# PROCLUS
->ON<-
## THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO.
---

> “Placing the soul in the middle, he extended it through the whole of the world; and besides this, he externally wrapped <note>original: "circumvested"</note> the body of the universe with the soul.”

God <note>original: "Divinity"</note> produces all things at once and eternally. Because of His very nature, and according to an eternal intelligence of all things as a whole, He generates all things from Himself: celestial beings <note>original: "supermundane"</note>, all worldly beings, intellects, souls, natural forces, bodies, and matter itself. 

Indeed, this "all-at-once" creation exists to a greater degree in the Creator's <term>Demiurge: the divine craftsman or architect of the universe in Platonic philosophy</term> production of things than it does in the sun's illumination <note>original: "For *hyliakes* (material) here, it is obviously necessary to read *heliakes* (solar)."</note>. In the case of the sun, the entire light proceeds from it all at the same time. But the sun, which imitates its Father through visible creation, clearly yields to an eternal and invisible production. 

As we have said, therefore, even though all things are produced simultaneously and eternally by the Creator's <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> handiwork, the order of their effects is still preserved. This is because in the Producing Cause, there was an eternal intelligence and order that existed before the things being arranged. Consequently, although all things come from a single cause at once, some hold primary importance while others have a secondary status. 

Some things proceed from the cause to a greater degree, and others to a lesser degree. Some are aligned with the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> through a state of union, others through contact, and others through participation. For one intellect is able to be born together <term>connascent: originating or growing together</term> with another intellect through union. However, the soul is naturally designed to be joined with intellect. And bodies are formed to par—

<summary>In this passage, Proclus explains how the divine Creator (the Demiurge) produces all levels of reality—from intellect to matter—simultaneously and eternally while still maintaining a hierarchical order.</summary>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.
<page-num>2</page-num>

—participate in it alone, just as things in the depths of the earth participate in the sun's brilliance. Since all these things—intellect, soul, and body—exist in the world and are produced all at once, and since there is an order among them proceeding from the Creator <term>Demiurge: the divine craftsman or architect of the universe</term>, our discussion of them follows two paths. Sometimes it begins from above, following the sequence of their "progression" <note>original: *proodos*; the process of higher causes producing lower effects</note> and ending at the outer limits of creation <note>original: "fabrication"</note>. At other times, starting <note>original: *ormomenos* (impelled); the text notes that the Greek should be *ormomenos* (starting/impelled) rather than *oromenos* (seen)</note> from the very last things, it returns to the highest points of the universe, following the natural order of things themselves. For all things proceed from and return to the principle and cause from which they first emerged, thus forming a certain divine circle of creation <note>original: "demiurgic circle"</note>.

In what was previously said, Plato described the order of the world's fullness according to their progression. He represented the Creator placing intellect in the soul and the soul in the body, thereby constructing <note>original: *sunetektaineto* (fabricated/built together); the text notes this should be read instead of *suneteinato* (stretched)</note> the universe. 

But in what he says now, he completes the world through "conversion" <note>original: *epistrophe*; the return or "turning back" of effects toward their divine cause</note>. First, by taking the opposing elements <note>original: "contraries"</note> in the universe, he adds two mathematical means <note>original: "media"</note> to them and unites them through proportion <note>original: "analogy"</note>. Next, making it a "whole composed of wholes," he surrounds it with an intellectual shape, makes it capable of sharing in a divine life, and gives it a motion that imitates the intellect. 

By these additions, he constantly makes the world more perfect. Finally, he introduces the soul into the universe and fills all things with life, though different natures receive different types of life. He also places intellect in the soul, and through this, joins the soul to its fountain <note>the source of all being</note>. For the soul of the universe, by participating in intellect, becomes joined with the "intelligibles" <note>the realm of pure, non-physical truth and being</note> themselves. 

Thus, he ends at the principle from which the worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note> intellect, soul, and the physical mass of the body all proceed. By dividing the universe into three parts—intellect, soul, and body—he first discusses the most subordinate of these, which is the method used when speaking of "conversion" (the return to the source). The discussion of the creation of the body is now finished, having described its essence, shape, and motion.

The theory of the soul is joined to this, just as the body itself is suspended from a divine soul. The "animation" <note>the act of giving life/soul</note> which the discourse now adds is the seventh gift of the Creator given to the world. However, I believe the discussion of the soul is twofold: one part describes its essence, while the other describes its communion with the body. Plato chooses the latter and sees fit to mention it before the former. He likely does this because the relationship <note>original: "habitude"</note> of the soul to the body is, in a sense, a middle ground between the discussion of the body and...

<summary>This page explains Proclus's view on the "divine circle," where the universe is created through a progression from the Creator and returns through a process of "conversion." It transitions from the physical creation of the body to the discussion of how the soul inhabits and animates the world.</summary>

# BOOK III. THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO
<page-num>3</page-num>

...the soul itself. It is necessary that the path leading to principles should pass through intermediaries <note>original: "media"</note>. Perhaps he also chose this approach because he did not want to connect the soul with the body in terms of time; nor did he want to join it to the world only when it was separate and existing by itself. Instead, he explains the soul's communion with the body before the soul's actual birth <note>original: "generation"</note>, which helps clarify this point. For the birth of the soul is enough to prove that the physical mass of the world is also uncreated <term>original: "unbegotten"; meaning it has no beginning in time</term> in terms of time. For if he attributes "generation" to things that are actually uncreated, then "generation" must mean something different for them. But if, before the apparent birth, he places both body and soul in the same condition, then such a birth is eternal, and the process of giving life is perpetual. The soul is not created in time, nor does the body exist at a different time than the soul. This concludes the discussion of the primary parts of the order of what has been said.

Regarding the middle position of the soul, however, different interpreters explain it in various ways. Some say the "middle" is the center of the Earth; others say the Moon is the middle, acting as the bridge <note>original: "isthmus"</note> between created <note>original: "generated"</note> and divine natures. Others say it is the Sun, placed like a heart; others, the sphere of the fixed stars <term>original: "inerratic sphere"</term>; others, the celestial equator <term>original: "equinoctial"</term>, as it marks the width of the world; and others, the zodiac. 

Indeed, some place the ruling power of the universe in the center; others in the Moon; others in the Sun; others in the equator; and others in the zodiac. Each has their reasons:
*   The first group points to the power of the center, which holds every rotation together.
*   The second points to the motion of the Moon, which changes the world of creation in various ways.
*   The third points to the life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note> heat of the Sun.
*   The fourth points to the easy motion of the equatorial circle.
*   The fifth points to the rotation of the stars around the zodiac.

Against all these views, however, **Porphyry** and **Iamblichus** write, criticizing them for understanding the "middle" as a physical location or a spatial distance. They argue that these views trap the soul of the whole world in a specific part, even though the soul is present everywhere equally, ruling and guiding all things through its motions. Among these divine men, **Porphyry** assumes this refers to the soul of the universe and interprets the "middle" according to the essence of the soul <note>original: "psychical essence"</note>; for the soul is the middle point between the intelligible <term>realities known by the mind</term> and the sensible <term>realities known by the senses</term> worlds. 

In saying this, however, he does not seem to address **Plato's** specific words. But if we assume the universe is completed by intellect, soul, and body—and is a living being possessing soul and intellect—we will find that in this system, the soul is indeed the middle. Therefore, **Plato**, having said this before, now seems to mean only that the soul of the world is arranged so that its energies extend through the universe, being assigned...

<summary>Proclus examines various literal and allegorical interpretations of the "middle" of the soul in the universe, ultimately favoring a metaphysical interpretation where the soul acts as the intermediary between the physical and divine realms.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul’s "middle" position in the universe, comparing different Neoplatonic interpretations of whether this refers to a literal center or a spiritual hierarchy.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.
<page-num>4</page-num>

...the middle order in it. For secondary natures share in those that come before them <note>original: "participate of those prior to them"</note>; just as the body, which is the last of all things, shares in the soul, which ranks in the middle, and the soul shares in the intellect, which comes before it. But the philosopher Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a hugely influential Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> thinks that by "soul," we should understand the soul that is "exempt" <term>set apart and not bound to the material world</term>, supermundane <term>existing above the physical world</term>, and liberated, which has dominion over all things. According to him, Plato does not speak of the "mundane soul" (the soul within the world), but of that which is "imparticipable" <term>an original source that cannot be divided or diminished by the things that depend on it</term>, and which is arranged as a monad <term>a single, indivisible unity</term> above all mundane souls. 

For this is the primary soul, and the *middle* is within it, as it is equally present to all things because it does not belong to any specific body, nor does it exist in any state of "habitude" <term>original: "habitudon"; a state of being related to or bound by something else</term>. Instead, it gives life to everything while remaining equally separated from all worldly natures. It is not less separated from some and more from others; since it has no binding relationship, it is similarly separated from all, even though all things are not separated from it in the same way. Among those things that share in its life, some receive more and others receive less.

Our preceptor <note>This likely refers to Syrianus, the teacher of Proclus.</note>, however, interprets *the middle* in a way more suited to the actual words of Plato. He argues that since the soul of the universe indeed has a supermundane aspect that is set apart from the universe (through which it is joined to the Intellect—which Plato in the *Phaedrus*, and Orpheus in his writings about *Hippa*, call the "head" of the soul), and since it also has a vast number of powers proceeding from this single source <note>original: "monad"</note> that are distributed throughout the world and appropriately present to every part of the universe—some at the center, some at the earth, some at the sun, and some in each of the celestial spheres—this being the case, he says that Plato's words refer to all of these. Thus, the soul gives life to the middle in one way, but to the entire physical mass in another, while still leaving something else—prior to these powers—that remains set apart from the universe. 

However, so that we do not pay only superficial attention to what Plato says, but instead showcase the variety of the soul's powers <note>original: "psychical powers"</note>, we must say this: the soul, which exists long before the body, is a "vital world" and is both a single unit and a plurality. Through its unity, it is superior to every physical connection; but through its plurality, it governs the different parts of the universe. *For by its guardian powers, it maintains the center; since the entire sphere is governed from that point and converges toward it.* *Furthermore*, everything turbulent in the world is collected around the middle and requires a divine guard capable of organizing it and keeping it within its proper boundaries. This is why theologians place the end-points of the highest Gods' progressions in that location; and the Pythagoreans call the middle "the tower of Jupiter" and "the guard-house of..."

<page-num>5</page-num>
<header>BOOK III.] TIMAEUS OF PLATO.</header>

Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus, used here to represent the Demiurge, the divine craftsman of the universe.</note>. *“But through its stable and, at the same time, life-giving <note>original: "vivifying"</note> powers, it contains the sphere of the earth. By its perfecting and creative <note>original: "generative"</note> powers, it contains the sphere of water. By its unifying and moving powers, it contains the air. By its pure <note>original: "undefiled"</note> powers, it contains fire. And by its intellectual powers, it contains all of heaven. Within these, it also governs the lunar sphere in one way, the solar sphere in another, and the sphere of the fixed stars in yet another. For the souls of each of these spheres govern their own specific parts of the world in harmony with the total soul of the universe.”*

Since this is how life is given <term>animation</term>, Plato—as he usually does—begins from the very last things and works backward <term>conversion; the Neoplatonic concept of the soul "turning back" toward its divine source</term>. He first gives life to the center, then to the universe, and finally leaves a portion of the soul outside the universe. 

Just as he constructed the body before the soul, and parts before the whole, he describes the animation of the world by starting from the very end. When describing the process coming down from above, he said that the Demiurge <term>the Creator</term> placed intellect in the soul and the soul in the body. However, in this current passage, he is teaching us about life through the process of "conversion" (returning to the source). Therefore, he first animates the middle, and afterward the entire universe. 

The "river of life" <note>original: "river of vivification"</note> flows all the way to the center. This is what the Oracles <note>Likely the Chaldean Oracles, a set of mystical texts highly regarded by Neoplatonists.</note> say when speaking of the middle of the five centers, which extends from the highest point all the way to the opposite side: *"And another fifth middle fiery center, where a life-bearing fire descends as far as to the material rivers."* 

Plato, therefore, begins with the things where life-giving ends and works back to the total production of life; before this, he examines the power of the soul that exists independently <term>exempt</term>. Because of this, we must not place the "ruling part" of the soul in the center, for that part is set apart from the universe. Instead, we should place a certain power of the soul there which acts as the guardian of the entire worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note> order. 

Nothing else in the universe is as capable of completely destroying the "wholes" <note>The major structural parts of the cosmos.</note> as the center and the power of the center. The universe performs an "harmonic dance" around this center, provided they are in good condition. Thus, it seems to me that Plato spoke divinely when he did not place "the whole soul" in the middle of the universe, but simply *soul*. These are different because "the whole soul" would mean the entire essence of the soul is in the center, whereas "soul" means he places one *power* of it in the middle, and different powers in different parts of the world. 

Therefore, when Plato says, *"placing soul in the middle,"* it is the same as saying he gave the center a share in the soul and extended the soul's total powers to the universe. The Demiurge left a power of the soul outside the universe that is more divine than all others; it is established within itself and contains and connects the whole world from an independent position. There is no need to be wordy <note>original: "prolix"</note> in searching for Plato’s meaning, since the philosopher himself says shortly after, when discussing the animation of the world: *“but soul, unfolding herself from the middle to the farthest edge of the universe, covered it all around like a veil.”*

<summary>This page explains that the Demiurge animates the world from the center outward, using different powers to govern the elements and celestial spheres. Proclus clarifies that while a power of the soul resides at the center to maintain order, the highest part of the soul remains independent and "veils" the entire universe from the outside.</summary>

<keywords>Jupiter, Demiurge, soul, animation, conversion, five centers, Chaldean Oracles, mundane order, celestial spheres, Timaeus</keywords>

<page-num>6</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE *TIMAEUS* [BOOK III.]</header>

*"...she herself is wrapped within herself."* This, however, does not differ at all from the words we are considering. For *to extend every way from the middle* is the same thing as being *spread out from the center to the edges of the universe.* In the first case, the soul, acting of her own accord, illuminates the center of the universe and its entire sphere through her own powers; in the second case, the Demiurge <term>the Creator</term> is the cause of life <term>animation</term> and introduces the soul into the universe. The same result is achieved by both: it is done through the Creator’s intellect and craftsmanship, but also through the soul’s own power of self-motion. Now, however, the philosopher [Plato] describes the bond derived from the act of creation <note>original: "fabrication"</note> alone. We specifically attribute "wholes" (universal things) and things that are good to a divine cause; however, we consider "partial" (individual) natures and things that are not good to be unworthy of direct divine production. We instead see them as dependent on other, more immediate causes, even though these also—as has been frequently noted—exist through the divine.

There is, therefore, a connection between a divine soul (and likewise a partial soul) and physical bodies. *That connection which exists according to a generous will, and does not stray from the progression of the intelligible <note>The realm of pure thought and forms</note>, is divine. But that connection which exists because the soul has shed its wings <note>original: "defluxion of the wings"; a reference to Plato's *Phaedrus*, where the soul loses its divine "wings" and falls into a body</note>, or through recklessness <note>original: "audacity" (Greek: *tolma*); the soul's impulsive choice to exist as an individual</note>, or flight, is without God—though even in this, there is an intertwining with the soul's power of self-motion and the will of providence.* 

Nevertheless, the connection with the body that follows the divine way is made clear through the presence of divinity; but the connection coming from the soul itself is apparent through the sign of wandering <note>original: "representation of aberration"</note> that it shows. Since the life of the world is two-fold—proceeding both from the Demiurge and from self-motion—Plato here rightly gives preference to the cause that exists according to divinity, as it is most suited to the nature of "wholes" <note>The original text mistakenly used the word for "others" (τοις αλλοις); Proclus notes it should be "wholes" (τοις ολοις), referring to universal systems.</note>. For the words "*placing, he extended, and he wrapped as with a veil*," are the names of the Demiurge's works. The first of these signifies the boundary <note>original: "termination"</note> of the soul; the second signifies the soul's middle <note>original: "psychical middle"</note> which moves through all things; and the third signifies the soul's state of being separate and superior <note>original: "exempt transcendency"</note>. For *to wrap as with a veil* indicates that the soul encompasses the world in every way, unites it through herself, leads it to a single life, and does not leave anything outside of her appropriate protection <note>original: "providence"</note>, nor lacking in her nature.

<margin>Stephanus 34B</margin>
> "**And causing circle to rotate within a circle, he established heaven [or the universe] as a single, unique, and solitary nature.**"

The philosopher Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist scholar and student of Plotinus</note> interprets the meaning of "circle rotating in a circle" well. He says it is possible for something that is *not* a circle to be moved in a circle, such as a stone being whirled around; it is also possible for a circle *not* to be moved in—

<summary>Proclus explains how the Demiurge establishes the World Soul's relationship to the universe, distinguishing between divine animation and the soul's own self-motive fall, while defining the soul's role as a protective "veil" over the cosmos.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the World Soul's relationship to the physical universe, specifically focusing on the world’s circular motion and its status as a divine, self-sufficient "God" based on the teachings of Plato and Iamblichus.</meta>

<page-num>7</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE *TIMAEUS* [BOOK III.]</header>

...a circle, like a wheel when it is rolled along. However, it is a unique characteristic of the world that, because it is circular, it moves in a circle by harmoniously revolving around its center. The divine Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who heavily influenced later interpretations of Plato.</note> interprets the meaning of these words even more appropriately. He says that the circle is twofold: one is of the soul <note>original: "psychical"</note>, while the other is physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note>, and that the physical circle moves within the circle of the soul. This interpretation is consistent with what has been said before and matches what is stated later. For shortly after this, Plato himself describes the motion of the physical world according to the circle of the soul, making the two types of circulation correspond to the periods of the soul. This is the interpretation agreed upon by both these philosophers.

Furthermore, it is highly appropriate to describe the total blessedness of the world using three titles, as the world exists according to a triple cause: the final cause, the paradigmatic cause <note>The "model" or "blueprint" cause</note>, and the demiurgic cause <note>The "maker" or "creator" cause</note>. 

These three titles are derived as follows:
1. The first title, ***one***, is taken from the final cause; for "the one" is the same as "the good."
2. The second title, ***single*** or ***only***, is taken from the paradigmatic cause. This is because "only-begotten" and "singleness" <term>original: μονωσις (monosis)</term> existed in the "all-perfect living being" <note>original: "animal"; referring to the divine Model of the universe</note> even before the universe was created. 
3. The third title, ***the solitary***, is taken from the demiurgic cause. This is because the ability to function independently and to govern itself proceeds from the goodness of the Demiurge <term>the Creator</term>. 

Therefore, the world is ***one*** insofar as it is united and turned toward the One. It is ***single*** insofar as it participates in the realm of pure thought <note>original: "the intelligible"</note> and contains all things within itself. And it is ***solitary*** insofar as it resembles its father <note>The Demiurge</note> and is able to sustain itself. 

From these three qualities, it is clear that the world is a God. For "the one," "the perfect," and "the self-sufficient" are the essential elements of divinity. Thus, by receiving these qualities, the world is itself a God. It is ***one*** according to its essential existence <term>original: hyparxis</term>; it is ***single*** or ***only*** according to its perfection, which is completed by all things in the physical world; and it is ***solitary*** because it is self-sufficient.¹ For those who lead a solitary life, being focused inward on themselves, find the hope of their well-being within themselves. That this is the meaning of the term ***solitary*** is evident from Plato’s own words:

<insert>348</insert>
> "Able through virtue to converse with itself, lacking nothing from the outside, and sufficiently known and friendly to itself."

In these words, Plato clearly reveals what kind of "solitariness" he attributes to the world. He uses the term to describe a being that looks to itself, relies on what it is naturally provided with, and focuses on its own inherent nature.

---

¹ The world is ***single*** (or alone) because there is no other world equal to it; but it is ***solitary*** because it is sufficient unto itself. Thus, in this context, "the alone" and "the solitary" do not mean the same thing.

<page-num>8</page-num>
# PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS [BOOK III.]

measure. For those who live in solitary places are the "saviors" of themselves, at least regarding human causes. In this same way, the universe is also solitary, as it is self-sufficient and preserves itself—not because it lacks anything <note>original: "diminution"</note>, but because it has an abundance <note>original: "exuberance"</note> of power. Here, self-sufficiency is being pointed out; and as Plato says, this is achieved "through virtue." 

For among all individual beings <term>original: partial animals</term>—such as ourselves—only the one who possesses virtue is able to keep company with himself and love himself with a parental affection. On the other hand, the wicked man <note>original: "vicious man"</note>, looking at his own inner baseness, is disgusted with himself and his own essence. He is distracted by external things and seeks the company of others because he is unable to face himself. On the contrary, the worthy man, perceiving himself as beautiful, rejoices and is delighted; by producing beautiful thoughts within himself, he gladly embraces his own company. For we are naturally drawn to what is beautiful <note>original: "domesticated to the beautiful"</note>, but we hastily withdraw ourselves from what is deformed. Hence, if the world possesses a virtue adapted to its own nature—in its intellectual and soulful essence, and in the perfection of its life—then by looking inward, it loves itself, remains present with itself, and is sufficient unto itself.

It is proper, therefore, to argue these points against those who believe that the objects of thought <term>original: intelligibles</term> exist outside of the mind <term>original: intellect</term>. For how can something be "blessed" if it must look to other things and, because it is deficient, remains dependent on external factors? Therefore, if the world is turned toward itself through virtue, must the divine Mind <term>original: intellect</term> not do this to a much greater degree? The Mind, therefore, intellectually perceives itself. This is one of those truths that is immediately obvious. 

It also deserves to be noted that when Plato gives a soul to the world <note>original: "gives animation to the world"</note>, he immediately grants it virtue as well. For the participation in a soul is immediately accompanied by a fullness of virtue in any being that exists according to its true nature. This is because the single cause of the virtues <note>original: Vesta (Hestia)</note> is aligned with the source of all souls <note>original: Juno (Hera)</note>, and the progression of this source is joined with the progression of the soul. 

Regarding virtue, there is one kind that is unified, primary, and all-perfect; another exists in the ruling gods who are beyond the physical world <term>original: supermundane Gods</term>; another exists in the "liberated" gods; and yet another is "mundane" (belonging to this world). It is through this mundane virtue that the whole world possesses pure intelligence, a life that never wanders from its path, an energy focused on itself, and a purity that is not mixed with the lower animals it contains. From this virtue, the world becomes known and friendly to itself. For knowledge must come before familiarity.

Since the universe is also intellectual, a living being, and a God: 
* Insofar as it is **intellectual**, it becomes known to itself.
* Insofar as it is a **God**, it is friendly to itself. 

For divine union is more perfect than mere knowledge. If, therefore, the universe is known to itself, it is intellectual; for that which is primarily known to itself is...

² Juno <note>The goddess Hera, who in Neoplatonic thought represents the "fountain" or source of souls.</note>

He argues that the world loves itself because it is beautiful and intellectual, and distinguishes between different levels of virtue from the gods down to the physical world.</summary>

## BOOK III.] THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO.

If the intellect is friendly to itself, it is unified. That which is unified is made divine; for **the "one" which exists within the intellect is a God.** Again, therefore, you have virtue, a knowledge of oneself, and a friendship with oneself existing in the world. The first of these (virtue) proceeds into the world from the soul; the second (knowledge) from the intellect; and the third (friendship/unity) from the deity. 

Hence, Plato very properly adds that because of these things, the world was created by the Demiurge <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the Craftsman or Creator god</note> as a blessed God. For the presence of the soul, the participation in the intellect, and the reception of unity render the universe a God. And the "blessed God" which he mentions now is the God **"who would exist at a certain time,"** <note>Plato, Timaeus 34b</note> possessing a soul, endowed with intellect, and unified. 

This unity, however, is present within the world according to the bond of analogy <note>mathematical proportion</note>; but it is present much more through the one soul and the one intellect in which the world participates. For through these, greater bonds and a more excellent union proceeded into the universe. And still beyond these unions, divine friendship and the supply of "the Good" contain and connect the whole world. **For the bond which proceeds from intellect and soul is strong, as Orpheus also says; but the union of the golden chain** [that is, of the divine series of succession] **is still greater, and is the cause of greater good to all things.**

Moreover, happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note> must also be understood in a way adapted to the universe. For since the world is suspended from the paternal intellect <note>the mind of the Creator</note> and the entire fabrication of things, and since it lives in conformity to those causes, it is consequently happy (<gloss>eudaimon</gloss>)¹ because of them. For the Demiurge is also called a "daemon" by Plato in the *Politicus*, and a "great daemon" by Orpheus, when he says,
> **One is the great daemon and the lord of all.**²

Therefore, he who lives according to the will of the father and preserves the intellectual nature—which was granted to him from that source—in an unchanging state is happy and blessed. The first and most perfect form of happiness is that of the world itself. The second is that of the mundane Gods <note>gods within the physical cosmos</note>, whom Plato in the *Phaedrus* calls "happy Gods following the mighty Jupiter." 

The third form of happiness is that of the classes of beings superior to us [namely, the happiness of angels, daemons, and heroes]. For there is one virtue belonging to angels, another to daemons, and another to the heroic classes; thus, the form of happiness is triple, being different according to each class. The fourth form of happiness is that which exists in pure souls <note>original: "undefiled souls"</note> who make blameless descents [into the realms of physical existence] and lead a life that is firm and untamed by the material world. The fifth is that of individual souls [such as ours]; and this form is multiform. For a soul that is an attendant of the Moon is not happy in the same way as a soul that is...

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.

dependent on the solar order; but as the form of life is different, so likewise perfection is defined by different measures. And the final form of happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note> is that which is seen in irrational animals. For every thing which obtains a perfection adapted to its nature is happy. For through its own proper perfection, it is joined to its proper guiding spirit <note>original: "dæmon"; here meaning a protective or governing divine power</note>, and partakes of that spirit’s providential care. Since there are so many forms of happiness, the first and highest must be placed in the world itself, which is what Plato now mentions. We must not, however, wonder that he immediately calls the world a God because of its participation in the soul. For every thing is made divine through that which is immediately above it; the corporeal world is made divine through the soul; but the soul through the intellect, as the Athenian Stranger <note>original: "Athenian guest"; the primary speaker in Plato's *Laws*</note> also says; (for he asserts that by receiving intellect, the soul becomes a *God*,) and the intellect is made divine through *the One*. Hence, the intellect is divine, but it is not a *God* itself.¹ *The One*, however, is no longer a *God* through anything else, but is primarily a *God*; just as the intellect is primarily *cognitive* <note>original: "gnostic"</note>, the soul is primarily *self-moving*, and the body is primarily in a *place*. But since these things are perfectly true and unique to Plato’s philosophy, it is necessary to examine what follows, where he establishes the intellect within the soul, just as he here places the soul within the body.

<margin>34C</margin>
> "But, indeed, divinity did not create the soul later in time, as we have just now tried to say, as if it were *younger* <note>original: "junior"</note> than the body. For he who joined these together would never permit the older nature to be governed by the younger."

Plato knew that the method of "conversion" <note>the process of looking back from effects to causes</note> always presents things that are second in order as if they were first. This is because the things we experience directly are secondary to those that are independent <note>original: "exempt"; meaning transcendent causes</note>; and the things more familiar to the listeners are inferior to invisible things. The cause of this, however, is that when we examine reality now, we are in a "fallen" condition. For when we are in the higher realms and look at the things here as if from a shadow, we are able to see their small and secondary nature because we are associating with the intellectual forms and have them before our eyes. But falling into the world of change <note>original: "generation"</note> and looking at things while in a passive, "lying down" <note>original: "supine"</note> state, we first perceive *symbols* and things close to our senses, as they are placed nearer to us. And beginning from these, we return through recollection <note>original: "reminiscence"; the Platonic concept of *anamnesis*</note> to the true beings and the essence that truly exists.

# BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

The observation from above, therefore, will be that of souls residing there <note>residing in the higher divine realms</note>; but the observation from beneath will be that of souls who have separated themselves from the intelligible world <note>original: "intelligible world"; the realm of pure ideas and forms that can only be understood by the mind, rather than the senses</note>. Furthermore, the judgment that originates from things fundamentally more ancient is the judgment of souls living according to intellect; but the judgment that proceeds from secondary natures up to first natures is the judgment of fallen souls. For truly existing being is near to souls that remain in the intelligible realm; but "non-being" is near to those in a fallen condition. For that which remains, remains in being, and that which falls from the intelligible is situated in non-being. To each of these souls, the realm in which it dwells is the most familiar.

Plato, therefore, knowing these things—and knowing that we return from lower to higher natures through a well-ordered progression—thinks it appropriate to mention the nature of things in which the "elder" is superior to the "younger." Through this common concept, he arranges the soul as prior to the body. He reminds us that the soul is older and the body younger through a logical proof. For if the soul rules over the body, it is more ancient than the body. And it certainly does rule over the body: for it leads everything in the universe through its motions. The body is "alter-motive" <note>original: "alter-motive"; meaning it is moved by something external to itself</note>, but the soul is naturally designed to move both itself and other things. It is, therefore, more ancient than the body.

If this is the case, however, it is necessary to conceive of the soul by itself, not as something generated after the body (as we might imagine it), but by giving it a heavenly origin. We should view the physical mass of the universe as being unfolded into the light from the soul. For the universe derived its existence through the soul, imitating the soul's progression through its own physical bulk, and imitating the soul's "conversion" <note>original: "conversion"; the Neoplatonic concept of a soul's return or turning back toward its divine source</note> through its circular shape. We shall discuss these things again, however.

But, if you are willing, let us now examine each word of Plato’s text. In the first place, regarding the *soul*, he shows that he speaks of *every* soul by adding the definite article *the*. For he does not say as he did before, "*placing soul in the middle*," but *the* soul. In the earlier instance, he was speaking of a power of the whole soul located in the center; but here, every soul is said to be more ancient than the body. 

Next, the terms *older* and *younger* are not to be understood in terms of time, as the philosopher *Atticus* <note>a 2nd-century CE Platonic philosopher who argued for a literal, temporal creation of the world</note> understood them. For the Father <note>the Demiurgus</note> created the soul and surrounded the body of the universe with it (as if with a veil) at the same time. Instead, these terms must be understood in the order of essence. For the essence that is closer to the Demiurgus <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine Craftsman or Creator of the physical universe</note> is "older." Even if you wish to understand "older" and "younger" according to time, the time that exists in the soul is older and more divine, while the time that pertains to the body is...

<summary>Proclus argues that the soul is "older" than the body because it is self-moving and governs the physical world, representing a higher level of reality. He clarifies that "older" refers to a hierarchy of importance and essence rather than just a sequence in time.</summary>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.

...younger. And the soul, as far as it is soul, is not time as measured by the body. Instead, the time belonging to the body is secondary to the time belonging to the soul. For just as there is a different form of motion in both, the time in each is also different. In the third place, Plato uses the expression "artificially produce" <note>original: "artificially produce"; referring to the divine craftsmanship or *technê* of the Creator</note> in the most proper sense when speaking of the soul. This clearly indicates that the soul is a self-moving thing, that it is full of rational principles <note>original: "reasons" (*logoi*); the formative laws or blueprints of reality</note>, and is inventive in all kinds of clever designs.

Furthermore, the power of more ancient natures ruling over younger ones descends into the universe from the intelligible realms themselves <note>the world of pure ideas and forms</note>. For there, Protogonus <note>the "First-Born," often identified with Phanes in Orphic theology</note>—who is so named by all the gods—is the king of all intellectual beings. And in the intellectual hierarchy, the eldest of the sons of Saturn <note>Cronus</note> is said to be the father of all things.

->But Zeus was born first, and he knows more.<-
<note>A quote from Homer's *Iliad* (13.355), used here to show that "older" in divine terms means "wiser" and "superior."</note>

For everywhere, that which is older is the symbol of a life that is more intellectual, total, and unified <note>original: "monadic"</note>. On the other hand, that which is younger represents a life that is divisible <note>original: "partible"</note>, moves toward secondary natures, and is multiplied. This is why, among the life-giving goddesses, they call one older and the other younger <note>Rhea is the older goddess, and Juno (Hera) is the younger</note>. And among the creator gods <note>original: "demiurgic"</note>, they name one as prior and the other as junior—whom they also call "recent" <note>The prior Creator is Jupiter (Zeus), while the junior is Bacchus (Dionysus)</note>. 

In the next place, the word *conjoined* clearly shows that the soul being discussed here is "mundane" <note>belonging to the physical world/cosmos</note>, and not "liberated" <note>the "liberated" or "super-celestial" gods are those who exist immediately above the physical world</note>, nor is it the one single soul that exists before the many. For that single soul is detached from all other souls, which orbit around it like a center; but the soul discussed here is joined to a body, a conjunction brought about by the will of the Father <note>the Creator/Demiurge</note>.

> “We, however, participating in many ways in things that are accidental and without design, assert things of this kind.”

What is the reason that we are unwilling to move our intellect away from things of a younger nature and toward those that are essentially more ancient? <note>original Greek: "Why do we treat younger things as if they were older, rather than moving toward things that are truly ancient?"</note> It is...

He applies this to various gods (like Rhea and Jupiter) to justify why the soul must be older than the body.</summary>

### BOOK III.] THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

This is because our intellect resembles someone who is asleep, and because we are filled with an irrational and disorderly nature. The words *accidental* <note>original: "casual"</note> and *rash* <note>original: "rashly"</note> are used to describe these conditions. Since we possess senses and are surrounded by objects of the senses <term>sensibles</term>—which nourish us—we first perceive things of a younger or more recent nature <term>junior nature</term> because they are more familiar to us. 

Through our senses, we are carried along *rashly* and *without a plan*; but because we are focused on the physical objects before us, we live in an *accidental manner*. For those higher beings who remain in the divine realm, their senses are *at rest*, and they have no perception of the material objects we deal with; therefore, nothing occurs to them by chance. But we, because we have physical senses and material objects before our eyes, live by chance and *without design*. As the saying goes, we form our judgments of things *while standing on our heads* <note>original: "with the head downward"; a reference to the inverted, confused perspective of the soul when it first enters a body (Timaeus 43e)</note>. This is consistent with what Empedocles says when lamenting our human fate:

->Many terrible words and worries blunt the mind.<-
<note>original: "Many dire words and cares obtund the mind."</note>

Many things invade us while we are essentially slaves, having become exiles from the divine. These things blunt and clog our ability to contemplate real, eternal beings. However, as Empedocles also says, that which is *accidental* and *without design* reaches us from the *outside*. For this reason, Plato says that we merely participate in these things, rather than them being part of our *essence*. In our true essence, we are intellectual beings. But since we also receive influences from more divine natures, Plato adds the word *much*, to indicate the vast and confusing nature of this kind of participation. For the participation of more divine natures introduces union, limits, and order to those who receive them.

> "But the Creator <note>original: "artificer" (the Demiurge)</note> of the world constituted the soul to be prior to and more ancient than the body, both in its creation <note>original: "generation"</note> and in its excellence <note>original: "virtue"</note>, as the master and ruler of the body’s servant-like nature; and he did so from certain elements in the following manner."

Porphyry <note>a Neo-Platonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note>, analyzing this, believes these words signify that the *soul* is older than the body in terms of its *creation*, but also superior to it in *excellence*. Both meanings, or either one, may be intended; the phrases "prior to" and "more ancient than" can be applied to its creation—

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.

*generation*; and again, either may be joined to the words *in virtue*. But *generation, when ascribed to the soul*, is not something that happens according to time; for Plato in the *Phaedrus* demonstrates that the soul is unbegotten <note>original: "unbegotten"; meaning it was not created at a specific point in time but exists eternally.</note> and indestructible. Instead, it is an essential progression from intelligible causes. For among beings, some are intelligible and unbegotten, while others are sensible <term>perceived by the senses</term> and generated. The intermediaries between these are both intelligible and generated. Some things are entirely incomposite <term>simple/not made of parts</term> and <term>indivisible</term> <note>original: "impartible"</note>, and for this reason they are unbegotten; but others which exist between these are intelligible and generated, being naturally both <term>indivisible</term> and <term>divisible</term> <note>original: "partible"</note>, and in another sense both simple and composite.

*Generation*, therefore, *in the soul* is one thing, but generation in the body is another. The former is prior and more ancient, for it is closer to the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine craftsman or creator of the universe.</note> of all things; but the latter is secondary and more recent, for it is more remote from the one [creative] cause of all. Furthermore, *virtue* is present with the soul, and it is also present with the body and the whole animal; but the virtue of the soul is more divine, while that of the body is lowly. The former is of a more ruling nature and is nearer to the unified causes of intelligible virtue; but the latter is of an attendant nature and is more remote from the intelligible realm.

*Generation, however, manifests progression, but virtue manifests perfection and conversion*; the former comes from the fountain of the soul,¹ while the latter is inherent in souls from <term>fountain-like</term> <note>original: "fontal"</note> virtue [that is, from Vesta]. The terms *prior* and *more ancient* also have a certain difference from each other. For *prior* signifies order alone, but *more ancient* signifies the transcendence of a cause in relation to the thing it caused. Therefore, not everything that is prior can also be called more ancient; only that which leads the essence of secondary natures is called more ancient. Both terms, however, are true of the soul. For she is assigned a prior order, being the sister of the body according to the progression of both from one <term>creation</term> <note>original: "fabrication"</note>; and she generates and adorns the body in conjunction with the Father. For the first offspring of causes produce the second offspring as they proceed, in conjunction with their own causes.

What, however, shall we say of the words *the lord and ruler*? Do they not both indicate that the soul supplies all things with good, that it provides in every respect for the body, and that it preserves its own proper good in a flourishing condition?² And how is it possible that Plato should not reveal these things through these words? For a *master* or *lord* always refers the good³ of those who are governed...

¹ It is necessary here to provide the words "of the soul." The fountain of the soul is Juno.

³ Instead of "refers the goods of those that are governed" <note>original: "ta tōn dioikoumenōn agathōn anapherei"</note> in this place, it is necessary to read "refers the good things of those that are governed" <note>original: "ta tōn dioikoumenōn agatha anapherei"</note>.

He also defines the soul as the "lord and ruler" that provides for the body while remaining rooted in divine virtue.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the soul's relationship to the universe, specifically distinguishing between its roles as a "ruler" and a "master," and how these roles prove the soul's eternal connection to the physical world.</meta>

<page-num>15</page-num>

<header>BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

he governs, to his own good. But a *ruler* looks to the good of those who are obedient to him and organizes all things with reference to it. The *nature of a master* <note>original: "despotic peculiarity"</note>, however, is present in the soul because she performs all actions for her own sake; but the *nature of a ruler* <note>original: "ruling peculiarity"</note> is present because she fills all things with goodness. For her caring power <term>providential energy</term> is not diminished by directing everything toward her own well-being. And her own goodness remains unchanged even as she completes her caring activities. 

In another way, she is also both a *ruler* and a *master*, for she originates from both the ruling and the primary soul <note>original: "fontal soul"</note>.¹ <margin>1. That is, she originates from Proserpine and Juno.</margin> Similarly, because the universe is her home, she is called a *master* <note>original: "despot"</note>. And because she guides all things through her movements, she possesses a *ruling power*. Furthermore, because she has authority over the whole of existence, she is a *master*; but because she makes all things like the divine intellect <note>original: "the intelligible"</note>, she *rules* over the universe. 

If, however, she was created this way from the beginning—as both a master and a ruler—then these qualities are essential to her nature. And if they are essential, they are always present within her. If these qualities were present only as potential, she would be imperfect—an idea that is unacceptable to suggest. But if they are present in *action* <note>original: "energy"</note>, then whatever she governs has always existed and has always been made beautiful by her. 

Therefore, if the universe was created to be governed by the soul, it exists alongside the soul <term>consubsistent</term>. For that which is governed is naturally joined to that which governs. Thus, through both, we can see that the universe is eternal <term>perpetuity</term>. We see that governing is not a random occurrence for the soul, nor is being governed accidental for the body. Instead, the soul is, by its very essence, the master of the body, and the body is the servant <note>original: "vassal"</note> of the soul. For this reason, they are naturally joined to one another; the body is moved to take part in the soul, and the soul is moved to care for the body.

Furthermore, the purpose of the phrase "*from certain things in the following way*" is to bring to light the *categories* <term>genera</term> and the elements that make up the soul, as well as the method of mixing them and the ratios <note>original: "reasons"</note> by which that mixture is divided. For physical nature was created by God <note>original: "divinity"</note> to consist of specific elements in a specific way; he skillfully designed a certain mathematical relationship <term>analogy</term> and physical bond between them. 

But if the Divine skillfully produced the soul from certain materials and in a certain way, he created both her *substance* <note>original: "subject"</note> and her *form*. It is therefore illogical to say that her essence is eternal <term>unbegotten</term> while her form is created <term>generated</term>, if she is made of specific elements. For Plato says that the Divine created both the "matter" of the soul, so to speak, and the logic <note>original: "reason"</note> by which she is given variety.

<summary>This page discusses the dual nature of the soul as both a master (acting for itself) and a ruler (acting for the good of the governed), arguing that the soul and the physical universe are eternally and essentially linked. Proclus explains that the soul's substance and form were both designed by the Divine through specific mathematical ratios and categories.</summary>

### PROCLUS ON THE BOOK III.

...with the forms she possesses, being bound by certain mediating links. If, however, divinity generates her "elements"—namely, essence, sameness, and difference—and from these the whole, then everything that is essential in the soul is generated.

> "From an essence that is always indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> and exists with unchanging sameness, and again from an essence that is divisible among bodies, he mingled from both a middle form of essence."

First, it is necessary to show <gloss>①</gloss> the cause through which Plato describes the "generation" of the soul, since according to him it is actually unbegotten <note>eternal and without a beginning</note>. <margin>②</margin> Next, we must appropriately divide the entire process of the soul's generation. Third, we must <gloss>③</gloss> demonstrate the middle nature of the soul. <margin>④</margin> Fourth, we must speak concerning the categories <note>original: "genera"</note> of those things from which Plato constitutes all other beings and the soul. Fifth, we must show how the <gloss>⑤</gloss> mixture of these categories is to be understood in the soul. Sixth, we must demonstrate what the <gloss>⑥</gloss> indivisible and the divisible natures are. Finally, seventh, we must unfold <gloss>⑦</gloss> the meaning of Plato’s words and prove that they agree with all that has been said before. If we can discuss all these details, we shall properly achieve the goal of this investigation. 

Let us begin, therefore, with the first point, because some of the ancients have criticized Plato. They assert that he does not rightly investigate the origin of an origin <term>principle of a principle</term>, or the "generation" of <unclear>an</unclear> unbegotten thing. For if we investigate the causes of primary natures and imagine a beginning for things that exist by themselves <term>self-subsistent</term>, we will ignorantly spiral toward infinity and find no end to our contemplation. Just as someone who thinks everything must be proven actually undermines the possibility of proof itself, so too does the person who investigates the causes of *all* things entirely undermine all beings and the order that proceeds from a definite starting point. 

Theophrastus raised objections of this kind against Plato regarding the soul's generation. He says we should not investigate the *why* in all physical inquiries. He adds that it would be ridiculous to wonder why fire burns, for what reason fire exists, or why snow makes things cold. But those who have written against Theophrastus in defense of Plato say that merely to know "the fact that" <note>original: "the *οτι*"</note> things exist in nature is irrational knowledge; it is an apprehension based on opinion or the senses. However, to add the "reason why" <note>original: "the *διοτι*"</note> and to investigate their causes is the true work of discursive reason <term>dianoia</term> and a scientific intellect. In this, right opinion differs from scientific reason.

---

\* <note>original: "viz. Merely to know that they exist, without knowing the διοτι, or why they exist."</note> This means merely knowing that things exist, without knowing the *reason why* they exist.

### BOOK III. THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO.

We, however, paying attention to what both of them say, think that the latter <note>Referring to the followers of Plato mentioned on the previous page</note> speak well. But first, we would ask Theophrastus himself: is the cause of nothing to be assigned, or is there a cause for certain things? For if there is no cause for anything, he would not only be undermining science—which specifically seeks to know causes—but he would also be accusing himself. In his work *Meteors*, he inquires where thunder comes from, why winds arise, and what the causes are of lightning, flashes of light <note>original: "corruscations"</note>, fiery whirlwinds, rain, snow, and hail. He rightly considers all of these to be deserving of a proper theoretical <note>original: "conjectural"</note> discussion. 

But if the cause of a certain thing is to be assigned, why are some physical phenomena to be examined through their causes, while others are presented irrationally without any cause? For it does not follow that just because it is obvious *that something exists*, we also know *why it exists*. 

Following this, we shall ask the lovers of Plato: are we to investigate the causes of everything, or not? If we must investigate everything, then we must also investigate the cause of *the One*, which we say is superior to the very concept of cause. We can learn *that the One exists* from first principles. For if the "One" is not the principle of all things, and instead "multitude" <note>manyness or diversity</note> is the principle, then what is it that unites things? Just as something that is "essentialized" <note>given essence or being</note> comes from Essence itself, and that which is "animated" <note>given life or a soul</note> comes from the Soul, so too that which is "united" must come from the One. But *why the One is one* cannot be explained <note>original: "unfolded"</note>, for it is more fundamental <note>original: "ancient"</note> than any cause. And if we are not to investigate the causes of everything, why should we investigate the cause of the soul and its progression from a cause, yet refuse to do so for other things?

Since we have questioned each of them separately, we shall now weigh the doubts concerning both. Why does Plato propose the origin <note>original: "generation"</note> of the soul and its progression from a cause, while Theophrastus condemns all teaching of this kind? Having considered this doubt, we say that for Theophrastus and the entire Peripatetic school <note>The followers of Aristotle</note>, the height of their speculation only reaches as far as the moving forms of the universe—whether it is proper to call these "souls" or "intellects." <note>That is, the souls of the celestial and sublunary spheres.</note>

But for Plato, these moving forms fall short of the highest rank among beings because they are "participable" <note>they are shared by or present in physical bodies</note>. Consequently, they are seen as having an order very far removed from first principles. Prior to these are the "intelligible" and "intellectual" orders of beings <note>The realm of pure ideas and thoughts</note> from which these moving forms derive their existence. And prior to these orders is the "number of the Gods" <note>The divine henads or unities</note>, who cause all beings to become united and connected, illuminating them with divine light. Finally, prior to this number is the indivisible "One," from which this divine number reveals itself through the various natures that receive it. For it is necessary that indivisible forms...

...should exist prior to those things that are shared <note>original: "participated"</note>, and prior to the unshared <note>original: "imparticipables"</note> things—their unities. For that which is united is one thing, while Unity itself is another; and prior to a multitude of individual unities, their single fountain exists.

Such, therefore, being the opinions of both these philosophers: Theophrastus, because he asserts that the soul is the principle of motion and does not admit that there is anything else prior to this principle, quite properly thinks that this principle ought not to be investigated further. For he grants that the universe is animated <note>endowed with a soul</note>, and is divine for this reason. "*For if it is divine,*" he says, "*and has the most excellent life, it is animated; since nothing is honorable without a soul,*" as he writes in his treatise *On the Heaven*. 

But Plato admits that there are "mundane" <note>cosmic or worldly</note> intellects prior to the celestial souls, and prior to these, intellects without any connection <note>original: "habitude"</note> to souls, and prior to all of these, the divine order itself. Hence, he quite properly describes the soul as being produced and generated from another principle; even though he also knew that "generation" of another kind occurs not only in bodies but also in souls, insofar as they participate in time. For time exists in divine souls as well, since, as Plato says in the *Phaedrus*, they survey reality itself through time. For all moving <note>original: "transitive"</note> motion has time joined with it. 

And so much for the first of the previously mentioned problems. For at the same time, it has been sufficiently demonstrated that Plato rightly describes the "generation" of the soul, even though it is essentially unbegotten <note>eternal and without a starting point in time</note>, and that the argument urged against this view is partly right and partly not. For to someone who admits that the soul is the first thing, it follows that they must reject its "generation." For what could it be generated from if there is nothing prior to it? However, this very claim—that the soul is the first of all things—is not true. 

For what Aristotle says concerning the body—that because it is finite, it always receives the power of being constantly moved, but does not receive the infinite all at once—must also necessarily be said concerning the soul. It does not act <note>original: "energize"</note> according to all things at once, so it does not possess all infinite power at once from which it acts; nor does it act according to every power simultaneously so as to possess a single, constant action. For every power has one corresponding action. Hence, it always receives the power to act perpetually, and for this reason, it does not always act with unchanging sameness, but differently at different times. *So, in short, it is true that everything which acts according to time always receives the power to act, yet does not receive the whole power at once, and for this reason is considered "generated."*

That the soul, however, is not the first of beings¹ is evident. For that which is first is present with all things, and it is necessary that all things should participate in it...

...of the principle of all; otherwise, if they did not participate in it, they would entirely perish. For essence and <term>hyparxis</term> <note>original: "hyparxis" — a term used to describe the primary "subsistence" or the very core of a thing's existence</note> are imparted to all things from the first principle. However, the soul is not present in all things, nor is it necessary that all things should participate in the soul. For among bodies, some are inanimate, and others are animated. 

It is likewise necessary that the first of all things should be one. For if it were a multitude, it would require a unifying cause to exist before itself, because a dispersed multitude cannot exist on its own. But the soul is a multitude. The first of all things is also beyond all essence, since every essence contains a multitude within itself—namely, "difference and sameness, life, and eternal energy." <note>These are the fundamental "kinds" or categories of being described in Plato's Sophist</note> But the soul is an essence. Everywhere, too, the first category <note>original: "genus"</note> is free from evil; but the category of partial souls <note>individual souls, such as those of humans, as opposed to the universal "World Soul"</note> is, at certain times, naturally capable of becoming evil. This can be demonstrated through many arguments. 

The design of Plato, however, for the reasons mentioned above, is to reveal the <term>psychical essence</term> <note>the fundamental nature or "being" of the soul</note> to us, to show how it exists, and to teach us what elements it is composed of and according to what "reasons." <note>original: "reasons" or "logoi" — the formative, rational principles that organize the soul</note> Regarding our body, it is easy to see that it contains a face and hands, thighs and feet, and all the other obvious parts. But to know how the body is composed from its internal parts—from what specific materials and in what proportions—requires medical and anatomical knowledge. In the same way, regarding the soul, it is not difficult to show what it is in terms of its general powers. However, to reveal its very essence, down to the elements of which it consists, and to examine the various "reasons" within it, requires the most accurate theory. This is exactly what Plato endeavors to do, "anatomizing" the <term>psychical essence</term> as it were, and laying it bare for those who are able to follow him. 

As we have stated, we may thus reply to the first of the inquiries. We can see that Plato very properly says the essence of the soul is "generated" <note>produced or brought into being</note> if we consider that he called <term>corporeal-formed nature</term> <note>physical matter</note> "generated" because it is always in a state of "becoming" and receives an infinite power of existing. The soul is also a thing of this kind; it is not able to receive the entire infinity of being all at once. This is evident because the soul lives in a "discursive" manner <note>discursive — reasoning step-by-step through time, rather than grasping all truths simultaneously and eternally</note>, producing different thoughts at different times, rather than having the entirety of an infinite life present at once. By always evolving its own life, it is clear that its essence is always "generated" (or in a state of becoming) and always advancing toward the infinite, without ever being infinite in itself. Hence, it always receives a life that is essential and entirely natural to it. For that which perfects a thing is entirely in accordance with that thing's nature. Moreover, if it...

the soul is **self-moving**, <insert>as Timaeus asserts, then we must admit that it gives to itself, all at once, the whole of the essential life which it possesses in itself. Thus, it will be both unbegotten and at the same time</insert> generated. It is, indeed, ever-living and ever-existent through the essence and life which it always possesses; but because it is always receiving these, it is always "coming into being" as essence and life. *For it exists in two ways: from itself, and from the beings that come before it. Through itself, it always exists; but through the beings prior to it, it is always coming into being. Or rather, through those higher beings, it has both—to be what it is, and to be generated—but through itself, it only has the quality of being what it is.* 

For the soul alone receives something perpetually from the beings prior to itself. Aristotle also rightly stated that nothing is the cause of itself if its well-being depends on time rather than an eternal existence, <note>In the original Greek: "Aristotle also rightly saying that nothing is its own cause, which has well-being according to time, but not eternally." The translator notes that Leonicus Thomæus incorrectly translated this as: "Therefore, Aristotle speaks most excellently when he says that no thing is its own cause, neither in time nor in eternity." This is an important distinction because, in this philosophy, an eternal nature *is* considered self-subsistent (its own cause).</note> so that the cause (which must come before the effect) does not simply exist at the same time as the thing being generated. 

Hence, both time and eternity exist in relation to the soul: eternity insofar as the soul is <term>unbegotten</term> <note>original: "unbegotten" — meaning it has no beginning in time and was not created like a physical object</note>, but time insofar as it is generated. On this account, the soul is eternal in a certain respect, as it is indestructible, but it is not "simply eternal" in the absolute sense, as Plato also says in the *Laws*. The second task proposed was to divide the entire "generation" of the soul in an appropriate manner. This, however, we shall accomplish later, once again taking our starting point from the nature of things themselves.

<margin>(2)</margin>
In every nature, therefore, there are **essence, power, and activity** <note>original: "energy" — here meaning the outward operation or manifestation of a thing's power</note>. **Essence** is that by which a thing exists—for example, the "fire-ness" that makes fire be fire. But **power** is one thing, and **activity** is another. For instance, one power dries, another heats, and others produce changes in different ways. It is necessary, therefore, that in the soul also, one thing should be essence, another power, and another activity. It is essential for anyone who wishes to understand and examine the soul in its entirety to speak about all of these. Regarding the generation of the soul, therefore, there will be three main topics: first, its essence; second, its power; and third, its activity. This will provide a complete investigation of the subjects we have proposed to consider.

<header>BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

We can see, however, that the nature of the soul (the psychical essence) is a certain threefold nature. Its foundational existence (<term>hyparxis</term>) <note>original: hyparxis; the primary, essential reality or 'being' of a thing</note> is one thing, and its internal harmony is another, by which its essential plurality is connected. The soul is not a single essence <note>original: *ουτε μιας ουσιας*; the text originally read *ουτε μιας αιτιας* (not of one cause), which the translator notes should be corrected to 'essence' for the argument to make sense.</note> like the divine Intellect, nor is it divisible to infinity like the physical bodies that come after it. Instead, it is divisible into more than one essential part; yet these parts are finite in number, since they cannot be further divided into others, as will become clear as we proceed. 

The *form* that results from these parts is yet another thing; thus, the essence of the soul is both one and threefold. Both the <term>monad</term> (the unit) and the <term>triad</term> (the three) are suited to it, since we divide the whole soul into three parts. Hence, its essence is one and triple: for foundational existence is one thing, harmony another, and form another. The first of these defines existence itself; the second harmonizes the many essential parts; and the third contains the specific character of the whole system. 

All of these, likewise, exist within one another. Foundational existence (<term>hyparxis</term>) contains a harmonized plurality within itself; it is neither lacking in plurality nor is it merely a disorganized crowd. Harmony itself is essential; it binds the essence together and gives it form. This also shows in what way the soul is a harmony and in what way it is not. It demonstrates that Plato is consistent with himself when he claims here that the soul is a harmony, while in the <term>Phaedo</term> he refutes those who maintain that it is. *For it is one thing to be the source of harmony for oneself and for other things, and quite another to be merely the harmony of something else.* The latter (the view refuted in the *Phaedo*) produces harmony in a subject—a harmony inseparable from the things it organizes and rooted in an external body. But the former produces an independent harmony that originates from itself and is directed toward itself. 

*The Form, likewise, encompasses the harmonic principles (reasons), contains the foundational existence of the soul, and is the primary principle by which the soul is what it is.* All these, therefore, are in each other—existence, harmony, and form—and the essence of the soul is one and triple. This is because it also consists of three categories: Essence, Sameness, and Difference. Furthermore, foundational existence is defined by "Essence," harmony by "Sameness," and form by "Difference," through which the soul is distinguished from all other things.

Since we find that the soul is triple from the beginning—possessing essence, power, and activity (<term>energy</term>)—and since its essence is also triple (consisting of foundational existence, harmony, and form), we can combine these into a <term>pentad</term> (a group of five). We arrange them as follows: foundational existence (<term>hyparxis</term>) is first, harmony is second, idea or form is third, power is fourth, and activity (<term>energy</term>) is fifth. For the <term>pentad</term> is suited to the soul as a middle ground, containing the bond between the unit (<term>monad</term>) and the...

ennead <note>original: ennead; a group or set of nine</note>, just as the soul is the bond between the intelligible and sensible essence. Adopting this same arrangement, we shall divide the entire theory concerning the soul into five categories:
1. Speaking concerning the essential existence (<term>hyparxis</term>) <note>The primary, foundational reality of a thing</note> of the soul.
2. Concerning the rational principles <note>original: reasons; the internal logic or 'logoi'</note> and the harmony within it.
3. Discussing the idea (or form) of it.
4. The many powers it contains.
5. Directing our attention to its activities <note>original: energies</note>.

For when Plato speaks about the physical body of the universe (<term>mundane body</term>), examining the physical nature of the world on its own, he first describes the underlying nature of matter and produces the elements of which the world consists. In the next place, he presents the harmony of the elements; for mathematical proportion (<term>analogy</term>), and the bond created through proportion, are an image of the soul's harmony. In the third place, he presents the "idea" of the world, showing it to us as a spherical "whole made of wholes." In the fourth place, he reveals to us the powers of the world; he gives the celestial spheres specific, divisible (<term>partible</term>) powers that act through local organs, but to the "animal of the universe" (the living cosmos as a whole), he gives complete and perfect powers. And in the fifth place, he describes the activities of the world, surrounding its body with a wise and intellectual motion. In the same manner, he divides the theory of the soul into these five categories. From this, it should be clear that Plato’s investigation of the soul's "generation" is very appropriate, as is the number and nature of its divisions.

<margin>(3)</margin>
Following this, however, we must discuss our third subject of inquiry: how and why we say the soul has a "middle nature." It is necessary to understand this before reasoning about the soul itself. Since many things proceed from **the One** <note>The ultimate source of all reality in Neoplatonic philosophy</note> down to formless and final matter, let us look at the characteristics of the first beings, the characteristics of the last, and what is assigned to the middle ground, and how they are adapted to the essence of the soul.

These are the characteristics of **intelligibles** (divine, non-physical realities): 
* Truly-existing being
* The eternal
* The indivisible (<term>impartible</term>)
* The immovable
* The entire and the perfect
* A super-fullness of existence
* An untiring and unrestricted life
* That which moves all things
* Similarity (<term>similitude</term>)
* Being present with all things while remaining distinct (<term>exempt</term>) from all things.

All these properties are revealed in the intelligible realm according to the progression of being. 

But again, there are certain other characteristics of **sensibles** (physical things perceived by the senses), such as:
* That which is not truly-existing being
* That which is temporary in its essence
* The divisible (<term>partible</term>)
* That which is moved by something else
* The partial (rather than the whole)
* That which is in need of another
* That which is always trying to "fill up" with existence
* That which lives only by participation
* That which is moved by another (<term>alter-motive</term>)
* Difference (<term>dissimilitude</term>)
* That which occupies space with its parts.

Between these two extremes, which are opposed to each other as the first things are to the last, there are

<meta>This page continues the analysis of the soul's essence, specifically defining the soul as an intermediate (a "mean") between the eternal, indivisible realm of Being and the temporal, divisible realm of physical matter.</meta>
