<margin>
<note>A vertical bracket and a downward-pointing arrow appear here in the original text, likely highlighting the following definition of the soul's intermediate nature.</note>
</margin>

...certain intermediates <note>original: media</note>, through which it is entirely necessary that the progression from the first to the last types of nature should be achieved. For things that are similar to their producing causes proceed before those that are dissimilar; this is because similarity is allied to *the One*, and all things strive after *the One*. 

The intermediates between these two extremes, therefore, have the following qualities:
* They are not true existence, yet they are more excellent than non-being, while still being inferior to real Being.
* In their essence, they are in a certain respect eternal, but they perform their activities in time. 
* They are indivisible <note>original: impartible</note> in their most divine part, but are distributed into parts according to the varied progression of their rational principles <note>original: reasons; here referring to 'logoi,' the formative patterns or blueprints within the soul</note>. 
* They move themselves and rule over things moved by external forces <term>alter-motive</term> <note>Moved by another</note>, yet they are inferior to beings that are completely immovable.
* They appear to the view partially in connection with their "wholeness." That is, they are in one respect a "whole" because they possess all rational principles, but they appear "partial" because of their diminished state and the way their activity transitions from one thing to another <note>original: transition of energy</note>. 

Such an intermediate also perfects itself while being perfected by natures higher than itself, and it is more perfect than things that are capable only of being perfected by another. Likewise, it fills itself with power and is filled by other things. It lives from itself and receives life from others, being more divine than those natures that live only by participating in life, but inferior to those that possess life fundamentally. Moreover, it moves other things but is moved by the highest natures; it is both similar and dissimilar at the same time, and it is both set apart from the lowest things and coordinated with them.

Since these are the specific characteristics of essences, let us consider where the soul should be placed: in the first or the last rank of things. If it belonged to the first rank of things, it would be true existence, entirely eternal and immovable, with every other quality belonging to real beings. In that case, we would not preserve the divisible nature of soul-based principles, nor "soul-time," nor self-motion, nor transitional activity <note>original: transitive energy; the movement of the soul's focus or action from one state to another</note>, nor anything of that kind—even though we clearly observe these things in all our souls. 

Now, we are investigating the qualities common to all souls that are essentially inherent in them, such as the characteristics mentioned above. So, if these are inherent in all souls, then souls do not belong to the first rank of things or to eternal beings, insofar as they are souls. 

But neither do they rank among the last of things. For if they did, we would make the soul moved only by external forces <term>alter-motive</term>, divisible, and composite, and only capable of being perfected by other things—yet we see the exact opposite even in our own souls. Our souls move and perfect themselves, and they conduct themselves as they please. Much more so, then, will divine souls possess the cause of their own perfection. They will lead all things by their own motions and will turn toward and know themselves—which is impossible for natures that are only moved by something else.

<summary>Proclus argues that the soul is an intermediate "mean" that bridges the gap between the eternal, unchanging realm of Being and the changing, physical world. He concludes that the soul must be self-moving and self-perfecting, distinguishing it from both higher divine intellects and lower physical objects.</summary>
<keywords>Proclus, Timaeus, soul, intermediate, the One, self-motion, rational principles, logoi, alter-motive, eternity vs time</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul as a bridge between two worlds: the eternal, unchanging realm of pure thought and the ever-changing physical world of the senses.</meta>

<page-num>24</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.</header>

If, however, it is impossible for the soul to be placed in either the first or the last of all things, we must grant it a certain middle position. This is very appropriate so that it may imitate its own primary causes. For the Goddess who is the cause of the soul holds a middle rank among the Gods, as she also appeared to theologians; she unites the two fathers,¹ and from her own depths <note>original: "bowels"</note> she releases the life of the soul. Therefore, just as we see the soul’s nature in the "fountain-like" <note>original: "fontal"</note> Gods, we may also see this "soul-principle" <term>psychical principle</term> shining through the ruling Gods. Thus, the soul properly proceeds as a medium between purely intelligible realities <note>objects of pure intellect</note> and sensible realities <note>objects of the senses</note>—between beings that are purely eternal and those that are simply created <note>original: "generated"</note>.

<margin>136</margin>However, you must not understand its middle nature to be the kind of thing that merely connects two extremes while remaining separate from the things it connects. For the soul is not "better" than intelligible realities; rather, it is their final result. Nor, on the other hand, is it inferior to both; for it transcends the sensible things that are moved by it. Instead, because it is a boundary or an end, it is the limit of the intelligible realm, but the starting principle of the sensible realm. 

By no means, however, should we say that it is a boundary or principle in the same way a point exists on a line. It is not inside the things it bounds like a point is inside two sections of a line. Rather, it is the boundary of the intelligible realm in one way—by appearing immediately after the intelligible "essential reality" <term>hypostasis</term>—and it is the principle of the sensible realm in another way—by being both separate from and the cause of motion for sensible things. 

In this way, it provides us with a certain analogy: just as things moved by others <term>alter-motive</term> relate to things that move themselves <term>self-motive</term>, so do self-moving natures relate to those that are completely immovable. The soul also holds the bond of all beings through its specific middle condition; it unfolds causes that were once united, while simultaneously gathering together the scattered powers of the physical world. It is contained by the immovable essence which always remains the same, but it itself contains all things that are moved by others and the entirely unstable world of change.

*It is likewise "intelligible" <note>pertaining to the realm of thought</note> when compared to created things, but "created" when compared to the intelligible realm. Thus, it displays both extremes within its middle nature, imitating in this respect the Goddess who is its cause.² For she is luminous on every side and has a face looking in every direction. She also holds the rudders of the universe, receiving the progressions of intelligible beings into her own bosom. She is filled by the "intelligible"³ <note>original: νοητης (noētēs)</note> life, while pouring out the rivers of the "intellectual"⁴ <note>original: νοερας (noeras)</note> life, and she contains within herself the very center of this progression.*

¹ The cause of the soul is Rhea, who unites the two fathers, Saturn and Jupiter. Juno is also a cause of the soul, but she is a secondary cause, contained within the life-giving fountain of Rhea.
² That is, Rhea.
³ For "intellectual" <note>original: νοερας (noeras)</note> here, it is necessary to read "intelligible" <note>original: νοητης (noētēs)</note>.
⁴ And instead of "intelligible" <note>original: νοητης (noētēs)</note> here, we must read "intellectual" <note>original: νοερας (noeras)</note>.

<meta>This page continues the argument that the soul exists as a middle ground between the eternal realm of pure intellect and the physical realm of time and change. It explores how the soul can be both "unbegotten" (eternal) and "generated" (created) at the same time.</meta>

<page-num>25</page-num>
<header>BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 25</header>
<sig>VOL. II. D</sig>

...of all beings. It is very appropriate, then, that the soul is considered both unbegotten <note>original: "unbegotten"—meaning eternal and without a beginning</note> and generated <note>original: "generated"—meaning something that comes into being or changes</note>. This was previously demonstrated by the two types of life found within her: the *essential* life and the *transitive* life <note>Essential life refers to the soul's core existence; transitive life refers to its movement and activity through time</note>. However, this can now be shown by looking at the soul as a whole and in its parts. For how can a true "being" be unbegotten unless it possesses the infinite power of existence all at once? And how can a physical body be "generated" unless infinite power is constantly flowing into it, because the body is unable to receive that entire power at one time?

<margin>About the soul</margin>
Therefore, because the soul is non-physical, it has an inherent, infinite power to exist; as a whole, it was not "created" in a single moment, but is immortal. Yet, according to its parts, it is always being "generated" to infinity. If the soul possessed the same total infinity at all times, there would be no difference between the whole and the part, the perfect and the imperfect, or that which contains and that which is contained. But this is impossible. Furthermore, the soul cannot be entirely in a state of "becoming," nor can only a part of it be eternal being; otherwise, the parts would be superior to the whole. *Conversely, the whole is an infinite being, while the part is always in the process of becoming.* 

So, the fundamental nature <term>hypostasis</term> of the soul possesses infinite power and is generated to infinity. In this way, it participates in true "being" while also being the first of all "generated" natures—since physical bodies, both as a whole and in their parts, are always in a state of becoming. It is not enough to say the soul is "generated" simply because it acts in separate parts; we must see how this quality exists in the very essence of the soul. Every natural action has an underlying essence that serves as its cause. Therefore, the soul also holds the "seed" of a life that exists within time, a quality common to every soul. It is necessary for this life to be "generated" and not just simply "be." *If this is the case, since the soul possesses being as a whole, it must be generated in its parts.* We have shown how this is true. This should be enough concerning the "middle" nature of the soul.

Let us also establish that the intelligible breadth <note>the vast range of pure thought</note>, the psychical multitude <note>the variety of souls</note>, and the sensible nature <note>the physical world</note> are separate from each other. Let the lowest things be dependent on those in the middle, and let those middle things be dependent on the highest. Let the soul also be the single bond that connects all beings, existing within them. For the "One" also binds all things together, but in a way that is distinct and superior. All things are united to each other because they are of a similar kind, derived from one cause, and extended toward...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the soul as a mediating force. Having established the soul as both eternal and part of the world of "becoming," the author now begins to analyze the fundamental "genera" or categories that compose the soul's essence, drawing on Plato’s "Sophist" and "Philebus."</meta>

<page-num>26</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.</header>

...one object of desire. However, the soul also binds different beings together because it exists within them. Just as in a mathematical proportion (analogy), the middle term relates to the things it connects, we must recognize the soul as the middle point of all existence—both binding others and being bound itself—because its nature is to move itself.

<margin>(4)</margin>
Now that we have discussed these points, the next step is to show how and from what "genera" <note>original: "genera"—the fundamental categories or "types" of being, such as Sameness, Difference, and Essence</note> this soul is formed, since it holds the connection between all beings. However, it is even more important to first discuss these genera themselves: what they are, where they come from, and how they function. It is necessary to understand the "wholes" (the big picture) before examining the "parts" (the details). 

This is the fourth topic we proposed to cover, and we will discuss it as clearly as possible. It has been proven in many other works—and will be shown by Plato later in this text—that the "intelligible world" <note>The realm of pure thought or divine ideas that exists beyond the physical world</note> contains the causes for all lower forms of nature. All "forms" <note>original: "forms"—the perfect Platonic Ideals or universal blueprints for all things</note> exist there, whether we describe them as existing in pure thought or in the intellect, for they exist in both ways. 

Among these forms, some are the most universal ("total") and apply to everything. Others are the most specific, acting as "atomic" or indivisible forms. Still others exist in between, applying to many things but not all. This is something the "Elean Stranger" <note>A character in Plato’s dialogue, the *Sophist*</note> also points out in the *Sophist*. 

For example, an individual human comes from the "Form of Man," and an individual horse comes from the "Form of Horse." However, the quality of "similarity" found in both humans and horses—and in many other things—comes from "Similitude" itself. The same is true for "Dissimilarity." Likewise, "Difference" and "Sameness," which are present in all existing things, come from the universal Sameness and Difference found in that higher realm. 

Therefore, some things originate from "atomic" forms, others from middle forms, and still others from the most universal forms. We see this in our own sciences: some focus on a single object (like medicine focuses on health), while others apply to many areas. For instance, arithmetic applies to philosophy, politics, the "tectonic" <note>original: "tectonic"—referring here to the art of construction or carpentry</note> arts, and many others. 

This is true not only for arithmetic but also for geometry (the science of measuring) and statics <note>The study of weights and balances</note>. Plato says that most, if not all, of the "fabricative" <note>original: "fabricative"—creative or manufacturing arts</note> arts require these sciences; without them, they would lack any precision. 

Yet there are other arts that apply to all disciplines—not just the creative ones, but also the "contemplative" <note>original: "contemplative"—theoretical or philosophical sciences</note> sciences. An example of this is the "art of division" <note>The logical method of categorizing things by dividing a genus into species</note>, as Socrates mentions in the *Philebus*. 

Just as some sciences are more universal than others, some higher causes are more "partial" <note>In this context, "partial" means specific or limited in scope compared to universal laws</note>. These partial causes lead specific groups of similar forms. Others are very broad, such as "Equality," "Similarity," and "Wholeness." Note, however, that even "Wholeness" is not common to absolutely everything; a part, as long as it is a part, is not a whole.

Since "Being" itself is the very first of the intelligible forms, the causes of existence hold the highest and most universal rank among the categories (genera) of being. These genera...</insert>

...there are five in number: *essence*, *sameness*, *difference*, *motion*, and *permanency*. For every being is given an essence; it is united to itself, yet separated both from itself and from other things. It proceeds from itself and its own proper principle, and it participates in a certain stillness and permanency as long as it preserves its own distinct form. Whether, therefore, there is a category of things that is intelligible <note>original: "intelligible"—belonging to the realm of pure thought or divine intellect</note>, or sensible <note>original: "sensible"—capable of being perceived by the senses</note>, or a middle category between the two, it consists of these five; for all things originate from them. Not everything is alive, nor is everything a "whole," a "part," or animated with a soul; but all things participate in these five fundamental categories. 

If essence were not present, no other category could exist, for they all exist within essence. If sameness did not exist, the whole of reality would be dissipated <note>original: "dissipated"—scattered or broken apart into nothingness</note>. If the difference of one thing from another were abolished, there would be only one thing, and that one thing would lack any variety. Likewise, if motion did not exist, things would be inactive and dead. And without <note>original: *ανευ* (aneu)—without. This word was omitted in the original Greek text.</note> *permanency*, things would be unstable and immediately hurried away into non-existence. 

Hence, it is necessary that in all things there should be each of these five, and that essence should stand as the first among them. Essence serves as the Vesta <note>The Roman goddess of the hearth, representing the stable, central point of the home or the universe</note> and the "monad" <note>A fundamental, indivisible unit or the number one</note> of these categories, holding a position similar to *The One* <note>The ultimate, absolute source of all existence in Neoplatonism</note>. After this, it is necessary that sameness and difference should exist; sameness is similar to the principle of *Bound* <note>The principle of limit, structure, and order</note>, while difference is similar to *Infinity* <note>The principle of unlimited potential, expansion, and variety</note>. 

In a similar manner, it is required that there should be *permanency* and *motion*. Permanency is especially visible in the *powers of beings*, while motion is visible in their *energies* <note>In this context, "power" is the internal capacity or potential to act, while "energy" is the actual outward expression or activity of that power</note>. Every essential power falls under the category of sameness, or difference, or both. For example, heat (and every power that separates things) falls under difference; but cold (and every power that collects things together) falls under sameness. <meta>This page continues Proclus's examination of the five primary "genera" or categories of being (Essence, Sameness, Difference, Motion, and Permanency). Having established that all things are composed of these categories, he now explains how they manifest differently across the various levels of reality, from the divine down to the physical.</meta>

<page-num>28</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.</header>

...acts. In short, since everything that exists in any way consists of both "bound" <note>original: "bound"—the principle of limit, order, and definition</note> and "infinity" <note>original: "infinity"—the principle of unlimited power and multiplicity</note>, it is given its essence and exists through a participation in both of these. It possesses a sense of sameness with itself through the union of these two, and difference through their separation. Because it is not the "First Principle" <note>Referring to "The One," the source of all things in Neoplatonism</note>, it proceeds from the source of all things and yet remains within it; thus, it is both in motion and permanent. These five categories, therefore, are present in every being simply because it is a being, though they exist differently in different levels of reality.

For **intelligible** natures <note>original: "intelligibles"—the highest level of reality, pure divine forms</note> possess all five of these essentially. **Intelligible-and-intellectual** natures <note>The middle rank between pure forms and pure mind</note> possess them according to *sameness*^1; **intellectual** natures <note>Natures characterized by mind and thought</note> according to *difference*; **psychical** natures <note>Natures related to the soul</note> according to *permanency*; and **corporeal** natures <note>Physical bodies</note> according to *motion*. 

However, this can also be viewed the other way around if we say that "life" is motion and "stillness" <note>original: "sluggishness"—used here to mean inactivity or stasis</note> is permanency. Souls are essentially "lives," but bodies are "moved by something else" <note>original: "alter-motive"—meaning they do not move themselves but are moved by external forces</note>. If, however, motion and permanency come before sameness and difference—as we might prove by other arguments—then we would call the progression of each thing from its cause^2 a "motion" that happens before any action begins, and we would call its staying within its cause a "permanency" that happens before the state of inactivity. If this is the case, then after the intelligibles, the intelligible-and-intellectual natures will exist according to *permanency*, but the intellectuals will exist according to *motion*. Souls will exist according to *sameness*, but bodies will exist according to *difference*. 

But if we say that life is motion and unchanging intelligence is permanency, then once again:
*   **Intelligibles** will be characterized by *essence*.
*   **Intelligible-and-intellectual** natures, being "lives," will be characterized by *motion*.
*   **Intellectual** natures, being rooted in the intellect, will be characterized by *permanency* (for physical things derive their stability from the intellect). 
*   **Psychical** natures will exist according to *sameness*, because they contain the bond^3 between the indivisible and the divisible.
*   **Corporeal** natures will exist according to *difference*, for in physical things, because they are divisible, conflict and separation have dominion. 

These five natures follow each other in order: **being**, **life**, **intellect**, **soul**, and **body**; this is because the universal categories that exist before specific forms are also five in number. This is enough to say concerning these five categories universally, though we should also note that these same things are called both "genera" <note>Categories or kinds</note> and "elements." The highest forms of these secondary natures are called "genera"; while they remain whole and separate from individual things, they are the causes of those things' existence. But each of the several...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the five primary "genera" or categories of being. Having explained how they exist in the divine intellect, Proclus now moves to the "fifth head" or topic: how these categories function within the human soul to allow it to perceive and understand both the divine and the physical worlds.</meta>

<page-num>29</page-num>
<header>BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

The things of which a whole consists are called "elements." For the primary categories <note>original: "genera"—the five fundamental classes of Being, Sameness, Difference, Motion, and Rest</note> within the Demiurge <note>The divine Creator or "Craftsman" of the universe in Platonic thought</note> give completion to his creative being and serve as its elements. Furthermore, they are the source-categories of all the forms contained in the intellects that proceed from him, as well as all those forms found in souls and bodies.¹

<margin>⑤</margin>
Let us now proceed to the fifth point, if you are willing, and consider how these primary categories exist within souls, and why Plato assumes them. It has already been shown that the soul is the medium between "beings" <note>Intelligible realities or pure forms</note> and "non-beings" <note>Sensible or physical matter</note>, and that it knows all things—both the intelligible and the sensible—whether it does so through the same rational principles or through different ones, as some suggest. Therefore, it is necessary that the <margin>mention before the categories</margin> essence of the soul should proceed from these primary categories of being. For if the soul did not originate from these, but from some other sources, it would not be able to know all things or apply itself to all things. <margin>></margin> Just as the soul knows a "man" according to the rational principle (or form) of a man which it contains, and it knows a "divine spirit" <note>original: "dæmon"—in this context, a benevolent intermediary spirit between gods and men</note> according to the form of such a spirit within it, so too does it know *being itself* through its participation in "Being," and it knows *difference* through its participation in "Difference." <margin>)</margin>

Consequently, the soul contains all the primary categories, but in a manner adapted to its own nature. It appears to me that, for this reason, Plato constitutes the soul out of the first categories, and out of numbers and harmonic ratios. He also places within it the principles of geometric figures and divine motions. He does this so that the soul—by already possessing the internal reasons for all academic disciplines and for dialectic <note>The highest form of philosophical reasoning and logic</note>—might understand all things: specifically the essences, the numbers, the harmonies, the figures, and the motions of <margin>></margin> which all wholes consist. 

It seems, likewise, that he constitutes the soul from the categories of being (which primarily exist in the divine realm) because the soul is allied to intelligible things. However, he gives the soul "figure" <note>Geometric shape or structure</note> because it is also allied to sensible things, for things that are truly shaped by figures are sensible objects. As a medium between the intelligible and the sensible, he binds the soul together with harmonic ratios. While the forms of "harmony" and "figure" also exist in the highest intelligible realm, "Harmony itself"² is not something that has been harmonized by an outside force, nor is "Figure itself" something that has been shaped into a figure. This is because things that exist in a primary, original state do not exist by "participation" <note>The philosophical concept of a lower thing "sharing in" the quality of a higher Form</note>. In sensible objects, harmony and the categories of being exist only in a divided, partial way. But in souls, they exist non-physically and yet in a composite manner;³ and this participation reveals their composite nature.⁴ For "participation" is a quality of composite things, while "incorporeality" (non-physicality) is the defining characteristic of simple, pure natures. It is necessary, however, for that which primarily participates—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the soul is composed of the five primary "genera" or categories of being. The previous page ended while explaining that the soul participates in these categories so that it can understand all levels of reality.</meta>

<page-num>30</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.</header>

<margin>✓</margin>
...participates in them in such a way. Plato, therefore, constructs the soul’s nature <note>original: "psychical essence"</note> from these primary categories. He first produces the underlying substance <note>original: *hypokeimenon*</note> of this nature from the "middle" versions of these categories. 

We can compare this to how the physical elements work. As we have said, all the elements exist in the heavens, in the world of change <note>original: "sublunary region"</note>, and even under the earth. However, they are not the same everywhere. Heaven consists of the "summits" or purest forms of the elements; the world of generation consists of the secondary forms; and the subterranean regions consist of the very last stages of the elements' progression. 

In the same way, all things consist of these primary categories, but they manifest differently:
*   **Intelligible natures** (pure intellects) consist of the first, indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note>, immovable, and entire versions of these categories.
*   **Self-moving natures** (souls) consist of versions that are both indivisible and divisible <note>original: "partible"</note>.
*   **Physical natures** (bodies) consist of the divisible versions. 

The nature of a thing matches the categories that form it. Indivisible natures come before those that are both indivisible and divisible, and those, in turn, come before purely divisible natures. The indivisible is closer to **the One**, because it is indivisible due to its unity. 

Since it has been shown that the soul’s nature is the "middle ground" of all beings, it appropriately consists of the "middle" versions of the primary categories: Essence, Sameness, and Difference. In the *Phaedrus*, when Plato weaves together the powers derived from these, he calls them a "charioteer and horses," because these define the very existence of the soul. We can also see "permanency" <note>Rest</note> and "motion" in how the soul acts, for they exist in its very essence. The soul creates itself, remains as it is, and moves forward; it is eternal. In this way, motion and permanency are even more fundamental to the soul than sameness and difference. It stays fixed among eternal things through permanency, yet it moves forward through progression. Through this progression, it branches out into a "united multitude." These primary categories of being are most clearly seen in how the soul operates.

The soul is not only the middle point between indivisible and divisible reality, but also between the realm of eternal, unchanging Sameness and the realm of "generation"—the world of things constantly becoming. 

Therefore, because the soul exists with unchanging sameness, it shares in "permanency" according to its essential nature. But because it is involved in the world of change, it shares in "motion." 

However, one might also argue that because "Sameness" and "Difference" specifically belong to the work of the Demiurge <note>The Divine Creator</note>, Timaeus describes the creation of these first. 

What, then, is the defining trait of each of these "middle" categories? We might say that since "Essence" consists of "Bound" <note>Limit</note> and "Infinity," when Bound prevails over Infinity, it produces the...

While a body is divisible and can be broken down infinitely, souls, by contrast, are divisible into finite parts, just as a number is divisible into units <term>monads: the indivisible units that make up a number</term>. Because of this, some philosophers have chosen to call the soul a "number"—divisible, yes, but into indivisible units rather than things that can be divided forever. <note>A large hand-drawn parenthesis mark appears in the right margin, encompassing the text from "Hence also" down to "it is partible ;"</note> Therefore, the indivisibility of the soul is twofold: it is indivisible as a whole, and it is indivisible at the level of its final, smallest parts. Yet, even in its matter, the division is not infinite; it ends at the final unit, which is indivisible.

If you are willing, this may also be viewed in another way. Since these intermediate types <note>original: "middle genera"</note> are three, when **Essence** prevails over **Sameness** and **Difference**, then—according to the specific mixture of these intermediaries—a divine soul is created. The degree of this dominance determines the range and variety of divine souls. But when **Sameness** and **Essence** together prevail over **Difference**, an angelic soul is generated. When **Sameness** alone predominates, a daemonic <note>original: "dæmoniacal"; in this context, it refers to "daemons," spirits that act as messengers between gods and humans, not necessarily evil beings</note> soul is produced. However, when **Sameness** together with **Difference** have dominion over **Essence**, an heroic soul is generated; and when **Difference** alone prevails, a human soul is produced. 

It is impossible for the extreme types to overcome the middle ground, because they cannot be joined to each other without that intermediary. Within each of these mixtures, the greater or lesser degree of the dominating qualities produces the wide range of souls. These matters, however, will be discussed more fully elsewhere.

<margin>6</margin>
In the next place, it remains to consider what the indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> and the divisible <note>original: "partible"</note> forms of essence are. Among the more ancient interpreters, there were differences of opinion on this subject. Therefore, let us first speak generally about these things, and afterwards in a way that is more specific to the subjects we are investigating. We can speak in both ways. 

We say, therefore, that every essence of the mind and spirit <note>original: "intelligible and intellectual essence"</note>—whether it is universal or individual, non-physical and distinct, and either preceding eternity or being eternal—is indivisible. On the other hand, all essences that act upon bodies are divisible. These include the lives of the physical world, natures that lean toward physical matter, or the natural laws <note>original: "physical reasons"</note> that are distributed throughout a body that lacks inherent qualities. All of these are divisible because of their connection to bodies. 

Some of these indeed exist within visible bodies as if they were qualities of a subject. Others have their own fundamental existence as forms of life but are inseparable from bodies, such as nature itself. Others are distributed into parts but unify themselves into an indivisible point, such as the faculty of sense. 

If you wish, you may say that the indivisible essence is threefold, existing according to **being**, **life**, and **intellect**. The essence that exists according to sensory perception takes the place of intellect; that which exists according to nature takes the place of life; and that which exists according to the physical forms distributed through the mass of bodies takes the place of being. Because these latter three are reflections <note>original: "images"</note> of the former three, they exist in an opposite order to one another. The intermediaries between these are the being, life, and intellect within souls. These souls preserve the order of the higher natures through their resemblance to them, but they have a distribution into parts equal¹ to the natures that...

...are secondary to them. We must, therefore, divide all things into three parts. By doing so, we must arrange the essence of the soul between the indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> and the divisible <note>original: "partible"</note> natures. The soul acts as the image of the former and the model <note>original: "paradigm"</note> for the latter. It stays still while also proceeding forward; it is both simple and composite; and it is separate from, yet joined with, physical bodies. The soul’s nature as a perfect middle ground is revealed through all these characteristics. Generally speaking, we can say that every essence between the **One** and the soul is indivisible, and every essence between the soul and physical bodies is divisible.

If, however, we need to define the divisible and the indivisible more precisely, we should speak as follows: The Demiurge <note>The divine "Craftsman" or creator-god in Plato's philosophy</note> created the universe as a living being, endowed with a soul and an intellect. He believed that a living thing is better than a lifeless one, and an intellectual being is better than one without intellect. Therefore, the universe has a physical life, which is why it is called a living being; because it is bound with "soul-bonds," it became alive. 

However, the soul itself is not mixed with the body. Socrates argues against the idea of such a mixture in the *Phaedrus*. Instead, the soul is divine. It is through the soul that the universe is alive, having both an innate life <note>original: "connascent life"</note> and a separate, independent life. Within it, there is also an immaterial <note>original Greek: *aulos*. The text notes a correction from *autos* (self) to *aulos* (immaterial).</note> and divine intellect. We must call this an "essential intellect" rather than a mere state or habit of the soul. The Demiurge did not create the soul as a mere state, but as something that moves itself toward the realm of the intellect, as Timaeus says later. 

Thus, the universe has a triple life: physical, soul-based <note>original: "psychical"</note>, and intellectual. The intellectual life of the universe is indivisible because it is eternal, understands all truths at once, is unchanging, and is unified by a supreme power that transcends all lesser things. In contrast, the physical life is divisible because it exists within physical matter, is mixed with the body, and turns toward material objects. The life of the soul is the middle ground between the two. It rises above the physical because it exists separately, wrapping around the bulk of the universe like a veil (as has been said and will be mentioned again). It reaches toward the intellect, yet remains lower than it. It gains understanding through time and unfolds the indivisible nature of the intellectual life, while also making contact with the physical body. By creating the world-soul from these intermediate parts, Plato shows that it is a bridge between the natures that are si— <note>The text cuts off mid-word "situated" or "similar," continuing on the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul as a mediating essence. It specifically defines the "Soul of the Universe" as the bridge between the single, universal intellect and the totality of physical matter, distinguishing it from individual souls like those of the sun, moon, or humans.</meta>

<page-num>34</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.</header>

...situated on each side of it, but it is not the medium between every intellectual and physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> essence. For it is not the medium for partial intellects <note>Individual minds or lower-level intellectual beings</note> and the forms which are distributed throughout the parts of the universe. It is also the unique characteristic of the Soul of the Universe neither to consist purely of numbers, nor of these or those "reasons" <note>original: "rational principles" or "logoi"</note>, nor of a specific number of circles. For all these things, and others, are common to every divine, demonic, and human soul. 

*But its unique quality is that its essence is the medium between the following extremes: the one universal <note>original: "mundane"</note> intellect and the whole of the divisible <note>original: "partible"</note> essence which is distributed among bodies.* 

It is the medium of these, not specifically in how the intellect "knows" <note>original: "is gnostic"</note> or gives life, nor in how nature serves as the life of bodies. This discussion is not about knowledge or types of life; it is about how these are certain "essences." The former is an indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> essence, while the latter is an essence divisible among bodies. For this reason, we also attempt to define both "being" and "generation"—the indivisible and the divisible—according to the essential existence <note>original: "hyparxis"</note> of the soul. In doing so, we set aside changes and activities <note>original: "mutations and energies"</note>. We do not seek to perceive the activities of the soul, but rather its essence, which is both unbegotten and generated at the same time. <note>Proclus argues the soul is "unbegotten" because it is eternal in essence, but "generated" because it exists within the realm of time and change.</note>

It is also evident that its essential "bound" <note>The limit or defining principle of its nature</note> is more unitary <note>original: "unical"</note> than the bounds found in all other souls, and that its "infinite" <note>Its power or potentiality</note> is more comprehensive than the infinites in other souls. For not every bound is equal to every other bound; some are more "total" (universal), while others are more "partial" (individual). Nor is every infinity equal to every power. Therefore, not every essence is equal to every other essence; one is total, and another is partial. 

The essence of the Soul of the Universe is more universal than any other soul-based <note>original: "psychical"</note> essence. The bound within it is the most universal of all soul-bounds, and its infinity is the most universal of all the infinites in souls. For the extremes of these are: the purely indivisible essence, and the essence that is purely divisible among bodies—not just among *some* bodies, but among *all* bodies. 

For example, the soul of the sun is the medium between a specific indivisible essence (not the Indivisible in an absolute sense) and a specific divisible essence (not every essence divisible among bodies). Plato, assuming this is the primary characteristic of the universal soul, connects the remaining details—such as number, harmony, and form—as belonging to the discussion of this specific kind of soul. Therefore, the "indivisible" should not be understood here as every intellectual essence, but only the essence of the universal intellect. Likewise, in the soul of the sun, it must be understood as the essence of the "solar intellect," and similarly in the soul of the moon and all other souls. For every bridge <note>original: "medium"</note> has its own specific, nearby shores <note>original: "proximate extremes"</note>, and will be the medium between those, rather than a medium for all extremes everywhere.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of how the soul acts as a bridge between the spiritual and physical worlds. It transitions from discussing the World Soul to how dæmons and individual souls also serve as "media" or intermediaries.</meta>

<page-num>35</page-num>
<header>BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 35</header>

In this way, dæmons <note>original: "dæmons"; in Neoplatonism, these are benevolent intermediary spirits that link gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense</note>—who are higher in rank than individual souls—exist as intermediaries between their own intellects and the bodies that are born with them. Therefore, if Plato had discussed any other kind of soul, he would not have said its essence is a medium between the indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> essence and the essence divisible among bodies in general, but rather between a specific indivisible and divisible essence belonging to individual natures. 

For grammatical articles <note>Proclus refers to the Greek practice of adding "the" (*to*) before a word to indicate a universal Form</note> indicate the transcendent and the whole, as Plato determines elsewhere. He asserts that when we say "*the* beautiful," we indicate the universal concept, but we mean something else when we just say "beautiful." The former indicates that which is independent <note>original: "exempt"</note>, while the latter indicates something ranked alongside others. 

If you wish to apply the views of the illustrious Theodorus here: the intellect exists without relation <note>original: "habitude"; meaning it is independent and not tied to anything else</note>; life associated with the body exists in a state of relation; and the soul is the medium between the two, being a sort of "half-relation." 

According to the great Iamblichus: the intellect is indeed independent; life associated with the body is organized alongside physical matter; and the soul is both independent of and, at the same time, organized with the life of the body. Every intellect, therefore, is indivisible, as it possesses a single essence, a single sameness, and a single difference, of which it is entirely composed. But every soul is divisible <note>original: "partible"</note> because every mixture of the elements that compose it is divided into many parts. Each of these parts is a compound of all the fundamental kinds <note>original: "genera"</note>; consequently, there are many essences, many samenesses, and many differences in each mixture, which are divided along with the parts within it. As for what these parts are and how many there are, Plato demonstrates this to us by using mathematical means, sections through intervals of nine-to-eight <note>original: "sesquioctaves"; a musical ratio representing a whole tone</note>, and mathematical remainders <note>original: "lemmas"; referring to the Greek *leimma*, the "leftover" interval in a musical scale</note>, as will become clear as we proceed.

<margin>The problem with the plurality of forms</margin>
Furthermore, it is evident that we say the intellect, insofar as it is intellect, is indivisible, because we believe that although a multitude of forms exist within it, they are distinct from it. We say the soul, insofar as it is soul, is divisible—not by looking at the forms within it at the same time, but by looking solely at the soul’s essence and the intellectual essence, and seeing each as separate from the other. 

Hence, the intellect that the soul participates in is called an "indivisible essence" by Plato. However, the body-shaped life that proceeds from the soul—which relates to the soul like a reflection—is said by him to be "divisible among bodies." For the intellect is like the sun, the soul is like the light coming from the sun, and the divisible life is like the brightness reflected from that light. We correctly consider these assertions more accurate than previous ones because it is necessary that the Demiurge <note>The divine Craftsman or Creator of the universe</note> should be the master of every indivisible and every divisible essence,¹ so that the recipient may have a place, and that the nature which consists of—

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of how different types of souls—supermundane, mundane, and human—are composed of "divisible" and "indivisible" elements. Proclus is debating with earlier philosophers like Iamblichus and Theodorus about which specific soul Plato is describing in the "Timaeus."</meta>

both may be mingled, and all such other particulars may be effected, as Plato adduces in what follows. Iamblichus, therefore, and together with him Theodorus, refer what is here said to the transcendent <note>original: "supermundane"</note> soul; but we are of the opinion that Timaeus generates through these things the soul of the universe, as the words also manifest.

<margin>(</margin>We think it requisite, however, that the lovers of contemplation should investigate what the divisible <note>original: "partible"</note> and the indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> are <note>The words "the divisible and" (original: *to meriston kai*) are omitted in the original Greek text.</note> in the transcendent soul. For a transcendent intellect is seated above every soul. But what is the divisible in the transcendent soul? For certain sensible bodies are not suspended from such souls. Because they are transcendent, the reverse of what takes place in human souls is true of them; since bodies are suspended from each human soul, through which they are also made worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note>. But a specific intellect is not established above human souls, which is why they do not always perceive through pure intellect. 

Bodies, however, are suspended from all the souls that exist between human and transcendent souls. Hence also they are worldly, being more filled <note>original: "redundant"</note> than transcendent souls by their connection to a body. And there is a *specific* intellect from which they are suspended, which is why they are not always fixed in the intelligible realm. For that which is immovable produces eternal energy. 

Hence, since the extremes—namely, transcendent and worldly souls—have a contrary mode of existence, and as it would seem, the latter being deficient according to the divisible, but the former exceeding according to the indivisible;—this being the case, we say that the divisible nature of transcendent souls is not that which is divided among bodies, but that which is divided among the worldly souls <note>"Of souls" (original: *Psychon*) is omitted in the original Greek text.</note> themselves. For they immediately transcend these, just as worldly souls transcend the divisible essence which exists among bodies. 

Hence, the transcendent souls are intermediaries <note>original: "media"</note> between intellects and worldly souls; intellects have an existence unmingled with body, but worldly souls experience transitions in their intellectual acts. *But the indivisible part of human souls—so far as such a thing exists in them—is found in the souls that are above them, which are always intellectual. Human souls are suspended from these higher souls and participate in them at certain times, as far as they are able. For through these higher souls, as intermediaries, they are likewise joined with the intellects that are above all souls, and thus become intellectual.*

These, however, as we have said, being the extremes, all the intermediate souls have a peculiar indivisibility and divisibility, whether they have a divine or spiritual <note>original: "dæmoniacal"; referring to *daemons*, the intermediary spirits in Neoplatonism</note> assignment; rational spirits, and prior to these the soul of the universe, are intermediaries between the whole worldly intellect (which has an indivisible essence) and the physical world.

# BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

...and the divisible <term>original: "partible"; the aspect of the soul that interacts with the physical, fragmented world</term> essence which exists around bodies. We assert these things based on all that has been said before, through which we have demonstrated their truth using the words of Plato himself, rather than our own personal opinions. *For those who reason based on the [Chaldean] Oracles <note>A collection of mystical verses from the 2nd century AD, highly influential on Neoplatonists like Proclus.</note>, it must be argued that transcendent <note>original: "supermundane"</note> souls ride in certain transcendent, ethereal, and empyrean <note>made of fire or light</note> bodies. Otherwise, how could those bodies be moved unless souls moved them in a manner more divine than that of worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note> souls? But if this is granted, it may also be admitted that partial souls <note>individual souls, like those of humans</note> have an indivisible intellectual essence above them, and a certain power of intellect which illuminates similar souls. It is because of this that they are "partial" and only intellectual at certain times, while the souls suspended from each total intellect are the only ones that are always intellectual.*

Furthermore, in order for these things to align with the Orphic doctrines, we must say that Orpheus does not attribute the term "indivisible" <note>original: "impartible"</note> to every intelligible or intellectual order. According to him, there is something superior to this name, just as some natures are more excellent than the names we give them. For he does not apply the titles of "king" and "father" to all the divine orders. Where, then, shall we first see the "indivisible" according to him, so that we may understand the divinely inspired <note>The original Greek text likely had a typo, *enthen* ("from there"), which the translator corrects to *entheon* ("divinely inspired").</note> conception of Plato? 

Orpheus, therefore, establishes a Demiurge <note>original: "Demiurgus"; a creator god. Here, identified as Bacchus/Dionysus.</note> of "all-divided" creation, who is analogous to the one father who brings the entire creation into the light. From him, he produces the whole worldly intellectual multitude, the number of souls, and physical bodies. This Demiurge generates all these things as a unified whole, but the gods who surround him divide and separate his creations. Orpheus says, however, that while all the other creations of the god were distributed into parts by the deities who specialize in division, the heart alone remained undivided through the providence of Minerva <note>The Roman name for Athena. In the myth, Bacchus/Dionysus is torn apart by Titans, but Athena saves his heart.</note>. Since he created intellects, souls, and bodies, and since souls and bodies undergo much division and separation into parts, it is only the intellect that remains united and indivisible. It is "all things in one," comprehending entire intelligible wholes in a single act of thought. Hence, Orpheus says that the intellectual essence alone, and the intellectual number, were preserved by Minerva. For he says,

> The intellectual heart alone remained.

He clearly calls it "intellectual." Therefore, if the undivided heart is intellectual, it will evidently be the intellect and an intellectual number—yet not every intellect, but specifically the worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note> intellect. For this is the "undivided heart" [of the world]; since of this also the...

<note>2. That is, Bacchus (Dionysus).</note>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.

The Creator <term>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine craftsman of the universe in Platonic philosophy</term> was divided God. Orpheus, therefore, calls the intellect of Bacchus the indivisible <term>original: "impartible"</term> essence of the God. However, he refers to his procreative organs <note>original: "genitals"</note> as the life which is divided among physical bodies; this life being physical and the producer of seeds. He also says that Diana—who presides over all generation in nature and acts as a midwife <term>original: "obstetricates"</term> to natural laws <note>original: "physical reasons" (logoi); the formative principles that shape matter</note>—extends as far as the subterranean realms, distributing the prolific power of Bacchus. But all the remaining body of the God forms the composition of the soul <note>original: "psychical composition"</note>, which is likewise divided into seven parts.

->All the seven parts they scattered of the boy;<-

says the theologian <note>referring to Orpheus</note> concerning the Titans; just as Timaeus also divides the soul into seven parts. Perhaps he also reminds us of the Orphic "Titanic distribution"¹ into parts when he says that the soul is extended² through the whole world. Because of this, the soul not only circularly covers the universe like a veil, but is also extended through the entirety of it. Hence, Plato very properly calls the essence which is immediately above the soul "indivisible." In short, he uses this name for the intellect in which the soul participates, following the Orphic fables and wishing to act as the interpreter of secret and mystical claims. Returning, therefore, to the words of Plato, it is necessary to show how what has been said previously aligns with his concepts.

Since intellect is an indivisible essence, it is striking how Parmenides, in the second³ hypothesis <note>The second hypothesis of Plato's "Parmenides" explores the relationship between "The One" and "Being."</note>, distributes *being* into infinite parts, and *the One* along with *being*. It is acknowledged by nearly all interpreters that the subject of that hypothesis is the nature that exists beyond souls. Or could it be said that the distribution into parts mentioned there signifies the progression of the *many unities*⁴ from the "One Being" [or being characterized by *the One*]? These unities proceed in a well-ordered manner from their proper principles into an appropriate multitude. Plato, however, does not intend to mean that the "One Being" derives its completion from these many unities in the same way that he says the soul, though one, has a multitude that ends within it. Rather, his meaning is that *the One Being* precedes the many unities and beings, and that the multitude of these is subordinate to it. He also means that both the "unical" <note>pertaining to unity or the One</note> and all essential numbers are causally contained within it; just as in this dialogue, he calls "Animal Itself" <note>The "Autozoon," the intelligible paradigm of all living things</note> one whole, but...

<note>² Instead of "ordered" (*tetagmenēn*) here, it is necessary to read "extended" (*tetamenēn*).</note>

...the four ideas are the parts of it. The "Animal-Itself" <note>original: "animal itself"; the Platonic Form of the Living Being which contains all other forms</note> does not derive its perfection from them; rather, they are contained within it, distributing the unity of that one being through their own multitude. Each of them possesses the power of a part of it, but all of them together are not equal to its total unity. For in this same way, both numbers—the one-like <note>original: "unical"</note> and the essential—are parts of that one being (as discussed in the *Parmenides*) without being "completive" of it, as if the whole consisted only of these parts. This is enough in answer to this doubt; let us proceed to the words before us.¹

<margin>7</margin>
> "From an essence always indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> and existing with unchanging identity, and again, from an essence which becomes divisible among physical bodies, he mingled from both a middle form of essence."

<margin>namely a Form</margin>
By the "indivisible essence," Plato means the intellectual essence, which in its entirety participates in eternity. By the "essence which is divisible among bodies," he means that which is inseparable from physical matter and is assigned its existence <term>original: "hyparxis"; the essential reality or "being" of a thing</term> within the whole of time. He shows this by saying that the former "exists with unchanging identity," and by calling the latter "that which is becoming." He does this so that he may call the soul not only indivisible and divisible at the same time, but also intelligible and the first of created things.

For eternal permanence is one thing; but that which exists according to temporal infinity is another, having its foundational reality <term>original: "hypostasis"</term> in extension. There is yet another which is mixed from both, such as the permanence of the soul. The soul is indeed unmoved in its essence, but it moves through its thoughts <note>original: "intellections"</note>. It is eternal according to its essence, but temporal according to its thoughts. It is likewise evident that the soul necessarily has something of this kind in its existence <note>original: "hyparxis"</note>, or it would not exhibit the characteristics of generation and temporal extension in its natural energies.

It appears to me that Plato, perceiving this in a wonderful manner, says that the Creator <term>original: "Demiurgus"</term> did not only make the soul a medium between the indivisible essence and the essence which is divisible among bodies, but also <margin>...could he say everything</margin> that he made it a medium between the essence which exists with unchanging identity and that which is generated, or "becoming." For how could he appropriately write the **Generation of the Soul** <term>original: "Psychogony"; the study or description of the soul's origin</term>,² if there was neither generation nor composition in the soul? How also would it be possible to take away parts from that which—

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.

...is essentially indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note>? For simple natures do not undergo any form of creation or coming-into-being. Even material forms are without creation and destruction, as Aristotle says. For through their simplicity, they preserve the characteristics of the primary forms even in the lowest levels of reality. However, it is possible to describe the coming-into-being of things that possess any kind of composition. Therefore, so that he might demonstrate these concepts which are quite rightly circulated regarding the soul, he calls it the middle ground between the eternal and the created <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: "hypostasis"; the essential reality, substance, or underlying foundation of a thing</note>.

<margin>[</margin>Prior to this, however, we should make the following division: concerning the indivisible and the divisible, it is necessary that either both should exist before the soul, or both exist after the soul, or both exist within the soul; or that one should exist before the soul while the other exists after it. Both cannot exist before the soul, because the soul is superior to the divisible life¹ that is coming into existence: [for she has a nature distinct from bodies, whereas divisible life is merged within bodies. Nor is it appropriate to say that both exist after the soul:]² for the indivisible essence is eternal and remains always the same. But the soul is not entirely eternal since, as Plato says in the *Laws*, she participates in the process of becoming. Nor are both within the soul, because it is impossible for things that differ so much from each other to combine into a single thing—namely, the inseparable and the separate from bodies, the uncreated and the created. Therefore, it remains that the one which is more excellent should exist before the soul, while the other which is less excellent should exist after it. Since, however, these qualities exist around the soul, it is necessary—as the soul does not consist of these external things—that it should consist of things analogous to them, which either exist separately from each other or are mingled together. But it is impossible for it to consist of them while they are separate from each other, for Plato clearly says that these are mingled together. Therefore, it is necessary that the essential part of the soul should consist of a mixture of these two. And since within the soul one thing is better and another is worse, that which is indivisible in it [is less excellent than the indivisible realm above it, and that which is divisible in it]³ is better than the divisible nature which exists after it. For being a middle ground, the soul possesses that which is more excellent in an inferior way, but possesses that which is less excellent in a superior way. And this indeed is evident.

...since it does not consist of these very things themselves, but † of others that are analogous to them. <image-desc>A double vertical pencil bracket is drawn in the right margin next to the first four lines of the page.</image-desc>

But it is evident that the essence of the soul does not consist of these things as its constituent parts. For once again, let us consider this very point. In the first place, <insert>①</insert> how is it possible for the indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> to be mingled with the divisible <note>original: "partible"</note>, and the eternal with that which is created <note>original: "generated"</note>? For these are, in a certain sense, opposites and extremely remote from each other, so that, as we have said before, they can by no means be joined together. In the second place, <insert>②</insert> would we not be making the soul secondary and subordinate to the things within it, <insert>←</insert> and the essence that is inseparable from the body more ancient than that which is separate, if it consists of an essence that is divided among bodies? Furthermore, <insert>③</insert> how can the soul be rightly called a "third thing"? For a "third thing" clearly exists alongside the other two, which must themselves be preserved and not destroyed. But things that are mixed together are no longer themselves; instead, a certain other <margin>judgment</margin> thing is produced from them, and not a "third" thing. For they themselves cease to exist, having been destroyed through the mixture. <insert>④</insert> Again, if the Demiurge <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine craftsman or creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy</note> <margin>making</margin> took a portion of the indivisible to create the soul, then that which is called an "indivisible essence" would no longer be indivisible. For how can anyone take a part of it, if it cannot be divided? But if he used up the whole of the indivisible essence to create the soul, he would no longer be acting for the good <note>original: "beneficent"</note>, because he would be consuming more divine natures—which are closer to himself and more primary <note>original: "causal"</note>—to form the <term>hypostasis</term> <note>the underlying foundation or essential reality</note> of less excellent natures. In addition to this, <insert>⑤</insert> if the soul derives its completion from a created, divisible nature, then that divisible nature would not only be divisible among bodies, but also among souls. Therefore, the indivisible and the divisible do not themselves form the soul, as some imagine. Rather, what Plato asserts is true: the Demiurge mixed a "middle" form of essence from the indivisible essence and from that which is divisible among bodies. Thus, the soul is divisible in relation to what is indivisible, but indivisible in relation to what is divisible, and this truly provides us with the soul's intermediate nature. <image-desc>A double vertical pencil bracket is drawn in the right margin marking the section from "Again, if the Demiurgus..." to "...middle nature of the soul."</image-desc>

Moreover, this "third thing" itself shows us the nature of the proportion <note>original: "analogy"</note> inherent in the soul. For if the same thing is both the middle and the third, and if this middle acts as the first and also as the last, then the soul is simultaneously the first and the last—a proportion that is naturally suited to produce beauty in the highest degree. And if this third thing is also the middle, it will clearly—since it is a single thing—be the midpoint between two extremes, rather than being a middle alongside something else. For it

...it would be the fourth, four things being proportional. But if three things are proportional of which the soul is the middle, it is not simply the middle of essence <note>unchanging reality</note> and generation <note>the world of change and becoming</note>. Rather, it is the middle of an essence which is entirely uncreated <note>original: "unbegotten"</note>, and of an essence that becomes divisible <note>original: "partible"</note> when associated with physical bodies. The soul itself is an essence that is both indivisible and becomes divisible—yet not because of bodies. Instead, it becomes divisible by its own nature and does not need bodies at all in order to be what it is. To consist of both of these is suited to the soul, not only (as some say) because it exists as a middle point between both, but because it is both: it is indivisible as an image <note>original: "iconically"</note> of the higher, but divisible as a model <note>original: "paradigmatically"</note> for the lower. For it possesses the rational principles of <margin>></margin> both. Therefore, all things exist within the soul in a coordinated way. Since, however, the Divine Intellect is all things, and the nature perceived by the senses is all things, Plato adds the phrase, "*in the middle*." By this, he shows how all things are to be understood within the soul: specifically, in a middle way, being neither the primary causes nor the very last forms of existence.

Again, in another way, the essence of the soul consists of both because it is produced by the total creative <note>original: "demiurgic"</note> intellect, in which the indivisible and the divisible exist as models and as causes. Since, however, the [world's] intellect also proceeds from the whole of this Intellect, the words "*in the middle*" reveal the unique character of the soul's reality <term>hypostasis</term>. And how is it possible that the words "*he mingled*" should not be suited to the soul's essence? This is true not only because its indivisible and divisible aspects exist in union—similar to how mixed things permeate each other—but also because the unique character of life accords with the soul. The Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note>¹ constitutes the soul in conjunction with the life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note> Goddess, and he mixes its various kinds in the Mixing Bowl <term>Crater</term> <note>original: "Crater"; the symbolic vessel in the Timaeus where the soul's ingredients are combined.</note>. Furthermore, the word *middle* shows² that the soul constitutes itself; it does not simply receive the mixture of its types from the Creator's energy as if it were merely a passive experience <note>original: "passion"</note>.³ The words "*a form of essence*" likewise clearly indicate to us how effects are contained within their causes. For if "essence" in the Creator is a general category <note>original: "genus"</note>, but in the soul it is a specific "form" or species, then the former contains the latter. But the Creator's essence may be called a genus because it is distinct from the form of the soul and generates it. By being distinct, it differs from the categories that exist alongside a species; but by generating this form, it transcends things that are of a different kind. For those things do not produce other categories. These genera and species, therefore, must be understood in another way. For they are productive, full of power, contain individual forms, and have a transcendent nature. Therefore, the "genus" is the essence...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s analysis of the soul's "middle" nature. He explains that the soul sits between the purely indivisible Intellect and the infinitely divisible physical world, possessing qualities of both without being a physical mixture of them.</meta>

<page-num>43</page-num>
<header>BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

...in the <term>Demiurgus</term> <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine Craftsman or Creator of the universe</note>; but the form or species of this is the indivisible essence. Likewise, the essence which is the medium between the indivisible essence and that which is divisible in relation to bodies is the second form. But the third is that which is divisible in relation to body. And the last is the nature that takes a bodily form. In these forms, there is a sequence of "prior" and "posterior" (before and after), because the basic types <note>original: "genera"</note> produce and give existence to the first, middle, and last forms. 

The entire intellectual essence is indeed indivisible as a single unit. In contrast, that which is divisible in relation to bodies is multiplied because it is distributed among them. The medium between these is both "one" and "not one." For the Intellect has one essence, one sameness, and one difference, insofar as it is intellect. But the parts that compose the whole soul are many and are fitted to one another. In each of these parts, there are also essence, sameness, and difference; there are as many essences, samenesses, and differences as there are parts. These parts are indeed countable, yet at the same time, they are many, and each of them is "one" and "not one." Pure Intellect, however, remains a single essence, a single sameness, and a single difference. 

The nature which is divisible in relation to bodies has one of these qualities in one place and another in another, being divided along with the objects it inhabits—just as a body itself is not merely divisible into many parts, but into infinite parts. But though the soul is divided into the essence of many things, it also possesses unity, having a <term>hypostasis</term> <note>a distinct, underlying reality or substantial existence</note> separate from bodies. 

So, once again, there are two intermediate levels here: one between truly existing essence <note>eternal reality</note> and what is truly "becoming" <note>original: "generation"; the changing physical world</note>, and another between the indivisibility of the former and the infinite divisibility of the latter. These levels are the soul and the essence which is divisible in relation to bodies (which is not the same as the physical world of "becoming" itself). The soul is indivisible to a greater degree because it turns back toward itself; however, the essence which is divisible in relation to bodies is more divisible because it belongs to something else and does not exist by its own power. Therefore, Plato says that the soul consists of both this [divisible essence] and the indivisible essence. He says this because the soul is a medium between things entirely free from bodies and things submerged in bodies, and between things that exist by their own power and those that belong to others. Thus, the soul both exists by its own power and relates to others.

<margin>||</margin>
We must certainly not say that it is a medium in the sense of having one part that is incorporeal and another that is corporeal, as Eratosthenes <note>a Greek polymath and head of the Library of Alexandria</note> believed. Nor should we follow Severus in ascribing "geometrical interval" <note>physical extension or dimensions</note> to the soul's essence. For a mixture can never be created between that which lacks dimensions and that which possesses <margin>||</margin> dimensions, or between the indivisible and a physical body. Just as a point and a line cannot be mixed, if there can be no mixture of the indivisible and a line, [then the soul cannot be a physical mixture].

▪ "Not" <note>original: "Ου"</note> is omitted in the original Greek.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s analysis of the soul as a "medium" essence. He argues that the soul maintains its unity even while being divided into various powers, and he critiques the views of earlier philosophers who defined the soul through mathematical or physical models.</meta>

<page-num>44</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.</header>

...much less can there be a mixture of it with another dimension [namely, the dimension of depth]. For that which is divisible in three ways is further removed from the indivisible than that which is divisible in only one way. We say, however, that the intellectual essence always remains one, that the divisible consists of many essences, and that the <term>psychical</term> <note>original: "psychical"; relating to the soul (psyche)</note> is both one and not one. It preserves the "one" while being multiplied, and maintains a multitude while being united. For the <term>Demiurgus</term> <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine Craftsman or Creator of the universe</note> did not divide it so as to exhaust the whole in the division, but preserved its unity within its multiplication, and its wholeness within its division. 

This is not surprising, since even in bodies—which are all divisible—there is, as the <term>Elean guest</term> <note>A character in Plato's dialogues *The Sophist* and *Statesman*, often identified as a follower of Parmenides</note> says, a certain "one" that connects the parts. Aristotle also asserts that in divisible natures there is something indivisible; so the soul will remain a whole and a unity all the more when it is multiplied and divided. Hence, as <term>Timaeus</term> says, it is also indivisible. But if its unity was not preserved, it would be purely divisible. This would be the case, for example, if you were to say that the <term>dianoetic</term> <note>the soul's power of discursive reasoning</note> and <term>doxastic</term> <note>the soul's power of forming opinions or beliefs</note> powers of the soul are two separate essences. Yet, at the same time, the whole soul is one single thing that acts both through reasoning and through opinion because it centers upon itself. We, therefore, driven by what Plato himself says, interpret the indivisible and the divisible essence in this way.

However, among those who came before us, some made the essence of the soul mathematical, seeing it as a medium between natural and supernatural things. Some of these, asserting that the soul is a number, claim it consists of the <term>Monad</term> <note>the "One," representing unity and the indivisible</note> as the indivisible part, and the <term>indefinite duad</term> <note>the "Two," representing multiplicity and the divisible</note> as the divisible part. Others, considering it a geometric <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: "hypostasis"; a fundamental reality or underlying substance</note>, assert that it consists of a point and an interval—the former being indivisible, the latter divisible. Aristander, Numenius, and their followers, along with many other interpreters, hold the first opinion, while Severus holds the second. 

Others again, such as Plutarch and Atticus, looking at the physical essence, say that the irrational part (which comes first in the order of physical theory) is the divisible essence, while the divine part of the soul is the indivisible. They make the rational essence consist of both: the divine part acts as that which organizes, and the irrational part acts as the subject. They also say that the soul is <term>unbegotten</term> <note>eternal or uncreated</note> in its essence, but "generated" or created in its form. 

Others, however, like Plotinus, who consider Plato's words in a more philosophical manner, say that the soul is a medium between intellect and sense; the former being indivisible, but the latter being divisible among bodies. Yet others, going higher and placing two levels of Intellect above the soul—one possessing the ideas of "wholes" and the other the ideas of partial natures—say that the soul is the medium between these as...
