deriving its existence from both. For so says Theodorus of Asine, who found this opinion in Porphyry as being derived from the Persians. Antoninus, the disciple of Ammonius, relates these things. To the first of these opinions, however, it must be said that since Plato does not define the soul as a "number," it is absurd to investigate the numerical principles of which the soul consists. To the second, we must say that Plato describes the soul as incorporeal when compared to any physical body, and that it has a self-moving essence; however, nothing that possesses <term>interval</term> <note>original: "interval"; *diastema*, referring here to spatial extension or physical dimensions</note> is a thing of this kind. To the third, it must be said that Plato does not believe the irrational part is older than the rational part. For the Divine, as he says, did not think it right that the older nature should be governed by the younger. To the fourth, we respond that this discussion does not concern the soul's knowledge, but the soul's essence. And therefore, it is not proper to say that the soul is merely a medium between the two <term>gnostic</term> <note>original: "gnostic"; relating to the power of knowing or cognition</note> powers: the intellectual and the sensitive. And to the fifth, we say that every intellect is unbegotten and separate from bodies. But Plato calls the soul a "generated" essence that is <term>partible</term> <note>original: "partible"; capable of being divided or partitioned</note>, giving it a division opposite to the essence that exists with invariable sameness, and to that which is divisible among bodies, thereby separating it from the essence which is external to bodies and always exists. As these details have been sufficiently discussed, let us consider what follows:

> “And again in the same manner, with respect to the nature of **Same** and the nature of **Different**, he established the soul in the middle between the indivisibility of these and the nature which is divisible among bodies.”

Essence, as we have said, holds the first rank among the "genera" of being, because it is, as it were, the **Vesta of being** <note>original: "Vesta of being"; Proclus likens Essence to Vesta (Hestia), the goddess of the hearth, who remains stationary at the center of the divine home.</note>. **Sameness**, therefore, holds the second rank, and **Difference** the third. Some consider Difference to have a higher dignity than Sameness. But Plato, in what he said previously, has clearly shown that the "similar" is better than the "dissimilar"; and now, by placing Sameness immediately after Essence, he directly gives it preference over Difference. And just as we said that the "middle essence" of the soul is inferior to the pure intellectual essence but transcends that which is divisible among bodies, we also say that the **Sameness** of the soul is inferior to the indivisible Sameness, but is more unified than physical Sameness. The same logic applies to **Difference**. Hence, in the essence of the pure Intellect, Sameness—being a unity—collects itself (as well as essential Difference) into the Essence which is there, and which is one. Just as Difference, being one, distinguishes itself and separates Essence and Sameness from each other. But in the soul, Sameness collects the differences into a unity...

...which are many in the many parts, and difference separates the various forms of sameness. I know, therefore, that some Platonists arrange sameness within <term>indivisible</term> <note>original: "impartible"</note> natures, but place difference within <term>divisible</term> <note>original: "partible"</note> natures, and thus they make the soul consist of both as a medium between sameness and difference. These thinkers, however, do not <note>The Greek word *Ouk* (not) is omitted in the original text.</note> attend to what Plato says here: that the soul is a medium between the indivisibility of sameness and difference, and the divisibility of that nature which is distributed among bodies.

It is likewise necessary to know that these are the <term>categories</term> <note>original: "genera"</note> of being, and that it is necessary for these to exist everywhere appropriately: in indivisible and divisible natures, in the media between them, and again in intellectual essences, in souls, in physical natures, and in bodily masses. For I would be ashamed to divide the categories as they do, placing one here and another there. For if they had said that sameness predominates in intelligible and indivisible natures, while difference predominates in sensible and divisible natures, they would have spoken correctly. But if they assert that indivisible things are entirely separate from difference, they will not be able to assign sameness to them either. For the *One* differs from the *Same*. <note>For if indivisible things have no difference, they will be identical to each other and will become the *One*. In the *One*, there is no difference. Thus, the *One* would not differ from the *Same*.</note> And if they say that divisible natures are separate from sameness, they undermine their very essence.

Following the reality of the matter, therefore, we must admit that the category of sameness exists with a <term>creative</term> <note>original: "demiurgic"</note> character, but its species are the indivisible, the divisible, and the medium between both. And again, the category of difference is also creative, but its species are the indivisible, the divisible, and that which is intermediate. Accepting this, we must assign these intermediate states to the soul and intertwine them with the middle form of essence in order to establish the soul’s existence. For in this way, I believe we will be able to align Plato's words with reality. For he says that just as in "essence," so too in the nature of "same" and the nature of "different," the <term>Creator</term> <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> mingled a third thing from both, and in the same manner. And just as there, that which was mingled from both was a specific kind or form of essence, so here, the medium between "same" and "different" is a form. For it is possible to be a medium not just as a form, but as a whole composed of extremes—such as an animal that consists of soul and body. So that you do not mistakenly think this is the case, he adds the phrase, "*and after the same manner*"; this indicates that here too, what consists of both is a form and not merely a composite whole.

> "And taking them as three beings, he mingled all of them into one idea."

He explains that the Soul's essence is a unique "form" created by the Demiurge through the blending of these principles.</summary>

That the three creative <term>genera</term> <note>original: "demiurgic genera"; these are the fundamental categories or classes of being used by the Creator.</note> are the causes of <term>existence</term> <note>original: "hypostasis"; a technical term for the underlying reality or substance of a thing.</note> for secondary and tertiary forms, I think Plato sufficiently demonstrates by saying, "*and taking them as three things*." For where do these things exist? Evidently in the **Demiurge** <note>The Divine Craftsman of the universe in Platonic philosophy.</note>. For he contains that which he takes, yet he receives them from superior causes. 

Since **Sameness**—which has a greater share of the form of "Bound"—consists of Bound and Infinity, and **Difference**—which has more of the form of "Infinity"—also consists of these, just as **Essence** proceeds similarly from both, it is evident that we must place the sameness and difference of <term>indivisible</term> <note>original: "impartible"</note> natures in Bound [rather than in Infinity]. However, we must place those of the "media" (the middle ground) equally in both, and those of <term>divisible</term> <note>original: "partible"</note> natures rather in the Infinite than in Bound. This is just as the first Difference possesses the Infinite while only slightly declining from Bound, and the first Sameness possesses Bound while only slightly declining from the Infinite. <gloss>1. In the original Greek text, there is an omission here of the phrase "of the infinite" <note>original: "του απειρου" / tou apeirou</note>.</gloss> 

Hence, Plato says that the Demiurge received them as three, being separated from each other. And since the forms that are in him <gloss>2. For the Greek phrase "in her" <note>original: "εν ταυτη" / en tautē</note> in this place, it is necessary to read "in him" <note>original: "εν αυτω" / en autō</note>, referring to the Demiurge.</gloss> hasten toward the creation of other things, he also constitutes other things from these. 

Therefore, if we understand "beings" as things that existed prior to the generation of the middle ground, we must say that these exist in him as causes; for these were in him before the things he generated. But if by "beings" we understand the "media" (the intermediaries), we must understand them as things already formed. For they are now "beings" because they were produced by him prior to the mixture, each distinct from the other; and Essence, Sameness, and Difference were now each generated by themselves. 

May not the words, however, be interpreted more simply? Namely, that the Demiurge was "*taking them being three*," for he created so many things from the three once the extremes were constituted by him according to the pre-existent causes he contains. He produced these categories according to his creative being, but he added "Idea" to all three according to his own internal unity and the divinity within him, which is the cause of unifying many things. You can see that each of the three was a "form," and that which was produced from the mixture of the three was one "Idea." Consequently, it is necessary to say that ***the soul is a form of forms***; and, in short, to conceive of nothing in it as composite or physical.

The triad, therefore, is suited to the very essence of the soul, since it was previously shown that the soul is **triadic** (three-fold). For we divided the whole of it into **Essence**, **Power**, and **Energy**. We further divided Essence into <term>existence</term> <note>original: "hyparxis"; the fundamental "peak" or essential reality of a being.</note>, **Harmony**, and **Form**; and existence into what is properly called **Essence**, **Same**, and **Different**. Nor should we wonder if we make a "part" of essence to be "essence" itself. For the one category of being is called Essence, but that which is generated from all the elements—

elements of being, is called essence. If, however, we should again inquire what it is that makes this one idea not just any random soul, but the <term>mundane soul</term> <note>The "World Soul" or the soul of the universe.</note> specifically, while elsewhere it makes a different soul; we reply that it is the *total* nature of the <term>genera</term> <note>The fundamental categories of being: Essence, Sameness, and Difference.</note> that are used. *For the world soul is a medium, not of random extremes, but of a total intellect and a total bodily nature, according to which the world is a living being; just as it is endowed with intellect according to its indivisible nature, and is animated according to its middle nature.* The dominance of essence also causes it to be the world soul; for this makes it divine. In the same way, the prevalence of Sameness alone produces a <term>daemoniacal</term> <note>original: "dæmoniacal"; referring to "daemons," which in Neoplatonism are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note> soul, and the prevalence of Difference alone produces a <term>partial soul</term> <note>A soul belonging to an individual, like a human or animal, rather than the whole universe.</note>. Therefore, a different relationship to the extremes produces a difference in the intermediate souls. And the mixture of these media, defined according to which element prevails, evidently changes the whole nature of the soul.

->“Forcefully harmonizing the nature of Difference, which was difficult<-
->to mingle, with the nature of Sameness.”<-

How is the nature of Difference difficult to be mingled? It is because it has a separating and dividing power, and is the cause of progression and multiplication. Every divine being begins its <term>activity</term> <note>original: "energy"; here meaning the actualization or outward working of a thing's power.</note> from itself. Hence, the nature of Difference also separates itself from other things and from itself, for it generates multitude within itself. On this account, it is said in the *Sophist* <note>Plato’s dialogue, the *Sophista*.</note> that it makes both other things and itself to be "non-beings" by separating them from other beings. 

Hence, it is difficult to be mingled, possessing this difficulty not by accident or any error, but by having an essence that is the cause of "otherness"—of the unconfused <term>reality</term> <note>original: "hypostasis"; the underlying substance or essential nature of a thing.</note> of forms, and of unmingled simplicity. Possessing such a power as this, it is a certain contrary both to Sameness and to Essence.<sup>1</sup> It is indeed contrary to Sameness because Sameness is the cause of union, communion, and connection, while Difference is the cause of separation, of an inability to be mingled, and of otherness. But it is also a certain contrary to Essence because Essence is *being*, but Difference is *non-being*, as is demonstrated in the *Sophist*. For the nature of Difference, being divided into minute parts, becomes the principle of non-being. 

So that we may not be confused by seeing a mixture of these categories all at once, Plato first mingles Sameness with Difference,<sup>2</sup> and says that the divinity harmonized the nature of Difference to that of Sameness, joining it harmoniously with "middle" Sameness. Afterwards, he—

He mingled both of these with essence. For Plato, having said that divinity adapted the nature of difference to that of sameness, adds, “*that he mingled them with essence, and made one thing from the three.*” Because essence connects the two <term>genera</term> <note>The fundamental categories or "kinds" of being.</note> of sameness and difference, and since these two are coordinated with each other, it is necessary that they should first be mingled with each other, and secondly, *that both should be mingled with essence.* This is the order of the mixture. 

The force employed in this mixture is not accidental, nor is it a violent or unnatural force; rather, it indicates a transcendence and abundance of power, for such is <term>demiurgic power</term> <note>The creative power of the Demiurge, the divine craftsman of the universe.</note>. This power is able to unite difference, to divide sameness, and to produce one harmony from both.

> “But having mingled these two with essence, and made one thing from the three, he again divided this whole into *appropriate parts.*”

Just as the equal and the unequal are joined with quantity;¹ and as all quantity is either equal or unequal—or rather, is equal and at the same time unequal, for every quantity participates in both at once; and as the similar and the dissimilar are joined with quality, and every quality is both similar and dissimilar; so also, sameness and difference coexist with essence. All essence participates in sameness and difference. These qualities are essential to things—that is, they belong to their very existence—rather than being mere matters of quantity or quality. 

Therefore, they are "essential," acting as the mediators between the divine genera and the specific traits found in quantities and qualities. Sameness is derived from <term>bound</term> <note>The principle of limit, order, and definition.</note>, while difference is derived from <term>infinity</term> <note>The principle of the unlimited, variety, and change.</note>. In the same way, similarity and equality are derived from sameness, while dissimilarity and inequality are derived from difference. 

For this reason, Plato, in his dialogue the *Philebus*, derives bound and infinity from [the highest] God, for they are divine genera. But in the *Sophist*, he calls sameness and difference the genera² of being. The former (bound and infinity) exist in relation to the *One* <note>The ultimate, absolute principle of reality in Neoplatonism.</note>, but the latter (sameness and difference) exist in relation to essence. 

Again, you see how much more venerable Plato is than all other <term>physiologists</term> <note>Early natural philosophers who studied the physical world.</note>, and even than Aristotle himself. Those thinkers make their first principles out of "contraries" (opposites), but they introduce opposites that are merely organic, material, and divisible. Even the most respected of them refer to opposites as "excess and defect" <note>Too much or too little.</note>, which wrongly assumes a lack of measure at the very source of all things. Measure is more divine than the lack of measure. But Plato refers opposites to—

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, specifically discussing how the Demiurge uses the principles of Sameness and Difference to form the World Soul’s essence and harmony.</meta>

sameness and difference, through which he understands all the opposites in the soul, in nature, and in the body. He places these within the Demiurge <note>The divine craftsman or creator of the universe.</note> so that he may grant them creative, world-making <note>original: "cosmurgic"; powers effective in the creation of the world.</note>, immaterial, and transcendent powers. Having placed them there, he forms the soul from them, producing from these that which serves as its subject and its very being—being as such, rather than being with a specific quality—so that it may imitate the primary, original Being. 

For he later assigns harmony, form, powers, and energies to the soul, thus completing the discussion of it. We are able to examine its status and its rank in the world (which is of a ruling nature) if we perceive how it contains worldly essences through all the fundamental categories <note>original: "genera"</note> within it; how it brings the whole world into harmony through its own internal harmony; how it encompasses all worldly forms and figures through its own shape <margin><unclear>this is now accomplished</unclear></margin>; how it is able to perfect all physical, rational, or artificial powers through the powers within it; and how it stirs worldly productions through its own proper energies.

Why, then, did Plato not say that the soul is a middle point between intellect and the senses? Because he says that intellect and sense are specific cognitive powers <note>original: "gnostic powers"</note>. His intention, however, was to describe the middle nature of the soul in terms of its essence <note>Its fundamental nature or being.</note>, and not merely its powers. 

Furthermore, why did he not say that the soul is a middle point between the ideal "Form" and things that are shaped by those forms? Because his purpose here was not to teach us the quality of the soul's form, but rather what its essence is. It is not the same thing to speak of a thing's essence as it is to speak of its form. Form shows an essence of a certain quality. 

Why, then, did he not place the soul as a middle point between "intelligible numbers" <note>Numbers as abstract, divine concepts in the mind of the Demiurge.</note> and "sensible numbers" <note>Numbers as they appear in the physical, countable world.</note>? Because in the following part of the discussion, he assigns a harmony to the soul. According to this harmony, the soul ranks as a middle point between separate numbers (and separate harmony) and the sensible numbers (and the harmony that cannot be separated from physical objects). <margin>||</margin> 

According to Plato’s view, the soul is neither "harmony itself" nor the harmony found within things that have been harmonized. "Harmony itself" is uniform, separate, and exists apart from all harmonized things, regardless of what they are; it is that alone which is called harmony itself. But the harmony found within things that are harmonized belongs to other objects and is naturally moved by external forces. The soul’s harmony is the middle point between these two. For the soul is that which is *first* harmonized. Because of this, it imparts harmony to other things. Anything that is able to give something to another thing is either the Form itself [which is shared] or is the first thing to participate in that Form. This harmony of the soul, therefore, is lower than intelligible harmony and the intelligible...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, focusing on the metaphysical composition of the soul and its place between the divine and the physical world through the lenses of number and harmony.</meta>

<page-num>51</page-num>

numbers; but because it goes beyond harmony perceived by the senses, it likewise goes beyond numbers perceived by the senses. If it is necessary to speak briefly about each of these, each is fourfold. For regarding number: the first is divine, the second is essential <note>Relating to the very essence or being of a thing.</note>, the third belongs to the soul <note>original: "psychical"</note>, and the last is physical. The first takes the form of oneness; the second is immovable; the third moves itself; and the fourth is moved by something else <note>original: "alter-motive"</note>. 

Regarding harmony, there is also a fourfold division: the first exists in the Gods, the second in truly existing beings, the third in souls, and the last in those things in nature which are harmonized by external forces. Therefore, if Plato had intended here to speak concerning the harmony of the soul, he would have said that it is a middle ground between indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> and divisible <note>original: "partible"</note> harmony. But since the current discussion concerns the very essence of the soul, he says it is a middle ground between "sameness" and "difference" <note>Two of Plato's "Greatest Kinds" or fundamental categories used to describe how things can be both self-consistent and distinct from others.</note>.

Here, it is also necessary to observe that in what is said now, Plato performs a sort of "turning back" <note>A Neoplatonic concept where an effect returns to contemplate its cause.</note> of the soul’s progression toward its original principles. There are two ways these mixtures are formed: 
1. The first is created by mixing the extremes (as we see in the mixture of essence, sameness, and difference). 
2. The second is created by gathering these components back into a single whole. 

In the first mixture, he began with essence and ended with the latter components; but in the second mixture, he did the opposite. He first harmonized the latter components with sameness, then harmonized both with essence, and finally ended with essence—the point from which he originally began. Everywhere, however, the "whole" is subordinate to the two principles <note>The principles of "Bound" and "Infinity."</note>. 

When he produces the soul from indivisible and divisible parts, he treats the indivisible as being like "bound" <note>The principle of limit, order, and definition.</note> and the divisible as being like "infinity" <note>The principle of multitude, change, and lack of limit.</note>. This is because infinity is the cause of many things (multitude), while bound is the cause of unity. When he harmonizes "difference" with "sameness," he treats difference as part of the category of infinity, and sameness as part of the category of bound. Likewise, when he mixes these two with essence, he treats essence as having the form of oneness, while sameness and difference are treated as a pair <note>original: "dyadic"</note> opposed to each other. 

He does not stop gathering this multitude together until he proves the whole to be one. For this "One" is even more excellent than essence itself and the dual principles of bound and infinity. Since this mixture is twofold—one part forming the elements themselves and the other forming the thing made from those elements—the philosopher Porphyry <note>An early Neoplatonist and student of Plotinus.</note> rightly asks whether the Creator <term>Demiurgus</term> made both of these in the "Mixing Bowl" <term>Crater</term> <note>Plato uses the metaphor of a mixing bowl (Crater) to describe where the Creator blends the ingredients of the soul. Proclus identifies this bowl with the goddess Juno/Hera.</note>, or if he made one outside of it and the other within it.

---

<note>¹ Instead of the original Greek phrase "everywhere the one of the principles holds the two," it is necessary, based on the translation by Leonicus Thomaeus, to read "everywhere the whole is subordinate to the two principles."</note>

<summary>Proclus explains the four levels of number and harmony—divine, essential, soul-based, and physical—and details how the Demiurge blends the soul's essence from the principles of Sameness, Difference, Bound, and Infinity.</summary>

<page-num>54</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.</header>

<margin>The nature of the soul's intellect</margin>
Regarding the universe, since it is not right to attribute the failings <note>original: "deteriorations"; the text suggests these are the shortcomings of individual, limited souls rather than the divine World Soul.</note> of individual souls to those that are divine, Plato adds that divinity divided the soul into appropriate parts. In this context, that which divides does so according to an intellectual cause, and that which is divided is divided in its very essence. This mode of division, therefore, is suited both to the divider and the thing being divided; it is beneficial and perfects the essence of the soul, introducing it to intellectual variety <note>original: "poikilia", referring to the complex diversity of the intelligible world</note> and making it all-perfect by inserting within it all the rational principles <note>original: "reasons"</note> of all beings.

If we assert these things correctly, it is not proper to separate the soul from its unity during its division, nor to assume its wholeness is "used up" <note>original: "consumed"</note> to create its parts—even though the words of Timaeus seem to suggest this when he says the mixture was consumed into these parts. We must not imagine that this was like dividing a physical object according to a ruler. All such modes of division are corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note> and are in no way suited to immaterial essences. Because everything created by the Demiurge <note>The 'Craftsman' or divine creator figure in Plato's Timaeus</note> must necessarily remain the same—since he always produces in the same manner, being immovable and eternal in his actions—it is necessary that the "whole" always remains a "whole." The creation of the parts must happen while the wholeness remains intact; the whole is not destroyed by being divided into parts. 

Therefore, we must conceive that the essence of the soul is simultaneously one and many; the whole remains while being distributed into parts, possessing continuity while being divided. We must not imagine that its continuity involves physical distance <note>original: "interval"</note>, for it is continuous and without physical size, much like the continuity of time. Nor should we think its division is like that of discrete units <note>original: "monadic numbers"</note>, for that would be a type of quantity that does not allow for continuity. Instead, we must combine these concepts as is appropriate for incorporeal <note>non-physical</note> natures, and we must view the soul as a "whole" existing in conjunction with its "parts." Plato also demonstrates that it is not proper to abandon unity during this division through the following words:

> "At the same time mingling each part from 'Same', 'Different', and 'Essence'.
> But he began to divide as follows."

If the basic kinds <note>original: "genera"</note> that constitute the soul are present in all its parts, then the whole—

$^3$ Namely, a thing of this kind is discrete quantity <note>quantity made of separate units rather than a continuous flow</note>.

<page-num>55</page-num>
<header>BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>

Because the soul consists of parts that share its own nature, it will not be separated from its continuity and unity. If physical bodies that are similar to one another stick together without any intermediate substance, how much more must the parts of an incorporeal <note>non-physical or spiritual</note> nature be united? In this case, the whole is governed by unity; the parts are not blurred together by the structure of the whole, nor is the wholeness destroyed by the separation of the parts. 

You may also conclude from these things that every part of the soul is both indivisible and divisible. If every part of it participates in all the "middle categories" <note>original: "middle genera"; in Neoplatonism, these are the primary categories of Being, Sameness, and Difference that bridge the gap between the One and the physical world</note>, then nothing in it can be found that does not consist of these three. The ancient philosophers, observing this, concluded that the soul is entirely being, life, and intellect. They believed that whichever of these three you focus on, you can infer that it contains the other two as well. Since everything in the soul moves through every other part, the whole is a single unit; its unity is perfectly complete, and every part reflects the whole. 

However, if each of the soul's many parts is considered a certain <term>essence</term> <note>the fundamental reality or "whatness" of a thing</note>, then the soul's essence is as multifaceted as its parts. Similarly, regarding "sameness" and "difference": in the divine Intellect <note>original: "intellect"; the higher realm of pure, eternal thought</note>, these are one, and for this reason, the Intellect is indivisible. In the Intellect, one thing is not a part distinct from another. But in the soul, both of these are divided according to a fundamental mathematical structure <note>original: "essential number"</note>. The parts of the soul are fitted to each other, making it a single entity formed from many parts.

Furthermore, we should consider that in the creation of the elements, the Demiurge <note>The 'Craftsman' or divine creator figure in Plato's Timaeus</note> began with essence, as we have noted. But when he composed the whole soul, he began with *difference*. He adapted the nature of *difference*—which is naturally difficult to mix with *sameness*—and blended both with *essence*. Yet, when he divided the whole into harmonic ratios <note>The mathematical proportions used to create musical or cosmic harmony</note>, he began with *sameness*. For Plato says¹ that the Demiurge divided each part that had been blended from sameness, difference, and essence. 

Starting with essence is entirely² suited to the generation of simple natures, since essence is simpler than other things. However, when composing a complex whole, it is appropriate to start with difference, because the creation of a whole from parts begins with the things that are subordinate to that whole. Finally, starting with sameness is suited to the <term>hypostasis</term> <note>the underlying existence or essential substance</note> of harmony. The Demiurge intended for harmony to result in the sameness and communion of those things that had been divided. In short, he wanted harmony to produce unity among the parts it organized.

These particulars, however, having been discussed by us as far as we are able,

² Instead of "of all" <note>original Greek: *pantōn*</note> here, read "entirely" <note>original Greek: *pantōs*</note>.

He describes how the Demiurge uses these principles—specifically starting with "difference" for composition and "sameness" for harmony—to create a balanced cosmic soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the mathematical and harmonic composition of the soul in Plato's Timaeus. Having discussed the soul's division into parts, Proclus now moves to the specific musical and numerical ratios that define its structure.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.

Next, it is necessary to establish the facts we should already know concerning numbers and the harmonic ratios of the soul, so that we do not attempt to interpret what follows in vain. Therefore, we must first set out the things usually mentioned in harmonic discussions—namely, what sound, interval, and system are—and note that the Pythagoreans did not derive the harmonies <note>original: "symphonies"</note> from just any source, but from specific numbers: specifically, from multiples and <term>super-particulars</term> <note>a ratio where the larger number contains the smaller once, plus one part of it, such as 3:2 or 4:3</note>. 

For they said that the <term>diatessaron</term> <note>a perfect fourth</note> is in a <term>sesquitertian</term> ratio <note>4:3</note>; the <term>diapente</term> <note>a perfect fifth</note> is in a <term>sesquialter</term> ratio <note>3:2</note>; and the <term>diapason</term> <note>an octave</note> is in a duple ratio <note>2:1</note>. Again, they said that the octave and the fifth combined is in a triple ratio <note>3:1</note>, while the <term>disdiapason</term> <note>a double octave</note> is in a quadruple ratio <note>4:1</note>. 

The octave and the fourth combined did not appear harmonious to them because it consists of a <term>multiple super-partient</term> ratio <note>a ratio where the larger number contains the smaller several times plus several parts of it</note>—specifically, the ratio of 8 to 3. In this case, 6 acts as a middle point between the two; it produces a duple ratio with the smaller number, but a <term>sub-sesquitertian</term> ratio <note>3:4</note> with the larger. 

These things, therefore, must be established beforehand, as well as the following:
*   The <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>9:8</note> is the ratio of a whole tone.
*   The sesquitertian ratio <note>4:3</note> consists of two tones and a <term>leimma</term> <note>original: "leimma," meaning "remainder"; a small interval in Pythagorean tuning slightly less than a semitone</note>.
*   The sesquialter ratio <note>3:2</note> consists of three tones and a leimma.¹ 

We shall later learn the exact ratio of the leimma. Furthermore, the Pythagoreans said there are three types <note>original: "genera"</note> of harmonies: the **diatonic**, the **enharmonic**, and the **chromatic**. 
*   The **diatonic** consists of a semitone (though what I call a semitone here is not strictly one, but a leimma), followed by a tone and another tone. 
*   The **enharmonic** consists of a <term>diesis</term> <note>a very small interval, roughly a quarter-tone</note>, another diesis, and a <term>ditone</term> <note>a major third or two whole tones</note>. 
*   The **chromatic** consists of a semitone, another semitone, and a <term>tri-semitone</term> <note>a minor third</note>. 

A diesis is effectively the fourth part of a tone, though not exactly a fourth, just as a leimma is not accurately a semitone. We shall demonstrate these things in the following sections.

Since there are three types, each being a specific way of dividing the <term>tetrachord</term> <note>a scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth</note>, Plato appears to have used the **diatonic** type alone. He chooses to divide the 4:3 ratios into 9:8 ratios and leimmas, rather than into enharmonic dieses—especially since some of the ancients called a semitone a "diesis." Plato also seems to have adopted this diatonic genus because it is more grand, simple, and noble than the other types, even though the enharmonic type appears better suited for formal education. And if I may offer my own prediction on this subject: the enharmonic genus presides over all life which is—

***

¹ After the word *leimmatos* <note>original: "λειμματος," meaning "of the remainder"</note> in the original Greek, it is necessary to add the words "but the sesquialter consists of three tones and a leimma," based on the translation by Thomæus. I refer the reader who wishes to thoroughly understand these points to my book, *Theoretic Arithmetic*.

# BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

...the divisible nature related to bodies,¹ just as the <term>diatonic</term> <note>a musical scale characterized by whole tones and semitones</note> presides over the rational life. Hence the <term>enharmonic</term> genus <note>a style of music using very small intervals, such as quarter-tones</note> is adapted to instruct and discipline the divisible life. But the <term>chromatic</term> genus <note>a scale using semitones</note> presides over the corporeal <note>bodily</note> idea itself. For this reason, it is considered effeminate and ignoble. 

The enharmonic genus, therefore, is deservedly used for education. This is why Socrates, in the *Republic*, thinks it appropriate to mention it specifically in what he says about harmony. Timæus, knowing this and having heard Socrates asserting these things on the previous day, establishes the essence of the soul through the diatonic genus, and not through the enharmonic; the latter, as we have said, is suited to teaching. For this reason, the ancients called the leaders (or teachers) of these disciplines <term>Harmonici</term> <note>original: "Harmonici"; those skilled in the science of music and harmony</note>. 

Aristoxenus, in the first book of his *Harmonic Elements*, says it happened that those who formerly employed themselves in music were truly called *Harmonici*. Because they were solely focused on harmony, they neglected every other pursuit. In this, Aristoxenus also asserts something surprising: that the ancients had no knowledge of the diatonic diagram. For he writes: "As proof of this, their diagram alone shows enharmonic systems, but no one ever saw a diatonic or chromatic diagram drawn by them." It is remarkable, however, that he should claim these things, since Plato presents a diagram according to the diatonic genus, as does Timæus himself. Perhaps, therefore, what Adrastus says is true; he mocks Aristoxenus as a man of coarse character,² but one who is eager to appear to be saying something new.

Plato, therefore, in the diatonic genus, makes a division of <term>tetrachords</term> <note>a series of four musical notes</note> and proceeds not only as far as the <term>diapason</term> <note>an octave</note>, but also as far as a quadruple octave and a <term>diapente</term> <note>a perfect fifth</note>, adding a whole tone as well. Or, according to Severus, Plato did not produce the tetrachords without a tone, but ended in a <term>leimma</term> <note>a "remainder" or minor semitone in Pythagorean tuning</note>, and not in a tone. 

If, however, someone should doubt how Plato extended the diagram to such a degree, let him pay attention to the words of Adrastus. For he says that Aristoxenus extended the range of his multiform diagram as far as the octave and a <term>diatessaron</term> <note>a perfect fourth</note> and the harmony of these, because he preferred the information of the ears to the judgment of the intellect. But more modern musicians extended the diagram as far as the fifteenth mode—that is, to three octaves and a tone. In doing so, they looked only to our practical use, thinking that those who compete in singing could not exceed this range, nor could their listeners judge clearly beyond...

² For "appearance" <note>original Greek: το εἶδος</note> here, it is necessary, based on the version by Thomæus, to read "character" <note>original Greek: το ἦθος</note>.

# PROCLUS ON THE TIMÆUS [BOOK III.]

...it. **Plato**, however, looking to nature, constructs the soul from all of these, so that it might proceed as far as solid numbers, as it ought to preside over bodies. For the progression as far as the quadruple <term>diapason</term> <note>an interval of four octaves</note> and <term>diapente</term> <note>the interval of a perfect fifth</note> necessarily follows the seven terms [or bounding numbers]. This is evident from the greatest term being twenty-seven. And so much for the answer to that doubt.

In short, there are three things into which the study of harmony may be divided. The first is the explanation of the seven parts. The second is the insertion of the two <term>media</term> <note>mathematical means or averages</note>. The third is the division of the <term>sesquitertian</term> <note>a ratio of 4:3</note> and <term>sesquialter</term> <note>a ratio of 3:2</note> ratios into <term>sesquioctaves</term> <note>a ratio of 9:8, representing a whole tone</note> and <term>lemmas</term> <note>original: "lemmas"; here meaning a limma, the mathematical remainder that forms a semitone</note>. 

Because of this, some, such as **Adrastus**, are accustomed to draw three triangles. In the smallest of these, they describe the seven parts, making the peak of the triangle one of the parts and distributing the other six around it. On one side, they describe the whole <term>duple</term> <note>double</note> order, and on the other, the whole <term>triple</term> order. Furthermore, in the second triangle, which is larger and contains the first, they increased the numbers and again inserted two media in a similar manner, arranging the double numbers separately from the triple numbers and placing one of the parts at the peak. 

In the third triangle, which encompasses both the others, they described the whole diagram in the same way. Others again, adopting a diagram in the form of the Greek letter **λ** <note>the "Lambda" diagram, commonly used to visualize the 1, 2, 4, 8 and 1, 3, 9, 27 series</note>, arrange the numbers successively, as if on the markings of a ruler, according to three centers—assuming the first, second, and third numbers, as we shall also do. This method is also adopted by **Porphyry** and **Severus**. 

These are the details that should be established beforehand, as well as the fact that Plato divides this topic into three parts. In the first part, he discusses the seven parts, containing three double and three triple intervals according to the <term>geometrical middle</term> <note>a progression where each term is multiplied by the same ratio</note>. In the second part, he discusses the insertion of the other two media—namely, the harmonic and arithmetic means—into each interval of the double and triple numbers. In the third part, he considers the division of the sesquitertian and sesquialter ratios into sesquioctaves and lemmas; the discussion of the parts of the soul extends as far as these.

It is necessary, however, to be well acquainted with what is said about the three media, to know their differences, and the methods through which they are discovered. The **arithmetical medium**, therefore, is that in which the middle term exceeds and is exceeded by an equal quantity <note>original: "ison" (Greek); this word was omitted in the source text but is restored here for clarity</note>, as may be seen in all numbers in a consecutive order, according to the definition of **Timæus** himself. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the mathematical structure of the soul as described by Proclus. # BOOK III. TIMÆUS OF PLATO

...the middle term is exceeded by the greater by the same fraction of the greater as the fraction of the less term by which it exceeds the less term—as seen in the numbers 6, 4, and 3. For here, 4 is surpassed by 6 by a difference of 2, which is the third part of 6; and 4 exceeds the smaller term, 3, by 1, which is the third part of 3. And the **geometrical medium** <note>Also known as the geometric mean.</note> is that in which the ratio of the greater term to the middle term is the same as the ratio of the middle term to the less term.

The methods for discovering these must now be explained by us. Let two terms be given between which we intend to find both an **harmonic** and an **arithmetical medium**; and let these terms have a <term>duple ratio</term> <note>A 2:1 ratio, such as 12 and 6.</note>, for instance 12 and 6. I take the difference <note>original: "excess"</note> of the greater number over the smaller, which is evidently 6. Dividing this into two equal parts, I add one half to the smaller number, making this the middle term. Hence, 9 is the arithmetical medium between 12 and 6. This is because the difference is three, both between the greater and the middle, and between the middle and the smallest term. 

Again, taking the difference of the outer numbers <note>original: "extremes"</note>, which is 6, I multiply this by the smaller term, and the result is 36. Dividing this by the sum of the outer numbers (which is 18), the result is 2, which is called the <term>breadth of the comparison</term>. <margin>The harmonic proportion may also be defined as that in which the difference between the greatest and middle term is to the difference between the middle and least term as the greatest term is to the least. Thus, in the numbers 6, 4, 3: as 6 minus 4 is to 4 minus 3, so 6 is to 3; namely, as 2 is to 1, so 6 is to 3.</margin> To the smaller term, I also add this 2, and I arrive at the harmonic middle, 8. For 8 is surpassed by the greater term 12 by the same fraction of 12 as the fraction of the smaller term 6 by which 8 exceeds 6. Specifically, 8 is surpassed by a third part of 12, and it exceeds 6 by a third part of 6.

Next, let there be a <term>triple interval</term> <note>A 3:1 ratio.</note>, such as 18 and 6 <note>original: "or" is omitted in the original Greek text.</note>. Adding these together, I get 24. Taking half of this, I find the arithmetical middle is 12. Again, taking the difference of 18 over 6 (which is 12), I multiply it by the smaller term, 6, and the result is 72. I divide this by 24 (the sum of the outer numbers), and 3, the "breadth of the comparison," is produced. Afterward, I add this to 6, and I have 9 for the harmonic medium, which exceeds and is exceeded by the same proportional part of the outer numbers. 

Similarly, if 1 and 2 were the outer numbers, by adding them together and taking half, I would have 1 and a half as the middle term of the arithmetical mean. But taking the difference of the greater term over one, and multiplying it by the smaller term (that is, 1 multiplied by 1), I get 1. Afterward, dividing <note>original: *paralabon* ("taking"); it is necessary to read *merizon* ("dividing") here.</note> this by 3 (the sum of the outer numbers), I shall...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's technical explanation of how to calculate mathematical means (arithmetic and harmonic) between the primary numbers of the soul's composition, building on the geometric ratios established by Plato in the Timaeus.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III. TIMÆUS OF PLATO]

...have the breadth <note>original: "breadth of the comparison," a technical term in Greek mathematics referring to the resulting value when one number is divided by another.</note> of the third part of 1; so that 3, when compared to 1, makes the third part of 1. Adding this 1/3 to 1, I shall have 4/3, which is the **harmonic mean** <note>original: "harmonic medium"</note> between 1 and 1/2, just as before. Hence, by employing these methods, we shall in an appropriate manner fill all the double and triple intervals with arithmetic and harmonic means. Timaeus has included these within the **geometric mean**, increasing them by inserting the other means.

In short, since Plato mentions the three means <note>original: "middles"</note> which are contained within the geometric mean, let the following theorem be added as a corollary to what has been said: If the analogy consists of four terms, and one of the intermediate numbers produces an **arithmetic mean**, the other will produce an **harmonic mean**, and vice versa. 

For example, let there be four terms, *a*, *b*, *c*, and *d*, such that the first, *a* <note>original footnote 1: *a* is omitted in this place in the original text.</note>, is to *b* as *c* is to *d*. Suppose that *b* is an arithmetic mean (so that *a*, *b*, and *d* are in arithmetic proportion). I claim that *c* is a harmonic mean. Because the product of *a* and *d* is equal to the product of *b* and *c*, and *b* is an arithmetic mean, the sum of (*c* multiplied by *a*) and (*c* multiplied by *d*) is double the product of *b* and *c* (as is the case in an arithmetic mean). This being the case, it follows that the sum of (*c* multiplied by *a*) and (*c* multiplied by *d*) is double the product of *a* and *d* <note>original footnote 2: As *a* is to *b* as *c* is to *d* by hypothesis, and therefore *ad = bc*. But *ca + cd = 2bc*; and because *bc = ad*, therefore *2bc = 2ad*.</note>. But this was the defining property of the harmonic mean: namely, that the product of the mean by the outer terms <note>original: "extremes"</note> is double the product of the outer terms. 

Again, let *c* be a harmonic mean; I claim that *b* is an arithmetic mean. Since the sum of (*c* times *a*) and (*c* times *d*) is double the product of *b* and *c*, the sum of *a* and *d* is double *b* <note>original footnote 3: Since *ca + cd = 2bc*, it follows—since *c* multiplies all three terms *ca*, *cd*, and *2bc*—that *a + d = 2b*.</note>. This constitutes an arithmetic mean, where the sum of the outer terms is double the middle term. 

Furthermore, of these four terms, let *b* be an arithmetic mean and *c* be a harmonic mean; I claim that as *a* is to *b*, so is *c* to *d*. Because the sum of (*c* times *a*) and (*c* times *d*) is double the product of *a* and *d* (due to the harmonic mean), but the sum of *a* and *d* is double *b* (due to the arithmetic mean), the product of *a* and *d* will therefore be equal to the product of *b* and *c*. Thus, *a* is to *b* as *c* is to *d* <note>original footnote 4: (*a + d*) × *c = 2ad*. But 2*b* × *c = 2ad*, and therefore *b* × *c = a* × *d*. Hence *a : b* as *c : d*. The truth of this may be seen in numbers by substituting 6, 12, 9, and 18 for *a, b, c, and d*.</note>. This was the specific characteristic of the geometric mean. Hence, those two means are contained within the geometric...

...middle, <note>original footnote 1: After the word "peculiar" [original: *idion*] in the original, it is necessary to supply from the version of Leonicus Thomæus the words: "the two means are therefore contained in the geometric mean."</note> and reciprocate with each other. Mathematical theory is neither to be entirely ignored [in this discussion] nor embraced on its own. The latter would fail to show us what Plato intended to represent through images, and the former would make the whole explanation useless. It is necessary to consider the essence of the subjects under discussion as if on a secure foundation. As we noted before, we will proceed in a middle way: first mathematically, in a manner suited to the subjects, and then we will explain the division shown in the text. 

The Pythagoreans <note>followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who believed the universe was structured by numbers and music</note> have a magnificent understanding of the division or section of the scale <note>original: "rule"</note> in this passage; specifically, that Plato reveals the essential causes and the reasons that generate mathematical theorems. Therefore, as I said, let us first mathematically exercise the reader's reasoning power by briefly explaining what many have asserted, while avoiding controversy and seeking the truth for its own sake. 

Our discussion will briefly cover these five points: multiple ratios; the means <note>original: "media"</note> that exist between them; the 4:3 <note>original: "sesquitertian"</note> and 3:2 <note>original: "sesquialter"</note> ratios which appear in the means; the 9:8 ratios <note>original: "sesquioctaves"</note> that fill these intervals; and the remainder <note>original: "leimma," the small interval or semitone left over in a scale</note>. It is necessary for the diagram to include all of these and be filled with all these ratios.

To proceed in order, we will take the ratios Plato first mentions, starting from the number one <note>original: "unity"</note>. # BOOK III. PROCLUS ON THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO

...but he alternately mixes them, as if proceeding in a straight line. If, however, Plato had stopped here, there would have been nothing further for us to discuss. But since he himself exhorts us to connect the double and triple intervals with harmonic and arithmetic means, and it is not possible to find these means between 1 and 2, some first number must be chosen which, being the smallest possible, may have both a half and a third part. Since every number can be doubled, this must therefore be investigated. 

Let us then assume 6, and its double 12; the former has the same ratio to the latter as 1 to 2. Between these (which are 1 and 2 multiplied by 6), by placing 8 and 9 as the means, we will find the mentioned middle points. For 8 exceeds and is exceeded by the same proportion of the extremes <note>The harmonic mean: 8 is 1/3 more than 6, and 12 is 1/3 more than 8</note>; but 9 exceeds and is exceeded by an equal number <note>The arithmetic mean: 9 is 3 more than 6, and 12 is 3 more than 9</note>. Hence, by multiplying 1 and 2 by six, we will find numbers that can contain these middle points. 

In a similar way, by multiplying the remaining double and triple numbers by 6 in the order mentioned before, we will find the terms that we can fill in with arithmetic and harmonic means. These "sextuple" <note>numbers multiplied by six</note> numbers will be produced from all the previously mentioned orders, provided we arrange the numbers correctly—specifically, that 48 should be placed before 54. In this respect, we depart from the arrangement of Plato, who places 9 before 8 in order to alternate between the double and triple ratios. We, however, make this change because it is more consistent with the quantity of <term>units</term> <note>original: "monads"</note> and the nature of increasing numbers. 

Therefore, 8 and 9 come between 6 and 12. Between 12 and its double (24), the harmonic mean is 16 and the arithmetic mean is 18. Between the third double¹ 24 and 48, the harmonic mean is 32 and the arithmetic mean is 36. 

In triple numbers, between 6 and 18 (the first triple ratio), the harmonic mean is 9 and the arithmetic mean is 12. Between the second triple (18 and 54), the harmonic mean is 27 and the arithmetic mean is 36. And between the third triple (54 and 162), the harmonic mean is 81 and the arithmetic mean is 108. The double and triple intervals are therefore divided by these two means. Consequently, these terms will follow each other in this sequence: 6, 8, 9, 12, 16, 18, 24, 27, 32, 36, 48, 54, 81, 108, 162.

If it were possible to divide the <term>4:3 ratios</term> <note>original: "sesquitertian ratios"</note> into <term>9:8 ratios</term> <note>original: "sesquioctaves"</note> and <term>remainders</term> <note>original: "lemmas"; the small interval left over when two 9:8 ratios are taken from a 4:3 ratio</note> using only the terms we have described, we would not need to go any further. But since this is not possible, we need another method. Since it was originally proposed to fill the double ratio with the mentioned means and with 9:8 ratios, it is necessary that the lower term of the double ratio should contain the 4:3 ratio along with two 9:8 ratios.

# BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

First, let us take the third number from one <note>original: unity</note> following an eightfold ratio, which is 64 <note>This follows the sequence 1, 8, 64</note>. From this number, it is possible to form two 9:8 ratios <term>original: sesquioctaves; a ratio representing a whole tone</term>. Every multiple number acts as a starting point for as many multiple ratios as the number of steps it is removed from one. However, 64 does not have a 4:3 ratio <term>original: sesquitertian; a ratio representing a perfect fourth</term> that results in a whole number.¹ By tripling 64, therefore, we get 192. The 4:3 ratio of 192 is 256, but its 9:8 ratio is 216, and the 9:8 ratio of 216 is 243.² 

The ratio of the remnant <term>original: leimma; the "leftover" interval in a Pythagorean scale, roughly a semitone</term> is what remains after subtracting the two 9:8 ratios (243 and 216) from the larger interval. Whenever two 9:8 ratios are taken from a 4:3 ratio, the ratio of the remnant is what is left. Now, the 9:8 ratio of 256 is 288. This number 288 maintains an arithmetic mean <note>The average: (192 + 384) / 2 = 288</note> between 192 and 384. The number 384 has a double <note>original: duple</note> ratio to 192 and a 4:3 ratio to 288. 

If it were possible to form two 9:8 ratios from 288, we might also fill this 4:3 ratio with 9:8 ratios and a remnant. At the moment, however, this is not possible, because its 9:8 ratio, 324, does not have an eighth part that is a whole number. Therefore, if we wish to keep the number one <note>original: unity</note> always undivided by fractions, it is impossible for it to have a 9:8 ratio. Its eighth part would be 40 and ½. By doubling this to make the half a whole number, we can then determine its eighth part. 

Because of this, however, we will be forced to double all the numbers that came before it and those that come after it. Consequently, instead of 192, we shall have 384; instead of 216, 432; instead of 243, 486; instead of 256, 512; and instead of 288, 576. The 9:8 ratio of 576 is 648, and the 9:8 ratio of 648 is 729.³ Afterward, the number 768, which is the double of 384, has the ratio of a remnant to 729. In this manner, the double interval is filled with 3:2 <term>original: sesquialter; a perfect fifth</term>, 4:3, and 9:8 ratios using the numbers 384, 432, 486, 512, 576, 648, 729, and 768. 

Therefore, if we wish to fill the entire diagram and list all the numbers in their proper order, we must use the following values:
*   Instead of the first part, we use 384.
*   Instead of the double of the first, 768.
*   Instead of the triple of the first (which is the 3:2 ratio of the second), 1152.
*   Instead of the quadruple of the first, 1536.
*   Instead of the fifth part <note>referring to the fifth number in Plato's series: 1, 2, 3, 4, 9</note>, which is triple the third, 3456.
*   Instead of the sixth part <note>the number 8 in the series</note>, which is eight times the first, 3072.
*   Instead of the seventh part <note>the number 27 in the series</note>, which is twenty-seven times <note>original: the twenty-seventh part of; here Proclus means the 27th multiple</note> the first, 10368.

# PROCLUS ON THE TIMÆUS [BOOK III.]

If we wish to take the aforementioned means <note>original: middles; in this context, it refers to the harmonic and arithmetic means</note> of the triple interval—namely, of 384 and 1152—then 576 will serve as the harmonic mean <note>original: harmonic middle; the Greek text originally had "arithmetic," which was a mistake</note>. Again, if we wish to take the same means for the double and quadruple intervals—that is, the means between the terms 768 and 1536 (the former being double 384, and the latter being quadruple)—the harmonic mean will be 1024, and 1152 will be the arithmetic mean. If we also wish to fill in the second triple interval, the terms of which are 1152 and 3456 (the former being double 576, and the latter being triple 1152), then 1728 will give us the harmonic mean, and 2304 the arithmetic mean. And if we wish to fill in the third double interval, consisting of the terms 1536 and 3072, then 2048 will be the harmonic mean and 2304 the arithmetic mean. 

But if we wish to fill in the third triple interval with similar means—specifically, the fifth and seventh parts—our extremes will be 3456 and 10368. The harmonic mean will be 5184, and the arithmetic mean 6912. If, once again, we should fill in each of the 4:3 ratios <term>original: sesquitertians; a ratio representing a perfect fourth</term> that arise from these means, as well as the 3:2 ratios <term>original: sesquialters; a ratio representing a perfect fifth</term>, along with 9:8 ratios <term>original: sesquioctaves; a ratio representing a whole tone</term> and a remnant <term>original: leimma; the Pythagorean semitone</term>, this will become clear after the full explanation. We will then present a complete diagram showing all terms in sequence, which contains 24 whole tones <note>original: sesquioctaves</note> and 9 remnants <note>original: leimmas</note>.

Having clarified these points, we shall observe this regarding the remnant <note>original: leimma</note>: since it is not possible to divide any superparticular ratio <term>a ratio where the numerator is one more than the denominator, such as 9:8 or 4:3</term> into two equal ratios using whole numbers, an exact semitone cannot be expressed in whole numbers. However, by taking the ratios that are adjacent to each other—namely, the 17:16 ratio and the 16:15 ratio—and demonstrating that the 17:16 ratio is greater than the remnant (which is itself less than an accurate semitone), we can infer that both the remnant and the 17:16 ratio are less than a true semitone. 

That the remnant is less than a semitone is demonstrated as follows: Let there be given the term 16 and its 9:8 ratio, 18. By placing 17 between them, it divides the 9:8 ratio into two unequal ratios, which are close to a semitone interval because 17 differs from the extremes by only one unit. It is evident that it creates a larger ratio with the smaller term (16), because in all arithmetic proportions, the ratio is greater when the terms are smaller. Therefore, the 17:16 ratio is less than a true semitone. Furthermore, the remnant is even smaller than the 17:16 ratio, as is evident from the terms provided by Plato. Since 256 has the ratio of a remnant to 243, as we shall demonstrate in what follows...

-> # BOOK III. THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO <-

It follows that we shall show that the primary ratio of the <term>leimma</term> <note>original: leimma; in Pythagorean music theory, this is the "remainder" or the interval of 256:243, slightly smaller than a semitone.</note> is found in these numbers. Since 256 exceeds 243 by 13 units, and this excess is less than a seventeenth part of 243 (because a seventeenth of 243 is more than 13), it follows that the ratio of the leimma is less than a semitonic interval. Consequently, the ratio that remains to complete a full tone—which is called the ratio of an <term>apotome</term> <note>original: apotome; the "cut-off" portion that remains when a leimma is subtracted from a whole tone.</note>—is necessarily greater than a semitone.

Furthermore, this may also be demonstrated in another way, as follows: Let the numbers 256 and 243 be given. Suppose we assume three numbers in a consecutive order following this ratio. From 256, we get 65,536; from 243, we get 59,049; and from the combination of both, we get 62,208. These three numbers are related by the ratio of the leimma. If that ratio were a true semitone, the ratio between the two outer numbers (the extremes) would be a perfect <term>tonic ratio</term> <note>original: sesquioctave or 9:8 ratio</note>. If the leimma is greater than a semitone, that interval will be greater than a tone; if it is less, the interval will be less than a tone. However, the <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>original: sesquioctave; a 9:8 ratio</note> of 59,049 is 66,430 1/8. This is greater than our larger term (65,536).

There is a third way to demonstrate the same thing: that a tone cannot be divided into two equal parts using the ratio of 256 to 243. If we take an eighth part of 243, which is 30 3/8, and add this to it, we get 273 3/8. This number has a sesquioctave ratio (9:8) to 243. You can see, therefore, that 256 has a smaller ratio to 243 than 273 3/8 has to 256. Specifically, 256 has a <term>superpartient ratio</term> <note>original: superpartient ratio; a ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number plus more than one part of it</note> to 243, exceeding it by 13/243. However, 273 3/8 exceeds 256 by 17 3/8 divided by 256 (which equals 139/2048). A ratio that exceeds by seventeen and a fraction is greater than one that exceeds by only thirteen, when calculated according to the ratio of excess. 

Therefore, a tone cannot be divided into equal parts. Instead, the smaller part is the *leimma*, as Plato calls it, and the part with the greater ratio is the *apotome*, as musicians are accustomed to call it. For if 273 3/8 has a 9:8 ratio to 243, but 256 has the ratio of the leimma to that same 243 (which is less than a seventeenth part), it is evident that 273 3/8 (the full tone) will have the ratio of the apotome when compared to 256. The apotome is the remainder of the leimma and is greater than the seventeenth part, which we have shown to be less than the ratio of the leimma. 

If we multiply these numbers by eight, we will find the first whole numbers that express the ratio of the apotome in primary ratios <note>original: en pythmesin (εν πυθμεσιν)</note>. Eight times 243 is 1944; eight times 256 is 2048; and eight times 273 3/8 is 2187. Thus, the ratio of the apotome in primary numbers is 2187 to 2048. We will need these three terms in a consecutive order for our diagram: 243, 256, and 273 3/8. But because of the fraction 3/8, we will use their octuples...

...numbers 1944, 2048, and 2187, in order that the terms may be expressed in whole numbers <note>original: "perfect unities"; meaning integers rather than fractions.</note>, and not in fractions. Since, however, it is necessary that the ratio of the <term>leimma</term> <note>original: leimma; in Pythagorean music theory, this is the "remainder" or semitone that results from subtracting two whole tones from a fourth.</note> should be 256 to 243, we may demonstrate it as follows: 

If two <term>sesquioctaves</term> <note>original: sesquioctave; a ratio of 9 to 8, representing a whole tone.</note> are taken away from a <term>sesquitertian</term> <note>original: sesquitertian; a ratio of 4 to 3, representing a perfect fourth.</note> interval, the terms that encompass the remaining interval will have a ratio to each other of 256 to 243. For example, let *a b* be sesquitertian to *e*, and let *c* be taken away, which is the <term>subsesquioctave</term> <note>original: subsesquioctave; the inverse ratio of 8 to 9.</note> of the sesquioctave *a b*. In a similar manner, let *d* be taken from *c*. I say that *d* will have the proposed ratio to *e*. 

From *a b*, let *c* be taken (which is equal to *z b*), and let *d* be taken (which is equal to *e b*). Since, therefore, *a b* is to *c* as *c* is to *d* (for they are both sesquioctaves), it will also be that *a z* is to *b z* as *b z* is to *b e*. Hence, the remainder *a z* will be to the remainder *z e* as the whole is to the whole—that is, as *a b* is to *b z*. But *a b* is a sesquioctave of *b z*. Therefore, *b z* is a sesquioctave of *e z*. 

Let *z h* be set equal to *z e*. Thus, *z h* is eight times <note>original: "octuple"</note> *h a*. Since *z e* is equal to *z h*, it follows that *e h* is eighteen times *h a*. <note>The math here follows Proclus’s specific geometric construction of ratios.</note> Again, since *z b* is a sesquioctave of *b e* (because *c* is a sesquioctave of *d*), *b e* is eight times *e z*. In terms of these numbers, if *z e* is 8, then *e b* is 64 and *z b* is 72—since 72 is a sesquioctave of 64. Furthermore, the whole *a b* is 81, for 81 is the sesquioctave of 72. 

These numbers, therefore, are quadrupled. Hence, if *a b* is 324, then *e b* (which is *d*) is 256—since 324 is four times 81, and 256 is four times 64. Because numbers that are multiplied by the same amount maintain the same ratio as their parts, and since *a b* is sesquitertian (4:3) of *e*, then if *a b* is 324, *e* will be 243. This is because 324 contains 243 plus a third part of it (which is 81). We have already shown that if *a b* is 324, then *d* is 256. Therefore, when *d* is 256, *e* is 243.

It is clear, however, that this ratio of the <term>leimma</term> is in its simplest terms. These are "prime" terms in relation to each other, which is evident through the process of subtraction: they eventually end in unity when the smaller is repeatedly taken from the larger. <note>Proclus is referring to Euclid's algorithm for finding the greatest common divisor; because the result is 1, the numbers 256 and 243 share no common factors.</note> Since they are prime terms, they are necessarily the smallest numbers that can express this specific ratio. Therefore, if two sesquioctaves are subtracted from a sesquitertian interval, the remaining terms will have the ratio of 256 to 243.

Having demonstrated this, let us arrange the following in order: *a b* for the tonic ratio (9:8), *b c* for the ratio of the leimma (256:243), *a d* for the ratio of what is called a semitone, and *d* to *c* for the ratio of the <term>comma</term>. <note>original: comma; a very small interval, defined here as the difference between the "true" semitone and the mathematical apotome.</note> This name is given to the ratio of the excess of the <term>apotome</term> <note>original: apotome; the "remainder" of a whole tone after a leimma is removed, roughly 2187:2048.</note> above a true semitone (which cannot be expressed perfectly in numbers). 

This, then, is proven. To what has been said, however, we must add that we have called the ratio of *d b* a "semitone," not because a sesquioctave (a whole tone) can be divided into two equal ratios—for no <term>superparticular ratio</term> <note>original: superparticular ratio; a ratio of the form (n+1)/n. The Pythagoreans proved that such ratios cannot be divided into two equal rational parts.</note> can be divided that way—but because the followers of <term>Aristoxenus</term> <note>Aristoxenus (4th century BCE) was a music theorist who argued that intervals should be measured by the ear rather than by strict mathematical ratios.</note> assume a semitone exists after two sesquioctaves. We have assumed the ratio of a semitone according to their position in order to discover what...

This is asserted for the reason we have already mentioned. It has been demonstrated that every <term>superparticular ratio</term> <note>original: superparticular ratio; a ratio where the numerator is one greater than the denominator, such as 3:2, 4:3, or 9:8</note> cannot be divided into two equal ratios. 

However, we must add this for the sake of thorough scholarship: the Pythagoreans do not admit that there is a "semitone" which, when added to two <term>sesquioctaves</term> <note>original: sesquioctave; the 9:8 ratio, representing a whole tone</note>, produces a <term>sesquitertian</term> <note>original: sesquitertian; the 4:3 ratio, representing a perfect fourth</note> ratio. Nor do they accept the symphony of the <term>diapason</term> <note>original: diapason; the octave</note> and <term>diatessaron</term> <note>original: diatessaron; the perfect fourth</note> <note>Together, these form an eleventh (an octave plus a fourth)</note> as the followers of Aristoxenus do. 

The musicians who came after him, the disciples of Ptolemy, agree with the Pythagoreans that what is called a "semitone" is not actually a half-tone. However, they reject the opinion that the octave and the fourth do not create a harmony. We must demonstrate the former point because it reflects Plato's opinion; however, since we are not required to prove the latter point—Plato having said nothing about it—we shall omit it for now.

Since we have shown the numbers in which the ratio of the leimma and the ratio of the apotome are first found, we must also show in what numbers the ratio of the comma is first discovered (this being the amount by which the apotome exceeds the leimma). According to the ancients, this ratio in whole numbers <note>original: "perfect [i. e. in undivided] unities"</note> is **531,441 to 524,288**. <gloss>1. Leonicus Thomæus <note>A 15th-century translator of Proclus</note> uses the number 524,298 in his version.</gloss> 

But if dividing a single unit <note>original: "if to divide unity makes no difference"; i.e., using fractions</note> is acceptable, let the ratio of the leimma be taken as 256 to 243. The sesquioctave (9:8 ratio) of 243 is 273 3/8, and the sesquioctave of 256 is 288. <gloss>2. The number 288 is omitted in the original Greek and also in the version by Thomæus.</gloss> 

Another leimma exists between 269 and 243 13/243. <gloss>3. Calculated as: $269 + \frac{13}{243} = \frac{65380}{243}$. The ratio is $\frac{65380}{243}$ to 256, which is the same as 256 to $243 \frac{37908}{65380}$.</gloss> This is the ratio of the leimma because 269 contains 256 plus 13 units, and 256 contains 243 plus 13 units. Because 256 consists of 243 plus 13 units (which are parts of 243), the 13 by which 256 exceeds 243 represents 13/243 of 243. Each of the thirteen units by which 256 exceeds 243 contains 1/243 of 243. Therefore, $269 \frac{13}{243}$ has the same ratio to 256 as 256 has to 243—being in a "superpartient" ratio to it. Consequently, the remaining value, 273 3/8, has the ratio of the comma to $269 \frac{13}{243}$. 

Thus, we have shown in which numbers (using divided units) and in which two leimmas taken from the whole tone the ratio of the comma is first found. It is evident from what has been said that we have achieved what we promised. The terms and all the intervals have been filled in using <term>harmonic</term> and <term>arithmetic middles</term> <note>Two ways of calculating a "center" between two numbers in Greek mathematics</note>, and the divisions of the <term>sesquialter</term> <note>original: sesquialter; the 3:2 ratio or perfect fifth</note> and sesquitertian ratios into whole tones and leimmas have been completed. In the <term>duple interval</term> <note>original: duple interval; a 2:1 ratio, which in music corresponds to an octave</note> between 384 and 768, the number 432 (which is in a <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>original: sesquioctave; a 9:8 ratio, representing a whole tone</note> ratio to 384) and 486 (which is sesquioctave to 432) fall between them. There is also 512, which forms a <term>leimma</term> <note>original: leimma; the Pythagorean semitone with a ratio of 256:243</note> with 486. Up to this point, the <term>sesquitertian</term> <note>original: sesquitertian; a 4:3 ratio, representing a perfect fourth</note> ratio consists of two whole tones and the leimma.

Furthermore, 576 is the sesquioctave of 512, 648 is the sesquioctave of 576, 729 is the sesquioctave of 648, and 768 has the ratio of the leimma to 729. From these, the <term>sesquialter</term> <note>original: sesquialter; a 3:2 ratio, representing a perfect fifth</note> is completed, consisting of three sesquioctaves and one leimma.^1 The entire double interval (octave) consists of five sesquioctaves and two leimmas. Again, using the previously described numbers 384 and 768, the number 512 creates an <term>harmonic mean</term> <note>original: harmonic medium; a mathematical average used in music theory to find the "middle" note of a symphony</note>, while 576 creates an <term>arithmetic mean</term>. Additionally, 864 is placed as the sesquioctave of 768, 972 is the sesquioctave of 864, and 1024 has the ratio of the leimma to 972. Then 1152 is the sesquioctave of 1024. Now, after the double interval, the sesquialter ratio is produced, creating a <term>triple ratio</term> <note>original: triple ratio; a 3:1 ratio, which in music is an octave plus a perfect fifth</note>—namely, the ratio of 1152 to 384. Within this triple interval, 576 is the harmonic mean between the extremes, while 768 is the arithmetic mean. *For a theorem of the following kind is universally proven: if we take a base number and find its double and its triple, and then find the arithmetic mean of the double interval, that same mean will be the harmonic mean for the triple interval. Furthermore, the higher number in the double ratio will become the arithmetic mean in the triple ratio.* For instance, in the numbers used above, 768 is the double of 384, but 1152 is the triple. Between the double terms 768 and 384, the arithmetic mean 576 is found; this same mean is seen to be the harmonic mean between the triple terms 384 and 1152. And 768, which was the double, becomes the arithmetic mean between the triple terms. Afterward, 1296 is the sesquioctave of 1152, 1458 is the sesquioctave of 1296, and 1536 has the ratio of the leimma to 1458. At this point, the second double interval (the second octave) is completed, being composed of the sesquialter and sesquitertian ratios. Its boundaries are 768 and 1536, and it is divided into five sesquioctaves and two leimmas. It likewise has 1024 for its harmonic mean and 1152 for its arithmetic mean.

Again, 1728 is the sesquioctave of 1536, 1944 is the sesquioctave of 1728, 2187 is the sesquioctave of 1944, and 2304 has the ratio of the leimma to 2187. The sesquioctave of 2304 is 2592; the sesquioctave of this is 2916, and 3072 has the ratio of the leimma to 2916. This 3072 is <term>octuple</term> <note>original: octuple; 8:1 ratio, or three octaves ($2^3=8$)</note> of the first part (384), completing the third double interval. Furthermore, the sesquioctave of 3072 is 3456. The second triple interval extends this far, having 1152 and 3456 as its boundaries, with 1728 as its harmonic mean and 2304 as its arithmetic mean. The <term>double</term> and <term>triple</term> intervals are therefore filled with middle terms, <term>sesquioctaves</term> (whole tones), and <term>leimmas</term> (semitones). This entire diagram contains nine <term>leimmas</term> and twenty-four <term>sesquioctaves</term>.
