The sequence extends as far as four <term>octaves</term> <note>original: diapason</note>, a <term>fifth</term> <note>original: diapente</note>, and a whole tone.

However, Adrastus—a scholar of the arts—arranges these figures, as we have mentioned, in the shape of the Greek letter **λ** (lambda). He places the numbers within specific triangles. In the innermost triangle, he places the ratios of the basic <term>unit numbers</term> <note>original: monadic numbers</note> <insert>that is, the numbers from one to ten</insert>. In the next triangle, he places six times those values, which provide two middle points for every double or triple interval. Finally, in the outermost triangle, he places the numbers that complete the entire diagram described above. 

What we have said will become clear from the illustration. However, we have chosen not to list all the above-mentioned numbers between the double and triple intervals, as we did not want to include an <insert>unnecessary</insert> number of terms. Arranging the terms this way and repeating the same numbers twice lacks a clear system. Many of the same middle points are found in both the double and triple intervals, because the triple intervals are themselves composed of double intervals and <term>perfect fifths</term> <note>original: sesquialters; 3:2 ratios</note>. 

Thus, we have clarified Plato’s meaning. We have identified two middle points between every <term>double</term> and <term>triple</term> interval. From these middle points, <term>perfect fifths</term> and <term>perfect fourths</term> <note>original: sesquitertian; 4:3 ratios</note> are formed. manner, the terms which comprise the whole diagram will be found to be thirty-four only.¹

Since, however, the Pythagorean Timaeus says that the terms of the diagram are thirty-six, and yet uses the same extremes <note>The outer limits or the lowest and highest numbers.</note> as Plato—namely, 384 and 10,368—let us show how the other two terms are inserted so that these philosophers do not appear to be in disagreement with each other. These men (the Pythagoreans) intended for there to be not only the ratio of the <term>leimma</term> <note>original: leimma; a Pythagorean semitone with a 256:243 ratio.</note> in the diagram, but also that of the <term>apotome</term> <note>original: apotome; the interval remaining when a leimma is subtracted from a whole tone (9:8).</note>, which they discovered twice: both in basic numbers and in those that are three times those values. By adding one term to each of these, they introduced this into the diagram. 

But Plato makes no mention of the <term>apotome</term>; for this reason, we are satisfied with the <term>leimma</term> and have only employed the thirty-four terms listed above. For how could he make use of the <term>apotome</term> while assuming the <term>diatonic genus</term> <note>One of the three ancient Greek musical scales, characterized by two whole tones and a semitone.</note>, given that the <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>original: sesquioctave; a 9:8 ratio, or a whole tone.</note> is not divided in this genus? The <term>apotome</term> is only produced when the <term>sesquioctave</term> is divided, because the <term>apotome</term> is the part of the <term>sesquioctave</term> that remains after the <term>leimma</term> is taken away. Therefore, since Plato does not mention the <term>apotome</term> and it cannot occur in the <term>diatonic genus</term>, it would be unreasonable for us to try to insert other terms just to have an <term>apotome</term>. The thirty-four terms are sufficient to complete the <term>sesquioctaves</term> and <term>leimmas</term>. It also appears that the number 34 is perfectly suited to the <term>diatonic genus</term>.

...in which alone the <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>original: sesquioctave; a 9:8 ratio, which represents a whole tone in music.</note> ratio is found. For it consists of the terms 18 and 16, which are in a sesquioctave ratio to each other. Although the <term>sesquialter</term> <note>3:2 ratio, a perfect fifth.</note> and <term>sesquitertian</term> <note>4:3 ratio, a perfect fourth.</note> ratios, as well as <term>leimmas</term> <note>original: leimmas; the Pythagorean semitone with a ratio of 256:243.</note>, are also found in the other musical genres, sesquioctaves are found only in this one of the three genres. Hence, this sesquioctave ratio very properly produces the number of the parts through its composition; and this being the second stage, it is adapted to the second progression of the soul from the first intelligible principles.

If, therefore, we take the smaller term of the third double (1536) and find its sesquioctave (1728), then the sesquioctave of that (1944), and again the <term>tritone</term> <note>An interval of three whole tones.</note> of the original (2187), there will be one interval between the extremes. However, because 2048 has a sesquitertian (4:3) ratio to 1536, but 1944 has the ratio of the leimma to it, it is necessary that 2187 should create an <term>apotome</term> <note>The interval remaining when a leimma is subtracted from a whole tone (9:8).</note> relative to 2048. For an apotome is, as we have said before, that which remains of a whole tone after the leimma is removed.

In a similar manner, by taking 4608 in the third triple—which contains the tritone¹ 6561—and also taking 6144 (which has a sesquitertian ratio to 4608 but a leimma ratio to 5832), we shall necessarily have the apotome in the ratio of 6561 to 6144. These numbers are triple the basic terms that we discovered earlier in the third double. It is evident that the ratio of the apotome is fundamentally found in those terms. For 2187 and 2048 are demonstrated to be the primary terms for each other by the mathematical theorem of subtraction; primary terms are necessarily the smallest possible whole numbers for a ratio. The large number of terms described by Timaeus is demonstrated by the philosopher Philolaus, but Plato’s diagram proceeds without using the ratio of the apotome. And that is enough concerning these details.

Since, however, we have observed before that if two numbers are assumed from one term—one being its double and the other its triple—then the <term>arithmetical mean</term> <note>The midpoint between two numbers, found by adding them and dividing by two.</note> between the double terms becomes the <term>harmonic mean</term> <note>A type of average used in music and geometry where the reciprocal of the mean is the average of the reciprocals of the numbers.</note> between the triple terms, and the double term itself acts as an arithmetical mean between the triple terms, we will now briefly clarify and demonstrate this theorem. Let *b* be the double of *a*, and *c* be the triple of it; and between *a* and *b*, let the arithmetical mean be *d*. I say that the result will be what was stated in the proposition. For since *b* is double and *c* is triple of *a*, if *a* is two, *b* will be four, and *c* will be six. Hence, if *b* is four, *c* will be six. By that much,

Therefore, *c* exceeds *b* by the same amount that *b* exceeds *a*. Hence, *b* is an **arithmetical mean** <note>The average of two numbers, where the difference between each consecutive number is the same (e.g., 2, 3, 4).</note> between *a* and *c*. Again, if *a* is two and *b* is four, the arithmetical mean between them is *d*; therefore, *d* will be three, relative to *a* being two and *b* being four.¹ But where *b* is four, *c* is six. Consequently, where *a* is two, *d* is three and *c* is six. Thus, *d* compared to *a* and *c* will produce a **harmonic middle** <note>original: harmonic middle; also known as the harmonic mean. In the sequence 2, 3, 6, the middle term 3 is defined by the fact that the difference between the terms is a consistent fraction of the terms themselves: 6 exceeds 3 by 3 (half of 6), and 3 exceeds 2 by 1 (half of 2).</note>.² For it is exceeded by the greater term by the same fraction of that greater term, and it exceeds the lesser term by the same fraction of that lesser term. This concludes the discussion on this particular point.

**Severus**, however, thinks that this diagram should not end in a whole tone, but in the **leimma** <note>original: leimma; the Pythagorean semitone, with a ratio of 256:243.</note>, because Plato ends his entire discussion concerning the division of the soul with this interval. In order to ensure it ends in the leimma, Severus adjusts some of the terms, making thirty-four of them in total. But since the half of a unit occurs in the thirty-fourth term, he doubles all the terms, making the starting number 768 (which is double 384). 

Of this number, he calculates the <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>A 9:8 ratio, representing a whole tone in music.</note> as 864, and the sesquioctave of that as 972. To this, he applies the ratio of the leimma, resulting in 1024. Then he takes the sesquioctave of this (1152); the sesquioctave of that (1296); and the sesquioctave of that again (1458). To this, he applies the leimma to get 1536, and places the sesquioctave of this as 1728, and the sesquioctave of that as 1944. To this, he likewise applies the ratio of the leimma, 2187. From this, he assumes the sesquioctave is 2304; the sesquioctave of that is 2592; and the sesquioctave of that again is 2916. To this, he adds 3072, which has the ratio of the leimma to it; then the sesquioctave 3456; and similarly 3888. 

To this, he again applies the leimma to get 4374; of this, he takes the sesquioctave 4608; then the sesquioctave 5184; and the sesquioctave of that again, 5832. To this, he applies the ratio of the leimma, 6144; and of this, he takes the sesquioctave 6912; then the sesquioctave 7776; and the sesquioctave of that again, 8748. To this, he applies the leimma 9216. From this, he calculates the sesquioctave 10368; then 11664; and again the sesquioctave 13122. To this, he applies the leimma 13824; then the sesquioctave 15552; then the sesquioctave 17496; and finally the sesquioctave 19683. To this last number, he applies 20736, which maintains the ratio of the leimma. 

He completes the diagram at this point, making the leimma the final interval; however, in these terms, there is first the <term>sesquitertian</term> <note>A 4:3 ratio, a perfect fourth.</note>, then the <term>sesquialter</term> <note>A 3:2 ratio, a perfect fifth.</note>, then the sesquitertian again, and finally the sesquialter ratio.

<header>BOOK III.] PLATO'S TIMAEUS.</header>

And again the **sesquitertian** <note>original: sesquitertian; a ratio of 4:3</note>, afterward the **sesquialter** <note>original: sesquialter; a ratio of 3:2</note>, and then three sesquialters in a following order, as is evident from the description above.

It happens, therefore, in this diagram, that there is a quadruple **diapason** <note>original: diapason; an octave, or 2:1 ratio</note>, that the **diapente** <note>original: diapente; a perfect fifth, or 3:2 ratio</note> occurs once, and that the **tone** <note>original: tone; a 9:8 ratio</note> is redundant. For three sesquialters make one diapason and a tone. The diagram, however, does not end in a tone, but in the **leimma** <note>original: leimma; the Pythagorean semitone (256:243)</note>. This was what was proposed to be accomplished. Severus, therefore, does not remove the tone, but he does not end the sequence with it. Thus, the whole diagram, according to all the terms, consists of a quadruple diapason, the diapentes, and one tone. 

If we also wish to represent these intervals in **monadic numbers** <note>Counting numbers or integers</note>, we must examine the progression as it extends up to twenty-seven. For 2 is the double of 1, 4 is the double of 2, 8 of 4, and 16 of 8; and the quadruple diapason extends as far as this. But 24 is the sesquialter of 16, and this is the diapente; and 27 has a **sesquioctave** <note>9:8</note> ratio to 24. Thus, the previously mentioned **symphonies** <note>musical intervals or harmonies</note> are completed in one part, reaching as far as twenty-seven. 

This, therefore, as I have said, is common to all the diagrams. But they differ from each other in this: some are in the form of the letter **λ** <note>The Greek letter "lambda," used to show the two branches of the soul's numbers (the powers of 2 and the powers of 3)</note>, while others are in a straight line. Among the ancients, Adrastus employs figures in the shape of a λ, but Severus uses straight lines, which in my opinion is better. For in the figures shaped like the letter λ, the same numbers are found twice in different places. But this is inconsistent with the reality of the subject. There are not two parts of the soul which are the same, yet all these numbers represent parts of the soul. 

They also differ in that some of the diagrams end in a tone, but others in the leimma. Some are also clearer, even though the same numbers are used twice, as is the case with those diagrams which distribute the double and triple^1 ratios along the sides of triangles. But others place each number only once in all the intervals, though this makes it more difficult to divide the double terms into **super-particular** <note>A ratio where the numerator is one greater than the denominator (e.g., 3:2, 4:3)</note> and **super-partient** <note>A ratio where the numerator is more than one greater than the denominator (e.g., 5:3)</note> ratios. We have, therefore, introduced these points to assist those examining the **psychogonic diagram** <note>The "soul-generating" diagram; the mathematical model of the soul's creation</note> from a mathematical perspective.

As we begin the more important explanation of the words of Plato, we think it necessary to speak first about the division itself—by which the soul is divided into these ratios—and to use logic to remove any obstacles to understanding the truth about it. Therefore, let no one think that this division is physical or corporeal. For it has already been demonstrated that the intermediate nature of the soul is separate from bodies, and at the—

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s discussion of the soul's structure. Having previously discussed the mathematical ratios (the musical intervals) of the soul, Proclus now moves into the metaphysical nature of how the soul is "divided" into parts by the Demiurge, emphasizing that this division is intellectual and immaterial, not physical.</meta>

### PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.

<page-num>74</page-num>

At the same time, the soul is distinct from every divisible essence <note>original: "partible essence"; referring to matter or things that can be physically broken apart</note> that is distributed throughout bodies. We must not suppose that while the soul is indeed better than bodies, it is divided in the same way as the dimensions and intervals by which bodies <margin>Proclus notes that in the Greek text, "themselves" (autēn) should be read as "them" (auta) to refer to the bodies.</margin> are measured. For things that have physical dimensions are not entirely present with themselves in their whole being; when they are divided, they cannot maintain a unified whole. But the soul, participating in an indivisible portion, is united to itself; it shows that all its elements remain the same in every one of its parts. 

Furthermore, this sectioning of the soul must not be thought of as a division of quantity or number. For the soul is indeed a "number," yet not a number based on quantity, but one that is essential, self-begotten, possessing the form of unity, and focused upon itself. Nor should the presence of these ratios in every part of the soul be compared to **seminal principles** <note>original: "spermatic reasons" (spermatikoi logoi); the biological blueprints or formative forces found in seeds and matter</note>. For these are imperfect, physically formed, and material; they fall entirely short of the immaterial and pure essence of the **rational principles of the soul** <note>original: "psychical reasons"</note>. 

Nor should anyone compare the previously mentioned parts of the soul to the theorems of science, just because each individual theorem contains the whole science of which it is a part. In this case, we are not considering the *knowledge* held by the soul, but the very *essence* of the soul itself. Nor is it proper to think that the differences in essences are like the distinctions between habits or traits. Habits vary entirely depending on the nature of the person who has them, but the soul's essences are established with unchanging sameness within the boundaries set by the **Demiurge** <note>The divine Craftsman or Creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy</note>. 

Therefore, it is necessary to trace the primary principle of this **soul-generating division** <note>original: "psychogonic division"</note> back to the Demiurgic cause and to those perfect measures that eternally exist in real beings. By looking at these, the Demiurge divides the soul. Just as he divided this universe according to intellectual models <note>original: "intelligible paradigms"</note>, he also separates the essence of the soul by the most beautiful boundaries, making it like the more ancient and primary causes. 

*The method of division, therefore, is immaterial, intellectual, and pure. It perfects the soul's essence, generates the many parts within it, collects those parts back into a single order through harmony, and connects the divided parts. It is simultaneously the cause of the unmixed purity of the soul’s many parts and the creator of a communion of rational principles that all converge into the same essence.*

And the Demiurge, indeed, appears to exhaust the whole by dividing it into parts. For in a certain sense, Timaeus says, "*that he consumed the whole from which he cut off these parts.*" This, however, is not actually the case; it is necessary to keep the soul indivisible <margin>Proclus notes that the Greek "divided" (diameriston) should be read as "indivisible" (ameriston) here.</margin> and to ensure that the wholeness remains intact.

<summary>Proclus explains that the "division" of the soul by the Demiurge is not a physical or quantitative breaking apart, but an intellectual organization that preserves the soul's unity and immaterial essence. He distinguishes the soul's internal ratios from biological blueprints (seminal principles) or scientific theorems, arguing it is modeled on eternal, divine patterns.</summary>

...ble, the division into many parts should be carried out. For if we assume only one of these—meaning the division into parts—we would make the soul something that is only divisible <term>original: "partible"; capable of being divided into separate pieces</term>. *The whole, therefore, is distributed into parts, and at the same time the whole remains.* Again, the indivisible <term>original: "impartible"</term> nature of the soul participates equally in what is indivisible and what is divisible. *For it is well said, as we have previously observed, by the divine Aristotle <note>original: "dæmoniacal Aristotle." In this context, "dæmoniacal" does not mean evil, but refers to a "daimon"—a being of superhuman or divine-like insight</note>, that there is something indivisible in divisible natures which connects them. Therefore, it is even more necessary that something indivisible should remain in things that have not only a divisible nature, but an indivisible one as well. For if this did not remain, that which consists of both would be only divisible.* 

It is evident, however, that it is necessary for the whole to remain during the generation of the parts, if the Demiurge <note>the divine Craftsman or Creator of the universe</note> is an eternally producing cause. He constituted the soul as one whole prior to its division. He did not destroy the whole in order to produce something else. Instead, he produces everything eternally and causes that which is produced to remain what it is. Hence, the "wholeness" is not destroyed when the parts are formed; it remains and exists before the parts. For he did not produce the parts before the whole and then generate the whole from them, but rather the other way around. The essence of the soul, therefore, is at once a whole and yet has parts; it is both one and many. This is the kind of division of the soul that Timaeus describes.

The method of explaining this, however, should match the essence of the soul. It should be freed from visible things and elevate itself to essential and immaterial harmony, moving from mere images to the original patterns <term>original: "paradigms"</term>. For the symphony that reaches the ears, consisting of physical sounds and vibrations, is very different from the harmony that is vital and intellectual. No one, therefore, should stop at mere mathematical theory. Instead, one should rouse oneself to a method¹ of investigation adapted to the essence of the soul. Nor should one think that we ought to focus only on mathematical intervals or the differences in motions. For these are distant concepts and are not at all suited to the subjects we are investigating. Instead, one should examine the claims themselves and consider how they indicate the "middle" nature of the soul <note>Proclus views the soul as a bridge or "middle" between the eternal, unchanging divine realm and the changing, physical world</note>, looking to the Demiurge's providence as their ultimate goal. 

In the first place, then, if you are willing to investigate in this way—since wholeness is threefold (one being prior² to the parts, another consisting of the parts, and another being within each of the parts, as we have frequently demonstrated elsewhere)—this being the case, Plato has already described the wholeness of the soul which exists prior to the parts. For—

He [the Demiurge] made it to be a single whole prior <note>The original Greek text here is *pro pantos merismou*, meaning "before all division."</note> to all division into parts—a whole which, as we have already said, remains what it is without being used up or destroyed in the creation of those parts. For the desire to dissolve something that has been well-harmonized is the sign of an evil nature. Dissolution occurs when the "whole" is consumed and broken down into its "parts." In the passage currently under consideration, however, he builds the soul as a whole *from* its parts, using the entire mixture to create the divisions of its essence. Through the harmony of these parts, he makes it a whole once again <note>original: "de novo"; anew</note> and ensures it is complete, formed from all its appropriate components. 

Shortly after this, he teaches us about the "wholeness" that exists within each of the parts. He does this by dividing the whole soul into certain circles and inserting into each circle all the "principles" <note>original: "reasons"; here referring to *logoi*, or the rational governing principles in Platonic philosophy</note> that he had already revealed to us. He had stated that in each part, there are three elements—Same, Different, and Essence—just as they exist in the whole. Therefore, every part, like the whole itself, is in a certain respect a "triadic" (three-fold) whole. 

It follows that the soul must possess three levels of "wholeness" because it animates the universe, which is itself a "whole of wholes," where each sub-section is a whole according to the wholeness inherent in a part. Because the soul animates the universe in two ways—both as a single whole and as a collection of complete parts—it requires two types of wholeness. It transcends the things it animates by having an existence external to them, allowing it to surround the universe in a circle, as *Timaeus* says, like a veil. Through the "wholeness" that exists prior to parts, the soul exists entirely above the universe; but through the other two types of wholeness, it connects the universe and the parts within it, which are also wholes.

Next, we must observe that Plato, proceeding from the beginning to the end, preserves the "monadic" (single) and "dyadic" (dual) nature of the soul simultaneously. He reduces its existence <term>original: "hyparxis"; essential being or reality</term> to Essence, Same, and Different, and he distributes its numbers through a two-fold division, starting from one part and moving into double and triple numbers. He also examines the "means" <note>the middle points or averages in a mathematical series</note>, and shows how one of them encompasses the other two.<note>This refers to geometric proportion, which encompasses both arithmetical and harmonical proportion. For example, if you take the numbers 1, 2, and 3 (which are in arithmetical proportion) and add a fourth term, 6, to create a geometric proportion (1 : 2 :: 3 : 6), then the set contains both an arithmetical proportion (1, 2, 3) and a harmonic proportion (2, 3, 6).</note> Based on each of these, he unfolds two types of ratios: the sesquialter <note>a ratio of 3:2</note> and the sesquitertian <note>a ratio of 4:3</note>. He then divides these further into sesquioctaves <note>a ratio of 9:8, which represents a whole tone in music</note> and "leimmas" <note>mathematical "remnants" or musical semitones</note>. In the following section, he similarly divides the single length of the soul into two, and its single shape into two periods <note>circular paths or orbits</note>. In short, he never fails to show that the soul is both one and two at the same time, and he does this with the greatest...

appropriateness. For the quality of being a single unit (monadic) belongs only to the intellect, which is why the intellect is indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note>. But the quality of being a pair (dyadic) belongs to the body; this is why, in the creation of physical nature, Plato began from the "duad" (the pair of fire and earth) and arranged two other types of elements between them. The soul, however, being a middle ground between intellect and body, is both a monad (a unity) and a duad (a duality) at the same time. The cause <note>The original text mistakenly used the word for "eternal" (*aidion*); it should be "cause" (*aition*).</note> of this is that in a certain respect it participates equally in both "Bound" and "Infinity." Just as the intellect is allied to Bound (limit), the body pertains more to Infinity because of its underlying matter and its ability to be divided forever. 

If people refer to the indivisible and the divisible in this way—as the monad and the indefinite duad—they are speaking in accordance with the reality of things. However, if they claim the soul is merely a number that is no different from simple mathematical units, they are far from describing the true essence of the soul. Therefore, the soul is both a monad and a duad: it foreshadows intellectual Bound through its monadic nature, while foreshadowing Infinity through its dyadic nature. Or, to put it another way, through the former it is the image of indivisible things, while through the latter it is the model for things that can be divided.

In addition to these points, we must also observe how a two-fold work of the Demiurge <term>The Divine Creator or "Craftsman" in Platonic philosophy.</term> is described here. He divides the soul into parts, creates harmony among those divided parts, and makes them agree with each other. In doing these things, he acts at one and the same time in the manner of Dionysus <note>Also called Bacchus; in Greek myth, he represents the "multiplicity" of the soul being poured out into the world.</note> and Apollo. For it is the role of Dionysus to divide, to produce parts out of wholes, and to oversee the distribution of forms; but it is the role of Apollo to bring all things to perfection through harmony. Since the Demiurge contains within himself the power of both these Gods, he both divides and harmonizes the soul. ...seven parts, the soul may have a mark of the Dionysian <note>original: Dionysiacal</note> lineage, and of the mythological tearing apart <gloss>The original Greek *sparagmonou* should be read as *sparagmou* (tearing apart/dismemberment).</gloss> of Bacchus. For it is necessary that it should participate in the Dionysian intellect; and as Orpheus says, by "bearing the God on its head," the soul should be divided in a way that corresponds to him. 

But the soul also possesses harmony in these parts as a symbol of the Apollonian <note>original: Apolloniacal</note> order. For in the stories of the tearing apart of Bacchus, it is Apollo who collects and unites the scattered parts of Bacchus, according to the will of the father [Jupiter]. In these numbers also, the three "middles" <note>In Greek mathematics, a "middle" refers to a mean proportion—arithmetic, geometric, or harmonic—that connects two outer terms.</note> are included. <gloss>Specifically, in the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 6—the set of seven (hebdomad), as Proclus observes, consists of 1, 2, and 4. And the numbers 1, 2, 3, and 6 are in geometrical proportion.</gloss> These being three, they foreshadow—not only in the soul but everywhere—the three daughters of Themis <note>Themis is the Titaness of divine law and order; her daughters are the Horae (the Seasons/Hours).</note>. 

The geometric middle, indeed, is the image of Eunomia <note>Eunomia translates to "Good Order" or "Lawfulness".</note> <gloss>Instead of "Eunomia" here, the Greek should read "of Eunomia".</gloss>. Hence Plato says in the *Laws* that she adorns politics and organizes them in an orderly manner; he likewise celebrates her as the judgment of Jupiter, adorning the universe and encompassing the true science of politics. But the harmonic middle is an image of Dice <note>Dice (pronounced "Dee-kay") is the personification of Justice.</note> or Justice, which distributes a greater ratio to greater terms, but a lesser ratio to lesser terms. This, however, is the work of justice. And the arithmetical middle is an image of Peace. For it is this middle, as it is also said in the *Laws*, which gives to all things an equality based on quantity and makes people at peace with one another. 

For the solid analogy [that is, the triplicate proportion] which exists prior to these is sacred to their mother Themis, who contains the powers of all of them. <gloss>The triplicate proportion consists of geometric proportion, and the geometric contains within itself the arithmetical and the harmonic proportions; therefore, the triplicate or solid analogy encompasses the three middles.</gloss> This is as much as can be said generally concerning these three middles.

These three middles <gloss>The word "middles" (Mesotetes) is omitted in the original Greek text.</gloss>, however, may be described—in a way adapted to what was observed before—as the sources of union and connection for the soul. In other words, they are unions, analogies, and bonds. Because of this, Timaeus calls them bonds. For prior to this, he had said that the geometric middle is the most beautiful of bonds and that the other middles are contained within it <gloss>Instead of "in these" here, it is obviously necessary to read "in this".</gloss>. Every bond is a type of union. If, therefore, the middles are bonds, and bonds are the unions of the things that are bound, then the conclusion is obvious. These middles pervade the entire essence of the soul <gloss>The words "soul's essence" (psychis ousias) are omitted in the original, but clearly should be included.</gloss> and render it a single unit made of many parts.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, specifically focusing on how the Soul is unified through three mathematical "middles" or proportions: the geometric, harmonic, and arithmetical. These proportions link the metaphysical concepts of Essence, Sameness, and Difference.</meta>

<header>BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>
<page-num>79</page-num>

...wholes, as they are granted a power to bind together things of a varied nature. However, because there are three of them, the geometric middle <note>In Greek mathematics, a "middle" refers to a mean proportion—geometric, harmonic, or arithmetic—that connects two outer terms.</note> binds everything that is essential in souls. For essence is a single principle <note>original: reason</note> that moves through all things, connecting the first, middle, and last levels of reality. Just so, in the geometric middle, one and the same ratio flows perfectly through the three terms that make up the proportion. 

But the harmonic middle connects all the divided "sameness" of souls, giving the outer extremes a shared logic and a natural connection. And "sameness" is seen more clearly in universal <note>original: total</note> natures, and less so in individual <note>original: partial</note> natures. 

The arithmetical middle binds together the vast diversity found in the soul's progression. it is less prominent in greater things and more present in lesser things, according to their order. For "difference" dominates in individual things, just as "sameness" has more authority in universal and superior things. These two middles (the harmonic and arithmetical) have a way of communicating with each other, just as sameness and difference do. Just as "essence" is the primary unit <note>original: monad</note> for sameness and difference, the geometric middle is the primary unit for the other two proportions. 

The geometric middle, therefore, is the union of the essences across all the terms; the harmonic is the union of the many "samenesses"; and the arithmetical is the union of the "differences." <note>original: It is here necessary to supply the words "as the arithmetical middle [is the union] of the differences" (original Greek: ὡς ἡ ἀριθμητικὴ τῶν ἑτεροτήτων).</note> Therefore, all of these extend through all the terms; otherwise, how could a unified whole be produced from them unless they were as closely united as possible? They are united essentially by the geometric middle, but in different ways by the other two. 

On this account, the arithmetical and harmonic middles serve as the completion <note>original: consummation</note> of the geometric middle, in the same way that sameness and difference contribute to the perfection of essence. Because the arithmetical and harmonic middles exist in opposition to one another, the geometric middle connects and, as it were, weaves* together their disagreement. 

The harmonic middle assigns, as we have said, larger ratios to larger terms and smaller ratios to smaller terms. This demonstrates that things which are naturally greater and more universal are also more powerful than things of an inferior nature. Conversely, the arithmetical middle assigns smaller ratios to larger terms and larger ratios to smaller terms. For "difference" prevails more in lower natures, just as "sameness" has greater authority in superior ones. Finally, the geometric middle extends the same ratio to every term. It illuminates and unites the first, middle, and last levels of reality by bringing the presence of essence to all things.

The Demiurge <note>The "Craftsman" or Creator-god in Plato's philosophy</note> therefore grants three connecting unions to the soul, which Plato calls "middles," because they bind together the middle order of all things.

* <note>Original Greek footnote: For "shines together" (*sumphainei*), it is necessary to read "weaves together" (*sunuphainei*).</note>

The geometric middle is presented as the primary unifying force that balances the opposing tendencies of the other two.</summary>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.
### TIMÆUS OF PLATO

<page-num>80</page-num>

And among these, the geometric mean <note>original: middle</note> gathers the multitude of essences together and causes essential progressions to be unified; for a single ratio is the image of union. But the harmonic mean binds all universal "samenesses" and their essential existences <term>hyparxes: the essential foundations or "flowers" of a thing's being</term> into one communion. And the arithmetic mean joins together the first, middle, and last differences. For, in short, difference is the mother of numbers, as we learn in Plato's *Parmenides*. These three—namely essence, sameness, and difference—exist in every part of the soul, and it is necessary to join all of them to each other through a medium and through binding principles <note>original: colligative reasons</note>.

<margin>¹ For example, 32 to 4 is a multiple ratio, which in its lowest terms is 8 to 1. But 8 is divisible, while 1, strictly speaking, is not. Proclus, therefore, in what he says here, refers to multiple ratios when they are reduced to their lowest terms.</margin>
<margin>² Thus, the superparticular ratio <term>superparticular ratio: a ratio of the form (n+1):n, such as 3:2 or 4:3</term> of 6 to 4 is, in its lowest terms, the ratio of 3 to 2. Both 3 and 2 are divisible. But this ratio is indivisible according to the difference of the terms, because that difference is 1.</margin>
<margin>³ For instance, the superpartient ratio <term>superpartient ratio: a ratio where the larger number contains the smaller plus more than one part of it, such as 5:3 (which contains 3 once plus two-thirds of 3)</term> of 5 to 3—which is "superbipartient"—is evidently divisible both according to the leading term <term>prologos: the first or greater term in a ratio</term> and the following term <term>hypologos: the second or lesser term in a ratio</term>. It is also divisible according to the difference between the terms, since that difference is 2.</margin>

Next, we say that the soul is a fullness of rational principles <note>original: reasons</note>, as she is simpler than sensible objects but more complex <note>original: composite</note> than purely intellectual realities. Therefore, Timaeus assumes seven types of ratios in the soul: equality, multiplicity, submultiplicity, superparticular, and superpartient ratios, as well as their opposites—the sub-superparticular and sub-superpartient—but not the ratios that are compounded from these. For compound ratios are suited to physical <note>original: corporeal</note> principles, because they are complex and divisible. The principles in the soul, however, do proceed into many parts, yet they maintain simplicity; they show unity even while being distributed into parts.

For this reason, they are not granted an existence <term>hypostasis: the underlying reality or substance</term> in the "monad" <note>the fundamental unit of one</note> or the indivisible in the same way that Intellect is. For Intellect alone is unified and indivisible. Nor does the soul's multitude of principles descend into complex ratios. A "multiple ratio" is divisible in only one way—by its leading term <gloss>1</gloss>; for the following term, being smaller, is indivisible and may even be the number one. But the superparticular ratio is divisible in two ways—by the leading and following terms—but it is indivisible according to the difference between them <gloss>2</gloss>. And the superpartient ratio is divisible both by the leading term, the following term, and according to the difference <gloss>3</gloss>. Thus, the first of these is divisible in only one way, the second in two ways <note>original: bifariously</note>, and the third in three ways <note>original: trifariously</note>. But equality is indivisible. The soul, therefore, builds the universe using these ratios: the physical <note>original: corporeal-formed</note> nature is created by that which is divisible in three ways; the nature of surfaces <note>original: superficies</note> by...

<header>BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

<page-num>81</page-num>

...that which is divisible in two ways <note>original: bifariously partible; likely referring to surfaces or planes</note>; every linear quality, by that which is divisible in only one way; and by the indivisible, the state of indivisibility which encompasses all things. For there is something indivisible even within things that can be divided. These points, therefore, are correctly stated.

It is necessary, however, to examine these in another way, starting with the premise that numbers which are simpler and closer to the monad <term>monad: the number one, representing unity and the source of all numbers</term> should be understood as more primary than those which are more complex <note>original: composite</note>. For Plato also, having placed one part before all the rest, relates all of them back to this one, and ends with terms that are especially complex and three-dimensional <note>original: solid</note>.

Having therefore established this premise, I say that equality—and the ratio of equality <note>the ratio of 1:1</note>—serves as the monad for all other ratios. Just as the monad is the basic unit of quantity in itself, equality is the basic unit of quantity in relation to other things. Accordingly, the soul introduces a common measure to all things that exist according to the same principles <note>original: reasons; here meaning "logoi" or rational structures</note>. This measure also brings with it a single Form: the image of "Sameness."

Furthermore, through the "multiple" and "sub-multiple" ratios <note>ratios like 2:1 or 1:2</note>, the soul governs the entire series of things, unifying and encompassing them. It displays each total Form of cosmic <note>original: mundane</note> natures by reproducing it across all cosmic beings. For instance, it produces the "solar form" and the "lunar form" in divine souls, in daemonic <term>daemonic: relating to "daemons," intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense</term> and human souls, in irrational animals, in plants, and even in stones themselves. It organizes the most universal categories <note>original: genera</note> through these more specific series.

According to the "superparticular" and "sub-superparticular" ratios <note>ratios where one number contains the other plus one part of it, like 3:2</note>, the soul organizes things that exist as "wholes" within the things that participate in them, and which are shared according to one specific quality contained within them. 

But according to the "superpartient" and "sub-superpartient"¹ ratios <note>ratios where the larger number contains the smaller plus more than one part of it, like 5:3</note>, the soul organizes things that are shared entirely by secondary natures, accompanied by a division into a large number of parts <note>original: multitude</note>. For example, a human participates in the category of "Animal," and the entire Form of "Animal" is within the human. However, it is not there alone; the whole is in the human according to one specific thing—namely, the human form. Thus, the Form is present to the participant as both the whole and as a specific part of it. 

On the other hand, what are called "common categories" <note>original: genera</note> participate in one category, but not in that one alone; they participate in it along with many other categories that are parts of the whole, rather than just one part. For instance, a mule participates in the species from which it has a mixed ancestry <note>original: co-mingled generation</note>. Therefore, each species either participates in one category through a single form—imitating the superparticular ratio (which contains the whole and one part of the whole)—or it participates in what is common along with many other things, thus imitating the superpartient ratio (which possesses the whole plus many parts of the whole). And besides these, there is no other way to participate in...

species or forms. Looking also to these things, we may be able to assign the specific causes of those natures which exist according to a single form—such as the sun, the moon, and man—as well as those that exist according to many forms combined. For there are many things of this kind in the earth and in the sea, such as animals with a human face and extremities resembling those of a fish, or animals in the form of dragons but with a lion's face. These have an essence mingled from many different things. Therefore, all these ratios <term>ratio: in Platonic philosophy, these "logoi" are the rational, mathematical blueprints of things</term> are appropriately contained beforehand within the soul, as they define all the ways that forms participate in the universe. Nor can there be any other ratios of communion besides these, since all things receive their specific distinction according to them.

Again, therefore, the group of seven <note>original: hebdomad</note> ratios corresponds to the group of seven parts. The soul is entirely "seven-fold" <note>original: hebdomatic</note> throughout itself: in its parts, in its ratios, and in its circles. For if the demiurgic intellect <term>demiurgic intellect: the divine Mind of the Creator</term> is a monad <term>monad: a single, indivisible unit or source</term>, and the soul primarily proceeds from that intellect, the soul will have the ratio of seven in relation to it. This is because the "hebdomad" or number seven is considered paternal and motherless <note>In Pythagorean numerology, the number seven was associated with the virgin goddess Athena because it is not produced by any other number within the first ten, nor does it produce any other number.</note>.

Perhaps equality imparts a shared sense of the "equal" to all the soul's ratios, so that all parts may communicate with one another. However, the *multiple ratio* <note>such as 2:1 or 3:1</note> indicates how the ratios that are more unified measure those that are more numerous; the unified ones extend through the entirety of the more complex ones. These indivisible ratios measure those that are more distributed into parts. 

On the other hand, the *superparticular* and *sub-superparticular* ratios <note>ratios where one number contains the other plus one part of it, like 3:2 (sesquialter) or 4:3 (sesquitertian)</note> indicate the difference by which whole ratios do not communicate with other whole ratios. Instead, they have a partial relationship, yet are joined according to one specific, principal part of themselves. Finally, the *superpartient* and *sub-superpartient* ratios <note>more complex ratios where the larger number contains the smaller plus several parts of it, like 5:3</note> provide an indication of the lowest nature. In these, there is a divided and multiplied communion of the soul's ratios because of their lower rank and inferiority. 

The more elevated of these rational principles are united entirely to one another. Those of the middle rank are joined not through their whole selves, but only according to their highest part. And those of the third rank join together in pieces according to their many divisions. I say, for instance, that "Essence" communicates with all the ratios, measuring all their progressions, for nothing in them is without essence. But Sameness <note>original: οὐδὲ (nor/not even); the author suggests reading ἢ (or/than). See footnote 1.</note>, being itself a "genus" or primary category, especially collects the highest points of these ratios into one communion. And Difference particularly measures their divisions and progressions. Therefore, the communion of the soul's ratios is exhibited everywhere <note>original: πλὴν (except/but); the author suggests reading πανταχοῦ (everywhere). See footnote 2.</note>. For it is either all-perfect, or it exists only according to the highest points, or according to their extension into a great multitude.

<header>BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

<page-num>83</page-num>

Furthermore, let us next examine how the seven parts ¹ are assigned their existence <term>hypostasis: the underlying reality or fundamental nature of something</term>. 

The first part is the most intellectual aspect and the peak of the soul, connecting it to "the One" itself and to the essential existence <term>hyparxis: the very core or "outflow" of a being’s existence</term> of the primary essence. For this reason, it is called "One," as it possesses the form of unity. Although its number branches out ² into a multitude, it remains held together by that union. It is likewise similar to the cause and center of the soul. For the soul remains stable through this part and does not separate itself from the whole of reality. 

The four-fold nature <term>tetrad: the number four</term> exists within the primary units <term>monads: single, indivisible units</term> because of its stability and its harmony with equality and sameness. However, the eight-fold nature <term>ogdoad: the number eight</term> exists in the units of the second order. This is due to a decrease in unity as the soul’s care <note>original: providence</note> extends down to the very edge of existence and to the most material things.³ Additionally, the three-fold nature <term>triad: the number three</term> is found in the units of the third order, serving to lead the multitude it contains back around to the "all-perfect" source. 

At the same time, these images show that the summit of the soul—though it takes the form of unity—is not "purely" one; instead, it is a multitude held together as one. Just as the unit (monad) is not without a multitude within it, yet remains a unity. But the "One" of the Gods is uniquely one. The "One" of the intellect is more "one" than "multitude," though it too is multiplied. But the "One" of the soul is equally one and many; just like the unity of the natures that come after it (which are divided among physical bodies) consists of more multitude than unity. Finally, the "One" found in physical bodies is not truly one at all, but rather a ghost and an image of unity. This is why the "Elean Guest" <note>The "Elean Guest" or "Stranger" is a character in Plato’s dialogue, *The Sophist*.</note> says that everything physical is broken into pieces; it only has a secondary <note>original: adventitious</note> unity and never stops being divided. 

The second part of the soul multiplies the part before it through generative expansions, which the two-fold nature <term>duad: the number two</term> represents, unfolding all the stages of existence. Therefore, it is called the "double" of the first part, as it imitates the "indefinite two" and the infinite nature of the intellect. 

The third part, in turn, turns the whole soul back toward its source; it is this third aspect that revolves back to the primary principles. Therefore, this part is measured by the first part because it is filled with unity from it, yet it is only partially connected to the second part. For this reason, it is said to be "triple" the first but "one-and-a-half" <term>sesquialter: a ratio of 3:2, or one and a half</term> times the second. It is only half-contained by the second (since it does not have equal power), but it is perfectly contained by the first. 

Furthermore, the fourth and fifth parts show that the soul specifically governs secondary natures. These parts are the intellectual causes of the non-physical forces that are distributed throughout bodies. They act as "planes" and "squares"; the fourth part is the square of the second, and the fifth is the square of the third part. And the fourth part, indeed, is—

The fourth part is the cause of progression <term>progression: the "proodos," or the process of the soul moving outward to create or influence lower levels of reality</term> and generation, while the fifth part is the cause of return <term>conversion: the "epistrophe," or the soul's intellectual turning back toward its source</term> and perfection. Both are planes <note>In Greek mathematics, a "plane" number is the product of two numbers (like 2×2=4 or 3×3=9)</note>; however, one is derived from the second part, existing as that part taken twice, while the other is from the third part, proceeding from it three times.¹ It appears that the first of these planes is imitative² of the generative natures that are divided among physical bodies. The second, however, is imitative of intellectual returns.³ For all knowledge turns the one who knows toward the thing being known, just as every nature desires to generate and move outward toward that which is lower than itself. 

The sixth and seventh parts contain within themselves the original causes of bodies and solid masses, for these numbers are "solids" <note>In this context, 8 (2×2×2) and 27 (3×3×3) are "solid" or cubic numbers</note>. The former comes from the second part, while the latter comes from the third part. But Plato, in his descriptions, turns the last parts back to the first and connects the furthest edges of the soul to its highest peak; he places one part as eight times the first, and the other as twenty-seven times the first. 

Thus, the essence of the soul consists of seven parts that are stable, proceeding, and returning. It serves as the cause for both the outward progression and the inward return of those essences that are divided among bodies, as well as the cause of bodies themselves. If you wish to put it this way: because the soul is assigned an underlying reality <term>hypostasis: the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing</term> between things that cannot be divided and things that can, she imitates the indivisible through the group of three <term>triad: the number three</term>, but first takes on the nature of the divisible from the group of four <term>tetrad: the number four</term>. Yet the whole of her consists of all these terms because the soul is the center of all things. 

It is also possible to divide these parts according to the "double" order <note>The sequence 1, 2, 4, 8</note> if you consider the summit of the soul and its stability, progression, and return,⁴ as well as the way things immediately following it turn back toward it, and finally the way solids are produced (or rather, the way their cause diminishes as it reaches the double ratio). You will find that this entire arrangement relates to the productive "two" <term>duad: the number two</term>. 

But again, the soul’s return to itself, and the return of the natures immediately following it, and the return of those even further removed back to the uniform and collective essence of the whole, all exist according to the "triple" order <note>The sequence 1, 3, 9, 27</note>. Therefore, the arithmetical and harmonic "middles" <note>The mathematical means used to bridge the gaps between the main numbers in the sequence</note> complete these essential intervals, which are examined according to existence itself. As we have said, some of these "middles" bind together the things that are the same, while others bind together their differences.

Furthermore, you may also say in a way that is closer to the things themselves: the soul, in one part, is united to the natures that come before it, and—

This first part is the summit of the soul. However, through the double and triple parts, the soul proceeds from the intellect and returns back to it;¹ and through the "double of the double" (the number 4) and the "triple of the triple" (the number 9), the soul proceeds from itself and returns to itself. By using itself as a bridge, it reaches its own guiding principles. Because it is filled by these higher principles, the soul is productive <note>original: "prolific"; the text corrects the Greek term from *monumos* (stable) to *gonimos* (productive)</note> ² of secondary natures. Just as its outward movement <term>progression: the "proodos," or the soul's movement toward creation</term> from itself depends on the natures that came before it, so too its return or "regression" to itself ³ depends on the return of those higher beings. 

The final parts (the "solids" 8 and 27), through which the soul creates the natures that come after it, are linked back to the very first part. This is done so that an endless circle may be revealed, with the end joined to the beginning. In this way, the entire universe becomes alive and, at the same time, filled with intellect, with the solid numbers aligned with the first principle. 

Moreover, Plato says that from these middle numbers, ratios of a "perfect fifth" <term>sesquialter: a 3:2 ratio</term>, a "perfect fourth" <term>sesquitertian: a 4:3 ratio</term>, and a "whole tone" <term>sesquioctave: a 9:8 ratio</term> become apparent. What else does he intend to show by this, other than the specific differences in the soul’s proportions? The perfect fifth ratios represent a shared connection starting from the highest parts. The perfect fourth ratios represent a shared connection through the middle terms. And the whole tone ratios represent this connection through the final terms. Consequently, the middle proportions are joined to each other by the whole tone ratio. When viewed as belonging to opposite groups, they have very little in common; yet, they are appropriately connected to both extremes.

Timæus also adds that all the perfect fourth ratios (4:3) are filled by the interval of the whole tone (9:8) in conjunction with the *leimma* <term>leimma: a "remainder" or semitone in ancient Greek music</term>. This indicates that the boundaries of all these ratios end in more specific forms of existence <note>original: "hypostases"</note>. This is because the soul contains the causes of the most divided and material things in the world. It establishes within itself the principles of their order and harmony, according to the divine will of the Creator <note>original: "demiurgic will"</note>. 

The soul, therefore, possesses the principles of harmonious outward movement and return, and of the division into things first, middle, and last. It is a single intellectual "ratio" that is made complete by all other ratios. Furthermore, it is consistent with these ideas that the entire harmony of the soul consists of four octaves <term>diapason: an octave</term>, a fifth <term>diapente: a perfect fifth</term>, and a whole tone. For since—

<meta>This page continues Proclus's technical commentary on how the Soul's mathematical structure (using ratios and intervals) allows it to harmonize the physical universe according to the divine patterns of the Intellect.</meta>

<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.</header>

Harmony exists in the world, as well as in the intellect and in the soul. For this reason, Timaeus says that the soul participates in harmony and *is* harmony. Consequently, the world participates in harmony based on the number ten <term>decadically: relating to the number 10, the "decad"</term>, while the soul does so based on the number four <term>tetradically: relating to the number 4, the "tetrad"</term>, and harmony pre-exists in the intellect as a single unit <term>monadically: relating to the number 1, the "monad"</term>. Just as the monad (1) is the cause of the tetrad (4), and the tetrad is the cause of the decad (10), so too the intellectual harmony provides for the soul's harmony, and the soul's harmony provides for the harmony of the senses.

Therefore, Timaeus conceived that a four-octave range <term>quadruple diapason: four octaves</term> is suited to the harmony of the soul, for the soul is the direct model <term>proximate paradigm</term> of the harmony found in the sensible world. Since five <note>original: "πέντε" (pente). The OCR originally had "πάντα" (all), which the translator corrects to "five."</note> figures and five centers in the universe complete the whole, the interval of a perfect fifth <term>diapente: a 3:2 ratio or perfect fifth</term> also grants the world the symphony found in its parts. Furthermore, since the universe is divided into nine parts, the whole tone <term>sesquioctave: a 9:8 ratio or whole tone</term> creates the communion between the soul and the world. 

Here you may see that the soul encompasses the world and makes it a whole according to its cause <note>Thomæus, a Renaissance translator, suggests inserting the phrase "the soul encompasses the world, and makes it a whole according to cause" here to fix a gap in the original Greek text.</note>—as one, as a group of four, as a group of five, and as divided into nine parts—harmonizing and causally containing the whole of it. For the monad (1), the tetrad (4), the pentad (5), and the ennead (9) <note>original: "enneas" (the number 9)</note> provide for us the complete set of numbers according to which all parts of the world are divided. This is why the ancients claim that the Muses and Apollo Musagetes <note>Apollo Musagetes: Apollo as the "Leader of the Muses"</note> preside over the universe; Apollo provides the single union of all its harmony, while the Muses connect the various stages of this harmony, making their number match the eight Sirens mentioned in Plato's *Republic*. 

Thus, between the monad (1) and the ennead (9), the universe is adorned according to the numbers four and five. It is adorned by four according to the four types of living beings <note>In the *Timaeus*, these are gods/stars, birds, water creatures, and land creatures.</note> which the divine model contains. It is adorned by five according to the five regular shapes <note>The five Platonic solids: the tetrahedron (pyramid), octahedron, icosahedron, cube, and dodecahedron.</note> through which the Demiurge <term>Demiurgus: the Creator or Craftsman of the universe</term> distributed all things. As Timaeus says, the Demiurge introduced the fifth idea <note>The dodecahedron, which represents the shape of the universe as a whole</note> and arranged it harmonically throughout the universe.

Starting again from the beginning, we may say that the Demiurge possesses two powers. One is effective at producing "Sameness" (as we learn in Plato's *Parmenides*), while the other produces "Difference." Through these, he both divides and binds the soul. He is also the ultimate cause of these actions, so that the soul may become the middle point of all "wholes." It is similarly united and divided, with two types of things existing above it—divine natures as pure unities, and beings as united things—and two things existing below it...

The exemplary <term>paradigmatic: serving as a model or archetype</term> causes are the "sections" and "bonds" of the Father.

For he <note>original: "εκεινος" (ekeinos). The translator suggests this refers to the Demiurgus rather than "each" (εκατερον).</note> first cuts, and then binds with unspeakable <term>ineffable: too sacred or great to be expressed in words</term> bonds. *These concepts are also dimly suggested by theologians when they speak of the Saturnian sections and bonds with which the maker of the universe is said to surround himself*, and which are mentioned by Socrates in Plato's *Cratylus* <note>In the "Cratylus," Socrates discusses the etymology of the gods; Neoplatonists interpreted the myths of Saturn (Cronus) "binding" or "cutting" as allegories for how the divine intellect organizes reality.</note>. The formal causes of the divisions are the numbers, for it is according to these that the parts are distinguished. But the formal causes of the bonds are the mathematical means <term>middles: intermediate terms in a proportion</term> and the ratios that complete them. It is impossible to observe contributing causes <term>concauses: secondary or joint causes</term> that function like matter within souls, because souls are bodiless <term>incorporeal: not composed of matter</term>.] <note>The translator Thomæus often omitted this bracketed section in his version, though it contains vital information about the "Chaldæan Oracles," which claim the Demiurgus "glitters with intellectual sections."</note>

With these points established, it is clear that the Demiurgus—acting with twofold powers (those of a dividing nature and those of a binding nature)—divides the triple-formed essence of the soul and the threefold mixture. While the whole remains exactly what it is, he uses the original causes of all division to make the soul consist of seven parts and seven members, contained within intellectual boundaries. 

The Demiurgus created the soul as the middle ground between an indivisible <term>impartible: cannot be divided</term> essence and that essence which is divisible among bodies. Because the indivisible essence is triple—existing in a state of staying <term>abiding: remaining stable in its source</term>, moving forward <term>proceeding: flowing out from its source</term>, and returning—he established a likeness of this triad in three parts of the soul. 

He hinted at the stability <note>original: "μονιμον" (monimon), correcting the OCR's "γονιμον" (productive)</note> of this essence through the first part. He represented its forward movement through the second part; for this reason, perhaps, the second part is said to be double the size of the first, because everything that moves forward must have a prior state of stability from which to move. Finally, he represented its return <term>regression: the soul's movement back toward its divine origin</term> through the third part. Thus, this part is three times the size of the first, because everything that returns must have already moved forward and existed in a stable state.

However, since the soul produces the essence that comes after it, it contains the complete <note>original: "ολας" (holas)</note> essences of that lower reality within itself. It contains the entirety of the bodiless essence—though that essence is inseparable from bodies—according to the fourth and fifth parts; but the...

<meta>This page continues the technical mathematical and metaphysical breakdown of the Soul's structure. Proclus is explaining how the "Demiurgus" (the Creator) uses specific mathematical ratios—the same ones used in music—to bind the different parts of the Soul and the universe together.</meta>

<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.</header>

...the whole of the bodily essence, according to the solid numbers <term>solid numbers: numbers representing three dimensions, specifically cubes</term>, namely the sixth and seventh parts. Or it may be said that because the soul is self-subsisting and self-activating, it produces itself and returns to its own principle according to square numbers; however, it produces all the divisible essence that comes after it according to cubic numbers. 

These seven parts are divided, as we have said, into groups of three and four. The single ratio of geometric proportion <note>original: "geometric analogy"</note> binds them in their essence. The "harmonic mean" binds them according to their similarity, and the "arithmetic mean" binds them according to their difference. 

These parts, however, are inserted between the geometric means and are said to complete the double and triple intervals <note>These refer to the musical intervals of the octave (2:1) and the twelfth (3:1), or the doubling and tripling sequences 1, 2, 4, 8 and 1, 3, 9, 27</note>. This is because all similarity and all difference are uniformly contained by the Soul's essence and the harmony that exists within it. 

From these "means" <term>middles: mathematical averages used as binding principles</term>, the various ratios known as the *sesquialter* (3:2), the *sesquitertian* (4:3), and the *sesquioctave* (9:8) become apparent. This collection of ratios acts as a binding and connecting force, just like the "means" do, but in a more specific way. While these are particular ratios, each of the "means" consists of many ratios, which are either the same or different. Just as a full proportion is more comprehensive than a single ratio, these "means" provide a greater cause for the soul to hold its inner complexity together, since they intellectually extend <note>The original Greek *dioikousan* (governing) is corrected here to *dieikousan* (pervading or extending through).</note> through the whole of it. Therefore, the 3:2 and 4:3 ratios are more specific bonds and are contained within the "means"—not as mathematical calculations of distance, but as a primary cause and a more complete existence <term>hypostasis: the underlying reality or substance</term>.

Furthermore, these bonds contain the second and third stages of the ratios. The *sesquialter* (3:2) ratio tightens the harmony of the ratios through the five centers. The *sesquitertian* (4:3) ratio demonstrates its power through the four elements that are everywhere, making all things intelligible and related to each other. Finally, the *sesquioctave* (9:8) ratio harmonizes the division into nine and eight. 

Because the world consists of eight parts and also of nine, the ancient writers sometimes established eight Sirens and at other times nine Muses as the rulers of the universe, since the harmony of the whole of things proceeds from these numbers. The 4:3 and 3:2 ratios are more fundamental than the 9:8 ratios because they provide a more perfect symphony and represent the harmonious structure of the world using smaller numbers. In our physical world, these divisions are separated from each other in the things that participate in them; but in the incorporeal "reasons" <term>logoi: the rational, spiritual blueprints of reality</term>...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, specifically focusing on the mathematical proportions used to describe the creation of the Soul. # PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.]

How these numbers develop the essence of the soul of the universe is not easy to explain for those who do not look to Plato’s specific concepts. This is clear from the disagreement among interpreters; the way modern commentators oppose the ancient ones demonstrates the difficulty of this theory. 

Some believe that the first seven terms—which we have assumed are like the numbers shown in the whole diagram—refer to the seven planetary spheres. Others link them to the distances of these spheres from the center of the earth, where they place the <term>monad: the number one, representing unity or the point of origin</term>. Others again refer them to the motions of the spheres. <insert>Others apply them to the sizes of the stars, while others adapt them to the speeds of the celestial orbs.</insert> <note>These bracketed words are missing in the original Greek manuscript and were added from the Latin translation by Leonicus Thomæus.</note> Still others refer them to different explanations of this kind. 

Their interpretations, however, face many difficulties. Among these is the fact that they do not agree with the observations and demonstrations of recent astronomers. Furthermore, Plato nowhere defines the size, distance, or speed of the stars; though he admits that one star is larger than another, he does not specify by how much or in what way. 

Most importantly, the subject he is discussing here is <term>psychogony: the generation or "birth" of the soul</term>, not <term>cosmogony: the generation of the physical world</term>. While it is necessary to achieve the same results in both the soul and the physical world in a certain sense, it is proper to first <gloss>original: *poteron* (whether); corrected to *proteron* (first)</gloss> examine the powers within the soul itself, as well as the underlying reasons for the things that happen outside of it. 

Additionally, their explanation of the numbers given by Plato is especially contradictory. In Plato's terms, the number in the fifth position is greater than the one in the sixth (for instance, 9 is greater than 8). <gloss>The original Greek text mistakenly used the word for "sixth" (*hektados*); it has been corrected to "eighth" (*oktados*) to match the number 8.</gloss> However, in the systems these interpreters propose, the fifth magnitude or interval (or whatever they choose to call it) is always smaller than the sixth. Therefore, their explanations do not match the terms Plato actually used.

After these, there is another group of interpreters who provide a more significant explanation of these details. Amelius—not adopting the opinion he says was held by Plotinus (which was shared in Plotinus's unwritten or oral lectures and has been sufficiently refuted by later thinkers) <note>The beginning of this sentence is missing in the original Greek but is supplied from the Latin version by Leonicus Thomæus.</note>—attempts to explain these terms in a different way. Since the soul encompasses all worldly natures—such as gods, daemons <note>original: "dæmons"; in Neoplatonism, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans</note>, and humans—Amelius says that, in one sense, the soul contains every worldly being according to the monad...

<summary>Proclus critiques various astronomical interpretations of Plato’s "psychogony," arguing that the mathematical ratios describe the Soul's internal essence rather than physical planetary distances or sizes. He begins to introduce the more metaphysical interpretation of Amelius, a student of Plotinus.</summary>

One of the philosophers who came after Amelius <note>Amelius was a 3rd-century Neoplatonist and a prominent student of Plotinus.</note> attributes this opinion to him. For the term "God" is used in many different ways: not only are the <term>superessential: that which exists beyond being itself</term> and the pure intellect called Gods, but also divine souls and divine bodies. He believes that the soul of the universe contains the divine number through its unity; however, it contains the <term>dæmoniacal: relating to dæmons, spirits that act as intermediaries between gods and humans</term> category through its <term>duad: the number two</term> and <term>triad: the number three</term>. Since dæmons depend on the Gods and watch over us, the soul uses the number two to activate their care for us, and uses the number three to guide their return to the Gods. As we have said, their relationship is twofold, because they exist between the Gods and us.

Furthermore, using the <term>tetrad: the number four</term> and <term>ennead: the number nine</term>, the soul cares for all human life. This life is also twofold, divided into a superior and an inferior part. By the nine, it gives order to the more excellent life, and by the four, it organizes the lower life. Finally, through the <term>octad: the number eight</term> and the number twenty-seven, it reaches out to everything, down to the lowliest of things. It brings tame animals to perfection through odd numbers and savage animals through even numbers. It orders each thing with appropriate powers: lesser things are everywhere governed by even numbers, while more sacred and powerful things—those more closely linked to the Gods—are governed by odd numbers.

Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a significant Neoplatonist philosopher and the primary editor of Plotinus's writings.</note>, however, in an impressive way (though these points were mentioned earlier), proves with many arguments that the soul is harmonized and that it fills the entire world with harmony. He draws this conclusion because the soul is a "multitude" (composed of many parts). Since it is a multitude, it must either be disordered or harmonized. It is correct to claim the latter and not the former. Since it is the creation of the <term>intellect: the divine mind or 'Nous'</term>, how could it be chaotic and unharmonized? He also reasons that the soul guides everything in the world according to <term>harmonic reasons: the underlying mathematical principles or ratios of harmony</term>, and links the birth of animals and their unified organization to the universe itself.

He does not explain what these "reasons" are that exist in the soul’s <term>hypostasis: its underlying reality or substance</term>, nor does he think they need much attention. He simply says the soul’s essence contains these harmonic principles, not just as copies of things or basic starting points, but as the glue that holds its many powers together. For if the soul is truly both <term>impartible: indivisible</term> and <term>partible: capable of being divided</term>, it must be both a single unity and a multitude. If it is a multitude, it must be either infinite or countable. It is impossible, however, for it to be infinite, because an infinite multitude is disordered. Therefore, it must be countable. But if it is countable, it must consist of either unharmonized or harmonized parts. It is, however, impossible that it should consist of unhar—

It therefore entirely consists of harmonized parts; but if it is made of harmonized parts, it must necessarily exist according to the most excellent harmony, since it is the first of all harmonized things. The most excellent harmony, however, is that which follows the <term>diatonic genus: the most natural and standard scale in Greek music theory, often considered the most stable and "venerable"</term>, for this is sacred, abundant, and grand. But the divine Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist who introduced a more religious and magical (theurgic) element into the philosophy.</note> extols these numbers with all his power, as exhibiting certain admirable characteristics. He calls the <term>monad: the number one; the principle of unity</term> the cause of sameness and union; the <term>duad: the number two</term> the supplier of progression and separation; and the <term>triad: the number three</term> the leader of the regression <note>In Neoplatonism, "regression" or "reversion" refers to the process by which a created thing turns back toward its divine source.</note> of the things that have proceeded. He also says that the <term>tetrad: the number four</term> is truly all-harmonic, containing all ratios within itself and unfolding the second orderly distribution of things. He states that the <term>ennead: the number nine</term> produces true perfection and similarity, being a "perfect number made from perfect numbers" and sharing in the nature of sameness. 

But he calls the <term>ogdoad: the number eight</term> the cause of universal progression and of pervading through all things. Lastly, he says that the number twenty-seven effects the regression of the lowest things back to the first, so that on each side of the tetrad (four) there may be permanency, progression, and regression—occurring primarily on one side and secondarily on the other. For the ennead (nine) has an alliance to the monad (one), being "a new one" <note>original: *$\epsilon\nu\ \nu\acute{\epsilon}o\nu\ \text{o}\tilde{\upsilon}\sigma\alpha$* (en neon ousa). Through the first set of numbers, therefore, the soul imparts stability, progression, and regression to simpler natures; but through the latter set, it imparts these to more complex natures. The tetrad (four) is the middle because it is a square, possessing permanency; but because it is "evenly-even" <note>An ancient mathematical term for a number that can be divided by two repeatedly down to the number one (like 4, 8, 16).</note>, it has progression; and because it is filled with all ratios from the monad, it has regression. These, however, are symbols of divine and secret things.

After this explanation, which is so admirable, the philosopher Theodorus <note>Theodorus of Asine (c. 275–360 AD), a student of Iamblichus who developed his own complex system of numerology.</note>, proceeding on a path peculiar to himself, says that the soul is the third principle after the one primary principle of all things. He identifies one soul as <term>fontal: acting as a fountain or source</term>, another as universal, and a third as the soul of this specific universe. He also says that the first of these is indivisible, the second is divisible, and that the third possesses all-various divisions. Since there is this triple difference in souls, that which is "soul itself"...
