And the third soul is that which is shaped <note>original: "fabricated"</note> through straight lines and circles. Having, therefore, made this division of the birth of the soul and the types of souls, he considers the distribution into parts and the seven terms as belonging to the universal soul alone. Likewise, referring these terms to the division of the universal soul, he thinks it necessary that celestial natures should be produced by this soul from the double order <note>original: "duple"</note>, but earthly <note>original: "sublunary"</note> natures from the triple order. 

For he assigns appropriate numbers to each of the elements: to earth indeed 7, to fire 11, to water 9, and to air 13. For the geometrical proportion—which is 1, 2, 4 [the sum of which is 7]—pertains to earth; perhaps indeed because of the name, and perhaps also because as earth contains the remaining elements, so the geometric proportion encompasses the other middle points. 

But the arithmetical proportion, which pertains to water, is 2, 3, 4; it connects with earth through the number 2, and also because it is especially friendly to large quantities and consists of an element that is the most numerous of all others, namely the <term>icosahedron: a three-dimensional shape with twenty triangular faces</term>. 

And the harmonical proportion, which pertains to air, is 3, 4, 6; this is because it connects with the arithmetical proportion through two of its terms, 3 and 4, which are the larger numbers in the former but the smaller terms in the latter proportion. Since, however, the harmonic middle is twofold, consisting either in the double ratio of the extremes or in the triple ratio—for Plato assumes it as the middle of either double or triple terms—by making the extremes 3 and 6 (according to the double of the extremes), he obtains the specific element of the air, namely the <term>octahedron: a three-dimensional shape with eight triangular faces</term>. This shape has 6 according to the angles, but 4 according to the base of the two pyramids, and 3 according to the surface <note>original: "superficies"</note> of the octahedron, which is <term>trigonic: triangular in shape</term>. 

But according to the other harmonic middle, which is 2, 3, 6, he obtains the element of fire; because these, according to the two terms 3 and 6, connect with the terms before them [3, 4, 6], which are there the extremes, but are here the...

...greater terms; and moreover, because the element of fire has 6 edges <note>original: "sides"</note>, but twice the <term>tetrad: the number four</term> in its angles and surfaces <note>original: "superficies"</note>, and a triangular base. Very properly, therefore, does the number 7 pertain to earth, 9 to water, 13 to air, and 11 to fire; these ratios are calculated from the numbers mentioned above, from which they are produced. For 7 consists of 1, 2, and 4; 9 consists of 2, 3, and 4; 13 consists of 3, 4, and 6; and 11 consists of 2, 3, and 6. Each of these has two terms in common with the number next to it, just as the physical elements have two sides in common. From the combination of these, a triple order is established. Among the middle terms of the proportions that are close to each other, one is greater than the other, which is also the case with the extremes. This is evident in the relationship between earth and water, and between fire and air,¹ as shown in the given terms.

Again, he attributes the number 15 to celestial natures. He assigns the <term>monad: the number one; unity</term> to the "circle of the same" <note>The "circle of the same" refers to the celestial equator or the sphere of fixed stars, representing eternal stability.</note>, but the double <term>hebdomad: a group of seven</term> to the "circle of the different" <note>The "circle of the different" refers to the zodiac or the planetary orbits.</note>. This is due to the twofold rotation of each—that is, the rotation of the spheres themselves and the stars contained within them, of which there are seven spheres and seven stars. 

These things, which are asserted mathematically, provide a theory that is quite elegant. However, how they are assimilated to the topics now being discussed, and how they may be interpreted in a Pythagorean manner, is not addressed by Theodorus in a way that would satisfy anyone who pays close attention to what Plato says. All these details are indeed cleverly invented, but he limits his analysis of the Platonic diagram to simple whole numbers <note>original: "monadic numbers"</note>. He fails to look at the ratios resulting from them, which would allow him to include everything: the middle terms, the <term>sesquialter: a ratio of 3 to 2, or a musical fifth</term> and <term>sesquitertian: a ratio of 4 to 3, or a musical fourth</term> ratios, the <term>sesquioctaves: a ratio of 9 to 8, or a musical whole tone</term>, and the <term>lemmas: the small intervals or 'leavings' in a musical scale, specifically the Pythagorean limma</term>. It is simply not possible to discover these in the basic numbers he uses in his distribution of the elements and the heavens.

After these points, therefore, let us examine another method of discussion. This mode is adopted by our preceptor <note>This likely refers to Syrianus, Proclus's teacher and predecessor as head of the Neoplatonic Academy.</note>; it generates not just one, but many admirable concepts, and it is the same method we used previously. He says that each of these things may be considered in two ways: first, in the whole soul of the universe as a single unit, according to its union; and second, in the many ratios and the multitude contained within it, according to its division. For the soul is both a unity and a multitude; it is both one reason and the sum of all-various forms. In this way, it imitates the <term>demiurgic: relating to the Demiurge, the divine craftsman of the universe</term> wholeness and the separation of the Father’s powers. First, therefore, we must understand what the soul is according to its whole self—remaining and proceeding...

---

¹ For example, in the numbers 1, 2, and 4 (which pertain to earth) and in 2, 3, and 4 (which pertain to water), the middle term 3 is greater than the middle term 2. This is also the case in the numbers 3, 4, and 6 (air) and 2, 3, and 6 (fire). Regarding the extremes, the extreme 2 is greater than 1, and the extreme 3 is greater than 2.

<summary>Proclus critiques Theodorus's numerical assignment of specific totals to the elements and heavens, arguing that a true Pythagorean analysis must account for the complex musical ratios (fifths, fourths, and tones) inherent in the soul's structure. He introduces a more comprehensive method from his teacher that views the soul as both a unified whole and a divided multitude of ratios.</summary>

# BOOK III.] THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 95

...proceeding from itself and returning to itself. It also providentially looks after both the immaterial and pure forms of worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note> natures, and all physical bodies and the divisible <term>partible: divisible into parts; the material realm</term> essence. Understanding this as well, we must say that the soul remains stable according to its first part, but moves forward <note>original: "proceeds"</note> according to its second part. This forward movement is understood as divine, not caused by emotion <note>original: "passion"</note> or weakness <note>original: "imbecility"</note>. Finally, it returns to itself according to its third part. For the power to make things perfect comes to beings from this return. 

Being completely perfect and firmly established <note>The original Greek uses *enidrymenēn* (ἐνιδρυμένην), meaning "seated" or "fixed."</note> in the realm of things known by the mind <note>original: "intelligibles"</note>, and remaining eternally within the Intellect, it also looks after lower <note>original: "secondary"</note> natures. In one way, it watches over the natures directly dependent on it; in another way, it watches over physical matter <note>original: "solid masses"</note> itself. It also cares for each of these in two ways. The natures that directly share in the soul's essence come from it and return to it. They go forth according to the creative <note>original: "prolific"</note> power of the soul's fourth part, but they return to their single cause according to the uplifting <note>original: "re-elevating"</note> power of its fifth part. 

We can also see these "solid numbers" in physical bodies. They go forth according to the number eight <note>original: "octuple"</note> of the first part—this being a <term>dyadic: based on the number two; dual</term> and solid number (2 cubed, or 2x2x2). It is simultaneously productive and able to reach out to all things. However, they return according to the number twenty-seven (3 cubed, or 3x3x3), which represents a solid turning back <note>original: "conversion"</note> because it is <term>triadic: based on the number three</term> and belongs to the nature of "Sameness" <note>In Platonic philosophy, "Sameness" represents stability, the eternal, and the divine, often associated with odd numbers.</note>. For such is the nature of the odd number. 

Therefore, there are three movements outward <note>original: "progressions"</note> and three movements back <note>original: "regressions"</note>, all surrounding the single and unified permanence of the soul. For this reason, there are also three even and three odd numbers that come from the <term>monad: the number one; the original unity</term> and are interwoven <note>original: "complicated"</note> with each other, because the soul itself also goes out and returns. As it goes out, it creates its own first containers and that which is first given shape <note>original: "invested with figure"</note>. In creating these, it gives them dimension <note>original: "interval"</note> and physical size <note>original: "bulk"</note>. But in its return to itself, it makes these shapes spherical. By making it this way, the soul produces the world within itself. It carries out this outward movement according to an even <note>original: *artiakōs* (ἀρτιακῶς)</note> number, but the return according to an odd number. Both of these are done "cubically" because this involves the creation and return of solid shapes. Therefore, the movement out and the movement back are threefold: the first is without shape, the second has shape in a primary way, and the third <note>The text suggests adding "primarily, or" (πρώτως, ἢ) to complete the sense of the degrees of shape.</note> in a secondary way; but all of these exist as they do in numbers.

Next, we must follow the theory according to the many parts within the soul and say that the ratios within it contain other ratios,

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s detailed commentary on the mathematical composition of the World Soul as described in Plato’s Timaeus. # PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.]

## PAGE 98

Some of these ratios are divided within the soul as wholes, while others are divided as parts. <note>Note 1: In the original Greek, it is necessary to read *merōn* (of parts) instead of *merē* (parts).</note> Some are universal <note>original: "total"</note>, others are generic, others specific, and others are partial. The universal ratios are those of the mathematical means <note>original: "middles"</note>; the generic ratios are those found in double <note>original: "duple"</note> or triple terms; and the specific ratios are those categorized under these. <note>Note 2: These are the *hypologi* (the second terms in a ratio), which were explained previously.</note> For each of these exists in many different ways <note>original: "multifarious subsistence"</note>. 

The partial ratios are the 9:8 ratios <term>sesquioctaves: a ratio of 9 to 8, representing a whole tone in ancient music theory</term> and the remainders <term>leimmas: from the Greek *leimma*, meaning "remnant"; the small interval left over when a scale is divided, similar to a semitone</term>. These are the parts into which all 3:2 <term>sesquialter: a ratio of 3 to 2, or a musical fifth</term> and 4:3 ratios <term>sesquitertian: a ratio of 4 to 3, or a musical fourth</term> are divided. 

We must also say that the soul contains the single unity of these ratios through its "essential monad" (its principle of oneness). It contains the division of the ratios through the progression of the "duad" (the principle of twoness); and it encompasses them <note>Note 3: Following the translation of Leonico Tomeo <note>original: "Thomæus"</note>, the original text here should include the words: "the progression of the duad, and the comprehension of them through..."</note> through multiple terms. For these multiple terms encompass the "super-particular" ratios <term>super-particular: a ratio where the numerator is one greater than the denominator, such as 3:2 or 4:3</term> and have an essence more universal than they do. In the same way, the super-particulars encompass the 9:8 ratios and the remainders; the former relate to them as species, while the latter are arranged as parts. 

To suggest that geometric proportion alone encompasses the other two means <note>the arithmetic and harmonic means</note> would imply that the soul’s entire essence is a kind of "divine geometry" <note>original: "demiurgic geometry"</note>. For elsewhere, Plato calls this analogy "the judgment of Zeus" <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>. Furthermore, it shows that when these two means are viewed alongside and included within the geometric mean, they arrange all things in an orderly way according to justice. However, when they are separated from it, they become the causes of confusion and injustice. 

For distributing equal portions to unequal things is entirely unjust, as is the joining of opposites without a certain geometric equality. Therefore, the harmonic mean requires geometric analogy to bring opposites together elegantly, just as Plato did when he harmonized fire and earth using the two intervening elements of air and water. The arithmetic mean likewise, when working together with the geometric, possesses correctness <note>original: "rectitude"</note> in its operations. In this way, what is unequal in unequal things becomes equal. <note>Note 4: For example, in the numbers 1, 2, 3, and 6, which are in geometric proportion, the numbers 1, 2, and 3 are also in arithmetic proportion. While the differences between the numbers are unequal (the difference between 2 and 3 is 1, but between 3 and 6 is 3), the ratio remains consistent. Therefore, by joining the arithmetic with the geometric mean, the inequality in the numbers is balanced out.</note> 

By distributing equals to unequals, the soul preserves its own unique character and shows a distribution based on merit <note>original: "desert"</note>, which is the special privilege of the geometric mean. Furthermore, we must say that the soul imitates the first principles of all things.

<summary>Proclus explains how the World Soul utilizes different mathematical means (geometric, arithmetic, and harmonic) to ensure cosmic justice, balancing opposites and distributing portions according to merit rather than simple equality.</summary>

Through the first part, which is the single cause of all wholes; through the double <note>original: "duple"</note> progression, the dual-natured principles that follow *the One*; through the even and odd numbers, the male and female aspects of the Gods; through the three-part <term>triadic: related to a group of three</term> division of each, the intellectual triads; and through the group of seven <term>hebdomad: a set or group of seven</term> terms, the unified and intellectual group of seven. 

Through the first part also, the soul makes <note>Note 1: The original text uses the word "calls" (*kalei*), but it is necessary to read "makes" (*poiei*) here.</note> the world to be a self-perfecting God; through the dual <term>dyadic: based on the number two</term> progression, it displays the multitude and variety within the world; through the division of even and odd numbers, it divides the whole of the male and female, from the Gods themselves down to the plants. According to the two and three <note>original: "duad and triad"</note>, it establishes the male and female among the Gods; according to the four and nine <note>original: "tetrad and ennead"</term>, it establishes those in the classes of beings superior to us; and according to the two cubes (8 and 27), it establishes the male and female which extend as far as the terrestrial and ultimate <note>Note 2: The original text uses "terrestrial" (*chthonion*), but as "land-dwelling" (*chersaion*) was used just before it, it is clearly necessary to read "ultimate" or "last" (*eschaton*).</note> species of life. 

But through the group of seven <note>original: "heptad"</note> terms, the soul connects and guards all things, provides for them intellectually, and disposes the wholes in an orderly and becoming manner, stably and invariably. Likewise, through this, it adorns the parts of these wholes, the parts of those parts, and whatever may exist among the very last of things—which are in themselves irrational and serve as the remnant <term>leimma: the "leftover" or remainder in a mathematical proportion; here, the final, least organized parts of creation</term> of the world's fabrication. Hence, in accordance with these concepts, we may be able to interpret the various words of Plato, and by looking to these, we may resolve many doubts. Let us, therefore, refer Plato's words one by one to these principles, according to the explanations of our teacher.

In the first place, we should note that the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: the divine Craftsman or Creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy</term> did not merely "insert" the parts into the soul, but rather "took them away" from it as if they were already <note>Note 3: The original text says "knew" (*edei*), but it is necessary to read "already" (*ede*).</note> within it. This action of taking them away and then using them to complete the essence of the soul indicates to us that this mixture is not merely the "subject" or "matter" of the soul. It is not like an object that is given a shape by an artist. Instead, because the soul is a "form" itself, it is the fullness of all forms. Thus, the ideas of "indefiniteness" and "matter"—which more recent interpreters claim exist in the realm of the intellect—have no place in this theory. 

Secondly, arranging all the other parts (the terms 2, 3, 4, 9, 8, and 27) in relation to the first part gives the highest dignity to the monad <term>monad: the number one, representing unity, the source, and the ruling principle</term>. It does not allow us to think of the monad as the public imagines it—as merely the smallest unit of quantity or the "matter" of a number. Instead, it leads us to consider the monad as the ruling principle of the soul's entire essence, the root of all the powers contained within it, and the Vesta <note>Vesta: The Roman goddess of the hearth; here used to mean the fixed, central, and sacred core of the soul.</note> of the soul.

number that completes it. Next, doesn't the phrase *the double of the first part* agree with what we have said? The double is formed entirely by the duad <term>duad: the number two, or the principle of duality</term> and is lower than the essential existence <term>hyparxis: the highest, most unified part of a being's essence</term> which is characterized by unity. It also moves toward multiplicity, increasing in quantity while decreasing in power. This is also how the soul's progression works. While the soul stays within its most divine part—and as Orpheus says, "establishing its head in intellect" <note>original: intellect/divine mind</note>—it moves outward from there according to its own duality. It moves into itself, creating the many rational principles and the various forms it contains. 

After moving outward, however, it returns to its source, creating a certain essential circle. Through this return <term>regression: the act of returning to a source</term>, it is linked to its own creative <note>original: "prolific"</note> power, by which it produced itself, and to the monad <term>monad: the number one; the principle of unity</term> that gives it stability and makes it a single whole. This is because the power that perfects and turns things back <note>original: "convertive"</note> is joined to both the creative cause and the unifying cause. To put it briefly: just as life comes from "Being," but "Intellect" is joined to both life and "Being," the soul moves out from its creative cause, but its return is toward both its causes. It relates in a ratio of one and a half <term>sesquialter: a ratio of 3:2, where the larger number contains the smaller once plus a half</term> to the cause immediately above it, but in a triple ratio (3:1) to the cause beyond that. It is fitting that the returning form should seek the whole of its source and reduce the division created by the 1.5 ratio. Since the "double" (2:1) is dominated by duality, the 1.5 ratio (3:2) is similar to it but reduces the degree of subordination.

Furthermore, it is clear that the "triple" (the number three) represents the third stage in the return from the original source. Additionally, because the triad <term>triad: the number three</term> is the first number and is essentially a whole—having a beginning, middle, and end—it is like the monad (the One), which holds all multiplicity in a unified way <note>original: "unically"</note>. Because of this, Plato shows that the soul, which consists of three wholes, is itself triple. He divides it into what stays still (abiding), what moves out (proceeding), and what returns (converting), following the division of the divine classes <term>genera: types or classes of divine beings</term>. In those divine classes, there are also three types: one that stays, one that goes out, and one that returns to its source. One cause creates stability and essence; another leads the way for creation and expansion; and the third brings perfection and raises lower natures back up to higher ones. In the words that follow, he shows how

The soul beautifies secondary natures based on its own essence. Before the soul gives out powers or energies, Plato shows that it contains these ratios within itself. From these ratios, and through them, it governs the first things that participate in its nature, as well as those things shaped by it in a secondary stage of separation. The soul itself functions entirely like a monad <term>monad: a single, indivisible unit representing unity and the source of all numbers</term>, while these lower things imitate its patterns of moving outward and returning. 

Before these lower things exist, the soul moves outward in a dual way <term>dyadically: in a pair or twofold manner</term> but returns in a triple way <term>triadically: in a group of three</term>. The part of the soul that moves outward is separated from the part that remains still; this is a "double" separation. However, the part that returns (or "converts") is separated from the source by only a half. <note>original footnote 1: It is necessary here to supply the word "ratio" (original: λόγον / logos).</note> <note>original footnote 2: For "them" (original: αυτὰς) in this place, it is necessary to read "its" (original: αὐτῆς).</note> <note>original footnote 3: That which moves outward is separated doubly from that which remains: the double ratio of 2 to 1 is "doubly separated" from 1. But that which returns is separated from the remaining principle by half, because the ratio of 3 to 2 differs from 1 by 1/2. Thus, the outward and returning movements are considered based on their relationship—their proximity and alliance—to unity. The outward movement relates to unity immediately, while the return relates to unity through the number 2 as a middle step.</note> 

Separation is the unique feature of moving outward (progression), while sameness and similarity are features of the return (conversion). When the soul returns, it becomes like the part that remains still. It becomes "all" instead of just "one." Instead of being a whole that exists *before* its parts, it becomes a whole made *of* parts. It seems to be triple the size of the part that remains, yet it has less power and simply contains all its internal parts.

> "Then a fourth part, double of the second; a fifth, triple of the third; a sixth, eight times the first; and a seventh, twenty-seven times the first."

The soul's perfect essence is understood through these numbers. One part of this essence stays still in the soul, another moves out from it, and a third returns to it. Because we need to examine its parts and the causes behind them, Plato explains these in great detail, showing us how the soul contains the "ideas" <term>ideas: the divine blueprints or forms of all things</term> of everything. 

Therefore, through the fourth and fifth parts, the soul understands the principles of everything that first participates in its nature. It contains their outward movement through the fourth part and their return through the fifth. <note>original footnote 4: The phrase "but their return through the fifth" was omitted in the original Greek and has been restored.</note> [Therefore, Plato relates the fourth part to the second, and the fifth to the third, because parts imitate the wholes they come from and exist in a similar way to them. <note>original footnote 5: These words are supplied from the version of the scholar Leonhardus Thomæus.</note>] Finally, through the sixth and seventh parts, the soul constitutes—as we have observed before—solid masses themselves; gene-

For the total form of the soul is completed by the progression of these parts. You may see how the numbers and the order of the progression are adapted to the soul. For both the last terms are triadic <term>triadic: relating to a group of three or the number three</term>. For the number eight itself is, in a certain respect, triadic, as it proceeds into the third order of powers. We have, therefore, the single wholeness of the soul in the mixture, its triple <note>original: τριπλοvν (triploun). In accordance with this, the soul also creates whole things according to each form of providence. In its wholeness, we shall find it containing the triple form, but in the triple, it contains the tetradic <term>tetradic: relating to a group of four or the number four</term> form, always gathering parts into a union through these wholes.

They likewise call actions of this kind "sections" and "bonds." According to these powers, therefore, the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: the divine Craftsman or creator of the material world in Platonic philosophy</term> is now said to cut off parts from the soul's wholeness, separating its essence into creative bonds. He is also said to bind those parts again with certain bonds through the "middles" <note>original: "media" or "means" in a mathematical sense</note>. Through these middles, he causes that which is divided to be connected, just as through the sections he causes that which is united to be divided. 

Plato’s words make it clear that these things are consistent with theological principles. Let us, however, see how they are so by considering more minutely what he says. Plato shows that the whole soul is, in itself, of the same essence, consists of similar parts, and is—so to speak—of the same color, being entirely intellectual and rational. He demonstrates this by making both the whole and its parts from the same mixture. The parts cut off from it are specific, divided essences within it. He also shows that there is a certain rank of first, middle, and last forms by adding the word *still*. 

We use the word *still* <note>Plato uses this to indicate a progression or a continuing of the process</note> when we see the same form becoming more hidden or dim; we do this with the celestial essence, because we perceive a certain change within it and yet a resemblance to divine bodies is preserved there. Therefore, so that we do not assume every "reason" <term>reason: here, *logos*, meaning a rational principle or mathematical ratio</term> in the soul has the same rank, Plato adds the word *still* to indicate what we have mentioned. For the further inward we go, investigating the "means of means" <note>the intermediate levels between already intermediate steps</note>, the more we will encounter specific, particular forms. This is because the things contained are more "partial" <note>more specific or individual</note> than the natures that contain them, and the containing natures are more divine than those they encompass. 

The world likewise imitates this: regarding the realm of generation <term>generation: the physical world of birth, death, and change</term>, it has a divine body, but surrounding that body is the whole soul. All these previously mentioned sections of the soul—both the generative (which are the double intervals) and the perfective (which are the triple intervals)—encompass more specific rational principles. Through these, the parts of the universe are ordered, reaching even to the very last of things.

> "So that in each interval¹ there are two middles <note>mathematical means</note>, one of which exceeds and is exceeded by the same proportional part of the extremes; but the other, by an equal number surpasses one extreme, and by an equal number is surpassed by the other."²

In these words, it must be observed in the first place that the two middles are—

...is said by Plato to be comprehended in the geometric middle. Afterward, he places the harmonic middle before the arithmetical middle, as it is superior to it. For although the arithmetical middle possesses spontaneity, simplicity, and an alliance to "sameness" (since equality is a form of sameness), and although Plato shows that in politics the arithmetical middle produces friendship because it embraces equality according to number—just as the harmonic is effective for justice, since it regards distribution according to desert <note>merit or what is deserved</note>—and even though the arithmetical middle is assigned "quantity in itself" <note>original: *posotes*, referring to absolute numbers</note> while the harmonic is assigned "relative quantity" <note>original: *pelikotes*, referring to magnitude or the size of parts relative to a whole</note> (the former being concerned with the absolute quantity of parts, the latter with relative quantity, since a third or fourth part is a feature of relative quantity); despite all this, the harmonic middle is still properly placed before the arithmetical because it is closer to the geometric middle. It provides sameness in the extremes and distributes greater ratios to larger terms and smaller ratios to smaller terms; because of this, it is better suited to distribution based on merit.

It must be said, therefore, that the harmonic middle binds together all the "psychical sameness" <note>the inherent consistency of the soul</note> and grants an unbreakable communion to celestial beings. It distributes greater powers and motions to the larger circles, and lesser powers to the smaller ones. For the spheres that contain others move swifter than the spheres they contain. 

Conversely, the arithmetical middle connects all the "difference" in the soul and grants a communion to sublunary <note>earthly, or below the moon</note> natures through an equal exchange. Among these earthly things, one thing is not acted upon any more than it acts upon others. This property of being changed into one another is equally inherent in all the elements of generation according to arithmetical equality. This equality also grants faster and greater motions to more refined natures, and slower, smaller motions to those consisting of larger parts.

> *“But as sesquialter <note>a 3:2 ratio, or a perfect fifth in music</note>, sesquitertian <note>a 4:3 ratio, or a perfect fourth</note>, and sesquioctave <note>a 9:8 ratio, or a whole tone</note> intervals were produced from those bonds in the former intervals, he filled all the sesquitertian parts with the interval of the sesquioctave.”*

It is evident from what has been said that from the two middles mentioned above—the harmonic and the arithmetical bonds produced in the intervals of the double and triple terms—the sesquitertian and sesquialter ratios appearing in those middles are divided by the interval of the sesquioctave. This will also be clear if you consider the terms 6, 8, 12, and 18.<sup>1</sup> For in these, the double and...

...triple interval consists of sesquitertian <note>a 4:3 ratio</note> and sesquialter <note>a 3:2 ratio</note> ratios. But how do these things align with what was said before? We reply that they must be understood as following from them. For just as the two "middles" divide the universe into two parts, these sesquitertian and sesquialter ratios establish a more specific order of things. These ratios organize things that exist as complete wholes but are also "parts of parts." Each is a whole according to the leading term <note>original: *prologos*</note>, but a part according to the following term <note>original: *hypologos*</note>, and a part of a part relative to the way the One transcends all else.

Within each of the celestial spheres, there are divine, dæmonic <note>original: *dæmoniacal*, referring to spiritual intermediaries between gods and humans</note>, and partial types of souls, such as our own. The secondary divine beings fully participate in the wholeness of those above them. However, the dæmonic beings—though they participate in the wholeness of the divine—only do so in a specific way. For this reason, they are called "more partial," as they cannot receive all the divine characteristics at once. Even more partial dæmonic beings participate in different characteristics at different times, rather than always keeping the same ones. 

Consequently, the soul contains the mathematical ratios of these beings in a partial way. It contains the "multiple" ratios <note>such as 2:1 or 3:1</note> by participating in the whole; it contains the "superparticular" ratios <note>where the numerator is one unit larger than the denominator, like 3:2 or 4:3</note> through its most important part; and it contains the "superpartient" ratios <note>more complex ratios where the numerator is larger than the denominator by more than one unit</note> through a diverse and divided connection between those who participate and the things being participated in. 

Through these ratios, the elements and the celestial spheres are organized. They participate in a "third wholeness" while simultaneously being parts of the two main sections of the universe, since every whole also contains parts within itself. Different characteristics belong to different spheres <note>For "a different sphere" here, it is necessary to read "of a different sphere."</note>, and different numbers correspond to different elements. The sesquioctave ratio <note>a 9:8 ratio, representing a whole tone in music</note> completes the sesquitertian and sesquialter ratios. It generates the full range of these cosmic parts and harmonizes them with their proper wholes. 

You can see, then, that just as in mathematics the geometric middle encompasses the other two middles, and those middles encompass the sesquitertian and sesquialter ratios, and these in turn encompass the sesquioctaves—in the same way, the soul's own wholeness creates the entire world. According to its essential duality <note>original: *duad*</note>, the soul divides the universe into two parts and produces the primary parts of the universe (which are themselves secondary wholes). According to the principles of the "third wholeness," it organizes and beautifies the spheres; and according to the numbers suited to these parts, it fills them with the appropriate forms and components.

We may also put it this way: This universe has whole spheres; and

<meta>This page continues Proclus's discussion on how the World Soul organizes the cosmos. He is explaining how specific musical and mathematical ratios (like the 4:3 and 3:2 intervals) correspond to different ranks of beings—divine, dæmonic, heroic, and human—within the celestial spheres.</meta>

<page-num>104</page-num>

It also has divine, dæmonic <note>original: *dæmoniacal*, referring to spiritual intermediaries</note>, and soul-governed <note>original: *psychical*</note> beings <note>original: *animals*, here referring to any living entity, including celestial ones</note> in each sphere. For there are distributions of partial souls within each of the spheres. However, the harmonic ratios of the whole soul harmonize the essences that are divisible around bodies, as well as the bodies themselves. For by its very essence [it contains all these, and the ratios which encompass them; <note>Note 1: These words are missing in the original Greek but were supplied from the Latin version by the scholar Thomæus.</note>] just as fire, being heat-producing <note>original: *calefactive*</note> by its very existence, is primarily hot. 

It contains, therefore, the *diatessaron* <note>a perfect fourth, or a 4:3 ratio</note> harmony, through which it harmonizes the essences that are divisible around the bodies of each of the spheres, and of the divine, dæmonic, and soul-governed beings in each, and also the bodies with one another. One thing does not encompass another by chance, nor do some things follow others randomly; rather, dæmonic beings follow divine beings, and soul-governed beings follow dæmonic ones. In accordance with nature, secondary essences are always adapted to primary ones. 

Thus, the *diatessaron* harmony exists in each of the spheres. The ratios of each sphere to the divine beings contained in it, and of those to the dæmonic beings, will be truly *sesquioctaves* <note>a 9:8 ratio, representing a whole tone in music</note>, possessing a perfect interval. These are simultaneously harmonious and adapted to physical bodies. For the *ogdoad* <note>the number eight</note>, having a triple interval <note>a reference to 2x2x2, creating a 3D solid</note>, has a body-like form, just as the *ennead* <note>the number nine, or 3x3</note> is a plane. However, each is related to equality. Secondary physical essences are always dependent on primary ones, participating in them and in the physical logic <note>original: *reason* or *ratio*</note> they contain. <note>Note 2: Proclus likely meant "in them" rather than "in it" here.</note> This is shown by the part which is said to be an eighth of the thing participated in. 

What remains, however, is the ratio of soul-governed to dæmonic beings, which has the relationship of the *leimma* <note>the "remainder" or a small semitone in Pythagorean tuning</note>; it is *superpartient* <note>a complex ratio where the larger number contains the smaller plus a specific fraction</note> and is adapted to thirteen parts. For these beings do not have a single, uniform life, since they ascend and descend, and enjoy the natures preceding them in a fragmented and inconsistent way. And since the number twelve is assigned to the worldly <note>original: *mundane*</note> Gods and to the natures superior to us, thirteen is adapted to those who do not rank among the Gods. 

*If, among the soul-governed beings themselves, some belong to pure souls (which Plato usually calls the souls of heroes), while others belong to common <note>original: *gregarious*</note> souls like our own, then the diapente <note>a perfect fifth, or 3:2 ratio; Note 3: This occurs because each sphere contains divine, dæmonic, heroic, and common souls, along with their appropriate bodies</note> will also be found in each of the spheres.* 

Heroic souls will maintain a *sesquioctave* ratio <note>9:8</note> toward the dæmonic beings because of their pure form of life; but the souls of the masses will have the ratio of the *leimma* toward them. Consequently, in each of the spheres, there will be *sesquitertian* <note>4:3</note>, *sesquialter* <note>3:2</note>, and *sesquioctave* <note>9:8</note> ratios.

He argues that these ratios ensure the cosmos is a perfectly harmonized and ordered system where secondary beings depend on primary ones.</summary>

Or rather, it could be said that the universe is divided into four parts, according to the four fundamental ideas of its model <note>original: "paradigm"</note>. However, in each of these four parts, there are all types of living beings <note>original: "animals"—in this context, Proclus uses this to mean any ensouled entity, including celestial ones</note>: the divine, the daemonic, the heroic, and human souls. All of these are harmoniously organized with one another and in relation to their own totality—whether that be the heavens, the air, the water, or the earth. This totality produces the <term>diapente</term> <note>a perfect fifth, or a 3:2 ratio</note>. Aside from this, it may be said that the <term>diatessaron</term> <note>a perfect fourth, or a 4:3 ratio</note> exists within the four species of living beings, just as Plato himself divides them—namely, into the universe as a whole and the various forms of living beings. Consequently, through these mathematical relationships, Plato provides us with ratios that encompass other ratios, which are perfect according to a single harmony. When the soul is filled with these ratios, it fills the visible world, making all things understandable <note>original: "effable"</note> and familiar with one another.

<margin>36B</margin>
> "Leaving a part of each of them. And then again, the interval of this part being assumed, a comparison of number to number is obtained from it—specifically, the ratio of 256 to 243."

What this <term>lemma</term> <note>here referring to the mathematical "leimma" or remainder</note> is, what ratio it holds, and how—by being adapted to concord—it becomes harmonious when arranged with the other ratios, is clear through the study of mathematics. Such a thing exists in the universe as a whole; the ratio of this "remainder" <note>original: *leimma*</note> is found in the lowliest of the living beings within it, regardless of the previously mentioned explanation regarding the fourfold division of the whole. This is because certain outflows and mixed remnants of the elements proceed from each of the celestial spheres into the subterranean regions. These remnants possess much that is chaotic, dark, and material, yet they still contribute to the overall structure and harmony of the world. 

Plato, therefore, places the cause of these remnants within the universal soul and calls it a <term>leimma</term> <note>Greek: *λείμμα*, meaning "remainder" or "leftover"</note>, which signifies the furthest point of reduction. Since theologians place the powers of the highest gods in that region—with Zeus <note>original: *Jupiter*</note> beautifying those parts to make them capable of participating in such mighty divinities—what should we think about the soul of the universe? Must it not, to a much greater degree, beautify everything that appears to be disordered? Must it not possess the cause of the underlying reality <note>original: *hypostasis*</note> of a disorderly nature and arrange it in a fitting manner according to this cause? 

How else could the soul govern the universe or guide all things in accordance with the divine Intellect, unless it organizes that which is disorderly and harmonizes even the very last of things with the single life of the world? Furthermore, if the causes of these things already exist within the <term>Demiurgus</term> <note>the Divine Craftsman or Creator</note>, as Orpheus says:
> ->The distant realms of dark Tartarus,<-
> ->And Earth’s furthest ends, his holy feet secure.<-

Why should it be surprising that the whole soul—possessing all such qualities in its own unique way, just as a divine intellect possesses them as a creator <note>original: "demiurgically"</note>—should contain beforehand the causes of the most remote parts of the world, even that which is, as it were, the residue or "sediment" of the whole? For the soul grasps the invisible world before it grasps the visible and physical world. Therefore, what the <term>leimma</term> <note>original: "leimma" (remainder)—in Pythagorean music theory, this is the small interval (semitone) left over when two whole tones are subtracted from a perfect fourth (a 256:243 ratio)</note> is becomes clear through these points. Consequently, the remainder is both fourfold and single. It is necessary that the soul should understand the logic behind both states—where the remainder exists as four parts and where it exists as one—since this mathematical logic must contribute both to the universe as a whole and to each of its individual parts.

If you also direct your attention to the specific numbers used in these terms, you will see that they maintain a remarkable correspondence. The progression into hundreds and "twos" <note>referring to the '200' in 256 and 243</note> manifests a complete descent and separation from the original cause. In the soul, this represents the most specific and individual parts; in the universe, it represents the final and most physical matter. 

However, the digits four and five in the "tens" place <note>the '40' in 243 and '50' in 256</note> connect these final, material things back to the primary natures and organize them according to their original principles. The <term>tetrad</term> <note>the number four</note> is assigned a creative and world-building quality. Meanwhile, the <term>pentad</term> <note>the number five</note> draws everything that has descended back toward powers that are closer to the nature of "the One." 

Furthermore, the three and the six in the "units" place <note>the '3' in 243 and '6' in 256</note> bring these things to perfection through "conversion" <note>the Neoplatonic concept of *epistrophe*, or the return of an effect to its cause</note>. Even if the ratio of 243 to 13 is <term>superpartient</term>¹ <note>a complex ratio where the larger number contains the smaller multiple times plus a remainder</note>, this number is not out of harmony with the universe. For after the complete progression of physical things, and a descent as far down as the earth—which is said to be the twelfth part of the world—everything that exists beneath it will be the thirteenth part of the whole. The forms of the elements that extend into the subterranean places will be suited to this number. 

Therefore, the most material part of the universe expands to its furthest extent, is made beautiful as it proceeds, and returns to its source once it has been beautified. In every part of the universe, there are these final, diminished classes of eternal natures to which the number twelve is assigned. It is very appropriate that they share a relationship and connection with one another according to the thirteenth ratio, since the number twelve was dedicated by the ancient philosophers to the worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note> Gods and to the classes of beings that always depend on them. The soul grasps all of these as a single unity within the ratio of the remainder. 

In addition to these things, the <term>ennead</term> <note>the number nine</note> of the units (which the numbers three and six produce for us) marks the end of the soul's mathematical ratios. Starting from the <term>monad</term> <note>the number one, representing unity</note>, they advance to the nine, and from units to tens, and from tens to hundreds. For the entire progression of the soul is...

It is also because the hexad is "circular" <note>a number whose powers always end in the same digit, e.g., 6 x 6 = 36</note>, in the same way as the <term>pentad</term> <note>the number 5; the original Greek text likely intended "pentad" here</note>.² The <term>pentad</term>, however, is the image of the intellectual circle, being masculine, while the <term>hexad</term> represents the psychical circle, being feminine.

Hence, all numbers are said to proceed from the inner depths of the <term>monad</term> as far as the divine <term>tetrad</term>, which brought forth the mother of all things—unchanging and tireless—which is called³ the sacred <term>decad</term>. 

The <term>tetrad</term> has for its "side" the <term>duad</term> <note>the number 2</note>, and doubling the square of it and adding 2 produces the number mentioned above (34) ;* this is an imitation of the soul, which is multiplied by itself along with its own creative power. Because it acts as a middle ground between harmonious and discordant intervals, it is suited to the "middle nature" of the soul. In short, the <term>sesquioctave</term> characterizes the <term>diatonic genus</term> <note>the standard musical scale</note>, according to which the entire soul is harmonized. But being recognized as the "second" ratio, it aligns with the rank of the soul, where the basic categories of being have a secondary existence.

Furthermore, in addition to these things, the whole diagram contains a <term>quadruple diapason</term> <note>four octaves</note>—which is the most complete of all harmonies—and a single <term>diapente</term> <note>a perfect fifth</note>, ending in one tone. This signifies the fourfold cause for dividing the world into four parts. This division proceeds from above—starting from the "Living Being" itself and the four primary ideas within it—through the soul and into the universe. It also signifies the perfect harmony in each part of the world; through which heaven is a single realm, in celestial agreement with itself, and the earth contains all things in a terrestrial manner, and...

### PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.

...In a similar way, each of the elements between these is organized. Since, however, the world is not only divided into four parts, but also contains <term>five figures</term> <note>the five Platonic solids: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron</note>—possessing a fifth idea along with the other four—the soul very properly contains within itself the <term>symphony diapente</term> <note>original: "symphony diapente"—the musical interval of a perfect fifth (a 3:2 ratio)</note> after the <term>quadruple diapason</term> <note>original: "quadruple diapason"—a range spanning four octaves</note>.

The remaining section is the division of the heavens into eight spheres, and of the whole world into nine. Over the eight spheres, the Sirens mentioned in Plato’s *Republic* preside; over the ninth, the whole group of Muses governs, under whom the Sirens serve. Again, therefore, a <term>tone</term> <note>a 9:8 ratio</note> harmoniously closes the entire <term>diagram</term> <note>the "psychogonic diagram," or soul-birth chart</note>. It is not possible to devise any other divisions than these which are delivered to us by Plato—I mean, the divisions into four, five, eight, and nine parts. Some of these are mentioned in this dialogue (*the Timaeus*), and some in the *Republic*. 

Very properly, therefore, the entire soul-generating diagram is composed of all the particulars mentioned above: a tone, the perfect fifth, and the four-octave range. This is so that you may see these ratios throughout the whole world, as they hold the power of the entire diagram. All of these are assumed according to all the divisions Plato made of worldly natures, which are threefold: according to ideas, according to geometric figures, and according to the spheres.

All the other <term>sesquialter</term> <note>original: "sesquialter"—a 3:2 ratio</note> and <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>original: "sesquioctave"—a 9:8 ratio</note> ratios, therefore, were the bonds of more specific orders. These were contained either in the five parts of the universe, or in its divisions into eight and nine—for instance, in the division into Gods, <term>daemons</term> <note>divine spirit-beings that act as intermediaries between gods and humans</note>, souls, natures, and bodies. 

Among the Gods, there are those who preside over different parts of the world. In each part, there are different orders of Gods, with those of the second rank being analogous to those who come before them. In a similar way, regarding the daemons, some belong to one series and others to another. The same thing occurs with souls, natures, and bodies. 

But the <term>diapente symphony</term> <note>the perfect fifth</note> and the <term>sesquioctave ratio</term> <note>the whole tone</note> are not included without reason after the four-octave range. They are included because they are common factors that comprehend and connect the "wholes" of the universe. I say, for instance, that the ratio of the ninth sphere to the eighth sphere comprehends and connects as a single ratio all the parts at once that are arranged according to a five-fold division, as well as all those divided into eight and nine. 

However, the <term>lemmas</term> <note>original: "leimmas" (remainders)—the small intervals, or semitones, left over in the tuning of the scale</note> of all the <term>sesquitertian</term> <note>original: "sesquitertian"—a 4:3 ratio, or a perfect fourth</note> ratios are either the final and most divisible reductions within each of the four parts of the distribution, or they are the common gifts of all these ratios into the lowest place of the universe. Through these, Gods, daemons, individual souls, and natures proceed into that region. There, they accord with each other according to the final and perfectly divisible harmony, such as we say <term>superpartient ratios</term> <note>ratios where the larger number contains the smaller number plus more than one part of it (e.g., 5:3 or 7:4)</note> possess. Hence, as Plato descends to this point, he adds that the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>the divine Craftsman or Creator</note>, while dividing the mixture, had now consumed the whole of it. For neither God nor nature does anything in vain.

<page-num>109</page-num>
<header>BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

The <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The "Craftsman" or Creator of the physical universe in Platonic philosophy.</note> therefore did not create a mixture of parts that was either excessive or lacking. Instead, he produced it in a way that was exactly sufficient for the completeness of the soul itself. For a whole made of parts is neither more nor less than its own constituent parts; it derives its completion entirely from the parts appropriate to it. Hence, the entire mixture consists of harmonic ratios, and all this harmony is, in essence, the fundamental model—the paradigm—for the harmony of the entire universe, following all the divisions found in the world.

Furthermore, the total number of the essential <term>monads</term> <note>In this context, units or fundamental building blocks of numerical value.</note> of the soul is 105,947,¹ proceeding according to all the orders of numbers:

*   **By tens (decadically):** This is so the soul may become "mundane" (belonging to the world), for the number ten is the number of the world.
*   **By fives (pentadically):** This is so it may turn back toward itself, for the number five has a self-returning quality. <note>In Pythagorean thought, five was seen as a "circular" number because its powers always end in five, symbolizing a return to the self.</note>
*   **By nines (enneadically):** This is so that it does not only ² contain the universe as a single unit (monadically), but also spreads out from that starting unit to the very last of things.
*   **By fours (tetradically):** This gathers the four-fold division of reality into one.
*   **By sevens (hebdomadically):** This turns all things back to the One (the monad). The number seven is uniquely linked to the One, being considered "motherless" and "virile." <note>The number seven was often called "Athena" by Pythagoreans because it is not "born" from any multiplication of numbers within the first ten, nor does it "breed" any other number within that group.</note>

In the Soul of the World, this entire number exists as a whole. In divine souls (the gods), whose energies are directed toward that ³ Soul, it exists both as a whole and in parts. In <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "dæmons"—benevolent spiritual beings that act as intermediaries between gods and humans.</note>, who act in even more specific ways, it exists the opposite way: partially and then as a whole. Finally, in human souls, it exists only in parts, and only <term>gnostically</term> <note>original: "gnostically"—referring to the soul's ability to know or perceive these truths, rather than the power to create them.</note>. 

For this is how all "Forms" (the ideal blueprints of reality) exist within these souls—such as the forms of humans, spirits, and gods. This allows these souls to know that all things exist within higher, more excellent natures both as something they create and, at the same time, as something they know. 

Therefore, this specific mixture belongs only to the Soul of the World. It exists in the same way within every divine soul, and similarly in the souls of spirits (daemons). Each of these has an Intellect placed above its own core essence, a specific "vehicle" (a spiritual or celestial body), and a life that revolves around this. If, however, we must define the unique nature of "partial souls" (such as individual human souls), they are a middle point between the "indivisible" which is above them and the "divisible" which comes after them,⁴ or they are partly one and partly the other. Although we have discussed this at length elsewhere, we will examine it specifically when we explain what Plato says regarding the birth of individual souls.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the construction of the World Soul from Plato’s Timaeus. It transitions from the calculation of the soul's numeric components to the geometric arrangement of those numbers into the cosmic structure of the heavens.</meta>

> “Having, therefore, cut all this double composition along its length, so as to produce two from one, he joined middle to middle, each to the other, like the letter X.”

First, it is necessary to show mathematically what kind of shape the soul has, and then afterwards introduce the theory behind these things. In this way, by being guided in an appropriate manner through our <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "phantasy"—in Neoplatonic thought, this refers to the faculty that allows the mind to visualize geometric and mathematical forms.</note>, we may prepare ourselves for a scientific understanding of what is being said. 

Therefore, imagine all the numbers as being written on a single ruler, just as musicians are accustomed to doing. Let this ruler contain the numbers through its entire depth and be divided along its length. Consequently, all the ratios will exist in each of the sections. If the division were made across the breadth, some numbers would necessarily be in one part and different numbers in the other. However, since the cut is made along the length, and all the numbers exist throughout the entire length, the same numbers will appear in both parts. For it is clear that "dividing the length" is not the same thing as "dividing *according to* length"; the latter means the cut runs through the entire length, whereas the former means the length itself is cut in two.¹ 

Let the ruler, therefore, be divided along its length in this way,² and let the two resulting strips be joined to each other at their midpoints—yet not at right angles, for the celestial circles themselves are not at right angles. Let these two strips also be curved so that their ends meet. Two circles will therefore be formed: one will be on the inside and the other on the outside, and they will be slanted (oblique) to each other. One of these is called the **Circle of the Same**, and the other is called the **Circle of the Different**. The first corresponds to the <term>equinoctial circle</term> <note>The celestial equator.</note>, and the other corresponds to the <term>zodiac</term> <note>The ecliptic, the apparent path of the sun and planets.</note>. For the entire Circle of the Different revolves along the zodiac, while the Circle of the Same revolves around the equator. This is why we imagine that the straight lines should not be joined at right angles, but rather like...

the letter **X** as Plato says, so as to cause the angles to be equal only at the intersection, while the angles on each side and the successive angles are unequal. For the <term>equinoctial circle</term> <note>The celestial equator.</note> does not cut the <term>zodiac</term> <note>The ecliptic, or the sun's apparent path.</note> at right angles. Such, then, in short, is the mathematical discussion regarding the figure of the soul.

Again, however, by surveying these things from the beginning, let us apply what Plato has said to the <term>psychical essence</term> <note>The fundamental nature or "being" of the soul.</note>. In the first place, we must observe that <term>continuous and discrete quantity</term> <note>In classical mathematics, "discrete quantity" refers to whole numbers (arithmetic), while "continuous quantity" refers to magnitudes like lines and shapes (geometry).</note> are divided from each other according to the mathematical sciences. They are, in a certain way, opposed to each other, so that it is not possible for the discrete to be continuous, or the continuous to be a discrete quantity. In the soul, however, both of these coincide—namely, union and separation. For the soul is both a <term>monad</term> <note>A single, indivisible unit.</note> and a number; it is one rational principle and one multitude; it is many things. As a whole, it is continuous; but as a number, it is divided according to the rational principles it contains. 

Through its continuity, the soul is made like the union of <term>intelligibles</term> <note>original: "intelligibles"—purely intellectual realities that exist beyond the physical world.</note>, but through its multitude, it is made like the separation between them. By ascending even higher than these, we shall find that according to its union, the soul possesses an image and representation of **The One** <note>The ultimate, absolute principle in Neoplatonic philosophy.</note>, but according to its division, it represents the multitude of the divine numbers. Hence, it possesses neither a purely arithmetical essence (for then it would not be continuous) nor a purely geometrical essence (for then it would not be divided). Instead, it must be said that it is both an arithmetical and a geometrical essence at the same time. 

Insofar as it is an arithmetical essence, it also essentially possesses the <term>harmonical</term> <note>The science of ratios and musical intervals.</note> essence. For the multitude within the soul is harmonized, and it encompasses both absolute and relative quantity within its own sameness. But insofar as it is a geometrical essence, it contains the <term>spherical essence</term> <note>The mathematical principles governing the movement of spheres.</note>. For the circles within the soul are both immovable and moved—immovable in their essential nature, but moved according to a vital energy. Or rather, the soul possesses both of these at once because it is **self-motive**. To be self-motive is to be both moved and immovable at the same time. For the soul moves itself; yet to move, or to be the cause of motion, belongs to an immovable power. 

The soul, therefore, essentially encompasses all sciences: geometry, according to its wholeness, its figures, and its lines; and arithmetic, according to its multitude and the essential "units" within it, as we have shown before. It also encompasses the harmonic science, according to the ratios of numbers, and the "spheric" science <note>Astronomy/Celestial mechanics.</note>, according to its twofold circulations. In reality, the soul is the essential, self-motive, intellectual, and united bond of mathematics, encompassing all things without being limited by physical shape and with undefiled purity. Hence, it encompasses figures without being bound by shape; it encompasses separated things in a united way; and it encompasses things that have spatial extension without itself having any extension. For these qualities belong to the essence of the soul, and it is necessary to examine everything within it in this manner.

Moreover, this should also be understood from what has been said: that all secondary natures are analogous to those that come before them, and that everywhere, *the one* precedes the multitude. For just as the theory of the <term>hyparxis</term> <note>original: "hyparxis"—the essential existence, foundation, or "subsistence" of a being.</note> of the soul began from its essence, and the theory of its harmony from the *one part*, so the doctrine concerning its shape places the "one length" prior to the two. And as sameness and difference arise from essence, so the triple and double ratios arise from the <term>monad</term> <note>The number one; the principle of unity.</note>; but from the "one length" come the circle of *the same* and the circle of *the different*. 

As the preceding things are to the preceding, so the succeeding things are to the succeeding, and all things correspond to each other—namely essence, harmony, and form. All things are indeed found everywhere because the <term>psychical life</term> <note>The life or animating force of the soul.</note> is, as it were, uniform and made of similar parts. However, *the same* and the triple ratio exist to a greater degree in the "circle of the same," while *the different* and the double ratio exist more in the "circle of the different." All the ratios are likewise everywhere, but in different ways in primary and secondary natures. In the primary, they exist intellectually, as a whole, and united; but in the secondary, they exist <term>doxastically</term> <note>original: "doxastically"—related to "doxa" or opinion/sensory-based belief, rather than certain knowledge.</note>, divided, and in parts. This concludes our discussion of these details.

Regarding this section, however, and the two lengths and circles, it is worth considering what they should be called. The divine <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A prominent Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who heavily influenced Proclus.</note> soars high in his thought and carefully investigates invisible natures—specifically, the "one soul" and the two souls that proceed from it. For every order is led by an <term>unparticipated unity</term> <note>original: "imparticipable monad"—a primary principle that remains pure and separate from the lower things that depend on it.</note> that exists prior to the things that participate in it; there is also a number appropriate to and born together with these unparticipated principles. The <term>duad</term> <note>The number two, representing duality or the first departure from unity.</note> also comes from unity, in the same way as it does among the Gods themselves. 

<term>Timaeus</term> <note>The main speaker in Plato’s dialogue, the "Timaeus."</note>, he says, has constructed the "one and <term>supermundane</term> <note>original: "supermundane"—above or beyond the physical world.</note> soul" through his <term>psychogony</term> <note>original: "psychogony"—the account of the generation or "birth" of the soul.</note> in words. From this soul, the soul of the universe and other souls are derived; he now produces the duality from this. For this division demonstrates the creative division of the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The "Craftsman" or Creator of the physical universe in Plato’s philosophy.</note>, which proceeds in sameness and perfection, generating the same patterns according to secondary numbers. 

The division according to length shows us the progression descending from the Demiurge on high. Through these, however, two souls are generated after the "one soul." Each of these has the same ratios, they are joined together, they exist within each other, yet they are also divided from each other. They likewise preserve a pure, unmixed state along with their union with each other. For they are united at their own centers, and this is the joining of center to center. 

But since these souls are also intellectual and participate in a divine intellect, the Demiurge—prior to the generation of the universe—bent them into a circle. He contained them within a motion according to "the same" and in "the same," making them intellectual, giving them a divine intellect, and inserting...

...the pair <note>original: "duad"</note> of souls, within the intellectual pair, which essentially transcends them. [Thus far the divine Iamblichus.]

We therefore admit that all this is well said as far as it pertains to the theory of things, for these details exist prior to the world. Hence, even in worldly natures, there is first the <term>monad</term> <note>The number one; a single unity.</note>, then the <term>duad</term> <note>A pair or the number two.</note>, and finally the <term>heptad</term> <note>A group of seven.</note>. For in the universe there is one soul, which is the Soul of the Universe. But after this, there are two souls, which divide the heavens into the "circulation of *the same*" and the "circulation of *the different*." And after these, there are seven souls, which distribute the planetary spheres in an orderly manner. 

However, we believe it is more in agreement with Plato’s words to understand what is being said here as referring neither to those souls that exist above the world, nor to the vast multitude of souls within the world, but specifically to the Soul of the Universe itself. Plato himself, shortly after speaking about all the divisions of the soul, says:

> "But when the entire composition of the soul was produced according to the intention of its composing <term>Artificer</term> <note>The Demiurge or Creator.</note>, he then fashioned within it the whole of a physical-formed nature."

In these words, he refers to the soul as "one," and this can be none other than the Soul of the Universe. For it is this soul which encompasses the entirety of physical nature. Therefore, the <term>demiurgic</term> <note>Creative or related to the work of the divine Craftsman.</note> divisions, and the two-fold lines and circles, must be understood as being within *this* soul; by doing so, we will not lack supporting arguments. 

Since the soul is the gatherer of all things—those that are immovable and those that are <term>moved by others</term> <note>original: "alter-motive"</note>, those that are indivisible and those that are divisible, the divine models and the final images, and those beings that truly exist alongside those that do not—its nature is very properly two-fold. It pertains partly to more excellent beings and partly to subordinate ones. Because these two types of being are entirely separated from each other, they require two <note>See footnote 3.</note> connecting means. 

In physical natures, these two joining links are separated from each other. However, in incorporeal natures, it is a single, two-formed essence that binds the extremes together. One part of this essence is joined to <term>intelligibles</term> <note>Purely spiritual or intellectual realities that can only be grasped by the mind.</note>; it is intellectual, scientific, shining with divine wisdom, <term>anagogic</term> <note>Leading the soul upward to higher spiritual realities.</note>, and understands the causes of things. The other part is close to divisible natures; it produces difference, comes into contact with the <term>sensible world</term> <note>The world perceived through the senses.</note>, oversees the care of secondary natures, is skillful, and contains everything else allied to these. All the mathematical ratios, however, are present in each of these parts. In this regard, the essence of the soul differs from the pure intellectual essence. For the intellectual essence is uniform and precedes—

<page-num>114</page-num>
<header>TIMÆUS OF PLATO. [BOOK III.</header>

...openly comprehends all forms as a unity <note>original: "monadically"</note>; but the former is a duality <note>original: "dyadic"</note> and contains the same principles <note>original: "reasons"</note> through reasoning <note>original: "dianoetically"</note> and belief <note>original: "doxastically"</note>. It contains them in one way in the "circle of the *same*," but in another way in the "circle of the *different*." [And thus the soul imitates its cause.]$^1$ For she is both a unity <note>original: "monad"</note> and a duality <note>original: "duad"</note> in relation to the "monad" [Saturn], who is the father of the intellectual gods. The soul is a unity in relation to the universe, but a duality in relation to the intellect. In short, division and multiplication themselves derive their existence <note>original: "subsistence"</note> from this goddess [Rhea]. The life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note> principle is therefore the cause of progression, variety, and multiplication.

For this reason, some philosophers—comparing things to the gods from whom they come—assign intellects to the masculine category and souls to the feminine category of the gods. For intellect is indivisible and follows the nature of the odd number, while the soul is divisible and has two forms. The former is like fatherly causes, while the latter is like fertile <note>original: "prolific"</note> causes. One is linked to limitation <note>original: "bound"</note>, and the other to the infinite. If I should be asked how the soul is one and how it has two forms, I would say that it is one because it is self-moving; for this is common to all life of the soul and to all the parts it contains. But I would say it has two forms according to its two-fold lives: namely, the life that is turned toward higher <note>original: "first"</note> natures, and the life that provides for <note>original: "providentially attends to"</note> lower <note>original: "secondary"</note> natures. I would also say that according to its essence it has one life, for self-motion is the essence of the soul; but I would distinguish its two-fold lives according to the "same" and the "different."

Why, however, did the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The Creator or divine Craftsman.</note> first create the soul in a straight line, but afterward in a circle? And in what way is a straight line suited to the essence of the soul? To this we reply that it is necessary to think of the soul as being like a straight line. For just as a straight line proceeds without curving and moves definitely from one point to another (since there is only one straight line between two points), and just as it is infinite in its own nature, so the soul is produced as an infinite power. Intellect also, like an indivisible point, guides the soul, encompassing it as a single whole and containing the soul's entire essence in an indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> way from the start. For what cannot be divided <note>original: "impartible"</note> belongs to intellect, while that which is primarily divisible <note>original: "partible"</note> belongs to the soul. A point and a line represent these two things. Hence, a straight line is very properly assigned to the soul, and afterward a circle (both of which we call "simple lines"), while a point is assigned to intellect. For from that point—
