<meta>Tim. Plat.</meta>

This is manifest. For they call the first of these the messenger of the Gods <note>Mercury</note>; the second, *the gate of ascent*; and the power which is in the middle of both is Venus’*, being the friendship or love which is the connecting medium of the universe. This is true whether the Sun comes before her and Mercury comes after, or the other way around <note>original: "vice versa"</note>. Perhaps, too, they will revolve with equal speed, insofar as all of them look toward one thing: the bond of the whole. Their energies will have this as their goal: to establish all things in one union, so that the universe may be filled with its proper causes. All things, therefore, are in the soul according to a unified comprehension <note>original: "unical comprehension"</note>. For the eight circles are powers that unitedly contain things that exist in a divided way in sensible things <note>things perceived by the senses</note>, both in the heavens and in each of the elements. And this much may be said in short concerning all the circles.

Again, however, considering the circle of the *different* by itself, we say that its division into six parts is most perfectly suited to the soul. For according to the doctrine of the *Pythagoreans, the soul is a hexad* <note>the number six</note>. They arrange the <term>monad</term> (the number one) as analogous to a point, but the hexad to that which is animated <note>given life</note>, and the <term>heptad</term> (the number seven) to that which is intellectual. But how is it possible we should not say that the number of seven circles is adapted to the soul? For the soul is produced by the life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note> Goddess Rhea, who is a monad, duad <note>two</note>, and heptad, containing within herself all the female Titans <note>original: "Titannidæ"</note>. Furthermore, this may be considered in another way: for the heptad is a number that produces opportunity <note>original: καιρος γαρ εστιν αριθμος; "for it is the number of opportunity"</note>, and it perfects and restores <note>original: "apocatastatic"</note> cycles. In this respect, therefore, it exists appropriately in relation to the soul, which produces and directs all things by its motions. 

If, however, this is the case, it is evident that these circles of the soul are gnostic <note>relating to knowledge or cognition</note> and, with much greater priority, vital powers of it—both tetradic <note>groups of four</note> and triadic <note>groups of three</note>. For through both, they contain all sensible things; through the triad, they know all the similarities in them, but through the tetrad, they know all the differences, variety, and categories <note>original: "genera"</note> which they contain. They also know through these whether sensible things, in whatever way they exist, participate in a certain truth, symmetry, or beauty from truly-existing beings <note>the realm of ideal Forms or Reality</note>.

Moreover, the existence of these seven geometrical terms in each of the circles gives a sevenfold <note>original: "septuple"</note> increase to the ratios. This is an indication of the self-moving nature of the soul. For the soul generates and multiplies itself, and is at one and the same time a heptad and a number proceeding from the heptad.

\* "Aphrodite" [Venus] is omitted in the original Greek, but both the translation by Thomæus <note>Niccolò Leonico Tomeo, a Renaissance scholar</note> and the logic of the passage require it to be included.

Furthermore, the fact that the circles of the soul <note>original: "psychical circles"</note> move in opposite directions shows that these powers extend everywhere, are productive of all things, and are the causes of the differences found throughout the world and of the opposites that exist in the realm of birth and change <note>original: "generation"</note>. For opposites exist within the soul, within the heavens, and within physical matter. Indeed, the process of birth and change is composed of these material opposites. These opposites, however, draw their existence from the soul's powers through the principles of the stars and planets <note>original: "celestial reasons"</note>. For in the things they create, some have the relationship of "the material from which," others "the instrument through which," and others "the primary cause by which,"¹ in the things produced by them.

Moreover, the similarity of the three circles and the difference of the four circles are chosen based on the nature of those numbers. For the number three <term>triad</term> brings things to perfection and returns them to their original form. But the number four <term>tetrad</term> is productive and the cause of all diversity. Therefore, all the numbers—namely the one <term>monad</term>, two <term>duad</term>, three <term>triad</term>, four <term>tetrad</term>, five <term>pentad</term>, six <term>hexad</term>, and seven <term>heptad</term>—exist entirely within the essence of the soul. Following all of these is the square of seven <note>forty-nine</note>.² All these numbers also end in the number seven. Thus, the soul's essence is in every way based on the number seven <term>hebdomadic</term>.

The "Circle of the Same" <note>the outer, uniform motion of the stars</note> is like the number one; but the "Circle of the Different" <note>the inner, varied motion of the planets</note> is, as we have said, like the number seven. For the first is the intellect in motion, but the second is a light directed by the intellect—just as the number seven is, according to the *Pythagoreans*. The first is also indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note>, similar to pure intellect, while the other is divisible <note>original: "partible"</note>; however, it still consists of both the indivisible essence and the essence that is divided among physical bodies. [However, the divisible nature is dominant]³ within it, for "difference" holds power there.

Thus, the one is like the number one and the other is like the number seven. This is not only because the number seven belongs to the soul’s essence through its similarity to the life-giving Goddess⁴ <note>namely, Rhea</note> (for she is a single power containing two groups of three within herself), but also because the initial division of the soul into parts is based on the number seven, as was shown previously. to dividing powers, in the same manner as the group of seven <term>heptad</term>. The latter, however, pertains to powers above the world <term>supermundane</term>, [but the former to powers within the world <term>mundane</term>.]¹

If, however, it is necessary to relate the entire structure of the soul to the divine orders—since the soul contains images of all of them—we must begin this comparison from the earlier part of this dialogue. There, it is said that the soul was created not as something younger than the body (as we might assume), but was made prior to it and more ancient in both its origin and its virtue, acting as the body's mistress and ruler. Because Timaeus begins his description there, he gives the soul a higher status than the creation of the physical body. 

It must be said, therefore, that the soul’s progression—insofar as it rules and is the mistress of the body—must be traced back to the ultimate Principle of all things. But insofar as it is granted a triple and unified reality <term>hypostasis</term>, we must relate it to the highest level <note>original: "summit"</note>² of the Intelligible realm <note>The realm of pure reality known by the mind rather than the senses</note>. Furthermore, because the soul is generated from "Essence," "Sameness," and "Difference," it relates to the entire expanse of the truly Intelligible realm. In that realm, "Essence" and "Being" occupy the highest point; "Eternity"—which causes all things to remain constant in the same state—occupies the middle; and the "Intelligible Living Being"—which allows itself to become diverse as it progresses into various living forms—is the end. For in that realm, as the *Parmenides* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the nature of Unity and Being</note> teaches us, the whole consists of dissimilar parts. 

This triple whole (the soul), which is a mixture of dissimilar elements, is a thing of this kind. Insofar as the soul is a self-generated and mind-accessible <note>original: "intelligible"</note> number, we must relate it to the highest of the Intelligible and, at the same time, Intellectual orders. For there, the first number exists in conjunction with "Difference." As theologians say, we must view that first order as being³ the cause of the series of things [and of other organized groups]⁴ which are divided according to number. In that same realm, the *Parmenides* gives existence to the whole of number, and from there unfolds all things into the light.

[...the harmo]nic middle <note>original: "harmonic middle." A mathematical proportion where the middle term relates to the extremes in a specific ratio. This God grants a different kind of bond to different things: a stronger bond to those that are greater, and a weaker bond to those that are lesser.¹ And another proportion, the arithmetical middle, is derived from the third of these Gods. This God, through his own light, grants a sense of community to beings of a third rank. Through this, things that are smaller in size <note>original: "bulk"</note> are more closely united, while things that are larger are united to a lesser degree.² This is the defining characteristic of the arithmetical middle. 

Furthermore, because the soul possesses this specific kind of form and structure, and moves in both a straight line and a circle (for the reasons we mentioned earlier), we must relate it to the "triad of intellectual figure." This is because straight and circular lines first exist within that divine group of three. Therefore, in the fundamental idea of the soul, lines and circles were included, both joined together and separate from one another. 

Again, insofar as the soul receives powers of unity <term>monadic</term> and powers of the number seven <term>hebdomadic</term>, we must relate it to the "intellectual group of seven" <term>intellectual hebdomad</term>. But because the soul acts as the middle³ between the realm of the mind <term>intelligibles</term> and the realm of the senses <term>sensibles</term>—making sensory things more like mental realities—we must relate it to the "ruling" (or "supermundane") order of gods. This divine series makes secondary natures similar to their unified, highest peaks. 

Finally, because the soul acts with two types of energy—one that provides care for sensory things and another that clings to mental realities—we must relate it to the "liberated Gods." These are the deities who "touch and do not touch" the universe. These brief observations will help those who wish to read the writings of our teacher <note>Referring to Syrianus, Proclus’s predecessor as head of the Platonic Academy</note>, in which Plato’s truly secret <note>original: "arcane"</note> concepts regarding these matters are explained.⁴

I am surprised, however, at those Platonists who think the soul should be physically divided into parts to match the celestial souls (namely, the one soul of the universe and the seven souls of the planets). How could such a division exist in non-physical <term>incorporeal</term> natures? Such a division would destroy the whole soul. That kind of distribution into parts is only possible for physical matter. I also wonder at those who think these souls are entirely "above the heavens" <term>supercelestial</term>, since Plato shows in the very next passage that he is speaking about a single soul that belongs to the world <term>mundane</term>. Therefore, I think it is better to start with the principle that it is necessary here—

...the whole should remain within these divisions, and that the discussion concerns the animation of the world <note>original: "mundane animations"</note>. Having assumed this, we can say that the single soul of the world is indivisible, yet simultaneously divided according to these powers: first into the pair <term>duad</term>, second into the group of three <term>triad</term> and group of four <term>tetrad</term>, and third into the group of seven <term>hebdomad</term>. For its division is made according to these numbers. This is our opinion on this subject.

However, the philosopher Theodorus of Asine, being deeply influenced by the doctrines of Numenius <note>Numenius of Apamea was a 2nd-century philosopher who linked Plato’s teachings with Pythagorean and even Eastern thought.</note>, speculates on the generation of the soul in a more unusual way, using letters, symbols <note>original: "characters"</note>, and numbers. But the divine Iamblichus criticizes every theory of this kind in his treatise refuting the followers of Amelius and Numenius. I cannot say whether he includes Numenius among those who adopted this method, or whether he encountered similar opinions in the writings of Amelius’s disciples. 

The divine Iamblichus says, first of all, that it is not proper to define the soul as every number, or as a geometrical number, simply because of the number of letters in its name. For the words *body* <note>original Greek: "soma"</note> and *non-being itself* <note>original Greek: "me on"</note> consist of the same number of letters. Therefore, "non-being" would also be every number. You may also find many other things composed of the same number of letters that are lowly in nature and completely opposite to each other; it is not right to confuse and mix all of these together. 

Secondly, he observes that it is not reliable to argue based on the shapes of letters. These shapes exist by convention <note>original: "subsist by position"</note>, and the ancient way of forming them was different from the current style. For instance, the letter Z—which Theodorus makes the subject of his discussion—did not originally have parallel top and bottom lines with a diagonal middle line. Instead, the middle line was at a right angle, as is clear from ancient letters. 

Thirdly, he adds that analyzing things into the primary ratios of numbers and dwelling on these merely shifts the theory from one set of numbers to another. For the "sevenness" <term>heptad</term> found in units is not the same as the sevenness found in tens or hundreds. Since this number exists within the name of the soul, why is it necessary to introduce an inquiry into primary ratios? By dividing, combining, or multiplying, one could relate anything to any number. In short, Iamblichus accuses this entire theory of being artificial and containing no sound reasoning. 

I am also aware of Aristotle's arguments against Plato's account of the soul's creation <term>psychogony</term>, and the solutions to those arguments offered by certain Platonists. However, I have not considered it necessary to mention them further here, as I have discussed them elsewhere. For the soul is not a—

In all the other points, the philosopher has most perfectly instructed us. But the last point was concerning the <insert>energies of the soul</insert>, which he adds in what is said here. 

Since, however, there is a twofold form of the soul's energy—namely, the <term>gnostic</term> <note>related to knowing</note> and the <term>motive</term> <note>related to movement</note>—he discusses each of these separately. <meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on Plato's Timaeus, focusing on how the Demiurge (the divine creator) joins the soul to the physical body of the universe according to the model of the divine Intellect.</meta>

...them in a specific relationship <note>original: "habitude"</note>. Regarding its shape, he assigns it to the soul which occupies a specific rank. Furthermore, I believe it is sufficiently clear from these points that he did not instruct us about souls beyond the physical world <note>original: "supermundane"</note>, as others claim who assert that he produces one and seven such souls. For he joins the soul, which was crafted according to the Father's intention, to the universe; and within it, he constructs the whole of a nature formed by body. This is indeed evident from the entire design of the dialogue. For the whole discussion concerned the world, and not progeny existing beyond the world.

You may also see how accurately Timaeus chooses each word. For the phrase, *according to the intellect*, shows that intellect is the model <note>original: "paradigm"</note> for the universe. For the "all-perfect living being" <note>original: "animal"</note> is the intelligible intellect, based on which this universe and its soul were established. These words also signify that nothing was created in vain, nor was there more or less than was appropriate. Instead, everything required to complete the soul's essence <note>original: "psychical essence"</note> was fashioned in a becoming manner¹, and the essence of the soul received the full extent of the creator's <note>original: "demiurgic"</note> will. 

While material things, because of their matter, break apart indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> forms—receiving a whole as a fragment and something without physical extension <note>original: "interval"</note> as if it had extension—the soul receives the entire creative <note>original: "demiurgic"</note> fabrication in harmony with the will of the Demiurge. The words *its composer* also show a universal energy. For the words "*according to intellect*" indicate completion, while *its composer* indicates an energy where the whole is always present at once.² 

Likewise, the words *the whole composition of the soul* show that nothing escapes the creator's art. Instead, the entire progression of the soul is governed by the form and power of the Demiurge. But the words " *in the next place*" or " *after this*" must not be understood as having a temporal meaning, but rather as signifying a logical or hierarchical order. For the soul's independent life is one thing, and its secondary life—which follows this and connects with the body—is another. In a divine essence, more perfect things precede those that are less perfect. Finally, the words "*within the soul*" prove that the world³ is born together with <note>original: "connascent with"</note> the soul and is its offspring. For if the world proceeds within the soul, she is the mistress of its existence, encompasses its entire essence, and works together with the Demiurge in its orderly arrangement.

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on Plato's Timaeus, focusing on how the Creator (Demiurge) joins the soul to the physical body of the universe. <header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.</header>

...distribution of body. For the soul of the universe is not $^1$ <note>original: "ou gar" (not for) instead of "to gar" (the for)</note> like individual souls <term>partial souls</term>, which receive bodies fashioned by other forces. Because of this, individual souls sometimes rule over their bodies, but at other times, they are incapable of governing their own organs. However, proceeding from her source, the soul produces her own habitation—or rather, her vehicle—together with her father <note>The Demiurge or Creator</note>. Hence, she also governs the universe and acts eternally, without anxiety or labor. For everything that creates according to its own nature <note>original: "essence"</note> does so with ease.

Moreover, the words *he fabricated* reveal that the production of the Creator <term>Demiurge</term> acts through solid and resisting substances. They also show how physical objects <term>sensibles</term> are formed from the outside. These words almost $^2$ <note>original: "mononouchi" (all but) instead of "mononchi"</note> represent him employing the tools of Vulcan $^3$ <note>original: "Hephaisteiois" (relating to Hephaestus/Vulcan) instead of "uphisteiois"</note>, by which he fashions the whole heaven from brass—depicting everything with forms, giving roundness to physical masses, and shaping each thing with an appropriate form. Since the creation <note>original: "fabrication"</note> of the universe is threefold: the *first* is that where the Creator produced it from the elements bound together by mathematical proportion <note>original: "analogy"</note>, making it a "whole of wholes"; the *second* is that where he decorated it with the entire system of spheres (since it is impossible for something made of elements not to be divided into spheres); and the *third* is that which completes the universe with celestial, aerial, aquatic, and terrestrial living beings <note>original: "animals"</note>. This being the case, Plato now reveals to us the "middle" stage of creation. For he who crafts the entirety of physical nature <note>original: "corporeal-formed nature"</note> within the soul—which is divided into circles—clearly crafted it by dividing it into spheres. Because the spheres are images of the circles in the soul, the Creator is said to have crafted the whole of physical nature within those circles. From this, it is also evident that the eight circles include the region below the moon <term>sublunary region</term>, since the Creator placed the entirety of physical nature within them. If this were not the case, Plato would have said that the Creator fashioned everything *celestial*, rather than everything *physical* within them. Therefore, everything below the heavens is included in these circles because it is divided along with the heavens, or because it is contained within the circle of the moon. Theologians also call the moon "earth" because of the close connection between the two. For instance, it is common to both the moon and the earth to block <note>original: "conceal"</note> the light.

<margin>36 e (II. 252)</margin>
> ->"And collecting center to center, he harmonized them to each other."<-

$^3$ Instead of "under-tools" <note>original Greek: *uphisteiois*</note> in this place, it is required to read "Hephaestean/Vulcanian tools" <note>original Greek: *Hephaisteiois*</note>.

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on Plato's Timaeus, focusing on the relationship between the World Soul and the physical universe. It explores how the Creator (Demiurge) centers the soul within the body of the world so that it can govern all parts equally and harmoniously.</meta>

<header>BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>
<page-num>145</page-num>

Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note>, interpreting the "middle" as the physical aspect of the soul, tries to match it to the center of the universe, even though Plato does not explicitly mention the physical here. If, however, we wish to interpret what is said in a way that better fits Plato's meaning, we must say that the Creator <term>Demiurgus</term> placed the center of the world within the soul. The soul itself holds a middle position between pure intellect and the physical body; therefore, placing the world's center in the soul's center is to "join middle to middle." 

That this is Plato's meaning is clear from what follows: he says that the soul was extended in every direction from the center to the furthest edges of the universe. From this, we can conclude that the entirety of the physical world is filled with life <term>animated</term> in the same way throughout. We can also conclude that the World Soul is completely independent of the body, allowing it to imitate the Creator, who is present in all things yet separate from them all. 

We can also assume that because the physical world is placed at the center of the soul, the soul's life-giving power flows equally in all directions. If the outer edges of the universe were only joined to the centers, some parts would be further from the soul and others nearer. However, it is necessary for all things to remain anchored in the soul and filled with life by it. This joining of "middle to middle" shows that the soul is equally independent of all things and equally distant from all. For if it were closer to some things and further from others, it would be tied to lower, secondary natures. 

Both assertions are therefore true: the physical body is at the center, and it is joined to the soul, which is also a "middle" or intermediate reality. Furthermore, the phrase "to collect" demonstrates the Creator's power to unify, the bond that makes the universe eternal. The phrase "to harmonize" indicates the peaceful association of the body with the soul. In this relationship, the soul performs its own divine functions, while the body maintains its proper order without disrupting or dragging down the divine thoughts <term>intellection</term> of the soul's essence. This is the truly harmonious form of communion. 

However, if in the union of a lesser nature and a more excellent nature, either one fails in its perfection and causes a disturbance in the activities of the superior nature, then such a union is disharmonious <note>original: *enharmonios* (harmonious); the text notes this should be *anharmonios* (unharmonious)</note>, disorderly, and confused. Because the soul exists according to harmonic ratios, the entire physical world is seen to be in "friendship" with it through mathematical proportion <term>analogy</term> and is harmoniously composed. What bonds could be more unbreakable, more eternal, or more divine than these? None—except perhaps the very will of the Creator who bound the soul in the first place, a will that remains independent of the very things it has bound.

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.

<margin>(II. 283)</margin>

> “But the soul, being interwoven in every direction from the middle to the furthest reaches of the universe, and covering it on the outside like a veil, while at the same time revolving within itself, initiated the divine beginning of an unceasing and wise life for all time.”

The method of animation <note>The process by which the soul gives life to the body of the world</note> according to "conversion" or "regression" <note>original: *epistrophe*; the soul’s return or turning back toward its source</note> begins, as we have said before, from below and proceeds to things on high. It starts from the lowest levels of existence and ends at the very peaks of reality; this is the perspective Plato adopts here. Because the soul proceeds from on high down to the deepest recesses of the earth, illuminating everything with the light of life, the world is "turned" back toward it. Beginning from the lowest things, the world is given life both at its center and throughout its entire span. 

In addition to this, the world enjoys the intellectual illumination of the soul from the outside. Thus, the soul is said to occupy the middle of the universe because it places its powers there as a symbol of its own presence. It is also said to extend itself to the furthest edges of the universe, as it gives life to every part. Furthermore, it is said to "circularly cover it as with a veil" because its powers are superior to and independent of material, divisible bodies. In doing so, it almost seems to project the *aegis* <note>The shield or breastplate of Athena (Minerva), symbolizing divine protection</note> of Minerva, from which

->“A hundred golden tassels flutter.”<- <note>original: *Iliad* 2.448</note>

Through this power, the soul also surrounds the entire world from the outside. To speak the truth, Plato uses these words to silence those who mistakenly believe the soul has a literally circular shape and physical dimensions. For how could a literal circle be "interwoven" with a physical body? How could it extend itself equally to cover the world like a veil and adapt itself to the entire span of the universe? This description immediately proves that the imagination of those who think of the soul in such physical terms is false.

Additionally, we must examine what we stated before: that being "interwoven with" and "covering the universe like a veil" makes the soul similar to the higher *intellectual life* <term>intellectual life</term>, which Plato previously said surrounds the two circles of the soul. For just as that higher life encompasses the soul, so the soul encompasses the universe. Furthermore, we must consider how the soul is made like those Gods to whom Parmenides <note>A Greek philosopher; here referring to Plato’s dialogue *Parmenides*</note> attributes the concepts of "similarity" and "distinction"...

->“Της εκατον θυσανοι παγχρυσεοι ηερεθοντο.”<-

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the World Soul's relationship to the physical universe, specifically addressing how the soul is both "interwoven" with the world and "covers it like a veil," emphasizing its transcendence over the material body it animates.</meta>

# BOOK III.] THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO.

...similar. The "interweaving" shows that the soul is present in the world through similarity. This is because every connection between basic realities <note>original: essences</note>, powers, and activities <note>original: energies</note> comes from this similarity. 

However, the act of "circularly covering the universe as if with a veil" signifies the soul’s transcendence. It shows us how the soul is incommensurable <note>Meaning the soul cannot be measured by or restricted to the physical dimensions of the world</note> to the world and, because of this, is unparticipated <note>original: imparticipable; meaning the soul remains independent and does not lose itself in the things it gives life to</note>. For anything that is incommensurable is certainly different from the thing it cannot be measured against. 

Perhaps, however, both conditions apply to both. To be "interwoven" is the characteristic of things that are partly similar and partly different. And to "circularly cover as with a veil"—while remaining inseparable—demonstrates intellectual comprehension, which is present in the universe in a secondary way. Through this comprehension, the universe imitates the Intellect, of which it becomes the first resemblance <note>Note: In the original Greek, the word "resemblance" is *genomenon* (neuter); the author suggests the original text incorrectly used the feminine form *genomenen*</note>. 

Therefore, the soul is present with the universe in a separate, independent manner. It illuminates all things without being itself turned toward <note>original: converted to</note> the things it illuminates, and without taking on any relationship or coordination with them. Such things are foreign to the whole soul [the soul that exists as a complete whole]. 

Because the body proceeds along with the soul, but the soul does not proceed along with the body; and since the soul, by its infinite power, encompasses the world—encompassing all spatial extension <note>original: interval</note> by its own lack of extension, encompassing everything divisible <note>original: partible</note> by its own indivisible <note>original: impartible</note> nature, and encompassing the complex by its own simplicity—the construction of the body depends on the creation of the soul, not the other way around. The essence of the soul is therefore the leader, as it is more closely allied to the Intellect, and the body depends on the soul as its cause. 

Is there any reason, then, why we should tolerate the kind of *interweaving* proposed by some, who imagine the soul is present in the body through divisible powers, "actualities" <note>original: entelecheia</note>, and lives that cannot exist apart from the body? Absolutely not. Every distribution of this kind is secondary to the one Soul of the universe. 

Even in our own case, the *actuality* <note>original: entelecheia</note> animates the body in one way, while the separate, rational soul animates it in another. The former is divided among the physical parts of the body, but the latter is established within itself, being indivisibly present everywhere and containing divisible lives through its own indivisible powers. 

But if we are to speak in a manner that fits the dignity of the whole soul of the universe, this *interweaving* is an unmixed union of the body with the soul. It is a communion, a connected encompassesment, and a giving of life by the soul that proceeds from the Demiurge <note>The Creator or "Divine Craftsman" in Plato's philosophy</note> and returns <note>original: being again converted</note> to him. For just as we must not understand the phrase "circularly covering as with a veil" as...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the World Soul's relationship to the physical universe. It specifically transitions from how the soul "covers" the world to how its internal, circular motion represents its unique capacity for self-knowledge and intellectual life.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS [BOOK III.]

...not accompanied by physical distance <term>interval</term> or limited to a specific place. Instead, it signifies that the soul is, in every way, similarly independent of the body; by being thus independent, it uniformly encompasses the body. Likewise, we must not understand the phrase *"being interwoven"* as literal physical contact, but as a manifestation of the life <note>original: animation</note> that flows through all things and the union of all things with the soul. For the soul, filling everything with itself and containing everything in a connected way, holds itself in purity before <note>In the original Greek, read *pro ton allon* (before other things) instead of *pros ton allon* (toward other things)</note> all other things and turns <note>original: converts</note> the world toward itself. 

Therefore, by an even greater priority, the soul itself is turned <note>original: converted</note> toward itself. For this reason, Timaeus adds that the soul is revolved <note>original: convolved</note> within itself. He does this to show the difference between the soul and the physical body of the universe. While the body of the universe also revolves, it does not revolve within itself, but rather within the total space that it occupies. The body revolves locally, but the soul revolves vitally and intellectually, understanding itself and finding all things to be within itself. For the soul is the fullness <note>original: plenitude</note> of the whole and contains the images of all things. When it perceives these things intellectually, it is said to "revolve in itself." This revolution indicates that its motion is both intellectual and restorative <term>apocatastatic; a return to a former or original state</term>, while its "revolving in itself" highlights the unique nature of self-motion. For even though the universe also revolves, it is moved by something else—that is, by the soul.

This provides a solution to the problem we were investigating. We had asked, looking at the entire account of the soul's creation <term>psychogony</term>, where Plato described the soul's unique capacity for knowledge <term>gnostic peculiarity</term>. He had already established its essential nature through the *triple mixture* and its vital nature through its *motion in the Same*. Therefore, through the soul's circular turning <note>original: conversion</note> toward itself, the Creator <term>Demiurgus</term> established its capacity for knowledge. Plato makes this even clearer in what he says now. To show how the soul knows all things, he says that it revolves within itself, and through this revolution, it began to live a wise and intellectual life. 

From this, it is immediately clear that the soul's turning toward itself is the same thing as the knowledge of itself and of everything that exists before, within, or proceeding from it. *For all knowledge is a turning <note>original: conversion</note> toward the object of knowledge, as well as an alliance and alignment with it. For this reason, truth is the agreement between the knower and the thing known.* However, since this turning back <note>original: conversion or regression</note> is two-fold—one returning toward *the Good* and the other toward *Being*—the vital turning of all things is directed toward *the Good*, while the intellectual <note>original: gnostic</note> turning is directed toward *Being*. Thus, when the former turns, it is said to possess *the Good*, while the latter is said to possess *Being*. *The grasp of truth is the comprehension of Being, whether that Being exists within the knower, or before it, or after it.* This, as I have stated, becomes clear to us from these points.

<summary>Proclus explains that the soul's "circular" motion is an intellectual process of self-knowledge rather than a physical movement, distinguishing the soul's self-driven life from the body's externally-driven motion. He defines truth as the alignment between the soul and "Being," achieved through this internal revolution.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the World Soul's internal activity. It contrasts the development of "partial souls" (like those of humans and animals), which must grow from imperfection toward perfection, with the Soul of the Universe, which begins its existence in a state of perfect, divine activity.</meta>

### BOOK III.] TIMAEUS OF PLATO. 149

In the souls of individual living beings <note>original: partial animals</note>, reason sometimes acts intellectually and turns inward toward itself, but this does not happen immediately from the moment of birth. In these creatures, growth proceeds from the imperfect to the perfect, and remembering <note>This refers to the Platonic concept of *anamnesis*, or the soul regaining knowledge it forgot at birth.</note> comes only after a period of forgetting. For this reason, Plato says that the World Soul initiated a divine beginning of a wise life, starting from the highest level and from its very first activities <note>original: energies</note>. For the soul possesses some activities that are divine and independent, while others are responsible for moving the universe. It also always possesses more perfect powers before it exercises secondary ones. Coming from the Demiurge <term>the Divine Craftsman or Creator</term> and beginning to act, it starts with those activities that are most divine. Through these, it directs the secondary powers—namely, the intellectual powers and those based on opinion <note>original: doxastic energies</note>. 

This beginning, however, is entirely divine. Any process that begins with imperfect things is clearly material in nature. [For among the Gods, more perfect activities precede those that are lower;¹] but the opposite is true for material things. In the material world, birth and growth begin with imperfect states and move toward perfection. *Therefore, although the human soul sometimes acts divinely, this divine activity is its final goal. At first, it is content to act according to right opinion; later, it acts with scientific knowledge; and finally, it acts divinely, awakening² the "one" within itself—that part of its essence which is even more excellent than its intellect.* 

But a divine soul has this divine activity as its very first function. Because of this, it directs all its secondary powers of knowing <note>original: gnostic powers</note>, always guiding the lower powers through the superior ones. With even greater priority, therefore, the Soul of the Universe initiated the divine beginning of a wise life. It acted first through its divine part [the "One" at the core of its being], and afterwards from above through its reasoning <note>original: dianoetic</note> part, moving that part and making it god-like <note>original: deiform</note> in nature. 

Constant activity is the result of this. Anything that is created, or that performs a divine act within time, naturally moves from the imperfect to the perfect. But that which begins with the most perfect and divine activities never stops acting in this way, nor is it ranked among things that exist only within the limits of time. Therefore, if the Soul of the Universe initiated a divine start to its activity, it acts incessantly, eternally, and with unchanging consistency. For whatever reaches its own perfection over time starts from an imperfect state, not from a divine beginning. From this, it follows that the life of a divine soul is wise. If the life of this soul is unending, it is defined by intellect and wisdom.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Soul of the Universe, focusing on its constant wisdom and its unique relationship with time. It distinguishes the World Soul from other divine souls by its encompassing nature, which spans the entire duration of time and all cosmic cycles.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.

We must accept one of three¹ things: either that its life is always wise, or always lacking in wisdom (which we cannot rightfully say), or that it is wise at one time but unwise at another. It remains, therefore, that a wise life in a divine soul is continuous and never² fails.

In another respect, wisdom is suited to this soul because it participates in divine wisdom. Life is also suited to it because the soul unfolds the indivisible nature <note>original: impartibility</note> of the intellectual life, extending its activities <note>original: energies</note> and moving through transitions. For the term *life* <note>original: βιος - *bios*</note> is most appropriately applied to the soul. If this word is ever used in reference to the pure intellect—as in the *Philebus* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning pleasure and the good life.</note> where a certain "life" of intellect is mentioned—it signifies the specific nature of that life. *For the word "life" reveals two things: the unique form of each life and the unfolding of the choices from which it develops.* It is, therefore, properly used for souls, because in them there is an unfolding of choice. Sometimes it is also used for the intellect, and in those cases, it indicates the specific character of intellectual life.

It might be argued, however, that all these qualities are present in every divine soul—namely, to have a divine beginning, to act incessantly, and to possess a wise life. In what way, then, does the Soul of the Universe surpass other divine souls? Plato, anticipating this question, adds the phrase: “*through the whole of time.*” For while all souls act through transitions and have different cycles <note>original: periods</note>, some longer and some shorter, the Soul that functions as a whole alone receives the first and unified interval of time. It possesses the complete and primary measure that encompasses the cycles of all other souls. 

Just as different divine bodies have different cycles, the cycle of the "divine generated nature"³ contains all of them within itself. It encompasses through its restoration <term>original: apocatastatically; the return of celestial bodies to the same relative positions</term> many cycles of Saturn, many of the Sun, and many of the Moon; indeed, all time exists within the single cycle of the universe. In the same way, other divine souls have their restorative cycles in more limited spans of time. 

Since the breadth of the intelligible world is finite, but the restoration is different for different souls—being shorter for some and longer for others based on whether their object of thought is more or less excellent—and since the restoration of the universe is measured by the entire span and evolution of time (beyond which there is no greater time, except by repeating the same cycle again and again, which makes time infinite), the Soul of the Universe is the first of those beings that perceive intellectually according to a single form.

² <note>The word "not" [μη] was omitted in the original Greek text.</note>
³ <note>This refers to the body of the entire world. The title "divine generated nature" applies primarily to the world as a whole, though it also refers to any celestial body that moves perpetually in a circle, whether in the heavens or in the sublunary realm.</note>

# BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 151

<margin>II. 289, 29</margin>
...is a participant in time. Since this is the case, it is necessary for this soul to receive the whole form and measure¹ of time. Therefore, it is necessary that the soul of the universe alone should act through the whole of time, while other souls act only according to a part of this whole, which defines the point where their cycle is completed <term>apocatastasis</term>. <note>original: apocatastasis — a term in Platonic philosophy referring to the restoration of a celestial body or soul to its original starting position, completing a cycle.</note> [This is similar to what we see in other forms. For whatever participates in a specific form primarily² receives the whole of it.] *Therefore, supermundane <note>supermundane: existing above or beyond the physical world.</note> souls—if such souls exist—perceive through thought with a sense of transition. (This is because every soul understands in this way, which is also how intellect and soul differ.) However, they can grasp more than one object of thought at a time. Since they are closer to the pure Intellect—which perceives all things simultaneously—it is necessary for them to understand more than one thing at once. But the soul of the universe is the first to perceive intellectually only one object at a time, which is what makes it a "mundane" <note>mundane: belonging to the physical world or cosmos.</note> soul.*

In this respect, then, all souls within the world differ from those above the world. Because of this, the soul of the universe, which understands one thing at a time, completes its cosmic cycle <term>apocatastasis</term> across the entirety of time, which encompasses the period of everything divinely generated. In the first sense, it is inferior to souls above the world; but in the second sense, it transcends all other souls within the world. While those souls have their cyclic periods within only a part of the whole of time,³ the soul of the universe perceives the one intelligible world⁴ through its intellect and, "running" as it were around it, completes its full period across the whole of time. 

For it is necessary, as the soul of the world, that its mundane intellect should unfold the whole intelligible world. For this reason, it completes the intellectual restoration <term>apocatastasis</term> of its worldly period according to the "perfect number," just as it completes its entire physical <note>original: corporeal</note> period. This universe imitates the invisible period of the world-soul through its own physical rotation. It completes its physical cycle in space at the same time as the soul completes its intellectual restoration. This is the famous and unique quality of the world-soul, which Plato reveals in these words to those capable of understanding him. This is how his words should be understood.

<summary>This page discusses the unique relationship between the Soul of the Universe and the entirety of time, explaining that while other souls operate in fragments of time, the World Soul spans its whole duration. It also differentiates between 'supermundane' souls, which can grasp multiple thoughts at once, and the 'mundane' World Soul, which perceives one object at a time as it orbits the intelligible world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*, specifically examining why the soul experiences thought as a sequence (transition) and how it relates to time, whereas the pure Intellect experiences everything simultaneously in eternity.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.
## TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 152

<margin>II. 290, 23</margin>
Once again, however, we must investigate what produces a transitive motion <note>transitive motion: a movement from one thing to another; here, the soul’s thought moving step-by-step through ideas.</note> in the soul, as well as an understanding that is not fixed like that of the pure Intellect, and time instead of eternity. To answer this, we must say that just as the soul has a divisible <term>partible</term> essence, it also has a life that is not unified, but is divided along with its essence; the same is true for its intelligence. For the soul, instead of being Essence itself, is "essentialized"; instead of being Life itself, it is "vitalized"; and instead of being Intellect itself, it is "intellectualized." It participates in these qualities primarily because they exist prior to the soul. 

In the pure Intellect, therefore, the essence is one and the life is one. Its understanding of essence is indivisible <term>impartible</term>, just like the essence itself. Because it is perfectly aligned with it—like a point upon a point—it has no transition. The intelligence of the soul, however, is not only indivisible but is also, as we have said, divisible. Lacking the strength to be perfectly aligned with what is indivisible, but instead distributing itself around the indivisibility of the Intellect, it constantly applies first one part of itself and then another to the fixed Intellect. It does this so that it may eventually grasp the whole of that which exists prior to it. 

In this way, therefore, it produces a "transition of activity" <note>original: energy; here meaning *energeia* or active operation.</note>. That which is divisible within the soul unfolds itself around that which is indivisible, and together with this transition, it generates time. This transition is carried out in two ways:
1. First, by unfolding around *the One*, where all parts of the soul possess *the One*. For however many parts the soul is divided into, the qualities of "essence," "sameness," and "difference" are contained within it in just as many ways. By applying each of its parts to *the One* and frequently coming into contact with it, the soul introduces transition into its thought so that its whole being may intellectually perceive what came before it. 
2. In the second way, its transition occurs as each part of the soul acts upon all things. Every part of the soul possesses these three: essence, sameness, and difference. Because the soul cannot align itself with the whole of each quality at once, it applies itself to each individually, so far as it participates in each. It connects to essence through the part of itself that is like essence, and to other things in a similar manner. This is how we resolve the doubt.

In addition to this, one might ask: how can Plato say that the soul lives through the whole of time, when he has not yet described the creation <note>original: generation</note> of time? To this inquiry, we must say that he is describing the creation of that specific time in which the "living nature" <note>animal nature: the soul-infused physical cosmos viewed as a living organism.</note> of the world participates. For he says that when the Father <note>the Father: referring to the Demiurge or Creator in Plato's Timaeus.</note> saw the universe moving and living, he established time for the purpose of measuring the motion within it. Therefore, since this life and motion are added <note>original: adventitious — meaning coming from outside or not inherent.</note> to the physical universe, time is also granted by its creator, from whom the universe receives life and motion through the soul. But the soul also receives these from the Father—namely, life and the motion which is...

<meta>Pencil mark "II. 290, 23" in top left margin. Vertical pencil line highlighting the section of the first paragraph from "essence is one" down to "transition of energy".</meta>

<summary>Proclus explains that the soul experiences time and sequential thought because its nature is "divisible," unlike the "indivisible" pure Intellect which exists in a single, eternal moment. He also clarifies that while the physical world's time is created by the Demiurge, the soul's relationship with time and motion is also derived from this divine source.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus's exploration of the soul’s relationship with time. He explains that while the Demiurge (the Creator) is the primary cause, the soul is "self-moving" and thus contributes to its own progression through time, acting as a bridge between eternal intellect and the physical universe.</meta>

# BOOK III.] THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 153

<meta>Tim. Plat. VOL. II.</meta>

...according to time. However, since the soul is something self-existing <note>original: self-subsistent</note>, it contributes something to its own progression into existence from its creator. Just as the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The divine "Craftsman" or Creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy.</note> moves the soul, and the soul is also self-moving, in the same way, the soul is the cause of its own movement according to time. 

Therefore, before the <term>Demiurge</term> gave time to this universe, the soul is said to move through the entirety of time. In this way, it brings "soul-time" <note>original: "animal time"; referring to *anima* (soul), the time associated with the life of the soul rather than mere physical duration.</note> into existence in conjunction with the <term>Demiurge</term>, just as it creates the life through which¹ motion exists in conjunction with him. The soul also governs according to nature that which lives and moves through it; its oversight is not accidental, and it never fails to provide for what it governs. We shall speak again concerning time later.

From these points, we may summarize the following: the Soul of the Universe moves the universe by establishing protective powers in its center, filling the whole of it with life <note>original: vivification</note>, and containing it from the outside through intellect. In this respect, it imitates its own cause, which generates three divine realms: the protective, the life-giving, and the creative <note>original: demiurgic</note>. 

However, the soul moves itself in a divine manner with even greater priority, beginning from its first activities <note>original: energies</note>; for this reason, it moves both itself and the universe without ceasing. Thus, it conducts itself and all of heaven wisely. Furthermore, the soul makes the single extension of time the measure of its own cycle, rotating the universe with unchanging consistency. For the universe completes its <term>apocatastasis</term> <note>The restoration of the stars and planets to their original positions; the completion of a great cosmic cycle.</note> at the same time as the <term>apocatastasis</term> of the soul. The universe does not complete this cycle before the soul does, because the same events take place again and again in the world,² and physical things are produced according to the thoughts <note>original: intellections</note> of the soul. Nor does it complete it after the soul, so that this restoration to its original state is not without a cause. For what else but the period of the soul could encompass the whole of it? If we assert these things correctly, the soul derives its divinity from "the One," its unceasing nature from eternity, its wisdom from the Intellect, and all its attributes from the single Cause of all things.³

<margin>II. 292, 30</margin>
> "And while the body of the universe was generated to be visible, the soul is invisible. It participates in rational activity and harmony, and it belongs among the intelligible and perpetual beings, having been created by the best of causes as the best of all created things."

# BOOK III.] PROCLUS ON THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 154

Since Plato later gives the soul all the qualities he previously gave the body—namely, essence, harmony, figure, powers, and motion—and joins both together to complete a single living being <note>original: "animal"; here referring to the universe as a living organism</note>; he briefly reminds us of the difference between the two so that you do not mistakenly assume that body and soul have equal status, being misled by terms that sound the same but have different meanings <note>original: "homonymous appellations"</note>. He is not merely being repetitive when he says that the body is visible but the soul is invisible. He shows that the body is the object of opinion <note>In Platonic thought, "opinion" refers to knowledge gained through the senses, which is less certain than "intellect."</note> because it is perceptible and created, but the soul is uncreated in relation to the body, yet created in relation to the intellect. 

For the soul belongs at the same time to eternal beings and created natures, but it is the last of the eternal beings, since time now has a place within it. That which is primarily an eternal being is eternal in two ways: both in its essence and in its activity <note>original: "energy"</note>. For its activity is not different from its essence. But that which is created is created in both ways, always coming into being and always acting, existing in a state of creation according to time. The soul, however, participates in eternity in one sense and in creation in another; but it acts in a temporal way. 

And indeed, the extremes—that is, eternal beings and created natures—are perpetual in only one way: the first eternally, and the second temporally. But the middle point between the two is perpetual in a twofold way, having a dual nature <note>original: "biformed"</note> and, for this reason, an ambiguous character. This is true not only according to the divisible <note>original: "partible"</note> and the indivisible, and according to its two circular motions, but also according to perpetual being and that which is created. Therefore, it belongs to eternal beings and is the best of created things, being produced by the best of causes. 

And again, you see the difference between the soul and the body. Plato had previously called the body the *most beautiful* of created things; but now he calls the soul the *best* of things created. 
<margin>I. 293, 29</margin>
It is common to both that they were created by the most excellent cause. The soul, however, being closer to its maker, is *the best*; but the body, being more distant from him, is indeed *most beautiful*, but not *the best*. For *the most beautiful* is secondary to *the best*, in the same way that *beauty* is secondary to *the good*.

In what is said here, Plato may seem to call the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The divine "Craftsman" or Creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy.</note> the best of intelligible and eternal beings, just as he calls the soul the best of created things. In doing so, he seems to testify to those who place one God before the world.¹ But even if someone understands these words in that way by reversing their order, it is nonetheless evident through logic that we must not place in—

---

¹ Proclus, in what he says here, is referring to the Christians.

<summary>Proclus distinguishes between the soul and the body, explaining that the soul is a "medium" that participates in both eternity and time. He clarifies that while the body is the most beautiful created thing, the soul is the best, as it sits closer to the Creator (Demiurge).</summary>

<header>BOOK III.] THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO.</header>

<margin>¹ Instead of *eidei* (in the form) here, it is necessary to read *eide* (forms/kinds). <note>original: "ειδει... ειδη"</note></margin>

...intelligible and eternal beings, as forms in the Demiurge <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine craftsman or creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy</note>. However, it would involve other essences existing after him, if the soul has the same relationship <note>original: "ratio"</note> to all created things that the Demiurge has to eternal beings. We would also have to assume that he looks toward things that come after him, even though in his speech to the younger gods—when he entrusts them with the creation of mortal beings—he orders them to imitate his own power in their generation. 

Therefore, he does not create immortal living beings by imitating things that come after him, but rather things that exist entirely before him, just as he wishes the younger gods to create mortal beings by imitating him. Or, if we wish to avoid this difficulty, we must admit that there are many intelligible gods who exist after the Demiurge—an idea that those mentioned above will not accept. 

Would it not be better, then, to claim one of two things? Either Plato says the soul belongs to the realm of intelligible and eternal beings because it is the best of all created things and is truly both indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> and divisible, due to its middle position between the two realms. Or, perhaps it belongs to—or primarily participates in—intelligible and eternal beings because he says it shares in rational activity <note>original: "energy"</note> and harmony. 

For the harmony within the soul is created; it is not Harmony itself, but something that has been "harmonized." Similarly, its rational activity is not an eternal being but something that is created, as it exists within time and moves from one thought to another <note>original: "transitive"</note>. How, then, does the soul participate in rational activity and harmony? And why is it that harmony and rational activity are not found primarily in the soul, but only through participation? 

I answer that it is because these qualities exist first within the Demiurge. For he produces the Muses and *Mousagetes* <note>original: *Mousagetes*, the "Leader of the Muses," a title for the god Apollo</note>, as well as the Mercurial series <note>The "chain" or succession of divine beings associated with Hermes/Mercury</note>. Therefore, the rational creative activity and harmony exist primarily in him; the former is associated with Mercury, while the latter is associated with Apollo. 

The soul, being filled by these sources, participates in rational activity and harmony. To speak plainly, I believe that *harmony must be understood to exist in three ways: as Harmony itself; as that which is first harmonized (being harmonious in its entire nature); or as that which is secondarily harmonized (sharing in harmony only in a certain way).* 

The first of these levels belongs to *intellect*; the second to the *soul*; and the third to the *body*. Similarly, the rational or reasoning activity exists in three ways: the first is original and primary; the second exists through participation; and the third exists as a representation or likeness. For there is even a certain trace of rational activity in some irrational animals. We likewise understand essence <note>the fundamental nature of a thing</note>, shape, and power in three ways. For essence, in its primary existence...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, focusing on how the soul occupies a middle ground. It explains how the soul participates in divine qualities like "figure" and "power" more fully than physical bodies do, and introduces the soul's two primary functions: movement and knowledge.</meta>

<page-num>156</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE *TIMAEUS* [BOOK III.]</header>

The first figure and the first power exist within the realm of intelligible beings <note>The "intelligible" realm refers to the world of pure, divine ideas that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses</note>. However, physical nature also participates in these qualities in a certain way. Even matter itself exists, which is formless, lacking in essence, and powerless. The soul, on the other hand, possesses each of these qualities through participation, but it participates in them completely throughout its entire being. For the soul is entirely strengthened, entirely shaped by figure, and entirely given essence <note>original: "essentiallized"</note>. In the soul, the formless does not come before the figured; nor does weakness come before power; nor does a lack of essence come before essence. If these deficiencies came first, the soul would not differ at all from material bodies. 

The soul, therefore, participates in rational activity <note>original: "energy"</note>, harmony, figure, and power, and it participates in each of these as a whole. In contrast, the body only participates in them partially. From these points, the soul's middle nature becomes clear. It is also evident why Plato rightly says that the soul was created by the best of causes, that it is the first and best of created things, and that it is invisible, yet remains the primary participant in intelligible harmony.

> “Since, therefore, the soul was blended from these three—namely, from the nature of the **Same**, the **Different**, and **Essence**—and was divided into parts and bound according to mathematical proportion <note>original: "analogy"</note>, it returns to itself by a circular activity. Consequently, when it touches upon something that has a scattered existence <note>original: "dissipated essence"; referring to physical objects that are spread out in space</note>, or when it touches upon that which is indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note>, it speaks concerning that thing, being moved through the entirety of itself.”

<margin>
Proclus
</margin>

We divide the activities <note>original: "energies"</note> of the soul into two types: moving activities and knowing activities <note>original: "motive and gnostic"</note>. Both of these are suited to the soul, as the divine <note>original: "dæmoniacal"; used here in the Greek sense to mean inspired or superhuman</note> Aristotle also says. 

Regarding the moving activities, we find that some are inherent in the soul itself, others proceed into the universe, and others exist somewhere between the two. Those that extend through the whole world, from the center to the edge of the universe, belong to the physical world <note>original: "mundane"</note> alone. Those that turn the soul are separate from the physical world. Finally, those that circularly cover the universe like a veil are both separate and inseparable—staying in place while also moving around the universe. 

Regarding the knowing activities, some relate to the highest things, others to those of a middle nature, and others to the lowest things. The soul knows itself, as well as the natures that exist before it and those that come after it. This is because the soul is the image of the things above it, but the model <note>original: "paradigm"</note> for the things below it. Hence, by perceiving and unfolding its own nature, it knows all things without ever having to depart from its own power. For it is not necessary for the soul to leave itself behind to understand...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the soul, moving from its "motive energies" (how it moves) to its "gnostic energies" (how it gains knowledge). It explores the relationship between the soul's internal structure and its ability to perceive both the divine realm and the physical world.</meta>

<page-num>157</page-num>
<header>BOOK III.] TIMAEUS OF PLATO. 157</header>

to any other place in order to perceive beings, but rather that it should see itself through the intellect. Enough, therefore, has been said concerning the soul's powers of movement <note>original: "motive energies"</note>. But here, and in what follows, Plato speaks concerning its powers of knowledge <note>original: "gnostic energies"</note>. It is evident that the soul—especially the soul of the universe—knows existing beings, since we see that they are also grasped by our own souls. However, if the soul knows, we must consider *how* it knows, and in what manner it understands "intelligibles" <term>intelligibles: divine realities or ideas that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses</term> and "sensibles" <term>sensibles: physical objects perceived by the five senses</term>—whether it uses the same or different powers, and whether it looks inward at itself and the rational principles it contains, or reaches out toward the objects of knowledge themselves, just as sight reaches out toward an external visible object.

In short, Plato refers to these intellectual movements of the soul as "contacts" with the objects of knowledge. By this, he indicates the immediate nature of their understanding and their inseparable union <note>original: "impartible communion"</note> with the things known. If every act of knowledge is a "contact," the soul will come into contact with both intelligible ideas and physical things by applying itself appropriately to each, yet not so as to grasp both through the same active focus <note>original: "projecting energy"</note>. For it does not reach physical things by focusing on divine ideas, nor does it reach divine ideas by focusing on physical things. However, both of these—to touch and not to touch—are the unique characteristics of the "liberated Gods," as we learn from the *Parmenides* <note>The "liberated Gods" in Neoplatonism are divine beings that exist between the celestial and the super-celestial realms, acting as intermediaries</note>. Therefore, we previously correctly asserted that the soul is made like those Gods through the powers of knowledge it possesses essentially, through which it knows things both superior and inferior to itself. 

Because Plato is now speaking about these powers, he first wishes to remind us of what has been said before. This reminder is not unnecessary but contributes to the explanation that follows. From these earlier points and the ones now being made, the discussion will be properly explained. The details he had previously discussed concerned the essence, the harmony, the form, and the powers of the soul. Thus, recapitulating, Plato says that the soul is entirely blended from three parts: **Essence**, the **Same**, and the **Different**. It has already been shown what this mixture is and that it is life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note>. For the singular cause of souls creates the soul in conjunction with the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: the divine "craftsman" or creator of the material world in Platonic philosophy</term>. It has also been shown how the "triad" <note>the grouping of Essence, Same, and Different</note> belongs to the soul, and from which categories <note>original: "genera"</note> it is formed—namely, the "middle" categories. The soul was also divided by double intervals according to the geometric mean <note>original: "geometric middle"</note> and was bound together again through the remaining mathematical means. For he called these proportions "bonds." Similarly, a circular motion was given to it through the circles which encompass its harmony and its form. In its harmony, the distribution into parts came before the mathematical relationship <note>original: "analogy"</note>; and in its form, the division came before the contact. That which

<page-num>158</page-num>

<meta>Pencil notation in left margin: I. 298. 7</meta>

...remains, however, is in each. For the binding <note>original: "colligation"</note> contains a representation of the loosening <note>original: "solution"</note>, since binding only applies to things that can be loosened. The distribution of this binding is also based on proportion <note>original: "analogous"</note>. For as we observed before, proportion <note>original: "analogy"</note> is the most beautiful of bonds. The soul is divided in the manner of the Titans <note>original: "Titannically" — in Greek myth, the Titans tore the god Dionysus apart; Neoplatonists used this to symbolize how the soul's unified power is divided as it enters the physical world</note>, but it is structured through harmony and joined together in a way that gives life <note>original: "vivifically"</note>. Furthermore, in the third place, the soul is divided into powers that allow it to return to itself through a circular motion <note>original: "circular energy"</note>. These twofold circles represent its powers. Having established these points, we must now demonstrate what follows.

Since the soul consists of three parts—Essence, Sameness, and Difference—and contains these categories as a middle ground between indivisible <term>impartible: something that cannot be divided into parts, like a spirit or a mathematical point</term> and divisible <term>partible: something that can be divided, like physical matter</term> natures, it knows both types of nature through them. The soul is the image of the indivisible and the model <note>original: "paradigm"</note> for the divisible. As Empedocles says:

> We see Earth by earth, and Water by water,
> Divine Air by air, and consuming Fire by fire;
> We see Love by love, and Strife by gloomy strife.
> <note>original: "Water by water, earth by earthly sight, / Ether divine we see by ether’s light; / Fire ever splendid we discern by fire; / View love by love, by strife contention dire."</note>

<margin>I. 298. 7</margin>
In the same way, we say that the soul, through its own Essence, knows all the essences it comes from and all those that come after it. Through its Sameness, it knows the similarity found in all divine, mental, and physical <note>original: "intelligible, intellectual, and sensible"</note> natures. And through its Difference, it knows the distinctions that run through everything. Because the soul is inherently harmonized, it uses its own inner harmony to understand both divine and physical harmony. Since it also possesses intellectual powers, it recognizes power wherever it exists. 

Therefore, based on what has been said, the explanation of the soul's powers of knowledge <note>original: "gnostic energies"</note> is now clear. Using what it possesses within its own being, the soul knows both the original divine models and their physical images. Through the rational principles <note>original: "reasons"</note> given to it by the Creator <term>Demiurgus: the "Craftsman" or Creator of the physical universe in Platonic philosophy</term>, it mentally understands the natures that exist both above and below it. 

By returning to itself through a circular motion, the soul comes into contact—as Timaeus says—with both indivisible and divisible essences. By looking inward, it discovers that it contains the rational structure <note>original: "reason"</note> of all things. All knowledge is achieved when the knower becomes like the thing being known. This likeness is achieved through the sharing of one Form <term>Form: in Platonic thought, the perfect, eternal template of a thing</term>. Therefore, there is a single rational principle shared by the knower and the object known; because they are the same, this principle joins them together. However, because the rational principles in knowing beings are diverse¹—depending on the rank and degree of their existence—knowledge itself takes on many different forms...

<summary>Proclus explains that the soul gains knowledge because its internal structure (comprising Essence, Sameness, and Difference) mirrors the structure of the universe, following the principle that "like knows like." By looking inward, the soul finds the rational blueprints for all reality, connecting it to both divine and physical existence.</summary>

<page-num>159</page-num>
<header>BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

...difference. Intellectual knowledge is indivisible <term>impartible: something that cannot be divided into parts, like a spirit or a mathematical point</term> and eternal because the internal principles <note>original: "reasons"—in this context, these are the *logoi*, or the rational, formative structures within the soul</note> of things within it are of this kind. However, the soul's knowledge <note>original: "psychical knowledge"</note> is unfolded and exists in step-by-step reasoning <term>discursive energies: the process of reaching a conclusion through a series of logical steps rather than through direct, instant intuition</term>; this is because the principles of the soul, through which it knows things, have an unfolding nature.

Furthermore, intellectual knowledge is uniform because its principles exist as single units <term>monadically: existing as a "monad" or a single, unified entity</term>, for they are the primary sources. But the soul's knowledge has two forms because its principles also have a twofold existence: reasoning <term>dianoetic: relating to the soul’s ability to think through things logically and mathematically</term> exists in one way, but opinion <term>doxastic: relating to belief or opinion based on sensory experience</term> exists in another. Therefore, knowledge is both one and twofold, according to the essential division of these principles. For if one of the soul's "circles" knows the realm of pure thought <note>original: "intelligible"</note>, but the other knows the realm of the senses <note>original: "sensible essence"</note>, what is it that declares these two are different from each other, and that the former is a model <note>original: "paradigm"</note> while the latter is merely an image? It is impossible for something that does not know both to speak about the difference between them, as we may learn in Plato’s *Theætetus*. 

Hence, as it is said in that text, the nature that knows things seen and things heard—the former through sight and the latter through hearing—and says that these are different from each other, must know both. Similarly, this reason <note>or logic</note> which is distinct from the two circles, speaking through the whole soul about both the intellectual and the sensory worlds and being common to both circles, is, I would say, the activity <note>original: "energy"</note> of the essential part of the soul. Because the soul is a single essence, it possesses this single power of knowing <term>gnostic energy: the capacity for knowledge or perception</term> which Plato calls "reason." This is why we simply call the whole soul "rational." 

This reason is therefore the soul's single knowledge. Through the "circle of the *same*," it knows the indivisible, but through the "circle of the *different*," it knows the scattered existence <term>dissipated essence: the physical world, where things are divided and spread out across space and time</term>. For although both circles exist between the indivisible and the divisible, the circle of the *same* shares more in the indivisible, while the circle of the *different* shares more in the divisible. This is the single, essential logic, just as the soul's essence is one, existing before the split into "same" and "different." Its life is also "self-motion," which exists in both circles; but its knowledge is "transitive" <note>transitive: here meaning knowledge that moves from one thought to the next, rather than being static</note>, and this is also common to both circles. On this account, the soul is not only twofold but also a single unity. So much, then, has been said to understand this entire doctrine.

Moving on to specifics, however, it must be observed that Plato says the soul consists of three parts and is mixed from them. This "mixture" indicates the union of these gathered parts; but the "number" indicates their unmixed purity. For they would not remain "three" unless they preserved their own nature unconfused. It must also be observed that when speaking of divisible natures, he says, "*when the soul touches on a certain thing having a scattered existence <note>original: "dissipated essence"</note>.*" For the phrase "to have" <note>original Greek: *to te gar echein* (το τε γαρ εχειν)</note> pertains to things which...

<summary>Proclus explains how the soul acts as a bridge between the eternal and the physical, using its unified "reason" to perceive both through the distinct functions of the "circles" of Sameness and Difference.</summary>
