# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.

...possess essence and being as if they came from the outside <note>original: "adventitiously"</note>, while the subject matter itself is non-essential and non-being. The phrase "a certain thing" <note>original: "το τινος" (to tinos)</note> is most suited to things that are in some way divisible <term>partible: having parts; the opposite of a single, unified spirit</term> and extended in space <note>original: "endued with interval"</note>. Furthermore, the term **to touch** is appropriately used because the soul sits directly over sensible objects <note>physical things perceived by the senses</note> and is suspended from intelligible truths <note>eternal, spiritual realities</note>. *This "contact" describes a type of knowledge that is clear, immediate, and established through a direct focus on the object of knowledge.* "As a contact," says one of the Gods. 

But concerning indivisible essences <note>original: "impartible essences"</note>, Plato was satisfied with only saying, "*and when on that which is indivisible*." This is because simplicity and uniformity are the unique traits of the indivisible essence alone. Moreover, the phrase **to speak** appropriately signifies the soul’s intelligence. For the soul is reason, but "to speak" is the active result <note>original: "ενεργημα" (energēma)—the boundary or completed state of an energy. Just as a "thought" is the result of "thinking," an *energēma* is the result of *energeia* (energy or activity)</note> of reason. This is the same way that "to perceive intellectually" is the activity of the intellect, and "to germinate" is the activity of nature. The activities of these essences are named using words derived from the names of the essences themselves.

<margin>✓</margin>
We should not, however, be ignorant of what Porphyry <note>a major Neoplatonist philosopher and editor of Plotinus</note> relates concerning the words *it speaks* and *it ends* <note>original: "περι του λεγει, και ληγει" (peri tou legei, kai lēgei)</note>. He mentions that he met one interpreter, Amelius <note>a student of Plotinus; his name was omitted in the original Greek text but restored here</note>, who instead of reading "it speaks being moved," read "it ends being moved." However, it is difficult to apply this reading to the soul, which moves incessantly, as we have observed before. Porphyry adds that he told Amelius the word "speaks" should be used, not "ends," and that Amelius was very much hurt by this correction. However, Porphyry later found a man named Socrates <note>not the famous philosopher, but a later scholar/scribe</note> who also used the reading "ends," just like Amelius. 

Despite this, we must write, "**it speaks being moved through the whole of itself**," and not "it ends being moved," as that Socrates and Amelius wrote, according to Porphyry’s account. This is because **to speak** is the essential <note>original: "ουσιωδης" (ousiodēs)</note> activity of reason. Therefore, the soul—being reason and a rational intellect—speaks and sees intellectually through its entire self when it comes into contact with either a divisible or an indivisible essence. It identifies what the object of its perception is because the soul itself is both indivisible and divisible. If the various "categories" <note>original: "genera"</note> within the soul were entirely separated from each other, the soul would not be able to use its knowledge of "being" to understand a specific "essence." But if those categories were entirely destroyed <note>original: "corrupted"</note>, there would be no definite knowledge of any beings at all.

<header>BOOK III.] TIMAEUS OF PLATO.</header>

Nor would it be possible to say that essence is one thing, but sameness is another. However, since the middle categories <note>original: "genera"</note> are mingled with each other without being confused, the soul understands each thing clearly and—as Plato says—through its entire self. If the soul speaks while being moved throughout its entire self, it is clear that it is both one and not one. It possesses knowledge common to both extremes yet different from them. As a single entity, it speaks about all things as a whole; yet, it is not entirely a whole, because it is not [completely] one. 

Likewise, in its knowledge of spiritual realities <note>original: "intelligibles"</note>, the circle of **the same** knows physical things <note>original: "sensibles"</note> by looking at their divine models <note>original: "paradigms"</note>. Meanwhile, the circle of the **different** knows spiritual realities by looking at their physical representations <note>original: "images"</note>. Because each part possesses its object of knowledge perfectly, it necessarily sees that one is the model and the other is the image. If it did not know that one was a model or the other an image, its knowledge would not be complete in itself. However, by knowing that something is a model, it knows what it is a model of; and by knowing that something is an image, it knows what it is an image of. It is therefore very appropriate to say that the soul speaks of all things through its entire self. That concludes the discussion of the things themselves.

However, some people mistakenly read the text as *ends*, rather than *it speaks through the whole of itself*. As Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–c. 305 AD) who edited the works of Plotinus</note> relates, Amelius <note>A student of Plotinus and a philosopher in his own right</note> read it this way and was unable to explain the meaning of Plato's words. We should add that while reading "it speaks while being moved" is easier, we might also read it as "it ends." The word **ends** <note>original: "λήγει" (lēgei)</note> signifies a single understanding drawn from many concepts regarding knowable things, reaching a specific and definite insight into each. The meaning of the whole would then be: *the soul, being moved, ends at the knowledge of each thing* [with which it comes into contact]. The goal of "being moved" is to reach a stopping point, yet the soul never stops moving and is always arriving at a certain understanding. Aristotle <note>The famous Greek philosopher and student of Plato</note> also noticed this in the movement of the heavens, saying that they are always moved *at their goal* <note>original: "in the end"</note>.

> "It also declares what any given thing is the same as, and what it is different from; to what it is most closely related, and in what way and how it exists. It explains how these things happen to exist or to be *acted upon* <note>original: "suffer"</note>, both in the world of changing things <note>original: "things which are generated"</note> and in relation to things that possess an eternal sameness of being."

There are three interpretations of these proposed words, all of which are reasonable, and it is necessary to show the power of each. The first interpretation treats the whole passage as one sentence; the second makes it two sentences (dividing the words as we do); and the third makes it three, form—

# PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS [BOOK III]

...ing the division according to each of the clauses <term>original: "colon"; here referring to a specific phrase or part of a sentence</term>. The first interpretation is as follows: “*When the soul touches on a certain thing which has a scattered essence <note>original: "dissipated essence"; referring to the physical world where things are spread out in space and time</note>, and when on that which is indivisible <note>original: "impartible"; referring to the eternal, spiritual world</note>,*” here the interpretation makes a small stop <gloss>meaning a comma</gloss> and then brings in the rest of the words: “*it says, being moved through the whole of itself, what that is with which any thing is the same, etc.*” 

For Plato asserts that the soul says all these things while being moved through the whole of itself, regarding both the indivisible and the divided essence. In both cases, it comes into contact with sameness and difference, relationships and qualities, actions and passions. All of these exist by analogy in both spiritual realities <note>original: "intelligibles"</note> and physical realities <note>original: "sensibles"</note>. 

The second interpretation makes the first sentence what we mentioned before: “*When the soul touches on a certain thing which has a scattered essence, and when on that which is indivisible.*” And the second sentence is: “*It also asserts, being moved, what that is with which any thing is the same, from what it is different, to what it is related, in what respect, and how it exists <note>original: "subsists"</note>, etc.*” This interpretation differs from the first because it separates what is said about "essence" (the core being) from what is said about "things pertaining to essence" (its properties). 

The third interpretation makes a rapid division of the clauses. It makes one division the phrase we mentioned before; the second, “*It also asserts what that is with which any thing is the same, and from what it is different;*” and the third includes all that follows. As we have said, the words have a threefold interpretation. However, we should direct our attention especially to the realities themselves.

<margin>Categories</margin>
It is evident, then, that sameness and difference exist in spiritual realities. But how do relationship, situation, quality, "when," and "passion" <note>These are several of Aristotle's "Categories" used to describe how things exist</note> exist there? For these are well known to exist in physical things, but how do they exist in spiritual ones? May it not be said that the categories of being manifestly exist in spiritual realities because they are the most "true" beings? 

You may also assume that relationship, situation, and so on, can be observed analogously in spiritual realities. Relationship can be seen, if you like, according to the "paternal" and "maternal" <note>metaphorical terms for the way higher divine principles produce lower ones</note>, and also the similar and dissimilar, the equal and unequal. However, you must not assume these are accidental relationships <note>original: "unessential habitudes"</note>, but rather relationships that are essential to spiritual beings. For the most fundamental relationship is there, where there is a more abundant union <note>original: "communion"</note>, and where all things exist in their primary form. 

Hence Plato says, “*and to what it is especially related.*” Furthermore, the phrase *in a certain respect* <note>original Greek: ὅπῃ (hopē)</note> applies to spiritual realities insofar as each of them is not completely *the One* itself, but exists "after a certain manner" <note>original Greek: πῃ (pē)</note>; for *the One* is simply and purely one. Again, the *same* which is there is also *different*, but it is not simply *different*; for if it were, "difference" <note>original Greek: ετερότης (heterotēs). The original text had a typo: ετεροητος</note> would be no different than sameness. The same logic applies to the rest of the categories. All things...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the soul identifies and categorizes the relationships between different levels of reality. It explores the philosophical nuances of how eternal forms (intelligibles) and physical things (sensibles) share in the qualities of sameness, difference, and "suffering" or participation.</meta>

# [BOOK III] THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO

"Therefore," he says, "all things exist, and each is one according to its essence <note>original: 'essence'; the fundamental nature or 'being' of a thing</note>, but they are all things through participation." And this is what the phrase "in a certain respect" means when applied to intelligible realities <note>original: 'intelligibles'; eternal things known by the mind rather than the senses</note>.

<margin>A. 304,1</margin>
Again, the question of "how it exists" <note>original: 'subsists'</note> is answered there according to the different ways things participate. For many things participate in the same unique quality in different ways. For instance, "permanency" <note>rest or stability</note> participates in "sameness," and "motion" also participates in it, yet not in the same manner; the former participates more, and the latter less. In the hierarchy of forms, intelligible realities participate in "the One" or in "essence" in one way, while intellectual realities <note>beings or forms characterized by the act of thinking</note> participate in another way. Among these, some participate differently from others, according to the measure of each one's essence. This is why we ask "how it exists." 

But the "when" exists there, either according to the operations of intelligible realities on sublunary natures <note>original: 'sublunary'; referring to the physical world below the moon, which is subject to change</note>—for these physical things sometimes participate in the forms and sometimes become capable of being shared by certain things—or the "when" exists according to the acts of understanding <note>original: 'intellections'</note> of the soul itself. For as the soul applies itself at different times to different forms, it perceives some at one moment and others at another. Eternal being sometimes approaches the soul in the same way that the intelligible world does. 

Likewise, each thing exists there "with reference to each other," insofar as all things are contained within one another and move through each other. All things are connected and adapted to one another; they may be dependent on a single source, or one may be the cause while another is the effect, or they may exist differently in some other way. 

And "to suffer" <note>original: 'passio'; in this philosophical context, 'suffering' does not mean pain, but rather the state of being acted upon or being a recipient of a quality</note> exists there insofar as things are filled by each other, and all things share their own unique characteristics with everything else. For Plato frequently describes "participation" using the word "suffering," as we may learn in the *Sophist* <note>original: 'Sophista'; one of Plato's dialogues</note>. For he says there that the "whole" is the "suffering one" (or that which is passive to "the One"), but it is not "the One" itself, because it merely participates in "the One." 

These things, therefore, are present in both intelligible and sensible <note>physical/perceivable</note> realities because, in both cases, it happens that each thing exists and "suffers" (receives influence) in relation to every other thing. Plato, therefore (as I have said), is accustomed to indicate participation by the word "suffering." As we have stated, he calls everything that participates "that which suffers the thing" in which it participates.

In short, the Soul of the Universe speaks through the whole of itself according to a single knowledge, encompassing both generated natures <note>physical things that are born and die</note> and those things that possess an eternal sameness of being. The soul asserts of each thing what it is, what it is the same as, and what it is different from. It also describes how each thing exists, whether through its existence, its actions, or its "passions" <note>the ways it is acted upon</note>. For among both real beings <note>eternal forms</note> and generated natures, one thing is affected by another to a greater degree, and one thing acts upon another to a greater degree.

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III]

...another. The soul perceives all of this intellectually, identifying some things through the circle of the **same**, but others through the circle of the **different**. It understands all sensible objects <note>original: "sensibles"; things perceived by the senses rather than the intellect</note> and their actions and experiences <note>original: "passions"; in this context, how a thing is acted upon or affected by outside forces</note> beforehand. Because the universe is a single living being, every part is interconnected <note>original: "copassive"; a philosophical term meaning that what happens to one part of the universe is felt by the whole</note>, so that all things that come into being are parts of the life of the universe, as if they were characters in a single drama. 

It is like a tragic poet who composes a play featuring gods, heroes, and other characters. The poet assigns specific speeches to those actors who are willing to play the part, while the poet alone understands the unified purpose behind everything that is said. We must imagine the World Soul in a similar way. By giving life to the entire world—which is both unified and diverse, like a many-headed creature speaking through all its heads in both Greek and foreign <note>original: "Barbaric"</note> languages—this soul understands the causes of everything that is created. It knows specific details through universal principles, accidental qualities through essential natures, and parts through the whole. 

However, it knows all things purely through its divine nature. A god, in their capacity as a god, understands individual things, things that go against nature, and indeed all things—even matter itself. For every thing, whatever it may be, is "one" because it originates from **the one** <note>In Neoplatonism, "The One" is the ultimate source of all reality</note>. Therefore, the knowledge of all things, simplified and immediate, is divine.

> “But reason becoming true according to **same**, and also being conversant with **different**, and revolving about **same** without speech and sound, in that which is moved by it.”

Atticus <note>A 2nd-century Platonist philosopher</note> interprets "reason" here as the soul’s power of attention. Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist</note> sees it as the "charioteer" who guides the two horses of the soul. Iamblichus <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist</note> believes it refers to the soul in its entirety. For the soul moves its entire self, and throughout its whole being, it serves as the rational principle <note>original: "reason"; here meaning the 'logos' or structural logic of beings</note> of all that exists. 

While all these interpretations seem to reflect Plato’s meaning, Porphyry’s view is more consistent with both this text and other works. The "reason" mentioned here is not the soul's essence itself, nor its active functioning, but rather the single power of the soul’s essence. This power makes the soul a unity, just as the soul is formed by two parts: sameness and difference. Why would there only be two circles—instead of three, to match the three elements—unless a single essence exists within both? The power of this single essence is this "reason," which is neither the essence itself nor the energy produced by the essence (which would be the third level of order).

# BOOK III] PLATO'S TIMAEUS.

Therefore, the soul’s reason knows both **sameness** and **difference** regarding both the eternal <note>original: "intelligible"</note> and the physical <note>original: "sensible"</note> essence. It is not "eternally true" like the pure divine intellect; instead, it "becomes true" regarding both, because its knowledge moves from one thing to another <note>original: "transitive nature"</note>. 

Thus, the phrase "according to sameness" signifies the difference between the knowledge of a divine soul and our own human knowledge. However, the word "becoming" highlights the difference between the knowledge of a soul <note>original: "psychical knowledge"</note> and that of the pure intellect. This reason, therefore, understands eternal truths and physical objects by coming into contact with their inherent sameness and difference. It flows through the entire soul, activating the **circle of the same** in one area and the **circle of the different** in another. Through the first, it contemplates eternal realities; through the second, it observes the physical world. 

In this way, it mirrors the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note>, of whom the *Chaldean Oracles* say: "Through his intellect he possesses eternal truths, but he introduces sensory perception to the worlds." Similarly, as the soul's reason moves through the soul—governing both itself and the whole soul concerning eternal and physical sameness and difference—at times it produces opinions and beliefs, and at other times it reaches toward pure intellect and science. It is "becoming true" rather than "being eternally true" in the way that the pure intellect is. 

Pure intellect is *really* true and remains the same. This is because it either knows both eternal beings and created things simultaneously, or because it is eternally consistent—unlike the reason found in individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls like ours. Our reason is not always true; it can be clouded by error and ignorance because of its connection to the physical world <note>original: "through generation"</note>. 

Alternatively, the soul’s reason is "becoming true" because it moves back and forth in its twofold knowledge. Yet it is also true "according to sameness" because it always grasps the complete form of every object it knows. Unlike our human reason, which must work through the forms it beholds one by one, the World Soul’s reason surveys the entirety of everything it sees at once. When we encounter different parts of the same object, we fail to see it as a unified whole <note>original: "according to same"</note>; instead, we only perceive things in pieces. 

Or it may be said that this reason follows "sameness" when it deals with both sameness and difference. It "becomes" true in the same way for both eternal and physical things, knowing both at once—how they are the same and how they are different—so that it can see and explain how the physical world originates from the eternal world.

Therefore, acting "according to sameness" shows that this reason is capable of knowledge <note>original: "gnostic"</note> through a single focused power <note>original: "projecting energy"</note> directed at both what is truly **different** and what is truly the **same**. By having a knowledge that moves between these concepts, this reason "becomes true." Its function is to describe what is truly the same and what is truly different within both eternal reality <note>original: "intelligible"</note> and physical nature. The task of this reason is to see exactly how eternal truths differ from physical objects. For there must be a certain something—

...which is capable of knowing <note>original: "gnostic"</note> both, so that it can state that intellectual realities <note>original: "intelligibles"</note> are one thing, but sensory objects <note>original: "sensibles"</note> are another. But " *it is carried along within that which it moves,* " as it proceeds into the two circles and moves both itself and them. For this motion <note>original: "lation"</note> reveals the progression from a single form of knowledge into a divided, twofold knowledge. However, this reason itself is a unified knowledge [or a knowledge patterned after the form of *the one*], covering both intellectual and sensory things. Or it may be said that it speaks within the soul because the intellectual is one thing and the sensory is another; or that it knows<sup>2</sup> both, existing before the two circles which understand intellectual and sensory things in a divided manner. Since the soul is both a single unit <note>original: "monad"</note> and a pair <note>original: "duad"</note>, it uses one form of knowledge to unitedly comprehend both intellectual and sensory things; and yet, it also understands some things through the **circle of the same** and others through the **circle of the different**. Just as the unified state <note>original: "monadic"</note> precedes the dual state <note>original: "biformed"</note> in essence, harmony, form, and power, so too in the activities of knowledge <note>original: "gnostic energies"</note>, this single reason is the primary leader of all specialized knowledge. These points have been frequently repeated by me because of the confusion modern interpreters face when explaining them.

Plato, pointing out these details, says that as reason itself becomes true, it revolves <note>original: "is borne along"</note> around both intellectual and sensory things within that which it moves—that is, within each of the circles. But it moves without speech or sound. For internal reason has no need for either of these; they are only necessary for the reason that is expressed through the mouth. It is as if he had said that this internal reason has a motion more perfect than any activity <note>original: "energy"</note> that manifests externally. For sound and voice are taken to be symbols of sensory motions. Therefore, internal reason—acting as the charioteer and moving each of the circles on its path—produces in us two types of knowledge, which Plato explains in the following section. However, if we follow the most accurate manuscripts and read *in that which is moved by itself*, rather than *in that which is moved by it* (meaning reason), this would refer to the whole soul, identifying it by its very definition. For the thing being defined is, in a certain respect, the same as its definition. Therefore, reason moves within the soul (for it is the soul that moves itself); at one moment it knows the **sameness** and **difference** of sensory things, and at another, of intellectual things. It seems that **sameness** and **difference** are the primary characteristics of knowledge, just as motion and stability <note>original: "permanency"</note> characterize life. Hence

<page-num>167</page-num>
### BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

Also, Plato particularly makes mention of these, because all knowledge has an alliance to them.

<margin>II. 309, 3</margin>
> "When it is dealing with a sensory nature <note>original: "sensible nature"</note>, and the **circle of the different**—proceeding with integrity <note>original: "rectitude"</note>—announces what it perceives to the whole soul; then stable and true opinions and belief are produced."

In what is said here, Plato speaks about the knowledge of sensory objects <note>original: "sensibles"</note>, and how the reason in the soul of the universe generates this knowledge: namely, by moving the **circle of the different**, and the rational principles <note>original: "reasons"</note> which preside over the orderly distribution of the whole, and by preserving this circle in a state of undeviating integrity. For "integrity" <note>original: "rectitude"</note> demonstrates "right opinion," as Porphyry interprets and Iamblichus admits. It likewise demonstrates the untamed and the unswerving <note>original: "non-verging"</note> in providential actions <note>original: "energies"</note>. For a tireless and rapidly-moving power is adapted to the intellect; but the inflexible and the uninclined are adapted to providence and productive <note>original: "prolific"</note> actions. And to the indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> essence, indeed, purity of intellect is adapted; but to the divisible <note>original: "partible"</note> essence, undefiled action. 

Porphyry, therefore, considers the circle which is moved with integrity to be indivisible; but that which is not accurately a circle, but in a certain respect participates in a straight line, to be divisible. For the knowledge of sensory objects tends toward external things, and is again reflected back to the soul itself. Hence, that which is not accurately a circle in the soul is neither a straight line alone (such as is the knowledge of the senses), nor a perfect circle (such as is the knowledge of discursive reason <note>original: "dianoia"</note>). 

Iamblichus, however, rejects all this, as pertaining to human and not to divine knowledge. When, therefore, the charioteer <note>The guiding faculty of the soul</note> moves the **circle of the different**, but this remains undeviating and turned toward itself, it excites the rational principles of sensory objects and announces to the whole soul the quality of each sensory object. Since the whole soul knows every sensory thing according to this—for the **circle of the same**, when it beholds intellectual realities <note>original: "intelligibles"</note>, also knows sensory objects as if from their cause, but the **circle of the different** knows them immediately and in a corresponding manner—when this is the case, then stable and true opinions and belief are generated in it. 

For the more divine soul, judiciously approving (or rather, imparting by illumination a more intellectual energy to) the circle of opinion <note>original: "doxastic circle"</note>, this circle possesses its own proper life with purity, and the knowledge in it is rendered stable. It previously comprehends in a stable manner those things that move through space, and it faithfully and stably understands things that are changing and accidental <note>original: "flowing and contingent"</note>.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s analysis of how the World Soul processes knowledge. <page-num>168</page-num>
# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK III.

*For opinion is indeed the activity and knowledge of the soul that forms opinions <note>original: "doxastic soul"</note>; but faith is the stable and unwavering judgment of that opinion.* And that is enough concerning this particular point.

However, it deserves to be investigated how the circle of *the different* is, as has been said, capable of knowing <note>original: "gnostic"</note> everything perceived by the senses <note>original: "sensible"</note>, and why the circle of *the same* is capable of knowing intellectual realities <note>original: "intelligibles"</note>, as will be explained. For even though we separate the powers of movement from each other—where one circle causes motion to the right and the other causes motion to the left—we must not separate the powers of knowledge in the same way. Instead, it must be acknowledged that they possess knowledge of both sensory and intellectual things. 

Might it not therefore be said that the vital motions relate to outward movements <note>original: "progressions"</note>, while the powers of knowledge relate to the return <note>original: "regressions"</note> to the source? The circle of *the same*, because it is closest to the intellectual realm and originates from it, is moved with life as it proceeds. Through its outward movement, it forms the primary cycle <note>original: "period"</note>, and through this, it moves the entire world. For the secondary cycles follow the primary ones. Aristotle’s claim is also true: the world of change <note>original: "generation"</note> is moved by both circles, receiving its unchanging qualities from the motion to the right, and its changing qualities from the rotation to the left. 

The circle of *the same*, therefore, turns back toward the intellectual realm; for this reason, it is capable of knowing intellectual truths. Thus, it is necessary that everywhere, a return <note>original: "conversion or regression"</note> follows a state of permanence. But the circle of *the different* remains within the circle of *the same*—for it is directly contained by it, just as the circle of *the same* is contained by the Intellect. It proceeds through a life-giving motion to the second realm that it moves—meaning the second rotation <note>original: "circulation"</note>;<margin>Namely, the rotation of the planetary spheres.</margin> and through this, it also moves the world of change, just as the circle of *the same* moves the universe through the sphere of the fixed stars <note>original: "inerratic sphere"</note>. 

However, when it turns back or returns through knowledge, it turns toward the life-giving motion of the circle of *the same* which is directly above it. By returning to it through knowledge, it is intellectually turned toward what the motion of the circle of *the same* governs through life. In this way, it gains knowledge of the entire world by connecting its own return <note>original: "regression"</note> to this circle of sameness which exists before it. Thus, one circle becomes capable of knowing intellectual truths, while the other becomes capable of knowing sensory things. For if the latter circle moves the cycle <note>original: "period"</note> of *the different*, it must know this cycle as well as the things it leads and what it follows as an intermediary. Similarly, if the circle of *the same* moves the universe, it must know what it is imitating <note>original: "assimilated"</note> as it lives this life. Therefore, for one of these circles, the return is from a part to the whole; but for the other,

# BOOK III.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 169

"...through one whole to another whole." This concludes our response to this inquiry, which requires deep contemplation.

Therefore, it is incorrect to believe that the soul of the universe receives its knowledge of sensory objects <note>original: "sensibles"</note> from the outside, or that it lacks the organs needed to perceive them. Such limitations belong only to individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls. Instead, we should understand that by turning inward toward itself, the soul possesses the rational principles <note>original: "reasons"</note> of sensory things, which are actively produced from within its own nature. 

For this reason, Plato accurately states that the "circle of the different" acts upon what is sensory, but not toward sensory essence <note>the material reality of things</note> itself. He does this to show that the soul contains the causes of sensory things within its own rational principles, rather than having a type of knowledge that is simply on the same level as sensory objects or trapped within them. These explanations are consistent with the things themselves. 

The phrase, "*enunciates to the whole soul*," however, agrees with the statement, "*it speaks, being moved through the whole of itself*." These phrases indicate that the "circle of the different" makes direct contact with sensory things, and through this, the entire soul gains knowledge of them. The word *autou* <note>original Greek: αυτου; meaning "of it" or "itself"</note> can be interpreted in many ways, as Porphyry <note>a Neo-Platonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note> observed, but it should probably be applied to *reason*. This is because opinions and the beliefs held by the circle as it moves correctly and reports on sensory things are the offspring of reason. While opinions and beliefs reside in the opinion-forming <note>original: "doxastic"</note> part of the soul, they belong to reason because they are set in motion, awakened, and maintained by it. This explains how reason is coordinated with the "circle of the different." 

Next, Plato speaks of reason's coordination with the "circle of the same," adding the following:

<margin>7, 312, 6</margin>

> "But when, on the other hand, the soul is occupied with the rational <note>original: "logistic"</note> power, and the 'circle of the same'—revolving with ease—reveals its perceptions, then intellect <note>intuitive understanding</note> and science <note>certain, demonstrable knowledge</note> are necessarily produced."

Plato creates a complete set of opposites:³ he sets the *rational* <note>original: "logistic"</note> against the *sensible*, the *easy revolution* of the circles against *straight or linear* motion, what *is* <note>eternal reality</note> against what is *generated* <note>constantly changing</note>, *indication* <note>revealing</note> against *enunciation* <note>reporting</note>, *intellect* against *opinion*, and *science* against *faith* <note>or belief</note>. 

The term *rational* <note>original: "logistic"</note> here, however, does not mean the process of reasoning as some might assume, but refers to the intelligible realm <note>the world of pure ideas</note> itself. Plato contrasts this with the *sensible* realm because the reasoning found there is more divine than the reasoning within the soul, as we have—

...is frequently observed, and in the realm of the intelligible <note>the world of ideas or things understood by the mind alone</note> it always exists as an active reality <note>original: "subsists in energy"</note>. It seems that he names the *rational* part the *reasoning* <term>original: "logistic"; the faculty of the soul that calculates or reasons</term> part, just as he later calls the *sensible* <note>objects of the senses</note> the *sensitive*. For the sensible object moves the senses, and the intelligible object moves the reasoning of the soul. 

Therefore, the reasoning faculty will be that which is understood by the soul’s power of reasoning; this prior cause of understanding is also called *reasoning* <note>original: "logistic"</note> by association. But he describes the intellectual as "revolving" <note>original: "voluble"; meaning easily turning or moving in a circle</note>, because it moves without hindrance, and also as circular, flourishing, and possessing perfection in its thoughts <note>original: "intellections"</note>. It acts upon divinity, takes the form of the Good <note>original: "boniform"</note>, and revolves around the intelligible as its center. "Hurry to join yourself to the center of resounding light," says one of the Gods. 

The word *being* signifies that which is filled with truly existing realities and is united to them. The word *indicates* signifies unfolding something into the light, teaching it, or producing it from a secret <note>original: "arcane"</note> source. Furthermore, by *intellect* here, we must understand intellect as a state of being <note>original: "according to habit"</note>. 

*For intellect exists in three ways: the first is divine, such as the creator-intellect <note>original: "demiurgic intellect"</note>; the second is that which is shared by the soul and is essential and perfect in itself; and the third is that which exists as a state of being, which is why the soul is called intellectual.* 

Science <note>original: "episteme"; structured, certain knowledge</note> is the primary knowledge that is filled by the intelligible world; it exists as an unchanging, steady, and immovable activity. It differs from "intellect," <note>original: "The word *Nous* (Intellect) is omitted here in the original Greek text."</note> because intellect is seen in the soul’s simple, direct focus <note>original: "projections"</note> alone. Through intellect, the soul immediately perceives the whole of each object of thought, because the ability to grasp things all at once is the unique characteristic of intellect. 

However, science is seen in the knowledge of causes. This is the hallmark of science, as is the ability to organize and divide various forms. It is evident that by having knowledge of beings, science also knows which of them act as causes and which act as effects. All knowledge of this kind is called science, just as the simple grasp of an object of thought is called intelligence. This is our explanation.

Iamblichus <note>a highly influential Neo-Platonist philosopher, c. 245–325 AD</note>, however, believes this intellect is more ancient than the soul, containing it from above and giving it perfection. He also argues against those who either immediately connect the soul to the all-perfect intellect (for it is necessary that there should be middle stages between higher natures and those that participate in them), or those who suppose intellect to be merely a state of the soul. ...it is necessary that before something exists in another thing, it must first exist in itself. This is rightly stated regarding things in general. However, it is more consistent with Plato’s words to view this "intellect" as a state <term>original: "habit"; a stable internal disposition or quality</term> within the soul itself. For Timaeus says it is produced from the activity <term>original: "energy"</term> of the *circle of the same* <note>In Plato’s Timaeus, the soul is composed of two revolving circles: "the Same" (representing identity and intellect) and "the Different" (representing diversity and sensation)</note>. 

But the Intellect created by the Demiurgus <note>the divine Craftsman or creator of the cosmos</note> must be considered superior to the soul, because he placed the soul within the body and the intellect within the soul in a proportional way. It is clear that this higher Intellect is more ancient than the soul, just as Timaeus says the soul is more ancient than the body. 

However, the "intellect" mentioned here is the result of reason moving toward the intelligible <note>the realm of pure, non-physical ideas</note> through the *circle of the same*. He says it is produced because that circle revolves with ease around what is grasped by the power of reasoning. Therefore, this specific intellect is not more ancient than the soul, but is a certain state of it, in the same way that science is. For this reason, he says it is generated in the soul, just like science, opinion, and faith. 

From everything that has been said, this one point may be summarized: *when reason deals with the intelligible, and the circle of the same reveals the nature of being to reason through its intellectual activity, then intellect and science are produced in the soul.* This must necessarily be the case, for a perfection suited to such activities exists alongside them. 

One might then ask: does reason focus on intelligibles at one time, but on sensibles <note>physical things perceived by the senses</note> at another? This is by no means the case for the universal soul [the Soul of the Universe]. It is always "on high" and is always directed toward intelligibles. It remains established there and provides for the sensible world through providence with an unrestrained activity. Because the *circle of the same* moves so easily, the *circle of the different* remains constant and upright in its path. 

We must also not overlook that Timaeus mentions "the circle of *the different* proceeding with rectitude" <note>moving in a straight or correct alignment</note>. In saying this, he is looking at the circles of a "partial" [human] soul. He asserts that when a human soul is in a fallen condition, its *circle of the same* is shackled and its *circle of the different* is distorted. By using these words here, he contrasts "rectitude" with "distortion," and "facility of motion" (which signifies being unencumbered) with "being shackled." Just as rectitude in the higher soul indicates a movement <term>original: "lation"; a moving from one place to another</term> that is not distorted by inferior things...

What does Plato intend to signify by the word *this*? Is it intellect and science? If so, he does not just mean the circle of the *different*. Or rather, does he not speak of the twofold pairings: [intellect and science]¹ and opinion and faith? For intellect and science are one of the pairings, and opinion and faith are the second. Through these, he encompasses every soul. Every thing, therefore, which is the recipient of intellect and science, opinion and faith,² is soul. For all these forms of knowledge are rational and transitive <term>moving step-by-step from one thought to another, rather than grasping everything at once</term>. And because they are rational, they are distinct from the irrational powers; but because they are transitive, they are subordinate to pure intellectual knowledge. 

For even if science and intellect exist in the realm of the "intelligibles" <note>the eternal, non-physical forms or ideas</note>, they are not *generated* in them in the same way he says they are in the soul. Sciences in the soul exist by participation; they participate in "science itself," because the soul’s very essence is formed through participation. For "middle" things <note>the soul is considered a 'middle' between the eternal and the physical</note> proceed from the first types <term>original: "genera"</term> and are harmonized in a similar way, since the harmony in the soul comes from "harmony itself." 

The soul likewise possesses "figure" <term>structure or geometric form</term>, similar to the first types. For intellectual figure contains all various figures within it. The soul also possesses powers in the same manner, for intellectual and intelligible powers exist prior to it. It likewise receives motion from the categories of being, and knowledge from the intelligence of the Demiurge <note>the divine Craftsman or Creator</note>, where "permanency" <note>stability or unchanging being</note> is also revealed. *For all knowledge is a certain permanency and a grasping of the thing known, and a fitting connection with it.* 

The motion of the soul, therefore, shares in the soul’s total knowledge, insofar as the soul knows itself³ and moves while looking toward itself; and knowledge shares in motion insofar as it moves from one thought to the next. Specifically, however, the power of motion is defined according to⁴ motion, while the cognitive <term>original: "gnostic"</term> power is defined according to permanency. And the circle of the *different* is related more to motion than to knowledge, but the circle of the *same* is related more to knowledge than to motion; this is because permanency belongs to sameness, while motion belongs to difference. <meta>This page continues Proclus’s discussion of the World Soul's composition. He is explaining how the soul participates in the "genera of being" (the fundamental categories of reality) and how its structure is defined by mathematical and harmonic ratios.</meta>

<page-num>173</page-num>
<header>BOOK III.] PLATO'S TIMAEUS.</header>

...the same, motion; just as in the latter there is sameness, and in the former difference. *But the whole soul participates through the whole of itself in the fundamental types of being.* As far, therefore, as these details are concerned, the <term>psychogony</term> <note>original: "psychogony"; the birth or generation of the soul</note> reaches its completion, being divided into the previously mentioned categories. For the <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: "hypostasis"; the fundamental reality or essential nature</note>, harmony, shape, powers, and activities of the soul have been discussed.***¹

Since, however, the soul is a plurality and the first of composite natures, it is composed not of infinite parts but of numbered things. These are not arranged randomly but are harmonized; because of this, numbers and harmony were very appropriately used in its creation. Since the soul also contains the principles of every mathematical proportion and every harmony—because it is the soul of the world—no proportion is left out [in its composition]. However, because it was formed by the Divine, the more divine of the musical scales was used: the diatonic, for it is filled with divine inspiration <note>original: "entheastic"</note>. 

At first, because "essence," "sameness," and "difference" were used, the "whole" of the soul that exists before its parts was established. But now, through the <term>psychogony</term>, we see the "whole" that exists within the parts. For the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>the Divine Craftsman of the universe</note> divides and then reunites the parts through mathematical proportions. Through the circles, the wholeness of each part is expressed. It must also be understood that the <term>Demiurge</term> in the *Timaeus* acts in cooperation with all the other creative Gods. For he cuts the soul into seven parts in the manner of the <term>Titans</term> <note>referring to the myth where the Titans dismember a god</note>; he reunites them in the manner of <term>Apollo</term>; he produces the body and gives it shape, containing within himself the power of <term>Vulcan</term> <note>original: "Vulcan"; the Roman name for Hephaestus, the smith-god who crafts physical forms</note>; and he sets the limits for rising and falling, and writes the laws of Fate, as he possesses the power of Necessity. 

In this study of the soul’s birth, it is necessary to apply what has been said to the essence of the soul itself, to the things governed by it, or rather, to both. For the natures found within the world are under the dominion of the powers that are essentially part of the soul. It is also necessary to investigate what the "middles" <note>mathematical means or averages</note> are; what the multiple, "superparticular," and "superpartient" ratios are; what the <term>leimma</term> <note>the "remainder" or leftover interval in a musical scale</note> is; and what the seven parts are. We must also ask why the diagram proceeds to a fourfold <term>diapason</term> <note>an octave</note>, a <term>diapente</term> <note>a perfect fifth</note>, and a whole tone.

Of the three types of "middles"—the geometrical, arithmetical, and musical—the solid proportion composed of all three is the equality of <term>Themis</term> <note>the goddess of divine law and order</note>, from whom every order is derived. These three "middles" proceed from the three daughters of <term>Themis</term>: <term>Eunomia</term> (Good Order), <term>Dice</term> (Justice), and <term>Irene</term> (Peace). The arithmetical middle comes from <term>Irene</term>, which exceeds and is exceeded by an equal amount. We use this in times of peace for contracts, and it is through this that the elements remain at rest. <meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the World Soul. Having established the ratios used by the Demiurge, Proclus now explains how the three mathematical "middles" or means—geometric, arithmetical, and harmonic—govern different aspects of the soul’s nature and the physical universe.</meta>

<page-num>174</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO. [BOOK III.</header>

Through Jupiter <note>referring to Zeus as the Demiurge or Divine Creator</note>, the world is adorned with geometrical analogies. Additionally, the harmonic mean comes from Dike <note>original: "Dice"; the goddess of Justice</note>, through which larger things have a larger ratio, and smaller things have a smaller ratio. Since the geometrical mean encompasses the other two, as has been demonstrated, the essence of the soul is adorned by this geometric mean. This is because the soul remains the same through its entire self, being everywhere both <term>partible</term> <note>original: "partible"; divisible, or able to be distributed through space</note> and <term>impartible</term> <note>original: "impartible"; indivisible, or unified in essence</note>.

The soul is also adorned according to the arithmetical mean. This is because its common powers, which move from the indivisible to the divisible—or from the divisible back to the indivisible—surpass and are surpassed by those states in equal measure. 

Furthermore, it is adorned by the harmonic mean¹ because some of the powers within the soul are more distant from their original causes and have a greater degree of transcendence, while others have less. 

Again, the sameness of forms exists appropriately everywhere throughout the whole world—physically and vitally—whether in a plant, an animal, or a stone; this is because the entire world is organized by geometrical proportion. However, the arithmetical mean is most visible in the <term>sublunary elements</term> <note>the four elements (earth, water, air, fire) found below the moon’s orbit</note>, which it balances according to their powers. Finally, the harmonic mean is seen in the world through the celestial spheres, their movements, and the distances between them. For Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the Greco-Egyptian astronomer</note> demonstrates that these intervals exist in harmonic proportion.

The one <term>Demiurge</term> <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine craftsman or creator of the material world</note>, who also creates whole systems, generates everything collectively and all at once, according to "sameness." Others, however, believed different powers were at work. 

There is significant disagreement and even opposition between these thinkers. There are some who, while uniting these powers, are unwilling to admit that "the One" exists without the power of plurality <note>original: "efficacy of multitude"</note>. There are others who, even though they divide these powers, cannot bear to say that the number of powers is disordered or incomplete. Instead, they willingly admit and demonstrate that these powers are contained within their own proper <term>monad</term> <note>original: "monad"; a fundamental, indivisible unit or "the One"</note> and are united and preserved by it.

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

The one <term>Demiurge</term> <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine craftsman or creator of the material world</note> grants to the <term>junior Demiurges</term> <note>original: "junior Demiurgi"; the secondary, celestial gods tasked by the primary creator with fashioning the mortal parts of the universe</note> who come after him several powers at once. He gives them an **assimilative power** when he orders them to imitate his own power in their acts of creation; a **generative power** when he commands them to produce and create animals collectively; and an **analyzing power** when he commands them to take back the parts borrowed from the elements once the physical bodies composed of them are dissolved. Finally, he grants them a **guardian power**, by which he immediately establishes the governors of the world as guardians of the cycles of time, and the earth as the guardian of day and night.

The Demiurge, who produced all things, generated them to exist alongside himself. He made them like their models, perfected them, and turned them back toward himself. The order of these things was not confused by their sudden appearance into the light of existence; rather, that order was even more strictly guarded and connected. For he does not deprive lower beings of the <term>providential care</term> <note>original: "providential care"; the divine foresight and protection extended by higher beings to the rest of creation</note> of more excellent beings, nor does he take away the authority of perfect beings over those that are imperfect. One does not come before the other in time; secondary natures are never left without divine oversight, and ancient, superior natures are never idle or unproductive—it is not as if the former had to wait to receive the care of the latter. 

However, because we are unable to understand—and even less able to explain—the eternal, generous energy of the Father toward the universe, we must be satisfied with speaking of him as acting in stages: at one time generating, at another adorning, at another perfecting, and at another making things like himself. The words of the philosopher [Plato] are prepared to work this understanding in us. For the world now participates in motion and life, according to the doctrine of the Father <note>original: "Father" (*patros*). The Greek text previously read "of the whole" (*pantos*), but Proclus notes it should be corrected to "of the Father."</note>. For the Soul that dwells within the world preserves its own specific types of knowledge, through which it knows both <term>intelligibles</term> <note>original: "intelligibles"; eternal truths and divine realities that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses</note> and <term>mundane natures</term> <note>original: "mundane natures"; things belonging to the physical, material world</note>. But motion and life do not thrive in the soul alone; the soul also imparts them to the entire physical body of the universe. 

Because the structure of the world was completely fashioned as a resemblance of the divine, intelligible Gods, the Demiurge was even more delighted and joyful. Because of this joy, he made the world possess an even greater and more perfect likeness to those eternal models. Therefore, he considered how he might make it, in a sense, perpetual. For the "eternal" or "perpetual" exists in two ways: that which is primarily perpetual (the divine model) and that which is secondarily perpetual (that which stretches out through the progression and evolution of time). # BOOK IV.] PLATO'S TIMAEUS. 177

...the one being eternal and the other temporal. Why, then, after all the previously mentioned benefits, does Plato introduce this eighth gift from the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine craftsman or creator of the material world</note>? Because it is the greatest and most perfect gift, and it brings the created image into the closest possible resemblance to its <term>paradigm</term> <note>original: "paradigm"; the eternal, divine model after which the world is patterned</note>. It is necessary for anyone explaining the birth of all things in words to move from the imperfect toward the perfect. 

In accordance with this principle, things that exist <term>essentially</term> <note>original: "per se"; by themselves or in their own right</note> are, in a sense, the opposites of things that are generated within others. For in those things that are self-contained and do not depend on anything else, the most "venerable" or ancient elements act as leaders. It is through these leaders that the final, creative, and other subsequent causes are revealed. However, in things that are shared or "participated in" by others, more imperfect qualities appear first. These serve as a foundation for more perfect natures and show themselves to have a later origin. This, then, is the overall ¹ design of the words we are considering.

Next, we must show the causes and the nature through which the Demiurge of the whole universe created Time alongside the soul and the physical world. We must also explain the specific good that Time provides and why it was created. This is particularly necessary because many—even among Plato’s followers—view Time as a vague form, nothing more than a way to measure motion. They fail to realize *that among the ten gifts the Father grants to the world, each subsequent gift is significantly greater than the one before it.* 

Therefore, if the Creator has already brought the world to life and made it a "blessed God," and only then grants it Time, it is clear that Time ² is superior to the soul itself and to the blessed life the soul provides. Furthermore, a life defined by Time will move in cycles. Thus, Time is not what the common crowd thinks it is; rather, it possesses a nature more divine than that of souls or any <term>psychical</term> <note>original: "psychical"; relating to the soul (from the Greek *psyche*)</note> benefit. We will reinforce this point again more fully.

Turning our attention to Plato's words, we must say that the Demiurge perceives the life, motion, order, and form of the universe through his intellect, rather than by looking at the physical world itself. For in short, the physical world cannot be understood purely through the intellect; because of its material bulk, it is instead an object of opinion combined with unreasoning physical sensation. Nor does the Demiurge focus on external objects during his <term>intellections</term> <note>original: "intellections"; acts of pure intellectual perception or divine thought</note>; but—

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, specifically focusing on how the created world serves as a physical likeness or "statue" of the eternal, intelligible Gods. It explores the relationship between the Demiurge (the creator), the eternal paradigm (the model), and the various levels of divinity that fill the universe.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.] PLATO'S TIMAEUS. 178

Every intellect <note>The word *nous* (intellect or mind) is omitted in the original Greek text in this place.</note> is turned toward itself. Therefore, because the creator intellectually perceives himself and contains within himself the generative and providential cause of all things, he surveys both the essence and the perfection of his own offspring by beholding himself. *But Plato says that the world was created as the statue or likeness of the eternal Gods.* This does not mean it is only the image of the gods who live within the world; for Plato is not just speaking about the physical nature of the universe, but also about the living and intellectual being which contains those worldly gods within itself. He says this because the world is the likeness of the *intelligible* Gods <note>The "intelligible" realm refers to the highest level of reality, consisting of pure being and divine ideas, which can only be grasped by the mind rather than the senses.</note>.

The world is filled with divinity from these Gods, and the progressions of the worldly gods into the universe are like rivers and illuminations flowing from the intelligible Gods. The world receives these progressions throughout its entire being, not just in its celestial part. For in the air, the earth, and the sea, there are presences of the terrestrial, aquatic, and aerial Gods. Therefore, the world is filled with divinity throughout its whole self, and for this reason, it is entirely a likeness of the intelligible Gods. It does not receive the transcendent essences of the universal Gods themselves—for even physical statues do not receive the separate natures of the total Gods—but because it is appropriately ordered, it receives the light flowing from them to secondary levels of existence, where the world has a proportional way of being.

By using the term "eternal" <note>original: "perpetual"</note>, however, Plato means all the intelligible Gods and not just the gods within the world. He makes this clear by immediately adding, "Hence, as that is an eternal animal," referring to the intelligible "Living Being" <note>original: "animal itself"; in Platonic philosophy, this refers to the eternal Model or Paradigm that contains the forms of all living creatures</note>. We can determine who these intelligible Gods are through a process of elimination. We must admit that they are either prior to the "Living Being" itself; or they are inside it (serving as the primary units of the four central Ideas found there); or they exist after it.

It would be ridiculous to place them before the "Living Being," because they would then encompass eternity, and Plato has not yet said the universe is modeled after that. But it is also impossible to place them inside the "Living Being." For how could Plato call the universe the "statue" or likeness of those Gods if he had not yet, in the order of his argument, modeled the various parts of the universe after them? He only does this later when he produces the specific components that fill the universe. If they were internal, he would not have said that the universe was *already* created as a likeness of these Gods, but rather that it *would be* in the future. 

Therefore, it remains that the "eternal Gods" are all those who exist after the "Living Being" and who stand between that eternal model <note>original: "paradigm"</note> and the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>the divine craftsman or creator of the material world</note>. The Demiurge made the universe similar to all of these, insofar as each of them contains the form of the world as a whole. This, then, is demonstrated.

<summary>Proclus explains that the physical world is a "statue" or divine likeness of the eternal, intelligible Gods, filled with their presence across all elements (land, sea, and air). He argues that these "eternal Gods" occupy a specific middle rank in the divine hierarchy between the eternal Model and the Creator.</summary>

# BOOK IV: PLATO'S TIMAEUS

Hence the world is the statue of the intelligible Gods <note>The "intelligible" realm refers to the highest level of reality, consisting of pure being and divine ideas, which can only be grasped by the mind rather than the senses.</note>, when it is understood as being joined with soul and intellect, and the deity that comes to it. But it is a statue in motion, full of life <note>original: "zoe" (life). The author notes it is necessary to read this as "zoes" (of life) for grammatical correctness.</note> and divinity. It is fashioned from all the things within itself, preserving everything, and filled with a complete and immediate abundance of all good things from the father <note>The "father" refers to the Demiurge or Creator.</note>. 

From nature, the world specifically receives motion above all else; but from the soul, it receives both motion and life; and from intellect, it receives intelligence, life, and the capacity to contain the worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note> Gods. From these worldly Gods, however, it receives what remains: namely, being fashioned in perfection as the most true statue, or resemblance, of the intelligible Gods. 

Furthermore, this makes it evident that Plato establishes the Demiurge <note>The Demiurge is the divine craftsman or creator of the physical universe in Platonic philosophy.</note> in a way that matches the most perfect of those who initiate others into the sacred mysteries. *For he shows him as the sculptor of the world, just as before he represented him as the maker of divine names and the speaker of divine symbols <note>original: "characters"</note>, through which he gave perfection to the soul. For these things are accomplished by those who are truly telestae <note>original: "telestae." These were initiators into the mysteries and "theurgists," priests capable of performing divine operations or rituals. Theurgy was the highest level of their sacred science.</note>, who complete statues through symbols and life-giving names, making them living and moving.*

Therefore, it was very fitting that the father of all things was delighted with his creation. Being filled with joy by it, he endeavored to render it even more similar to its eternal model <note>original: "paradigm"</note>. However, he did not admire the finished object itself, but rather his own power. It was this power that caused the universe—which had been moving in a confused and disorderly manner—to become orderly, alive, filled with intellect, and divine. 

Just as he knows the world by knowing himself, so by admiring his own creative <note>original: "demiurgic"</note> power, he makes his creation wonderful and the true statue or resemblance of the perpetual Gods. *For in a certain respect, the universe is said to be a "statue"* <note>original Greek: "agalma"</note> *because the divinity is "delighted with it"* <note>original Greek: "para to agallesthei ton theon ep' auto." Proclus is playing on the Greek words for "statue" and "delight."</note>. 

He was delighted and exulted, but not because he rejoiced in something outside of himself; for how could he, being pure intellect, look outward? Instead, his delight was produced from being filled with his own good-natured will, and from his generous power reaching out to provide a boundless and unenvying supply of more perfect goods. Plato also clearly indicates this by saying that the Demiurge, because he was delighted, endeavored to render the universe still more [perfect].

# BOOK IV: PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS

...similar to its paradigm <note>In Platonic philosophy, a "paradigm" is the eternal, perfect model or "blueprint" of which the physical world is a copy.</note>. For he was primarily delighted through his own internal thinking, understanding and kindly embracing the intelligible universe <note>The "intelligible universe" refers to the realm of pure ideas and divine truth that can only be grasped by the mind.</note> with a simple, unhindered, and focused grasp, through his permanence within and perfect union with it. But he was delighted in a secondary way—if it is appropriate to say so—because of the readiness <note>original: "aptitude"</note> of those natures that receive the supply of goodness flowing outward from him.

<margin>1. Instead of "elements" <note>original: στοιχεια (stoicheia)</note> in this place, it is necessary to read "coordinate" <note>original: συστοιχα (systoicha)</note>.</margin>
<margin>2. That is, if we wish to receive his helpful enlightenments. For these are always offered in the same way, because, as Proclus observes, divinity possesses an unchanging nature. Therefore, when we receive the good that he constantly offers us, he is said to be "delighted"—his delight actually signifying our own correct reception of this good.</margin>

Here you can see how Plato describes the three causes for how goodness is shared, proceeding from the Father <note>The "Father" refers to the Demiurge, the divine creator.</note> into this world. The first cause is the one that comes from the *power* of the "effective cause" <note>The "effective cause" is the creative force that makes things happen.</note>. It is the *Demiurge* who now creates time through his own generous and productive abundance, desiring to fill everything with primary, intermediate, and final goods. The second cause arises from the readiness <note>original: "aptitude"</note> of the thing receiving the goodness. The giver of good is then "delighted" when the receiver is properly prepared to take it in. And the third cause comes from the *symmetry*—the harmony and agreement—between both *power* and *readiness*. 

Because of this, although the Gods always offer to all things the goodness that is appropriate <note>original: "co-ordinate" or συστοιχα (systoicha)</note> to their natures, we do not always receive it. This is because we are not always suited for its reception, and our state of being is not always equal to its power. However, if we wish for the divine to "rejoice" in us, as he is naturally inclined to do, and to be delighted by us, we must make ourselves ready to receive the goodness he offers. We must do this even though he himself remains unchanging. This ensures that the divine gift is not ineffective for us, even though nothing can actually block the divine power. A fuller examination of these matters belongs to a different discussion.

Now, however, let us see how the universe becomes more like its paradigm <note>The eternal model.</note> through the creation of time. Since the paradigm is primarily eternal, it is clear to everyone that if the physical <note>original: "sensible"</note> world did not receive a secondary kind of everlastingness <note>original: "perpetuity"</note>, it would be less like the intelligible realm. Likewise, it is easy to see that any nature created through change <note>original: "mutation"</note> would be unable to last even for a moment if it were separated from time, let alone be everlasting. Therefore, a certain kind of everlastingness is necessary for anything that is to be in a still greater...

# BOOK IV: PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS

But for that which is indeed perpetual, yet does not possess its perpetuity all at once in the same way as the intelligible realm, the whole extension of time is necessary. Furthermore, whoever considers the nature of time will understand more clearly¹ how time contributes not only to the endurance of the whole world and its major parts, but also to the perfection and happiness of each of them, and encompasses all these at once. <margin>Stephanus 37D</margin>
> "The nature of the Living Being itself <note>original: "animal itself"; in Greek philosophy, the universe is seen as a living organism, and its "Living Being itself" is the eternal, divine model of life.</note> was eternal, and it was impossible to adapt this perfectly to that which is generated <note>Created or physical things.</note>. Hence, he [the Demiurge] formed the design of producing a certain moving² image³ of eternity;⁴ and as a result of this, while he was adorning the universe, he made this eternal image proceeding according to number—an image of eternity abiding in unity—which we call 'time'."

That the "Living Being itself" is the fullness of the multitude of intelligible beings, and that it possesses an unchanging consistency of existence, is a point frequently and fully asserted; it is not considered at all doubtful by Platonic philosophers. However, what "eternity" is, and what the "moving time" which imitates it is, are things that are extremely difficult to understand and to explain sufficiently to others. Nevertheless, it is necessary to recount the more elegant opinions of the ancients about this and to add, if we are able, anything that may contribute to the clarification and distinct consideration of the matters to be discussed.

Most people, therefore, have a concept and shared perception of time as a result of looking at the motions of the earth and the stars. They are of the opinion that time is something related to motion—for instance, the number or the duration of motion, or something else of that kind. But the more excellent thinkers, proceeding to the consideration⁵ of eternity, perceived that there is not simply motion in the universe, but a perpetual and orderly motion that circulates with unchanging sameness. From this, they conceived that this unchanging sameness was inherent in moving things because of a certain other cause, and not...

But if it is always in motion, the permanence of its motion must be derived from something else. Either this chain would continue infinitely <note>original: "ad infinitum"</note>, or there must be something immovable which serves as the cause of perpetual motion for things that are always moving. <note>In this passage, it is necessary to read "or to infinity" (η επ' απειρον) instead of "if to infinity" (ει επ' απειρον).</note> And the activity <note>original: "energy"</note> of this immovable being is no longer measured by time, but is eternal.

For the unique characteristic of things that exist according to time is that they are always in a state of generation—or *coming into being*—whereas eternal natures *exist always*. Common understanding suggests that the word "eternity" is named for "existing always," just as it thinks "time" <note>Greek: *chronos*</note> derives its name from "dancing" <note>original: "παρα την χορείαν" (*para tēn choreian*). Proclus is referencing a common ancient etymological theory linking time to the rhythmic movement of a dance.</note>, because dancing is a measured motion that exists within the process of generation. For this reason, it seems to me that the general public formed their first concept of time, while the wise formed theirs of eternity—the former directing their attention to the nature which is always in motion, and the latter to the nature which is always stable. Now, however, we must show what each of these is, in a manner most consistent with the teachings of Plato.

Aristotle, admitting that time is the "number of motion," asserts that it is so not in terms of the one who counts, but in terms of the thing being counted. Therefore, he rightly asks what it is that does the counting, if time is the thing being counted. He answers this inquiry unsatisfactorily <note>original: "weakly"</note> by saying that it is a certain soul which counts time. <note>In defense of Aristotle, however, one might say that when he asserts that a certain soul counts time, he is not speaking of time in its primary form. Instead, he refers to time as it is experienced by material things—the kind of time that the general public, as Proclus observes, can perceive and feel.</note> For before there can be a perpetual number, there must be a perpetual "counter" <note>original: "numerator"</note>, so that he may always produce that which is created as something that always exists.

While accepting time as the number of motion, Aristotle also says that eternity is intelligible <note>In this context, "intelligible" refers to the realm of pure reality that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses.</note>, taking its name from *existing always*, and possessing and encompassing the whole of time. Therefore, he also says that the existence and life of all things depend on this—some things more obscurely, others more clearly. At present, however, it is necessary for us to see specifically what eternity and time are according to Plato. # BOOK IV: PLATO’S TIMAEUS

...it exists among the <term>intelligibles</term> <note>These are realities grasped by the mind or intellect rather than the physical senses.</note>. This is the specific characteristic of Plato’s philosophy.

It is clear to everyone, then, that eternity is more venerable, primary, and, in a sense, more stable than the <term>animal itself</term> <note>original: "animal itself." In Platonic philosophy, this refers to the "Absolute Living Being," the divine blueprint or Form containing all possible forms of life.</note>, even though "animal itself" is the most beautiful and most perfect of intelligible beings, as Plato has said before. For if an "eternal being" is said to exist and be eternal because it participates in eternity, but eternity is not said to participate in "animal itself"—nor does it take its name from it—it is evident that the former is secondary, while the latter is more simple and more primary. 

Eternity does not participate in "animal itself" because eternity is not an animal; similarly, time is not a visible animal, nor is it any other kind of living being. It has already been demonstrated that "animal itself" is "only-begotten" and eternal precisely because eternity is more excellent. The "eternal" is neither identical to eternity nor more excellent than it. Just as we all say that anything possessing an intellect or a soul is secondary to Intellect and Soul itself, so too is the "eternal" secondary to Eternity. Someone might then ask: what will eternity be if it is more venerable than "animal itself," which is called the most beautiful and perfectly complete of all intelligible things?

Perhaps it may be said that "animal itself" is the most beautiful because it receives the very height of beauty through its intense participation in it, but it does not receive the height of the **Good**, for it is not said to be the *most excellent*. Thus, it may be subordinate to that which is best. To this we may add that it is not simply the most beautiful of all intelligibles, but specifically of *intelligible animals* (living beings). Therefore, eternity <note>original Greek: *ho aiōn* (the eternity). There is an omission of this phrase in the original text.</note> is not an animal; rather, if it is life, it is infinite life.

Furthermore, it is not necessary that whatever is "perfect in every respect" should be the first principle. To be "perfect" means to possess all things—having a beginning, middle, and end. However, that which exists above such divisions is "super-perfect." Therefore, nothing prevents eternity from being superior to "animal itself"—even though that being is the most beautiful of all intelligible animals and perfect in every way—if eternity itself is most excellent and super-perfect.

Furthermore, "animal itself" does not <note>The word *ou* (not) was omitted in the original Greek text here.</note> have a rank prior to the entire multitude of intelligible animals. For this reason, Plato says:
> "*For to that which is the most beautiful of intelligibles and in every respect perfect.*"

But eternity is prior to the entire multitude of intelligible animals. These beings are "eternal," but eternal natures participate in eternity; eternity itself is not ranked alongside the multitude but rather has a status superior to them. It unites the many and is said to "abide in one," as it is free from the plurality of...
