...multitude. However, <term>Animal Itself</term> encompasses all such living beings as are <term>intelligible</term> <note>These are realities grasped by the mind rather than the physical senses.</note>. For this reason, it also requires eternity so that, through it, it may participate in union, containing power, and a stable and unchanging life. Hence, Plato says that it is eternal, yet he does not add that it contains "multitude" within itself; instead, he speaks of it in the singular. This indicates that union is particularly present within it because of eternity, so that the entire essence of intelligible living beings shines forth as a single nature, thanks to eternity.

If these points are correctly asserted, then eternity will not be a single specific <term>genus</term> <note>A fundamental category or "Great Kind" of being, as described in Plato's *Sophist*.</note> of being—as some think it is—such as <term>essence</term> (being), <term>permanency</term> (rest), or <term>sameness</term>. All of these are merely parts of the "Animal Itself," and each has an opposite. For instance, essence is opposed to non-being; permanency is opposed to motion; and sameness is opposed to difference. But nothing is opposed to eternity. Furthermore, all these categories—sameness, difference, permanency, and motion—are equally eternal. This would not be the case if eternity were simply one of them. Motion and permanency are not "equally eternal" in the same way they are equal to eternity itself. Rather, all intelligible things are equally perpetual and eternal beings. 

Eternity, therefore, is not opposed to any of these, nor to anything that comes after it. As for **time**, which may seem to exist in a way that is the opposite of eternity: in the first place, time does not revolve around the same things as eternity, but rather around things that do not receive their connection from eternity. In the second place, time is an *image* of eternity, not its opposite, as we have already noted and shall demonstrate. 

Therefore, eternity is neither a single genus of being, nor the entire collection of the genera of being. If it were a multitude, it would still require the union of that which "abides in one." But eternity *is* that which "abides in one." If it were a collection, it would simultaneously abide and not abide in one: it would abide as eternity (the cause of union for beings), but it would not abide because it consisted of a multitude. 

In addition to everything already said, it is the **Intellect** that is composed of <note>original footnote: "The Greek words *synistatai ek* ('is composed of') appear to be missing in this place in the original text."</note> these genera and perceives their completion. However, the concept of Intellect is different from the concept of Eternity, just as the concept of the **soul** is different from that of **time**. The activity of the Intellect is <term>intransitive intelligence</term> <note>Thought that happens all at once, without moving from one idea to the next.</note>, while the activity of eternity is <term>impartible perpetuity</term> <note>Indivisible, unending existence.</note>. This is how these things are distinguished from one another. But those who mix everything together and claim there is only one Intellect between the soul and "the Good" are forced to acknowledge that Intellect and Eternity are the same thing.

...consists of all the five genera, since all these are eternal, and eternity is above them? We reply: what else can it be but the encompassing source <note>original: περιοχὴ (periochē)</note> of the <term>intelligible unities</term> <note>The "intelligible unities" are the highest, most unified forms of existence in the divine mind.</note>? By "unities," I mean the Ideas of <term>intelligible animals</term> <note>The divine archetypes or "blueprints" for all living things.</note> and the primary categories of all these mental Ideas. Therefore, eternity is the single encompassing source of these ideas and the peak of their variety. It is the cause of their unchanging stability. It does not exist within the multitude of these intelligible beings, nor is it merely a collection of them; rather, it is present with them transcendently <note>original: "exemptly," meaning existing in a superior, independent state</note>, organizing and, in a sense, shaping them by its own nature, making this very collection a single "whole." 

For the diverse variety of divine Ideas is not produced immediately after **the Good** <note>The ultimate, supreme principle in Platonic philosophy, which is beyond all many-ness.</note>, which is entirely without any representation of multiplicity. Instead, there are certain intermediate levels of nature. These are more unified than the "all-perfect multitude" of Ideas, yet they display the "labor" <note>original: "parturiency," the state of being about to bring forth offspring</note> and the emergence of the offspring of all "wholes," and they contain within themselves a power that holds everything together. The Gods know the exact number and nature of these levels divinely, but the mystical tradition of the *Parmenides* <note>One of Plato's most difficult dialogues, which Proclus interprets as a map of the divine hierarchy.</note> teaches us about them in a human and philosophical manner. We refer the reader to that work for an accurate discussion of these details. 

But now we shall demonstrate, through the philosopher's own words, that eternity is superior to the <term>Animal Itself</term> <note>The "Animal Itself" (Autozōon) is the divine blueprint of the universe containing all life.</note>, and that it sits immediately above it. Because the "Animal Itself" is said to be "eternal," it must be secondary to Eternity. Furthermore, because there is no eternal nature prior to it, it is immediately following Eternity in the hierarchy. 

How, then, is this evident? We reply: because there is nothing temporal (existing in time) prior to **Time**, which is the image of eternity. The physical world primarily participates in time, and the "Animal Itself" primarily participates in eternity. For if, as eternity is to time, so the "Animal Itself" is to the world, then, as mathematicians would say, we can alternate the proportion: as eternity is to the "Animal Itself," so time is to the world. 

But time is first participated in by the physical world; for time had no existence whatsoever before the orderly arrangement of the universe. Therefore, eternity is first participated in by the "Animal Itself." Likewise, time is not the "sensible animal" <note>The physical, living universe.</note> which encompasses all other physical living things—that is, it is not the universe itself—because time is generated *along with* the universe. That which is created alongside something is not the same as the thing it is created with. If this is the case, then eternity will not be the "intelligible animal" either. Hence, eternity will not be an "animal" at all, otherwise there would be two "all-encompassing" intelligible animals. It has already been demonstrated by Plato that the "Animal Itself" is <term>only-begotten</term> <note>original: monogenēs, meaning unique or the only one of its kind.</note>. In short, eternity will not be an animal. For if it were, it would either be an animal different from, or the same as, the "Animal Itself." However, it is not possible to assert—

It also gives things the ability to revolve and act out of love <note>original: "in an amatory manner"</note> around the first principle of all things. I am unfolding <note>original: "evolve"</note> these thoughts within the deepest reaches of my reason.

Therefore, it is even less possible for anything else to abide within it. In short, nothing exists inside it <note>All things are contained by the One, but nothing exists separately within it. # BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 187

...every known nature. Now, however, eternity is not said to abide in *the absolute One*, but simply in "one." This implies that it does not abide directly in *the Good* <note>The "Good" is the Neoplatonic term for the ultimate, absolute source of all reality, often identified with the "One."</note>. Does the "abiding of eternity in one" signify its unified nature, as if it stays within its own unity to show that it is a "unified multitude"? Or, in short, does it indicate the "number" of that which does not move outward <note>original: "proceed"—in Neoplatonism, this refers to the process where a higher principle produces a lower one while remaining itself unchanged</note>? If so, it would be the cause of union for the multitude of spiritual realities <note>original: "intelligibles"</note>. 

Indeed, we also say this is true, so that eternity may grant itself stability and wholeness before any eternal beings exist. For this is what it means *to abide in one*: to have the whole of existence present at once and to possess the same unchanging <term>hyparxis</term> <note>original: "hyparxis"—a technical term for the essential existence or the very "peak" of a thing's being</note>. Every divine nature begins its activity from within itself. Therefore, eternity will establish itself in "one" and hold itself together in the same way, existing before all other eternal beings. 

Consequently, it is not "being"—as Strato the physiologist <note>Strato of Lampsacus (c. 335–c. 269 BC), a Greek philosopher who focused on natural science</note> claims—that is the cause of permanence, but eternity. And it is the cause of a permanence that is not always in a state of "becoming" or physical change, but one that exists immutably in "one," just as Timaeus says.

However, eternity does exhibit a <term>duad</term> <note>a "duad" is a pair or a duality</note>, even though we often try to hide it. This is because the concept of "always" is joined to "being" through "sameness." Thus, eternity <note>original: *aion*</note> is defined as "that which always is" <note>original: *ho aei on*</note>. It appears, then, that eternity has the <term>monad</term> <note>a "monad" is a single, indivisible unit</note> of *being* existing before it, as well as *the one being*. Eternity abides in this "one," as our teacher <note>Proclus likely refers to his own mentor, Syrianus</note> also thought. It does this so that it may be "one" before it becomes a "duad," never departing from its unity. 

The duad, which represents the potential for multitude within itself, is united to "the one being" in which eternity dwells. Meanwhile, the multitude of spiritual realities is united to eternity itself, which holds all their highest points together in a transcendent and unified way. It is clear that the concepts of "the one being" and "eternity" differ. For *to be always* and *to be simply* are entirely different things. If something *always is*, then that thing certainly *is*; but the reverse is not true—if something *is*, it does not necessarily follow that it *always is*. 

Therefore, *to exist* is a broader and more general category than *to exist always*. For this reason, simple existence is closer to the cause of all beings, to the unity within beings, and even to the world of change and matter. These three things, therefore, follow in order: 
1. **The one being**, which is the single unit of all existence; 
2. **Eternity**, which acts as a duality, joining "always" with "existence"; 
3. **The eternal**, which participates in both existence and "always" but is not "perpetual being" in its primary form like eternity itself. 

"The one being" is the sole cause of existence for all things, whether they truly exist or not. But eternity is the cause of permanence in that existence. Strato, therefore, should have asserted this; he should not have defined "being" as the per-

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

permanence <gloss>1</gloss> of beings. He writes this in his treatise *Concerning Being*, thereby transferring the unique quality of eternity to "being." For even in created things <note>original: "generated natures"</note>, it is not the same thing to be born and to remain in existence after being born. The characteristic of "becoming" <term>generation</term> <note>the process of coming into existence in the physical world</note> is for a thing to constantly show one condition after another. However, the characteristic of becoming that stays or remains permanent is "time," the medium in which that process exists. And what time is to the world of becoming, eternity is to the world of true essence. Regarding the unfolding, however, of that great divinity—Eternity abiding in one—let this suffice.

But why does Plato say, "*the nature of the living being itself was eternal*," and not *is*, even though the word "now" is better suited to eternity than the past tense? He uses this style of speaking elsewhere; for example, when he says of the Creator <term>Demiurge</term> who is always good, "he *was* good." This signifies that he does not possess goodness starting from a specific point in time, but that he always was so. It also shows that in divine natures, the results are already assumed and united with the beginnings, existing before any passage of time <note>original: "extension"</note>. 

At this point, however, the word *was* is used more appropriately. Since Plato describes the ordering of the universe as a hypothesis, the intellectual realities <term>intelligibles</term> existed before that ordering—not earlier in time, but higher in rank and status. Anything that exists alongside these intellectual realities shares that status; for this reason, he says, "*it was*." 

But again, by using the word *being* <gloss>2</gloss> <note>original: *ousa* (ουσα)</note>, he makes up for the "weakness" of the past-tense <note>original: "imperfect"</note> verb. He treats this "being" as essential and no less real than the "present." He also adapts his language to the nature of eternity: he points to its perfection through the word *was*, and to its essential existence by introducing the word *being*. So much for the specific words Plato employs.

Why, however, was it impossible to perfectly apply the "eternal" to the "created"? Is it not because everything created may be said to have its existence in constant change <note>original: "mutation"</note>, while that which is perfectly eternal is unchanging and never born? Since these natures are opposites, if someone tried to forcefully connect the perfectly eternal with that which is created, they would fail to make the created thing unchanging and would instead destroy its nature. 

Is eternity, then, present within the physical world <note>original: "sensible"</note> in a certain way, rather than entirely? How could we not acknowledge this? For that which shares in the image of eternity also shares, in some respect, in eternity itself—though not in the same way as things that participate in it directly. In short, superior causes always bring order to the realms of their subordinates, so that eternity—

<summary>Proclus explains Plato's use of the past tense "was" to describe the eternity of the archetypal Living Being, arguing it signifies a state of perfection beyond time. He further explores how eternity provides permanence to true essence while its image, time, provides a form of permanence to the changing physical world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, specifically discussing the relationship between Eternity and Time. The previous page established that Eternity is the measure of true essence, while Time is the measure of the physical world of "becoming."</meta>

<page-num>189</page-num>
-> BOOK IV.] TIMAEUS OF PLATO. <-

Likewise, [Eternity] is present in a certain respect with the natures that are adorned by time. For according to one all-perfect boundary, it is present with intelligible realities <term>intelligibles</term> <note>original: "intelligibles alone"; refers to things perceived by the mind rather than the senses</note> alone. However, it is also capable of being present with worldly <term>mundane</term> things in a manifold way, according to divided perfections and definite measures of life, and especially according to the essential natures of the celestial souls. The world itself also receives eternity—not as it is in its own nature (which is why the world is not called "eternal" in the same sense)—but as far as it is able, it receives its indivisible <term>impartible</term> presence and illumination. This, therefore, is the supreme <term>transcendent</term> good in eternity, arising from a divine cause and encompassing power. Because of this, eternity encompasses fragmented <term>partible</term> beings—even those that seem contrary to its own nature—through a chain <note>original: "concatenation"</note> of causes. And thus much for this particular point.

But how is time said to be the image of eternity? Is it because eternity remains in unity, while time moves according to number? This, however, shows their difference <term>dissimilitude</term> rather than their similarity. For Plato contrasts almost every quality of eternity with those of time: *moving* is contrasted with *staying* <note>original: "proceeding, to abiding"</note>; *according to number* with *unity*; and the *image* with the *original thing itself*.

It is better, therefore, to say that divinity produced these two—eternity and time—as the measures of beings: the former for spiritual <term>intelligible</term> beings and the latter for worldly beings. Therefore, just as the world is said to be the image of the intelligible realm, the worldly measure (time) is called the image of the intelligible measure (eternity). Eternity, however, is a measure based on unity, while time is a measure based on number. For each one measures: the former measures things that become one, while the latter measures things that are counted. The former measures the permanence of beings, but the latter measures the *duration* <note>original Greek: "parapasin"; the translator notes this should be "paratashin," meaning extension or duration</note> of created <term>generated</term> natures.

These apparent oppositions between the two do not show that the measures are unrelated; rather, they indicate that secondary things are produced by more honorable and ancient natures. For movement <term>progression</term> comes from staying still <term>permanency</term>, and number comes from unity. Is time not the image of eternity for this reason: that it brings worldly natures to their perfection, just as eternity is the container and guardian of true beings? Those things that are unable to live according to the pure intellect are brought under the rule of Fate, so that by fleeing from the divine, they do not become perfectly chaotic. Similarly, things that come from eternity but cannot share in a steady perfection—which is complete all at once and always the same—fall under the dominion of time. Yet, they are moved by time toward their own <note>The original text uses the singular "his/its own," but the translator notes it should be the plural "their own."</note> appropriate activities, by which they are enabled to reach the goal suited to them through certain cycles of restoration <term>apocatastatic periods</term> <note>original: "apocatastatic periods"; referring to the cosmic cycles where the stars and planets return to their original positions</note>.

<summary>Proclus explains that Time is the "image" of Eternity because both serve as measures of existence—Eternity for the spiritual realm and Time for the physical world. He argues that Time guides changing things through cycles of restoration so they can participate in divine perfection as best they can.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, specifically examining why Plato describes the creation of time as a "contrivance" or "plan" of the Demiurge (the divine creator). It explores the paradox of how time can be "movable" while remaining rooted in a stable, eternal principle.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS [BOOK IV.

It is also right that Plato calls the production of time the *conception* or *contrivance* <note>original Greek: *epinoia* (επίνοια); a thought, purpose, or design</note> of the Demiurge <note>the "Craftsman" or creator of the physical universe</note>. For to grant an external and temporal kind of eternity to beings that are not naturally eternal—and to give perfection to things that are imperfect, and a circular <term>apocatastasis</term> <note>original: "apocatastasis"; a restoration or return to a starting point, as in a planetary orbit</note> to things that move in a straight line—does not seem to fall far short of *invention* and *contrivance*. Hence, in the passages that follow, he says that the deity *contrived* the generation of the parts of time. 

But how is the image of eternity said to be movable?¹ Is it² because the whole of it is moved and everything in it is in motion? Or is this not impossible? For nothing is moved entirely as a whole; this is not the case even with things that undergo essential changes, because the underlying subject of those things remains. Therefore, it is even more likely that things moved by other types of motion—whether they are growing, changing in quality, or moving from place to place—will remain the same in their essence. For if no part of them remained stable, their motion would vanish along with them, because all motion must exist within a certain thing. 

Therefore, as we have said, nothing is entirely moved. This is especially true for perpetual natures, which must be rooted in their own proper principles and remain stable within themselves if they are to be continually preserved. But it is particularly necessary that the image of eternity should have a perpetual consistency and stability; so it is impossible for time to be movable in its entirety, since that is not possible for anything else. It is necessary, therefore, that some part of it should remain still, since everything that moves does so because it has something within itself that stays stable. 

Hence the <term>monad</term> <note>original: "monad"; a single, indivisible unit or the ultimate principle of a thing</note> of time remains suspended from the Demiurge. But because it is full of measuring power and wishes to measure the motions of the soul’s <term>psychical</term>³ essence—as well as the existence, energies, and experiences <term>passions</term> of the physical and corporeal essence—it proceeds according to number. Time, therefore, remains stable in its indivisible <term>impartible</term> and inward energy, but it proceeds according to number through its external energy, which is shared by the things it measures. That is to say, it proceeds according to a certain intellectual number—or rather, according to the "primary number" which Parmenides <note>a pre-Socratic philosopher who wrote about the nature of being and the "One"</note> would say rules over the intellectual order, just as the "One Being" rules over the mental <term>intelligible</term> orders. It proceeds, therefore, according to that number. Because of this, it also distributes an appropriate measure to each⁴ of the worldly <term>mundane</term> forms.

You may likewise say even more directly, that true time proceeds accord—

² There is an omission here in the original Greek of the word "or" (*e*).
³ For "soul" (*psyches*) here, read "of the soul" (*psychikes*).
⁴ Instead of "to each" (feminine: *hekaste*), it is necessary to read "to each" (masculine/neuter: *hekasto*).

<summary>Proclus argues that time cannot be entirely in motion because all movement requires a stable foundation; therefore, time has an eternal "monad" rooted in the Demiurge while it measures the physical world through number.</summary>

# BOOK IV.] THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO.

...ing according to true number, participating <gloss>1 original: *metechonta* (participating)</gloss> in its numbers, and being itself intellectual number. Socrates speaks of this and hints at it when he says that swiftness itself and slowness itself exist within *true number*. It is by this true number that things measured by time differ, moving more swiftly or more slowly. Therefore, Timaeus does not <gloss>2 the word "not" (*ou*) was omitted in the original Greek</gloss> say much about this specific number—since Socrates had fully explained it the previous day—but focuses instead on the number that proceeds from it. 

For while that other form is "truly existing number," he says that this time "proceeds according to number." It proceeds, therefore, according to "intelligible number," by which it measures its participants. Conversely, the time found in physical things <note>original: "sensibles"</note> proceeds according to that which measures, being itself the thing that is measured. It still retains the image of essential time, through which all things are measured by the greater or lesser numbers of their lifespan. Thus, an ox lives for one duration, while a human lives for another; the sun returns to its original position in one period, the moon in another, and all other things complete their cycles according to different measures.

Therefore, time is the measure of motions—not merely as a tool we use to measure (which is our mental concept of time, not time itself), but as a creative force that defines the existence of life and every other motion occurring within time. It measures things and makes them similar to their <term>paradigms</term> <note>original: "paradigms"; the eternal blueprints or divine models of all physical things</note>. Just as time relates itself to the likeness of eternity (which contains the divine causes), it also directs the things it completes—those that revolve in cycles—toward a more sacred imitation of eternal principles.

How then, being such a great God, could time be merely the measure of motion—or rather, of <term>generation</term> <note>3 original: *geneseos* (generation); the realm of physical birth, change, and decay</note>—as some have thought? Those people failed to perceive its power or its creative <note>4 original: *demiurgikes* (demiurgic); related to the Demiurge or divine creator</note> presence within all things. When they claim that time is the cause of decay rather than creation, and of forgetting rather than preservation, they are only speaking of accidental effects, not its essential nature. In this, they resemble people who are asleep, unable to reason out the benefits time provides to the soul, the body, the whole of heaven, and all of creation.

*The <term>Theurgists</term> <note>original: "Theurgists"; practitioners of "god-working" or divine rituals intended to unite the soul with the gods</note> also confirm our claims. They state that Time is a God and provide us with the instructions for his worship, by which we are enabled to call him forth to become visible. They also honor him as both older and younger, and as a God who revolves in a circle and is eternal—not just as an image of eternity, but as a being that eternally receives eternity into itself.*

<summary>This page discusses the metaphysical distinction between "true number" and the time that measures physical life, arguing that time is a creative, divine force rather than just a human measurement or a cause of decay. Proclus invokes the authority of both Socrates and the Theurgists to define Time as a "revolving and eternal God."</summary>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

*They likewise add that time intellectually perceives the entire number of all the natures moved within the world. According to this number, time revolves and restores all moving substances to their original state through faster or slower cycles <note>original: "periods"</note>. Furthermore, they assert that time is infinite in power. For to circulate again and again without end is the function of an infinite power. Along with these points, they also say it has a spiral form, because it measures according to a single power both those things that move in a straight line and those that move in a circle—just as a spiral line, in a single form, contains both the straight and the circular line.*

We must not, therefore, agree with the opinion of those who consider time to exist only in our thoughts, or who treat it as a mere accidental property. Nor should we agree with those more respected thinkers who come closer to the truth but claim that time is generated by the "Universal Soul" acting in a step-by-step <note>original: "transitively"</note> way, or acting collectively without transitions to measure the celestial revolutions and the cycles of other souls. Even though they are close to the truth, we must not agree with them. 

First, Plato—with whom we all wish to agree on divine matters—says of the <term>Demiurgus</term> <note>The Divine Craftsman or Creator in Plato's philosophy</note> that he established time once the world was already organized in both soul and body. He did not create it within the soul as he did the musical <note>original: "harmonic"</note> ratios. He does not describe the divinity shaping time within the soul in the same way he says that he fabricated the physical nature within it. Instead, after speaking about the soul’s essence, harmony, power, motions, and all-encompassing knowledge, he then generated the essence of time to guard, measure, and make all these things similar to their <term>paradigmatic</term> <note>pertaining to the "Paradigm" or eternal model of the world</note> principles. 

For what benefit would worldly things gain from being beautiful if they did not last? Or from imitating the eternal Idea <note>the "paradigm"</note> if they did not unfold it through time and receive piece-by-piece what is actually one whole <note>original: "partibly receiving impartible intellection"</note>? On these accounts, therefore, the philosopher attributes the origin of time to a "demiurgic" <note>divine/creative</note> cause, not a "psychical" <note>related only to the soul</note> one.

Secondly, looking at the nature of things, you could say that if the soul had generated time, the soul would not participate in time in a way that allows it to be perfected by it. It is clear that the soul is perfected by time and measured by its own activities. This is because anything that does not receive the fullness of its energy all at once requires time for its perfection and its <term>apocatastasis</term> <note>original: *apocatastasis*; a Greek term meaning "restoration" or the completion of a cosmic cycle</note>. Through time, everything gathers the specific "good" it is meant to have—which it is unable to receive as a single whole without the passage of time. Thus, as we noted before, eternity and time are the measures of permanence and perfection...

<summary>Proclus argues that time is a divine creation of the Demiurgus rather than a byproduct of the soul or a human concept, serving to help worldly things imitate eternal perfection through cycles.</summary>

# TIMÆUS OF PLATO. [BOOK IV.

...of beings. The former is the single and undivided comprehension of the "intelligible unities" <note>Divine, non-physical realities accessible only to the mind</note>, while the latter is the boundary and creative <note>original: "demiurgic"</note> measure of eternity—or of the varying degrees of permanence found in things that proceed from these higher realities. 

If, therefore, the soul understood every object of its knowledge in a single flash of insight <note>original: "projecting energy"</note>—just as the Divine Intellect and the Gods do—and if it acted with an energy that was always the same, understanding things all at once without shifting from one thought to another <note>original: "intransitively"</note>, it might perhaps have produced time. However, in that case, it would not have *needed* time for its own completion. 

But the soul actually understands or perceives things intellectually through a sequence of steps <note>original: "with transition"</note> and in cycles <note>original: "apocatastatically"</note>. One soul requires the whole of time, while another requires only a certain part¹ of it, to fulfill its intellectual and life-generating <note>original: "genesiurgic"</note> functions. If we assume that no cause depends on its own offspring for its own completion, then the soul would be both perfect and imperfect before it even created what follows it. It would have to be perfect in order to create—since nothing imperfect can generate something else—but it would also be imperfect because it would never share in the very thing (time) that supposedly makes it perfect. It is completely absurd to say that causes depend on the things they produce. Therefore, let this be your strongest argument: time is not the child of the soul, but rather the soul is the first thing to participate in time.

Next, however, it is necessary to understand that even lifeless <note>original: "inanimate"</note> objects participate in time. They do not only participate when they first come into existence (in the same way they take on a specific form or quality); even when they seem to be entirely without life, they still participate in time. This is not simply because they are part of the larger, living universe and are affected by its movements. Rather, they participate in a specific span of time in an essential way, precisely because they are lifeless and are in a constant state of decay until they are completely destroyed. 

For time is present everywhere. An architect can predict how long a wall will last, and a weaver can tell the lifespan of a shirt—or, in short, of any garment.² In a similar way, every craftsman can say what the duration of his own work will be, though he cannot speak as precisely as one can regarding the works of nature. But the prophet speaks about the duration of all things, as he is able to see the span of time <note>original: "temporal interval"</note> distributed to all things by the universe. 

In addition to these points, since changes in the soul <note>original: "psychical mutations"</note> and the body <note>original: "corporeal mutations"</note>, as well as states of motion and rest—and in short, all such worldly things as are the opposite of...

# PROCLUS ON THE TIMÆUS [BOOK IV.

Because things that differ from each other are measured by time, time must be independent of all of them. For something that is one and the same, yet shared by many different things—and specifically by unlike things—while existing by itself beforehand, must be shared in an independent manner. Furthermore, because time exists in all things, it is everywhere undivided <note>original: "impartible"</note>; it is everywhere a single being, undivided in number, and belongs to no specific thing that exists within it. Aristotle also recognized this when he showed that in things that can be divided <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: μεριστοῖς (meristois)</note>, there is something non-physical <note>original: "incorporeal"</note> and undivided that is everywhere the same, which he identified <gloss>2</gloss> as *the now* or a single instant.

Furthermore, if time were not a fundamental substance <note>original: "essence"</note> but merely a secondary attribute <note>original: "accident"</note>, it would not display such creative <gloss>3</gloss> <note>original: "demiurgic"</note> power. This power causes some things to be produced perpetually, while others have a longer or shorter lifespan based on whether their nature is stronger or weaker; it distributes the appropriate measure of duration to all beings. If, however, time is a creative substance, it is neither the whole "Soul of the Universe" nor just a part of that soul. The concept of the soul is different from the concept of time, and each is the cause of different—not <gloss>4</gloss> the same—things. For the soul provides life and moves all things; thus the world, as it relates to the soul, is filled with life and shares in motion. 

But time <gloss>5</gloss>, which drives creative effects toward their perfection and measures them as whole units—and which provides a kind of eternity <gloss>6</gloss> <note>original: "perpetuity"</note>—cannot be secondary to the soul. This is because the soul itself shares in time, not in its basic nature, but through its changing activities <note>original: "transitive energies"</note>. Indeed, the Soul of the Universe is said to act without ceasing and to live wisely throughout the whole of time. Therefore, it remains that time is a fundamental substance and is not inferior to the soul. 

After all, we must consider this: if eternity was the child of Intellect (or a certain intellectual power), then we would have to say that time is a similar power belonging to the soul. But if eternity is the independent measure of the many "intelligible" realities <note>the highest, non-physical forms</note>, and is the container of the permanence and perfection of all things, then time must have this same relationship to the soul and the soul-level of reality <note>original: "psychical order"</note>. They differ only in the way that all things that flow out <note>original: "proceeding"</note> differ from the causes that remain stable <note>original: "abiding"</note>. For eternity possesses a greater transcendence than time,

# BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

with respect to the things that are measured by it. For the former <note>Eternity.</note> contains, in a transcendent way, both the fundamental natures <note>original: "essences"</note> and the unities of intelligible beings <note>original: "intelligibles"; these are realities that can only be grasped by the mind, not the senses</note>. The latter <note>Time</note>, however, does not measure the fundamental natures of the primary souls <margin>These are the "supermundane" or celestial souls that exist above the physical world.</margin>, as it instead exists on the same level as them and was created alongside them. As some Platonists also say, time does not measure the intellectual activities of these primary souls; even though Plato clearly states that the Soul of the Universe leads a divine and wise life through the whole of time. 

Intelligible beings are also more closely united to eternity than physical <note>original: "mundane"</note> natures are to time. Their union is so profound that some of the more contemplative philosophers have believed eternity to be nothing other than the one total Intellect (which contains all other individual intellects). However, no wise person is willing to admit that time is the same as the things that exist within time, because of the great separation and difference between them.

What then will time be, if it is neither something belonging to motion, nor a byproduct of the soul's activity, nor, in short, the offspring of the soul? Furthermore, time is not—as some who innovate in divine matters suggest—the soul's "circle of the *different*," while eternity is the soul's "circle of the *same*." <note>In Plato's *Timaeus*, the Soul of the World is composed of two "circles" or motions: the "Same" (representing the fixed stars/sameness) and the "Different" (representing the planets/change).</note> I have heard that the philosopher Theodorus held such views. However, anyone who tries to correct this opinion will never admit that these parts of the soul are identical to eternity and time. Instead, they will grant that the circle of the *different* leans toward temporal things, while the circle of the *same* leans toward eternal natures. 

Since we do not approve of any of these opinions, what is time? It is perhaps not enough to say that it is the measure of physical natures, nor to list the benefits it causes; rather, we must try to grasp its unique character to the best of our ability. Shall we say, therefore, that its nature is most excellent, perfecting the soul and present in all things? Is it an intellect that is not only staying still, but also moving? It remains still in its internal activity—through which it is truly eternal—but it moves in its external activity, by which it defines all change <note>original: "bounds all transition"</note>. 

For eternity remains stable in both its internal activity and the activity it directs toward eternal beings. Time foreshadows <note>original: "adumbrates"</note> eternity in one of these ways, but is separated from it in the other, because it both remains still and is moved. Therefore, time is something that is simultaneously intellectual and created, and something that is both divisible and indivisible <note>original: "partible and impartible"</note>. Since we already accept that these contradictions exist within the nature of the soul, we can only grasp this "middle nature" of time by using opposites to examine it. Why, then, should this be considered strange?

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s investigation into the nature of time, specifically examining Plato’s description of time as an "eternal image" and how time acts as a bridge between the eternal realm and the world of motion.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

If we perceive the nature of time to be partly immoveable and partly moved—or rather, if not we, but the philosopher <note>Plato</note> before us perceived it—he would show that its intellectual source <term>monad: a single, fundamental unit or source from which other things derive</term> remains in a state of sameness because it is *eternal*. However, he would also show that time’s activity <note>original: "energy"</note>, which flows outward and is shared by the soul and the entire world, is *moved*. 

We should not imagine that calling time "eternal" merely means it is an image of eternity. For what would have hindered Plato from simply saying that time is the *image* of eternity, rather than the *eternal image* of it? He wished to demonstrate this very fact: that time has an eternal nature, yet it is not eternal in the same way as the "Living Being itself" <note>original: "animal itself"; the divine, intelligible model of all life in Platonic thought</note>. For that Living Being is eternal in both its essence and its activity. But time, in its inward activity, is eternal; while in its externally proceeding gift to the world, it is moveable. 

For this reason, practitioners of divine ritual <term>theurgists: those who perform sacred rites to connect with the divine</term> also call time eternal, and Plato very correctly describes it as *not only* eternal <note>original: Plato "properly denominates it not eternal only"; Proclus is correcting the text here to suggest Plato means it is both eternal and something more.</note>. For one thing <note>the soul</note> is essentially moveable by itself and is the sole cause of motion for those things that participate in it; such a thing is the soul. It alone, therefore, moves itself and other things. But another thing is exclusively immoveable, keeping itself unchanging and acting as the cause of constant sameness for other things, and for those things that are moved because of the soul. [And this thing is the Intellect.] 

Therefore, it is necessary that there be a medium between these two extremes—between that which is immoveable in both essence and activity <note>Intellect</note>, and that which is moveable both by its own nature and in what it gives to other things <note>Soul</note>. This medium must be something that is at once immoveable and moved: immoveable in its core essence, but moved in its participants. Time is exactly this kind of thing. 

For if there is something present in things that are measured—like "number in that which is numbered"—what is the reality that does the numbering? It is absurd to say it is merely a "partial soul" <note>an individual human soul</note> that does this. For the part of our soul that counts time is a later development, just as the part of us that counts our fingers comes after the fingers themselves. The counting is not done by the one who *makes* the five fingers, but by the one who counts the fingers that nature has already produced. We, however, are searching for the cause of time itself being the thing that is numbered. Time, therefore, is that which remains immoveable and, by its very existence, unfolds the sequence of things that are numbered.

In short, if the time we see is moveable, and everything that is moveable is moved by being part of something else—since it is the object, not "motion" itself, that is moveable—then it is necessary that there should be a Time that exists by itself, so that there can be a "moveable time." So far, therefore, as it is *truly* time, and—

¹ Note: The original Greek *monos* ("only") should be read as *ou monos* ("not only").
² Note: Instead of "number as the thing numbered," the text should read "as number in that which is numbered."
³ Note: A grammatical correction to the Greek word for "so many."

<summary>Proclus argues that time is a mediating force between the unchanging Intellect and the moving Soul, possessing an eternal essence while producing motion in the physical world. He explains that for time to be measurable, there must be a primary, self-existing Time that remains still while unfolding the sequence of events.</summary>

<header>BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

Insofar as time exists in itself, it is unmoving <note>original: *akineton* (immoveable). The translator notes the Greek text should be corrected here from *kat' ekeinen* to *akineton*.</note>; but insofar as it exists within the things that participate in it, it is moveable, and together with them, it unfolds itself into them. Hence, time is indeed eternal—essentially a single source <term>monad: a single, fundamental unit</term> and a center—according to the activity <note>original: "energy"</note> that remains within it. At the same time, however, it is continuous, a number, and a circle, according to its outward-flowing and shared activity. *It is, therefore, a kind of intellect that proceeds forth, rooted indeed in eternity, and for this reason it is also said to be eternal. For it would not be able to help the things of this world become more perfectly like their divine models <term>paradigms: the eternal blueprints of reality</term> unless it was first superior to and independent of them.* 

But it *proceeds and flows abundantly into the things that are guarded by it.* For this reason, I believe the most accomplished practitioners of divine ritual <term>theurgists: those who perform sacred rites to connect with the divine</term> celebrate time as a God—as Julian does in the seventh book of his treatise *On the Zones*—and they revere it by those names through which it is *revealed in the things that participate in it.* It makes some things older and others more recent, and it turns all things in a circle. Since time is the image of eternity, it would be ridiculous if it were only this temporal image that exists within things that are counted. For how is it possible that a thing of this kind, which exists as a property of a subject, could be the image of a deity as great as Eternity? This is especially true since time rather *appears* to be a property of a subject [than is so in reality], and is itself an accidental quality of that which is itself an accident.

If, however, intellect is secondary to eternity, and the soul is the resemblance of intellect, how is it possible that time (the image of eternity) should not be something more excellent and more fundamental than the soul? For as intellect is related to the soul, so eternity is related to time. And conversely, as time is related to the soul <note>original: the Greek is corrected from "before soul" (*pro psyches*) to "to soul" (*pros psychen*)</note>, so eternity is related to the intellect <note>original: the Greek is corrected from "before intellect" (*pro nou*) to "to intellect" (*pros noun*)</note>. 

Time does not participate in the soul <note>original: the Greek is corrected to clarify "time does not participate in it"</note>, just as eternity does not participate in intellect; rather, it is the other way around. Therefore, because time has a certain intellectual nature, it rotates the things that participate in it—both souls and other things—according to number. For time is eternal, not only in its essence but also in its internal activity, in which it is always the same. But through the activity by which it is shared by external things, it is moveable, extending itself along with them and adapting its gift to them. Every soul, however, moves from one state to another, both in its internal activities and its external activities through which it moves bodies. It appears to me that it was named *Time* <note>original: *Chronos*</note> by those who perceived its true nature; they wished to use this name to say that it is a *certain dance* <note>original: *choron* (dance/choir). The translator notes the text should be corrected from *chronon* (time) to *choron* here to make the pun work.</note>, and as it were, a *dancing intellect*.

<summary>Proclus argues that Time is a divine, intellectual force superior to the soul, acting as a "dancing intellect" that flows from eternity to organize the world into cycles. He notes that while time appears to move within objects, its essential nature remains eternal and unmoving.</summary>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

...and, as it were, a dancing intellect <note>original: *kai oion choreuonta noun*</note>. But by a further division, they named it "time" for the sake of concealment. Perhaps, likewise, they gave it this name because it at once remains still and proceeds with a measured motion; it remains still in one part of itself, but proceeds in the other, as if it were half intellect and half dancing <term>saltant: dancing or leaping</term>. Hence, by combining both parts, they signified the wonderful and creative <note>original: "demiurgic"</note> nature of this God. 

It appears, likewise, that just as the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: the Divine Craftsman or Creator of the universe</term>, being intellectual, began from the intellect to organize the universe, so time, being beyond the physical world <term>supermundane: existing above or beyond the material world</term>, began from the soul to perfect it. For it is evident that time is not only within the world, but is, by a much greater priority, beyond it; because as eternity is to the Living Being itself <note>original: "animal itself" (the Platonic paradigm or eternal blueprint of all life)</note>, so time is to this world. The world is animated and endowed with intellect, and is entirely the image of the Living Being itself, in the same way that time is the image of eternity.

If, therefore, time exists, it both remains still and proceeds in a measured motion. And through its remaining still, the harmonious "dances" of the cosmos are infinite and restorative <term>apocatastatic: relating to the restoration of things to their original state at the end of a cycle</term>. For since time is the first intellect that "dances" about the whole creation of things, insofar as it exists invariably the same and is essentially intellect, it is said to be eternal. But insofar as it dances, it rolls souls, natures, and bodies in a circle; and in short, it is periodically restored to its original state. For the world is moved, indeed, because it participates in the soul; but it is moved in an orderly manner because it participates in intellect. For as Plato also says in the *Laws*,

> *that the soul, receiving a divine intellect, governs with righteousness and wisdom.*

And the world is moved periodically, by moving from the same point back to the same point. Because of this, it may be said to imitate the permanence of intellect in its "sameness" through the imitation of eternity by time. And this is done to make the world more similar to its eternal model <term>paradigm: an eternal pattern or blueprint</term> which remains as one; specifically, to be cycled back periodically to one and the same thing through its circulation according to time. 

From all these details, you also have all the causes of time according to Plato. For the Demiurge is the effective cause of time; eternity is its model; and its end (or final cause) is the circular return <term>circumduction: the act of leading around in a circle</term> to one thing of all the natures that are moved according to their cycles. For that which does not remain as one unit aspires after the circular return to unity, desiring through this to obtain *the One*, which is the same as *the Good*. For reason requires—if it is appropriate to call what is necessary "reasonable"—that the progression of things should not be a single straight line, forming a line that is infinite in both directions. Instead, the progression should be definite and enclosed, "dancing" about the Father of all things and the primal unit <term>monad: a single, fundamental unit</term> of time, unfolding all the power of creation, and again returning to its original condition, and doing this frequently, or rather infinitely. For from where would the participants of time derive the power of being restored to their original condition, unless...

The demonstrations of the most wise <note>original: "sagacious"</note> legislators agree with this, as do the words of Plato himself, who says that time—imitating eternity in these things and circulating according to number—was then brought into being <note>original: "generated"</note>. *For time, circulating the first of all changeable <term>moveable: here meaning things that change or move in the physical world</term> natures through an energy that flows outward and then returns to its original state after its power has fully unfolded, likewise restores the cycles of other natures to their original condition.* 

Time, through its entire progression, revolves <term>convolves: rolls or rotates</term> the soul, which is the first thing to participate in time. However, through specific parts of itself, it revolves other souls and natures, the orbits of the stars, and finally, the entire realm of birth and change <note>original: "generation"</note>. Because time circulates, all things are turned in a circle. **Of the circulations, however, some are shorter, but others longer.**

Furthermore, if the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: the divine craftsman or creator of the cosmos</term> himself made time to be the changing <note>original: "moveable"</note> image of eternity and gave it existence according to his divine thought <term>intellection: the act of the intellect or divine mind</term> regarding eternity, it is necessary that the changing nature of time be circular and proceed with a rhythmic, measured motion. This ensures it does not stray from eternity and can unfold the Creator’s <note>original: "father"</note> thought concerning it. 

In short, since the changing nature of time encompasses all motions, it must be defined <note>original: "bounded"</note> well before the things that it measures. For it is not the absence of measure, but the primary measure itself that measures all beings; similarly, infinity does not give limits to things, as that is the role of the primary "Bound" <note>In Platonic philosophy, "Bound" and "Infinite" are the two fundamental principles from which all reality is composed.</note>. 

But time does not move according to the soul, nor according to nature, nor according to physical and visible substance; if it did, its motions would be divided into parts and would not encompass the whole of things. Furthermore, such motions would partake in irregularity <note>original: "the anomalous"</note> to some degree and would themselves require time to exist. This is because the motions of the soul, nature, and the body are all observed *within* time; they are not the primary progression that measures the whole universe, but are instead found in specific qualities of life, physical movement <term>lation: change of place or local motion</term>, or external influence <term>passion: the state of being acted upon by an outside force</term>. 

The motion of time, however, is a pure progression—undifferentiated, imperceptible, unbroken <note>original: *aklastos*, corrected from *achalaistos*</note>, orderly <note>original: *eutaktos*, corrected from *ataktos*</note>, equal, similar, and constant. It is beyond both steady and unsteady motions, being equally present in both. It is not changed in quality by any alteration <term>alliation: change or variation</term> in those motions, but remains the same, separate from all inequality. It empowers all natural motions, measuring them and returning them to their original state. It also exists unmixed with the things it measures, in accordance with...

to the unique quality of intellectual activity <note>original: "energy"</note>; instead, it proceeds by moving itself and passing from one thing to another. In this respect, it belongs to the order of the soul <note>original: "psychical order"</note>, but it exists within the things that are defined and perfected by it, acting as a primary <note>original: "primordial"</note> cause. It is not, however, closely related in *all respects* to any single being. For the measure of all things must be somewhat similar and related to everything, yet it must not be the same as any of the natures it measures.

The motion of time, therefore, proceeds by unfolding and dividing a power that is otherwise indivisible and eternal, revealing it piece by piece. For just as a specific number <note>The number ten, or the decad.</note> receives all the forms of the "monad" <term>monad: a single, indivisible unit or source from which all numbers arise</term> in a divisible way, and then turns and leads them back to itself; so too does the motion of time. Moving according to the measures within the "temporal monad," time joins the end to the beginning in an infinite cycle. It possesses a divine order—not an order that is merely *arranged* (as the philosopher Iamblichus says), but an *arranging* order. It is not an order that follows earlier things, but one that is the primary leader of everything that is fully realized. 

At the same time, however, it is not measured by anything that has physical extension <note>original: "interval"</note>. It would be ridiculous to say that things of more ancient nature and dignity are measured by things that came after them. Instead, the motion of time is measured only by the "temporal monad"—which the progression of time is said to reveal—and, with even greater priority, by the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: the divine creator or craftsman of the cosmos</term> and Eternity itself. Time is said to be the image of Eternity, and it is made to move in relation to it. 

Therefore, in relation to Eternity—which is perfectly motionless—time is said to be moving. This is similar to saying that the soul is divisible when compared to the Intellect because it acts upon physical bodies. It is not that the soul is *only* divisible, but that when compared with the Intellect, it appears to be so, even though the soul itself is indivisible compared to physical matter. In the same way, although time is eternal by nature, it is called "moving" when compared to Eternity itself. 

Because of its order and the continuous way it progresses, we should not think of "before" and "after" in time the way some people do. These concepts must not be strictly viewed only through changes in motion (like the movements of the stars), nor in the unfolding of lives (as in the soul), nor in the gradual progression of physical creation <note>original: "corporeal generations"</note> (as in nature), nor anything else of that kind. (For these are the characteristics of orders that come *after* time <note>original: "μετ' αυτων" (with them); Proclus notes it is necessary to read "μετ' αυτον" (after it)</note>). Instead, time must be viewed according to the priority of causes and the connection within its continuity...

...of its offspring, and according to a primary <note>original: "primordial"</note> energy and a power capable of producing all kinds of motions.

Time, therefore, is not inherently <note>original: "by itself, [or essentially]"</note> changeable, but it appears to move through the way physical motions participate in it, and by which those motions are measured and defined.¹ Just as one might say that the soul is divided among bodies, insofar as there is a certain divisible participation of the soul within those bodies, for which the soul itself provides the cause. In this same way, time is considered "moveable" because it holds the cause of the activity <note>original: "energy"</note> that proceeds from it—an activity that is partly seen in physical motions and is divided along with them. Therefore, just as motions become "temporal" by participating in time, so too is time called "moveable" because it is shared by motions. Natural philosophers <term>physiologists: in this context, early scientists or philosophers who studied the physical world (nature)</term>, looking only at this effect, mistakenly believe that time is merely the "numbering of motion," because they cannot perceive the underlying cause of this.

In the first place, therefore, it must be stated that the universe does not exist solely in a state of motion; it is necessary that something within it should remain completely still so that, while it stays permanent, other things can move. It is demonstrated in the *Theaetetus* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of knowledge.</note> that it is impossible for anything to be moving in every single respect. Therefore, it is necessary for something to exist before the kind of time that is shared with and co-extends with motion. It is impossible for this prior state to be inactive. But if it is active and *also* moves, it would require yet another thing to measure its own motion. ***If, however, it acts <note>original: "energizes"</note> without moving, this will be the true, unique characteristic of time.*** In the second place, we are convinced by common tradition that the Seasons are Goddesses and that the Month is a God, both of whom we worship in temples. We also say that Day and Night are divinities, for whom we have prayers <note>original: "invocations"</note> given to us by the Gods themselves. Therefore, it is even more necessary that Time itself should be a God, since it encompasses the Month, the Seasons, and Day and Night. In the third place, if time is something that is "numbered" (measured), there must be a "numberer" (measurer) that exists before the thing being numbered. Just as the ability to number must exist before anything is actually numbered, and an active numbering must happen before a result is reached—if this is the case, then true Time is the actual number or law that governs all cycles and measures each of them. In the fourth place, everything that possesses a soul also participates in time, but the reverse is not true: even inanimate things <term>inanimate natures: things without a soul or life-force, such as rocks or simple matter</term> participate in time. Therefore, it must be admitted that time exists on a level beyond the soul. But the soul is prior...

How, then, can something of this nature be the "image of eternity"? This must be discussed again, given the difficulty of obtaining knowledge about such matters. According to the divine Iamblichus, time displays the infinity of eternity (which exists as a "now," is all things at once, dwells in the eternal present, and is the unquantifiable measure of things known through the intellect <term>intelligibles: things that can only be understood by the mind/intellect, rather than the senses</term>) through a circular progression, continuity, and sequence. It also does this by distinguishing beginnings, middles, and ends, yet without abandoning any of the things it encompasses. And just as time is not merely "moving" in a simple sense, but moves in relation to eternity, it is also not merely a simple "image." Rather, the whole of time can rightly be called the image of eternity. Because time is a true essence—one that measures, understands, and returns all movements to their original state—it is simultaneously called an "eternal image." *It also appears to be the primary image.* 

The "all-perfect intellect" <term>Intellect (Nous): in Neoplatonism, the divine mind or the second principle after "The One."</term> cannot properly be called the image of the First Cause <note>The "First Cause" refers to "The One," the absolute source of all existence in Neoplatonism.</note>. After all, what can be compared to that which has no form at all? Instead, time is the first participant of the intellect, acting as an indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> nature between the all-perfect intellect and the realm of physical objects <term>sensibles: things that can be perceived by the senses</term>. 

In short, if an "image" must belong to things that "participate" (since an image seeks to preserve the form of an older and more sacred nature from which it draws its specific character), then an image cannot exist among the "first essences." These first essences do not participate in anything; rather, other things participate in them. They are not created within those that participate in them but exist in another way, turned inward toward themselves. Therefore, images do not exist only in physical things. Intermediate natures <note>Proclus refers here to the "middle" levels of reality, such as Soul and Time, which bridge the gap between the divine Intellect and the physical world.</note> also participate in the primary natures; it is not only physical things that are made to resemble the primary natures through the mediation of these middle natures.\* 

Therefore, time is called the image of eternity, and the entire world is called the image of the "Living Being itself" <note>original: "animal itself" (Greek: autozoon). In Plato's Timaeus, this refers to the eternal, intelligible model of all living things.</note> in both soul and body. Consequently, if we follow Porphyry and other Platonists who believed that only physical things participate in truly existing beings, we would only look for "images" in the physical world. However, if we follow Amelius—and Numenius before him—who argued that there is also "participation" within the intellectual realms, then images must exist there as well. But if, as the divine Plato suggests, images are found neither in the very highest beings nor solely in physical things, then Iamblichus (who surpasses almost all other philosophers in every subject) will be proven correct here too. He encourages us to observe how "participation" works in both the intermediate and the lowest levels of existence. This should be enough for now regarding eternity and its image, which is at

<margin>37E</margin>
> "He also designed the creation of days and nights, and months and years, which did not exist before the universe, but which were established together with it. All these are parts of time,¹ and *was* and *will be* are created types <note>original: "species"</note> of time."

It is perfectly clear that before the creation of the universe (and I am speaking here of the universe as viewed together with the soul and the total life of the world), there was an indivisible <term>impartible: that which cannot be divided into parts</term> essence staying in eternity, in the same way that eternity stays in unity. This essence was not a part of the proceeding and participated time <note>participated time: time as it is experienced by physical things, rather than time as an abstract principle</note>. 

However, what day and night, month and year actually are—and why these are called "parts" of time, while *was* and *will be* are called "types" and not parts—will require a more detailed discussion and a deeper consideration. 

If we should say that a "day" is simply air lit up by the sun, we would first of all be talking about something that *happens* during the day, rather than what the day *is*. For when we speak of a long or a short day, we are not describing an increase or decrease in the amount of air. Furthermore, it is difficult to see how "illuminated air" would be a literal part of time. 

But if we say that a day is the temporal interval <term>interval: a span or stretch of time</term> during which the sun travels from east to west, we might avoid those first objections, but we will run into even more difficult problems. For if we look at the interval itself without any relation to the sun and call that a "day," it remains confusing why that same interval—being the same everywhere—does not result in it being "day" everywhere at once. 

If we look at it only in connection with the sun's motion, then it would always be "day" in the heavens, and there would never be "night." Yet, how is it possible for a part of time not to exist everywhere? For it is clearly stated here that night, day, and month are parts of time. 

If, however, we do not just connect the interval with the sun's rotation, but say that "day" is the motion of the sun from east to west, and "night" is its motion from west to east, then the universe would have neither days nor nights (which are defined as parts of time). a whole that remains within itself, and through every part of its progression, is present to the whole world. For one and the same "now" is everywhere the same. It is necessary, therefore, that day and such other things as we call parts of time should be everywhere the same, though they are experienced <note>original: "participated"</note> in a divided and scattered way by physical creations <note>original: "sensible fabrications"</note>. Looking at these physical things, some people adopt the more common rather than the more accurate meaning of these names.

Hence, as our father <note>Proclus refers to his teacher Syrianus as "father."</note> philosophizes, these things are not asserted for the purpose of overturning observable facts <note>original: "subverting the phenomena"</note>. For Timaeus says *what is usually said by the common people. But our father, referring these—as he is accustomed to do—to more fundamental realities <term>hypostases: the underlying fundamental realities or essences of things</term>, says that day and night are creative <term>demiurgic: relating to the Demiurge or divine creator</term> measures of time. They excite and call together all visible and invisible life and motion, as well as the orderly distribution of the sphere of fixed stars <term>inerratic sphere: the outer heaven of stars that do not wander like planets</term>. For these are the true parts of time; they are essentially present with all things and contain the primary cause of the apparent day and night, each of which is different in the time we can see.* And Timaeus, looking also at this, reminds us how time was generated together with the universe. Hence he uses the plural "days and nights," as he also does with "months and years." These, therefore, are obvious to everyone. For their invisible causes exist in a single, unified way before they become many and move in endless cycles. The unmoving causes of these likewise exist before the things that are moved, and their intellectual causes exist before the physical ones. This is how day and night must be understood according to their primary existence.

*But it must be said that a "month" is that which rotates the lunar sphere and every completion of the circuit around the zodiac, being truly a divine measurement of time. And a "year" is that which completes and contains the whole middle level of creation, according to which the sun is seen to possess the greatest power, measuring all things together with time.* For neither day, nor night, nor month—and much less a year—exists without the sun, nor does anything else belonging to the world. And I do not say this only in reference to the visible creation (for the visible sun is the cause of these measures), but in the invisible and higher creation, the more true sun measures all things together with time. In reality, it is the "time of time," according to the divine message <note>original: "oracle of the Gods"</note> concerning it.

That Plato knew not only these visible parts of time, but also the divine parts sharing the same names <note>original: "homonymous"</note>, is evident from what he says in the tenth book of the *Laws*. For he there shows that the seasons and months are divine, in conjunction with all the other worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note> Gods, because they possess divine lives and divine intellects presiding over them in the same manner as the universe. But it is not surprising if he now speaks mainly about the visible parts of time, because his current goal is to discuss natural philosophy <term>physiologize: to study or explain the nature of physical things</term>. Let these, therefore, be the parts of time, some of which are suited to the fixed stars, while others are suited to the stars that revolve about the poles of...

the zodiac, and others to other Gods, or the attendants of the Gods, or to mortal animals, or to the more elevated or lower parts of the universe.

Plato, however, says that *was* and *will be* are types <note>original: "species"</note> and not parts of time, in the same way that days, nights, months, and years are. For divine orders that complete the entire progression of time govern these latter parts. Therefore, he calls them "parts of time." But *was* and *will be* are observed entirely within each of these parts. Consequently, they are certain types because they do not have a particular substance <note>original: "matter"</note>; I mean, they do not have a substance specifically related to the day, or night, or anything similar. 

If, however, these are types of time that were created together with the universe, then "was" had no existence before the creation <note>original: "generation"</note> of the universe. But if "was" did not exist before it, neither did motion; for in all motion, there is a "was" and a "will be," because there is a "before" and an "after." If, then, motion did not exist before the universe, neither did "disorderly motion." Therefore, Atticus <note>Atticus was a second-century Platonist who believed the world had a beginning in time.</note> and his followers argue in vain when they say that time existed before the world was created, but was an "unarranged" time. For wherever there is time, there is also the past and the future. And wherever these exist, the *was* and the *will be* are entirely present. 

Furthermore, the *was* and the *will be* are types of time created by the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: the divine craftsman or creator of the physical universe</term>. This is why Plato calls them *generated* (or created). Therefore, there was no specific time before the creation of things. It is necessary, then, that the much-celebrated "disorderly motion" of Atticus and his followers either did not exist within time (if it existed at all), or that there simply was no time when it was produced. 

However, if motion exists, it is necessary that there should be a time in which it occurs: one part of it having the past <note>original Greek: *proelthon* ("having gone forward"); the text should be read as *parelthon* ("the past").</note>, another the present, and another the future. Thus, it is not possible that there could have been motion before the creation of time, since there could not even have been "disorderly time." For disorderly time would still have the *was* and the *will be*—the former being the past, and the latter being the future. 

Or, if time possessed only "the is" without past or future, it would be eternity rather than time, and "disorderly motion" would then be eternal—which is impossible. For Aristotle has sufficiently demonstrated that all motion is within time, both that which is disorderly and that which is orderly; each inevitably has a "before" and an "after" so that the motion may remain what it is, and not become a state of stillness <note>original: "permanency"</note> instead of motion. 

Plato clearly teaches us that the *was* and the *will be* did not exist before the creation of things. As I have observed before, he states that just as days and nights were created as parts, so the *was* and the *will be* were created as types of time. Atticus and his followers, however, claim that "disorderly motion" was uncreated <note>original: "unbegotten"</note>. Therefore, if there was then—

<summary>Proclus argues that time and motion began simultaneously with the universe's creation, refuting the philosopher Atticus's claim that a "disorderly" time or motion existed before the world was formed.</summary>
