<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, further examining why "was" and "will be" are considered forms or species of time rather than just parts, and how the stars act as instruments in time's progression.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

If time were uncreated <note>original: "unbegotten"</note> at a certain point, then the concepts of *the past* (the was) and *the future* (the will be) would also be uncreated. Therefore, the *past* and the *future* did not exist before the creation of the world but were simultaneous with it. In this view, time is one and the same—the numerical measure of both chaotic and ordered movements—and exists without any inherent difference between the two. This conclusion is demonstrated through these logical methods as a natural consequence.

However, if you wish to examine these as specific "species" or forms of time—in the way they appeared to our teacher <note>Proclus is likely referring to his own teacher, Syrianus.</note>—then consider a "perfect period" <term>perfect period: a complete cosmic cycle where all celestial bodies return to their starting positions</term> and the entire progression of time. In this view, one part has already become the past, while another is yet to be the future; thus, you can see the *past* and the *future* as distinct forms of time. 

If we do not look at it this way, but only partially understand Plato’s words, the majestic and complete idea of time will not be clear to us in each of its forms. Instead, we would only see what happens to specific things subject to birth and change. Unless, of course, the *past indicates the order of time that brings things to completion*, while the *future indicates that order which reveals things*, just as the *present indicates the order that holds everything together.* For time reveals things that do not yet exist, holds together those that are currently present, and *brings to completion those that are past, providing a fitting end to their cycles.* This concludes our discussion regarding the parts and forms of time.

Regarding the word *contrived*, we have previously noted that time is truly the result of divine and demiurgic <term>demiurgic: relating to the Demiurge, the divine craftsman of the universe</term> craftsmanship. Through this "contrivance," changing natures are able to endure throughout the whole and participate in perfection, eternity, protection, measurement, and comprehension. 

Yet, one might ask: do divine natures not measure themselves? <note>original: "For εαυτο (itself) here, read εαυτα (themselves)." Proclus is correcting the Greek text to ensure the reflexive pronoun is plural, referring to "divine natures."</note> Specifically, do the celestial bodies that revolve in the heavens not define their own movements? We must readily admit that they do. While material and perishable things receive their existence and the length of their life from external sources, divine natures receive these both from the original causes and from themselves. 

This is why Plato, when he begins to discuss the specific times revealed in the heavens, says that "*the stars were created to cooperate in the production of time.*" He further states that "*they were created as instruments of time*" and, thirdly, that "*they were produced to distinguish and guard the numbers of time.*" In these phrases, the term *cooperate* shows that while time existed before the stars, it is revealed to the world through them. Because time is "in" them, it is unfolded through their motion. Similarly, the term *instruments* indicates that the whole of time was produced—both that which remains still and that which moves forward.

<summary>Proclus argues that the past and future are essential forms of time that bring completion and revelation to the world, while explaining that stars act as the divine instruments that measure and manifest time's progression.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, transitioning from a discussion on the forms of time (past, present, future) to the specific roles of celestial bodies as the "instruments" and "measures" of time created by the Demiurge.</meta>

# BOOK IV.] THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO.

By the father and maker of all things, time was created for the purpose of measuring mundane <term>mundane: relating to the physical world or the cosmos</term> natures. The bodies that revolve in the heavens are partial measures and are contained within this single time. Each body, in its own special way and acting as an organic tool, works in conjunction with time to produce the things appropriate to it. In short, all secondary creation <note>original: "fabrication"</note> has this relationship to the single and indivisible production of things. 

Each of the bodies that revolve in the heavens is said to contribute especially to its own measurement. For instance, *the sun, though it contributes to all things because of its ruling dignity, particularly contributes to the year. It constitutes the year in conjunction with the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: the divine Craftsman or Creator of the universe</term> and the whole of time, acting as its own peculiar measure. But the moon contributes to the month, and the inerratic sphere <term>inerratic sphere: the outer shell of the cosmos containing the fixed stars, which do not wander like planets</term> contributes to the day and night.* The way the rest of the heavenly bodies operate is also evident; although neither night—and much less day—can exist without the sun, nor a year without the inerratic sphere and the zodiac. At the same time, however, some measures are better suited to certain celestial bodies than to others.

The stars may also be called the "instruments of time" because time possesses an effective power <note>original: "effective dignity"</note> over them and through them, organizing the world of generation <term>generation: the realm of birth, change, and decay</term> as if through tools. From this, it is evident that time is not merely something participated in, or just the "number of motion," since the governors of the world (the stars) act as instruments in relation to it. Rather, time is an invisible God, eternally acting upon all motions and the entire cycle of the world, using these divinities as more specific measures of itself. 

The assertion that the stars were created to distinguish and guard the "numbers of time" clearly shows that the "one time" proceeds from the Demiurge and his will. While remaining one, whole, and uniform, time becomes multitudinous according to number through the motion of these stars. Each of the measures adapted to it is, in a sense, cut and divided from the whole of time—which always remains the guardian of each measure through its steady and orderly motion. In reality, however, the celestial Gods are guarded by the numbers of time; they obtain through these numbers the distinction of their periods and the timing of their return to their original states <note>original: "restitutions to their pristine state"</note>. Yet, since we endeavor to gather the truth of invisible things from visible ones, we infer that the numbers of time are "guarded" through the circulation of the stars.

Not only does Plato agree with these points, as we have observed, but the theurgists <term>theurgists: Neo-Platonic practitioners of "god-working" rituals intended to purify the soul and unite it with the divine</term> also agree. They celebrate Time as a mundane God who is eternal, boundless, both young and old, and possessing a spiral form. Furthermore, they describe Time as having its essence in eternity, as always remaining the same, and as possessing...

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

...infinite power. For how could it otherwise encompass the infinity of visible time, and lead all things back to their previous condition in a circle, and renew them? How could it also recall things which grow old through time to their proper measure, being at once comprehensive of things that are moved in a circle and those that move in a straight line? A spiral is a thing of this kind; and hence, as I have observed before, time is celebrated by theurgists <term>theurgists: practitioners of divine magic or ritual intended to unite the soul with the divine</term> as having a spiral form. 

For they do not only honor time as a God, but day and night, month and year are also considered Gods by them. For regarding things which circulate perpetually, it is entirely necessary that there should be an unchanging <note>original: "immoveable"</note> cause; and a different cause for things that are specifically different. On this account, therefore, they have passed down to us assemblies <note>original: "congresses"</note>, prayers, and sacred laws for ritual purification <term>telestic: relating to the rites or mysteries of initiation and purification</term>. It is necessary, likewise, not to look at all these details superficially, but to revere them as divine, invisible, and unchanging causes that exist before these moving natures which are visible to all men. Plato himself in *The Laws* bears testimony to the truth of this by speaking of these causes as Gods. 

*For from the Greeks we receive the sacred rites of Month, and we learn that by the Phrygians, Month is celebrated as Sabazius <term>Sabazius: a nomadic horseman and sky-father god of the Phrygians and Thracians</term>, and also in the middle mysteries of Sabazius.* 

For that which they first beheld to be the measurer of a perpetual circulation, they understood to be a God, and they honored this through the mysteries and all-sacred worship, in the same manner as they also honored the seasons. For they were able to perceive the divinity of the seasons from their effects, though the divinity of the year was not as easily seen. For while men who were divinely wise have likewise celebrated the year, it was not easy for all men to know and worship it because of the difficulty of understanding the long cycle <note>original: "period"</note> which is measured by it. 

This is also the case with the whole of time, because of our ignorance of the single cycle of all things. Thus, the investigation of this whole as an existing being and as a God is attended with extreme difficulty. However, if an unchanging cause precedes perpetual motion, it is necessary that prior to eternity <note>original: "perpetuity"</note> itself, there should exist that which unitedly defines the whole of it and which numbers it; eternity itself being that which is numbered.

> “These things however, through forgetfulness <note>original: "oblivion"</note>, are not rightly transferred by us to an eternal essence. For we say that it *was*, and *will be*, though in reality, to this the term *it is*, alone applies <note>original: "pertains"</note>.”

In the first place, it deserves to be remarked that Plato again considers the eternal as the same with the intelligible essence <term>intelligible essence: the realm of pure being or reality accessible only to the intellect</term>; he does this so that we may be more clearly convinced that when he asserted the world was generated as the statue...

# BOOK IV. TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 209

...of the eternal Gods, he meant by the eternal, the intelligible Gods <note>intelligible Gods: divine beings or principles that can only be understood through the intellect, rather than the senses</note>. In the next place, it must be observed that because he perceived that men have no sound concepts or assertions about these matters, he himself returns to true conceptions of things. At the same time, he refines the use of words through which the teacher¹ necessarily awakens recollection in the minds of those who are well-disposed. 

What is said here, therefore, because of the mildness² of Plato's character, does not seem to severely accuse the assertions of mankind. For the expression "not rightly," being common to both the accuser and the accused, is not usually intended to bring great disgrace. The words of the text, however, have a sharp³ and piercing power. For regarding those things which the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: the "Craftsman" or Creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy</term> granted to the lowest of beings (because of their inability to receive a more venerable understanding), if men endeavor to apply these to the essences that dwell in eternity, they engage in a kind of "war of the giants" <note>This refers to the Gigantomachy, the mythological battle where giants tried to overthrow the gods; Proclus uses it as a metaphor for intellectual arrogance</note>. In doing so, they defame the will and power⁴ of the Demiurge and, in reality, are rushing to hurl rocks and oaks against the heavens. 

Why, therefore, are the terms **"was"** and **"will be"** not applied to eternal things? Because the measure of eternal things is firm and immovable, and it causes the things measured by it to be exempt from all change <note>original: "mutation"</note>. But why does **"it is"** alone, in reality, belong to them? Because what they are, they always are—neither losing nor receiving anything, whether in their essence, their life, their intelligence, or, even more so, in their union. 

Shall we say, then, that of these three—**"was,"** **"is,"** and **"will be"**—the extremes do not apply to eternal things, but the middle term alone? Or is this not the case at all? For neither does the "is" which is grouped with "was" and "will be" apply to eternal things. Instead, that which is exempt from all of these has no representation of time whatsoever. It is defined according to the eternal measure itself and must be attributed to the Gods and to eternal things. For just as there are two kinds of "always"—one eternal and the other temporal—likewise, "is" is twofold: one being suited to truly existing beings, and the other to worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note> things. When, therefore, Plato says that to this [eternal reality] the term "it is" alone applies, we shall find his statement to be more scientific if we emphasize the word *alone*. For it will then mean: to this, the "alone is" pertains; namely, the "is" which is by itself exempt from any connection to the categories of time.

# PROCLUS ON THE TIMÆUS [BOOK IV.] 210

How did humanity come to err so greatly in this regard, attributing qualities to the intelligible Gods <note>intelligible Gods: divine principles or beings that can only be understood through the intellect, rather than the physical senses</note> that do not belong to them at all? The entire cause is our forgetting of divine natures, brought about by the loss of our spiritual wings <note>original: "defluxion of our wings." This is a reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, where the soul is said to lose its "wings" and fall into a physical body</note>, our lapse from grace, and our entanglement with mortal bodies. 

For this reason, Plato also says, "that these things, through oblivion, are not correctly attributed by us to an eternal essence." Theurgists <term>Theurgists: practitioners of "divine work" or rituals intended to unite the human soul with the divine</term>, however, are not affected this way, for it is not permitted for them to be. Instead, they worship Time itself as a God. As we have mentioned, they name one type of time "zonic" <term>zonic: relating to the planetary zones or spheres</term>, and another "azonic" <term>azonic: "un-zoned," referring to powers that exist outside the specific planetary spheres</term>, which measures the cycle of the third of the ethereal worlds. 

They also honor a certain "archangelic" time in the middle of the ethereal worlds, and another "ruling" time which presides over the first of those worlds. Beyond all these, they speak of a "fontal" <term>fontal: acting as a "fount" or source</term> time. This time is the leader of the empyrean world <term>empyrean world: the highest, most spiritual region of heaven, often associated with light or fire</term>; it conducts and defines its cycle, proceeding from the fontal Goddess [Rhea] <note>Rhea: in Neo-Platonic thought, she represents the divine source of life and movement</note> herself, who generates all life and all motion. She produces fontal time and causes it to preside over all moving natures, measuring the cycles of all things down to the very last of beings. 

For even these lowest beings are measured according to cycles. Regarding things that are entirely perishable <note>original: *pamphthartôn*. The text notes a correction from *pamphorôn* (all-bearing) to *pamphthartôn* (perishable)</note>, Plato teaches us that everything living is generated from that which is dead, and everything dead from that which is living. There is a cycle for all things and an *apocatastasis* <term>apocatastasis: the restoration of a thing to its original state or the completion of a cosmic cycle</term> of generated natures—not only for those that are incorruptible. Even an individual who was generated from non-being according to a specific cycle eventually departs back into non-being, since motion from a starting point back to that same point constitutes a cycle.

Time, therefore, measures all things and defines the cycles of all things, down to the very last of beings. The Demiurge <term>Demiurge: the "Craftsman" or Creator of the physical universe</term> added this to moving natures so that they might imitate the continuous permanence of Intellect in eternity <note>The original Greek text is corrected here from the nominative "eternity" to the dative "in eternity"</note> itself. This imitation is achieved through the periodic progression from a starting point back to that same point, which Time grants to all moving beings. 

The general public, however, frequently confuses the nature of things. They fail to distinguish between what is suited to truly existing beings and what is suited to generated (temporary) things. In particular, ignorance concerning eternity and time produces this terrible confusion and error. The similarity between these things also contributes to the mistake. This is because the lowest natures are not completely separated from the highest; instead, they are suspended from them, proceed according to them, and take on the form of their images. # BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO. [PAGE 211]

People who lack a systematic knowledge of likenesses <note>original: "similitudes"; the philosophical study of how physical things resemble divine originals</note> tend to reason falsely and mistake one thing for another. They are persuaded to engage with mere images as if they were the original patterns <note>original: "paradigms"</note>, and they believe that a primordial essence is nothing more than its visible image. 

Therefore, when we perceive physical objects <note>original: "sensibles"</note>, we see a mixture of "being" and "non-being." In one sense, "being" dominates when we say a thing *is*. In another sense, "non-being" dominates when we claim that a thing *was* or that it *will be*. We incorrectly transfer these temporal terms to the eternal order of real beings. In that eternal realm, nothing is in the past, nothing will be in the future, and nothing will change. There is no progression of time there, nor any representation of existence based on what is lacking <note>original: "privation"</note>. Instead, there is true essence and truly existing being—an unchanging sameness of existence where everything exists in the "now." All ends exist simultaneously, not as different things in different places, but as one and the same with their subjects. For in these divine realms, where the whole of the <term>hyparxis</term> <note>hyparxis: the most fundamental level of a thing's existence or essence</note> consists of beauty and goodness, well-being is the same as existence.

> "But the terms *was* and *will be* are appropriately used for the process of 'becoming' <note>original: "generation"</note> that proceeds through time. These terms represent motions. However, it is not fitting that the nature which always exists with unchanging sameness and immobility should, through time, become either older or younger. Nor should it be said that it was generated in the past, is being generated now, or will be generated in the future. It should not receive any of the qualities that the process of 'becoming' applies to things moving within the physical world. These temporal terms are merely generated forms of time that imitate eternity and circulate according to number."

According to Plato, these three things pertain to the process of becoming because of time: 
1. The *was* and the *will be*.
2. The process of *becoming younger and older*.
3. Having *been generated formerly*, *being generated now*, or *being generated hereafter*. 

Regarding these, the divine Iamblichus says that time produces the first category in the physical world because it proceeds from real being. He says time produces the second because it is driven by life, and the third because it is dependent on the intellectual order. 

While these points are made with great wisdom, Iamblichus first investigates whether it is more appropriate to view them as three categories or as two. He considers if the phrase "to have been generated formerly" should be understood alongside "younger or older," and if the expressions "to be now generated" and "to be hereafter" should be grouped similarly. This is to ensure we do not mistakenly apply these concepts to the Gods—not only regarding their "becoming," but also regarding any part of time or generation. Next, returning to the beginning of everything Plato is now saying, it must be consid— <note>The text cuts off mid-word "considered" and continues on the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*, specifically examining why we use the terms "was," "is," and "will be" when discussing the physical world (the world of "becoming" or "generation") versus the eternal realm of "being."</meta>

# BOOK IV.] PROCLUS ON THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO [PAGE 212]

...considered whether we can correctly say there are only two parts to the world of becoming <note>original: "generation"</note>—the *was* and the *will be*—or if we should also include that which sits between them: the *is*. This "*is*" is not explicitly named here because the *eternal is* belongs to the world of thought <note>original: "intelligibles"</note>. It is avoided so that using the same word <note>original: "homonymy"</note> for two different things does not cause confusion in the discussion.

Furthermore, it is clear to everyone that every image shares in some way the qualities of its original model <note>original: "paradigm"</note>, but the whole world shares in the qualities of the intelligible realm in a particularly significant way. Therefore, if "true being" exists in the intelligible realm, "being" must also exist, in a certain sense, within the physical world <note>original: "sensible world"</note>. 

The *is*, however, is not counted along with the *was* and the *will be*. This is because what "properly is" does not exist among physical things; it has only a secondary existence derived from the intelligible world. Thus, it is more suited to that higher realm than to physical objects. Additionally, the goal was to show the unique characteristics of each nature, rather than how one might share traits with the other. Even though the *was* and the *will be* are defined more by "non-being" than by "being"—the former as "no longer existing" and the latter as "not yet existing." 

Do physical things, then, fully share in "being" in some way? Or should we say they are not named based on how they fall away from being, but because "non-being" dominates them? In this case, they are only suited for the world of becoming and do not belong to the realm of truly existing beings at all. Furthermore, the <term>monad</term> <note>monad: a single, indivisible unit; here representing the unified "is" of eternity</note>, or the *is*, is more closely related to eternity and the intelligible world. Conversely, the <term>duad</term> <note>duad: a pair or duality; here representing the "was" and "will be" of time</note> of the *was* and the *will be* relates to the world of becoming and time. 

*The power and strength of time’s energy is great: it coordinates that which no longer exists with current beings, and that which does not yet exist with things that are present. All these things become a continuous flow through time. The "present" is passed into the "was" by time, yet even then it is not swept away into total non-existence. Because of time, it remains, in a certain way, coordinated with things that have being.*

How, then, in the world of becoming, can the *was* and the *will be* be appropriately called "types" <note>original: "species"</note> of time? Perhaps we should say that the types of time are one thing—for the progression of time itself and the intervals that measure everything are simpler—while the things arranged within time-bound natures are another. For the phrase "time was" and "the war was" do not mean the same thing; just as "downward" in terms of general space is not the same as "downward" in relation to the earth. The former is simple and unified, while the latter is complex and dual. One contains the other, and the other is contained. 

In the same way, regarding the *was*, the element of time itself contains and measures and is simple; but the event that occurs within the world of becoming is contained, measured, and shares in time, but it is not time itself. It is clear that the entire world of becoming is contained by time, just as time itself is contained by the intelligible world. And time is said to come forth from the intelligible world according to number, making its progress according to the...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's discussion on the linguistic errors humans make when describing the physical world (generation) versus the eternal world (being). ...forms and measures that are in them. But generation <note>original: "generation"; here referring to the physical world of change and "becoming."</note> is said to proceed in time, as it is measured and perfected by time. Again, time—because it imitates eternity—is said to circulate (just as the heavens, because they imitate the divine intellect, are said to have a spherical form) and to have as its categories *the "was"*, and *the "will be"*, and other such things allied to these. It is evident that these are simple and are the primary guides of those natures that are carried along within the world of change. For that which holds the measures of all change within itself inserts images and impressions of them into the things that move according to it. 

The world of change, therefore, loses its vitality, and for this reason, it requires the renewing help of time. It is also imperfect at first and needs time to make it more perfect and older. But the intelligible realm <note>original: "the intelligible"; the world of pure, eternal forms.</note> is always perfect, always flourishing, and always has an unchanging way of existing. For this reason, even there, something "older" exists:

->But Zeus was born first,<- <note>original: "Jove"; quoting Homer's Iliad 13.355.</note>
->and likewise that which is younger:<-
->August Hebe pours the nectar for them.<- <note>Quoting Homer's Iliad 4.2. Hebe is the goddess of youth.</note>

Yet these qualities of "older" and "younger" are not present in that realm because of time. Plato also very accurately adds that it is not fitting for the intelligible to become either older or younger through time, nor, in short, for that which was never "born" <note>original: "unbegotten"</note> to be generated, or to have been generated, or to be generated in the future. In a single word: the world of change, though it is not "essence" <note>original: "essence"; meaning true, unchanging Being.</note> itself, still participates in essence; but it is by no means proper for true essence to be filled with change. Hence, it is not right to apply things suited only to the temporal world of change to truly existing beings.

> "And in addition to these things, we also claim that a thing which *was* created, *is* created; that what exists *in the process of becoming*, *is* created; that what *will be*, *is* to be; and that *non-being is non-being*; none of which assertions are accurate. Perhaps, however, a thorough discussion of these things is not suited to the present discourse."

Before this, Plato blamed the Greek custom of applying words suited to the changing world to truly existing beings. But now he accuses the common people of doing the opposite: applying terms suited to the eternal, intelligible realm to the world of change. Their error is either twofold or is one single, great illegality. For when they say that a thing which *was* created *is* created, and that what *will be* is *to be*, they erroneously apply the unique quality of eternal essences to things that change.

<summary>Proclus explains that while the physical world (generation) moves through time and needs it for "renewal," the eternal realm (the intelligible) remains unchanging and perfect. He critiques the linguistic error of applying the eternal "is" to the changing physical world.</summary>

# BOOK IV.] PROCLUS ON THE TIMÆUS [PAGE 214]

...natures. For this word ***is*** pertains to superior divine beings; just as to be generated, or to exist in a state of becoming, pertains to sensible things <note>original: "sensibles"; things that can be perceived by the physical senses rather than the intellect.</note>. They likewise erroneously confuse the parts of time and subvert its natural order by making the *now*, or the present time, the same as the past. 

But when they say that what exists in a state of **becoming** actually ***is***, they fall into the first error alone. Though this is an error of the greatest consequence, yet—if it be lawful to speak this way—it is a still greater error to say that non-being ***is***. For if "generation" <note>original: "generation"; the process of physical birth, change, and becoming.</note> is a middle ground between non-being and being, it is a smaller error to apply the characteristics of "being" to "generation" than it is to apply them to "non-being." 

One apology, however, may be made for these mistakes based on nature. Because "non-being" participates in the "generation of being"—just as everything temporal appears to participate in eternity—it is common to refer these things to eternity and to truly existing being, both of which are free from all time intervals and division into parts. And again, it is common to try to stabilize and hold onto "generation," which is otherwise swept along in constant motion and exists only in time. 

It is not at all surprising, therefore, if people wishing to stabilize those things that have already been generated among the ranks of "beings" should say that they ***are*** generated. Likewise, because they wish to rank things that are not yet generated with things currently in existence, they say that such a thing ***is*** to be generated. Through these two ways, non-being is able, in a certain respect, to approach and be ranked alongside "beings"—specifically through the participation in being and through the present temporal interval, both of which may appear to introduce actual existence. 

This is how the frequent use of these words in this sense began. Nevertheless, this mixing of terms has nothing accurate or scientific about it (as Plato says). By this, he signifies—at least as far as it applies to the current physical investigation—that a more thorough study of these matters belongs to another discussion. Most interpreters think that other discussion is "logical." For in logical discussions, it is common to ask whether "non-being" can be an object of opinion. 

As Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Proclus.</note> says, however—and I am persuaded by him—this discussion is actually **theological**. For in the *Sophist* <note>original: "Sophista"; one of Plato's dialogues.</note>, much is said about every variety of non-being, and likewise in the *Parmenides*, the investigation of which Timaeus also proves to be appropriate. 

Now, however, as he separates and distinguishes things from each other—dividing them into that which is "always being" and that which is "generated and perishes," or into "image" and "paradigm," and the "eternal" and the "temporal"—he also wishes to give names adapted to each of these. He does this so that he neither transfers qualities of temporal generation to more simple and divine essences, nor mixes the transcendent goods of superior natures with things that are swept along in motion and change. But he leaves the more profound investigation of these details for more appropriate opportunities. For this was the custom both with Plato himself and, prior to Plato, with the Pytha- <note>The text cuts off here, likely referring to the "Pythagoreans."</note>

# BOOK IV.] THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO. 215

...goreans <note>original: "goreans"; the conclusion of the word "Pythagoreans" from the previous page.</note>. Aristotle also, especially emulating this custom, discusses philosophical problems in a way adapted to the design of his treatise.

> "Time, therefore, was generated together with the universe, in order that by being generated together with it, it might also be dissolved together with it, if ever a certain dissolution of it should take place. It was also generated according to the model <note>original: "paradigm"; a perfect pattern or blueprint.</note> of an eternal nature, so that it might be as similar to it as possible. For the model of time is [real] being throughout all eternity. But the universe was generated, is, and will be forever through the whole of time."

Plato says that time was generated together with the universe—which is now animated <note>original: "animated"; meaning it possesses a soul (the World Soul).</note> and endowed with intellect—because the world first participates in time according to the soul and its physical nature. But the words, "*that being generated together with it, it may also be dissolved together with it, if ever a certain dissolution of it should take place*," clearly show that the universe is unbegotten and incorruptible <note>meaning it was not created at a specific moment and cannot be destroyed.</note>. 

For if it was generated, it was generated in time. But if it was generated *with* time, it was not generated *in* time. For time itself was not generated in time, otherwise there would be a time prior to time. If, therefore, the universe was generated together with time, it was not "generated" in the usual understanding of the word. For it is necessary that everything which was generated must come after time. The universe, however, is by no means posterior to time. 

Again, if everything that is dissolved <note>original: "dissolved"; broken down or destroyed.</note> is dissolved at a certain time, but time cannot be dissolved in a part of itself, then time can never be dissolved; consequently, neither can the universe. For the universe is indissoluble as long as time is indissoluble. Besides, time is indissoluble because of its simplicity of nature—unless someone wishes to name its progression and its return to the Demiurge <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine craftsman or creator of the material world.</note> (which are motions contrary to each other) as its "generation" and "dissolution." 

Thus, the universe also has dissolution and generation only according to its cause. It is just as if someone, wishing for the revolutions of the "Circle of the Different" <note>original: "the circle of the different"; in Plato's cosmology, this refers to the orbital plane of the planets, as opposed to the "Circle of the Same" or the fixed stars.</note> to be odd in number, should say that the heptad <note>original: "heptad"; the number seven.</note> exists alongside them. He might say that if the heptad ever became an even number, the revolutions would also become even—meaning by this that the orbits will never actually fall into an even number. In the same way, we must now understand the absolute indissolubility of the world and time, because time has a nature that cannot be dissolved.

One reason, therefore, that time was generated together with the universe is so that the universe may be indissoluble and perpetual. But a second cause is,

...so that it may be most similar to its paradigm <note>original: "paradigm"; the eternal model or blueprint upon which the physical universe is based.</note>. For Plato says that the universe itself is most similar to its paradigm. How, therefore, does the universe become more similar to the "Animal-itself" <note>original: "animal itself"; the Platonic Form of Living Being that contains all other living things.</note> through time? Because, says he, just as intelligible realities <note>original: "intelligibles"; things known by the mind rather than the senses, such as the Forms.</note> receive all the power of eternity—which now unites and contains them all at once, collectively and in a unified way—so also the world sustains all the measured motion of time in portions and in a divided manner. Through this, the world also *was*, *is*, and *will be*. It does not possess all three of these states throughout the whole of time, but experiences each in a specific portion of time. 

However, it receives each of the three across the whole of time because of the past and future periods, and because it is of the nature of things generated <note>original: "things generated"; things in the physical world that are subject to change and "becoming" rather than eternal "being."</note>; it possesses perfection in generation according to every part of time. And it exists indeed, or *is*, because in the whole of the present circulation of time, it participates in *being*. But it *will be* because the measured motions of the whole of time will never cease, and the circulations conjoin and assimilate <note>meaning to make similar.</note> time to intelligible causes. If, however, the universe exists forever through the whole of time—and *is*, and *was*, and *will be*—it *is* and *will be* in the time to come because it is indestructible. Hence, it was generated throughout *all* past time, being effectively "unbegotten" <note>meaning it has always existed and was not created at a specific start date.</note>. For it is similarly present with all time according to each of these three states <note>The states of "was," "is," and "will be."</note>. 

If this is not admitted, then it will no longer exist infinitely in the future, nor was it generated from infinity in the past. And those people are ridiculous <note>Proclus here alludes to the ancient Christians who tried to prove, using the authority of Plato, that the world was produced at a certain time and will at a certain time be destroyed.</note> who say that the world was once created and that it will cease to exist at a certain time, since Plato ascribes to it the whole of time, including both [the past and the future]. You see that he now attributes the three parts of time to the world and does not refuse to ascribe *being* to it. Hence, it is evident that when he previously attributed the "*is*" to an eternal nature and not to generation, that "*is*" is exempt from all temporal extension. Being established according to the eternal itself, it pertains to intelligible realities; since he grants that the whole of the "*was*" and the "*will be*" are forever present with sensible things <note>original: "sensibles"; physical things perceived by the senses.</note>, according to their participation in truly-existing being.

For how was that which is comprehensive and perfecting, and which makes the image more like its paradigm—how was this generated for the sake of that which is comprehended and made similar? # BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

...any other thing, it would be more honored than the goals themselves, and higher natures would exist only for the sake of lower things. However, no such arrangement is found in the philosophy of Plato. For time was not created solely for the sake of the universe, nor was the universe made solely for the sake of time; rather, each was created for its own sake, for the sake of the other, and for the sake of both together. To ensure the entire creation <note>original: "fabrication"</note> reached perfection, both the universe and time were produced in a complete and finished state. 

Furthermore, each contributes significantly to making the other more like its own eternal model <note>original: "paradigm"; the divine blueprint for reality.</note>. For time could not imitate eternity without the existence of the universe; otherwise, how would it move forward, or what existing things would it ever measure, connect, or perfect? Likewise, without the existence of time, the universe could not imitate, as much as possible, the all-perfect and eternal nature of the "Living-Being-Itself" <note>original: "animal itself"; in Platonic thought, this is the eternal Form of Life that contains all living species.</note>. 

Therefore, each was created not just for itself or for the other alone, but for the sake of the entire creation, so that each might become as perfect and as similar to its model as possible. More accurately, each was created for the sake of Goodness and the "Father of All" <note>Referring to the Demiurge or Creator god.</note>, which is why the production of things is perfect. Because each was created to relate to the other, they both contribute greatly to the stability, order, and well-being of all things in the physical world. 

This is the extent of Plato’s philosophy concerning time, which is the single, whole measure of all things, moving and proceeding from the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> alone and its own fundamental source <note>original: "monad"</note>. In what follows, he discusses the time that unfolds in the heavens, which is divided among the various movements <note>original: "lations"; from the Latin *latio*, meaning the act of carrying or moving.</note> of the stars. This celestial time would not exist without the revolution of the "Circle of the Same" and the "Circle of the Different" <note>These represent the celestial equator and the ecliptic (the path of the sun), the two primary motions in Plato's cosmology.</note> around that one invisible time, which provides and preserves the measure adapted to each of these circles. Next, so that this secondary time could enter the visible world and be understood through its smaller parts <note>original: "partial measures"</note>, the Creator made the planets, among which the sun and moon are included. From all this, we can see the great honor the philosopher—or rather the Creator of all things Himself—gives to that primary, unified time.

->“For this reason, then, and from such a rational plan <note>original: "discursive energy"</note> of divinity regarding the birth of time, in order that time might be created, He produced the sun, the moon, and the five other stars called planets, for the purpose of distinguishing and guarding the numbers of time.”<-

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

As we have frequently observed, the creation <note>original: "fabrication"</note> of things is twofold. One is invisible, singular, and simple; it is super-mundane <note>Existing above or beyond the physical world.</note> and universal. The other is visible, diverse, and multiform; it is distributed into parts <note>original: "μεριζομενης" (merizomenēs); the OCR text "περιζομενης" is likely an error.</note> within the world. 

This creation has two types of energies. The first is primary, unchanging, and intellectual. The second is secondary; it proceeds through motion and revolves around the intellect. While the first is independent of its results, the second is organized alongside them. Because of this, time also proceeds to beings in two ways: there is super-mundane time and mundane time. 

The first type of time stays still and moves forward at the same time, while the second is carried along by motion. That which we experience <note>original: "participated"</note> is also twofold: one exists as a simple experience, while the other exists within the cycles of the stars, which produce months, days, nights, and years. 

Because there is this difference between types of time, Plato—having already shared his ideas about the single and simple essence of time—is now about to discuss the variety of time. This is the time that is experienced in parts, and the study of the planets helps us understand it. It is through the motion of these planets dancing around the sun that the time we know is fully realized. Plato introduces this as a "ninth gift" to the world. 

However, to show that this version of time is lower than the super-mundane version, he says it was formed by the discursive reasoning <note>original: "discursive energy"; the process of the mind moving from one idea to another.</note> of the Divine. Furthermore, he says that it distinguishes and protects the "numbers of time" through the motion of the stars. We must pay attention to both points:
1. The distinction of many different measurements of time after the one super-mundane time.
2. The defense and perpetual preservation of these same measurements, which is why he says the stars were created.

The Demiurge <note>The "Craftsman" or Creator of the universe in Platonic thought.</note> produced the first kind of time by looking toward eternity and acting according to a single, simple intelligence. But he produced the second kind of time, as Plato says, from reason and discursive thought <note>original: "και διανοίας" (kai dianoias)</note>. By using the term *dianoia* <note>Dianoia refers to the distributive power of the mind—the cause that divides a single unified truth into a multitude of specific parts.</note>, he indicates the divided nature of this thought and how it spreads out into many things from a single intelligence. 

For a divine intellect is one thing, and divine reason is another. The intellect is unified, but reason is multiplied. The intellect understands things as whole, while reason divides that unity into a multitude. The intellect stays within itself, while reason unfolds itself into the light. Therefore, if this secondary time is visible everywhere, it is very appropriate to say it comes from the Demiurge's reason, which receives its progression from the intellect. Reason reveals the cause, but *dianoia* (discursive thought) reveals the...

<summary>Proclus distinguishes between "super-mundane" time, which is unified and eternal, and "mundane" time, which is divided into measurable units like days and years by the movement of the planets. He explains that while the higher time stems from divine intellect, the lower time stems from the Demiurge's discursive reasoning.</summary>

### BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

knowledge in the Demiurge <note>original: "Demiurgus," the divine craftsman of the universe</note>, which possesses a twofold nature. Truly-existing time—which is the total number of all the cycles in the universe—is one thing; but the time that flows from this and proceeds according to number is quite another.

Furthermore, truly-existing time encompasses all measures in a unified way. According to these measures, the cycles of both souls and bodies are completed, as is the single measure of the entire cosmic restoration <note>original: "apocatastasis," the point at which all celestial bodies return to their original positions</note>. For there is a specific cycle for that which is divinely created, which a perfect number encompasses, as Socrates mentions in the *Republic*. But secondary time defines and maintains the measures in souls and physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> natures. It distributes measures adapted to each of these. By doing this, it divides the single power of the first time but guards the measure belonging to each soul and each physical nature. In accordance with this, it also creates restorations. There is one measure for the solar cycle, another for the lunar, and another for the cycle of atmospheric phenomena <note>original: "meteors," referring to things occurring in the air or sky</note>. For in these too, there is a certain circle that mirrors the celestial circle. Different animals also have different cycles. For they have their own periods and measures of life, as the divine <note>original: "dæmoniacal," meaning divinely inspired or possessing supernatural genius</note> Aristotle says. These, therefore, are the conclusions we can now draw concerning the difference between these types of time.

It also appears that Plato does not say, "*in order that time might be generated*," without reason. He says it to show that invisible time existed beforehand as a whole, singular, and intellectual number, prior to the time that is experienced <note>original: "participated"</note> and which proceeds according to number. Everything that is created, therefore, exists invisibly in its cause before its actual generation. Thus, "generation" signifies a progression into things that participate in it, through which time reveals different forms <note>The original Greek text likely meant "forms of things" (eidon) rather than just "forms" (eide)</note> in primary and secondary ways. It also signifies that time proceeds from universal <note>original: "total"</note> to more specific <note>original: "partial"</note> natures, even down to the lowliest things, such as animals and plants. 

To us, however, the whole of time becomes known through specific but orderly measures. The "whole" of time is difficult to understand, and that which is disorderly cannot be used to measure other things. But since, as we have said, the cycle of the planets—and especially the solar circle—contributes to the creation of secondary time (or rather, to the understanding of the many measures within it, such as months and years, by which we are accustomed to measure time), Plato says that the sun, the moon, and the five planets were first created by the Demiurge. <meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Book IV of Plato’s Timaeus. It transitions from discussing the general nature of time to the specific roles of the celestial bodies—the fixed stars, the Sun, the Moon, and the planets—in establishing the measurable cycles of the physical world.</meta>

<page-num>220</page-num>

### PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

Every fixed star is spherical and completes its cycle around its own center according to a specific measurement of time. However, these measurements are not known to us in the way those of the planets are, according to which they make their cycles around the zodiac. Regarding the fixed stars, we do not know the length of their periods around their own proper centers. 

Therefore, Plato speaks about the planets and says they were created so that they might work together to produce visible time. They reveal different measurements for different things, with the Sun being granted a primary and governing status, especially regarding the creation of time. For this reason, he is called "the time of time" by theologians, because he reveals the primary form of time; the cycle of the seasons is completed according to his movement. 

The Moon holds the second rank, as she directly influences the movement, growth, and decay of everything in "generation" <note>original: "generation," referring to the physical world of change, birth, and death</note> through her powers. Thus, just as the Sun is said to change his forms every hour and in every sign of the zodiac,¹ the Moon changes her form every day. As the theologian says, she undergoes as many changes in a single month as the Sun does in a year. The other planets, through their various motions, link the diversity of the physical world into an orderly sequence. For different effects follow from the restoration <note>original: "apocatastasis," the point at which a celestial body returns to its starting position</note> of different planets, which complete their own lives in a cycle according to different measurements.

However, because the planets revolve with one continuous, steady, and unceasing motion—yet the order, consistency, and sameness of these motions are hidden because they appear to move forward, move backward, and stand still—for this reason, Plato says they are called "planets" <note>original: "planetes," meaning "wanderers"</note>. From this, you may conclude that it is the stars themselves—not the celestial spheres in which the stars move—that appear to advance and recede, and which move higher or lower. They contain within themselves, as orderly patterns <note>original: "paradigms"</note>, all the various disorders—

---

¹ This is well explained by Iamblichus in *On the Mysteries* <note>original: "De Mysteriis"</note>, page 152, as follows: 
> "Since every part of the heavens, every sign of the zodiac, and every celestial movement—along with every measurement of time by which the world moves—receives powers descending from the Sun, some of which are intertwined with these things themselves, while others remain pure and unmixed, symbolic teaching indicates this by claiming that the Sun is diversified according to the signs of the zodiac and that he changes his form every hour. Yet, at the same time, it points to his unchanging, stable, never-fading, and unified gift of goodness to the entire world. But because those who receive the indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> gift of the God are affected by it in different ways and receive many different types of power from the Sun according to their own specific motions, the symbolic doctrine proves through this variety of gifts that the God is one. It displays his single power through many forms of power. For this reason, it also says that he is one and the same, but we must admit that the changes in his form and his appearances actually exist within the things that receive him. On this account, it claims he changes every hour according to the sign of the zodiac, because these things are changing in relation to the God, based on the many ways they receive his influence."

<summary>Proclus explains that while fixed stars have their own unknown cycles, the Sun, Moon, and planets were created to produce "visible time." He details how the Sun's singular power is experienced as diverse changes by the physical world, a concept further explained by a passage from Iamblichus.</summary>

<header>BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>
<page-num>221</page-num>

...orderly motions of the sublunary <term>sublunary</term> region—namely, the motions there that are upward and downward, or backward and forward. For as Plato says in the *Laws*, those people sin against divinity who dare to attribute "wandering" to the celestial Gods because they do not understand their order, their harmonious dance, and the regularity of their motion. 

Irregularity only appears to exist in them because of their local motion <note>original: "lation," an archaic term for movement from one place to another</note> and the contrary circulation of their revolving circles, whether this is due to epicycles <term>epicycles</term>, eccentrics <term>eccentrics</term>, or other causes. Not all these hypotheses have the same¹ probability. Indeed, some of them are far removed from the simplicity of divine natures, and others are merely mechanical contrivances devised by modern thinkers to account for the motion of the celestial spheres. 

It seems that Plato, in the *Republic*, makes the "whirls" concentric and mentions these seven circles alone, without mentioning epicycles. By doing so, he attributes a kind of irregularity to the stars themselves, yet it is an irregularity that possesses arrangement and order. This is because this irregularity returns to its original state in orderly periods of time; the planets act as intermediaries between things that move with perfectly regular motion and those that move irregularly in every respect. Therefore, they are granted a motion that is "regularly irregular" or "irregularly regular."

Time, therefore, is revealed and makes its progression into the universe through all the celestial spheres—not only through the planets but also through the fixed stars. However, Plato specifically mentions the planets in the creation of time because they differ from the fixed stars in the variety of their cycles, and they differ from earthly natures because their motions are always invariably the same. The first point is shown by the distinction of many different measurements of time, and the second is shown by the perpetual preservation of the same periods and restorations <term>apocatastases</term>. 

For it is necessary to observe that these same patterns continue while the many measurements of time remain. These measures, therefore, have an orderly arrangement following the single measure of the entire cosmic period. The primary unit <term>monad</term> of time is itself a perfect and whole number. From this unit, in each circulation, there is a specific measure—whether it be Saturnian, Jovian <note>related to Jupiter</note>, or Lunar—receiving its unique character from the soul and the motivating deity that resides in each of the spheres. 

Just as one number pertains to the sun, another to a horse, and another to a plant, the universal <note>original: "mundane"</note> number is common to all of them. For this reason, we say that time is the same everywhere. The world has one life, just as it has one nature and one intellect. If, however, it has one life <note>original Greek: "ζωη" (zoe), referring to the fundamental principle of life</note>, it will also have one manner of living <note>original Greek: "βιος" (bios), referring to the lived course or duration of life</note>. If this is the case, it will likewise have one temporal measure. And just as each of the parts within the world lives according to the nature of the whole, so too it is...

---

¹ For "these," read "this." <note>The original Greek text likely had a gender/number error; "αυται" (hautai) should be read as "αυτο" (hauto).</note>

<summary>Proclus explains that celestial "irregularity" is actually an orderly, harmonious dance that defines different measures of time (Saturnian, Jovian, etc.), all of which are unified under one universal temporal measure.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, transitioning from the discussion of orderly celestial motions to the metaphysical structure of time and the hierarchy of the celestial governors (cosmocrators) and the soul.</meta>

<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.</header>

...measured according to total time. And this is the common measure of all things. But after this single unit <note>original: "monad," the primary source of a series</note> there is a triad <note>original: "triad," a group of three</note>, the *summit* of which is the measure of the first circulation; the *middle* is the measure of the entire circle of the *different* <note>In Platonic cosmology, the "Circle of the Different" refers to the paths of the planets, as opposed to the "Circle of the Same," which refers to the fixed stars.</note>. For all the planets, as parts of one living being, share one life <note>original: "ζωη εις" (zōē eis)</note>, one period, and one apocatastatic <term>apocatastatic</term> time <note>A period of time after which the stars and planets return to the same relative positions they occupied at a specific previous time.</note>. And the third part, or the *extremity*, is the measure of the circulation which takes place in the realm of generation <note>the physical world of birth, death, and change</note>. For because of this, the changes of the elements, the transformations of moveable natures, and rebirth are all granted a substantial existence <note>original: "hypostasis"</note>. After this triad, however, time proceeds according to various other numbers, measuring whole systems and distinguishing all things by appropriate measures. These things, therefore, we shall consider again.

It should not go unnoticed that Plato, having established the existence of whole systems and not yet mentioned individual living beings, first creates the planets, and afterwards the fixed stars, in the generation of individual beings. For what are called the planets are *cosmocrators* <term>cosmocrators</term>—governors of the world—and are granted a total power. And just as the fixed sphere <note>original: "inerratic sphere," the sphere of the stars that do not "wander"</note> contains a number of star-like beings, so each of the planets is the leader of a multitude of beings, or other things of this kind. 

From this, the puzzle may be solved: how does the one sphere [of the fixed stars] contain a multitude of stars, while in the many spheres of the planets, each sphere carries only one star? For it must be said that there [in the fixed stars] the sphere is a single unit <note>original: "monad"</note> that is one, containing within itself an appropriate multitude; it is sufficient to contain that multitude, as it is the first multitude. But in the planets, the leadership is twofold: one is the sphere [in which the planet is carried], and the other is each of the world-governors, being a single unit organized alongside a multitude. For lower natures require a greater number of leaders, and the multitude within each is invisible because of their lower rank. And in the sublunary <term>sublunary</term> region, there is a still greater number of orders which lead the various classes <note>original: "genera"</note> in each of the elements, as we may learn from the *Theogony* <note>The "Theogony" refers to traditional accounts of the origins and genealogies of the gods.</note> that has been passed down to us. Let these things, therefore, be accepted as evident.

But we must consider what is said about the generation of time: if time comes after the soul, how is the soul moved according to time? And if time exists before the soul, how can it be said to be "generated" <note>brought into being</note>? For Plato has said that the soul is the best of all generated things. But if time is on the same level <note>original: "co-ordinate"</note> as the soul, why is it that eternity is not on the same level as, but rather prior to, the intellect? It must be said—

---

¹ The sphere is a leader, an organized unit <note>original: "monad"</note>, and a complete whole; but each of the world-governors <note>original: "cosmocrators"</note> is a leader and a unit, but is not a complete whole.

<summary>Proclus explores the metaphysical structure of time and the hierarchy of celestial bodies, distinguishing between the unity of the fixed stars and the complex leadership of the planets (cosmocrators). He also raises a philosophical problem regarding whether time exists before or after the soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, transitioning from the metaphysical definition of time as a "measure" to how time relates to the soul and the physical creation of the planets.</meta>

<header>BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

In answer to this, we say that time is indeed prior to the soul, just as eternity is prior to the intellect. However, the soul is the finest of all generated <note>original: "generated," meaning things that have come into being or are subject to change, as opposed to eternal things</note> natures—specifically those that are *essentially* generated. This is true not only because they are present alongside secondary natures, but also because they have a generation according to their internal activity and an essence that can be divided into many parts, just as Plato himself has taught us.

But time, as we have demonstrated, is *essentially* an eternal intellect. It is participated in <note>original: "participated," meaning shared in or experienced by lower levels of reality</note> through a created manner—not all at once, nor immovably like the *intellects* that precede it, but through movement. For this reason, just like the intellect, time perfects the soul and is produced through these participations; it flows abundantly into those that participate in it and makes generations appear as things that are numbered. Thus, because it aligns completely with the cycles of creation,¹ it can be shown to be "generated."

Furthermore, because it proceeds according to number, time is said to be "movable." Yet it is not the same as number itself, because time exists prior to the things that are numbered. For these reasons, Plato calls time "eternal" here because it is eternal according to its internal activity, the entirety of which it possesses in the present moment. But in his work the *Laws*, he says that the soul is indeed indestructible, yet not "eternal," because it is not granted an unchanging internal activity.

> "But the divinity, having made the bodies of these stars, placed them—being seven in number—in the seven orbits formed by the periodic motion of the Circle of the Different."

It is clear that Plato refers to the sun, the moon, and the other five stars as living beings endowed with souls and intellects. This is evident from his addition that the divinity made the "bodies of each of them," implying the stars themselves are intellectual and vital. He does not say that he made *the bodies themselves*,² but the *bodies of them*. 

It must be said, therefore, that their "orbits" <note>original: "circulations"</note> are either epicycles <term>epicycle</term><note>In ancient astronomy, a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used to explain the complex paths of planets.</note>, or evolving circles, or the entire spheres in which each star is placed. Alternatively, as the divine Iamblichus <note>A prominent Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) known for his mystical and systematic approach to Plato.</note> understood it, these orbits signify the intellectual souls of the planets themselves. Just as the divinity previously fashioned the entire mass of the world within the soul, he now places these seven bodies within the seven intellectual souls, simultaneously appointing souls and intellects to govern these bodies. However, since much earlier than this, Plato represented the—

This correction changes the text from "the number that ran together with those [souls]" to "the numbers that ran together with their [generations]."</note>
² <note>original: "For *autēn* (her/it) here, it is necessary to read *auta* (them)." This confirms the text is referring to the multiple bodies of the stars.</note>

<summary>Proclus explains that while time is an eternal intellectual principle, it is experienced as "generated" and "movable" by the soul. He then discusses Plato’s creation of the seven planets, arguing they are living, intellectual beings whose bodies are governed by divine souls.</summary>

# PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS [BOOK IV.]

Regarding the period of the Circle of the Different <note>In Platonic cosmology, the "Circle of the Same" represents the uniform, eternal motion of the fixed stars, while the "Circle of the Different" represents the varied, wandering motions of the planets.</note> in the whole soul, as it presides over these seven divine bodies, Plato very properly adds—reminding us of what had been said before—that they are "in the seven circulations formed by the periodic motion of the Circle of the Different in the whole soul." And again, he demonstrates this by speaking in the singular number. For this circle is undivided, even though it is said to have been "cut." It does not lose its unity despite being divided into seven smaller circles.

Perhaps, however, it is better to say that the Demiurge <note>The divine craftsman or architect of the universe.</note> established the bodies of the world-rulers <note>original: "cosmocrators," the planetary gods who govern the world.</note> within the powers of the universal soul, but not yet within their own individual souls or their specific spheres. For the words "formed by the periodic motion of the circle of the different" show that this circle does not revolve these bodies simply by its own motion. This circle, being one and divided into seven parts, moves around the lives of these divine bodies. 

Further on, Plato says that the fixed stars are placed in the wisdom of the Intellect, which is the soul of the Circle of the Same. For that circle is the most powerful and excellent, as it is the one to which the Demiurge granted authority. The wisdom of this circle is an intellectual life. Thus, he now places the seven planetary bodies in the seven circles of the universal soul. Again, through these details, it becomes evident how the simplicity of the soul is preserved even in relation to physical cycles. For the single Circle of the Same animates both the fixed sphere <note>original: "inerratic sphere," the outer shell of the universe containing the fixed stars.</note> and the stars it contains according to a single union. 

In a similar way, each of the seven planets, according to one common power, animates both the spheres and the stars they contain. <note>original Greek: "ὁμοίως κατὰ δύναμιν μίαν καὶ ταῖς σφαίραις." The translator notes this was likely defective and suggests it should read: "similarly, according to one common power, it animates the spheres."</note> At this point, Plato is speaking of the soul that is common to all of them; but shortly after, he also describes the soul peculiar to each one, when he says "that being bound with living bonds, they became animals." <note>In this context, "animals" refers to self-moving, living celestial beings possessing their own souls.</note> For at that stage, they are no longer merely animated as parts of a whole, but as individual living beings through their own distinct souls.

> “And the moon indeed, he placed in the first circulation about the earth; but the sun, in the second above the earth; and the star called Lucifer <note>The "Light-Bringer," known today as the planet Venus.</note>, and that which is sacred to Mercury, in circulations proceeding with a swiftness equal to that of the sun, though they are assigned a contrary power. Hence the Sun, Venus, and Mercury mutually catch up to and are caught up by each other.”

From what is said here, it is evident what order the study of Spherics <note>The ancient study of the geometry of the heavens and celestial spheres.</note> gives to the—

For he arranges the Moon after the Sun; <note>The original text says "the Sun after the Moon," but as the footnote points out, the context requires the Moon to follow the Sun.</note> since there is a certain most abundant communion between these divinities in the visible production of things. [as Orpheus says]. Perhaps the <term>Chaldean Oracles</term> <note>A collection of mystical poems from the 2nd century AD, highly regarded by Neoplatonists like Proclus.</note> also teach us this, since they everywhere arrange the Moon after the Sun, and the air after the Moon, both when they describe their order from above and from beneath. For they say, "The ethereal course, the immense impulse of the Moon, and the aerial streams." And again, "O ether, Sun, spirit of the Moon, and you leaders of the air." And elsewhere, "Of the solar circles, <note>original Greek: ηλιακων τε κυκλων</note> the lunar rattlings, and the aerial bosoms." And afterwards, "The portion of ether, of the Sun, of the rivers of the Moon, and of the air." In another place they also say, "The broad air, the lunar course, and the perpetual pole of the Sun." 

Perhaps, therefore, as I have said, it is possible to be convinced by the Oracles that the Sun is immediately above the Moon, just as the Moon is above the air—the whole of heaven having the nature of fire. This was also the opinion of Plato, <note>original: "ο και Πλατωνι δοκει"</note> who, after describing the celestial realm, arranges the ethereal form in what he says shortly after regarding the four types of being [within the "Animal-Itself" or the living universe]. 

Unless, however, it is not strictly necessary for the Sun to be immediately above the Moon based on the analogy to <term>ether</term> <note>The "fifth element," thought to be the substance of the celestial spheres.</note>; for ether itself is not immediately above the Sun. Therefore, this analogy alone might not allow the Sun to be placed directly above the Moon. Nevertheless, ancient tradition <note>original: "rumor"</note> gives this order to the Sun. For Aristotle held this opinion, as did Eudoxus and his followers. 

If, however, some who adopt the hypotheses of mathematicians should think it right to arrange the Sun in the middle of the seven planets—as the one who collects and binds the groups of three on each side of him—it must be noted <note>original Greek: εστωσαν</note> that there is no real stability in what they say based on mathematics alone. For their claim—that Venus and Mercury would be obscured if they were located after the Sun (just as the Moon is sometimes obscured by the Sun)—is proven false by showing that when they are in <term>conjunction</term> with the Sun according to longitude, they entirely

differ according to latitude. And this is the cause of their not being obscured. However, as it does not necessarily follow that the Sun has a middle position among the planets, mathematicians cannot provide the same level of proof for this as they are accustomed to obtain for most other things.

Ptolemy, therefore, says in his *Syntaxis* <note>original Greek: Μεγαλη Συνταξις της Αστρονομιας, or *The Great Construction of Astronomy*. By the Arabians, it was called the *Almagest*.</note> that it is appropriate, based on sound and probable reasoning, to place the Sun in the middle of the seven planets. He suggests this so that among the five planets other than the Sun and Moon, there may be those that are perfectly separated from him, and after him, those that are in conjunction with him and lead the way or follow him like attendants. But in his *Hypotheses* <note>original Greek: Υποθεσις των Πλανωμενων, or *The Hypothesis of the Planets*. This work was illustrated by John Bainbridge with a Latin version and mathematical figures (London, 1620).</note>, he does not strongly argue for the truth of this, nor does he infer it from the intervals between the planets—neither in that work nor in his *Syntaxis*. Therefore, much attention should not be paid to mathematicians when they reason only from probability. 

But the theurgist <note>Julian the Chaldean, a 2nd-century mystic believed to have authored the *Chaldean Oracles*.</note> clearly says "that the Demiurge <note>The creator or "craftsman" of the universe in Platonic thought.</note> suspended six zones, and for the seventh hurled the fire of the Sun into the middle"; and it is not lawful to disbelieve what he says. Plato, however, looking at the abundant connection and "born-together" progression of the Sun and Moon from the same cause, as well as their entry into the world, describes them to us as being joined together. Plato was not the author of this hypothesis that the Moon exists immediately after the Sun; rather, as Eudemus relates, Anaxagoras was the first to hold this opinion.

Again, this is also a subject of inquiry: for what reason do the Sun, Venus, and Mercury revolve with equal speed? Some say from a mathematical perspective that the <term>epicycles</term> <note>Small circles used in ancient astronomy to explain the complex paths of planets while they orbited the Earth.</note> of these three stars are connected and that their centers are in one straight line. Therefore, just as there is one <term>apocatastasis</term> <note>original Greek: apokatastasis; the completion of a full orbital cycle or a return to a starting point.</note> of the motion of a single straight line, the epicycles of these planets also make the same <term>apocatastasis</term>. Of the epicycles themselves, the outer ones are smaller while the middle epicycle is larger, so that both their uniform and irregular motions are in the same ratio. 

But the interpreters of Plato—Porphyry and Theodorus—who investigate the cause of this, refer the principle of the equality and inequality of these planets' courses to their "lives." For according to them, the inequality or equality of their swiftness comes from their intellects tending directly through many mediators toward true essence and ending in the same...
