<meta>This page continues the discussion of planetary movement and speed. It explores the metaphysical theories of Porphyry, Theodorus, and Iamblichus regarding how different planets relate to the concepts of essence, intellect, and life.</meta>

### BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

[...the same] thing, though through different media, or from their tendency toward different goals. For the Sun, being "essence," proceeds toward "intellect" through "life." Venus, being "intellect," proceeds through "life" toward an intellect different from itself. And Mercury, being "life," also proceeds toward "intellect." However, the intellect in which these three terminate is essential in the first case, intellectual in the second, and vital in the third. Because of this, they move with equal speed; although they appear to leave and precede one another, they ultimately end in the same state.

Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, however, may be considered to differ in dignity, and for this reason, they do not move with equal speed. Their varying speeds may also arise from the fact that they do not revolve through equal media. For example, if Saturn, being essence, should proceed immediately to essence, but Jupiter should proceed to it through intellect alone, and Mars through both intellect and life, then Saturn proceeds without a medium to essence, Jupiter through one, and Mars through two. Thus, they will not move with equal speed.

Among the planets, the first triad <note>A group of three; in Neoplatonism, gods and principles are often organized into triads.</note> is elevated to essence; the second is elevated to intellect; and the Moon is elevated to life, which encompasses all "generation" <note>The world of change, birth, and physical matter.</note> and extends as far as the deepest parts of the earth. These views are held by Porphyry and Theodorus in accordance with their own hypotheses. They assert that essence, life, and intellect are present everywhere, and that each of the gods participates in these three, though a different characteristic dominates in different divinities. They also argue that the energy of each god is different and that their spiritual elevation occurs through different media <note>original Greek: δι αλλων μεσων</note>.

The divine Iamblichus, however, does not accept the introduction of "epicycles" <note>Small circles whose centers move around the circumference of larger circles; a mathematical device used by ancient astronomers to explain planetary motion.</note>, viewing them as too mechanical and foreign to Plato’s meaning. Nor does he accept the concepts arising from essence, life, and intellect, which he sees as uselessly employing separations, entrances, exits, and complications, as if in a dream, and not conforming to Plato's work in any way. For where does Plato ever claim that the elevation to essence is through life, intellect, and essence? Where does he categorize Saturn according to essence, Jupiter according to intellect, and Mars according to life?

Rejecting these assertions, Iamblichus offers a simpler theory. He says that the Moon is positioned first in the region <note>original Greek: εις τον περι γην τοπον</note> around the earth, acting as the mother and the "nature" of generation. All things are influenced by her; they grow as she waxes and diminish as she wanes. He further states that the Sun is positioned above the Moon because the Sun clearly fills the Moon with power and acts as the father of generation. But above [the Sun]...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of why the Sun, Venus, and Mercury appear to move at the same speed. It explores their roles in the metaphysical hierarchy and how they contribute to the harmony of the cosmos.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

Next to the Sun are Venus and Mercury. These planets are "solar" in nature, working together with the Sun in the creation of the universe and contributing to the perfection of all things. For this reason, their course is as swift as that of the Sun, and they revolve around him because they share in the production of things. However, they are also contrary to him. This is not only because of their movement <note>original: lation</note> in their epicycles <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used in ancient astronomy to explain planetary orbits.</note>, as we have previously observed and as mathematicians say. Nor is it only because one is the cause of bringing hidden things into the light while the other is the cause of concealment, as astrologers strongly claim. They are contrary for these reasons, but also because of the divine power itself,¹ which we mentioned before. There is a certain wonderful and transcendant power in the Sun; because of this, it is unique and cannot be measured against other things. But the powers of Venus and Mercury provide balance <note>original: symmetry</note> and a good temperament through their illumination. By always revolving in conjunction with the Sun, they make the solar motion harmonious. Both planets are causes of communion: Mercury is shared in both day and night productions, possessing both masculine and feminine power, while Venus possesses a binding power that joins together things that are separated from each other.

You may also say that because the Sun does not slow down, speed up, or become stationary, while Mercury and Venus use advancing and receding motions and are sometimes stationary, they are assigned powers that appear contrary to the Sun. This is not true in the sense that they proceed similarly to the first three monads <note>Primary units of reality. In Neoplatonism, these refer to Beauty, Symmetry, and Truth.</note>, which are in the "vestibules of *the good*," as we have noted before. For the Sun, as we learn in the *Republic*, gives existence to light, which is the image of truth. But Venus is the cause of beauty in created things <note>original: generated natures</note>, which is an imitation of intelligible beauty. And Mercury is the cause of symmetry <note>Proportion or harmony.</note> to all things, existing as the rational principle <note>original: reason</note> for things in the physical world. For all symmetry proceeds according to one ratio and according to number, of which this god (Mercury) is the giver. 

Since those primary monads exist in relation to and in conjunction with each other, these planets naturally desire to be with each other and revolve together. On this account, they also surround and are surrounded by one another, through their cooperation in the divine work of crafting <note>original: demiurgic works</note> the universe. But if at one time they move swifter and at another slower—and when one² is moved swifter the others are not, nor when one is moved slower the rest are also slower—then those that are moved swifter are properly said to overtake <note>original: comprehend</note> those that move slower, and...

...and conversely, the latter are said to be enclosed <note>original: comprehended</note> by the former. Indeed, there is one single period (or cycle) for all things; but because the parts of these periods differ in speed—some being fast and others slow—they cause different planets at different times to overtake and be overtaken by each other, according to the different stages of their cycles. 

Therefore, from these points and from what was said previously, we can conclude that, according to Plato, the motion of the sphere of the fixed stars <note>original: inerratic sphere</note> is single and uniform,¹ but the motions of the seven planets are uniform in themselves, yet appear irregular <note>original: anomalous</note> when compared to each other—except for three of them that move at the same speed. For before Plato introduced the seven planets, he stated that their circles were equally swift. Socrates demonstrates that the motion of each is uniform in the *Republic* when he says that a Siren <note>In Plato’s "Myth of Er," a Siren sits atop each of the eight celestial spheres, singing a single note to create the "music of the spheres."</note> presides over the eight circles, uttering one voice in one tone; this shows that a uniform motion is common to all of them. 

The seven planets, however, move around their own centers and also through the depth of their spheres. Both the other four planets and the first three overtake and are overtaken by each other because of the inequality of their specific motions. If they moved simply as spheres with uniform speed, they would never experience this; instead, they would always maintain the same distance from one another. This is why Plato says they proceed through the heavens with changes <note>original: mutations</note> in their motions.

Therefore, above this harmonious triad—which is formed by Venus uniting and leading into communion the work of Mercury (which is relaxed in nature) and the work of the Sun (which possesses intense power)—there is another triad, consisting of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars. Saturn and Mars are the extremes and are opposites: Saturn is the cause of binding, while Mars is the cause of division; one causes cold, while the other causes heat. Jupiter is placed in the middle and brings the creative <note>original: demiurgic</note> productions of Saturn and Mars into an excellent balance <note>original: temperament</note>. 

However, if you wish to examine the middle position of the Sun in another way, imagine two groups of five <note>original: pentads</note> on each side of him: those below the Moon, and the group of four <note>original: tetractys</note> elements. Do this so that you may understand that the heavenly <note>original: etherial</note> nature is different from what is strictly called "air," or so that you may also include the nature of earthly fire <note>original: sublunary fire</note>. This fire helps manage the natures of all the elements, moves all things, and stimulates their growth. For whatever lacks fire is dead, since extreme cooling <note>original: refrigeration</note> is the opposite of life. But above the Sun are the governors of the...

...the entire realm of generation <note>The physical world of birth, death, and change.</note> shares certain qualities that neither the Sun nor the Moon possesses: namely, forward and backward <note>original: "advancing and receding"</note> motions. Through these motions, the nature of sublunary <note>Earthly things existing below the sphere of the moon.</note> substances is changed in every possible way by the adding and taking away, and the increasing and decreasing, of generative powers, of life, and of their very essence. 

The Sun, however, is positioned in the very center <note>In the Platonic system, the Sun is placed in the middle of the seven planetary spheres.</note>. He brings to completion the works of the Gods who come before him, while he activates, revives, and variously alters the powers that come after him. *Therefore, the theologian <note>Proclus usually refers to Orpheus as "the theologian."</note> calls him the guardian of the universe. The theologian assigns to him creative <note>original: demiurgic</note>, pure, soul-lifting <note>original: elevating</note>, perfecting, and many other cleansing <note>original: cathartic</note> and separating powers. By these powers, as he revolves perpetually, the Sun brings order to the universe.*

> "Regarding the other stars, if anyone should wish to investigate the reasons why the Creator <note>original: Demiurgus</note> established them all, the effort would be greater than the discussion for which they were introduced. Perhaps we will discuss these things later when we have time, in the manner they deserve."

By the *other stars*, it is clear that Plato means Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. The word *established* shows us that their creation <note>original: fabrication</note> is eternal and indestructible. However, if you read it as *they established* <note>original: ἱδρύσαντο (hidrusanto)</note>—as found in some manuscripts—this suggests that the universe was created and decorated by both the Creator and other divine causes. 

A little earlier, Plato said that the divinity distributed the seven celestial bodies and the cycle of the "Circle of the Different" <note>The plane of the ecliptic where the planets move, as opposed to the "Circle of the Same" or the fixed stars.</note> in an orderly way. In addition to this, he distributed the individual souls of the stars, which he called "circulations." According to the reading *they established*, these stars were created by all the divine causes working together with the Creator. He made the entire world into a statue and placed the statues of the individual <note>original: partial</note> Gods within it. 

At this point, it is necessary to remember what we usually say about the order of all things in the world: the sphere of the fixed stars <note>original: inerratic sphere</note> is the cause of constant, unchanging existence for all things. Of the triad <note>A group of three.</note> below it—Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars—the first (Saturn) is the cause of connection, the second (Jupiter) is the cause of symmetry, and the third (Mars) is the cause of separation. Furthermore, the Moon is a single unit <note>original: monad</note>, the cause of all birth and decay <note>original: generation and corruption</note>. But the elements involved in birth form a triad under...

...this monad <note>original: monad; refers here to a single organizing principle or "oneness."</note>. The intermediate parts <note>original: media</note> between this group of three planets and the Moon are the planets that revolve with equal speed. And the Sun, indeed, reveals truth into light, as we have frequently said. But Venus reveals beauty; and Mercury reveals the balance <note>original: symmetry</note> of rational principles, according to the analogy¹ of the unities in the entrance of *the Good*. 

If you wish, you might also say that among the beneficial planets, the Moon is the cause of nature for mortals, being herself the visible image of the source-nature <note>original: fontal nature</note>. But the Sun is the Creator <note>original: Demiurgus</note> of everything perceived by the senses, because he is the cause of sight and visibility. Mercury is the cause of the motions of the imagination <note>original: phantasy</note>; for the Sun is the producing cause of the essence of imagination itself, insofar as sense and imagination are one. But Venus is the cause of desiring appetites <note>original: epithymetic; referring to the lowest part of the soul concerned with physical needs</note>; and Mars is the cause of the spirited impulses <note>original: irascible; referring to the part of the soul concerned with anger, courage, and pride</note> that are according to nature. Of all vital powers, however, Jupiter is the common cause; but of all cognitive <note>original: gnostic</note> powers, Saturn is the cause. For all irrational forms are divided among these. Therefore, the causes of these powers are previously contained within the celestial natures.

Someone, however, might reasonably wonder from what has been said where Plato places the soul of the fixed sphere <note>original: inerratic sphere; the outermost sphere of the universe where the stars do not wander</note>. One might fear that he would make the World Soul the same as the soul of that specific sphere, as Aristotle later did. For we have the individual souls of the stars through the previously mentioned orbits, and a little further on, Plato speaks about them. For he says that, being bound with living <note>original: animated</note> bonds, they became living beings. 

May we not say, therefore, that as he places twofold circles and twofold orbits in the whole soul of the universe, he also gives existence to twofold souls along with them? One is the soul of the fixed sphere, and the other is the soul of the entire planetary sphere, acting as one orbit. And again, assuming seven circles within the circle of the *Other* <note>original: different</note>, he had seven souls along with them, carried as if in vehicles in the seven spheres. For the life <note>original: animation</note> just now described was not of the spheres themselves. Hence, in what he said regarding the fixed sphere, he mentioned the life of the stars, but omitted the life of the entire spheres, as they are included in the circles of the whole soul. 

Because of the style of discussion usual among the ancients, he omits the detailed explanation of the various levels of life. For universal life is one thing; that which follows this, which is "universal-partial" life, is another; "partial-universal" life is another; and the last of all is "partial" life <note>Proclus is describing a hierarchy of souls, from the World Soul down to individual human souls</note>. According to all these forms of life, the whole world and its parts are living beings. It might also be said that Timaeus, having heard Socrates discuss these levels of life in detail the day before, felt that a specific elaboration of them would be redundant.

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

Socrates, therefore, placed souls which he called Sirens over the eight whirls <term>original: whirls; the rotating concentric spheres of the cosmos</term>. And again, he places one soul over the fixed <term>original: inerratic; referring to the sphere of the stars that do not "wander" like planets</term> portion of the world; one over the whole planetary region; and one over the whole heaven. In doing this, he reveals the specific souls of all these regions. He animates the fixed sphere in two ways: first as a single circle with a motion opposite to that of the seven planetary circles, and second as a sphere that contains the multitude of the fixed stars, being a "universal world" that is also "partial" <note>This refers to the idea that the sphere is a whole entity but also a specific part of the greater universe.</note>. This is sufficient as an answer to that specific doubt. However, the reason why Plato considers a further discussion of the stars to be unnecessary is clear: his goal was simply to show what "secondary time" is, and how and from where it is perfectly achieved.

> "When, therefore, each of the natures necessary for the joint creation of time had reached a local motion suited to its condition, and they became living beings through the connecting power of vital bonds, they then learned their prescribed order."

What the animation of the bodies of the seven "world-rulers" <term>original: cosmocrators; the planetary gods who govern the physical world</term> is, and what their order is, has already been shown. But Plato uses these words to explain to those capable of understanding him how each of them is a living being, how each is suspended from a more divine soul, and what each contributes to the perfection of the universe. 

Each of them is assigned an appropriate life and motion. Since the sacred law of the Creator <term>original: demiurgic; relating to the Demiurge or Divine Craftsman</term> distributes to every mortal nature that which is suited to it, what shall we say concerning the leaders and rulers of the universe? Must it not be that they receive from the Father <note>The "Father" here refers to the Demiurge, the creator of the world.</note> what is adapted to them and what constitutes their "good"? Being radiant with beauty, they not only cooperate with the Father in the generation of time, but they also lead and govern the entire world. 

How is it possible that in speaking this way about them, we should not be speaking correctly? In addition to these things, they do not only receive the beautiful and the good from the creative source <term>original: demiurgic monad</term>; because they are "self-moving," they also impart these qualities to themselves. They begin the gift of "good" from within themselves. Plato indicates this when he says "*that each of them arrived at a local motion adapted to its condition*." This means each defines for itself the measure of life, order, and motion it is assigned in the universe. 

Each of the seven celestial bodies has a twofold life: one is inseparable from the body, while the other is separable. One life is intellectual and established within itself in a leading and ruling manner. The other life is distributed throughout the body, which it contains and moves. According to this second kind of life, each is a living being <note>original: animal; in the classical sense of "anima" or a soul-bearing creature</note>, but according to the first kind...

...a God. Since this is the case, Plato separates these two things. He considers the divine and intellectual soul—which never departs from the realm of pure intelligibles—as one thing. But the "animal" [the celestial body] which is suspended from this soul, receives its life *from* it, and is its image, he considers as another. He says **"that being bound with vital bonds, they became animals, and learned their prescribed order."** For a divine soul learns the creator's <note>original: demiurgic</note> will and understands the works of the Father <note>original: Proclus notes that in the Greek text, "father" (patros) should be read instead of "the whole" (pantos)</note>. It also cooperates with him in the production of worldly <note>original: mundane</note> natures by perceiving him through the intellect and being filled by him with divine powers. For it is not possible for either an intellect or a soul to provide for the whole universe in a transcendent <note>original: exempt; Proclus notes the Greek should be read as "exeremenos" (transcendent) rather than "exertemenos" (suspended)</note> manner in any other way than by participating in divinity and through a divinely-inspired life.

Their cooperation, therefore, in the production of time shows that they are assigned a secondary power in the creation <note>original: fabrication</note> of it; their Father possesses the primary power. For he generates the entirety of time, but they produce the parts that make up time along with him. The cycles <note>original: periods</note> of these stars are the parts of the whole of time, just as they were created as parts of the world. 

But the "animal bound with vital bonds" is the animated body, which receives life from the soul assigned to it according to the creator's <note>original: demiurgic</note> distributions. For if in our case the "animal" is different from the "man"—if the visible Socrates is one thing, but the true Socrates another—this is even more true for the Sun and Jupiter [as distinct from their visible orbs], which consist of both body and soul. 

Hence, Socrates in the *Phaedrus* criticizes those who claim that a divine animal consists merely of body and soul. "For out of ignorance, and without sufficiently understanding," he says, "we imagine a God to be an immortal animal that has a soul and a body, and these are joined together <note>original: connascent</note> through the whole of time." 

And if it is necessary to speak what appears to me to be the truth: 
1. The unity within each being—which is the unspeakable participation in the fountain of all "unical" numbers <term>unical numbers: the "henads" or divine unities that precede all other numbers and forms</term>—is *primarily* a God. 
2. But *secondarily*, it is the Intellect, which contains everything in a stable <note>original: Proclus notes the Greek should be "monimos" (stably) rather than "omonymos" (homonymously)</note>, uniform, and unchanging way. 
3. And *in the third place*, it is the Soul, which is filled by the Intellect and unfolds the Intellect's single, unified understanding. 

The first of these is truly a God; the second is most divine; and the third is likewise divine, but it illuminates the "animal" [the celestial body] with the specific quality of deity. According to this, the animal is also divine, being bound with vital bonds—which you may say are life-giving, creative, and unbreakable bonds, as Timaeus says further on. For the divine bodies are completely bound within souls; they are contained by and established in them. This "binding" also indicates that the bodies are held stably and unchangeably within the souls, and the undis- <meta>catchword: undis-</meta>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s "Timaeus," specifically examining how the celestial bodies (the planets and stars) act as "joint-creators" of time. # PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

...joined communion of these bodies with souls. Divine bodies, however, being as they are, cooperate with the Creator <note>original: Demiurgus</note> in the production of time. They call forth the unified and invisible power of time and allow it to progress into the world, which brings many temporal measures into the light. Because of this, the whole of time reaches its completion, imitating the time that consists of numbering, since time itself consists of being numbered. In short, it becomes what it is from many numbers, so that it may be similar to that which is truly "total time," which encompasses all cyclical restoration numbers <term>apocatastatic numbers; these refer to the numbers that mark the completion of a cosmic cycle or the return of planets to their original positions</term>. The *cooperative creation* <note>original: joint fabrication</note>, therefore, indicates a production that proceeds to its end and represents a perfect energy.

> “According to the angled motion <term>oblique lation</term> of the circle of the *different*, which moves under the influence of the circle of *the same*, these orbs should—by their revolution—form partly a *larger* and partly a *smaller* circle; and that the orb which formed a *smaller* circle should revolve *faster*, but that which produced a *larger* circle should be *slower*.”

You may say that the angled motion <note>original: oblique lation</note> of the circle of the *different* signifies a motion following the tilt of the zodiac. For the motion of the planets follows the poles of the zodiac—to speak mathematically. Such an explanation should not be dismissed by those who discuss the celestial bodies. 

Or, according to a more inward understanding of the matter, you may say that this tilt manifests the cause of "coming-to-be" <note>original: generation</note> and the change <note>original: mutation</note> which exists beforehand in the celestial orbs. For "coming-to-be" participates in difference and variety from the revolution of the circle of the *different* (meaning from the orbits of the planets); but it participates in sameness and a state of being which is always the same from the circle of *the same* (or the fixed sphere of stars <term>inerratic sphere</term>), as Aristotle also says. 

For if only the circle of *the same* existed, there would be no change or coming-to-be; instead, all things would be uniform and, being always generated, would remain invariably the same. And if only the circle of the *different* existed, all things would lack stability and would be in continual motion. Therefore, in order that there may be both permanence and motion—and that this whole may be, as it is said, an "unchanging change" and a "motionless motion"—the universe has both of these cycles. 

The variety of "coming-to-be" becomes apparent through the cycle of the circle of the *different*, while connection <note>original: communion</note> and immutability are seen through the circle of *the same*. But of these again, one is achieved through the "soul’s circle of sameness" and the other through the "soul’s circle of difference." And of these also, one is through intellectual sameness, but the other through the Creator's <note>original: demiurgic</note> difference. And of these last, the one is through intellectual—

# BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 235

...intelligible boundary, but the other through intelligible infinity. In this manner, therefore, the *obliquity* <term>the tilt of the planetary orbits relative to the celestial equator</term> must be understood.

And here you may see what the difference is, as delivered by Plato, between the movement <note>original: psychical lation</note> of the *circle of difference* belonging to the soul and that belonging to the body. For he calls the former *straight*, but the latter *oblique*. The former is pure and unyielding <note>original: undefiled and inflexible</note>, but the latter directly governs the variety of generated natures; it has a visible variation <note>original: inequability</note> and a certain position and relationship with respect to the universe. 

Because the revolution of the circle of the *different* is like this, it proceeds <note>original Greek: πρόεισι (proeisi). The translator notes that the original Greek text likely meant "proceeds" rather than simply "is."</note> through the circle of the *same* and is governed by it. It is moved by invisible causes and by the unchanging <note>original: inerratic</note> sphere itself. Or rather, it receives its motive powers through that sphere and is governed by it because it is turned <note>original: convolved</note> according to the single, unchanging motion of that sphere. This is the mathematical explanation. 

But in another sense, you may say that the nature of "the same" and "the similar" has dominion so that the world may be one; so that all things may be as eternal as possible; and so that the world may imitate the "Living Being itself" <term>the Intelligible Paradigm or the "Animal itself," the perfect model upon which the physical world is based</term>, in which all things have an eternal existence. For if the circle of the *different* had dominion over the circle of the *same*, there would be less of the immutable than of the mutable in the universe, and the world would not receive all the eternity of which it is capable. In that case, it would be less similar to the "Living Being itself." Therefore, the movement <note>original: lation</note> of the circle of the *different*, being governed by the movement of the circle of the *same*, proceeds <note>original Greek: πρόεισι (proeisi)</note> within it, circulates through its inner curve, and revolves together with it.

> “And with respect to the seven bodies, some of them being slower and others swifter; those that revolve in a smaller circle revolve more swiftly; but Saturn, revolving in a larger circle, moves more slowly.” <note>original Greek: κινειται τα επτα σωματα... (kinetai ta hepta somata...). This portion of the text was missing from many older printed editions and the Latin translation by Marsilio Ficino.</note>

Plato says this while looking at the cosmic restorations <term>apocatastases; the points at which planets return to their original relative positions</term> of the planets. Hence, he says that they revolve swifter or slower, rather than simply stating they move swifter but revolve slower. For when the ratio of circle to circle is the same as the ratio of time to time, then the...

<summary>Proclus explains that the "Circle of the Same" (the fixed stars) governs the "Circle of the Different" (the planets) to maintain cosmic eternity and order. He also introduces Plato's observation that planets in smaller orbits move faster than those in larger orbits, like Saturn.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of celestial mechanics in Proclus's commentary on Plato's "Timaeus," specifically focusing on the mathematical relationship between the size of a planet's orbit (its circle), the time it takes to complete a revolution, and its resulting speed.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

Bodies in motion are equally swift when their distances and times are proportional. For example, let one circle be double the size of another, and the time taken for its revolution be double the time of the other. In this case, the larger circle—moving in double the time—will cover a distance equal to the smaller circle's entire orbit in exactly the same amount of time the smaller one takes to cover its own. Therefore, they are equally swift. For things are considered equally swift when they move over the same distance in the same amount of time. 

But when the ratio of one circle's size to another is greater than the ratio of their revolution times, the motion of the larger circle is faster. Let us assume this is the case,<sup>1</sup> and let the ratio of circle to circle be the same as the ratio of time to a specific duration. This duration will be shorter than the first time mentioned, because the same distance has a greater ratio to a smaller time. Therefore, the larger circle will pass over the same distance as the smaller circle in this shorter duration. As has been demonstrated, if the ratio of circles is equal to the ratio of times, the motion of the smaller is equal in speed to the larger. However, the motion of the smaller circle was originally performed in more time than this new duration. Since the same distance is covered by one circle in more time and by the other in less, the motion of the smaller circle is slower than that of the larger one. 

Conversely, if the ratio of one circle to another is less than the ratio of their times, the motion of the larger circle will be slower than that of the smaller. If you set the ratio of circle to circle equal to the ratio of time to a second duration, you will find that duration to be longer. A value has a smaller ratio when compared to a larger number. Thus, the larger circle will take more time to cover the same distance as the smaller circle, and it is therefore slower. 

Because these principles hold true, Plato does not at this point investigate the specific conditions of the planets regarding their swiftness and slowness, as that would require a much more extensive study. Instead, he adds that there is a different <term>apocatastasis</term> <note>original: apocatastasis; the periodic return of a celestial body to its original starting position</note> for different planets—some are slower and others are faster. This variation in speed is caused either by the irregular <note>original: anomalous</note> nature of their motions or, more accurately, by the fact that the stars<sup>2</sup> are all moving with equal speed <note>original: celerity</note>, but the ratio of their orbits differs from the ratio of their orbital times.

In short, this much should be understood concerning the motion of the stars: they do not simply have a rolling motion on their spheres, for such motion is not suited to spherical bodies. Nor do they remain fixed in one place, for then how would they be part of a circular system? Instead, they rotate around their own centers, imitating the rotation of the universe itself, according to Plato's view. This occurs without the need for the complex theories <note>original: hypotheses</note> used by astronomers, as I have noted before. For if Plato believes that the fixed stars move in this way, through an imitation of the—

Since the universe moves in this way, he will certainly grant that those stars assigned to govern the universe and held in high honor imitate the world as a whole. Therefore, these stars rotate around their own centers; meanwhile, the spheres that contain them—acting as moving rulers—carry them along, some faster and some slower. However, Plato assigns them a more complex motion because they are intermediaries <note>original: "media"</note> between things that move in a straight line and things that only move in a circle. He moves each of them around its own center and through its specific sphere so that they may rise high or come near the earth and revolve toward the northern and southern regions. Because of these various movements, they are considered lower than the fixed stars, even though they are otherwise granted a free status and power.

> “But because of the motion <term>motion</term> <note>original: "lation," from the Latin "latio," meaning movement or carrying.</note> of the circle of the 'Same,' the orbits that contain them appear to be overtaken because of the revolution of the spheres that move more slowly. For all their circles revolve with a spiral motion because they are moving in two opposite directions at the same time. Consequently, the sphere that has the slowest revolution appears nearest to the sphere that moves in the opposite direction, which is the swiftest of all the spheres.”

Revolution, as we have frequently observed, is twofold: one moves from the east to the west, and the other from the west to the east. Anyone who understands both of these revolutions will know the difference between the common motion of the heavens and the unique motion of the individual stars, as well as which of them move faster or slower. He will look to their unique motions and realize that those moving forward through the zodiac <term>moving forward</term> <note>original: "in consequentia"; refers to the natural West-to-East motion of planets through the constellations.</note> are the swiftest. Thus, he will not mistakenly believe that Saturn is faster than the Moon. Instead, he will see that the Moon moves further toward the east; Saturn is overtaken <note>original: "comprehended"</note>, while the Moon does the overtaking.

However, a person who imagines there is only one simple motion for all stars (from east to west) will see Saturn and the Moon together at one time, but later see Saturn further to the west as if it had moved a greater distance. Such a person will claim the Moon is being overtaken by Saturn—in other words, that the faster is being overtaken by the slower. This error arises from only looking at the period of the circle of the "Same" <note>In Plato's cosmology, the "Circle of the Same" is the outermost sphere of fixed stars that rotates daily from East to West.</note>, which possesses great power and strength. Such people fail to consider the unique motions of the planets and do not perceive that the planets do not transition backward <term>moving backward</term> <note>original: "in antecedentia"; refers to the apparent East-to-West motion.</note>, but forward through the zodiac. In asserting this, the "Athenian Guest" <note>A character in Plato’s "Laws" who is often identified with Plato himself.</note> blames the common people and those ignorant of astronomy. “For it is disgraceful,” he says, “if we watch a racecourse <note>original: "stadium"</note> and do not know which of the racers runs faster and which...

For the bodies that revolve with the greatest speed <term>speed</term> <note>original: "celerity"</note> appear to be overtaken <note>original: "comprehended"</note> by those that revolve more slowly; in reality, however, those who can observe their actual motion will see that they are the ones overtaking the others. But the movement <term>movement</term> <note>original: "lation," from the Latin *latio*, meaning the act of carrying or movement.</note> of the circle of *the Same* <note>The circle of "the Same" refers to the sphere of the fixed stars, which moves from east to west.</note>, overcoming the body nearest to it, causes that body to appear most rapid in its motion. The body nearest to it is the one that is the least distant from it.

For example, if the Moon and Saturn happened to be near the *Cor Leonis* <note>original: "Cor Leonis," the "Heart of the Lion," known today as the star Regulus.</note>; then the Moon, moving with its own unique motion, will move away from this fixed star; Saturn, however, will be seen in roughly the same place for many nights. The astronomer, therefore, knows that the Moon moves away from this star more rapidly because of the motion of the *Cor Leonis* in the order of the zodiac signs <note>original: "in consequentia," meaning movement in the natural order of the zodiac signs, from west to east.</note>. But someone ignorant of astronomy will imagine that the Moon and Saturn, being moved with the universe in the same direction, do not complete their cycles <term>cycles</term> <note>original: "apocatastases," referring to the restoration of a planet to its original starting position.</note> in the same way. They might think that one, being swifter, arrives in the west before the other, while the other, being slower, arrives further to the west. This would be the conclusion according to common opinion. However, it might actually be true that Saturn is the swifter if—as we noted before—the ratio of Saturn's orbit to the Moon's orbit is greater than the ratio of the time it takes for one to complete its cycle compared to the other. For the body closer to the sphere of the fixed stars will be swifter, for the reasons already mentioned.

But what is the meaning of the claim that the planets "*revolve with a spiral motion, because they are moved in two opposite directions at the same time?*" And how can we accept the idea of "opposition" within a circular motion? The fact that each planet is moved by two local motions is not the cause of the spiral motion; rather, this arises because they move in the oblique circle (that is, the zodiac) toward the celestial equator <term>celestial equator</term> <note>original: "equinoctial."</note>. Thus, if someone supposes that the Sun moves with the universe toward the equator, the cause of this would not be a spiral motion, even though there is a counter-rotation <note>original: "anti-circulation."</note>. Nor should we simply admit that a motion contrary to a circular motion is a motion of a different kind. For many excellent arguments have been raised against that view. Therefore, might the phrase *moved at the same time in two opposite directions* mean that they are not only moving east and west at the same time, but also that they move in terms of latitude <note>original: "breadth"</note> and distance <note>original: "depth"</note>, becoming nearer to or farther from the earth, and moving more to the north or to the south? For these two motions, in conjunction with the overall movement <note>original: "lation"</note>...

The spiral motion is likewise adapted to the planets, which are intermediaries <term>media</term> between the fixed stars and sublunary <note>sublunary: literally "below the moon," referring to the Earthly realm where things are subject to change and decay.</note> bodies. The fixed stars move according to a circle alone, while sublunary bodies move in straight lines. Again, it is natural for the planets, being intermediaries, to move both unevenly and uniformly according to their length, breadth, and depth. This is so that they may provide the models <term>paradigms</term> for the natures that move in all various ways coming after them, and may imitate through their circular motion the uniform existence of the natures that came before them. These things, therefore, are manifest to every one.

It is, however, not at all surprising that opposition <term>contrariety</term> should exist in the heavens prior to the oppositions found in the revolution of the circle of the *Different* <note>In the Timaeus, the "Circle of the Different" refers to the ecliptic or the orbital plane of the planets.</note>. In the very categories of being, there is said to be an opposition between sameness and difference, motion and stability, and in the principles of these themselves: bound and infinity. For these are opposites because, at their furthest points, there is a certain conflict and disagreement, even though they always possess the power of acting together. It is by no means surprising, therefore, that there should also be an opposition of these motions in the heavens. For we are not now discussing those opposites which are hostile to and destructive of each other; those are physical and divisible natures. Instead, we mean simply those which cause opposites, and those which are most distant from each other. This is also a certain mode of opposition in nature; for the fact that the apparent motion of the heavenly bodies is one thing, and their true motion another, indicates the prior existence of "non-being" and its intertwining with "being." 

The figure of the spiral, likewise, is no pointless or accidental thing; it completes the middle ground between bodies that move in straight lines and those that move in a circle. For the circle alone, as we have said, belongs to the sphere of the fixed stars <term>inerratic sphere</term>, while the straight line belongs to the realm of physical change <term>generation</term>. The spiral exists in the planetary region, as it is a mixture of the circumference and the straight line. The motions according to breadth and depth are the immediate causes and models for motions in the sublunary region—namely, upward, downward, and diagonal motions. Perhaps likewise the theurgist <note>Julian the Theurgist (2nd century AD), traditional author of the *Chaldean Oracles*, who described Time as having a spiral, youthful, and aged character.</note> Julian, in honoring Time as having a spiral form and as being both young and old, directed his attention to this, believing that the periods of time were especially to be understood through the motion of the planets. This concludes our discussion on these particulars. But Plato adds the following in the next section:

> "...in order that the motion of the eight revolutions might be visible, the divinity ignited a light—which we now call the Sun—in the second orbit from the earth. Plato here identifies the single governing cause for the creation of visible time. Just as the Demiurge <note>Demiurge: The "Craftsman" or creator deity in Platonic philosophy who shapes the material world based on eternal forms.</note> established invisible time, the Sun produces the time that is visible and which measures the motion of physical bodies. Through its light, the Sun brings every interval of time into visibility, defines all cycles, and reveals the measurements for the restoration of things to their original state. <note>original: "restitutions of things to their pristine state" refers to the "Great Year," the cycle after which all planets return to the same relative positions.</note> Therefore, the Sun is deservedly a clear measure, as it especially reveals the progression <note>original: Greek *periodon* (cycle) should be read as *proodon* (progression).</note> of time according to number throughout the universe. It has a more precise cycle than that of the five planets, as its motions are less irregular than theirs. It is also more precise than the Moon, because the Sun always ends its movements to the north and the south at the exact same points. Because it has a more precise cycle, it is rightfully the "measure of measures"; it defines <note>original: Greek *gnōrizein* (to know) should be read as *horizein* (to bound or define).</note> the periodic measures of the other planets and the speed of their motions relative to one another. It also imitates the everlasting stability of eternity to a greater degree by always revolving in the same manner. In this way, the Sun differs from the planets.

The Sun is also a more obvious measure than the measure of the sphere of fixed stars <note>original: "inerratic sphere," meaning the stars that do not "wander" like planets.</note>. Although the sphere of stars has its own appropriate measure, its own interval, and one unchanging number for its specific motion, the light of the Sun makes this measure and the entire unfolding of visible time clear and known. This is why Plato says, "*In order that there might be a certain conspicuous measure.*" For while there is a certain measure in the other planets, it is not clear or obvious. But the Sun reveals both time and other intellectual realities to the light. However, you must not conclude from this that the Sun's light was created solely for the sake of measurement. How could the whole exist for the sake of its parts? How could governing natures exist for the sake of those they rule, or eternal things for the sake of those that decay? Rather, we should say that light, possessing a power of manifestation, unfolds the whole of time and calls forth its...

# BOOK IV.] THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO.

This supermundane monad <note>monad: A single, indivisible source or unit of being; here, the Sun is the singular principle of measurement.</note> acts as a single measure for the cycles of physical bodies. This makes time something that can be perceived by the senses. Thus, it is the light of the Sun that allows everything in motion to have a clear and obvious measurement. This is its primary benefit to the universe. After benefiting the universe as a whole, it also benefits individual parts in a secondary way. It provides the birth of number and measurement to those beings capable of participating in them. While irrational beings lack these, the various classes of daemons <note>daemons: In Greek philosophy, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern malevolent sense.</note>—who follow the cycles of the Gods and of humans—do participate in them. 

The supply of goodness through the solar light begins from the highest realms and descends down to individual parts. If you wish to speak of invisible things starting from what is visible, the Sun's light gives splendor to the entire world; it makes the physical nature divine and fills it entirely with life. It leads souls through undefiled light, giving them a pure and uplifting power, and it governs the world through its rays. It also fills souls with empyrean <note>empyrean: Relating to the highest part of heaven, often associated with pure fire and light.</note> fruits. For the order of the Sun is derived from higher, supermundane <note>supermundane: Existing above or beyond the physical world.</note> realms. Because of this, Plato does not describe the Sun as being physically manufactured here; instead, he says the Demiurge <note>Demiurge: The "Craftsman" or creator deity who shapes the material world according to eternal forms.</note> "enkindled" it, giving it existence from his own essence and releasing a life from the solar fountain that extends through space and is continually renewed. *This is also asserted by theologians regarding the firmaments that exist beyond our world.*

For this reason, it seems to me that Plato describes a two-fold creation of the Sun. One occurs alongside the seven governors of the world <note>the seven governors: The seven classical "planets" known to the ancients: the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> when the Demiurge fashions their bodies and places them in their orbits. The other creation occurs through the "enkindling" of light, through which he gives the Sun a power that is beyond the physical world. It is one thing to create the physical mass of the Sun itself, and quite another to create it with a ruling characteristic, by which the Sun is called the king of all visible nature and is established as a symbol of the "One" or the "Fountain of Good." 

Just as this fountain—being superior to the essence of things that can be understood by the mind—illuminates both the mind and those intelligible things, so too the Sun—being superior to visible nature—illuminates both what is seen and the power of sight. But if the Sun is beyond a visible essence, it must have a nature that exists beyond the world. For the world is visible and tangible, and has a physical body. Therefore, we must view the Sun in two ways: as one of the seven planets, and as the leader of all things; and as both of this world and beyond it. In this second role, the Sun brilliantly radiates a divine light. For in the same way that the "Good" luminously radiates truth, which makes the higher intellectual orders divine; and as Phanes <note>Phanes: In Orphic mythology, the first-born god of light and creation who emerged from the cosmic egg.</note> in the teachings of Orpheus sends out a light that fills all the intellectual Gods with intelligence; and as Jupiter enkindles an intellectual and de-

...demiurgic light <note>demiurgic: Relating to the Demiurge, the divine craftsman or creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy.</note> in all the supermundane <note>supermundane: Existing above or beyond the physical world.</note> Gods; thus the Sun also illuminates everything visible through this undefiled light. The cause that illuminates is always in a higher order than the natures being illuminated. For "the Good" is not just something to be understood by the mind, nor is Phanes <note>Phanes: An Orphic deity of light and generation, often identified as the first-born of the universe.</note> merely intellectual, nor is Jupiter <note>original: Jupiter; here referring to Zeus, the king of the gods who acts as the demiurge.</note> simply supermundane. Because of this reasoning, the Sun—being supermundane—emits the fountains of light. According to the most mystical doctrines, the entirety of the Sun belongs to the supermundane orders; for within those orders, there is a solar world and a total light, as the *Chaldean Oracles*^1 assert, which I am convinced is true. And that is enough concerning these matters.

However, we must return to the words of the text and explain them as follows: The phrase, “*in order that there might be a measure*,” does not refer to a humanly invented measure, but to that which itself measures and defines physical <note>original: corporeal</note> motions and produces visible time. The words, “*that the motion of the eight circulations might be manifest*,” refer to this same measure. This measure moves through and calculates the measurements belonging to the paths of the eight circulations <note>eight circulations: The orbits of the seven classical planets (including the Sun and Moon) and the sphere of the fixed stars.</note>. For we say that the common *apocatastasis* <note>original: apocatastasis; a Greek term meaning "restoration" or "reconstitution," referring here to the completion of a full cosmic cycle where all celestial bodies return to their original positions.</note> of the eight revolutions takes a specific number of years. 

We gain knowledge of the solar year through light. Through light, we know which part of the zodiac the Sun occupies, which part he leaves, and where he goes. Thus, by the movement of light, we also know the amount of time the Sun takes to pass through his own circle and complete his revolution, and how many years it takes for all the periods of the eight circles to be finished. Likewise, by this we are able to measure the solar period and the shared period of the other circulations, which is the same as measuring their joint restoration. 

Furthermore, the words, “*the divinity enkindled a light*,” show us the non-temporal *hypostasis* <note>original: hypostasis; the fundamental reality or underlying substance of a thing.</note> of light, which proceeds from an invisible cause and from the demiurgic essence <note>demiurgic essence: The fundamental nature of the divine creator.</note>. Again, the words, “*in order that the heaven, or world might in the most eminent degree become universally apparent*,” have the following cause. It is necessary for the whole world to be filled with solar light as much as possible. However, the mass of the earth is naturally dark. Therefore, it is necessary for the Sun to be nearer to the earth to relieve its darkness. For whatever is closer provides more light. And when the source of light is larger than the object being lit, it is able to share its light more extensively. But the words, “*in the most...*”

The phrase "to a supreme degree" signifies that the Sun illuminates all the world *as much as possible.* He is not able to illuminate the whole earth at once, but does so partially through his circular motion. In the shortest amount of time, however, he illuminates the whole earth at once according to the equinoctial circle <note>equinoctial circle: The celestial equator, the great circle of the celestial sphere in the same plane as Earth's equator.</note>. For when he rises and sets, giving light to more than half the earth, he illuminates the entire earth in this single circulation. 

But if by the word *heaven*, we understand that which moves in a circle, the Sun does not illuminate the whole of this at once either. For there are also shadows there, caused by the shading <note>original: obumbrations</note> of the stars and the Moon. Nothing in the world is free from shadow except the Sun, just as nothing in the physical world exists without matter. Only supermundane <note>supermundane: Existing above or beyond the physical world.</note> natures are without shadow and immaterial. Therefore, the Sun is truly shadowless and not subject to the processes of generation <note>term: generation—The physical realm of birth, death, and constant change, as opposed to the eternal, unchanging divine realm.</note>; all other bodies receive different additions of light at different times.

One might ask: why did the divinity not kindle a light in the first of the orbits starting from the earth? We reply that the brilliant splendor of the Sun is inherently too great for the realm of generation to handle directly. But the Moon, being a middle ground between the two and the first to receive the Sun's light, makes that light proportionate to the realms of generation. For the Moon, as Aristotle says, is like a lesser Sun. However, because it is located immediately above the realm of generation, it must not be the most splendid and luminous of bodies. For it is not appropriate for a body of that supreme kind to be so close to that which is obscure and dark; rather, that which is secondarily bright should be there. This secondary body always has its own proper light, but when participating in a superior light, it shows change <note>original: mutation</note>, and does so in an orderly manner. 

That which possesses arrangement and order is more excellent than that which is without order. Through this change, the Moon serves as the model <note>original: paradigm</note> for the very changeable nature that matter introduces to created things—just as the position of the earth introduces the absence of light. These subjects, however, allow for a much broader discussion.

But that the stars, and all of heaven, receive their light from the Sun may be easily understood. For when a common quality exists in many things, it comes from a single cause. It exists from that cause in one way as something separate <note>original: exempt</note>, but in another way as something coordinated within the system. This latter mode of the cause's existence is the one in which it primarily shares that single form. But that which shares primarily is that in which the form exists first, or especially. Therefore, if light exists especially in the Sun, this will be the primary light; and from this, the light in all other things will be derived. So much for this particular point. We have, however, shown the—

What Proclus demonstrates here—that all light in the physical world is derived from the Sun—completely refutes the common modern opinion that the fixed stars are actually other suns.</note>

<summary>Proclus argues that the Sun is the primary source of all light in the universe and that the Moon acts as a necessary intermediary to soften this light for the physical world. He disputes the idea that stars are independent suns, viewing them instead as participants in the Sun's primary light.</summary>

meaning of the words, “*that the heaven might in the most eminent degree become universally apparent.*” For if by *heaven* you understand that which revolves in a circle, the Sun does not always illuminate the whole of the Moon, but only during the time from the conjunction to the full moon. But if you understand by it the whole world, then, as we have said, the Sun only accurately illuminates the whole earth in one day when he is in the equinoctial circle <note>equinoctial circle: The celestial equator.</note>, and in rising and setting, is diametrically opposite to the earth. It remains, therefore, to see what the *number* is which is produced by the motion <note>original: lation</note> of the "Same" and the "Similar" <note>the Same and the Similar: Platonic terms referring to the celestial motions of the fixed stars (the Same) and the planets (the Other/Similar).</note>, through the protective oversight of day and night. This number then, is neither intellectual nor based on discursive reasoning <note>original: dianoetic</note>, but is based on opinion <note>original: doxastic</note>, providing a record of the numbers which pre-exist in the eternal Forms. For there are many differences in the many types of generated numbers. And just as we know the number of invisible time through reasoning, so by that which is based on opinion, we grasp the number of visible time.

<margin> [A vertical bracket marks this paragraph in the left margin.] </margin>

> “Night therefore, and Day were produced in this way, and because of these, the period of the one most wise circulation was completed. And the Month was produced when the Moon, having completed her circle, came into conjunction with the Sun. But the Year was produced when the Sun, in revolving, had completed his circle. A few people only, however, understand the periods of the other stars, give names to them, and measure them in relation to each other, regarding the numbers adapted to this purpose; so that, I might say, they do not know that time is actually the wanderings of these bodies, which employ motions <note>original: lations</note> infinite in multitude and admirably diversified.”

Through the generation of light, nights and days began their progression, and the smallest measure of time is divided by these intervals. For the period, he says, of the "one most wise circulation," is completed by night and day. The act of understanding <note>original: intellection</note> of the sphere of the fixed stars <note>original: inerratic sphere</note>, or the "circle of the Same," is the one most wise circulation; but the *period* of this circle is the actual physical rotation of that sphere. For "circulation" is both an energy and a period of time. The act of understanding, however, is of a more primary nature; the period is the effect of that understanding, imitating the divine circulation. This, then, is the span of day and night. By this measure, however, years and months are calculated. For we measure greater intervals by smaller ones; just as by years, the entire restorative <note>term: apocatastatic—The "Great Year" or cosmic cycle when all celestial bodies return to their original relative positions.</note> time of the universe is measured. It is likewise necessary to observe how the unique nature of these measures is a middle ground between the unified Forms and the forms which exist within the multitude of...

individuals. For some forms are indeed in one thing, yet not always in the same thing according to number, but in many things. However, a Year and a Month are always in one thing according to number, because of the mutual rotation of individuals (that is, the sun and moon) in a circle. One month succeeds another, and one year follows another; yet each cycle is always one. These things, therefore, do not require much discussion.

Perhaps, however, someone may doubt how Plato says that Night and Day formed the period of one "most wise circulation." For this is the very thing for which Aristotle accuses Plato: calling a circulation "time," even though Plato now adds time to the universe when it is in motion as being something different from that motion. But if the motion of the universe is different from the time of the universe, the motion of each body that moves in a circle must also be different from the periodic time of that motion. This, therefore, may be the cause of doubt in the words before us. 

Likewise, how is the period of the <term>sphere of fixed stars</term> <note>original: inerratic sphere</note> the swiftest, while the bodies nearer to it are slower according to their <term>restoration</term> <note>original: apocatastasis; the return of a celestial body to its original starting position in the sky</note> than those that are farther from it? 

In answer to the first doubt, it may be proper to say that "period" signifies two things: at one time it means motion itself, but at another, it means the measure and condition of motion. This is just as a *medimnus* <note>original: medimnus; an ancient Greek unit of dry volume, roughly 55 liters.</note> and a *cotyle* <note>original: cotyle; an ancient Greek unit of liquid volume, roughly half a pint.</note>, and other such measures, are named in two ways—both as the container and the amount. Hence, the period of the <term>sphere of fixed stars</term> must not be called its motion, but rather the temporal interval of that motion. 

It may also be said that when Plato calls the wanderings of the heavenly bodies "time," he means nothing else than that their periods *are* time. For these are things that are numbered. And time, as the philosophers also say, is that which is "numbered of motion." It is just as if one said, "those oxen are a number of such a size." For in this way, periods are time, being a number of a certain magnitude.

But in answer to the second doubt, it may be said that Plato is assuming the apparent <term>restoration</term> of the <term>sphere of fixed stars</term>, which creates the space of a day and night, since there is another true <term>restoration</term>. For the point which rises now does not rise at the same hour as the one following it, nor do the other points exist in a similar way; yet all of these contribute to the <term>restoration</term> of the <term>sphere of fixed stars</term>. Not all the points in that sphere, nor all the fixed stars, complete their <term>restorations</term> according to the same period. However, it is necessary that they should if we assume an accurate <term>restoration</term>, which takes place over a great length of time. For it is evident that all the stars in the <term>sphere of fixed stars</term> are moved by it and have <term>positions</term> <note>original: habitudes</note> relative to each other and to the sphere itself. These stars exist differently at different times and, along with these changes, have at different times a different <term>orbital motion</term> <note>original: lation</note> toward the centers; and...

### PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

It is also true that their <term>restoration</term> <note>original: apocatastasis; the return of a celestial body to its original starting position</note> to the exact same state in every respect is completed over a very long period of time.

Furthermore, one might also wonder why Plato calls the measure of the <term>movement</term> <note>original: lation</note> of the <term>sphere of fixed stars</term> <note>original: inerratic sphere</note> "Night and Day." For this measure is derived from above—from the one intelligible cause of the universe and from the first <term>model</term> <note>original: paradigm</note>. However, Night and Day as we know them exist in the <term>earthly realm</term> <note>original: sublunary region; the area below the moon</note>. 

In answer to this doubt, it may be said that the interval of time which exists primarily in the circulation of the sphere of fixed stars, along with the solar light, are what produce Day and Night. Therefore, the whole measure of time is defined by things that occur last and are known to us. For this specific space of night and day is one thing, while that which exists in invisible time is another. The former is merely the image and final result of the latter. 

According to <term>Orphic theology</term> <note>the mystical teachings attributed to the mythical poet Orpheus</note>, there are many levels of Night and Day: intelligible, intellectual, super-mundane, celestial, and earthly. Some of these exist prior to the <term>crafting of the world</term> <note>original: fabrication of things</note>, while others are included within it, and others proceed from it. Similarly, some are invisible while others are visible. This is also true for the Month and the Year: those that are invisible are of one kind—serving to measure, connect, and perfect the intellectual and physical cycles of the Sun and Moon—while the visible ones are of another kind, acting as the limit and measure of the sun's revolution. 

The same applies to the other Gods. For there is one invisible <term>number</term> <note>here meaning a mathematical or harmonic principle</note> belonging to Saturn and another visible one; and likewise, there are invisible and visible numbers for Mars, Jupiter, and Mercury. For the Month itself, and also the Year, which exist within each planetary cycle—being each a single unit and always the same—are Gods who unchangeably define the measure of motion. For how could these cycles always remain exactly the same unless they came from an unchangeable cause? From what else could the differences in their <term>restorations</term> <note>original: apocatastases</note> be derived, except from different unchangeable causes? And what produces this unceasing, infinite repetition, if not the infinite powers contained within the "Month" and the "Year"?

It must also be accepted that this entire series of time exists under one "First Time," which defines the cycle of a divinely generated (or perpetually circulating) nature. This First Time is itself "true number," as we have noted before. We must understand that the visible periods are derived from these invisible periods; the visible ones proceed according to the "thing being numbered" from the invisible ones, which are able to both count and generate them. Astronomy beautifully teaches all of this, apprehending <term>through reasoned opinion</term> <note>original: doxastically</note> the number of the periodic restorations of each body. It also compares the ratios of these periods to each other; for instance, observing that the cycle of Saturn is two and a half times as long as the cycle of Jupiter.

This also applies to the other planets. Since they each have different <term>restorations</term> <note>original: apocatastases; the return of a celestial body to its original starting position in the sky</note>, they maintain different ratios to one another. Ancient sacred traditions also revere those invisible cycles, which are the causes of the visible ones. These traditions provide the divine names of "Night" and "Day," as well as the causes that form them, the invocations used to reach them, and the divine manifestations of "Month" and "Year." Therefore, we should not look at these cycles superficially. Instead, we should view them as divine beings that the laws of sacred institutions and the oracles of Apollo command us to worship and honor with statues and sacrifices, as historical records tell us. When these deities are honored, humanity receives the benefits that come from the cycles of the seasons and other divinities. Conversely, neglecting their worship results in an unnatural state for everything on Earth.<gloss>1</gloss> Plato, likewise, in his work *The Laws*, declares that all of these—the Seasons, Years, and Months—are gods, just like the Stars and the Sun. We are not introducing a new idea by suggesting that we should focus on the invisible powers of these cycles before we look at their visible effects. This concludes our discussion on these points.

Let us, however, return to the text. Plato mentions "Night" before "Day" to symbolize the invisible and <term>intellectual</term> <note>pertaining to the realm of pure thought or divine intellect, rather than the physical world</note> measures of time. Common tradition also places Night before Day. This is why we use the term *<term>nycthemeron</term>* <note>original: nycthemeron; a 24-hour period consisting of one night and one day</note>, because in their primary causes, Night exists before Day.<gloss>2</gloss> Regarding the phrases "*thus*" and "*on account of these*": the word "*thus*" points to the cause that produces Night and Day—which is light acting together with the <term>sphere of fixed stars</term> <note>original: inerratic sphere; the outermost sphere of the heavens which was thought to be unmoving relative to the other stars</note>. The words "*on account of these*" indicate the final purpose: so that the 24-hour cycle of night and day can serve as a clear measure for all celestial movements. Plato calls "the one most wise circulation" the revolution of the <term>circle of the Same</term> <note>in Plato's cosmology, the outer sphere of the universe that represents eternal, unchanging reality</note>, because it is uniform, rooted in the divine intellect, and most closely resembles the permanence and sameness of pure intel-

> “At the same time, however, it is no less possible to conceive that the perfect number of time will then accomplish a perfect year when the speeds of all the eight cycles, being completed with reference to each other, shall reach a summit, as they are measured by the circle of that which exists according to the same and the similar.”

After the <term>Creator’s</term> <note>original: demiurgic; referring to the Demiurge or divine craftsman of the universe</note> generation of the spheres, the cycle of the seven bodies, their animation, and the order which the Father placed within them—and also after their various motions, the time measurements of their several periods, and the differences of their <term>restorations</term>—the discussion proceeds to the <term>singular unit</term> <note>original: monad</note> of time's many parts. This is the one number by which all motion is measured, under which all other measures are included, and according to which the entire life of the world, the diverse evolution of bodies, and the whole of the <term>soul's</term> <note>original: psychical</note> life are defined, in accordance with an all-perfect cycle.

Afterward, they add to these the <term>restorations</term> of Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn; and finally, they add the <term>restoration</term> of the <term>sphere of fixed stars</term> <note>original: inerratic sphere</note> to the one shared <term>restoration</term> of the planets. They speak in this manner if the <term>restoration</term> times compared with each other are primary numbers. But if they are not primary, then by assuming a common measure, they see how this measure fits into each of the given <term>restoration</term> times. However, it is not proper to examine the entire time of the world solely in this way. Instead, we should scientifically examine it through the intellect and the active processes of reason as a single number, a single unfolded power, and a single perfecting progression that extends throughout the entire life of the world. This progression reaches the end, returns to the beginning, and converges upon itself; for this reason, it makes the measured motion circular. For just as the <term>monad</term> <note>original: monad; the principle of unity or the number one</note> limits the infinity of numbers and encompasses the undefined nature of the <term>duad</term> <note>original: duad; the principle of duality or the number two</note> beforehand, so too does time measure the entire motion and join its end back to its beginning. 

Therefore, it is called a "number," and "perfect." For a month is a number, as is a year, but they are not perfect numbers because they are only parts of other numbers. But the time of the universe's full cycle is perfect because it is not a part of any other period; it is a whole, designed to imitate eternity. For eternity is primarily a state of wholeness. Eternity presents its entire wholeness to beings all at once, whereas time does so through extension. For temporal wholeness is an unfolding of the wholeness that remains concentrated in eternity. 

The entire time of the world, therefore, measures the single life of the universe, by which all the speeds of the celestial and <term>sublunary</term> <note>referring to the region below the moon, i.e., the Earth and its atmosphere</note> circles are concluded. For these circles also have periods that reach the peak of their restoration at the movement of the "circle of the same" <note>the celestial equator or the sphere of fixed stars</note>. These are referred to this circle as their starting principle, because it is the simplest of all. For these restorations are observed in relation to specific points on that circle. 

Thus, for instance, all of them complete their restoration at the equinoctial point¹ or at the summer tropic. Even if the joint restoration is not considered to happen at the exact same point, but rather in reference to it—for example, when rising or reaching its highest point—all will still have a configuration related to it. The current order of things is a specific restoration of all the heavenly bodies, though the alignment is not seen at a single point but in relation to the same point. However, there was a time when it occurred at a single, specific point; if this happens again, the entirety of time will reach its end. A specific restoration of this kind seems to have been mentioned. Thus, it is said that Cancer is the horoscope of the world, and this year is called "Cynic" <note>meaning "pertaining to the dog"</note>, or the Year of the Dog, because among the constellations, the bright star of the Dog <note>Sirius</note> rises together with Cancer. > "Therefore, in accordance with and for the sake of these things, those stars that travel through the heavens in revolutions were created, so that this universe might most closely resemble the perfect and <term>intelligible animal</term> <note>original: intelligible animal; the ideal "Living Being" or Form that contains all other life forms within it</note> by imitating an eternal nature. Other forms were indeed crafted up until the creation of time, according to the likeness of that which they were modeled after."

It is evident from what has been said that the world became more perfect through the creation of time, imitating the all-perfect Living Being according to the principle of eternity. We also see that physical generation derived its existence through the <term>motion</term> <note>original: lation; the movement or orbital path of a heavenly body</note> of the seven <term>world-rulers</term> <note>original: cosmocrators; the seven "planets" known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon</note>. For from this motion, the variety found in the world of change was brought into the light. What remains of Plato’s observations concerning time deserves our attention: specifically, that time proceeds in a manner analogous to the soul, being both eternal and created. Just as the soul belongs to the category of eternal beings yet is the best of created natures, so too is time both eternal and created—so far as it is mingled with souls and bodies, and so far as it proceeds and...
