For it is a proceeding number and a circle; but in and of itself, it is both a monad <note>original: monad; a single, indivisible unit or source</note> and a center. For the Demiurge <note>original: Demiurgus; the divine craftsman or creator of the material world</note> produced a medium of this kind between things that are immovable and things that are moved, following his own likeness. For he is also a medium between the abiding and proceeding Gods,¹ fashioned after the paradigm <note>original: paradigm; the eternal model or blueprint of the universe</note>; because this model is also a medium between the intelligible and intellectual Gods,² between eternity and number,³ and the *eternal and perpetual Gods*.⁴ For it participates in eternity—specifically, it is the primary participant and the monad of "intelligible animals" <note>this refers to the ideal Forms of all living things within the divine mind</note>. Consequently, because the world was created to be perpetual throughout the whole of time, it was perfectly likened to its paradigm. For just as its paradigm received the full gift of eternity—since everything that primarily participates in a thing receives the entirety of its gift—so too the world lives through the whole of time, and lives according to its complete, perfect number. Therefore, it is also perpetual. For everything capable of receiving the entire evolution of time is indestructible. And the whole of time is the perfect number of the <term>restoration</term> <note>original: apocatastasis; the return of all celestial bodies to their original starting positions</note> of the universe, as we have frequently observed.

Furthermore, we must also understand from what has been said that Plato was very far from conceiving time in the way the Stoics and many of the Peripatetics <note>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy</note> understood it. The Stoics supposed time to be a mere mental concept—fleeting and very nearly non-existent. To them, time was one of those "signified" ⁵ things that they looked down upon as ineffective, having no real existence, and existing only in the mind. The Peripatetics, however, assert that time is an "accident" <note>original: accident; a property or quality that is not essential to the nature of a thing</note> of motion. Yet we might ask: of what motion? Is it a property of continuous motion? But time is everywhere, while motion exists only within the things being moved. Is it then a property of *all* motion? If so, there would be many different "times." And what would be the single unit (monad) connecting them? How can time be the numerical measurement of motion? For if that were so, time would only exist as a relationship; it would be something relative, and if the one doing the numbering did not exist, neither would time. Plato, therefore, perceiving that all these assertions are unworthy...

¹ <note>original: "The Demiurgus is a medium between the intelligible Gods, who are characterized by *permanency*, and the supermundane Gods, who are characterized by *proceeding*; just as the mundane Gods are characterized by *regression*. See my translation of Proclus on the Theology of Plato."</note>
² <note>i.e., between the intelligible triads of "being itself" and "life itself," and the intellectual order.</note>
³ <note>original: "viz. Between the middle triad of the intelligible order; for in this eternity first subsists, and the summit of the intelligible and at the same time intellectual order."</note>

# PROCLUS ON THE TIMÆUS [BOOK IV.

The theory concerning time gives to time an existence from above <note>original: supernally</note>, originating from the intelligible and intellectual Gods. Time is a super-mundane intellect <note>meaning an intellect that exists beyond the physical world</note> that holds all soul-based <note>original: psychical</note> life together. It measures the cycles of both the soul and the body, and it perfects the movement of these cycles as they unfold through space. From this single unit <note>original: monad</note>, he also establishes different measurements of time based on the triad <margin>1. That is, according to the past, the present, and the future.</margin> and the heptad <margin>2. That is, according to the seven planets.</margin>. He creates all of these around the single concept of time that measures the unified life of the universe. He also grants time such great power that it makes the world more like its eternal model <note>original: paradigm</note> through its influence. For the purpose <margin>3. Instead of the Greek phrase "ena kai" (one and), which appears here in the source text, it is necessary to read "eneka" (for the sake of).</margin> of generating these various times, he creates the Sun and the other *world-rulers* <note>original: cosmocrators; refers to the celestial bodies that govern the physical laws of the universe</note>. These beings call forth invisible time, bringing it into the light, distributing it into parts, dividing it, and constantly cycling it with unchanging consistency.

However, since he says that the planets traveling through the heavens have orbits <note>original: revolutions</note>, let us consider whether he thinks their motion is varied. They move around their own centers and revolve through the heavens in three dimensions—length, width, and depth—passing through their own spheres, which are parts of the heavens that complete the universe. He does not say they move *in* the heavens as if they stayed in one spot, but *through* the heavens, moving along celestial arcs and changing their positions entirely. Additionally, they always rotate around their own centers to create a "mixed" type of motion. In this way, they serve as a middle ground between the fixed stars (which always occupy the same place) and the things below the moon <note>original: sublunary natures</note> (which do not rotate around a fixed center). 

It is therefore clear that, according to Plato, all the celestial spheres share the same center as the universe itself. The apparent unevenness in the motions of the seven planets comes from their orbits. Their movement changes in various ways—speeding up or slowing down, moving forward, rising higher, or coming closer to the earth—all without needing the complex invention of epicycles <note>original: epicycles; a geometric model where a planet moves in a small circle which itself moves along a larger circle, used in ancient astronomy to explain planetary paths</note>. Plato makes no mention of these, and nature always requires a middle ground <note>original: medium</note>. The middle ground between perfectly uniform, orderly things and those that are irregular and chaotic is something that is both irregular *and* orderly. This is the nature of planetary motion: it shows an unevenness that nevertheless follows a perpetual, fixed order—alternating between fast and slow, and moving either toward the same point or in opposite directions. While some have used certain epicycles or uniform eccentric orbits <note>original: eccentrics; circular orbits where the center is not the Earth</note> as hypotheses to explain these motions...

<summary>Proclus explains how time is a divine intellect that governs cosmic cycles through the Sun and planets. He argues that planetary motion is an "orderly irregularity" that functions without the need for complex epicycles, maintaining that all celestial spheres are concentric.</summary>

# BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

To understand how the various movements of the stars, their circular paths <term>epicycles: small circles whose centers move around the circumference of larger circles</term>, and their off-center orbits <term>eccentrics: circular orbits that are not centered on the Earth</term> all work together is a beautiful idea suited for rational minds. However, this level of detail is outside the scope of the "nature of wholes"—the universal perspective—which was Plato’s sole focus.

> “But because the universe did not yet contain all the living beings <note>original: animals</note> produced within it, it was still unlike its model. Therefore, its creator <note>original: artificer</note> corrected this flaw by imprinting it with forms, based on the nature of its eternal model <note>original: paradigm</note>.”

It is clear and appropriate that Plato mentions the "Living-Being-in-itself" <note>original: animal itself; the Platonic Form that contains all other life</note> three times while likening the world to it. He describes the universe as "only-begotten" (unique), "perfectly perpetual" (eternal), and "all-perfect" (complete). The "Living-Being-in-itself" is defined by these three traits. Since it holds the third rank among "intelligible" <note>purely divine or mental</note> realities, it receives the quality of being "only-begotten" from the first rank of that order (the "One Being"). It receives "eternity" from the second rank. Finally, it possesses "all-perfection" from its own nature. 

We must carefully examine what this "all-perfection" means. As we have often noted, "wholeness" is three-fold and originates from the highest divine realms <note>original: supernally from intelligibles</note>. Because this world is the image of the most beautiful divine reality, it must reflect each of these three types of wholeness:
1.  **Wholeness prior to parts:** The unity that exists before anything is divided.
2.  **Wholeness made of parts:** The unity formed by the assembly of different elements.
3.  **Wholeness within a part:** The way a single part can reflect the nature of the whole.

The Creator <note>original: Demiurgus</note> had already organized the world according to the first kind of wholeness. He made it a living being with a soul and an intellect, bringing order to the previously chaotic and confused matter by introducing soul, mind, and divine unity. 

As the explanation continues, he also gave the world the second kind of wholeness (made of parts). He established the two primary celestial rotations, joined the elements together through mathematical proportion <note>original: analogy</note>,¹ and organized the soul's movements according to numerical structures: the one (monad), three (triad), four (tetrad), and seven (heptad). The universe is composed of these parts, which make it a complete "Whole" or "All." In the passage we are reading now, he gives the world the third form of wholeness. For it is necessary that each part of it should itself become a whole, and that it should have all—

---

¹ Instead of "through irrationality" <note>original: di alogias</note> in this passage, it is clearly necessary to read "through mathematical proportion" <note>original: di analogias</note>.

<summary>Proclus explains how the Creator organizes the universe into a "whole" by mimicking the three levels of wholeness found in the divine, eternal model of life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the physical world is made to resemble the "Living-Being-in-itself" (the eternal Form of life). It explains that the world contains all types of creatures—celestial, aerial, and terrestrial—to achieve "all-perfection."</meta>

# BOOK IV.] PROCLUS ON THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

The universe contains things appropriately within itself: the heavens in a celestial way, the air in an airy way, and the earth in an earthly way. In this way, the whole is present within each part. Through this, the world is even more closely aligned with its eternal model <note>original: paradigm</note>, which encompasses all living beings <note>original: animals</note>. For that model is both a unity <note>original: monad</note> and a collection <note>original: number</note>. 

It is necessary that the world should contain all living beings within itself so that it may become perfectly similar to the "all-encompassing" nature of its model. It achieves this not only by receiving the full systems <note>original: plenitudes</note> of the world and existing <note>The original Greek text used a word meaning "standing apart" (aphistamenos), but it should be read as "subsisting" or "existing" (hyphistamenos).</note> as a "whole of wholes," but also by containing the individual living beings. Through these individuals, every part of the world is completed, including all the divine, spirit-like <note>original: demoniacal; referring to daemons, intermediary spirits in Greek philosophy</note>, and mortal ranks. In this way, the most perfect similarity between the world and the "Living-Being-itself" is achieved. This is the tenth gift given by the Demiurge <note>the divine craftsman of the world</note> to the universe, and it is the greatest gift of all. 

We do not say, however, that the Demiurge brought the world from a state of being "unlike" the divine to a state of being "like" it. If we said that, it would mean the imperfect existed before the perfect in the divine creation of things. Rather, the order of this discussion follows a logical hierarchy of forms. It places the primary causes before the secondary and tertiary goods <note>The discussion presents the concept of a "whole" before its "parts," followed by a "whole consisting of parts," and finally the "whole existing within a part."</note> so that the world may be stamped—as if by a seal—with all the unfolded forms of the divine realities. 

Since the eternal model was a unity and contained all divine living beings, the world must not only be "only-begotten" (unique) and a "whole of wholes," but it must also contain all physical living beings. Here, the discussion of the "giving of life" <note>original: vivification</note> proceeds, filling all parts of the universe with the appropriate kinds <note>original: genera</note> of animals, organizing all these kinds by their proper numbers, and generating all those numbers to match the likeness of the eternal model.

> "Whatever ideas intellect perceived in that which is 'the living being itself,' it reasoned that this universe must contain those same types and that same number of ideas."

<note>The beginning of this commentary is missing in the original text. Due to an error in the historical printing, this extant portion was inserted in the wrong place (page 266) as if it belonged to a different section regarding "Night and Day."</note>

The third type of "wholeness" is given to the world through the process of creation <note>original: fabrication</note>. This process weaves parts together with wholes, and individual numbers <note>The original text uses a grammatical form meaning "to the numbers" (tois arithmois), but it should be read as the direct object "the numbers" (tous arithmous).</note> with unities. It makes each part of the universe its own "world," ensuring that even what exists in a single part is, in its own way, a "whole" and an "all."

# BOOK IV.] THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

The world is granted this quality because it is similar to the "Living-Being-itself" <note>original: animal itself; refers to the eternal Form of Life/the Living-Being mentioned in Plato's Timaeus</note>; for that model is also a complete unity <note>original: monad</note> and a specific number. It is likewise an all-perfect intellect existing in the realm of thought <note>original: intelligible intellect</note>, and a full collection <note>original: plenitude</note> of causes within that realm, which it produces so that they may remain eternally within itself. For the many things that remain within their cause are of one type, while those that go forth and are divided into parts are of another. 

For the Demiurge <note>the divine Craftsman of the universe</note> himself establishes some types of Gods within himself, but produces others from himself into second and third ranks. And the father of the Demiurge (Kronos <note>original: Saturn; the Neoplatonists identified the Greek god Kronos with the Roman Saturn</note>) creates some model causes of creation to stay within himself, but he produces others as the actual creative <note>original: demiurgic</note> causes that are ranked before the "wholes" of the universe. His grandfather, Ouranos <note>original: Heaven; referring to the god Uranus</note>, also keeps some causes within himself but leads others forth into a separation from himself. <note>original: Instead of "to these, the separation from himself" (τοις δε, την αφ' εαυτου διακρισιν), it is necessary to read "leads them forth into a separation from himself" (τους δε, προσαγει εις την αφ' εαυτου διακρισιν).</note> 

Theologians <note>referring to ancient mythological writers like Orpheus</note> show these things through mystical names, calling them either "concealment," "absorption," or "nurture in Fate." Therefore, long before these, the pure Intellect <note>original: intelligible intellect</note>, who is the father of all things, generates some causes within himself and reveals them, but produces others from himself and establishes the ranks of the Gods that come after him. <note>original: For "establishes with their own orders of the gods" (ταις μεθ' εαυτων ταξεσιν υφιστησι των θεων), it is necessary to read "establishes the orders of the gods that come after him" (τας μεθ' εαυτον ταξεις υφιστησι των θεων).</note> He contains unified, whole, and all-perfect causes within his own mind, while producing other orders that are multiplied and divided into parts through their differences. 

Hence, since every fatherly rank of divinity creates in this way, this world also—being an imitation of those higher orders and dependent on them—possesses one type of **entirety** <note>original: allness</note> that exists before individual living beings. But it also possesses another kind of entirety that is completed by those individuals. Together with the first kind, it receives the second kind so that it may be as similar as possible to its creative and model cause. This is the way in which this takes place.

But the words, "**in that which is the Living-Being-itself**," we have explained before, and we have shown what our opinion is regarding the nature of that Living-Being. Now we also say that within the range of the higher reality <note>original: intelligible breadth</note>, one part is the peak, which is unified and hidden <note>original: occult</note>. Another part is the power of that peak, which goes forth while still remaining where it is. A third part reveals itself through activity <note>original: energy</note> and shows within itself a vast number of higher forms <note>original: intelligible multitude</note>. 

Of these three, the first is "Pure Being," the second is "Pure Life," and the third is "Pure Intellect" <note>original: intelligible being, life, and intellect</note>. However, Pure Being itself cannot be the "Living-Being-itself," because the "many" are not found there, nor is the group of four fundamental ideas <note>original: tetrad of ideas</note>. Instead, because of its unique oneness and unspeakable <note>original: ineffable</note> union, Plato calls it the **One**. In short, the "Living-Being-itself" is said to share in <note>original: participate of</note> eternity, but the first...

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

Being-itself <note>The most fundamental level of reality in Neoplatonism</note> does not participate in anything, unless someone should say that it participates in the *One*, a point which is worth considering. For might not that which is above Being be superior even to this name [*the One*]? But Being-itself is primarily that which it is, and not something created through participation. 

Therefore, Being-itself cannot be the "Living-Being-itself" <note>original: animal itself; refers to the *Zoon*, the eternal Form of the Living Being</note> for the reasons mentioned above. Nor can "Intelligible Life" be the Living-Being-itself. For a "living being" is secondary to Life; a thing is said to be a living being through its participation in life. In short, if the Living-Being-itself were the second level, then Eternity would be Being-itself. This, however, is impossible. For *the One Being* is one thing, and *Eternal Being* is another; the former is the monad <note>unity</note> of Being, but the latter is a dyad <note>pair</note>, having the quality of "always" intertwined with Being. The former is the cause of existence for all things, while the latter is the cause of their permanence in that existence. 

If, therefore, neither the "One Being-itself" is the Living-Being-itself, nor that which is immediately after it (for that is Eternity, which is intelligible power, infinite life, and "Wholeness-itself," through which each of the divinities is simultaneously a whole), it is necessary that the third level, [or the *intelligible intellect*], should be the Living-Being-itself. It is necessary that the Living-Being-itself should be a form of intellect in a certain way, since the physical image of it exists entirely in conjunction with the senses. Sensation is the image of intellect; therefore, in that which is primarily a living being, Intellect primarily exists. 

Hence, if the Living-Being-itself is secondary to Life, it necessarily exists according to the *intelligible intellect*. For being intelligible, and as Plato says, "a living being, the most beautiful of intelligibles, and only-begotten," it will occupy this rank. For all things after this form are produced in conjunction with other things and fall short of "intelligible totality" <note>the state of containing all things in a unified way</note>.

The Living-Being-itself, therefore, is the *intelligible intellect*. It contains within itself the intellectual orders of the gods, collecting, uniting, and perfecting them,¹ and acting as the most beautiful boundary of the intelligible realm. It also reveals to intellectual natures the unified and unknown cause of the intelligibles, stirring itself toward "Ideas" and all-various powers, while producing all the secondary orders of the gods. 

For this reason, Orpheus calls it the god Phanes <note>An Orphic creator deity whose name means "the one who reveals" or "brings to light"</note>, as he "reveals" the intelligible unities; Orpheus gives it various forms, as it shows within itself the first cause of intelligible living beings. He also inserts into it multiform Ideas, as it is the first to contain intelligible Ideas, and calls it the "Key of Intellect," because it defines every intelligible essence and holds together intellectual life. From this great god, the Demiurge <note>the divine Craftsman</note> of the universe is suspended; the Demiurge is himself, as we have said before, an intellect, but an *intellectual* intellect, and specifically the cause of intellect. Hence, the Demiurge is said to "see" the Living-Being-itself: for "sight" is the...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the hierarchy of the divine, specifically focusing on how the Demiurge (the divine Craftsman) relates to the "Living-Being-itself" (the eternal model) and how different theological traditions describe this relationship.</meta>

<page-num>257</page-num>

# BOOK IV.] THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

This is a characteristic of the intellectual Gods. For the theologian <note>Referring to Orpheus</note> calls the "intelligible intellect" <note>The highest level of intellect that serves as an object for others</note> eyeless. He says of it:

->In his breast feeding eyeless, rapid Love.<-

For the boundary of its activity is the intelligible. But the Demiurge, being an intellect, does not rank among "participated" intellects <note>Intellects that are bound to specific souls</note>; this is so that he may be the Demiurge of the universe as a whole, and so that he may be able to look toward the *Living-Being-itself* <note>original: animal itself; the eternal Form that serves as a model for the world</note>. Being "imparticipable" <note>An independent, transcendent principle</note>, however, he is truly an intellectual intellect. 

Through simple intelligence, he is united to the intelligible; but through various ways of thinking, he moves toward the creation of secondary natures. Hence, his intelligence is called "vision," as it is not divided into many parts and shines with intelligible light. But his second activity is called "dianoetic" <note>discursive or rational reasoning</note>, as it proceeds from simple intelligence and advances to the creation of his works. 

Plato says that the Demiurge "looks" to the Living-Being-itself. Orpheus, however, says that he "leaps to" and "absorbs" it, through the direction of Night. For through Night—who is both intelligible and intellectual—the intellectual intellect is joined to the intelligible realm. You must not, however, assume from this that the Demiurge looks at something external to himself, for that is not permitted for him. Rather, being turned toward himself and toward the fountain of ideas within himself, he is also joined to the "monad" <note>the single, unified source</note> of all the various orders of forms. 

For "intellect is not without the intelligible, and does not exist separate from it," according to the Oracle <note>The Chaldean Oracles</note>. If we say that our own soul knows all things by looking into itself, and that things prior to the soul are not external to it, how could the demiurgic intellect not survey the intelligible world in a much greater degree by perceiving himself? For the Living-Being-itself is also within him—not as a single unit, but according to a certain divine number. Hence, being intellectual himself, he is said by theologians to "absorb" that intelligible God. This is because every intelligible thing, the divisions of forms, and the "intelligible number" are perceived by him. Plato also indicates this when he describes the ideas of the Demiurge as "*such and so many*." By "such," he shows the specific characteristics of their causes; by "so many," he shows their separation according to number.

If these things are indeed so, it is not proper to admit, as some do, that there is an infinity of forms in the intelligible realm. For that which is "definite" is more closely allied to first principles than the "indefinite," as Plato also indicates. First natures are always more concentrated in quantity, but they surpass in power those things that come after them. Nor should it be said that those who separate the Living-Being-itself from the Demiurge make the intelligible realm external to the intellect.

<meta>This page continues Proclus's exploration of how the Demiurge (the divine Craftsman) relates to the "Living-Being-itself" (the eternal Model). Proclus argues that the Model is not external to the Creator but exists within his intellect in a more divided, creative form.</meta>

<page-num>258</page-num>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.
<meta>By</meta>

We do not claim that the object of vision is secondary to the one who sees just to make it external to the viewer; rather, we assert that the object is prior to the viewer. Higher divine "intelligibles" <note>Objects of pure thought or divine realities</note> are perceived intellectually by various beings as existing within those beings themselves. This is because the soul, when it enters into itself, is said to discover all things—and as Socrates says, it discovers both God and wisdom. <note>original: This is asserted by Socrates in the *First Alcibiades*.</note> Therefore, the *Living-Being-itself* <note>original: "Animal itself"; the eternal Form of all life</note> is prior to the Demiurge <note>The divine Craftsman of the world</note> and is not external to him. In that higher realm, all things exist as a unified, intelligible whole; but within the Demiurge, they exist intellectually and with distinction. 

In the Demiurge, the individual causes of the sun and moon already exist, not just the single idea of the "celestial Gods" which brings all heavenly types into being. This is why the *Chaldean Oracles* <note>A collection of mystical verses highly regarded by Neoplatonists</note> say that the creative energies are carried along like swarms of bees, emerging and spreading throughout the bodies of the world. A divine intellect unfolds the *total distinction of these things as they exist in the intelligible realm* <note>original: "For *en tō nō* (in the intellect) in this place, it is necessary to read *en tō noētō* (in the intelligible)."</note> into the vast multitude of creative forces. These observations should be taken as natural conclusions of our argument.

Next, however, it is worth discussing the opinions of earlier interpreters who suggest a more unusual meaning for Plato's words. For example, Amelius identifies a "triad" <note>a group of three</note> of creative intellects from this text. He calls the first "that which is," based on the phrase "*that which is the Living-Being*"; he calls the second "that which has," based on the words "*in that*," because the second intellect does not *consist* of the Ideas, but rather the Ideas enter into it; and he calls the third "that which sees," based on the word "*perceived*." 

However, Plato says that the Ideas are *inside* the Living-Being; he does not say that the Living-Being is one thing and the place where the Ideas are contained is another. Therefore, "that which is" is not different from "that which has," if one is the Living-Being and the other is the realm where the Ideas exist. 

Furthermore, Numenius <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who influenced Neoplatonism</note> ranks the "First God" according to the Living-Being and says that he thinks intellectually for the benefit of the "Second God." He ranks the Second God as "Intellect" and says he builds the world for the benefit of the "Third God." The Third God is ranked by Numenius according to his "dianoetic" <note>discursive or reasoning</note> activity. 

It is clear that these three have essential differences. However, Plato does not make such a division here, where one thing is an intellect perceiving purely and another is an intellect using reasoning. Plato does not separate the activities from the beings who perform them, since activities flow from the beings themselves. Or rather, in divine beings, their essence and their activity are one and the same. To think through reasoning and to perceive purely are simply the boundaries of the activities <note>original: *energēmata*</note> of the demiurgic intellect. Therefore, it is not at all right to...

<summary>Proclus argues that the eternal Model exists within the Demiurge's mind and critiques the complex hierarchies of Amelius and Numenius, asserting that the Creator's essence and activity are unified.</summary>
<keywords>Proclus, Timaeus, Demiurge, Living-Being-itself, Amelius, Numenius, Chaldean Oracles, Intelligible vs Intellectual, Dianoetic, Neoplatonism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, transitioning from a general discussion of the Demiurge (the Craftsman) and the Model to a specific analysis of the four types of living beings that populate the universe.</meta>

<header>BOOK IV.] THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

Some have argued that these distinctions are divided in a contrary way within the Demiurge <note>The divine Craftsman or Creator</note>, since they align with his *hypostasis* <note>original: "hypostasis"; the essential nature or underlying reality of a divine being</note>. However, the divine Iamblichus has sufficiently refuted these people, adding that Plato does not make the kind of distinctions among divine natures in the *Sophist*, *Philebus*, and *Parmenides* that they claim. Instead, Plato discusses each of the divine orders mentioned there separately, and he keeps his hypotheses distinct from one another. He discusses the "one" separately, the "whole" separately, and continues in a similar way, defining each hypothesis with its own appropriate terms. Our goal, however, is not to disprove the opinions of others. Instead, we remind ourselves that the subjects we intend to consider are: what the one intelligible paradigm <note>The eternal Model or Blueprint used by the Creator</note> is, who the whole Demiurge is, and how the two are united. Let us therefore see how, in the following text, the multitude of models and the many ways things are created are presented.

> “But these ideas are four: one, the race of the celestial Gods; another, winged animals that wander through the air; the third, the aquatic species; and the fourth, those that walk on land and belong to the earth.”

Just as a single unit <note>original: "monad"</note> leads the intellectual multitude within the mind of the Creator, and just as a unified form exists in the Model prior to any number, so too does discourse—the interpreter of divine matters—imitate the nature of the things it describes. First, it grasps the entire object of knowledge collectively through an inspired conception; afterward, it unfolds what was concentrated and develops that single act of understanding through words. It also divides what is united according to the nature of the things themselves—at one time explaining their union, and at another, their separation. For it is not naturally possible for human speech to comprehend both of these aspects at once. 

Plato’s discourse is affected in this same way. First, in a divinely inspired manner, he reveals the entire number of intelligible ideas; afterward, he distributes the progressions contained within that number into parts. For the intelligible multitude shines forth precisely where the first "monads" of ideas are found. We have previously shown that this is Plato’s usual method in many instances, such as when he uses the phrases, “*it was generated,*” “*he was good,*” and “*one.*”

Turning our attention from words to realities, let us consider first what this "four-fold" <note>original: "tetrad"</note> structure of ideas is and where this number comes from. Next, we will consider what these four ideas are and how they exist in the *Living-Being-itself* <note>original: "animal itself"; the eternal Form of all life</note>—specifically, whether the perfection of that Living Being is completed through them, or whether...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's detailed breakdown of the "Intelligible Paradigm" (the divine model for the universe) and how it organizes the different levels of existence into numerical patterns like the monad (one), duad (two), and tetrad (four).</meta>

<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.</header>

...they exist in some other way. By proceeding in an orderly manner through these reflections, we shall discover Plato's divinely inspired concept. 

It is necessary, therefore, to return to the previously mentioned demonstrations. In those, we said that the first, most unified, and simplest intelligible essence of the Gods descends from above from the "unity of unities" <note>The ultimate source or "The One"</note> in a way that is ineffable and incomprehensible to all things. We identified three parts: the first <note>original: "one thing"; referring to the "One Being" itself, the peak of the intelligible order</note> is hidden and paternal; the second <note>original: "another"; referring to "Intelligible Life," in which eternity exists</note> is the unified power of the whole and an unlimited measure; and the third <note>original: "a third thing"; referring to "Animal Itself" or the "Intelligible Intellect," the conclusion of the intelligible order</note> moves into active expression <note>original: "energy"</note> and diverse powers, acting as both a father and a creator <note>original: "effective"</note>. 

The first of these is a *monad* <note>a single, indivisible unit</note> because it is the summit of the entire intelligible range and the fountain and cause of divine numbers. The second is a *duad* <note>a pair or duality</note> because it both remains and moves forward within the intelligible categories, linking "eternity" <note>original: "the *ever*"</note> with "being." However, the subject we are currently investigating is the third part, which is the *tetrad* <note>a group of four</note>. This tetrad receives the hidden cause of the monad and reveals its own internal, stationary power. Things that exist in the monad in a primary, unified, and stationary way are displayed by the tetrad in a distributed way—now separated by number and produced into secondary natures. 

Because this third level is adapted to its preceding causes and fully participates in them, it is not merely a tetrad. As a monad, it is greater than a simple four and is granted a paternal superiority; as a duad, it is creative and fertile. Therefore, insofar as it is called "Animal Itself" <note>the archetypal "Living Being" that contains the blueprints for all life</note>, it is the monad (the source unit) for the nature of all living beings—whether they are vital, intellectual, or physical. But insofar as it encompasses both the male and female principles at once, it is a duad. These principles exist appropriately in all ranks of living beings: in one way in the Gods, in another in daemons <note>original: "dæmons"; intermediary spirits</note>, and in another in mortals. It is necessary that the primary units of these beings exist fundamentally within the single, all-encompassing nature of "Animal Itself." 

Furthermore, insofar as it creates the four fundamental "ideas" (types) of living beings from this duad, it is a tetrad. The fourfold creation <note>original: "fabrication"</note> of the world follows these ideas, and the primary creative cause of the whole is a tetrad. Therefore, when Plato teaches the fourfold power of the Paradigm <note>the Model</note>, he says there are four primary ideas of worldly things, all contained within the single idea of "Animal Itself." In that realm, "Animal Itself" is one idea (a monad), but the male and female principles form a duad.

If you wish, you can also find "genera" and "species" <note>general classes and specific types</note> in Plato’s division. He refers to two of the ideas—the intellectual <note>the celestial or heavenly</note> and the air-wandering—as genera...

<note>2. That is, Intelligible Life, in which eternity exists.</note>

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the "Intelligible Paradigm," specifically focusing on why the number four (the tetrad) represents the most fundamental set of ideas that the Creator uses to build the universe.</meta>

<header>BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

...but the remaining two are species <term>species: specific categories or types within a larger genus</term>, as they are subordinate to the former two. The concept of "Animal Itself" <note>original: "animal itself"; the divine, living model of the universe containing all possible life forms</note> is also a tetrad <term>tetrad: a group of four</term>. At this level, the intelligible forms reach their limit.

After this point, however, ideas proceed according to different numbers. There is an appropriate number of them in each order; a smaller number is comprehensive of more universal <note>original: "total"</note> ideas, while a larger number consists of ideas that are more specific <note>original: "partial"</note>. Divine natures are more concentrated in quantity but possess a transcendent power. The forms of secondary natures are more numerous than those that come before them: intellectual forms are more numerous than intelligible forms, super-worldly <note>original: "supermundane"</note> forms more than intellectual ones, and worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note> forms more than super-worldly ones.

Therefore, worldly forms are those that have reached the furthest point of distribution, just as intelligible forms receive the highest degree of unity. Every progression away from the source diminishes power but increases variety <note>original: "multitude"</note>. Thus, if Timæus had been discussing a specific intellectual order, he would have mentioned a different number, such as seven <note>original: "hebdomadic"</note> or ten <note>original: "decadic"</note>. But since he is speaking of the intelligible cause of ideas, which encompasses all intelligible living beings, he says that the primary ideas are four.

The tetrad exists there, proceeding from the intelligible monad <term>monad: the primary "One" or single source of all being</term> and filling the creator’s <note>original: "demiurgic"</note> group of ten. As the Pythagorean hymn says:

"Divine number proceeds from the hidden depths of the undecaying monad, until it arrives at the divine tetrad, which produced the mother of all things—the universal recipient, ancient and venerable—placing a boundary around all things, unchanging and untiring, [and which both the immortal Gods and earth-born men call the sacred decad.]¹"

The hymn calls the uniform and hidden cause of the "One Being" the "undecaying monad" and the "hidden depths of the monad." However, it calls the "divine tetrad" the emergence into light of that intelligible variety which the "duad" <term>duad: the number two, representing the first step toward variety</term> (the bridge between the one and the four) unfolds. And the world itself, which receives the images of all the divine numbers granted to it from above, it calls the "decad" <term>decad: the number ten, representing a completed whole</term>. These words can be understood by looking at how the world was constructed. This concludes our discussion of the tetrad itself.

Next, let us show what these four ideas are and what kind of things they bring into existence. The interpreters differ in their opinions on this subject. Some assert that the progression of these ideas leads into the Gods and the mortal classes <note>original: "genera"</note>, specifically following the literal meaning of Plato’s words. Others, looking at the nature of things, say the progression leads to the Gods and the classes of beings superior to us <note>such as angels or daemons</note>, because...

---

¹ The words within the brackets are supplied from the Commentary of Syrianus on *Aristotle's Metaphysics*. The original Greek is: *Immortal Gods and earth-born men* <note>original: "Αθάνατοί τε θεοί, καὶ γηγενέεις ἄνθρωποι"</note>.

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the "Intelligible Paradigm," explaining how the four primary classes of living beings (celestial, aerial, aquatic, and terrestrial) are derived from the divine model and how various philosophers interpret their hierarchy.</meta>

<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV</header>

...these classes <term>original: "genera"</term> exist prior to mortal beings, and it is necessary that the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> should not produce mortal beings directly from divine natures. Others again, combining both these opinions and following what is written in the *Epinomis* <note>a dialogue often associated with Plato's Laws, discussing the nature of the gods and the heavens</note>, assert that Gods exist in the heavens, daemons <note>original: "dæmons"; in Neoplatonism, these are mediating spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense</note> in the air, demigods in water, and men and other mortals on earth. 

However, since there is such a difference of opinion among the interpreters, we admire those who love these subjects, but we shall endeavor to follow our leader, Syrianus <note>Proclus’s teacher and predecessor as head of the Neoplatonic Academy</note>. We say, therefore, that the celestial class of Gods includes all the heavenly types, whether they are divine, angelic, or demonic. The air-wandering class includes all the beings that are organized in the air, whether they are Gods assigned to the air, or daemons that follow them, or mortal animals that live in the air. The aquatic class includes all the groups assigned to the water and all that are nourished in water. And the land-dwelling <note>original: "pedestrious"</note> class includes all the groups that preside over the parts of the earth, and all the animals that are formed and generated in the earth. 

For the Creator is entirely the cause of all worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note> natures and the common father of all of them. He generates divine and demonic natures through himself alone, but he delivers the creation of mortal natures to the "junior gods," as they are able to generate these through an immediate action <note>original: "proximate energy"</note>. The Paradigm <note>the eternal "blue-print" or model of the universe</note> is not the cause of only some animals; rather, it possesses the most universal causes of all animals. Indeed, if it were the cause of the divine and demonic classes, but not the cause of the mortal classes, then mortals would not be generated. In that case, the universe would be imperfect, as it would not contain all the classes of animals. For the universe is similar to its Paradigm and is all-perfect because it imitates the four ideas of the Living Being Itself <note>original: "animal itself"; the divine, intelligible model of all life</note>.

If, on the contrary, someone should say that these classes include both Gods and mortals, how shall we agree with Plato, who, after discussing the creation of the celestial animals, says:

> "But to speak concerning the other daemons, and to know their generation, exceeds our ability;"

having also mentioned the Gods that proceed into the sublunary world <note>the realm of change and decay below the moon</note>. For here, after the aerial class, he arranges the aquatic, and after this, the land-dwelling class. 

In the generation of mortal animals, however, he no longer preserves this order. Instead, generating all of them through the human soul, he leads it into the land-dwelling class after its life <note>original: "polity"</note> in the heavens, so that he may fully produce man. After the human soul has acted wrongly, he again conducts it to the winged, land-dwelling, and savage classes, and afterwards to the aquatic tribe. Hence, it seems that these three classes are not only the aerial <note>The original text "aprea" is a typo for "aeria" (aerial).</note> natures of mortal beings, but that they are the causes of...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the Creator (Demiurge) derives the four primary classes of living beings from the "Intelligible Paradigm" and how these categories manifest across different levels of reality, from the gods down to mortal animals.</meta>

<header>BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

These exist prior to other things, and within them the same order of the three ideas is preserved, as secondary natures proceed from those prior to them through a decrease in power <term>original: "diminution"</term>. It is necessary, therefore, that all things should be generated through these ideas—namely, both the divine and mortal classes <term>original: "genera"</term>—and that the intelligible ideas, being the most universal <term>original: "total"</term>, should give existence to all classes. It is likewise necessary to apply the words before us appropriately according to each level of order. 

For instance, the class of Gods is understood in one way when referring to those properly called Gods, and in another way when referring to the classes superior to us that are arranged in the heavens. For we say that there are celestial angels, daemons <note>original: "dæmons"; in Neoplatonism, these are mediating spirits between gods and humans</note>, and heroes, and that all these are called "Gods" because the divine characteristic <term>original: "peculiarity"</term> predominates over their own specific nature. 

Again, the "winged and air-wandering" class exists in one way among the aerial Gods, in another among aerial daemons, and in another among aerial mortal animals. For the intellectual characteristic of these Gods is called "winged," but their providential characteristic is called "air-wandering," as it extends through the entire sphere of the air and holds the whole of it together. But in daemons, the *winged* quality signifies the rapidity of their energy, and the *air-wandering* quality manifests their being present everywhere without hindrance, proceeding through all things. And in mortal natures, the *winged* quality manifests motion through a specific organ <note>i.e., physical wings</note>, which alone makes use of the surrounding environment; but the *air-wandering* quality refers to the various ways they move through physical space. For nothing hinders partial souls <note>individual souls, like those of humans or animals, as opposed to the World Soul</note> which live in the air from wandering through the air. 

Furthermore, the "aquatic" quality in divine natures indicates a providential oversight and government that is inseparable from water. Hence, the Oracle also calls these Gods *water-walkers* <note>original: "υδροβατηρας" (hydrobatēras)</note>.$^2$ But in the classes that follow the Gods, it signifies that which holds together the nature of moisture. 

Moreover, the "pedestrian" <note>land-dwelling or earth-walking</note> quality in one context signifies that which occupies the final seat of existence and proceeds through it—such as the terrestrial nature—which stably governs it and brings it to perfection through various powers and lives. But in another context, it indicates that which governs and regulates different parts of the earth at different times through its own specific motion. This concludes the discussion concerning the names.

From these points, however, it may be assumed that the "Intelligible Animal" itself <note>The Paradigm or world of pure Ideas from which the Creator draws his model</note> is entirely different from the one in the Creator <term>original: "Demiurgus"</term>. For the former does not contain the separate ideas of mortal animals. For the Creator made mortal—

...animals, being willing to make worldly natures like all the forms contained within himself, in order that he might make the world completely perfect. But he contains the distinct ideas of these, producing mortal beings from immortal natures.$^1$ He knew, therefore, the mortal natures. And it is evident that he knew them by his own internal forms; and that he thought it fit the younger Gods should create them by looking to him, and not to the "Animal-itself" <note>original: "animal itself"; the Intelligible Paradigm, or the perfect, abstract blueprint of all life</note>, because he has within himself separate ideas for both mortal and immortal natures. 

In the "Animal-itself," therefore, there was the aerial, the aquatic, or the land-dwelling <term>original: "pedestrious"</term> form—there being one single idea for each (that is, one for all air animals, one for all water animals, and one for all land animals). But in the Demiurge <note>The Creator-God</note>, these ideas are divided. Some are the specific blueprints for immortal air-animals, while others are for mortal ones; the same is true for those that are aquatic and terrestrial. 

Hence, the variety of forms in the "Animal-itself" is not the same as the variety in the Demiurge, as can be seen from these arguments. We must also consider how these classes <term>original: "genera"</term> are divided. They are organized into a group of one <term>original: "monad"</term> and a group of three <term>original: "triad"</term>, setting the highest celestial class against the three total classes below it. They are also divided into two pairs <term>original: "duads"</term>. He calls the celestial and the winged types "classes" <term>original: "genera"</term>, but the aquatic and land-dwelling types "species," because they have a lower rank, just as a species is subordinate to a class.

Moreover, it is also necessary to observe that he omits the "idea of fire" in what he says now, because the divine class already includes the highest form of fire according to its own nature. Among the elements below the moon <term>original: "sublunary"</term>, fire alone does not have a stable, appropriate place; instead, it exists only in a state of constant change <term>original: "mutation"</term> and always requires fuel from air and water. The upper region is the natural place for fire. However, our earthly fire is not there. If it were, it would be seen, since fire is naturally visible. Nor can it reach that height, since it is extinguished by the surrounding air, which is different from it. 

If, therefore, it is necessary for there to be a stable "wholeness" of fire—a fire that has a permanent form somewhere rather than just existing in a state of coming-into-being—and since earthly fire is not like this, it follows that true fire exists only in the heavens. There, it remains as it truly is and always possesses its proper place. The upward motion we see in fire on Earth is not its natural motion, but the motion of fire that is in an unnatural state. This is also supported by the *Sacred Discourse of the Chaldeans* <note>The *Chaldean Oracles*, a collection of spiritual texts central to later Neoplatonism</note>, which links the "aerial bosoms" with the "lunar rattlings" and assigns the celestial region to fire, according to how the elements are distributed throughout the world. The fire that exists in the world of change <term>original: "generation"</term> is a kind of outflow from the celestial fire, trapped in the gaps of other elements.

elements; there is no sphere of fire existing by itself. Instead, the highest layers of the air imitate the purity of the upper fire. We say, therefore, that these heights are sublunary fire <note>Fire existing below the moon</note>, and that the place of fire is beneath the heavens. This region is most similar to the celestial depths, just as the lowest part of the air is most similar to water, because it is thick and cloudy. This also seems to have been Aristotle’s understanding; for he chose to name the fire found here in this way. But he calls the fire that is immediately under the heavens—which he says revolves along with the heavens—*fiery-formed*. 

If this is the case, however, it is necessary to ask him: where does that which is truly fire, and which ranks as a "whole" <term>original: "wholeness"; a complete, universal element rather than a partial or mixed one</term>, exist? For it cannot be the fire found here, since that is not a whole, nor is it truly existing fire, because the fire which is truly so is not merely "fiery-formed." He must therefore be forced to admit that fire which is truly fire—and which is pure light—exists in the heavens. 

You should not be surprised, however, if the thinnest and purest fire is in the upper layers of the air, just as the thickest and most turbid fire is in the depths of the earth. This does not mean that this fire is a different "whole" from the air; rather, because it is so thin, it is carried within the tiny pores of the air. It is not visible for two reasons: first, because it is not distinctly formed, and second, because it does not resist our sight since it consists of the smallest parts. This is also the case with the light of the eyes. 

Truly existing fire, therefore, is in the heavens. But the purest of the fire below the moon is in the air close to the heavenly bodies, which Plato later calls *ether* <note>original: "æther"</note>. And fire of the thickest nature is contained in the depths of the earth. Since Plato has now spoken concerning the four classes <note>original: "genera"</note> in common, let us look at how he constructs each of them in what follows.

> “The idea, therefore, of that which is divine, he created mostly from fire, so that it might be most radiant and beautiful to behold. [But making it like the universe, he made it round.”*]

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the composition of the celestial bodies, specifically exploring why the Demiurge (the divine craftsman) used fire as the primary element for the stars and the heavens.</meta>

<page-num>266</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.</header>

The Demiurge <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine craftsman or creator of the universe</note> first established the celestial world, producing it for the most part from the "idea" or archetype of fire. To understand this, we must first discuss its essence (what it is made of), second its shape, third its position, and fourth its motion. 

The discussion of its essence has caused much disagreement among the interpreters. For in what way does it possess the "idea of fire" for the most part? Is it as some say—that it is a mixture of all the elements, but consists mostly of fire? Or is it because every celestial category <note>original: "genus"</note> consists of all the elements, but the greatest part of it is fiery? It is possible to argue either of these points, just as if we were to say that all things consist of every category of being, but that "intelligible" things <note>Realities understood by the mind rather than the senses</note> possess the most "sameness" <note>Unity or unchanging nature</note>. 

Or is it not as a person would interpret who truly observes reality itself—that a state of being "mostly from the idea of fire" signifies that fire most abundantly possesses the character of the "fifth body" <note>The quintessence or aether, which Aristotle proposed as a fifth element distinct from the four earthly ones</note>, acting as the recipient of many creative powers with which each of the divine bodies is filled? Or shall we say, as others do, that divine animals <note>The stars and planets, viewed as living beings</note> consist of fire, but of a fire that has an essence possessing spatial extension <note>original: "interval"</note> and multiplicity? For the "intelligible" has the form of unity, but the physical is multiple because it is divisible and possesses physical bulk. 

Or perhaps—and this is the truest of all these views—we should look to all these concepts and see one truth as the result of all of them. For we believe all the elements exist in the heavens, but "immaterially"—at least as far as the immaterial can exist in physical things. We also say that the elements exist in the heavens, but only according to their "summits" <note>Their highest, purest, and most essential forms</note>. For if the forms of fire, air, water, and earth exist in the realm of Intellect, it is necessary that the heavens should be the first participants in this group of four <note>original: "tetrad"</note>. 

As the process of fabrication <note>creation by the Demiurge</note> proceeds, it also creates the final form of the elements, which is truly material. We likewise assert that the nature of the stars consists for the most part of fire. For although all the elements are in them, fire predominates; this is because, among the elements of the physical world, fire acts as the "form" (the organizing principle) relative to the other elements. 

It is necessary, therefore, in the celestial Gods <note>The stars and planets</note>, that the fiery characteristic should be most abundant, so that "form" may have dominion over the underlying substance. There should be the least of the other elements, because this smaller portion holds the rank of a "subject" <term>original: "subject"; the underlying material that is shaped and ruled by the "form"</term>. Thus, a terrestrial <note>earth-like</note> nature is present there as a certain solid essence and tangible bulk; for this reason, it is solid enough to be visible to our sight. The fiery nature is also there, illuminating and giving shape to that bulk and space. But the elements between these (air and water) exist there to connect the extremes and cause them to be one. Fire, however, rules over all the other elements because the "form" found there overpowers the material substance, holds it together, and preserves it on all sides, being itself full of life and the power of self-motion. Hence also it is full of divine and creative—

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s analysis of the celestial bodies, specifically refuting critics who argue against Plato’s claim that stars are composed primarily of fire. It completes the word "Demiurgic" from the previous page.</meta>

<page-num>267</page-num>
<header>BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

productive powers of the Demiurge <note>original: "urgic"; completing the word "Demiurgic" from the previous page, referring to the divine craftsman of the universe</note>, and proceeds into a state of multiplicity and spatial extension <note>original: "interval"</note>, defining in every way that which possesses dimensions and encompassing the physical bulk of the body.

Nor should we fear those skilled in logic <note>original: "dialectic"</note> who, by looking at only a small part of nature, criticize Plato for saying that fire tends to move upward, while the stars move in a circular motion. An upward tendency has no place in the fire of the heavens, just as self-motion does not belong to "intelligible fire" <note>Fire as a pure, non-physical idea in the divine mind</note> nor to fire that is purely physical in form. For the "reason" <note>original: "logos"; the internal form or productive principle</note> within the Intellect is intellectual fire. Movements correspond to the essence of the things themselves. If divine fire is what has the power to form the stars, it is not the same as this material and coarse sublunary <note>Earthly, or below the level of the moon</note> fire. If it is most brilliant and beautiful, it is different from this dim fire, which is mixed with the ugliness of matter. For the most basic matter is darkness and deformity, but this divine fire is most brilliant and beautiful—both of which are undeniable signs of truth. For the super-luminous, transparent splendor of light is an image of divine goodness, and its beauty is an indication of intellectual symmetry. 

Divine fire, therefore, is very different from that which is not divine. Thus, it appears that truly existing fire is found in the highest place; for this reason, the stars are fiery and are assigned the place of fire. The "summit" <note>The highest or purest form</note> of earth is also there. On the contrary, the whole of the earth <note>original: "τῃ" (te); the translator notes this should be "γῃ" (ge), meaning the element of earth</note> is here in our realm, which participates as much as is possible for earth in the lowest form of fire, which is most terrestrial and coarse. Likewise, the fire in the heavens possesses the "summit" of earth—the earth there being superior to the darkness and coarseness of this earthly world. This is also consistent with the teachings of Ptolemy <note>A famous Greco-Egyptian astronomer</note> and Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher</note>: every body, when it is in its proper place, either stays fixed or moves in a circle. Moving upward or downward are only the motions of bodies that are *not* in their proper places and are striving to get there. Thus, each of the other elements, when in its proper place, will either remain fixed or move in a circle. If a body were of a fiery nature and moved upward, it would be in a place where it does not belong.

We must not, therefore, doubt the theologians who place an "empyreal" <note>Fiery or made of pure light</note> essence in the heavens, for there are many types of fire. Simply to claim that the celestial body is a "fifth body" <note>The "quintessence" or aether, a concept from Aristotle</note> is not to say anything clear about it, other than that it is different from the four earthly elements. Plato, however, reveals its entire nature by placing the "summits" (the purest versions) of the elements in the heavens. Thus, the logical argument <note>original: "syllogism"</note> of those who think they can disprove Plato’s doctrine—that the stars consist mostly of fire—is itself disproven; it fails because it does not realize that the premise "fire must move upward" does not apply to celestial fire.

<summary>Proclus defends Plato’s view that stars are primarily made of fire by explaining that celestial fire is a divine, brilliant essence that naturally moves in circles, unlike the coarse, earthly fire that moves upward. He argues that the heavens contain the purest forms of all elements, governed by different laws of motion than those found on Earth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s analysis of the composition of the stars and the universe. It moves from discussing the nature of fire to explaining why the stars (the parts) are shaped like the universe (the whole) based on the Neoplatonic principle of "wholeness prior to parts."</meta>

<page-num>268</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.</header>

...upward. For it is not proper to define the nature of fire based on fire that is in an unnatural state <note>original: "preternatural subsistence"</note>—that is, fire that is struggling to return to its natural place. Instead, it must be defined by fire that is in a condition consistent with its nature. A thing of this kind is either fixed in place or revolves in a circle. 

The Demiurge <note>The divine craftsman or creator of the material world</note>, however, making each of the stars¹ similar to the universe, made each of them round. He gave them a twofold similarity: one to their own collective wholeness, and the other to the eternal model <note>original: "paradigm"</note> from which they are suspended. The parts of these stars also have a twofold similarity: one to the whole star, and the other to the essential idea of their wholeness. In the same way, an individual <note>original: "partial"</note> soul is made to be like the World-Soul and like the Intellect. But the World-Soul, which is one and encompasses everything, is made like the single and total Intellect. Total Nature is also modeled on the Soul, while an individual nature is modeled on its own whole and on the Soul. 

Consistent with this, each of the stars is made like the whole world and like its own specific eternal model. However, the similarity is different in each case. Each star is like its model according to its entire essence, but it is like the world in its shape and its motion. Each star is crafted to be round, just as the world is spherical. In the realm of physical things <note>original: "sensibles"</note>, the universe is primarily a sphere. Through this shape, it imitates both the Demiurge and the intelligible model. For both the Creator and the model, by converging upon themselves, constitute this "visible animal" [the world]. This inward-turning quality <note>original: "convergency"</note> connects the circle with a state of excellence, because the universe expresses as much as possible every unique characteristic of its model. And that is enough concerning these details.

If, however, we wish to investigate the cause of why a part of the universe was created to be similar to the whole, we will not lack arguments to show why it was made that way. This does not happen in all things. For it would not have been best for the eye to be created with a shape similar to that of the whole body, nor is that true of the heart or the head.² 

But where the "wholeness" exists prior to the "parts," it is possible for the parts to be like the whole, and for them to possess excellence through this similarity. On the contrary, where the whole is simply built out of its parts, the individual part does not possess excellence by being like the whole. The universe, however, is a "whole prior to parts"³—it is complete because it contains all the individual types <note>original: "partial genera"</note> within itself...

...of animals, according to the third species of wholeness,¹ as we have before observed. This is because the "Animal itself" <note>The Intelligible Animal, or the divine archetype of all living beings</note> is also a whole and is completely perfect as a monad <note>A single, unified entity</note>, yet it encompasses all intelligible animals through the previously mentioned tetrad <note>The four primary classes of living things: heavenly gods, birds, aquatic creatures, and land animals</note>.

> "He placed it also in the wisdom of the most excellent and powerful nature, so that it might follow that which is best, and distributed it in a circle about all heaven; causing it to be a *true world*, diversified through the whole of itself."

In what is said here, Plato speaks concerning the position of the stars. He explains that they are placed in circles on all sides within the revolution of the "Circle of the Same" <note>The outer sphere of the heavens that moves uniformly</note>, and that, as the poets say, they revolve in an orb around the heavens. Some of them are arranged in a different order from others, exhibiting an admirable variety. 

If, however, you wish to speak more grandly than this, you may say that the Demiurge <note>The divine craftsman of the world</note> placed the stars in the divine soul of the fixed sphere <note>original: "inerratic sphere," referring to the sphere of the fixed stars</note>, thus animating them and giving them their own proper life and intellect. In the same way, he inserted the planets into the orbits caused by the period of the "Circle of the Different" <note>The inner orbits of the planets, which move differently from the fixed stars</note>. Since these are divine animals, it is necessary that they should have an intellectual soul and a divine intellect. 

We can learn that they are not only animated by the Soul of the Universe, but that each also has a specific soul presiding over it, by considering the animals here on Earth. Among our animals, the most excellent are those that are not only animated by the total World-Soul but also have a specific individual soul that illuminates them with life. For instance, a human being is superior to animals that are only animated by the collective World-Soul and represent the final, lowest stage of the creation of things. 

Therefore, some animals are preserved in two ways <note>By both the World-Soul and an individual soul</note>, while others are barely preserved by the World-Soul alone. If this is true, and if celestial bodies are more excellent than our own bodies, they will be animated to an even greater degree by both the World-Soul and their own specific souls; this is because they are similar to the entirety of the heavens in which they revolve. But if this is the case, all of them move in a circle around their own centers. And if we admit this—and that every perpetual motion has a perpetually moving cause—then there are as many moving causes as there are bodies in perpetual motion (as Aristotle says). If this is true, it is necessary that each of the stars has its own specific soul by which it is moved. If they also move in an orderly manner, it is—

<meta>This page continues the analysis of the celestial bodies' relationship to the "Circle of the Same" and the "Circle of the Different." It explains why stars must possess divine, rational souls to maintain their orderly motion and how these individual souls relate to the universal World Soul.</meta>

<page-num>270</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.</header>

It is necessary that their souls should be intellectual <note>governed by higher reason or "nous"</note>; for if they moved in a disorderly manner—which we cannot rightly say about divine bodies—their souls would be irrational. Therefore, it is necessary that each of the stars should have a divine presiding soul. Through its own intellect, each star is united to the universal intellect that encompasses everything. For since even mortal bodies, such as our own, share in reason and intellect, what ought we to think of divine bodies themselves?

Each star, therefore, through its own soul, is placed within the motion <note>original: "lation," meaning the movement of a body from one place to another</note> of the "Circle of the Same." Plato very properly calls this circle *most excellent and powerful* because it governs all other rotations and revolves all of them through intellectual power. For just as the race of stars is revolved by the motion of the fixed sphere <note>original: "inerratic sphere," the outer shell of the heavens where stars stay in fixed positions relative to each other</note>, their individual souls are also contained by the single soul of the "Circle of the Same," and their intellects by its intellect. 

For again, it is necessary that the unity <note>original: "monad"</note> which is organized alongside a multitude of parts should exist in harmony with the higher Unity that stands apart from and above that multitude. Since the first of the four primary "Ideas" <note>the four classes of living beings: gods/stars, birds, water-dwellers, and land-dwellers</note> is the independent Unity, the vast number of stars arising from it is contained by the fixed sphere, which acts as a secondary, organized unity. 

Similarly, in each of the celestial spheres, the entire sphere acts as a unity, while the "cosmocrators" <note>original: "cosmocrators," meaning "world-rulers," often referring to the planets or the spirits governing them</note> are the leaders of the many beings within each. For in each sphere, a number of beings similar to the choir of the fixed stars exists within their own specific orbits. It is not surprising that while the fixed stars form a single unified whole, the planets are both a whole group and individual leaders. Because the motion of the "Circle of the Different" <note>the inner orbits of the planets, which move differently from the outer stars</note> is more varied, there are more individual leaders. 

In this way, the diversity of leaders increases as the "multitude" expands. In the sublunary region <note>the realm below the moon, including Earth</note>, there is an even greater number of leaders. For the unities in the heavens generate corresponding numbers of beings below them. 

As we have said, therefore, the act of giving life to the stars places them within their own specific souls. But it also connects them with the universal soul of the motion of the "Circle of the Same," raises them to the World Soul, and establishes them in the Intelligible Paradigm <note>the divine blueprint or "Form" of the universe</note> itself. The divine philosopher Iamblichus also clearly recognized this; he placed the wisdom of "that which is most excellent and powerful" within this divine blueprint. 

Furthermore, the fixed sphere was created as a *true world* because it is more properly a "world" <note>an ordered system</note> than the sublunary region, which always lacks its own order and is continually changing. The sphere of the fixed stars is a world so diverse that it expresses the variety of the divine mind, a variety which it receives uniformly throughout itself, imitating the beauty of the celestial paradigm...

patterns. To *distribute*, and to distribute in a circle, are actions suited to the fixed stars: for the latter signifies *intellectual distribution*, while the former signifies the *creator's order* <note>original: "demiurgic order," referring to the work of the Demiurge or divine craftsman</note>. On this account, theologians place Eunomia <note>the goddess of good order</note> in the fixed sphere <note>original: "inerratic sphere"</note>, as she separates the multitude within it and always preserves each of the stars in its proper order. Hence, also, when celebrating Vulcan <note>the Roman name for Hephaestus</note> as the maker of the heavens, they join him with Aglaïa <note>the Grace of Splendor</note>, as he adorns and gives brilliance and joy to all of heaven through the variety of the stars. 

And again, of the Seasons, they place Dice <note>Justice</note> over the planetary region, because it is just that irregularity should be reduced to regularity according to reason; but of the Graces, they place Thalia there, as she always causes their lives to be perfectly flourishing. They also give the oversight of the sublunary region <note>the area below the moon, including the Earth and its atmosphere</note> to Irene <note>Peace</note>, as she pacifies the war of the elements; but they give Euphrosyne, of the Graces, the role of granting to each element the ease of acting according to its nature.

> "But he adapted to each of them two motions. One is in the same place, according to the same things, through which they always intellectually perceive <note>original: "dianoetically perceive," meaning to think through a matter using reason</note> 'the same' about 'the same things.' But the other is a forward motion, driven by the dominance of the 'same and similar' circulation. He likewise rendered them immovable and stable regarding the other five motions, so that each of them might become as excellent as possible."

The discussion of motion follows the discussion of how these bodies are given life <note>original: "animation"</note>. Because each of the stars has a soul, each is also granted a specific motion. For the soul is the principle of motion. The discussion of motion is also connected to the theory of shape <note>original: "figure"</note>. For a body that has an appropriate circular shape, and receives this from the creator <note>original: "demiurgic cause"</note>, must necessarily have an activity and a circular movement <note>original: "lation"</note> adapted to that shape. 

Every natural body moves by its own essence, and not by accident; since nature is the principle of motion and change <note>original: "mutation"</note> in anything where it exists primarily by itself and not accidentally. The body of the stars, however, is immovable according to all other motions, as it is perpetual throughout all time. It is only capable of receiving local motion, and specifically circular motion, as it moves in its own place.
