<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the motions of the stars, specifically explaining why they possess both an individual rotation and a collective movement with the rest of the heavens.</meta>

<page-num>272</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.</header>

How can a star, through its own unique motion, share the same essence as the whole of heaven? And how else can it imitate the universe except by moving around its own center? It is necessary, therefore, for the stars to move with two types of motion: one that is intrinsic to them, around their own centers, and another that happens in harmony with the whole celestial system.

What, then, are these two motions? There are different opinions concerning them. Some say that both motions are physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note>, while others assert that one belongs to the soul <note>original: "psychical"</note> and the other is physical. It is better, however, to consider both the soul's motion and the physical motion as twofold. For the soul of these divine living beings <note>original: "divine animals," referring to the stars as living, ensouled entities</note> has its own distinct life, and through its own specific activity <note>original: "energy"</note>, it is connected with the <term>intelligibles</term> <note>the realm of pure, eternal ideas or forms that can only be understood by the mind</note>. In addition to this, it revolves together with the collective soul of the universe. In divine natures, those parts that function as individual units act according to their own powers while also acting in conjunction with the whole. 

Therefore, the soul of the stars moves in two respects. Likewise, the body of each star revolves around its own center—imitating the specific activity of its soul and its intellect—and is also moved with a forward-advancing motion. This latter motion imitates the cooperative activity of the soul of the fixed sphere <note>original: "inerratic sphere"</note> as it moves as a whole, and it reflects the way the intellect of this soul is established within the Universal Intellect. 

Thus, a twofold motion must be assumed for both the starry soul and the starry body. The starry soul is especially wise regarding the same eternal truths; it always perceives intellectually in the same manner, yet it also moves forward by following the movement of the whole. Because it participates in a more divine power, it returns to the very summit of the <term>intelligibles</term>, which act as leaders and exist before the soul, being apprehended and perceived by it. Similarly, the starry body moves toward the leading parts of the cosmos in harmony with the entire celestial circulation. However, it also has a perpetual motion originating from itself, which resembles <term>dianoetic</term> activity <note>rational or discursive thought; the process of reasoning from premises to a conclusion</note> and intellectual, eternal motion. Through its rotation in one place, it shares the same motion as the universe; but by always proceeding logically through the same cycles, it maintains a consistent purpose, participates in the same soul, and is always directed back toward the same intellect.

It is necessary, therefore, to divide the words of Plato according to these doctrines in the following way: He gave each of the stars two motions. One is in the same place and concerns the same things—by "the same," we understand the motion around the star's own center. Then, we must add that it is always thinking rationally <note>original: "dianoetically perceiving"</note>, perceiving within itself the same truths about the same things. For it is evident that the soul's motion, which is here...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the motions of the stars and celestial spheres, explaining how individual celestial bodies harmonize their specific movements with the universal rotation of the heavens.</meta>

<page-num>273</page-num>
<header>BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>
<sig>Tim. Plat. VOL. II. 2 M</sig>

...signified, has always a <term>dianoetic perception</term> <note>original: "dianoetic perception"; this refers to rational, discursive thought or the soul’s ability to reason through ideas</note> of true realities. For this is shown by the words, "*about the same things, and the same thing*." Unlike our human souls, the soul of a star does not think differently about the same subjects at different times. 

Furthermore, we must say that the **advancing motion** refers to the physical movement of the star, by which it passes entirely from one place to another. And afterward, when the text mentions making a stop, we must add: *Through the domination of the same and similar circulation*. He calls this circulation the motion of the circle of "**the same**" (the universal motion) belonging to the total soul of the universe. The soul of each individual star is governed by this universal motion, and by imitating it, the star is moved toward what lies ahead of it. This is truly what it means to be led by its own intellectual activities <note>original: "energies"</note> and to align <note>original: "co-assimilate"</note> itself with these divine cycles. 

It is clear, however, that this advancing motion only applies to things that move entirely from one place to another. For the stars themselves have an advancing motion, but the sphere of the fixed stars <note>original: "inerratic sphere"</note> does not, since it only rotates in a circle. Similarly, the planets move with an advancing motion, but the spheres that carry the planets do not move in that way <note>The original text corrected "planets" to "spheres of the planets" here for clarity</note>.

Again, we may see the order of these things by the number of their motions. The motion of the entire universe is uniform; the motion of the fixed stars has two forms; and the motion of bodies below the moon <note>original: "sublunary bodies"</note> is varied and lacks a definite pattern. For although each planet moves with a uniform motion, the mixture of many cycles—both the cycle specific to each planet and the one it shares with the sphere of the fixed stars—causes its movement <note>original: "lation"</note> to appear varied. 

It is necessary for the causes of variety and the principles of opposites <note>original: "contrariety"</note> to be contained within the heavens beforehand. Otherwise, how could the heavens contain the power of creation <note>original: "generation"</note>? How could they govern the changing nature of the elements on Earth unless they held the cause of opposites within themselves? 

However, because the heavens are immaterial (so far as this is possible for things perceived by the senses), the opposites within them are not hostile to one another and do not struggle. Instead, they exist together in harmony. The same celestial body is moved by two different circulations. Neither of these is a mere accident; both circulations are essential to its nature. In the heavens, nothing is an "accident" <note>in philosophy, an "accident" is a non-essential property, like hair color</note>, since everything there is immaterial and everything derives its existence from the divine craftsmanship <note>original: "fabrication," referring to the work of the Demiurge or Creator</note>. Therefore, both shape and motion are essential there. Since, therefore, the heavens are immaterial—by which I mean...

<summary>Proclus explains that stars possess both an individual rational soul and a physical motion that harmonizes with the universal rotation of the heavens. He argues that celestial variety and "opposites" exist in perfect harmony to govern the changes occurring in the world below the moon.</summary>

...that they are exempt from this <term>sublunary matter</term> <note>original: "sublunary matter"; refers to the physical matter found below the moon, which ancient philosophers believed was corruptible and unstable</note>, which is powerless <note>original: "inefficacious"</note>, possesses a false beauty, and is deformity itself. Since this is the case, they hold within themselves contrary motions simultaneously. For by existing outside of this sublunary matter (which cannot maintain stability), opposing forces meet in them and are united to each other. But in this sublunary matter, there are hostile conflicts because matter is too weak <note>original: "imbecility"</note> to receive the presence of both forms at once. This concludes the discussion concerning the motions of the stars.

<margin><image-desc>Vertical pencil mark in the margin alongside the start of the paragraph.</image-desc></margin>
It is clear, however, that the five motions which Plato removes from the <term>fixed stars</term> <note>original: "fixed stars"; stars that appear to stay in the same position relative to one another in the "inerratic" or un-wandering sphere</note> are: upward and downward, backward, and motion to the right and left. For he had previously removed the six motions from the <term>inerratic sphere</term>. To the fixed stars, however, he gave an "advancing" motion so that they might move along with the motion of the universe. But to the planets, he gives not only a direct advancing motion but also a <term>retrograde motion</term> <note>original: "retrograde motion"; the apparent backward movement of a planet through the sky</note>; for it is only because of this latter motion that they are said to "wander" <note>The word "planet" comes from the Greek word "planētēs," meaning "wanderer."</note>. Nor should we <insert>wonder</insert> if what he previously called "to the right hand," he now calls "to the front" <note>original: "anterior part"</note>. For in relation to the whole rotation <note>original: "circulation"</note>, it is toward the right; but in relation to the stars themselves, it is toward the front. 

And it seems that, so far as the world is one, it has one motion centered primarily on **Intellect** and wisdom. But because it is divided into the sphere of fixed stars and the planetary region, it has—through a twofold rotation—a motion to the right and to the left. Furthermore, because it contains individual living beings <note>original: "partial animals"</note>, both fixed and wandering, it has both direct and retrograde motions. The former is the motion of the fixed stars, while the latter belongs to the <insert>planets.</insert> It also seems, as far as it is possible to predict from these principles, that each of the fixed stars moves similarly to the inerratic sphere—about its own center—but rotating toward the west. In this way, as each star is moved by the whole sphere, it moves toward what is in front of itself. For according to nature, the direction in which a thing is moved is considered to be "in front" of that thing. Therefore, the direction in which each of the stars rotates is toward the west, so that its motion may be similar to that of its whole system. Just so, the east is "in front" of the planets, toward which they move according to their nature. 

An "advancing motion," therefore, belongs to the fixed stars and not to the planets. For there is something external to the former; since one thing in them is the leader, but the other follows.$^1$ The entire sphere of the fixed stars, however, transcends all <term>rectilinear motion</term> <note>original: "rectilinear motion"; movement in a straight line</note> and is moved only in a circle. You may also say that the planets have a unique motion, and that this is toward the east; but at the—

---

$^1$ That is: In the fixed stars, the whole sphere is the leader, but each individual star within this sphere follows the sphere itself.

<page-num>275</page-num>
# BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

At the same time, they orbit completely through the depth of their spheres. Likewise, the east is in front of them, but through the <term>inerratic sphere</term> <note>original: "inerratic sphere"; the outermost celestial sphere that carries the fixed stars and does not "wander" like the planets</note>, they have a <term>retrograde motion</term> <note>original: "retrograde motion"; an apparent motion of a planet in a direction opposite to that of other bodies within its system</note>, which is contrary to their own proper motion.

Of the six possible directions of motion, Plato ascribes to the fixed stars the one that moves toward the front. From this, you may infer that this motion is more honorable than the rest. As Aristotle says, the motion of the most excellent being is itself most excellent. Therefore, of all types of motion, local movement (change of place) is the best. Among local motions, the first is circular, and the second is the "advancing" or direct motion. This latter motion belongs to the fixed stars; however, each star remains immobile and stable regarding the other five directions of motion. Plato mentions both of these points so that you do not think this immobility is due to weakness, sluggishness, or a lack of something. Instead, you should understand that the fixed stars possess this stability because of their transcendent nature. This becomes evident from what follows, for he says it is "in order that each of them might become as much as possible most excellent."

If an immobility regarding the other five motions serves the ultimate end of the beauty and goodness of the celestial bodies, then it is not a lack of life or a deprivation. Rather, it is a power that holds mastery over variety. The circle of the inerratic sphere encompasses all motion, regardless of how it is carried out. The advancing motion of the stars within it clearly reveals the principle of moving forward in a straight line. Meanwhile, the variety of the planets conducts and governs all the unpredictability of the world of generation, moving it in every possible way through their orbits. Therefore, Plato ascribes this specific kind of motion to the fixed stars.

However, let those who claim the stars move in the **order of the signs** <note>original: "*consequentia*"; the direction following the sequence of the zodiac signs, from west to east</note>, or with a retrograde motion around the poles of the zodiac over a period of a hundred years—as Ptolemy and Hipparchus before him did, relying on observations—take note. The Egyptians before them used observations, and even before the Egyptians, the Chaldeans were taught by the Gods prior to making observations. These ancient groups held a similar opinion to Plato concerning the motion of the fixed stars. The <term>Oracles</term> <note>original: "Oracles"; likely referring to the Chaldean Oracles, a collection of philosophical and mystical revelations from the 2nd century AD</note> do not say it just once, but frequently speak of the "advancing procession" of the fixed stars. For they say:

> "The monthly course, and the starry advancing procession."

And again:

> "The advancing starry procession was not created for your sake."

The <term>theurgist</term> <note>original: "theurgist"; here referring to Julian the Theurgist, the reputed author of the Chaldean Oracles</note> likewise, in his doctrinal treatises, when speaking about the **third father**¹ says:

> "He established the numerous multitude of fixed stars, binding fire to fire. But he fixed them with a stability² free from any wandering motion."

In these words, he clearly testifies that the fixed stars move in the same place, and—

---

¹ This refers to Jupiter the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine creator or craftsman of the physical universe in Platonic thought</note>.
² For "fixed again" <note>original: *pēxe palin*</note> in this place, it is necessary to read "fixed the wandering" <note>original: *pēxē de planēn*</note>.

<summary>Proclus defends Plato's view that fixed stars possess a specific "advancing" motion and stability in other directions, citing ancient Egyptian, Chaldean, and oracular wisdom to support a divinely-ordered cosmos over purely observational astronomy.</summary>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

...about the same things; so that the opinion of Plato derives credibility from both. To this we may add that the observable phenomena are sufficient to convince anyone who has eyes to see. For it is evident that if the fixed stars moved around the poles of the zodiac with a retrograde motion <note>original: "retrograde motion"; an apparent backward movement through the signs of the zodiac, or westward</note>, the constellation of the Bear—which never sets in these regions and has been celebrated since the time of Homer as always shining in the same way—ought to have moved more than fifteen degrees, and not stayed around the pole of the equinoctial. The star Canobus <note>original: "Canobus"; now commonly spelled Canopus</note>¹ also should no longer appear to make a short circuit above the horizon to those living in the "third climate"²; but as Posydonius says, it ought to appear to those in Rhodes as passing right along the horizon. 

However, the Bear is always visible, and Canobus preserves the same position. Therefore, the motion of the fixed stars in <term>consequentia</term> <note>original: "consequentia"; moving in the "consequence" or order of the zodiac signs, i.e., eastward</note>, which is so highly celebrated by these modern thinkers, is not true. If they argue that the baneful motions of the planets and the calculations of birth charts <note>original: "nativity"; a horoscope or map of the sky at the time of a person's birth</note> prove this retrograde motion of the fixed stars, and they think they are speaking in agreement with the phenomena, we must tell them that those who do not hold this opinion also agree remarkably well with the phenomena. 

Furthermore, in creating rules for the motions of the planets and in studying the doctrine of birth charts, they do not actually need this hypothesis of the fixed stars moving in <term>consequentia</term>. The *men I particularly allude to are the Chaldæans* <note>original: "Chaldæans"; ancient Babylonian astronomers and astrologers famous for their long-term observations</note>, *who had observations spanning entire world-periods.* Why, then, should we accept as evidence the records of a few observations—views of a "juvenile" nature that lack great accuracy—when the vast, extended observations of the Chaldeans bear witness to the doctrine of the ancients concerning the motion of the fixed stars?⁴ For those who do—

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s defense of the stability of the fixed stars. He is responding to contemporary astronomers who used the "phenomena" (observed data) of precession—the slow shifting of the stars over centuries—to argue that the sphere of the fixed stars actually moves.</meta>

Those who believe this are unaware that it is possible to derive something true from false hypotheses. One should not assume that a conclusion which matches the phenomena <note>original: "phænomena"; the observable appearances or movements of the heavenly bodies</note> is sufficient proof that the hypotheses themselves are true.

> "And for this cause, such of the stars as are fixed <note>original: "inerratic"; stars that do not "wander" like planets</note> were generated, being divine living beings <note>original: "animals"; in the Platonic sense, an "animal" is any living being endowed with a soul</note>; and on this account, they always remain revolving in the *same* way. But the stars which both revolve and have a wandering motion, as we have before mentioned, were produced according to these same principles."

The cause of the stars' creation encompasses all their most essential principles: the model <note>original: "paradigmatic"</note>, the creator <note>original: "demiurgic"</note>, and the purpose <note>original: "final"</note>. It is from all these that the stars were created as they are, with the specific motions they possess. The sphere of the fixed stars exhibits a uniform motion that always proceeds in the same manner. Calling them *divine living beings* indicates that both intellect and a divine soul are present within them; and even prior to these is the "unity" or "oneness," according to which each star is a God. Because each is a living being, it has a soul by which it is moved; but because each is also a *divine* living being, it is dependent upon a divine intellect. For it is not intellect alone which—

<margin>
...with three motions: their own proper motion, the motion of the spheres that contain them, and the motion of the universe. However, he adds: my teacher Ammonius <note>the celebrated Ammonius Hermæas, who was the disciple of Proclus</note>, while observing the stars through an astrolabe while I was present in Alexandria, found that the star Arcturus had moved since the time of Ptolemy. It had moved exactly as much as necessary at a rate of one degree every hundred years. Therefore, it is more accurate to say that the starless sphere which contains all other spheres—which was unknown in the time of Aristotle—moves with one simple motion from the east, rotating all the other spheres along with it. But what we call the "fixed sphere" is moved by two motions: the motion of the universe from the east, and its own motion from the west. All the stars within it move with these two motions, as well as their own spinning motion. In the same way, the successive spheres and the stars within them move; the spheres have two motions, but the stars have three.
</margin>

I am, however, decidedly of the opinion of Proclus: that the records of a few observations and the views of a "youthful" science should not be used to oppose the vast, ancient observations of the Chaldeans. Their records embraced an entire "world period" <note>original: "mundane period"</note> of 300,000 years. What Proclus asserts here about the Chaldeans is also confirmed by Cicero in his first book *On Divination*, who says they had records of the stars for 370,000 years; and by Diodorus Siculus <note>*Historical Library*, book 11, page 118</note>, who says their observations spanned 473,000 years.

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

...makes it to be divine, since there are likewise angelic and demonic intellects. The divine intellect of this entire system differs from an intellect that is not divine in this way: it is dependent upon a deity, which is what causes it to be a divine intellect. But the *revolution always remaining in the same place* exhibits a permanence in the heavens, according to which the stars always occupy the same locations in the sky, moving about their own centers, and also possessing a fully realized energy and an unceasing life. 

Therefore, those who claim the stars are inanimate, or imagine that the souls of the celestial bodies are changeable like ours, or that they were created at a specific point in time, stray from the meaning of Plato. For if a certain living being <note>original: "animal"; in the Platonic sense, any entity with a soul is an animal</note> is divine, it must have a divine soul and is not merely animated by the "soul of the universe" alone. For the Earth itself is also a divine living being, since the Earth is the oldest and most venerable of the Gods; and there are likewise certain living things within it which possess <term>actualities</term> <note>original: "entelecheias"; the state of a thing whose essence is fully realized</note> derived from the soul of the universe alone, but these are not "living beings" <note>meaning they lack an individual soul of their own</note>. Furthermore, because the stars remain in motion forever, they did not acquire a soul at a specific time, nor will they ever lose it. For the term *always* demonstrates an immunity to change over time, regarding both the past and the future. This concludes the discussion concerning the fixed stars.

<margin>||</margin> Regarding the planets, however, Plato reminds us again that they have various motions, yet these are orderly and follow specific measures and boundaries. Their simplicity encompasses a multitude, their order connects their variety, and their measure defines their "wandering" <note>the word "planet" comes from the Greek word for "wanderer"</note>. 

What does Plato mean by reminding us of this, and what does it indicate to us? Some say it shows that although the planets in one respect surpass the fixed stars—insofar as they are assigned a ruling and <term>world-governing</term> <note>original: "cosmocratoric"</note> dignity in the universe and, as theologians say, an <term>unbound</term> <note>original: "azonic"; referring to gods who are not tied to a single sphere or "zone"</note> authority (for in each of the world-governors there is an "unbound" order of Gods)—yet at the same time, they are inferior to the fixed stars due to their wandering and the diverse variety of their motions. We also say there is nothing absurd in admitting that the same thing may both surpass and be surpassed by another, depending on the different ways they are viewed. But we should consider whether Plato, by speaking of the planets before the fixed stars and describing their order, motion, powers, periods, and <term>restorations</term> <note>original: "apocatastases"; the return of a planet to its original starting position</note>, and then resuming the mention of them after the fixed stars...

# BOOK 4: THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO

[He] does not do this because the discussion of the planets is secondary to that of the fixed stars, due to the complexity of their movements. <note>original: "variety of their motion"; footnote 1 notes that the Greek text should read "motion" (kinēseōs) rather than "commonality" (koinēseōs).</note> Therefore, it is a shared quality of both the fixed stars and the planets that all of them are "divine living beings." <note>original: "divine animals"; in Platonic philosophy, an "animal" is any entity composed of a body and a soul.</note> This is clearly stated about both groups. Specifically, it is said of the fixed stars that they move with a specific motion in the same place and around the same things. In contrast, it is said that the planets have "revolutions" as they travel through the heavens, just as he says now that they possess a revolving motion. 

From this, he clearly believes that the planets move closer to or further from the Earth by their own power. Their revolutions across the width of the sky are caused by their own forward movement, rather than being carried by external mechanisms like <term>evolvents</term> <note>hypothetical spheres used in ancient astronomy to explain planetary motion</note> or <term>epicycles</term> <note>small circles whose centers move around the circumference of larger circles</note>. This also stems from their singular nature, which possesses both a unified and a diverse motion. Through this nature, they move forward and backward, changing their paths during their revolutions in a spiral and multi-faceted way. 

Consequently, their <term>lation</term> <note>original: "lation"; the act of moving from one place to another</note> is threefold: 
1. The motion where they rotate around their own centers while also moving in terms of width and depth. 
2. Their circular rotation to the left, driven by their own individual spheres. <note>Footnote 2 notes that the Greek word for "spheres" (sphairōn) was omitted in the source but is necessary for the meaning.</note> 
3. The motion where they are carried by the "Circle of the Same" <note>the celestial equator, representing the uniform motion of the universe</note> as it overpowers the "Circle of the Different" <note>the ecliptic, representing the individualized paths of the planets</note>. 

This concludes the details on these points, which are theories specific to the philosophy of Plato.

If, however, you were to ask about the nature of the planets—both the stars themselves and their entire spheres—and whether the stars have the same nature as the spheres or a different one, we reply by returning to Platonic principles: that the whole of heaven is composed of all the elements. However, in one region, fire combined with earth is dominant, while in another, fire is combined with the "summit" <note>the highest or purest form</note> of water, and in another, fire with the summit of air. Because of these combinations, there is an immense variety. 

Therefore, some things in the heavens are more visible than others; these are the ones where fire is combined with solid matter. Others are less visible <note>original Greek: "aoratotera"; footnote 3 notes the original text mistakenly used "more visible" (aratōtera) here.</note>, and these are the ones where fire is combined with transparent radiance and the <term>diaphanous</term> <note>a material that is translucent or allows light to pass through</note>. For this reason, it is possible to see the bodies in the higher regions just as objects can be seen through the air. However, the bodies that combine fire with transparency overwhelm our sight through their extreme brightness. **If**

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, specifically discussing the nature of the elements in the heavens and how the motions of the planets—including their "satellites"—contribute to the creation and measurement of time.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE TIMÆUS [BOOK 4]

Indeed, <note>original: "however"; footnote 1 explains that the Greek should be read as "if indeed" rather than "if however" (reading *ei dē* for *ei de*)</note> these things are rightly asserted by us: the spheres of the stars properly have a more thin and transparent <note>original: "attenuated and diaphanous"</note> nature, while the stars themselves have a more solid essence. Fire predominates everywhere, and the power of fire characterizes all of heaven. 

However, the fire found there is neither burning <note>original: "caustic"</note>—since this is not even true of the highest sub-lunar elements, which Aristotle usually calls "fiery-formed"—nor is it destructive <note>original: "corruptive"</note> of anything, nor is it the opposite of earth. Instead, it shines with life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note> heat and the power to illuminate, possessing purity and transparent splendor. For intense heat <note>original: "the vehement"</note> is one thing, and pure light is another, as Socrates shows in the *Philebus*. Therefore, the fire found in the heavens is light; we should not confuse our discussion of it by focusing on the dense and dark fire of the region below the moon. In this way, the study of the planets will align with what has been said before.

There are, however, other divine living beings <note>original: "animals"; these are what the moderns call *satellites*.</note> following the orbits of the planets, and the seven planets act as their leaders. Plato includes all of these in his discussion here. For these also revolve and "wander" in the same way he previously mentioned regarding the seven planets. They revolve alongside their primary stars and complete their cycles <term>apocatastases</term> <note>the return of a celestial body to the same position; a full cosmic restoration</note> together with their guiding principles, just as the fixed stars are governed by the overall rotation of the unchanging <note>original: "inerratic"</note> sphere. 

He says these planetary bodies, created in harmony with the fixed stars, were made for the sake of generating time. They help produce it by introducing various measurements of time into the world through their irregular and eternal motion. Of these measurements, "Time" itself is the overarching whole, possessing one grand cycle <note>original: "periodic number"</note> that contains all various smaller cycles within it. 

When Plato asserts that the fixed stars rotate on their centers alongside their forward motion, he does not say they help produce time in the same way, even though they have their own cycles of restoration <note>original: "apocatastasis"</note> by which all of time is measured. Rather, discussing the planets from a physical perspective <note>original: "physiology"</note>, he focuses specifically on details where our senses can witness the varying motions of the planets. We cannot rely on our senses to understand the different mathematical ratios <note>original: "numbers"</note> of the fixed stars' motions or the long periods they take to complete their revolutions. Therefore, he specifically mentions that the planets were created for the sake of time because of the evidence we can actually see, as he himself points out.

***

<note>original: For ει δε (ei de - "if however") here, it is requisite to read ει δη (ei dē - "if indeed").</note>
<note>original: And these, as we have before observed, are what the moderns call *satellites*.</note>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, addressing the nature of fire in the celestial regions and the relationship between the fixed stars and the planetary spheres.</meta>

# BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 281

But we have already answered those who deny that the heavens consist of fire on the grounds that fire naturally tends to move upward. Therefore, it is necessary to remind them again—since they are so fond of arguing—that their reasoning is absurd. They are looking at the fire found here on Earth, which exists in a state outside of its natural place <note>original: "preternatural subsistence"</note>. For even if you consider the fire that exists immediately below the moon, moving upward is not its natural state; rather, its nature is to remain in its own place. Moving upward leads toward a natural state, but the motion itself is not the state of nature. For a body’s tendency toward health is not "nature" itself, but rather the state of being well; recovering from illness <note>original: "to be convalescent"</note> is only natural for a diseased body. Similarly, for fire that is not yet perfectly fire, it is natural to move upward; but for fire in its active state <note>original: "fire which is in energy"</note>, it is natural to remain on high. Once it is settled in that place, if it were to move at all, it would only move in a circle. But if it is true, as Aristotle says, that the highest part of the fire in the region below the moon <note>original: "sublunary region"</note> moves in a circle along with the *ether* <note>original: "*æther*"</note>, this demonstrates even more clearly that fire has a circular nature. For if this fire also always moves in a circle as much as it is able, it does so according to its nature. That which is against nature <note>original: "preternatural"</note> cannot be perpetual, and anything forced or violent is against nature. If, therefore, the fire immediately below the moon is of this kind, why do they doubt the nature of the heavenly bodies and so frequently point to the upward motion of fire?

Aristotle, however, asks why the sphere of the fixed stars is a single unit that contains many stars, while in each of the planetary spheres—which are numerous—there is only one star. The solution to this, according to his opinion, can be found in his own writings. But we have already said something about this, and now, in agreement with what was asserted before, we say that each of the planets is a "whole world," containing within itself many divine classes <note>original: "genera"</note> that are invisible to us. The visible star has leadership over all of these. In this way, the fixed stars differ from those in the planetary spheres: the fixed stars have one monad <note>original: "monad"; in this context, a single unifying principle or primary unit. The text notes this monad is the sphere of the fixed stars itself.</note> which serves as their "wholeness." But in each of the planetary spheres, there are invisible stars that revolve together with their spheres. Thus, in each planetary sphere, there is both a "wholeness" and a leader that is granted a distinct superiority <note>original: "exempt transcendency"</note>. Since the planets are secondary to the fixed stars, they require a twofold governing power <note>original: "prefecture"</note>: one that is more general <note>original: "total"</note> and another that is more specific <note>original: "partial"</note>. You may infer that there is a multitude of beings corresponding to each sphere by looking at the extremes: if the fixed <note>original: "inerratic"</note> sphere has a multitude corresponding to itself, and the Earth is the "wholeness" of all terrestrial things, then the same must be true for the spheres in between.

¹ And this one monad is the sphere of the fixed stars.

<header>PROCLUS ON THE</header>
<header>[ BOOK IV. TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 282</header>

If there are living beings <note>original: "animals"; in this context, the word refers to any "ensouled" being, including stars and divine entities</note>, it is necessary that each [intermediate] "wholeness" <note>A Neoplatonic term for a universal or complete entity that contains parts within itself</note> should entirely possess certain partial living beings coordinated with itself; it is through these that they are also called "wholenesses." These intermediate natures, however, are hidden from our senses, while the extremes are manifest: one of them through its transcendently luminous essence, and the other through its connection to us. If, likewise, partial souls are distributed <note>original: "disseminated"</note> among them—some around the sun, others around the moon, and others around each of the rest—and if, prior to these souls, daemons <note>original: "dæmons"; here meaning mediating spirits or guardian entities, not "demons" in the modern sense</note> complete the groups <note>original: "herds"</note> of which they are the leaders, then it is evidently well said that each of the spheres is a world. Theologians also teach us these things when they say there are Gods in each sphere who exist prior to the daemons, some of whom are under the government of others. For instance, they assert concerning our mistress the Moon, that the Goddess Hecate is contained in her, as well as Diana. Likewise, in speaking of the sovereign Sun and the Gods who are there, they celebrate Bacchus <note>Dionysus</note> as being present.

->The Sun's companion <note>original: "assessor"</note>, who with watchful eye surveys<-
->The sacred pole.<-

They likewise celebrate the Jupiter <note>Zeus</note> who is there, Osiris, the solar Pan, and others with which the books of theologians and theurgists <note>Those who practiced "divine work" or rituals to communicate with the gods</note> are full. From all this, it is evident that each of the planets is truly said to be the leader of many Gods, who fulfill its specific orbit <note>original: "peculiar circulation"</note>.¹ In this way, therefore, we resolve the doubt.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Book IV of Plato’s Timaeus. The discussion focuses on the hierarchical distinction between the fixed stars and the planets, categorized by their relationship to the "Circle of the Same" (Intellect) and the "Circle of the Different" (Soul/Nature), and concludes with a classification of the twelve primary mundane Gods.</meta>

<header>BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 283</header>

Based on what has been said, it is necessary to conclude one thing: that the fixed stars, according to Plato, are superior to the planets not only in their location but also in their dignity. Concerning the fixed stars, he says that the Demiurge <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the Creator or Divine Craftsman of the universe in Platonic philosophy</note> placed them within "the wisdom of the Circle of the Same." However, concerning the planets, he says that the Demiurge placed them in "the circulations made by the period of the Circle of the Different." <note>In the Timaeus, the "Circle of the Same" represents the uniform motion of the celestial equator (pure intellect), while the "Circle of the Different" represents the ecliptic and the varied motions of the planets.</note>

Thus, the fixed stars alone live in union with the intellectual life of the Circle of the Same. The planets, however, live according to the revolution of the Circle of the Different. This is entirely the case for the planets because, while they do rotate in conjunction with the fixed <note>original: "inerratic"</note> sphere, they also rotate together with the period <note>original: "period" (referring to the Greek text μετα δε της του θατερου περιοδου, meaning "along with the period of the different")</note> of the Circle of the Different. Therefore, if the fixed stars immediately participate in a more divine life, while the planets participate through the medium of a lower life, it necessarily follows that the former are of a superior dignity and the latter are subordinate.

From this, it seems—if we are to infer anything from these points—that the souls of the fixed stars possess both circles (for as Plato says, our souls also have the Circle of the Same and the Circle of the Different). Yet, they live more according to the former circle. For this reason, they live to a greater degree in union with the circle that resembles the whole soul of the universe. In contrast, the souls of the planets live to a greater degree according to the latter circle. Consequently, their bodies move with various motions and are placed within the revolutions of the Circle of the Different. These conclusions may also be reasonably made by those who look only at their motions, which is the specific focus of physical theory.

Similarly, the [Chaldean] theurgist <note>Julian the Theurgist, a 2nd-century figure believed to have received the Chaldean Oracles</note> teaches us concerning the wisdom of the fixed stars and the planets. Speaking of the creation of the fixed stars, he says: "The Father established the numerous multitude of fixed stars, not by a laborious or painful tension, but so that they might be moved <note>original: "πηξῃ δε πλανην ουκ εχουση φερεσθαι", meaning "to be carried by a fixing that has no wandering"</note> with a stability free of wandering motion." By using the word *established*, the theurgist reveals a motion that remains in the same state and according to the same laws. Concerning the planets, he says: "The Father made the planets six in number—"

---

That all the other mundane <note>worldly or cosmic</note> Gods exist within the twelve mentioned above, and that the first triad of these is demiurgic (or *creative*): Jupiter, Neptune, and Vulcan. The second triad is *defensive*: Vesta, Minerva, and Mars. The third is *life-giving* <note>original: "vivific"</note>: Ceres, Juno, and Diana. The fourth is *uplifting* <note>original: "elevating"</note> and *harmonizing*: Mercury, Venus, and Apollo. I say, if we unite this with the preceding theory, there is nothing in the ancient theology that will not appear admirably sublime and beautifully connected—accurate in all its parts, scientific, and divine.

<note>2. Instead of "πηξει δε πλανην ουκ εχουση χρωμενων" ("using a fixing that has no wandering"), it is necessary to read "πηξῃ δε πλανην ουκ εχουση φερεσθαι" ("to be carried by a fixing that has no wandering"), as corrected in Patricius's collection of the Chaldean Oracles.</note>

<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.</header>

...and for the seventh, he cast into the midst the fire of the sun, suspending their erratic motion in orderly zones. He calls the irregular <note>original: "anomalous"</note> nature of their motions *disorderly*, but the motion which governs the zones in which they are arranged, he calls *orderly disposed*. By this, he represents to us the conversion <note>original: "circumduction," meaning the act of leading or bringing around</note> of disorder into order. For the planets do not move irregularly because of weakness <note>original: "imbecility"</note>, as inanimate things do, but through the will of the powers that preside over them. He also shows us their different acts of intelligence <note>original: "intellections"</note>, which he calls "zones," through the order in which they are arranged. And he says that the apparent irregularity <gloss>1</gloss> of their bodies is led in a circle by these powers to an appropriate order, because each of them is preserved by their divine powers.

<margin>40 B 8 - C 3</margin>
> "But he designed <note>original: "machinated"</note> Earth to be our nurse. She is gathered <note>original: "conglobed"</note> around the pole that extends through the universe, and she is the guardian and creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> of night and day. She is the first and most ancient of the gods <gloss>2</gloss> born within the heavens."

The natural science <note>original: "physiology"</note> concerning the Earth is closely connected with the discussion of the motion of the stars. It is not that Timaeus only now creates the Earth through these motions—for he had already established it when he represented the world as consisting of all the elements, both the extremes and those in the middle—but because the consideration of the Earth contributes to the discussion of the progression of the planets and fixed stars, of time, and the temporal periods, since it was created as the guardian of night and day. <margin>True</margin> For all heaven dances around it and revolves in a circle about it; and as a physical body, the Earth is the center of the universe. We must distinguish between two types of centers: the indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> center is one thing, as in a geometrically true sphere, which encompasses the physical world on all sides and represents the power of the sphere (having an arrangement similar to the poles). The physical center is another thing, which nature established in the middle. All the stars move in a circle around this physical center and transmit their energies to it, and this physical center is what we call the Earth. Therefore, since Plato has spoken concerning the circulation of the heavenly bodies, he very properly joins to that discussion the study of the—

<header>BOOK IV.] THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO.</header>

...earth. Furthermore, according to another perspective, the nature of the earth acts as a mother to the celestial order. For just as Heaven produces things as a father, Earth produces them as a mother. All "meteors" <note>In this context, "meteors" refers to all atmospheric phenomena, such as rain, wind, and lightning, through which the cycle of life is completed.</note> derive their existence from Heaven, as if from a father who governs every material and changing essence from above. However, they also derive from Earth as a mother. Earth provides the physical matter for these atmospheric vapors from the substances that collect within her, just as Heaven gives them their structure and form <note>original: *morphē*</note>.

For this reason, Plato very appropriately pairs the discussion of the earth with that of the heavens. He looks at the very nature of things—the harmony and connection between the two—and examines how they are joined by their shared origins. Moreover, through the order of his discussion, he makes the power of analogy clear in reality. He does this by placing the discussion of the planets first and in the middle, and by delivering the discussion of Earth before that of other sublunary spirits <note>original: "dæmons." In Platonic philosophy, these are intermediate beings between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note>. In this way, the extremes become the beginning and the middle, and the middle parts are shifted into the order of the extremes; analogy is especially suited to accomplish this. In every way, therefore, the study of the Earth’s nature is inherently linked to the theory of the Heavens. This concludes the discussion regarding the order of these topics.

However, what is the Earth? Where does she come from? Why is she called our "nurse," and why is she the "most ancient and first of the Gods"? If we can understand these questions, we will have a sufficient theory about her for our current purpose. Earth, then, originates primarily from the "intelligible earth," which contains all the divine orders of the Gods as a single unity and is eternally established in the "Father" <note>This refers to the "Father" as the concepts of *ether* or *limit*, which form the highest level of the divine intellectual hierarchy.</note>. It also originates from the "intellectual Earth" which is paired with Heaven and receives everything Heaven produces. Because it is analogous to these higher realities, it also remains perpetually in the center of the heavens. Being surrounded on all sides by them, it is full of generative power and creative <note>original: "demiurgic," referring to the Demiurge or divine craftsman</note> perfection.

The true Earth, therefore, is not merely this physical and dense material mass. She would not be "the most ancient of the Gods" simply because of her physical size, nor would she be the first of the Gods arranged within the heavens. Nor is she merely the soul of this physical body. She would not be, as Plato says, "extended around the pole of the universe," since that describes the body of the earth, not the soul. But if it is necessary to speak the highest truth concerning her:

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, Book IV. Proclus is arguing that the Earth is not merely a lump of matter but a "divine animal"—a living, rational being with its own soul and intellect, which serves as a nurturing force for all life on its surface.</meta>

<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.</header>

...the Earth is a living being <note>original: "animal." In Platonic philosophy, "animal" refers to any "animated" or living thing (from the Latin *anima*, meaning soul), including plants and the planet itself.</note> consisting of a divine soul and a living body. Therefore the whole Earth is, as **Plato** says, a living being. For within it, there is an immaterial and separate intellect; a divine soul dancing around this intellect; an ethereal body directly suspended from the soul that gives it form; and finally, this visible physical mass. This mass is filled with life in every part by the "vehicle" <note>original: *ochēmatos*. In Neoplatonism, the "ochēma" or "astral vehicle" is a subtle, intermediate body that connects the immortal soul to the physical body.</note> of this soul. Being filled with this vehicle, the Earth generates and nourishes all kinds of living beings. For some living beings are rooted in it (like plants), while others move about upon it (like animals and humans).

**Aristotle**, recognizing this as well, was ashamed not to grant the Earth a natural life. For how is it that plants live while they remain in the earth, but die when separated <note>original: "divulged," here meaning uprooted or detached</note> from it, unless this earthly mass was already full of life? It is also necessary to assume as a universal principle that "wholes" are given life before "parts." For it would be ridiculous if a human being participated in a rational soul and intellect, but no soul were assigned to the Earth and the air—a soul that sits above <note>original: "supernally riding in"</note> and governs the elements, keeping them within their proper boundaries. For "wholes," as **Theophrastus** says, would have less authority than "parts," and eternal things would have less power than those that can decay <note>original: "corruptible natures"</note>, if they lacked a soul. Therefore, we must admit that both a soul and an intellect exist in the Earth; the soul makes it fertile, while the intellect holds it together at the center of the universe.

Earth herself, therefore, being a divine living being, is also full of intellectual and soul-based <note>original: "psychical"</note> essences and immaterial powers. For if an individual soul has an immaterial vehicle in addition to its material body—as we have shown elsewhere—what should we think of a soul as divine as that of the Earth? Is it not true that, by a much greater priority, visible bodies are connected to this soul through other vehicles acting as intermediaries? And is it not through these that the visible bodies are able to receive the light of the soul?

Since this is the nature of Earth herself, she is said to be our "nurse." First, she possesses a power that is in some way equal to that of **Heaven**. For just as Heaven contains divine living beings within itself, Earth is seen to contain terrestrial living beings. Secondly, she is our nurse because she inspires our lives from her own specific life. For she does not only produce fruits and nourish our bodies through them, but she also fills our souls with her own light. Because she is a divine living being and the creator of us—who are individual living beings—she nourishes and holds our physical mass together through her own body, but she perfects our souls through her own soul. Likewise, by her own intellect, she awakens the intellect that is within us; and thus, according to the whole...

<note>For according to **Plato**, plants are also considered "animals" (living beings) because they possess life.</note>

<summary>Proclus argues that the Earth is a "divine animal" possessing its own intellect and soul, which acts as a "nurse" to humans by nourishing both our physical bodies and our rational minds.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, Book IV. Proclus is explaining how the Earth acts as a "nurse" to living beings and discussing its physical and metaphysical position at the center of the universe, specifically addressing the Greek terminology used to describe its stability.</meta>

<header>BOOK IV.] TIMAEUS OF PLATO.</header>

By her own nature, the Earth becomes the nurse of our entire makeup. On this account, it appears to me that Plato calls her our "nurse," indicating by this her intellectual power to provide nourishment. For if she is our nurse, and we are truly souls and intellects, she will—in those respects especially—be the one who perfects our essence, moving and stimulating our intellectual part. 

However, being a divine living being <note>original: "animal." In this context, it refers to a being with an "anima" or soul.</note> and containing within herself many individual living beings, she is said by Plato to be clustered <note>original: "conglobed"</note> about the pole which extends through the universe; this is because she is held and compressed around its axis. In this sense, the axis is also called the "pole." The term "pole" is used here because the universe revolves around it. However, because the pole (strictly speaking) is a single, indivisible point, while the axis is a "pole with interval" (just as one might say a line is a moving point), Plato says the pole "extends through the universe,"¹ as it passes entirely through the center of the Earth.

But the word *illomenēn*,² <note>original: ἰλλομένην</note> which he uses here, reveals that which is clustered and held together. It does not mean "that which is moved," as Aristotle mistakenly supposed. For Plato specifically maintains that the Earth is immovable; in the *Phaedo*, he adds the reason why it is established without motion:

> "For he says that an object which is balanced, when placed in the center of a uniform environment, cannot move more or less in any one direction. Instead, existing in a state where it is equally affected on all sides, it will remain free from any tendency to tilt."

The Greek usage of words also confirms that *illomenēn* signifies *synagomenēn* <note>original: το συναγομενην</note>—that which is gathered or clustered—and not that which is moved. For the Greeks call bonds *illadas* <note>original: ἰλλάδας</note>. Timaeus himself likewise says in a later passage "that the hairs which are rooted and clustered <note>original: "conglomerated"</note> in the head, within the skin, are 'compacted' (*illesthai* <note>original: ἴλλεσθαι</note>)." From these examples, it is evident how he applies the word *illesthai* to the Earth in this current passage. 

Furthermore, if (as some say) the statement that "Vesta alone remains in the house of the Gods"³ refers to this Earth, then Plato is very far from suggesting the Earth moves. Even if we do not admit that the Vesta mentioned there is the Earth itself, it must still be granted that there is a guardian power in the Earth with the nature of Vesta. For just as we say that in the Heavens, the poles⁴ are held together by Vesta, the same is true among the elements.

---

¹ Plato says *dia pantos* (through all), and not *dia tou pantos* (through the whole): for Proclus observes that he could not have used the latter phrasing without a specific "soft breathing" sound in the pronunciation.
² See what is said by Simplicius concerning this word in the notes to my translation of Aristotle’s treatise *On the Heavens*, p. 236.
³ This is asserted in Plato’s *Phaedrus*.

# PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS [BOOK IV.

the **Earth**. Just as the super-worldly **Vesta** <note>Vesta is the Roman equivalent of Hestia, the goddess of the hearth and stability</note> is related to the great leader of the twelve Gods <note>likely referring to Jupiter/Zeus</note>, so in the physical world is the **Earth** related to the **Heavens**. Similarly, if we direct our attention to the **Pythagorean Timaeus** <note>the character in the dialogue or the text attributed to him</note>, we will find even more reason to deny that the **Earth** moves. For he says "that the **Earth** is established in the middle." And how is it reasonable to interpret the word *illomenēn* <note>original: ιλλoμενην - typically meaning "wound" or "turned"</note> as meaning *eiloumenēn* <note>original: ειλoυμενην - "revolving"</note>, thereby claiming the **Earth** revolves, while staying consistent with the doctrine of **Plato**?

Let **Heraclides Ponticus**—who was a student of **Plato**—hold that opinion; for he did attribute a circular motion to the **Earth**. However, let it be admitted that **Plato** himself established it as immovable. For if he had defined the "perfect year" to consist not only of the eight planetary periods but had also counted the earth as the ninth, giving it a cycle of return <note>original: "apocatastasis" – the completion of an astronomical cycle or restoration to a starting point</note> alongside the others, and forming one grand cycle from all of them together with the "circle of the same" <note>the celestial equator</note>, then we might understand the **Earth** as moving according to **Plato**. Since he did not do this, we should instead interpret the pole, the axis, and the **Earth** that is held around them in a different way.

It is necessary, based on these statements, to turn to the nature of the **Earth** and view the poles as powers that grant stability to the universe. These powers draw the entire physical mass toward an "intellectual love" <note>a Neo-Platonic concept of the physical world being attracted to the divine</note>, connecting that which is divisible and uniting without gap that which is extended through space. 

This is why **Plato**, in the ***Republic***, describes the spindle of **Lachesis** <note>one of the Fates</note> as being made of adamant <note>an indestructible, diamond-like legendary stone</note>, signaling, as we have said, their inflexible and untamable power. We must also consider the axis as a single divinity that brings together the centers of the universe; it binds the whole world together and drives the divine orbits. It is the center around which all whole things dance and revolve, sustaining all of **Heaven**. For this reason, it is called **Atlas**, as it possesses an unchanging and tireless energy. 

The word *tetamenon* <note>original: τεταμενoν</note>, or *extended*, used here by **Plato**, indicates that this single power is **Titanic**, guarding the circulation of the entire universe. But if, as the divine **Iamblichus** says, we take "the pole extended through the universe" to mean the **Heavens**, we still remain faithful to **Plato's** thought. For as **Plato** says in the ***Cratylus***, those skilled in astronomy call the **Heavens** the "pole" because of their harmonious revolution. According to this view, you may call **Heaven** the pole extended...

### BOOK IV: PLATO’S TIMAEUS

...through the universe, as being curved through the whole of itself because it is without angles <note>meaning it is spherical</note>. For in this way, the surface of a circle is extended. Around this, however, the **Earth** is shaped into a sphere—not just in terms of its location, but through a desire to become like the Heavens, converging toward the middle. This happens so that just as **Heaven** moves around the center, the **Earth**, by tending toward the center, may become similar to that which is essentially spherical, making itself as much of a sphere as possible. Hence, she is compressed by **Heaven** in such a way as to be entirely extended toward it.

<margin>—</margin>
According to each of these concepts, therefore, **Plato** explains the cause by which the **Earth** is held in the middle. The axis is a power that connects the **Earth**, and the **Earth** is compressed on all sides by the circulation of **Heaven**, being pulled together into the center of the universe. The **Earth** being such, **Timaeus** afterward clearly shows what use she provides to the universe; for he calls her the "guardian and maker of day and night." And indeed, it is evident that she is the maker of night. For she produces a conical shadow <note>the Earth's shadow in space which creates night</note>, and her size and shape are the causes of the dimensions and quality of that shadow. 

But in what way is she also the maker of day? Or does she not produce this "day" which is joined with night? For it is around her that the sunrises and sunsets are observed. It is clear that **Plato** assumes this "day" is intertwined with night, as he places the former under the latter; just as he said earlier, *“night, therefore, and day were thus generated.”* The **Earth**, therefore, is the maker of both, producing both in conjunction with the **Sun**; the **Sun** is the primary cause of day, but the **Earth** is the cause of night.

Being the maker, she is also their guardian, preserving their boundaries and their opposition to each other, as well as their increases and decreases according to a certain proportion. Because of this, some name her **Isis**, as she equalizes inequality and brings the increase and decrease of both day and night into a proper ratio. Others, looking to her fertile power, call her **Ceres** <note>original: "Ceres" – the Roman name for Demeter, goddess of agriculture</note>, such as **Plotinus** <note>a major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD)</note>, who calls the intellect of the **Earth** "**Vesta**" <note>Hestia, goddess of the hearth and stability</note>, but the soul of it "**Ceres**." 

We, however, say that the first causes of these divinities are intellectual, ruling <note>original: "hegemonikas" (ηγεμονικας). The original text notes that "daimonikas" (δαμονικας – demonic/spirit-like) should be read as "hegemonikas" (ruling/governing).</note> and liberated; but from these causes, illuminations and powers extend to the **Earth**. Hence, there is a terrestrial **Ceres** and **Vesta**, and a terrestrial **Isis**, in the same way that there is a terrestrial **Jupiter** <note>Zeus</note> and a terrestrial **Hermes**. These earthly deities are arranged around the single divinity of the **Earth**, just as a multitude of celestial gods proceeds around the single divinity of the **Heavens**. For there are progressions and endings of all the celestial...

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

The Gods descend into the Earth; and all things exist in her terrestrially, just as they are contained in the heavens celestially. For the intellectual Earth receives the fatherly powers of Heaven and contains all things in a generative manner. Thus, we say that there is a terrestrial Bacchus and a terrestrial Apollo, who is the source of prophetic <gloss>1. original Greek: *mantika* (prophetic)</gloss> waters in many parts of the earth, and of openings in the ground which predict future events. But the healing <gloss>2. original Greek: *paioniai* (Paeonian/healing)</gloss> and judicial powers which proceed into the Earth render other places of a purifying or medicinal nature. It is impossible, however, to enumerate all the other powers of Earth, for divine powers are indeed inexplicable. But the orders of angels and demons <note>original: *dæmons*; in this context, these are intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil</note> that follow these powers are even more numerous; they are assigned to the whole earth in cycles and dance around its one divinity, its one intellect, and its one soul.

It remains, in the next place, for us to examine how Earth is said to be the "most ancient" and the "first of the Gods" within the heavens. This will be taken literally by those who are accustomed to looking only at its material, gross, and dark bulk. But we, indeed, grant them that there is such a material element in the bulk of the Earth; however, we think it proper that they should also look to the other benefits of the Earth through which it surpasses the privileges of the other elements—namely, its stability, its generative power, its harmony with the heavens, and its position in the center of the universe. 

For the center has great power in the universe as the point that connects every rotation. Hence, the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras who held specific mystical views on numbers and cosmology</note> call the center the "tower of Jupiter," because it contains within itself a demiurgic <note>original: *demiurgic*; relating to the Demiurge or the divine craftsman of the world</note> guard. We shall likewise remind our opponents of the Platonic hypotheses concerning the earth mentioned by Socrates in the *Phaedo*. There, he says that the place where we live is hollow, dark, and bound by the sea; but that there is another "true earth" containing the dwellings of the Gods and possessing a beauty resembling that of the heavens. 

We ought not, therefore, to wonder if the Earth is now called the "most ancient" and the "first of the Gods" within the heavens, since she possesses such great altitude and such surpassing beauty. As Socrates later says, she was fashioned by the Demiurge to resemble a sphere covered with twelve skins <note>referring to the dodecahedron, a 12-sided geometric solid</note>, just as the heaven, according to the *Timaeus*, was painted by the Demiurge to be similar to a dodecahedron. We must likewise understand that the Demiurge gave to Earth alone among the elements the ability to contain all the elements separately, causing her to be an entire world, variegated in a way analogous to the heavens. For she contains a river of fire, of air, and of water, and of another "earth" which has the same relationship to her as she has to the universe, as...

# BOOK IV.] THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO.

Socrates says in the *Phaedo* <note>original: Phædo</note> that if this is the case, the Earth greatly surpasses the other elements by imitating the heavens and possessing within herself in a terrestrial way everything that is contained in the heavens in a celestial way.

To this we may also add that the Demiurge <note>original: Demiurgus; the divine craftsman or creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy</note> produced these two elements—earth and fire—first; he created the other elements for the sake of these two, so that they might act as bonds <note>the mathematical or structural links between the extremes of fire and earth</note> between them. All four elements exist both in the heavens and in the sublunary <note>the region below the moon, consisting of the Earth and its atmosphere</note> region. However, in the heavens they take on a fiery characteristic because fire predominates there, as Plato says. In the sublunary region, they take on a terrestrial quality. For the depth of the air and the vastness of the water are spread around the earth and possess many earthly properties, which is why they are naturally dark. Therefore, fire predominates in the heavens, but earth predominates in the sublunary region. 

Since, however, the realm of generation <note>the world of physical change, birth, and decay</note> is naturally linked with the heavens, the "end" of the heavens is the earth (meaning the moon), insofar as there is an "earthly" element in the heavens. Conversely, the "beginning" of generation is fire, as it exists within the world of change. For it is common to call the moon "Earth," as it has the same relationship to the Sun that the Earth has to fire.

> "But [the Demiurge]," says Orpheus, "fashioned another infinite earth, which the immortals call *Selene* <note>original Greek: the moon</note>, but those on earth call *Mene* <note>another ancient Greek name for the moon</note>."

It is also common to call the highest point of the realm of generation "fire." Aristotle does this when he calls the ether "fire." In other places, however, he does not think it proper to call ether fire, but rather "fiery-formed," as we have often noted. Therefore, the lowest part of the heavens is not entirely free from change <note>original: mutation</note> because of its closeness <note>original: propinquity</note> to the realm of generation; at the same time, the beginning of the realm of generation moves in a circle, imitating the heavens.

Furthermore, we must consider that we should not judge the worth <note>original: dignity</note> of things by their location, but by their powers and essence, as we have shown elsewhere. By what characteristics, then, should we judge what is superior? What others but those shown by the divine orders? For true superiority belongs to the Gods. From the divine orders, therefore, we must recognize certain powers: the monadic <note>unified or single</note>, the stable, the all-perfect, the prolific <note>fruitful and productive</note>, the connective, the perfective, the all-extended, the life-giving <note>original: vivific</note>, the adorning, the assimilative <note>making things similar to the divine</note>, and the comprehending power. These are the characteristics of all the divine orders. According to all these qualities, however, Earth surpasses the other elements, so that she may justly be called the most ancient and the first of the Gods.

Again, a twofold nature of things may be observed: one according to "progression," which always makes secondary things subordinate to those that came before them; and the other according to "conversion" <note>the return of an effect back to its divine cause</note>...

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

...which joins the extremes to the primary natures through similarity, and creates one continuous circle of the entire world of generation <note>original: generation; the realm of physical birth, change, and decay</note>. Since the world is also spherical—and a figure of this kind is characteristic of things that exist according to conversion <note>original: conversion; the Neoplatonic concept of an effect "turning back" toward its divine cause</note>—Earth must likewise be joined to the heavens within it, through one circle and one similarity. In this way, the center is most similar to the poles. For while the heavens entirely encompass all wholes by moving around the poles, the Earth is assigned a permanent place at the center. <margin>||</margin>For in the realm of generation, it is appropriate that what is immovable should be considered more "ancient" <note>meaning more fundamental or higher in the divine hierarchy</note> than what is moved. Therefore, based on all these concepts, it can be said that *Earth*, as the counterpart to *Heaven*, is the most ancient of the Gods within the heavens. She is within them because she is encompassed by them on all sides. Just as the Demiurge <note>the divine craftsman</note> fashioned the whole of physical nature within the soul of the world, he also built the Earth within the heavens, compressed and contained by them, and working together with them to create the whole.

However, insofar as she is the *first* of the Gods, she shows a sign of transcendence in her essence; but insofar as she is the *most ancient*, she exhibits the high status she has been assigned. For how is it possible not to admit that she is assigned a great portion in the world and is very honorable, since within her are the "tower of Jupiter" <note>original: Jupiter (Zeus); likely referring to the core or central guard-post of the universe</note> and the "progression of Saturn" <note>original: Saturn (Cronus)</note>? For not only is Tartarus—which is the furthest extremity of the earth—surrounded on all sides by Saturn and the Saturnian power, but so is everything else conceived to be below this. For Homer says that this region is held together by the "sub-Tartarean" Gods. He does not mean that he places Gods physically beyond Tartarus, as the words might suggest; rather, he means that Tartarus itself is encompassed by them on every side.

Furthermore, we can examine the analogy between our Earth and the "Intellectual Earth" <note>The divine, archetypal reality of Earth in the realm of pure Intellect</note>. Just as the Intellectual Earth contains and gives life to the "perfective," "guardian," and "Titanic" orders of Gods (of which the Orphic theologians <note>followers of the mystical teachings attributed to Orpheus</note> write extensively), our Earth likewise possesses various powers. As a nurse, she imitates the "perfective" order, which is why the Athenians are accustomed to call her *kourotrophos* <note>original: κουροτρόφος</note>, or *the nourisher of youth*, and *anesidora* <note>original: ἀνησιδώρα</note>, or *the one who sends up gifts*, because she produces and nourishes plants and animals. But as a guard, she imitates the "guardian" order; and because she is gathered around the pole that is *extended* <note>original: τεταμένη; tetamené</note> through the universe, she imitates the *Titanic* order. Since the Intellectual Earth generated Aigle and the Hesperian Erytheia <note>original: Erithya</note> before other divinities, our Earth is also the creator of day and night. The similarity between the latter and the former is evident.¹ And this is enough regarding these particulars.

# BOOK IV.] THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

If you are also willing to understand in another way that she [Earth] is the first and most ancient of the Gods—since she derives her existence <note>original: subsistence</note> from the first and most ancient causes—this reasoning will also be likely true. This is because primary causes extend their activities <note>original: energies</note> to the furthest reaches of things; furthermore, the last things in existence often mirror the pattern of the first, because they receive their order from them alone. Thus, Plato's claim is true in every way, whether you choose to look at the physical mass of the Earth or the powers she contains. 

It is also necessary to consider that the word *machinated* <note>original: machinated; from the Greek 'memēchanēmenē,' suggesting a clever, purposeful, or artificial design</note> testifies to the great intellectual power employed in the creation <note>original: fabrication</note> of the Earth. We find that neither the Sun by itself is able to create night and day, nor can the Earth alone (for the lack of light is one thing, but "night" is another). Instead, the production of both through the Sun and the Earth is the work of a divine design <note>original: demiurgic machination; the purposeful crafting by the Demiurge, or Creator-God</note>. The placement of the Earth in the center, the "dance" of the Sun, and the rotation of the sphere of fixed stars around it produce days and nights for the Earth. Furthermore, the Earth's position in the center ensures that the change of nights and days is consistent; this would not be the case if someone moved the Earth from its situation in the middle and established it elsewhere. These things, and many more besides, can be understood through this word "machination."
