<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, Book IV. Having previously discussed the Earth's central role in the cosmos and its divine nature, Proclus now addresses why Plato avoids detailed astronomical calculations and how to interpret the metaphorical "dances" and "motions" of the stars.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.

...hypotheses and astronomical <note>original: astrological</note> observations in which they do not speak in accordance with Plato. This is because the philosopher currently avoids discussing these details, as a great work still remains to be accomplished and it is not proper to dwell on these specific things. For astronomy is one thing, and natural science <note>original: physiology; here meaning the study of the physical nature of things</note> is another, as Aristotle also determines in the second book of his *Physics*. 

To this may be added that much time is required, first to study these things through images <note>original: models or representations</note>, and only afterward to explain the reasons for them. For, as he says, to speak about them without studying their physical models is a useless effort. It is necessary to behold these divine bodies with the abacus,¹ the armillary sphere,² the model globe,³ and the astrolabe,⁴ and thus betake ourselves to the theory of the entire universe. Observation is likewise necessary, which instruments provide to those who are skilled in these matters. For these reasons, therefore, the philosopher avoids the discussion of these specific details.

What he says now, however, must be considered in two ways: mathematically and philosophically. It pertains both to the physical and the soul-governed <note>original: psychical</note> motions of the stars. If you are willing, let us first consider the *measured motions* or *dances* of these divine bodies mathematically, and then philosophically. By these "dances," therefore, we must understand their orderly and harmonious orbits <note>original: circulations</note>, for the sake of which Plato inserted the discussion of the Earth. For he does not say that the Earth, being formed into a globe <note>original: conglobed</note>, dances, but that the stars dance around the Earth. For they dance while being moved with one harmonious motion around the same center. 

By their *concursions* <note>original: meetings or conjunctions</note>, we must understand their alignments in longitude, even when they differ in latitude or depth—meaning their joint risings and settings. The "*revolutions and advancing motions of their circles*" signify their direct and retrograde motions. In their direct motions, they proceed to their restorations <note>original: apocatastases; the return of a planet to its original starting position</note>; but in their retrograde motions, they appear to circulate among themselves. He refers here to the planetary spheres as "circles" according to which the stars move, rather than "epicycles" <note>original: small circles whose centers move around the circumference of larger circles</note>. For he nowhere mentions these, nor does he mention the "eccentrics" <note>original: circles whose center is off-center from the Earth</note> of the circles. For it would be ridiculous to suggest there are certain little spheres moving in each main sphere with a motion contrary to it, or to admit that they are parts of a sphere encompassing—

¹ A mathematical table on which the ancients drew lines and figures.
² In the original, *on the ringed sphere* <note>original: επί της κρικωτής σφαίρας</note>, which is clearly what moderns call the *armillary sphere*.
³ By the "paradigm" <note>original: model</note>, I suppose Proclus means an astronomical globe, or what is now called the celestial globe.
⁴ The astrolabe is a mathematical instrument representing nearly the entire celestial system on a flat surface, which is why it is also called a *planisphere*.

--- Page 301 ---
<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Book IV of Plato’s Timaeus. It follows a discussion of the "dances" or orbits of the stars, arguing that their complex movements are not the result of mechanical "eccentric" circles but are directed by the souls that inhabit them.</meta>

[...danc]ing indeed around the center, but not moving about it. For this would violate the common axiom of physics: that every simple motion is either *around* the middle of the universe, *away* from the middle, or *toward* the middle. But this hypothesis of "eccentrics" <note>An astronomical theory where celestial bodies move in circles whose centers are not the Earth</note> either divides the spheres into arcs moved in opposite directions—thereby destroying the continuity of each sphere—or it introduces circles to the celestial bodies that are of a different nature than the bodies themselves. This would connect motions from things that are dissimilar and lack any "sympathy" or natural connection with each other, due to the difference in their compositions.

It is necessary, however, to consider whether these things actually exist in this way. We must give our opinion on this subject, which requires much discussion. Plato attributes different movements to the stars without requiring mechanical contrivances of this kind, as he considers them unworthy of a divine essence. Instead, it is necessary to see this variety as stemming from the motion of the souls that give them form <note>original: informing souls</note>. Their bodies are moved faster or slower according to the will of these souls, and not—as the common people think—because of any physical weakness <note>original: imbecility</note>. This inequality and diversity of motion is also carried out in orderly cycles of time. The stars themselves move around their own centers while proceeding in various ways through their specific spheres. In this way, because they are intermediaries between bodies that are <term>inerratic</term> <note>fixed stars that do not "wander" or change their relative positions</note> and those that move in a straight line, they may have a mixed motion. They are carried along according to height and depth, and with both forward and retrograde motion, all within regular cycles of time. For Plato says that, “the stars, as they advance through the heavens, have their own revolutions.” But if they proceed *through* the heavens, it is evident that all of them move through the depth of their spheres. For bodies that travel through a certain space do not stay in one spot but pass from one part of that space to another. Furthermore, if they have rotations, then their various changes are the revolutions they make within their spheres according to breadth and depth.

The spheres themselves, however, only move toward the east, and not around the same poles as the sphere of the fixed stars. In the *Republic*, Plato describes the single axis of these spheres as a "distaff" and the poles of the eight spheres as "spindles." He says that there is one simple motion around these, just like the motion of the sphere of the fixed stars. Later in that same dialogue, he says that the Fates <note>The three goddesses of destiny: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos</note> preside over these circles, and that a different Fate moves each one differently. Here in the *Timaeus*, however, he rotates one of the spheres laterally and the other diagonally <note>original: diametrically; referring to the motion of the "Other" along the ecliptic</note>, in the same way as the "circles of the soul" <note>The "Same" and the "Other," the two components of the World Soul described earlier in the Timaeus</note>, in which he established the causes of the whole spheres themselves and the planets. For this reason, he moved them obliquely, following a diagonal path. Thus he says that some of the planets move in a similar way, while others move dissimilarly, in the same manner as the spheres. The difference, therefore...

Such, therefore, is the construction <note>original: fabrication</note> of the sphere according to Plato: the seven spheres have a joint revolution and possess that difference which we have mentioned regarding the single circulation of the <term>inerratic sphere</term> <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, so called because they do not "wander" or change position relative to each other.</note>. In accordance with this, the fixed stars move only around their own centers; but the planets both move around their centers and proceed through the depth of the spheres in which each is placed, revolving in various ways upward and downward, and with a retrograde motion <note>The appearance of a planet moving backward in the sky.</note>. Each of these, as well as their poles, moves in another circle around the zodiac <margin>For *around the oblique* here, it is necessary to read *around the oblique circle* [the zodiac].</margin>; but the spheres in which they exist all move similarly to the inerratic sphere; that is, they are moved about one pole which is common to all of them. 

The sphere of the fixed stars is moved by itself with one motion; but the planetary sphere moves with a twofold motion—one being its own motion, which is oblique <note>tilted relative to the celestial equator</note>, and the other being a revolution in conjunction with the inerratic sphere. Regarding the stars themselves, those that are fixed revolve around their own centers and also have an advancing motion along with their sphere. But the planets revolve in conjunction with the inerratic sphere, and each is moved together with its own sphere toward the east, revolving by itself according to its breadth and depth, and around its own proper center. For it is necessary that each, being spherical, should move with this motion, imitating its own "wholeness," just as the fixed stars are coordinated with the inerratic sphere. To this may be added that, as they proceed through the heavens, they also have—as Plato says—all kinds of various revolutions.

These things therefore being true, as we have demonstrated before, the theories <note>original: hypotheses</note> of epicycles or eccentrics <note>Mathematical models used by ancient astronomers to explain why planets seem to change speed or direction.</note> are not useless. Instead, they break down complex <note>original: various</note> motions into simple ones, so that we may easily understand the <term>apocatastases</term> <note>The completion of a planetary cycle; the return of a celestial body to its original position.</note> of complex motions. These cycles are not easily understood on their own, but are only to be grasped by comparison to the fixed stars. 

Hence, it is an excellent technique to discover which simple motions produce complex ones, and through them to investigate the measurements of such complexities. It is just as if someone, unable to measure a spiral motion around a cylinder, instead assumed a straight line moving around it and a point on that line measuring its movements; they would then find the total amount of motion along the spiral in a given time. This is the goal of those who employ "evolvents," epicycles, and eccentrics—using simple motions to discover the nature of a complex motion. These things

# [BOOK IV. THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO.]
->Tim. Plat. VOL. II. 2 P<-

These matters, however, deserve to be more fully considered, and for this reason, those who love philosophical contemplation should rouse themselves to a more precise understanding of them.

By their "conjunctions," we should understand their meetings and the *configurations* <note>original: σχηματισμους (schematismos). The Greek text previously used a word meaning "business dealings" (χρηματισμους), which the author notes is an error for "configurations."</note> they form with one another—whether they are arranged in a triangle <note>trine aspect (120°)</note>, a square <note>quadrature aspect (90°)</note>, a hexagon <note>sextile aspect (60°)</note>, or are diametrically opposite <note>opposition aspect (180°)</note>. Plato, by mentioning only their conjunction and their position in a straight line, uses these extremes to encompass all other possible geometric relationships. Their *obumbrations* <note>shadowing or eclipses</note> refer to the positions in which they darken us or other celestial bodies. For when one body is positioned in front of another, it stands before what is behind it. Thus, the stars cause darkness for us when they pass under one another. When Plato speaks of them "*becoming concealed*" <note>original: κατακαλυψεις (katakaluptseis); an error in the Greek source used "seizures" (καταληψεις) instead of "concealments."</note> and emerging again to our view at set times, we should understand this as their disappearance under the sun's rays and their reappearance into light. Those who are skilled in these matters say that both events are powerful and signify great changes in the world. To discuss all these details *without using visual models*—that is, without the help of astronomical instruments—would be a useless effort.

After this mathematical theory, let us examine what Plato says from a philosophical perspective. The *dances* of souls represent their being filled with divine inspiration <note>original: Bacchic mania; a state of sacred frenzy or spiritual ecstasy</note> and their cycles around the <term>intelligible</term> <note>the realm of pure, non-physical ideas or intellect</note>, as well as their intellectual restorations <note>original: apocatastases; the completion of a soul's cycle or its return to a prior state</note>. For as Socrates says in the *Phaedrus*, by following their more divine leader, they also move in harmony. Their *concursions* <note>meetings or encounters</note> are their intellectual perceptions of one another. For in that realm, all things are radiant; they see each other, and no soul is ignorant of the concerns of another. Furthermore, they align their own forms—like imprints or types—to the "intelligibles" which serve as their perfect models.

The *revolutions and advancing motions of their circles* represent the ways souls turn from themselves toward the pure Intellect, and from that Intellect back toward themselves. Both these movements happen perpetually: they know the Intellect through themselves, and they know themselves through the Intellect. Their *conjunctions* and *diametrical stations* are their unions with the intelligible realm (by which they are joined to one another) and also their outward progressions. When they join the "one" of their own essence to the "one" of the Divine Intellect, there is a "synod" or union of both. In these unions, it is necessary for the centers of the things joined to be aligned in a single straight line. However, when they move from that state to care for and oversee lower nature <note>providential inspection</note>, they move into a position opposite to this union. Yet, because they always remain the same, and both stay in place while simultaneously proceeding forward, they are both connected to and diametrically opposed to the divine source. But—

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV. THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO.]

*The shadowings <note>original: obumbrations</note> they cast on each other and on us act as the intermediaries <note>original: media</note> between divine souls and ourselves. For not all are directly united to one another; some are joined through many intermediary steps, and others through few. Their periods of hiding and their emergence into the light at specific times are their restorations <note>original: apocatastases; the return of a planet to its original position at the end of a cycle</note> and the start of new cycles.* According to these cycles, they bring about revolutions and transformations in the world, causing widespread destruction <note>original: copious corruptions</note> and major changes, as Plato explains in the *Republic*. To assert all these details without looking at the physical imitations of these things seen in the heavens would be a pointless task. It is necessary to move from observable phenomena toward the memory <note>original: reminiscence; the Platonic idea that learning is the soul remembering eternal truths</note> of invisible realities. Just as we use physical instruments and shadows to begin studying the celestial bodies, we use the stars themselves to recall the invisible orbits of the soul. The heavens serve as a bridge between the physical world <note>original: generated natures</note> and the realm of pure intellect <note>original: intelligible natures</note>.

Since Plato says that the shapes and movements of the stars cause terror and provide signs of the future for those who can interpret them, we must note that they signal the past as well. For this reason, he mentions activities that are primarily significant in themselves. The philosopher Theophrastus <note>a student of Aristotle</note> said that in his time,^1 the theories of the Chaldeans <note>ancient Babylonian astronomers and astrologers</note> regarding these matters were highly respected. They predicted both specific events—such as the life and death of individuals—and general ones, like storms or fair weather. He adds that, according to them, the planet Mercury signifies cold^2 when seen in winter, but intense heat in the summer. In his book *On Signs*, he states that they predicted everything, from the smallest details to general trends, by watching the stars. 

Let us now conclude our discussion of the nature of the visible and created Gods, as we have said enough about them. The goal of science^3 is to use appropriate language and provide only as much detail as is necessary for the theory being discussed. Plato follows this principle here. In these words, he finishes describing the celestial bodies and "starry animals" <note>the living beings of the stars</note>. This is why he also included his description of the Earth, because it produces time alongside the celestial orbits. This concludes those specific points. Here, the study of the visible and created Gods—whom we call the stars or celestial beings—comes to an end. He calls them

# [BOOK IV.] THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

They are visible because they belong to the physical world <note>original: "mundane"</note>, and they have aspects of perceptible things <note>original: "sensibles"</note> suspended from their intellectual essence. However, they are also "generated" <note>meaning: created or brought into being within time</note> because they possess a soul, which Plato calls the first of all generated natures. These beings are not visible in every part of their existence; rather, there is something about them that is indeed created, yet remains invisible. 

Plato demonstrates that his discussion of the Earth was intended to help explain the measured motion of the stars around it. He shows this by immediately adding, after his comments on the Earth, the phrase: "**And the natures successive to these**." <note>original Greek: *και τα τουτοις εφεξης* (kai ta toutois ephexēs)</note> <margin>1</margin> Through this phrase, I believe he clearly shows his design was to speak about the celestial Gods and the classes of beings <note>original: "genera"</note> that attend them. These attendants are sometimes hidden by the brilliance of the leading Gods, and at other times, when they become visible, they produce terror and provide signs of future events. <margin>2</margin> For what is said here is specifically adapted to these attendants according to an appropriate definition.

<margin>40 d</margin>
->“To speak, however, concerning the other spirits <note>original: "dæmons"</note>, and to know their origin, exceeds our ability.”<-

Now intending to speak about the sublunary Gods <note>term: **sublunary gods** refers to divine powers presiding over the elements below the moon, such as air, water, and earth</note>, Plato says that the discourse about them is marvelous and exceeds our ability. He suggests it transcends everything passed down to us by tradition, especially if we intend to discover their origin <note>original: "generation"</note> and describe it to others. 

He previously said of the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> that it is difficult to discover him and impossible to speak of him to all men; he now says the same of these sublunary Gods—that knowing and speaking of their origin surpasses our ability. What, then, does Plato mean by this? Since he has already delivered such many and marvelous teachings concerning the whole of heaven and the eternal model <note>original: "intelligible paradigm"</note>, how is it that he now claims that speaking of the Gods who craft the world of change <note>original: "fabricators of generation"</note> is a task beyond our power? 

Perhaps it is because many natural philosophers <note>original: "physiologists"</note> considered these sublunary elements to be inanimate things, moved only by chance and lacking any divine care. These thinkers acknowledged that the celestial bodies, because of their orderly motions, participate in Intellect and the Gods; however, they left the realm of change <note>original: "generation"</note> to be viewed as something unstable and indefinite, deprived of any providential oversight.

### PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.]

...thus Aristotle afterwards, acting alone, placed immovable causes over the celestial rotations <note>original: "circulations"</note>, whether eight in number or more; but he left these elements inanimate <note>meaning: without a soul or life-force</note>.

In order, therefore, that we might not be affected in the same manner as they were, Plato beforehand celebrates and proclaims the generation of the sublunary gods <note>term: **sublunary gods** refers to divine powers presiding over the elements below the moon, such as air, water, and earth</note> to be divine and intellectual. He does not require this kind of explanation when speaking of the celestial gods. Perhaps it may also be said that souls more quickly forget things nearer to themselves, but have a greater remembrance of superior principles. For the higher principles operate upon souls to a greater degree through their excellence of power, and they appear to be present with them through their energy. 

The same thing also happens with respect to our physical sight. For though we do not see many things situated on the earth, we nevertheless appear to see the sphere of fixed stars <note>original: "inerratic sphere"</note> and the stars themselves, because they illuminate our sight with their light. The "eye of the soul," therefore, becomes more forgetful of and blind to more proximate principles than to higher and more divine ones. Thus, all religions and sects acknowledge that there is a first principle of all things, and all men invoke God as their helper; but all do not believe that there are gods existing after this first principle, or that a providential energy proceeds from them into the universe. For the *one* <note>referring to the Neoplatonic "One," the ultimate source of all existence</note> is seen by them in a clearer manner than the multitude of gods. Others again believe indeed that there are gods, but after the gods, while they admit the demonic class <note>original: "dæmoniacal genus"</note>, they are ignorant of the heroic order <note>term: **heroic order** refers to a class of souls or beings ranking between demons and ordinary humans</note>. 

In short, the greatest work of science is to subtly distinguish the intermediate levels <note>original: "media"</note> and the progressions of beings. If we are correct in asserting these things, Plato, when speaking of the celestial gods, very properly indicates nothing of the difficulty of the subject. However, intending to speak of the sublunary gods, he says that it "surpasses our ability." For the discussion of these is more difficult because we cannot gather anything about them from visible <note>original: "apparent"</note> objects; rather, it requires a divinely-inspired energy and intellectual intuition <note>original: "projection"</note>. And so much for this doubt.

Again, however, someone may doubt why Plato calls the sublunary gods "demons" <note>original: "dæmons"; in Greek philosophy, *daimon* refers to a guiding spirit or divinity, not an evil entity</note>. For some have been led by this to place gods in the heavens but to assign the management of the sublunary region only to demons. However, that he conceived that these sublunary beings are also gods may be easily seen from what he adds: "*Let the generation therefore, of these Gods, be admitted to be as follows.*" 

In short, he does not appear to have spoken particularly about those powers properly named "demons," as he does not have the physical principles for them from the senses, which is where physical discussions must begin. Hence, he mentions the name of "demons" in one place where he calls our rational soul the "demon" of the animal; but in another, as...

### BOOK IV.] THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO

Here, Plato refers to the gods who produce generation as daemons <term>daemons: in Greek philosophy, "daemons" (daimones) are intermediate spiritual beings that bridge the gap between the high gods and humanity. They are not the "demons" of later folklore.</term>. One might ask—and this doubt must be addressed first—why he doesn't mention those who are daemons by their very nature? Is it because Socrates already presented this to his listeners the day before [in the *Republic*], where he spoke about the souls that oversee human lives and those that punish offenders in Hades <note>the underworld</note>? 

Therefore, he omits these details because they are already clear. However, what he said there reminded him of the daemons he had previously praised. Similarly, after assigning a specific soul to each of the eight spheres, he omits the animation of the entire sphere of fixed stars <note>original: "inerratic circle"</note> as a single unit, and the stars within it. He also omits the entire planetary sphere and its individual planets, because Socrates had already discussed them. This approach is based on a sound reasoning.

Returning to our earlier inquiry: why does Plato call these gods who produce generation "daemons"? Theodorus considers this differently; he says they are called daemons when they exist in "habitude" <term>habitude: a state of relation or connection to the physical world, rather than existing in pure, detached contemplation.</term>, but are called gods when they exist without it. He places them in the sublunary parts of the world [the region below the moon] and asserts that some of them animate the universe differently than others. 

However, our teacher Syrianus believes they should be considered daemons in relation to the celestial gods. They are dependent on the celestial gods and work with them to provide for their assigned domains. This arrangement is classically Platonic. For in the *Symposium* <note>original: "Banquet"</note>, Plato calls Love a daemon because he is an attendant of Venus and comes from the truly-existing god Porus [Plenty]; yet in the *Phaedrus*, he acknowledges Love as a god in terms of how he elevates our lives.

In the next place, according to another perspective, we may say that there are daemons in the celestial regions and gods in the sublunary region. In the celestial realms, the nature <note>original: θειον (theion) — divine</note> is indeed divine, even if daemons are also produced according to that nature <note>The original Greek text suggests a grammatical correction here: reading the masculine "according to that" (κατ' εκεινον) instead of the feminine (κατ' εκεινην).</note>; but in the sublunary realm, the entire multitude consists of daemons. In the heavens, the divine quality predominates, while here in the realm of generation, the daemonic quality prevails. Some people, looking only at this, have divided the divine and the daemonic strictly between the heavens and the realm of generation. They ought, however, to have arranged both in both; but in the former indeed the divine nature, and in the latter the...

The demonic nature predominates, although <note>The Greek word *kaitoi* (meaning "and yet") was mistakenly omitted in the original Greek text.</note> in the latter, the divine quality is also present. For if the entire world is a blessed God, then no part that makes it complete lacks divinity or the care of providence. And if all things participate in deity and providence, the world is granted a divine nature. If this is the case, then specific orders of Gods preside over its various parts. For if the heavens <note>If the heavens require intermediaries to participate in a single soul and intellect, the elements below the moon require them even more, given their lower status compared to the heavens.</note> participate in one soul and one intellect through intermediate souls and intellects, what should we think about the elements below the moon? How is it possible that these would not participate in the world's single deity to an even greater degree through certain middle divine orders?

Furthermore, it would be absurd if the <term>telestic art</term> (the art pertaining to mystic ceremonies) could establish places on earth suitable for oracles and statues of the Gods—and through certain symbols could cause things created from fragmented and decaying matter to become ready to share in the divine nature, to be moved by God, and to predict future events—but that the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>original: Demiurgus; the divine Craftsman of the universe</note> of the whole did not place divine souls, intellects, and Gods over the entire elements, which are the incorruptible fulfillments of the world. For was he unwilling? But how could he be unwilling, since he wished to make all things similar to himself? Was he then unable? But what could have hindered him? For we see that this is possible even through the works of the telestic art. But if he was both willing and able, it is evident that he gave existence to Gods who have roles within, and are the watchful guardians of, the world of generation <note>generation: the physical world of birth, change, and decay</note>. Since, however, the category of <term>daemons</term> <note>original: dæmons; intermediate spiritual beings that bridge the gap between gods and humans</note> always accompanies the Gods, there are also daemons who are the makers of generation. Some of these rule over entire elements, while others are the guardians of specific climates, others the rulers of nations, others of cities, others of families, and others are the guardians of individuals. For the protection of daemons extends even to the most minute detail.

Having therefore resolved the problem regarding their nature, let us next consider the order of these gods below the moon. For if they are Gods, and are called daemons for the reason mentioned above, where must we place them? Should it be, as we said before, below the moon, or prior to the celestial <note>The Greek word *ouraniōn* (meaning "celestial") was omitted in the original text.</note> Gods? This might appear to be proper for two reasons: one, because Plato indicates that he is ascending to a higher order by saying that it exceeds our ability to speak concerning them, having already spoken concerning—

...concerning the celestial Gods; but the other reason is that he follows the accounts of those who have passed down *theogonies* <note>original: Theogonies; genealogies or accounts of the origins of the gods</note> to us. For these writers, speaking of times before the world and the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>original: Demiurgus; the divine Craftsman or Architect of the universe</note>, described these generations of Gods as originating from Heaven and Earth. In answer to this question, however, we must say that he brings them into being after the celestial Gods, and because of this, they are born from Heaven and Earth. This is why he said that Earth was the oldest of the Gods within the Heaven: because from Earth and Heaven together, he was about to produce the other Gods that the heavens contain.

We can demonstrate this from the Demiurge addressing his speech to these Gods, and to all the rest, as being produced by him within the universe. However, regarding why Plato says he follows the traditional theogony and why he omits speaking of the <term>sublunary deities</term> <note>Gods presiding over the realm below the moon, including the Earth</note>, we must attribute this to the fact that he had no clear evidence for their existence from <term>phenomena</term> <note>original: phænomena; observable natural events or appearances</note>. He did have such evidence for the celestial divinities, based on the orderly nature of their planetary cycles, which is suited to the government of Gods. It is beyond the scope of <term>physiology</term> <note>In this context, the study of nature or natural philosophy</note>, therefore, to speak of beings for whom natural effects provide no firm basis for belief. Thus, Plato says, speaking as a natural philosopher, that it surpasses his ability to speak of these.

If, however, he says he follows those who are divinely inspired—and since they speak of the <term>supercelestial Gods</term> <note>Gods existing beyond the physical universe</note>, he adopts a similar theogony even while discussing sub-celestial divinities—we should not find this surprising. For he knew that all the ranks of the Gods extend down to the very last of things, starting from the primary arrangement of their progression, constantly generating sequences from themselves that correspond to the higher deities from which they originate. Therefore, although the ranks of these Gods celebrated by theologians are above the world, they also exist within the visible universe.

Just as this visible heaven is connected to the <term>supermundane</term> <note>original: supermundane; existing beyond the material world</note> heaven, so too our earth is connected to the earth that exists there [in the divine realm], and the ranks originating from the one are connected to the ranks proceeding from the other. From this, we can also assume that according to Plato, as well as other theologians, primary natures—as they emanate—produce lower things in cooperation with their own causes. For these sublunary Gods, coming from the Demiurge, are also said to be born from the Heaven and Earth that first came from him. The Demiurge, therefore, tells all of them that they should create mortal beings, imitating his own power <note>original footnote: It is obviously necessary here to read "his own" [heautou] instead of "their own" [heauton].</note> in their generation. Thus, they all originate from a single creative cause, even though those of a secondary rank also originate from the Gods who come before them. It follows from this that not everything produced by the junior Gods is mortal, since some of these...

<summary>Proclus explains why Plato uses traditional genealogies (theogonies) to describe the origin of gods, arguing that while natural science cannot prove the existence of sublunary deities, they exist as reflections of higher, supermundane divine orders.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on Plato's Timaeus, focusing on the hierarchy of divine beings. It explores how "junior Gods" (subordinate deities) generate both mortal and immortal beings, and investigates the origins and nature of rational and irrational spirits (dæmons).</meta>

<page-num>304</page-num>

<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.</header>

...proceed from other junior Gods <note>lower-ranking deities created by the Demiurge</note>; however, the opposite is true: everything mortal is created by these divinities. Furthermore, it follows from this that the junior Gods produce some things according to their unchanging <term>hyparxes</term> <note>original: hyparxes; essential modes of existence or foundations of being</note>, while they produce others according to their changing states. They could not be the source of immortal beings if they produced everything through their changing states, because it is true that everything which originates from a changing cause is itself inherently changeable.

From this concept, we may also solve the question of whether "irrational spirits" <note>original: dæmons; in Greek philosophy, these are intermediate spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil</note> exist, as practitioners of <term>theurgy</term> <note>original: theurgists; those who perform divine rituals to invoke or work with the gods</note> claim, and what their origin is. If they come from the junior Gods, it might be asked: how are they immortal, given that these Gods are the fathers of mortal natures? But if they come from the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>the divine Architect or Craftsman of the universe</note>, how are they irrational? For he is a father who acts in conjunction with Intellect <note>the divine Mind</note>. 

The solution to this inquiry is that they derive their existence from the junior Gods, and yet they are not mortal for that reason, since some of the junior Gods generate other Gods. Perhaps these beings are called spirits <note>dæmons</note> for this very reason: so that we may know that the spirits properly referred to by that name are established by the junior Gods. Yet, irrational spirits also proceed from the one Demiurge. For as the character <term>Timaeus</term> <note>The speaker in Plato's dialogue</note> says, the Demiurge is the cause of all immortal natures. If, however, the one Demiurge grants intellect to all things, then even in these spirits there is a certain final trace of that intellectual quality, insofar as they act with ease according to their imagination. This imagination is, as it were, the "last resounding echo" <note>original: apechema; the translator notes the original Greek text likely meant "echo" rather than "vehicle"</note> of the divine Intellect. 

For this reason, imagination <note>original: phantasy</note> is said by Aristotle to be a "passive intellect," and others have rightly asserted the same. Thus, among the spirits properly called "dæmons," those that are irrational are half-mortal. Plato, however, has already laid out the principles for us to solve the inquiry concerning the lowest classes of spirits. If there is a certain class of spirits that uses reason, it is evident that we must attribute this to the one Demiurge—whether they were produced directly by him, or through certain intermediate Gods that he created. 

The celestial Gods are the sources of celestial spirits, while the sub-celestial Gods are the sources of sub-celestial spirits. As Plato teaches us, in accordance with the <term>theogonies</term> <note>traditional accounts of the origins and genealogies of the gods</note>, some sub-celestial Gods are the fathers of others. Therefore, it is not at all surprising that these Gods should generate spirits of their own rank—and not only irrational ones, but also rational spirits—since they are the creators of Gods, just as the celestial Gods are the creators of celestial spirits. Consequently, it is necessary that the study of spirits should derive its entire arrangement <note>The translator notes the original Greek text likely meant "arrangement" (diataxin) rather than "way of life" (diaitan)</note> from these principles.

<summary>Proclus explains the hierarchy of divine creation, arguing that subordinate "junior Gods" can produce both mortal and immortal beings. He also clarifies that spirits (dæmons) derive their nature—whether rational or irrational—from their specific divine origins within the celestial and sub-celestial ranks.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on Plato's Timaeus, specifically discussing the hierarchy of spirits (dæmons) and the necessity of believing the ancient "theologists" or poets who spoke of the gods' lineages.</meta>

<page-num>305</page-num>

<header>BOOK IV.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

->From these considerations, conformably to Platonic doctrines:<-

From what Plato has said concerning the Gods of generation <note>original: genesiurgic Gods; deities responsible for the process of birth and becoming</note>, it becomes evident what his answer would be if he were asked about the generation of spirits <note>original: dæmons; in Greek philosophy, these are intermediate beings between gods and humans, not necessarily evil</note> truly so-called. In short, he who understands the class of spirits that exist according to their relative state <note>original: habitude; referring to spirits that have a relationship with the material world</note> will, with much greater priority, know the spirits that exist according to their essential foundation <term>hyparxis</term> <note>the essential, primary mode of a being's existence</note>, and which complete the structure of this universe. 

How, also, is it possible that he should not grant that there is a class of spirits defined by their relative state? For he says that our soul is assigned the rank of a spirit—in reference to the mortal animal—by the powers that fabricated mortal natures. It is necessary, therefore, that there should be an essential "spirit-life" prior to that which exists according to a relative state; those who grant the latter must also admit the existence of the former. Plato, however, who [verbally] establishes the rulers of the universe, is also of the opinion that their perpetual attendants received their <term>hypostasis</term> <note>real or essential existence</note> together with them and from them.

<margin>40 D</margin>
> “It is therefore necessary to believe the men of old, who, being the offspring of the Gods as they themselves assert, must have a clear knowledge of their parents. For it is impossible not to believe in the children of the Gods, even though they should speak without probable arguments and necessary demonstrations.”

We may gather from this that he who simply believes in things which seem difficult to know, and which are of a doubtful nature, follows a path of abundance. He recurs to divine knowledge and deific intelligence, through which all things become clear and known. For all things are contained in the Gods. Furthermore, that which encompasses all things beforehand is also able to fill other things with the knowledge of itself. 

Hence, Timæus here directs us to the "theologists" <note>the ancient poets and writers like Orpheus or Hesiod who described the genealogy of the gods</note> and to the generation of the Gods celebrated by them. Who, therefore, are they, and what is their knowledge? They indeed are the offspring of the Gods and clearly know their progenitors; they are the offspring and children of the Gods because they preserve the form of their presiding deity according to their present life.¹ For Apollonian souls <note>original: Apolloniacal; souls following the nature of the god Apollo</note>, by choosing a prophetic or ritualistic <note>original: telestic</note> life, are called the children and offspring of Apollo. They are children, so far as they are...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on Plato's Timaeus, specifically discussing why certain souls are called "children of the gods" and the nature of divinely inspired knowledge versus scientific or probable knowledge.</meta>

<page-num>306</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK IV.</header>

...souls pertaining to this God and adapted to this series; but they are called progeny because they demonstrate that their present life is conformable to these characteristics of the God. All souls, therefore, are the children of the Gods, but not all souls know their presiding God. Such souls, however, as have this knowledge and choose a similar life are called the children and progeny <note>original: *engonoi*; progeny or descendants</note><sup>1</sup> of the Gods. Hence Plato adds the phrase, "as they say," for they reveal the divine order from which they came. Thus the Sibyl <note>A legendary prophetess of antiquity.</note><sup>2</sup> uttered oracles as soon as she was born; and Hercules appeared at his birth with demiurgic symbols <note>symbols representing the "Demiurge" or the creator's power to shape the material world</note>. 

But souls of this kind turn themselves back toward their progenitors and are filled by them with deific <note>divine or god-like</note> knowledge. Their knowledge, however, is "enthusiastic" <note>original: enthusiastic; in this context, meaning "divinely inspired" or "possessed by a god" (from the Greek *enthousiasmos*)</note>, being joined to the deity through divine light and set apart from all other knowledge—both that which is merely probable and that which is demonstrative. For the former (probable knowledge) is concerned with nature and the universal principles found in specific things; but the latter (demonstrative or scientific knowledge) is concerned with an incorporeal essence and the objects of formal science. Divinely inspired knowledge alone, however, is truly joined with the Gods themselves.

<margin>40E</margin>
> “But since they declare that their narrations are about affairs to which they are naturally allied, it is proper that, complying with the law, we should assent to their tradition. Let, therefore, the generation of these Gods according to them be admitted and described by us in this way.”

From these words, one who considers them accurately may assume many things. For example, one might assume that divinely inspired knowledge is perfected through familiarity with and alliance to the Gods. For the sun is seen through "solar-form" light <note>light that shares the same nature as the sun</note>, and divinity becomes apparent through divine illumination. It may likewise be inferred that the divine law defines the orders of the Gods which the divinely inspired concepts of the ancients reveal. According to this law, souls who act—even if not acting with divine inspiration—are persuaded by those who are inspired. Complying with this law, Timaeus says at the beginning of this dialogue that he shall invoke the Gods and Goddesses. From these words we may also infer that all the kingdoms, both in the heavens and the sublunary <note>the region below the moon, typically referring to the Earth and its atmosphere where things are subject to change and decay</note> region, are...

<meta>This page begins Book V of the commentary, transitioning from the discussion of the celestial gods to the sublunary deities—those who govern the realm of change and physical birth below the moon.</meta>

# BOOK V.

---

The theory of the sublunary <note>original: "sublunary"; referring to the realm below the moon, including the Earth, which is subject to change, birth, and decay</note> gods is immediately connected with that of the celestial gods. Because it is suspended from the celestial theory, it possesses a perfect and scientific character. For the choir of gods that produces generation <note>original: "generation"; the process of coming into being or birth in the physical world</note> follows the gods in the heavens. In imitation of the celestial circle, they also revolve the circle of generation. This is because secondary natures follow the natures that come before them in an indivisible and united progression. 

However, because the divinities that govern generation exist directly from the celestial gods, they are also directed back toward them in an inseparable union. This is just as the celestial gods are directed toward the super-celestial deities from whom they were directly generated; and the super-celestial are directed toward the intellectual gods by whom they were adorned and distributed; and again, the intellectual are directed toward the intelligible gods, from whom they were ineffably <note>original: "ineffably"; in a way that is too great or sacred to be expressed in words</note> revealed, and who indescribably and secretly contain all things.

Of this entire, truly golden chain <note>A traditional Neoplatonic metaphor for the hierarchy of existence linking the highest divine principle to the lowest matter</note>, the summit is indeed the category of the intelligible gods, but the end is that of the sublunary deities. These deities govern generation in a way that is not itself generated, and they govern nature in a supernatural manner. The demiurgic <note>original: "demiurgic"; referring to the Demiurge or the divine "Craftsman" who shapes the material world</note> intellect now gives existence to these deities; the dominion of the gods extends from the heavens above down to the very last of things. 

Regarding these sublunary deities of whom we propose to speak, it is necessary to observe first that all of them preserve the generative and perfecting energy of their creating cause, as well as his demiurgic and stable productive power. They likewise receive their measures, boundaries, and order from their father. And such things as he governs in a universal and transcendent way, they govern in a way that is divided—

---

1. In the original text, for the word "superintending" <note>original: επιτροποντων (epitropontōn)</note>, it is necessary to read "governing as guardians" <note>original: επιτροπευοντων (epitropeuontōn)</note>.

<summary>This page introduces the hierarchy of sublunary gods, explaining how they are linked to the celestial and higher deities through a "golden chain" of cause and effect. It establishes that while these gods govern the changing physical world, they themselves operate according to eternal, divine principles.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the sublunary gods, specifically how they are structured in a hierarchy that mirrors the higher divine orders and how they govern the physical world of change and birth.</meta>

<page-num>309</page-num>
<header>BOOK V.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

...according to their allotments <note>original: "allotments"; refers to the specific divine roles or provinces assigned to each deity</note>, they fabricate, generate, and perfect. Some of them are close to the celestial gods, while others proceed to a greater distance from them. Therefore, some preserve the essence of these gods as much as possible within the sublunary realm <note>original: "sublunary order"; the realm of change and physical birth beneath the moon</note>, while others are established according to their own specific powers. For in every order, the summit corresponds to the order that came before it. Thus, the summit of the intelligible gods is unity; the summit of the intellectual gods is intelligible; the summit of the super-worldly <note>original: "supermundane"</note> order is intellectual; and the summit of the worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note> order is super-worldly.

Some of the sublunary gods are more closely united to the demiurgic monad <note>original: "demiurgic monad"; the single, primary source of the Craftsman-God, the Demiurge</note>, while others are more distant from it. Hence, some, being similar to it, are the leaders of this entire series, while others have a more partial resemblance to it. For the Father <note>The Demiurge, or divine Craftsman</note> established powers in every level of existence that correspond to his own arrangement; since in all the divine orders, there exists a primary cause that corresponds to the Good.¹

According to these causes—which correspond to the unspeakable principle of all things and are called "monads" <note>original: "monads"; single units or primary sources from which others flow</note>—the sublunary gods proceed, organizing and distributing the physical world <note>original: "generation"</note> in a fitting manner. Some fulfill one aspect of their Father's will, while others fulfill another. For some fulfill his connective will, others his life-giving <note>original: "prolific"</note> will, others his moving <note>original: "motive"</note> will, others his protective <note>original: "guardian"</note> will, and others fulfill different aspects of the Demiurge’s <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine Craftsman of the universe</note> will regarding the entirety of the sublunary region. 

Some of these gods rule over souls, others over spirits <note>original: "dæmons"; in this context, intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil beings</note>, and others over gods. However, all of them are intellectual in their core essence, but worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note> in their specific divine assignments. They are also perfecters and powerful, governing the physical world <note>original: "generation"</note> in a way that is itself eternal <note>original: "unbegotten"</note>. They govern mindless beings with intellect and lifeless things with life. For they organize all things according to their own divine essence, and not according to the weakness of the things receiving their influence. 

Furthermore, Plato clearly believes that these gods use certain other bodies that are simpler and more eternal than the four elements, because he says they appear when they please and become visible to us. It is also obvious that he gives them souls, as he says that every worldly god is joined to a body through a soul. For he first called the world itself a "God" only after he had established a soul within it. And again, it is evident that he connects intellects to them—through which their souls are intellectual and are immediately turned toward the Demiurge—as seen in the Demiurge's speech to them.²

If it is also necessary for the whole world to be perfect, then we must understand that along with the divine races, there is also the spirit-like <note>original: "dæmoniacal"</note>...

--- Page 316 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the hierarchy of divine beings, specifically moving from the sublunary gods to the intermediary orders of angels, demons, and heroes that bridge the gap between the divine and the human.</meta>

<page-num>310</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.</header>

This order was created prior to our souls (which Plato describes shortly afterward), and it is divided into three parts: **angels**, **demons** <note>original: "dæmons"; in this context, these are not evil spirits, but "daimons"—mediating spirits that guide and distribute divine energy</note> properly so-called, and **heroes**. This entire order fills the middle space between the Gods and humans, because there is a total separation between our concerns and those of the Gods. The Gods are eternal, whereas humans are frail and mortal. Furthermore, while humans are satisfied with enjoying a partial exercise of intellect, the Gods ascend into total and perfect intellect itself.

Because of this, there is a **triad** <note>original: "triad"; a group of three</note> that connects our human concerns with the Gods. This triad follows the three primary causes of all things, although Plato usually refers to this entire group as "demonic." 

1.  **The Angelic:** This corresponds to "being" or the "intelligible" world <note>the realm of pure thought and reality</note>, which is the first to emerge into the light from the unspeakable and hidden fountain of all beings. Therefore, it reveals the Gods themselves and announces what is hidden in their essence.
2.  **The Demonic:** This corresponds to "infinite life." Because of this, it exists everywhere across many levels and has a diverse, multiform nature.
3.  **The Heroic:** This corresponds to "intellect" and "conversion" <note>original: "conversion"; the process of a soul turning back toward its divine source</note>. Thus, it acts as the overseer of purification and provides a magnificent and elevated¹ life.

Furthermore, the angelic order proceeds according to the intellectual life of the **Demiurge** <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the Craftsman-God who shaped the universe</note>. It is essentially intellectual, interpreting and transmitting divine wisdom to lower beings. The demonic order proceeds according to the Demiurge’s providence over the whole of creation; it governs nature and ensures the order of the entire world is completed correctly. Finally, the heroic order proceeds according to the "converting" providence of these powers. Therefore, this class of beings is also elevated; it raises souls to a higher state and causes a grand and vigorous energy.

Since these are the natures of these three classes, they are all dependent on the Gods. Some depend on the celestial Gods, while others depend on the divinities who oversee the realm of generation <note>the world of physical birth and change</note>. Every God is the leader of a multitude that shares his specific character. 

*   **For the heavenly Gods:** Their angels, demons, and heroes are also heavenly.
*   **For the creators of generation:** Their intermediaries have the quality of producing generation.
*   **For the elevating Gods:** Their intermediaries have the power to elevate souls.
*   **For the demiurgic Gods:** Their intermediaries are demiurgic (creative).
*   **For the vivific Gods:** Their intermediaries are "vivific" <note>life-giving</note>.

The same applies to the rest. Among the elevating Gods, those who have the character of **Saturn** have Saturnian angels, demons, and heroes; those who are **Solar** have Solar intermediaries. Likewise, among the life-giving Gods, those who are **Lunar** have servants who are Lunar, and so on.

<note>¹ For the Greek phrase *e psyches* (of the soul) in this place, it is necessary to read *hypseles* (high or elevated). <note>original: "η ψυχης... υψηλης"</note></note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the hierarchy of divine beings, explaining how the names of major Gods are applied to the lower orders of angels, demons, and heroes that serve them. <page-num>311</page-num>
<header>BOOK 5] PLATO'S TIMAEUS. 311</header>

...the Aphrodisiacal—or those who possess the characteristics of Venus <note>the goddess of love and beauty</note>—they are called Aphrodisiacal. For they bear the names of the Gods from whom they depend, as they are in a continuous connection with them and receive the same essential idea, though in an appropriate lower state. This is not surprising, since individual souls also, when they recognize their patron and leading Gods, call themselves by their names. Where else did the names for the followers of Asclepius <note>original: "Esculapiuses"; referring to those under the influence of the god of medicine</note>, the followers of Bacchus <note>original: "Bacchuses"; followers of the god of wine and ecstasy</note>, and the Dioscuri <note>the twin sons of Zeus, Castor and Pollux</note> come from? [These were heroic men who took the names of the deities from whom they descended.]^1 Therefore, just as with the celestial gods, it is also necessary to observe a corresponding group of angels, demons, and heroes for each of the Gods who create the physical world <note>original: "fabricators of generation"</note>. We must accept that the multitude dependent on them keeps the name of the "monad" <note>the primary source or unit</note> that produced them. Hence, there is a celestial God, angel, and hero; and the same is also true on the earth.^2 In a similar manner, we must say that Ocean and Tethys <note>primordial sea deities</note> extend through all the divine ranks, as do the other Gods. For there are also groups belonging to Jupiter <note>original: "Jovian"</note>, Juno <note>original: "Junonian"</note>, and Saturn <note>original: "Saturnian"</note>, which are called by the same name of life. It is not absurd to give the name "man" to both the "intelligible" man <note>the perfect idea of humanity in the divine mind</note> and the "sensible" man <note>the physical human being</note>, even though there is a great distance and interval between them.

This concludes our general discussion of the Gods and demons who create physical life. We did this so we could look at the discussion of demons and Gods together. For Plato includes both these categories <note>original: "genera"</note> under the same names. It seems he calls the same powers both "demons" and "Gods" so we understand that the demonic category is dependent on these Gods, and we may address them as Gods. He does this in other places too, showing that this theory applies everywhere and that the eye of science views all things at once in an unbroken connection.

However, it is clear that we should still maintain the specific differences between these categories. We should view every "genesiurgic" <note>original: "genesiurgic"; responsible for the creation of physical life and generation</note> God as having goodness itself, accompanied by intellect, soul, and a divine body. A portion of each of these is given by these Gods to things in the "sublunary" realm <note>the region below the moon, i.e., the Earth and its atmosphere</note>. In this respect, the sublunary gods are more plentiful <note>original: "redundant"; meaning they have a more complex or multiplied presence in the lower world</note> than the celestial gods. We must also view every [rational] demon as being more excellent than our own souls, and as having an intellectual—

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the hierarchy of divine beings, specifically how the lower orders of angels and demons relate to the primary Gods, and shifts into an explanation of the soul's "ethereal vehicle" and the Orphic tradition of divine succession.</meta>

<page-num>312</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.</header>

...intellectual soul and an ethereal vehicle; since a certain thing of this kind is, as Plato says, attached to the human soul.
> “The Demiurge <note>the divine craftsman or creator of the physical world</note> therefore, he says, caused the soul to ascend into its vehicle.”

For it is necessary that every soul, before entering mortal bodies, should use certain everlasting, easily-moved, and circular bodies, as they possess an inherent power of movement. But we have previously spoken concerning irrational demons <note>original: "dæmons"</note>, and shown which Gods should be conceived as their makers. Regarding the demons that use rational souls, it is evident that the Demiurge must be considered their cause. Plato does not always distinguish clearly between the life-generating <note>original: "genesiurgic"</note> divinities and demons. At times, he calls the celestial powers "gods" even if they are demons; at other times, he calls the sublunary powers <note>those existing below the moon in the physical world</note> "demons" even if they are Gods. He does this to make the discussion apply to both the life-generating Gods and the demons who are directly dependent on them. However, we have already suggested other probable reasons for this.

It now remains to show what understanding we should have of the Gods mentioned here by Plato. Among the ancient writers, some referred to these descriptions as fables; others saw them as the founding fathers of cities; some viewed them as guardian powers, some as ethical allegories, and others as various types of souls. However, these views are sufficiently disproved by the divine Iamblichus <note>a prominent Neoplatonist philosopher, c. 245–325 AD</note>, who demonstrates that they stray from Plato’s meaning and the truth of the matter. Therefore, we must say that Timaeus, being a follower of Pythagoras, follows Pythagorean principles. These, in turn, are the Orphic traditions. For what Orpheus delivered mystically through secret stories, Pythagoras learned after being initiated by Aglaophemus <note>a priest of the Orphic mysteries</note> into the mystic wisdom which Orpheus received from his mother Calliope <note>the Muse of epic poetry</note>. *For Pythagoras says these things in "The Sacred Discourse."* 

What then are the Orphic traditions, since we believe the doctrine of Timaeus about the Gods should be referred to them? They are as follows: Orpheus described the kingdoms of the Gods who preside over the whole of reality according to a perfect number—namely, Phanes, Night, Heaven, Saturn, Jupiter, and Bacchus. Phanes is the first to hold a scepter, and the first king is the celebrated Ericapaeus <note>another name for Phanes, representing the primordial creative power</note>. The second is Night, who receives the scepter from her father [Phanes]. The third is Heaven <note>Uranus</note>, who receives it from Night. The fourth is Saturn <note>Cronus</note>, who, as they say, attacked his father. The fifth is Jupiter <note>Zeus</note>, who subdued his father. And after him, the sixth is Bacchus <note>Dionysus</note>. All these kings, starting from the highest realm of the intelligible and intellectual Gods, proceed through the middle orders and into the physical world.

...so that they may adorn mundane <note>world-related or physical</note> affairs. For Phanes <note>a primary Orphic deity representing the first light and the creator of the universe</note> is not only in the realm of intelligibles, but also in the realm of intellectuals, in the demiurgic <note>the level of the divine creator</note>, and in the supermundane <note>above the physical world</note> order; and in a similar manner, Heaven and Night exist there as well. For their distinct characteristics extend through all the intermediate levels of existence. 

And with respect to the mighty Saturn, is he not arranged prior to Jupiter? And does he not, after the Jovian <note>relating to Jupiter</note> kingdom, divide the Bacchic fabrication <note>This refers to the Orphic myth of Dionysus/Bacchus being torn apart by Titans, which Neoplatonists interpreted as the division of divine unity into the multiplicity of the physical world</note> in conjunction with the other Titans? He effects this in one way in the heavens, and in another way in the sublunary <note>below the moon; the earthly realm</note> region; in one way in the sphere of the fixed stars <note>original: "inerratic sphere"</note>, and in another way among the planets. Jupiter and Bacchus act in a similar manner. *These things, therefore, are clearly asserted by the ancients.*

If, however, we are right in these assertions, these divinities have every where an analogous existence. Anyone who wishes to survey their progressions into the heavens, or the sublunary region, should look to the first and principal causes of their kingdoms. For from those causes, and according to them, their generation is derived. It is necessary, therefore, that we also should look to these. 

Some, therefore, say that Plato omits investigating the Gods who are analogous to the two kings in the heavens—I mean Phanes and Night. For it is necessary to place them in a superior order, and not among the mundane Gods, because they are the leaders of the intellectual Gods prior to the world's existence. They are eternally established in the *adytum*, as Orpheus says of Phanes, *who by the word "adytum" signifies their secret and unmanifest order.* <note>original: "adytum" — a Greek word for the innermost, most private part of a temple; here it refers to a hidden or secret divine realm.</note> 

Whether, therefore, we refer the circulation of "same" and "different" [mentioned by Plato in this dialogue] to the analogy of these, as male and female, or paternal and generative, we shall not wander from the truth. Or whether we refer the sun and moon, as opposed to each other among the planets, to the same analogy, we shall not err. [For the sun, indeed, through his light preserves a similarity to Phanes, while the moon is similar to Night. Jupiter, or the Demiurge, in the intellectual realm, is analogous to Phanes in the intelligible order. And the life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note> crater <note>a mixing bowl or vessel; here representing a source of life</note> Juno is analogous to Night, who produces all life in conjunction with Phanes from hidden causes; just as Juno is in labor with, and emits into light, all the soul contained in the world.]* For it is better to conceive both of these as existing prior to the world, and to arrange the Demiurge himself as analogous to Phanes, since he is said to be modeled after him according to the production of universal realities <note>original: "wholes"</note>; but we should arrange the power conjoined with Jupiter (meaning Juno), which is generative of all things, as analogous to Night, who produces all things invisibly—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how divine hierarchies are reflected across different levels of reality. It explains why Plato begins his genealogy of the gods with Heaven and Earth rather than earlier Orphic figures like Phanes and Night.</meta>

...probably from the father Phanes <note>The first-born god of light in Orphic tradition</note>. After these, however, we must consider the remaining ones as analogous to the intellectual kingdoms.

If, likewise, it should be asked why Plato does not mention the kingdoms of Phanes and Night—to whom we have said Jupiter and Juno <note>Zeus and Hera</note> are analogous—it may be readily answered that the tradition of Orpheus contains these. For this reason, Plato celebrates the kingdom of Heaven and Earth as the first, as the Greeks were more accustomed to this than to the Orphic traditions. As he himself says in the *Cratylus*, where he particularly mentions the genealogy of the gods <note>original: "theogony"</note> by Hesiod, he goes back as far as this kingdom, according to that poet. 

Beginning, therefore, from this genealogy as it is better known, and assuming Heaven and Earth as the first kingdoms above the world, he produces the visible Heaven and Earth to correspond to those in the intellectual order, and celebrates the latter as the most ancient of the gods within the former. From these also, he begins the genealogy of the sublunary gods <note>deities whose domain is below the moon, in the earthly realm</note>. These things, however, if the divine wills it, will be clear from what follows. 

At present we shall only add that it is necessary to examine all these names either as divine or spirit-like <note>original: "dæmoniacally"; referring to "daemons," which in Neoplatonism are intermediary spirits between gods and humans</note>, according to the assignments of these divinities in the four elements. For this group of nine <note>original: "ennead"</note> is in ether and water, in earth and in air, in every variety, according to both the divine and the spirit-like character. And again, these names are to be examined in relation to water and air, and likewise terrestrially within the earth, so that all these powers may be everywhere, according to an all-encompassing mode of existence. For there are many modes of divine and spirit-like providence, and many assignments according to the division of the elements; otherwise, if all things were not everywhere, the balance of the same and the similar would be destroyed. And so much for these details. But let us now return to the text of Plato and explore its meaning to the utmost of our ability.

<margin>40E</margin>
> “That Ocean and Tethys were the offspring of Heaven and Earth.”

As this whole world is vast and diverse, reflecting <note>original: "adumbrating"</note> the intellectual order of forms, it contains these two extremes within itself: Earth and Heaven. The latter has the role of a father, while the former has the role of a mother. On this account, Plato calls Earth the most ancient of the gods within the heavens, so that, consistently with this, he might say that Earth is the mother of all that Heaven is the father of. At the same time, he shows that partial causes are not only subordinate to their offspring—as Poverty <note>original: *Penia*</note> [in the *Banquet* <note>The *Symposium*</note> of Plato] is to Love—but are likewise...

...superior to them, as alone receiving the offspring proceeding from the fathers. These two extremities, therefore, must be conceived in the world: Heaven as the father, and Earth as the mother of her common progeny. For all the rest terminate in these, some giving completion to the celestial number, while others complete the entirety of Earth. In the same manner, in each of the elements of the world, these two principles—Heaven and Earth—must be admitted. They exist as air in the air, as water in the water, and as earth in the earth, and according to all the modes mentioned above, in order that each may be a perfect world, adorned and distributed from analogous principles <note>original: "αλογων" (unreasoning), which the translator notes was a typo for "αναλογων" (analogous)</note>. 

For if man is said to be a microcosm <term>microcosm: the idea that a human being is a "little world" reflecting the structure of the entire universe</term>, is it not necessary that each of the elements, with a much greater priority, should contain within itself in its own way all that the world contains as a whole? Hence, it appears to me that Plato, immediately after speaking about Heaven and Earth, presents the theory of these Gods, beginning from those two divinities; for the other divinities proceed in a way analogous to Heaven and Earth. These two divinities, however, are the total causes of all the Gods that are now produced. And these divinities that are the progeny of *Heaven* and *Earth* are analogous to the whole of each. These two likewise, as we have before observed, are in each of the elements as air, or as water, or as earth. For Heaven is in Earth, and Earth is in Heaven <note>This is a very ancient Egyptian doctrine. And hence Athanasius Kircher, in his *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, says that he read the following words engraved on a stone near Memphis: "Heaven is above, heaven is below; everything which is above is also below. Grasp this, and you will be blessed." <note>original: "Coelum sursum, coelum deorsum, quod sursum id omne deorsum, hæc cape et beaberis"</note>. 

Conformably to this also, the celebrated *Smaragdine Table* <note>The Emerald Tablet</note>, which is of such great authority with the Alchemists, and which—whether originally written or not by Hermes Trismegistus—is doubtless of great antiquity, says that all that is beneath resembles all that is above. The table itself is as follows: 

"It is true without a lie, certain, and most true: that what is beneath is like that which is above, and what is above is like that which is beneath, for the purpose of accomplishing the miracle of the 'one thing.' And as all things were from one through the mediation of one, so all things were generated from this one thing by adaptation. Its father is the sun, its mother the moon. The wind carried it in its belly. Its nurse is the earth; it is the father of every perfection <term>telesmi: from the Greek 'telesmos,' meaning perfection, completion, or a consecrated object</term> of the entire world. Its power is complete if it is turned into earth. You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the dense, gently and with great ingenuity. It ascends from the earth to heaven, and descends again to the earth, and receives the power of the things above and below. Thus you will have the glory of the whole world, and therefore all obscurity will flee from you. This is the strength of all strength, for it will overcome every subtle thing and penetrate every solid thing. Thus the world was created. From this will come wonderful adaptations, the manner of which is this. Therefore I am called Hermes Trismegistus, having three parts of the philosophy of the whole world. What I have said concerning the work of the sun is complete." <note>original: "Verum sine mendacio, certum et verissimum: quod est inferius, est sicut id quod est superius... Completum est quod dixi de opere solis."</note></note>. And here indeed, Heaven exists in an earthly way, but there Earth...

celestially. For *Orpheus* calls the moon "celestial earth."¹ Nor is it surprising that this should be the case. For we may observe the same things everywhere according to their analogous forms in the realm of the intelligibles <term>intelligibles: the highest level of reality consisting of pure, non-physical forms or ideas</term>, in the intellectuals <term>intellectuals: a level of divine beings or principles characterized by active thought and consciousness</term>, in the supermundane <note>original: "supermundane" — referring to the realm above the physical world</note> order, in the heavens, and in the process of generation, all in conformity with the proper order of each level.

Regarding each of these divinities, however, some of the interpreters of Plato understand *Earth* to be this physical mass which is the object of our senses. Others see it as that which has an arrangement analogous to matter and is supposed to exist prior to the natures that are generated. Others see it as "intelligible matter" <note>original: "intelligible matter" — the underlying "substance" or potentiality within the realm of pure thought</note>; others, as the power of the intellect; others, as life; others, as an incorporeal form inseparable from the earth; others conceive it to be the soul; and others, the intellect itself. 

In a similar manner, with respect to *Heaven*, some suppose it to be the visible heavens; others, the motion around the center of the universe; others, a power proceeding in harmony with motion; others, that which possesses intellect; others, a pure and separate intellect; others, the nature of cosmic circulation; others, the soul; and others, the intellect. 

I also know that the divine *Iamblichus* <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD): An influential Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher</note> understands *Earth* to be everything stable and firm within the essence of the mundane Gods; this stability, through its active energy and perpetual circulation, encompasses more excellent powers and total lives. But by *Heaven*, he understands the total and perfect energy proceeding from the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: the divine "Craftsman" or creator of the physical universe</term>. This energy is full of its own appropriate power and exists around the Demiurge, acting as the boundary of itself and of all whole things. 

I also know that the admirable *Theodorus* establishes both these powers in the "first life," which exists according to habitude <term>habitude: a term used by Theodorus to describe the relationship or disposition between a higher soul and its lower manifestations</term>. For in the life of the World Soul (which exists according to habitude), when the soul descends into itself, it ends once more in the "source-soul" <note>original: "fontal soul"</note> with a distinction; three primary habitudes are immediately to be found there.

You must separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the dense, gently and with great skill. It ascends from earth to heaven, and again descends to the earth, and receives the power of things superior and inferior. <meta>This page continues Proclus's detailed breakdown of the three types of "wholeness" in the divine order, specifically how the principles of Heaven and Earth act as boundaries and containers within the different levels of reality.</meta>

<page-num>317</page-num>
