surveyed, together with the wholeness. The first of these consists of the wholeness found on each side; it possesses the type of wholeness that exists before its parts and ends in the complete source soul <note>original: "fontal soul"—the primary source from which all other souls flow</note>. The second preserves the entire source soul but divides itself into parts, possessing the type of wholeness that is made up of its parts. And the third distributes the source soul while remaining a whole itself. 

Earth and Heaven are contained within the first of these three. The material nature in this first level is called "Earth," as the ancient theologians used that name for matter. Heaven, however, is a specific type of intellect. It separates the lowest things from the highest through its disposition <note>original: "habitude"—the relationship or orientation of one thing toward another</note> and brings the visible heaven into being through that same disposition. Similarly, within us, the soul’s disposition toward the body is what preserves the body. Understanding this, I believe we must hold fast—as if to a strong anchor cable—to the teachings of our teacher, Syrianus. By doing so, we will avoid confused and mistaken ideas and align ourselves with the most pure insights of Iamblichus.

First, we should remember that Plato is now discussing the sublunary gods <term>sublunary gods: divine beings whose realm is below the moon and who oversee the world of change, birth, and death</term>. These gods are present everywhere and emerge according to the same pattern as the highest "intelligible" and "intellectual" kings. Second, we must say that just as the highest Heaven serves as the boundary and container for the intellectual gods—holding the "measure" that flows from *the Good* <note>original: εκ τ' αγαθου (*ek t'agathou*). The text notes that the original Greek should be corrected from *ek t'autou* ("from the same") to *ek t’agathou* ("from the Good")</note> and the intelligible gods into the intellectual ranks—in the same way, the Heaven Plato mentions here is the boundary and container of the gods who fabricate generation <note>those responsible for creating the physical world</note>. It encloses within one limit the demiurgic measure, as well as the influence that flows from the celestial gods to those divinities assigned to the realms of generation, linking them all to the divine celestial government. 

For just as the Demiurgus <term>Demiurgus: the divine Craftsman or creator of the physical universe</term> relates to *the Good itself*, so does the singular divinity of this Heaven relate to the intellectual Heaven. Therefore, just as "measure" and "limit" flow from *the Good* through Heaven to all the intellectual gods there, here a limit is passed down to the gods who create generation and to the more excellent classes <note>referring to angels, demons, and heroes</note> from the Demiurgus and the highest of the mundane gods <note>gods belonging to the physical cosmos</note>. This happens through the connecting medium of this Heaven <note>The original Greek phrasing here is corrected to read: "I mean through the [medium] of this Heaven..."</note>. For the Heaven that extends through everything is assigned this role: in one sequence of things, it acts in a unified and hidden <note>original: "occultly"</note> way, while in another, it acts openly and distinctly. In one rank, it brings "limit" to souls; in another, it brings it to the works of nature.

and in another manner relative to other things. In the air, indeed, it effects this primarily; in the aquatic orders, secondarily; and in the earth and terrestrial works, it effects this to an ultimate degree. There are also combinations of these. For the divine mode of existence, as well as the demonic <note>original: "dæmoniacal"—referring to 'daemons' or spirits that act as intermediaries between gods and humans</note> mode, are different in the air and in the earth. In one place, the mode is the same across different orders; but in another, the mode is different within a single allotment <note>original Greek: ληξεως (lēxeōs). The original text likely contained a typo, "lexeos" (speech), which the author corrects here to mean a divine station or realm.</note>. And this is enough regarding the power of Heaven.

In the next place, directing our attention to Earth and invoking her aid, we shall derive the entire theory concerning her from her first emergence <note>original: "evolution"—here meaning manifestation or unfolding</note> into light. She first becomes manifest, therefore, in the middle triads <note>original Greek: τριαδαις (triadais)—groups of three divine principles</note> of the intellectual Gods, together with Heaven, who contains the whole intellectual order within himself. She likewise proceeds in a manner analogous to the Intelligible Earth <note>original Greek: νοητων (noētōn). The text corrects a typo from "noerōn" (intellectual) to "noētōn" (intelligible), referring to the highest realm of pure being.</note>, which we find to be the first of the intelligible triads. Because she ranks among the life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note> orders, she is aligned with the first principle of infinity. But she is the receptive vessel <note>original: "receiving bosom"</note> of the generative deity of Heaven and the central point of his paternal goodness. She also reigns together with him and is the power of him who ranks as a father. 

The Earth, however, which is analogous to her and presides in the sublunary regions <term>sublunary regions: the world below the moon, characterized by change and the four elements</term>, is, as it were, the prolific power of the Heaven pertaining to the realms of generation. She unfolds into the light his paternal, definitive, measuring, and containing providence—a providence that extends prolifically <note>original Greek: γονιμως (gonimōs)</note> to all things. She likewise generates all the sublunary infinity <note>original Greek: απειριαν (apeirian). The text corrects a typo from "aporian" (difficulty/poverty) to "apeirian" (infinity).</note>, just as Heaven, who belongs to the category of "Bound," introduces termination and an end to secondary natures. 

Bound <term>Bound: the principle of structure, unity, and limit</term> and End define the subsistence <note>original: "hyparxis"—the essential foundation or 'being' of an entity</note> of every thing, by which Gods and demons, souls and bodies, are connected and made to be one, imitating the singular unity of "Wholes" (the ineffable principle of all things). On the other hand, Infinity multiplies the powers of every being. For there is much "bound" in all sublunary natures, and likewise much "infinity," which—through divinity and after the Gods—extends to all things. We have, therefore, these two orders which generate divine or demonic progressions in all the sublunary categories and elements; they form one kingdom in the same manner as they do in the higher intellectual orders.

From these, however, a second pair <note>original: "duad"</note> proceeds: Ocean and Tethys. This generation is not effected by physical mating, nor by any conjunction of things that were once separated, nor by division, nor according to a certain cutting-off <note>original: "abscission"</note>; for all these concepts are foreign to the gods.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the divine hierarchy, moving from the general principles of Heaven and Earth to the specific union between them that results in the generation of further deities like Ocean and Tethys.</meta>

<page-num>319</page-num>
<header>### BOOK V.] TIMAEUS OF PLATO.</header>

...from the Gods; rather, it is accomplished according to a single union and indivisible joining of powers. Theologians are accustomed to calling this union "marriage," for marriage—as the theologian Orpheus says—is appropriate to this level of reality. He calls Earth the "first Nymph" and her union with Heaven the "first marriage," since there is no marriage among the divinities who are united in the highest degree. Thus, there is no marriage between Phanes <note>original: "Phanes"—the first-born Orphic god of light and generation</note> and Night, who are united in a purely intelligible sense <note>original: "intelligibly united"—meaning they exist as a single unified concept before any division occurs</note>. However, marriage does exist among the Gods who show a division of powers and actions while still remaining united.

For this reason, marriage appears to be suited to the Heaven and Earth we are currently considering, as they reflect <note>original: "adumbrate"</note> the intellectual Heaven and Earth. The sacred laws of the Athenians, also recognizing this, ordered that the marriages of Heaven and Earth should be celebrated as a preparation for initiation into the mysteries. Focusing on these principles in the Eleusinian mysteries <note>The most famous of the secret religious rites of ancient Greece, centered on Demeter and Persephone</note>, they looked upward to the heavens and exclaimed, "O son!" but looking downward to the earth, they cried, "O parent!" <note>The exclamation "O son!" likely signified the divine and celestial origin of the human soul, while "O parent!" referred to its terrestrial origin through its union with a physical body.</note>

According to this union, combined with separation, Heaven and Earth produce Ocean and Tethys through their goodness. Or rather, they do not produce them immediately; prior to these two single principles <note>original: "monads"</note>, there are two groups of three <note>original: "triads"</note> and two groups of seven <note>original: "hebdomads"</note>, among which Ocean and Tethys are found. The single principles and the groups of three remain with the "father" principle. But among the groups of seven, Ocean and Tethys remain while simultaneously proceeding forward. All the others, however, move into a different order of Gods.

This is the way they exist in the intellectual realm. But here, Plato completely omits the causes that stay within the "father" principle; instead, he presents to us those that both proceed and remain, because his intention is to speak of the Gods who are the craftsmen of the world of change <note>original: "fabricators of generation"</note>. For these Gods, progression, motion, and "difference" are appropriate, as is the pairing of male and female. This allows for birth and growth <note>original: "generation"</note> to occur, for matter to be organized <note>original Greek: *kosmoumenēs*—meaning to be ordered or beautified. The original text corrects a typo from *kosmoumenous*.</note> with forms, and for "difference" to be balanced with "sameness." Thus, Plato begins with the pair <note>original: "duad"</note>, works through it, and returns to it again. The pair is suited to material natures and the concept of "difference" because of how forms are divided within matter. Having mentioned a pair, he begins with Earth, as it is more suited to things involving birth and growth.

With respect to these two divinities, Ocean and Tethys, who remain in...

<page-num>320</page-num>

...their causes, and at the same time proceed from them <note>The original Greek text is corrected here from "from her" (*ap' autēs*) to "from them" (*ap' autōn*).</note>. Some say that Ocean is a physical essence; others, that it is a nature that spreads swiftly; others, that it is the motion of a watery essence; others, that it is the ether itself because of the speed of its motion; and still others, that it is the deep, conceptual foundation <note>original: "intelligible profundity"</note> of life itself. 

The divine Iamblichus <note>A transformed Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who influenced later Platonic thought</note>, however, defines Ocean as the "middle source of divine movement." This cause is first shared by intermediary souls, lives, and intellectual acts, as well as by spirit-like elements such as air and fire. 

Regarding Tethys, some say she is a watery essence; others, a highly changeable nature; and others, the purity and radiance <note>original: "hilarity"—in this context, it refers to the unmixed, joyful vitality of the cosmos</note> of the universe. But the divine Iamblichus asserts that she is a productive power that establishes an effective foundation for action. Her stable intellectual insights are shared by souls, natures, and powers. She is also shared by certain solid containers of earth or water, which provide a foundation for the elements. 

Theodorus <note>Theodorus of Asine, a student of Iamblichus</note>, however, places Earth and Heaven in the first part of the previously mentioned "first triad" <note>A group of three related divine principles</note>, according to their state of being animated. By this, I mean he places them in the first category of "wholes that exist before their parts." He considers Heaven to be analogous to the intellectual nature, and Earth to the material nature. Of the remaining deities, he calls that which exists as a "whole made of parts" Ocean; but the third, which exists as the "wholeness found within a part," he names Tethys.

We, however, returning to our own principles, say that the causes of these deities exist among the intellectual Gods, and they are likewise present in the physical universe. Ocean everywhere distinguishes the higher orders from the lower; because of this, poets rightly call it the boundary of the earth. But the Ocean we are discussing now is the cause of motion, progression, and power. It provides the peak and fruitful abundance to intellectual lives; it gives speed and vigor to the energies of souls, as well as purity to their births; and it grants ease of movement to physical bodies. 

Among the Gods, Ocean provides a cause for movement and providence; but among angels, it provides an unfolding intellectual speed and vigor. Again, among spirits <note>original: "dæmons"—intermediary beings between gods and humans</note> it is the supplier of effective power; but among heroes, it provides a magnificent and flourishing life. It also exists in each of the elements according to its own specific character. Hence, the "aerial Ocean" is the cause of all changes in the air and the cycle of weather phenomena <note>original: "circle of the meteors"</note>, as Aristotle also says. But the "watery Ocean" gives existence to fertility, ease of movement, and all kinds of powers. For according to the poets:

->From this all seas, and every river flow.<-

And the "terrestrial ocean" is the producing cause of generative perfection, of the...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the divine roles of Ocean and Tethys in Neoplatonic philosophy, specifically how Tethys acts as a principle of separation and stability while Ocean acts as the source of all motion.</meta>

<page-num>321</page-num>
<header>BOOK V.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

...separation of forms, and of birth <note>original: "generation"</note> and decay <note>original: "corruption"</note>. Whether there are certain earthly orders that are life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note> and world-making <note>original: "demiurgic"</note>, Tethys is the source of their distinction. Or, if there are powers that connect the productive principles of the earth and serve as the overseeing guardians of birth, she also awakens and multiplies these, calling them into motion.

With respect to Tethys, as her name indeed demonstrates, she is the most ancient ancestor <note>original: "progenitor"</note> of the gods, in the same way that it is right to acknowledge the mother-goddess Rhea. For theologians name another goddess, Maia, as existing before her. Thus Orpheus says:

->Maia, supreme among the Gods, immortal Night,<-
->What do you mean to say?<-

But according to the etymology of Plato, she is a certain source-like <note>original: "fontal"</note> deity. For her name signifies that which is undefiled and pure, and that which filters <note>original: "percolates"</note>.

Since Ocean produces all things and is the source of all motions (which is why he is called the "generation of the gods"), Tethys separates the singular <note>original: "unical"</note> cause of his motions into primary and secondary movements.

Hence Plato says that she derives her name from *leaping* and *filtering*. For these are names of separation, in the same way he speaks in the *Sophist* <note>A dialogue by Plato</note> of the words "to card" and "to separate threads in weaving with a shuttle" <note>original Greek: *to xainein kai kerkizein*</note>.

Ocean, therefore, produces all motion collectively—whether it is divine, intellectual, soulful <note>original: "psychical"</note>, or physical. Tethys, however, distinguishes between internal and external motions; she is so named because she causes material movements to "leap" and be "filtered" out from those that are immaterial.

Hence, the characteristic of separating is assigned to the female, and the quality of being unified¹ to the male. Plato would assert such specific traits of Ocean and Tethys, and indeed does so in the *Cratylus*. But according to the divine Iamblichus, Tethys must be defined as the provider of position and a firm foundation.

From all that has been said, however, it may be summarized that Tethys is the cause of stability and the firm grounding of things within herself, separating them from the motions that proceed externally. In short, Ocean is the cause of all motion—intellectual, soulful, and physical—for all lesser <note>original: "secondary"</note> beings. But Tethys is the cause of all the separation of the streams flowing from Ocean. She imparts to each a proper purity in the motion assigned to it by nature. Through this, each thing—whether it moves itself or moves other things—moves in a superior <note>original: "transcendent"</note> manner. *Theologians reveal that Ocean is the provider of all motion when they say that he sends forth ten streams, nine of which flow into the sea.* This is because it is necessary that nine of the motions should be—

...corporeal, but that there should be only one essence that is separate from bodies, as we are informed by Plato in the *Laws*.¹ Therefore, the mighty Ocean excites to motion those divine natures he generates and makes them effective. But Tethys distinguishes these, keeping the generative causes pure from their offspring and establishing them in activities <note>original: "energies"</note> more ancient than those that extend into the external world. And that is enough regarding each of these divinities, Ocean and Tethys.

However, since we have said that these are generated from the prior divinities, Heaven and Earth, but this is not brought about through a physical union <note>original: "copulation"</note> like that found in the world of the senses <note>original: "sensibles"</note>, nor by a union like that of Night and Phanes in the realm of pure intellect <note>original: "intelligibles"</note>, it follows naturally that their offspring are separated from each other in a way similar to their parents, and each takes on a resemblance to both. For Ocean, being the male, is likened to the paternal cause, Heaven; but as the provider of motion, he is likened to the maternal cause, Earth, who is the cause of progressions. And Tethys, being the female, is likened to the reproductive <note>original: "prolific"</note> cause; but by providing a firm foundation <note>original: "establishment"</note> for her offspring in their respective lives, she is likened to the creative <note>original: "fabricating"</note> cause. For the male is equivalent to the monad <note>A single, indivisible unit</note>; but the female to the duad <note>A pair or principle of multiplicity</note>. Stability is suited to the former, while motion is suited to the latter. Therefore, a pair <note>original: "duad"</note> proceeding from a pair, and being made like the pair that generated it, defines and distinguishes its own causes and all the numbers that come after it, so that everywhere we may credit the order of Ocean and Tethys with the power of defining and separating. For this reason, theologians also tell us of many Oceans.³

However, one might wonder why these gods are generated from Heaven and Earth rather than from the soul of the universe. For Plato nowhere assigns a specific <note>original: "peculiar"</note> soul to the heavens. The solution to these doubts is this: it must be said that the soul which arises from the *psychogony* <note>The creation or birth of the soul</note> is the world-soul <note>original: "mundane soul"</note> of all parts of the universe. For Plato says that the divinity built the entire physical nature within this soul, not just the heavens. However, as the soul of the universe, it primarily illuminates the heavens, and—

# BOOK V.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

...gives life to the sublunary region <note>The region below the moon, consisting of the four changing elements of earth, water, air, and fire</note>, which hangs down from the heavens. Therefore, this soul is primarily heavenly. You can find a clear example of this in the human soul. For Plato says that the soul which governs our entire living being is assigned the head as its dwelling place; from there, it rules over the whole body and channels sensation, as if through a tube, to every part of the physical frame. Since Socrates had established the Fates over the fixed stars <note>original: "inerratic"</note> and the planetary spheres on the previous day, Plato does not now introduce a specific soul for each of them. Instead, because he has already used them, he forms these rotations of the universal soul. However, he assigns unique souls to the stars themselves within those spheres, because Socrates had said nothing about them in the *Republic*, and their specific way of being alive was unknown to his listeners. It was appropriate to elaborate on details that were unknown to them, rather than discussing obvious points at great length. <note>Five lines in the original of the above paragraph are likewise illegible, because they are in such a mutilated state.</note>

<margin>HOE</margin>
> “But from Ocean and Tethys were produced Phorcys, Saturn, Rhea, and others who exist along with them.”

In the previous generation, a pair <term>duad</term> that generates and moves (Ocean and Tethys) was produced from a pair that limits and defines (Heaven and Earth). But in this second generation, a multitude that returns to its causes through a group of three <term>triad</term> is generated from that pair, indicating a perfectly complete progression. This multitude is also divided into a part that corresponds to "limit" <note>original: "bound"</note> and a part aligned with "infinity." Within this group, the triad represents the limit, while the "nameless number" represents its infinite aspect. Even within the triad itself, one part is like the single unit <term>monad</term> and limit, while another is like the pair <term>duad</term> and infinity. In the previous progression, the offspring followed only the patterns of limit and the intellect; but in this stage, there is also a mixture of the indefinite. After establishing the limit from the triad, Plato adds, “*And such as exist together with these,*” which points to the complete development and separation of these triple orders. Thus, the offspring of this progression are threefold <note>original: "triadic"</note> because of how they return to their source, and twofold <note>original: "dyadic"</note> because of the influence of the infinite and indefinite.

Since these differ according to their intellectual causes in the same way as the previously mentioned orders, we must note that Ocean and Tethys were called the siblings—not the fathers <note>The Greek word for "father" (original: *Patros*) is erroneously printed in the source text instead of "fathers" (original: *pateres*).</note>—of Saturn and Rhea. This is because the descent of these gods began with Heaven and Earth, and the entire order of Titans originates from them.

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.

...derived; let us see why Plato here gives existence <note>original: "subsistence"</note> to Phorcys, Saturn, and Rhea, from Ocean and Tethys. For he may seem to say this in a way that is not consistent with Orphic principles. For "Earth secretly bore from Heaven, as the theologian <note>Referring to Orpheus, the legendary founder of the Orphic mysteries</note> says, seven pure beautiful virgins with rolling eyes, and seven sons who were kings with fine long hair. And the daughters, indeed, were Themis, and the joyful Tethys, Mnemosyne with thick-curled hair, and the blessed Thea. She likewise bore Dione, who has a very graceful form, and Phoebe, and Rhea, the mother of king Jupiter. But the venerable Earth brought forth those celestial youths who are called by the name of Titans, because they took revenge upon the mighty starry Heaven. And she also bore Coeus, the great Crius <note>original: "Crœus"</note>, and the strong Phorcys, and likewise Saturn, and Ocean, Hyperion, and Iapetus." 

Since these things were written by the theologian before Plato, why does Timaeus produce Saturn and Rhea from Ocean and Tethys? In answer to this <note>The original Greek text uses "towards" (*pros*) in response to the question, rather than "how" (*pos*)</note>: as we have previously arranged Ocean and Tethys above Saturn and Rhea—acting as the intermediaries <note>original: "media"</note> between them and the fathers, and as guardians of the boundaries of both, as they are usually praised—we must first say that it is not surprising that the same divinities should be brothers and yet, because of their superior dignity, be called the fathers of certain gods. For those who are first, when they emerge from their causes, help produce the natures that follow them, working alongside those original causes. 

In this way, all souls are indeed sisters, according to a single creative <term>demiurgic</term> cause and the life-giving <term>vivific</term> principle and fountain from which they proceed. At the same time, divine souls produce individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls together with the Creator <term>Demiurge</term> and the life-giving causes, because the divine souls emerged into the light first and remained in their complete state, receiving the power to create natures similar to themselves. Furthermore, among the gods themselves, all the offspring of Saturn are brothers, according to the one generative source <term>monad</term> by which they were produced. Yet at the same time, Jupiter is called "father" in the works of the divine poet Homer, by both Juno and Neptune:

->One word permit me, thundering father Jove; <note>Homer, *Iliad*, Book 19, line 121</note><-

And,

->What mortal now in all the boundless earth,<-
->O father Jove, will give counsel to the immortals? <note>Homer, *Iliad*, Book 7, line 447. Proclus’s text contains a minor Greek variant here, using the word for "favor" or "kindness" (*era*) rather than the name of the goddess Hera.</note><-

For in the first verse Juno calls Jupiter "father," and in the second Neptune does so. Therefore, it is not at all strange if Ocean and Tethys are called both siblings...

...and fathers of Saturn and Rhea, because they preserve the paternal characteristics among their brothers. First, the doubt may be resolved in this way.

Next, it could be said that among the divine groups of seven Titans <note>original: "Titannic hebdomads"</note>, Ocean both remains in his source <note>original: "abides"</note> and moves forward <note>original: "proceeds"</note>, staying united with his father and not leaving his kingdom. However, all the rest, delighting in their outward movement, are said to have carried out the will of Earth but to have attacked their father, separating themselves from his kingdom and entering another level of reality <note>original: "order"</note>. Or rather, of all the heavenly classes <note>original: "genera"</note>, some only remain in their primary states <note>original: "principles"</note>, such as the first two groups of three <note>original: "triads"</note>. [Orpheus says,] "For as soon as Heaven understood that they had an implacable heart and a lawless nature, he threw them into Tartarus, the deep abyss of the Earth." Therefore, through his overwhelming power, he hid them in the unapparent realm. But others both remain in and move forward from their origins, like Ocean and Tethys. For when the other Titans set out to attack their father, Heaven, Ocean stopped them from following their mother's orders, doubting their correctness.

> "But Ocean [says Orpheus] stayed within his dwelling place, considering what he should do, and whether he should strip his father of his power and unjustly maim him alongside Saturn and the other brothers—who followed their dear mother—or if he should leave them and stay quietly at home. After much hesitation, however, he stayed peaceably at home, being angry with his mother, but even more so with his brothers."

Therefore, he remains while simultaneously moving forward along with Tethys, for she is joined with him as the first offspring. But the other Titans are drawn toward separation and outward movement. The leader of these is the mighty Saturn, as the theologian <note>Referring to Orpheus, the legendary founder of the Orphic mysteries</note> says. He shows that Saturn is superior to Ocean by saying that Saturn himself took control of the celestial Olympus, and that having taken his throne there, he rules over the Titans. Meanwhile, Ocean received all the middle territory <note>original: "allotment"</note>. For he says that Ocean lives in the divine streams that are lower than Olympus, and that he surrounds the Heaven that is there—not the highest Heaven, but as the myth says, that which fell from Olympus and was situated there.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s analysis of the Titan genealogy. He is specifically examining the relationship between Ocean, Tethys, Saturn (Cronus), and Rhea, and how they transition from the "intellectual" realm of the mind to the "flowing" realm of the physical world.</meta>

# BOOK V.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

Ocean and Tethys, therefore, insofar as they remain and are united to Heaven <note>Uranus</note>, produce the kingdom of Saturn <note>Cronus</note> and Rhea in conjunction with him. But insofar as they are established in the primary power of their mother <note>Gaia/Earth</note>, they produce Phorcys in conjunction with her. <note>original: "with him" [Heaven], but the Greek text should read "with her" [Earth].</note> For Earth produces Phorcys together with Nereus and Thaumas <note>original: Thaumanta; corrected to Thaumantos</note>, by being joined through love with the sea <note>original: ponton; corrected to pontō</note>. Phorcys is not a "child of Heaven," but Ocean is, as is evident from the *Theogony*. <note>original: The Greek text here is erroneous; it says "Phorcys is not a child of Heaven, but Phorcys is," when it should say "but Ocean is." Hesiod’s Theogony identifies Ocean as the child of Heaven and Earth.</note>

Furthermore, insofar as Tethys is full of Earth—acting as a kind of Earth herself—she may be said to produce Phorcys in conjunction with Ocean. This is because Ocean also contains the "intelligible" (the realm of pure thought) within himself. Therefore Tethys, as a participant in Earth’s nature, and Ocean, as the source of the sea, give existence to this God <note>Phorcys</note> alongside Saturn and Rhea. 

However, if any arguments demonstrate that in the higher intellectual order, Saturn is above Ocean or Rhea is above Tethys, it must be said that such an arrangement belongs to that higher level. In that realm, the causes of "intellection" (pure thought) are superior to the causes of motion. But here in the physical world, on the contrary, all things are in a state of change and flow. Therefore, in this context, Ocean is properly placed before Saturn, since Ocean is the fountain of motion, and Tethys is placed before Rhea. In this way, the philosophical doubt may be resolved.

To speak about each of these Gods individually: Theodorus refers the souls that exist in relation to the physical world <note>original: "subsist in habitude"</note> to these divinities, and he arranges them as presiding over the three divisions of the world. 

*   **Phorcys:** Theodorus places him in the starless sphere <note>The *Primum Mobile*, or the outermost shell of the universe</note> as the force that moves the rotation <note>original: "lation"</note> of the universe. However, he would first have to prove that Plato was aware of a "starless sphere" before arranging Phorcys within it. 
*   **Saturn:** He places Saturn over the motions of the stars, because time <note>original Greek: *Kronos* (the god) erroneously printed for *chronos* (time)</note>—and the birth and decay of all things—comes from these stellar motions. 
*   **Rhea:** He places Rhea over the material part of the world, because through her materiality, she has an "overflow" or redundancy compared to the divinities that come before her. 

However, the divine Iamblichus <note>A simplified Neoplatonist philosopher</note> arranges them in the three spheres between the heavens and the earth. While some of the lower gods divide the region below the moon into two parts, these deities divide it into three. 

*   **Phorcys:** According to Iamblichus, he presides over the entirety <note>original: "whole essence" rather than "material essence"</note> of the "humid essence" (watery elements), containing all of it as a single whole. 
*   **Rhea:** She is a divinity who connects flowing and airy spirits.

# BOOK V.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

...the middle arrangement according to Plato, because in immaterial essences, the middle and the center hold greater authority than the powers situated around the middle. We certainly admire this intellectual explanation by Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was an influential Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who organized the gods into a complex hierarchy.</note>, but we think it is appropriate to observe these Gods everywhere—in all the elements and in all levels of the cosmic order. In this way, we can see what they have in common and how they extend through all things. 

We say that Phorcys is the overseeing guardian of every generative essence and of physical—and, so to speak, seed-like—productive principles, being the cause of physical birth <note>original: "generation"; the process of coming into being in the physical world.</note>. These generative principles exist in each of the elements, and different ranks of Gods and spirits <note>original: "dæmons"; in this context, these are intermediary divine beings, not evil spirits.</note> preside over them, all of whom Plato includes under the name of Phorcys. 

However, King Saturn <note>Saturn is the Roman name for the Greek Titan Cronus.</note> divides these forms and productive principles, turning universal powers into more specific ones. Thus, he is not only associated with "animal" as a general concept, but specifically with those that walk on land <note>original: "pedestrious"; meaning land-dwelling or walking on feet.</note>, those that live in water, and those that fly. Even among land animals, he is not just the cause of land-dwellers generally, but specifically of humans and horses. This is because the productive principles within him are more specific than those in the celestial deities. Among the intellectual Gods, he is assigned the power to multiply and divide the objects of pure thought. Therefore, he is the leader of the Titans, as he is primarily defined by this quality of division.

Next, we say that Rhea receives the hidden powers of King Saturn, leads them out toward secondary levels of nature, and rouses these fatherly powers to create visible objects. In this way, her primary rank is set in motion; it is filled with power and life, and it brings into the visible world the causes that remain hidden within Saturn. Consequently, Saturn is the universal provider of intellectual forms; Rhea is the source of all souls and every type of life; and Phorcys is abundant with the physical principles of nature. 

Since, however, another group of Gods belongs to their kingdom—whom Saturn and Rhea encompass—Plato adds the phrase, "*and such as exist together with these*." By this, he does not only include spirits, as some suggest, but implies that both the angelic and the spiritual ranks of Saturn have their own vast numbers—one group being angelic, the other spiritual. The multitude within the Gods is divine; that in the air is aerial; and it is the same for the other elements and the other more excellent classes <note>original: "genera"; types or categories of beings.</note> arranged under these Gods.

By the words "*such as exist together with these*," Plato also seems to refer to the remaining Titans: namely Coeus and Hyperion, Crius, and Iapetus, as well as the remaining Titanesses <note>original: "Titannidæ"</note>: namely Phoebe, Theia, Mnemosyne, Themis, and Dione, who emerged into the light alongside Saturn and Rhea. He also refers to those who emerged with Phorcys: Nereus and Thaumas, the highly active Eurybia, and those who especially sustain and connect the entirety of physical creation. Furthermore, it is worth noting that it is not appropriate to strictly debate the arrangement in

# PROCLUS ON THE TIMÆUS [BOOK V.]

...these divinities, and whether Saturn <note>original: "Saturn"; the Roman name for the Greek Titan Cronus, whom Proclus views as a representative of pure intellect.</note> or Phorcys is the superior deity; for they are united and similar to each other. But if it is necessary to make a distinction, it is better to adopt the arrangement of the divine Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian philosopher who refined the hierarchy of the gods in Neoplatonism.</note>. He states that Saturn is a monad <note>original: "monad"; a single, unified source or principle of "oneness."</note>; but Rhea is a certain duad <note>original: "duad"; a principle of duality or "twoness" that allows for multiplication.</note>, calling forth the powers that are within Saturn; and that Phorcys gives perfection to their progression. It now remains, therefore, that we direct our attention to the other kings who produce the visible, sublunary <note>original: "sublunary"; the region of the universe below the moon, meaning the physical world of change and death.</note> order of things; for such is the arrangement they are assigned.

<margin>41 A</margin>
> "But from Saturn and Rhea, descended Jupiter, Juno, and all such as we know are called their siblings, as well as their other offspring."

This is the third progression of the Gods who are the creators <note>original: "fabricators"; referring to the Demiurge or divine craftsman.</note> of physical birth <note>original: "generation"; the process of coming into being in the material world.</note>. However, it is the fourth order overall, closing as a tetrad <note>original: "tetrad"; a grouping of four, considered a number of completion.</note> the naming of the leading Gods. For the tetrad encompasses the divine orders. As a duad <note>a pair</note>, this progression is compared to the first kingdom, because both are dyadic in nature. Within this progression, however, there exists an all-perfect state according to its development, and an unlimited state according to its number.

But here, Plato not only adds the words "such as," as he did in the previous progression, but also the word "all," to indicate that they extend to everything. For we use the term <term>to hoion</term> <note>original: "το οἷον"; meaning "such as" or "of the sort."</note> when speaking of things that are united, but we use the term <term>to pantas</term> <note>original: "το παντας"; meaning "all."</note> when speaking of things that are now divided and multiplied. The universal <note>original: <term>το ολικον</term> ("to holikon"); meaning the "total" or "whole."</note> also pertains to this progression. For the Gods named here, and those that proceed everywhere alongside them, are characterized by this form of creation. *For all divine creators <note>original: "Demiurgi"; the gods who shape the world.</note> are universal.* Who, therefore, are they, and what kind of order do they possess?

The divine Iamblichus asserts that Jupiter is the one who perfects all physical birth. He claims Juno is the cause of power, connection, fullness, and life for all things. Their siblings are those who work with them in the creation of life, being themselves "intellects" <note>pure divine minds</note> and achieving their completion through a perfection and power similar to Jupiter and Juno. 

But Theodorus <note>Theodorus of Asine, a student of Iamblichus who often disagreed with him on the structure of the soul and the gods.</note>, again dividing the life that animates the whole in its various states, and organizing it into groups of three as he usually does, calls Jupiter the power that governs the upper region as far as the air. He calls Juno the power who is assigned the aerial part of the world. Their siblings are those who complete the remaining parts of the world. For Jupiter is the essence of the soul that exists in a material state, because there is nothing more vital than essence. But Juno is the intellectual part of such a soul, because the natures on the earth are governed by the productive powers...

...productive principles proceeding from the air. And the other number is the psychical <note>original: "psychical"; here meaning "relating to the soul" (psyche), rather than the modern paranormal sense.</note> distributed into particular parts.

We, however, following <note>original: *hemeis de epomenōs*</note> what has been asserted before, say that according to Plato there are many orders of Jupiter <note>Jupiter is the Roman name for the Greek king of the gods, Zeus.</note>. For one is the Demiurgus <note>The "Demiurge" is the divine Craftsman or Creator of the universe.</note>, as it is written in the *Cratylus*; another is the first of the Saturnian triad, as it is asserted in the *Gorgias*; another is the "liberated" god, as it is delivered in the *Phaedrus*; and another is the celestial god, whether in the sphere of the fixed stars or among the planets. Moreover, as the first Jupiter brought the power of his father (which was concealed in the hidden realm) into the visible creation—being stirred to this action <note>The original Greek *dianoētheis* ("having thought") is corrected by the translator to *diakinētheis* ("being moved or excited").</note> by his mother Rhea—in the same way, the Jupiter described here (who is the creator of physical birth) causes the hidden divisions and separations of forms made by Saturn to become visible. 

Rhea calls these forms forth into motion and birth; and Phorcys <note>A primordial sea god whom Proclus interprets as a power that organizes matter.</note> inserts them into matter, produces sensible <note>original: "sensible"; things that can be perceived by the five senses.</note> natures, and adorns the visible essence. He does this so that there may not only be divisions of rational patterns <note>original: "productive principles"; or *logoi*, the underlying blueprints of reality.</note> in natures, in souls, and in the intellectual essences that come before them, but also in physical things. ***For this is the unique characteristic of divine crafting.*** 

If it is necessary to speak what appears to me to be the truth: Saturn produces intellectual divisions, Rhea produces those relating to the soul, and Phorcys produces those relating to the physical body. For all seminal rational principles <note>original: "spermatic productive principles"; the biological and physical "seeds" or blueprints of life.</note> are under the domain of Nature. But Jupiter, by adorning the sensible and visible divisions, gives a specific distinction to those beings in the sublunary <note>The region below the moon; the earth and its atmosphere, characterized by change and decay.</note> region that are entirely alive, and he causes them to move. 

However, since these physical forms which are created and perfected are unfolded in many ways—being moved and changed according to all kinds of developments—the queen Juno <note>Juno is the Roman name for Hera.</note> is joined with Jupiter. She gives perfection to this motion of visible natures and to the unfolding of forms. For this reason, myths represent her as sometimes sending "mania" <note>Divine madness or frenzy.</note> to certain people, while ordering others to undergo severe labors (like Hercules). She does this so that through intellect being present in all things, and through individual souls acting divinely in both thought and practice, every stage and all the creation of the sublunary region may reach complete perfection.

Such, therefore, being the nature of this pair, there are also other creative powers which divide the visible <note>The original Greek *aphanē* ("unapparent") is corrected here to *emphanē* ("apparent" or "visible").</note> world of birth into three parts: one is assigned the government of air; another that of water; and another that of earth, according to their divine allotments. # PROCLUS ON THE [TIMÆUS] BOOK V

...these gods, because they also preside over the visible creation <note>original: "fabrication"</note>. Furthermore, there are others who are the descendants of these; this is the final progression of the divinities mentioned by Plato in this passage. For this reason, they are listed anonymously. By doing this, Plato indicates how the divine power diminishes as it reaches this final division. 

Just as among the gods who exist above the physical world, the divisible <note>original: "partible"; meaning specific or individual parts of a whole.</note> proceeds from the total creation, and the line of kings ends there; in the same way, among the sublunary gods <note>The gods presiding over the realm "below the moon," which includes the Earth and its atmosphere.</note>, the descendants of Jupiter <note>Roman name for Zeus.</note> proceed from the "Jovian order." Among these descendants is the choir of "divisible creation." Because the previously mentioned Demiurgi <note>original: "Demiurgi"; the divine craftsmen or creators.</note> produce sensible <note>original: "sensible"; things perceptible by the senses.</note> things as a whole, it is necessary for other deities to exist who distribute different powers and unique characteristics to different parts of nature, dividing the sublunary world into a vast multitude. 

This is why Plato calls them simply *others*, and does not use more general terms like *such as* or *all*, because they are associated with all types of diversity. In what Plato has written, we find the entire system of analogous kingdoms: Heaven and Earth hold the first rank, followed by the sublunary kingdoms—the celestial, the Saturnian <note>relating to Saturn/Cronus</note>, and the Dionysiacal <note>relating to Dionysus</note>. 

Between these two kingdoms, the order of Ocean is placed first. Ocean defines and distinguishes all the progressions coming from the "fathers" (the primary causes); he remains still while also proceeding forward, mirroring the intellectual foundations <note>original: "hypostases"</note> of those gods. What need is there to go any further? All the divine governments are delivered here, each joined with its proper group. Heaven terminates and defines, Earth strengthens and supports, and Ocean moves all generation. Meanwhile, Tethys establishes everything in its proper motion: 
*   Intellectual essences move with intellectual motion; 
*   Middle essences (souls) move with psychical motion; 
*   Corporeal (physical) things move with physical motion.

Ocean moves all these things collectively <note>original footnote translated: Instead of the Greek "tou okeanou panta kinountōn athroōs" (plural), it is obviously necessary to read "tou okeanou panta kinountos athroōs" (singular: "Ocean moving all things collectively").</note>. 

Saturn <note>Cronus</note> alone divides things intellectually; Rhea gives them life; Phorcys distributes the "spermatic" productive principles <note>The divine "seeds" or blueprints that determine the forms of physical life.</note>; Jupiter perfects things that are visible from those that were hidden; and Juno <note>Hera</note> unfolds them according to the many changes of visible nature. 

Thus, through this "ennead" <note>A group of nine: Heaven, Earth, Ocean, Tethys, Saturn, Rhea, Phorcys, Jupiter, and Juno.</note>, the entire sublunary world is completed and perfectly arranged. This arrangement is divine because of the gods, but it is also "angelic" (as we say) because of angels, and "demonic" because of demons <note>original: "dæmons"; in Neoplatonism, these are intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil.</note>. The gods themselves exist in relation to bodies, souls, and intellects; angels exercise their providence over souls and bodies; and demons are assigned to the crafting of nature and the care of physical bodies. 

Furthermore, the number nine (the ennead) is perfectly suited to the process of birth and generation. It proceeds from the "monad" <note>The number one, representing the source or unity.</note> all the way to the furthest extremities without turning back; this lack of "retrogression" is the defining characteristic of physical birth. For the "reasons" <note>original: "reasons" (logoi); the rational, productive principles of the universe.</note>—that is, the productive principles—fall into matter and are unable to return by themselves to the principles of their origin.

Moreover, the pair <note>original: "duad"</note> is also a group of three <note>original: "triadic"</note>, since three paired orders were assumed;¹ this demonstrates the combination of the perfect and the imperfect, and of Limit <note>original: "bound"</note> with Infinity. For all celestial natures are definite and, as Aristotle says, are always at their completion <note>original: "in the end"</note>. But things in the world of physical change <note>original: "generation"</note> proceed² from the imperfect to the perfect, and receive the same boundaries in an indefinite way. 

Besides this, the group of four <note>original: "tetrad"</note> arising from the birth of these divinities is adapted to the orders of the creators <note>original: "fabricators"</note> of the sublunary region. This is so that they may hold a multitude of things together as a unity, and contain the divisible <note>original: "partible"</note> in an indivisible way, as well as being adapted to the natures that exist in physical change. For the sublunary elements are four; the seasons according to which physical life evolves are four; and the centers of the world are four. In short, the number four has an abundant dominion over the world of physical change.

Why, however, it may be asked, does Plato include all the multitude of the gods who create physical life in this group of nine <note>original: "ennead"</note>? I answer that this group of nine completes the entire creation of the physical world. For in the sublunary realms, there are bodies and natures, souls and intellects, and these exist both as wholes and as parts. All of these are present in both respects in each of the elements,³ because wholes and parts exist alongside one another. 

Heaven and Earth, however, generate the invisible <note>original: "unapparent"</note> essences of these—that is, of both the wholes and the parts. Heaven does this according to union and Limit <note>original: "bound"</note>, while Earth does so according to multiplication and Infinity; together, they are the leaders that bring all things into being. But Ocean and Tethys bring completion to both the common and the divided motions of these things. 

There is, however, a different motion for different things: for the universal <note>original: "total"</note> intellect, the universal soul, and universal nature, and similarly for the individual <note>original: "partial"</note> versions of these. With the sublunary wholes thus organized and distributed, Saturn <note>The Roman name for Cronus</note> intellectually divides the individual natures from the universal ones. Rhea, as a life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note> deity, calls forth this division from the intellectual realm into all kinds of diverse progressions,⁴ reaching down to the very last forms of life. Phorcys then produces the "Titanic" separation, directing it toward the productive principles of the physical world. 

After these three come the fathers of composite natures. Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus</note> organizes the world of the senses as a whole, imitating the higher Heaven. For the Jupiter in the intellectual order proceeds in a manner analogous to the "Intellectual Heaven" in the royal series of gods. Finally, Juno <note>The Roman name for Hera</note> moves all wholes, filling them with power and unfolding them according to every progression—

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.]

The gods who follow these higher orders create the individual parts of the sensory world <note>original: "sensibles"</note>. Some do so according to one characteristic and some according to another—whether creative <note>original: "demiurgic"</note>, life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note>, perfecting, or binding <note>original: "connective"</note>. They unfold and divide themselves all the way down to the lowliest things, following the pattern of the Saturnian order. For the characteristic of division originates from the dominion of Saturn <note>In Neoplatonism, Saturn/Cronus represents the intellectual level that divides the unified ideas of the higher realm into distinct forms</note>.

<margin>41 A</margin>
> "When, therefore, all such gods as revolve visibly, and those who become visible whenever they please, were generated, the one who produced this universe addressed them in this way."

Plato has included in his discussion all the gods of the world—both those in the heavens and those who preside over the realm of change and physical birth <note>original: "generation"</note>. Having brought them forth from the creative source <note>original: "demiurgic monad"</note>—some individually, some in groups of seven <note>original: "hebdomadically"</note>, and others according to the number nine <note>original: "ennead"</note>—he now turns them back toward the creative cause. He gathers them around the one Father, through whom they are all related to one another, and fills them with creative thoughts <note>original: "demiurgic intellections"</note> so that they may imitate the providence of the Father. This will become clear later. For now, however, it is evident that he calls the celestial gods "those that revolve visibly." This is because their vessels <note>original: "vehicles," referring to the *ochema* or soul-carrier</note> are like the sun <note>original: "solar-form"</note> and imitate intellectual splendor.

But why does Plato describe the gods below the moon <note>original: "sublunary deities"</note> as "those who become visible when they please"? Should we say it is because these material elements are cast before them like veils¹ of the splendor of the celestial vessels that are directly attached to them? For it is clear that since they are part of the world, they must also necessarily possess a worldly, starry vessel. However, their light shines forth to our view only when they intend to benefit the places that receive their illumination. 

If Plato says that they become visible "when they please," it must be that this appearance is either an unfolding into the light of their non-physical <note>original: "incorporeal"</note> powers, or of the bodies that are completely subject to them. But if it is an unfolding of their non-physical powers, this would also be true of the visible gods. For the visible gods are not always apparent through their non-physical powers, but only sometimes, and when they choose. Therefore, it is not correct to distinguish the gods below the moon from the visible gods based on something they both have in common; we must distinguish them by what is unique to each. If, however, they produce a brilliant unfolding of certain bodies whenever they please, they must necessarily use other bodies prior to these material elements; and which then...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, specifically discussing the "sublunary gods"—those who govern the realm of change and physical elements below the moon—and the subtle bodies or "vehicles" they inhabit.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.] TIMAEUS OF PLATO

The gods become visible to us when it seems appropriate to the powers that use them. Consequently, other bodies more divine than those that are apparent are distributed beneath the invisible gods; and according to these, they are said to be, and are, worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note>. Through these bodies as intermediaries <note>original: "media"</note>, they ride within and govern these elements. For they impart to the elements as much of themselves as they are able to receive, and they contain the forms and natures of these elements within their own powers. 

Since none of these higher bodies is an object of the senses, and it is necessary that the vehicles of rational souls should be of this kind, it is evident that they must use other vehicles prior to these visible bodies. Furthermore, if no body at all were attached to them, it would be strange—since the celestial souls use bodies—that these divine sublunary souls should be exempt from all bodies, even though they are worldly gods. 

But if they also have something corporeal, they either have these visible bodies or other bodies that exist prior to them. If they only had the former, how would it be possible for them to ascend into (or be immediately connected with) bodies that are generated and subject to decay? For if these bodies had a sensory perception of an unnatural state <term>preternatural disposition</term> within them, caused by perceiving the life of the powers using them, they would not allow those powers to remain inactive. But if they do not have such perception <note>The original text notes: "For 'indeed' [Greek: *men*] here, it is necessary to read 'not' [Greek: *mē*]."</note>, they will not be animals. For every animal is capable of sensation, according to Plato. 

For this reason, Plato also grants a sense of the lowest kind to plants and calls them animals. But the idea that everything attached to a soul is animated and is an animal is also asserted by Plato. If, therefore, such bodies as are objects of the senses were immediately attached to the divine sublunary gods, it is doubtful how this would be possible. They must, therefore, have other bodies prior to these visible ones. This is what Plato reveals when he says, *"that they become apparent when they please,"* meaning that at other times they remain invisible to us. This concludes the commentary on the words of the text.

Regarding all the gods that govern the realm of change and generation, we must not say that they have a nature <note>original: "essence"</note> mingled with matter, as the Stoics <note>An ancient school of philosophy that believed God was a physical force or "breath" pervading all matter.</note> claim. For nothing that inclines toward matter is able to govern with intellect and wisdom, nor is it properly a producing cause, but rather an instrument of something else. 

Nor should we say that they have a nature unmixed with matter but have powers and activities <note>original: "energies"</note> mixed with it, as Numenius <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who influenced Neoplatonism by bridging Plato and Pythagorean thought.</note> and his followers assert. For the activities of the gods agree with their natures, and their inner lives exist before their external activities. Even an individual soul, before the life that is inserted into the animal attached to it, contains a more fundamental life within itself; and prior to the external motion through which it moves other things, it is moved by a motion turned back upon itself <note>In Neoplatonism, "conversion" or "turning back" refers to the way a higher being remains anchored in its own perfect nature even while acting upon lower things.</note>. The sublunary gods...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, specifically discussing the "sublunary gods"—those who govern the realm of change and physical elements below the moon—and the subtle bodies or "vehicles" they inhabit.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V. TIMAEUS OF PLATO]

These gods, therefore, are entirely unmixed with matter. They organize things that are mixed in an unmixed way, and they govern things that are created in an uncreated manner. They also contain divisible things <term>partibles</term> in an indivisible way. They are the causes of life, the providers of intellect, the replenishers of power, and the givers of soul. They are the primary leaders of all that is good and the sources of order, providence, and the highest administration. 

They also give existence to more excellent beings that surround them; they are the leaders of angels, the rulers of spirits <note>original: "dæmons," referring to intermediary spirits rather than evil beings</note>, and the overseers <note>original: "prefects"</note> of heroes. Through this triple army, they govern the entire realm of physical change <note>original: "generation"</note>. If, therefore, we assert that the specific order of these divinities concerning the physical world is the basis and seat of the total Gods, we shall be correct. We shall also not err in asserting that they connect <note>original: "convolve"</note> the end of the divine descent <note>original: "decrement"</note> back to the beginning. 

Such, then, is the nature of these divinities. Plato, looking toward the Gods who are both intelligible and intellectual, as well as those properly called intellectual, observed four common progressions among them. But they also contain powers derived from the gods beyond this world <note>original: "supermundane"</note>, whether they proceed from the twelve leaders or from certain other deities.

From the heavenly choir of Gods, a certain order likewise proceeds into the realm of physical change which, as the divine Iamblichus says, is doubled as it moves forward. For from the twenty-one leaders, forty-two governments of Gods—who are the fabricators of the physical world—are derived according to each elementary assignment. But from the thirty-six rulers of ten <term>decadarchs</term>¹, seventy-two sublunary rulers proceed. Other Gods follow a similar pattern, being double the number of the celestial Gods but possessing less power. 

It is also necessary to examine their threefold progressions, their fivefold divisions, and their divine production according to the group of seven <term>hebdomad</term>. For they receive an organized distribution in a threefold, fivefold, and sevenfold manner, analogous to the whole world. This is so that each of the elements may be a world in itself and may truly be an imitation of the universe. This, then, is the concise doctrine concerning the sublunary Gods, according to their twofold essences, lives, and assignments—just as Plato also makes their ruling offspring <note>original: "progeny"</note> twofold <term>dyadic</term>.

In the next place, let us consider the words of the Father [the Demiurge], and the reason for which they proceed. These "words" are not those that come through a mouth, for such a thing is unsuited to a non-physical and separate essence. Nor are they merely physical laws, for these are not primarily granted to worldly natures by the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note>,

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, focusing on the nature of the "speech" or "words" delivered by the Demiurge (the Creator) to the junior gods, explaining how these words act as a transmission of divine power.</meta>

# [BOOK V.] TIMAEUS OF PLATO

...but by the single nature of the universe. Nor are these words "psychical" (relating to the soul), for the one soul of the world—and all other souls that undergo a process of birth <term>generation</term>—already contain these within themselves. Nor are they "intellectual"; for, in short, <note>1</note> the intellect of the universe and all the individual intellects that compose it contain these within themselves. Rather, we must say—in a manner worthy of the speaker—that these words are creative <term>demiurgic</term> and divine. They cause all the gods who are born to become creators themselves and to be defined by the power of the God who is speaking. For words are the transmission of powers from primary to secondary natures; they communicate divine providence and that wondrous life which the Demiurge <note>original: "Demiurgus of wholes," referring to the Creator of the entire universe</note> already possesses within himself. Such, then, are these "words," as we have described them.

Their ultimate purpose, however, is to make the gods who receive them into creators themselves. Just as the rational principles <term>logoi</term> <note>original: "reasons [or productive powers]"</note> that move from art into matter create artificial forms—and just as those from nature create physical forms, those from the soul create living things, and those from the intellect create intellectual things—in the same way, the rational principles (or words) that come from the gods make all the classes <term>genera</term> that follow them divine. 

Since some of the gods belong to the creative <term>demiurgic</term> order and others to the life-giving <term>vivific</term> order—and while some are defined by an unchanging and pure life, others have different traits—the nature of their words is defined by the specific character of the speaker. For these words are either creative, or the source of a divine life, or the provider of stability and purity. Therefore, because the one who now delivers these words is the Demiurge, the words carry a creative power that matches his nature and turns those who receive them into creators <term>Demiurgi</term>. 

For although there are different ranks of the gods within the world <term>mundane Gods</term>—namely, the creative, life-giving, binding, perfecting, guarding, judging, and purifying <term>cathartic</term> orders, just as there are among the gods established above the heavens (since the lower gods follow the pattern of the higher ones)—at the same time, all of them share in all these powers. However, different gods are defined more or less by their specific unique traits. Thus, each god shares in creative power because they are all aligned with the creative unity <term>demiurgic monad</term>; they share in life-giving power because they are illuminated by the life-giving source <term>vivific fountain</term>; and the same applies to the other powers. 

If the speaker were a life-giving god, we would say that he filled his listeners with divine life through his words. But since the one delivering this speech is the Demiurge, he imparts his creative character to the other gods. He spreads his single act of creation <term>fabrication</term> among the many gods of the world and makes them the creators of other mortal species. Meanwhile, as divinely inspired poetry says, he himself remains eternally in his high watchtower on the summit of Olympus.

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.]

...therefore are the words, and this is the end of this creative <term>demiurgic</term> speech. It now remains that we should proceed to the development of the words themselves.

### "Gods of Gods."

<margin>41 A</margin>
The purpose of this speech is to instill creative power and providence into the worldly classes <term>mundane genera</term> of Gods, to lead them forward to the creation of the remaining kinds of animals, and to place them in charge of mortals. This makes them analogous to the Father of All <note>original: "father of wholes"</note> and his orderly distribution of the universe. It is necessary that some things should be primarily produced by the creative unity <term>demiurgic monad</term>, while others are produced through intermediate causes. The Creator <term>Demiurgus</term> indeed produces all things from himself at once and eternally, but the things produced in order—those proceeding first from him—produce the beings that come after them <term>natures posterior to themselves</term> alongside him. 

Thus, for instance, the celestial Gods produce the Gods below the moon <term>sublunary Gods</term>, and these generate mortal animals; at the same time, the Creator fashions these mortals in conjunction with the celestial and sublunary divinities. By the very act of speaking, he understands all things, and by understanding all things, he also makes the mortal classes of animals. However, because these animals are mortal, they require another immediate generating cause, and through this, they receive their progression into existence. 

The character of these words is divinely inspired <term>enthusiastic</term>, shining with intellectual insights, pure and venerable as if perfected by the Father of the Gods. They differ from and transcend human concepts; they are delicate and yet astonishing, full of grace and beauty, and simultaneously concise and perfectly accurate. Plato, therefore, carefully crafts these imitations of divine speeches. He shows this also in the *Republic*, when he represents the Muses speaking sublimely and the prophet ascending to a lofty seat. He adorns both those speeches with brevity and dignity, employing the precise power of rhetorical clauses <term>colons</term> <note>original: "colons" (Greek: kōla), referring to short, rhythmic members of a sentence</note>, directly reflecting divine thoughts through this form of words. 

In the words before us, he omits no excellence—neither the grand and robust style in the sentences and names adapted to these devices, nor the magnitude of the concepts and figures of speech that complete this idea. Besides this, a great deal of clarity and purity, the unfolding of truth, and the illustrious qualities of beauty are mingled with the idea of magnitude. This style is especially suited to the subject matter, the speaker, and the listeners. For the objects of this speech are the perfection of the universe, the imitation of the "All-Perfect Living Being" <note>original: "all-perfect animal," referring to the divine Paradigm or blueprint of the universe</note>, and the generation of all mortal animals; meanwhile, the Maker of all things exists beforehand and...

...adorning all things through their superior transcendence <note>original: "exempt transcendency"</note>; while the secondary creators <term>fabricators</term> add what was missing to the formation of the universe. Since everything is great and divine—both the beings and the objects created—and since they shine with beauty and are distinct from one another, Plato has used words perfectly suited to this style of speech.

Homer also, when acting under divine inspiration <note>original: "energizing enthusiastically"</note>, portrays Jupiter speaking and turning the two-fold orders <term>co-ordinations</term> of Gods toward himself. Jupiter becomes, as it were, the center of all the divine types <term>genera</term> in the world, making all things obedient to his intellect <term>intellection</term>. For this Goddess, pervading everywhere, gathers the divine assembly <note>original: "divine number"</note> and directs it back toward the creative source <term>demiurgic monad</term>. For the Gods are both separate from worldly affairs and yet eternally provide for all things; they are simultaneously above the world because of their supreme transcendence and yet extend their care <term>providence</term> everywhere. For their pure, unmixed nature is not without the power of care, nor is their care mixed with the material world. Through their superior power, they are not overwhelmed by the subjects they govern, and through their benevolent will, they make all things similar to themselves; while permanently abiding, proceeding, and remaining separate from all things, they are nonetheless present to all things in the same way.

Therefore, since the Gods who govern the world—and the spirits <term>daemons</term> who attend them—receive this pure essence and the task of administration from their father; he sometimes directs them toward himself directly and illuminates them with a separate, pure form of life. This is why I believe he orders them to be separated from all things, to remain elevated in Olympus, and to favor neither the Greeks nor the Barbarians. This is the same as saying they must transcend the two-fold orders of worldly <term>mundane</term> natures and remain unchanging in pure thought <term>undefiled intellection</term>. But at other times, he directs them to care for secondary natures through Themis, calling on them to lead the worldly struggle <term>battle</term> and urging different Gods to different tasks. These divinities, therefore, especially require the help of Themis, who holds the divine laws that link divine care <term>providence</term> to the whole of existence. <meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the speech of the Demiurge (the Creator) from Plato's Timaeus. <header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.</header>

...through this one speech, he encompasses these two-fold modes of discourse. For the Demiurge <term>the Creator-Craftsman</term> keeps the Gods pure and unmixed with lower <note>original: "secondary"</note> natures, yet causes them to provide for and give existence to mortals. He orders them to create in imitation of himself; in such an instruction, both these aspects are included. Specifically, they remain pure through their imitation of the Father, for he is separate and exempt from the entire physical world <note>original: "mundane wholes"</note>. However, their providential energy is expressed through the command to create, nourish, and increase mortal beings. 

Or rather, we may see both qualities in each action. In imitating the Demiurge, they provide for lower natures just as he does for the immortals; and in the act of creating, they remain separate from the things they create. For every creative cause is superior to the things it generates. Anything that is mixed with or dependent upon the things it creates would be weak <note>original: "imbecile"</note> and ineffective, unable to properly organize and build them. This concludes the general discussion regarding the speech as a whole.

Let us then, in the first place, consider what we are to understand by the phrase "**Gods of Gods**," and what power this phrase possesses. This invocation gathers the many gods and turns them back toward their single source <term>monad</term>. It calls upward those natures that have proceeded into the work of creation, and establishes a boundary and divine measure within them. This is clear to those who are not entirely unacquainted with such philosophical discourses. 

However, how those who are assigned parts of the world by their Father are called "Gods of Gods"—and according to what concept—cannot easily be explained to the general public; for these names contain the unfolding of a single divine intelligence. For this reason, some scholars mistakenly join the words "*of Gods*" with what follows, incorrectly interpreting the whole phrase as, "*of the Gods of whom I am the Demiurge.*" It is not proper to represent the Demiurge as the "builder" <term>fabricator</term> of some things but the "father" of others (implying the latter are less honorable). These scholars claim that Plato, by calling the Demiurge the "builder of Gods" but the "father of works," separates the two as if they were different and the latter were less worthy. 

[However, they do not speak correctly;] for the role of the "father" <term>paternal characteristic</term> is more ancient and venerable than the role of the "builder" <term>demiurgic characteristic</term>. Nor is it right to introduce these repetitions when the speech flows continuously. When there are many words in between, there might be a reason for such a parenthesis, but otherwise, it is unnecessary. Others say that the worldly <term>mundane</term> Gods are "of the intelligible <term>purely intellectual</term> Gods" because they are images of them—just as the whole world is the "statue" of the eternal Gods, according to the *Timaeus*. Yet, these people do not speak correctly either, because they do not say anything particularly distinguished about these Gods. In that case, what Plato says could be applied to every mortal nature as well. For all things are "of the Gods," as they are images of the intelligible world. And if it were necessary to refer the words "*of Gods*" to them, I should think it would be...
