<meta>This page continues the analysis of the speech of the Demiurge (the Creator-Craftsman) from Plato’s Timaeus. It focuses on the specific meaning of the address "Gods of Gods," debating whether it refers to all gods within the physical universe or only to a specific elite group of "leaders."</meta>

# BOOK V.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 339

It is more appropriate to call them *Gods of the God*, as they alone are produced directly by the one Demiurge <term>the Creator-Craftsman</term>, while mortal natures are not produced by him; for the one who speaks is the Demiurge himself. Therefore, it would be more proper to speak in the singular rather than the plural number. 

However, others say that the most complete unities of the worldly <term>mundane</term> gods are called "Gods of Gods," "leaders of leaders," and "kings of kings" by the Father, as they are similar to the Father himself. This is because he also, according to the poets, is the "father of fathers" and the supreme ruler. Yet, it is easy to reply to these interpretations: Plato shows the Demiurge speaking to *all* the worldly gods, or the attendants of the gods, and not to some of them alone. For if all the gods—both those who visibly orbit in the sky and those who become visible only when they wish—gather themselves around the one Demiurge, and the Demiurge addresses them, then it is not right to understand the words "Gods of Gods" in a limited way, as if they applied only to the leaders.

If, therefore, none of the assertions mentioned above match Plato’s true meaning, we must show what his meaning actually is. It will be better here to refer to the explanation of these words provided by our teacher <note>likely referring to Syrianus, Proclus’s mentor</note>. He says that all the worldly gods are not simply "Gods," but are entirely "Gods who participate." This is because they contain a part that is separate, invisible, and beyond the world <term>supermundane</term>, as well as a part that is their visible "statue" <note>the physical celestial body, such as a planet, seen as a vessel for the divine</note> which has an orderly place in the world. 

The invisible nature of these gods is the primary God; for this must be understood as that which is indivisible and one. But the vehicle <term>the subtle or physical body of a soul</term> which hangs from their invisible essence is a God in a secondary sense. If we consider humans to be twofold—having an inner soul and an outer visible person—then we must say the same, even more so, of the worldly gods. Divinity in them is twofold: one part is invisible and the other is visible. This being the case, we must say that "Gods of Gods" is an address to all the worldly divinities, in whom there is a connection between invisible and visible gods; for they are "Gods who participate." 

In short, since two types of orders are produced by the Demiurge—some being beyond the world and others within it, and some existing without participating in a body while others do—we can see the distinction. If the Demiurge were addressing the orders beyond the world, he would have simply called them "Gods," for they are separate, invisible, and do not participate in bodies. But since the speech is directed to the worldly gods, he calls them *Gods of Gods*, as they are participated in by other visible divinities. 

Daemons <note>original: "dæmons"; intermediate spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern evil sense</note> are also included in this address; for they too are gods according to their rank relative to the gods, whose specific <unclear>peculiarity</unclear> they share without division. Similarly, Plato, in the *Phaedrus*, when he calls the twelve gods the leaders of daemons, at the same time...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the speech of the Demiurge (the Creator-Craftsman) from Plato’s Timaeus. It explores why the Demiurge addresses the lesser deities as "Gods of Gods" and how these beings bridge the gap between the invisible, eternal realm and the visible, physical world.</meta>

<page-num>340</page-num>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.

He names all the attendants of the divinities "Gods," adding, "*and this is the life of the Gods.*" All these, therefore, are "Gods of Gods," as they possess a visible <note>original: apparent</note> nature connected with an invisible <note>original: unapparent</note> one, and a worldly <note>original: mundane</note> nature connected with one that is beyond the world <note>original: supermundane</note>. This concludes the discussion of the general meaning of these words.

However, since we have stated that these words are "demiurgic" <term>creative or craftsman-like</term>, it is necessary that they be understood in a way that fits the creative care <note>original: demiurgic providence</note> of the Creator. If these words are "intellectual conceptions" <term>noetic thoughts in the mind of the Creator</term>, and these thoughts themselves are acts of creation, what does the Demiurge <term>the Creator-Craftsman</term> actually achieve in the multitude of worldly gods through these first words of his speech? Is it not evident that this action of his is "deific" <term>god-making</term>? For this single divine thought—which is the first and simplest to come from the Demiurge—deifies all who receive it. It makes them creative gods, "participated" gods <note>gods who derive their divinity from a higher source</note>, and gods who are simultaneously invisible and visible. As has been said, this is the meaning of "Gods of Gods." The term "Gods" is not used alone because they are not only invisible. Nor is the word "Gods" simply repeated—as if one were to say "Gods and Gods"—because such a phrasing would be artificial and disconnected from the unity of the divine. These matters have now been sufficiently discussed.

To ensure our interpretations are consistent, it is also necessary to observe that every worldly <note>original: mundane</note> god has a living being <note>original: animal</note> attached to him, which is why he is called "worldly." He also has a divine soul that rules over its attached body <note>original: vehicle</note>, and an immaterial, separate intellect <term>pure mind</term>. Through this intellect, he is united to the realm of pure thought <note>original: the intelligible</note>, so that he may imitate the higher world in which all these things are contained. Because of the living being attached to him, he is a part of the physical universe; but through his intellect, he belongs to the realm of pure being <note>original: intelligible essence</note>. Through his soul, he connects the unified <note>original: impartible</note> life within him to the life that is distributed <note>original: divisible</note> throughout the physical body.

Since each worldly god has this three-part composition, Plato does not represent the Demiurge here as speaking only to intellects; for intellects exist in a state of eternal union with the Divine Mind and were never "born" or "made" <note>original: unbegotten</note>. Soul, however, is the first of "generated" <term>created or brought into being</term> things; and shortly after this, the Demiurge addresses them, saying, "*since you are generated.*" Nor does he represent the Demiurge as speaking only to the living beings attached to these gods' souls, for they belong to the physical realm and cannot receive divine intelligence directly. Nor does he represent him as speaking only to souls on their own, for they are entirely immortal; yet the gods he addresses now are said by him *not* to be immortal in every possible way <note>see footnote 2</note>. Therefore, if I must say what I believe...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the speech of the Demiurge (the Creator-Craftsman) from Plato’s Timaeus. It explores the relationship between the Creator and the "junior gods," explaining how these lesser deities receive divine instruction and participate in the creation of the material world.</meta>

<page-num>341</page-num>

<header>BOOK V.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

...me to be the truth, the words of the Creator <note>original: Demiurgus</note> are addressed to the being composed of soul and animal—that is, to the divine animal which shares in a soul. For the pure intellect does not understand the Creator's will through logical reasoning, but through direct intelligence—in other words, through intellectual vision. It does not learn through a turning toward the truth <note>original: conversion</note>, but through a union with the Universal Intellect, because it is itself an intellect and is, so to speak, of the same nature <note>original: same colour</note> as that Universal Intellect. 

But since the soul is based on reason rather than being pure intellect itself, its essence requires the activity <note>original: energy</note> of reasoning and a rational turning toward the intelligible <note>original: νοητῷ (noētō)</note> realm. Therefore, the Creator’s speech is directed toward these souls, as they are essentially rational and consist of rational principles. This speech applies to them in two ways: first, because they are "participated" by bodies (meaning they are the gods over those physical forms); and second, because they "participate" in higher intellects (meaning they are gods derived from intellects which are themselves gods). They both share in higher intellects and are themselves shared by physical bodies. 

Because of this, the claims that they are "generated" (created) and not entirely immortal—along with everything else in the speech—are appropriate for them, since they have a specific relationship and connection with worldly <note>original: mundane</note> natures and are shared by them. However, commands like "learn and generate," and other such instructions that are more divine than created things, apply to them as intellectual beings.

<margin>41A</margin>
> "I am the Creator <note>original: Demiurgus</note> and father of these works; whatever I have created is indissoluble <term>cannot be destroyed</term>, because such is my will in its making."

To summarize, Plato appears to divide the activity <note>original: energy</note> of the one Creator <note>original: Demiurgus</note> into three parts during his total production of the "junior gods." These are: 
1. The god-making <note>original: deitic</note> power.
2. The power that provides connection.
3. The power that provides a likeness to the "Universal Animal" <note>the Platonic concept of the living universe as a single organism</note>. 

The Creator’s speech shows that those who come from him are gods. Furthermore, the statements about what can and cannot be dissolved define a middle ground between the two. This provides an organization and connection that fits the ranking of the worldly <note>original: mundane</note> gods. The words calling them to create mortal beings make them the sources of perfection for the universe. It also makes them the makers of secondary living creatures, following the pattern <note>original: paradigm</note> of the original model. 

Through these three activities <note>original: energies</note>, the Creator raises his offspring toward all the intelligible gods and establishes them within the intelligible triads <term>groups of three divine principles in Neoplatonic philosophy</term>. Within the "One Being"—the highest point of these...

<summary>Proclus explains that the Demiurge’s speech is directed at the rational souls of the junior gods, who act as intermediaries between pure intellect and the physical world. He outlines a three-fold process—deification, connection, and imitation—by which the Creator establishes these lesser gods to complete the universe.</summary>

<keywords>Proclus, Timaeus, Demiurge, junior gods, intelligible triads, deification, mundane gods, rational soul, Platonic philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the Creator (Demiurge) establishes the lower gods within the divine hierarchy. It specifically explores how these gods participate in the "intelligible triads"—the highest levels of reality—to receive their immortality and creative power.</meta>

<page-num>342</page-num>

<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.</header>

...triads through the first of these activities <note>original: energies</note>. For that is primarily made divine <note>original: deified</note> in which the "one" is the deity, and "being" <term>Being: The first and most basic level of existence that emerges from the ultimate source.</term> is the first to participate in it. For the *One itself* is the only deity that exists without any relationship <note>original: habitude</note> to anything else and cannot be shared or participated in. However, the *One Being*, where the first participation occurs, is "God born of God." 

*Being* is a deity as the peak of all that exists, but the "one" within it is a deity that comes from the *One itself*, which is the primary God. Through the second of these activities, the Creator <note>original: Demiurgus</note> establishes his offspring in the second of the intelligible triads <term>Intelligible triads: Groups of three divine principles that exist in the realm of pure thought, above the physical world.</term>—that is, within eternity itself. For eternity is what grants this unbreakable <note>original: indissoluble</note> permanence to everything that remains forever whole. 

Because of this, all worldly <note>original: mundane</note> natures are held together according to the Creator's <note>original: demiurgic</note> will. They possess a quality of being unbreakable through their participation in him. However, the things that are inherently unbreakable are different from these worldly things, and those that are truly immortal exist for his sake. 

He establishes them in the "all-perfect Living Being" <note>original: animal; this refers to the *Autozon*, the Platonic archetype of all life</note> (the third of the intelligible triads) through the third of these activities. For the life-giving <note>original: vivific</note> power makes the worldly gods like this "Living Being" and places within them the models <note>original: paradigms</note> of the living creatures they create. This is indeed one goal of the divine creation <note>original: fabrication</note>: to turn and perfect the many gods who come forth from the source. After this unity, there is a threefold design that establishes them in the three intelligible orders.

Therefore, this second creative <note>original: demiurgic</note> intelligence, following the first which makes things divine <note>original: deific</note>, shines upon the worldly gods. It gives them a firm foundation, an unchangeable <note>original: immutable</note> power, and an eternal essence. Because of this, the whole world and all the divine territories <note>original: allotments</note> remain always the same, sharing in an unchangeable nature and never-fading <note>original: undecaying</note> power through their Father. 

For everything created from an unmoving <note>original: immoveable</note> cause is unbreakable and unchangeable. In contrast, all the offspring of a cause that can change <note>original: moveable</note> are themselves subject to change. Therefore, among worldly natures, those that come from the Creator’s <note>original: demiurgic</note> cause alone are permanent because they were created according to a standard that never varies; they are free from any essence that can change or vary. 

However, those things that come both from this cause and from other changing principles are unchangeable only to the extent that they come from the Creator. They are subject to change insofar as they come from those other principles. For those natures that the Creator alone brings forth, he crafts to be unchangeable and unbreakable, both by their own nature and by his own power and will. For he gives them a guarding and preserving power, and he binds their essence together in a way that is superior <note>original: transcendent</note> and set apart. For all things are preserved in two ways: by the power he possesses and by his divine care <note>original: providential goodness</note>, which is truly able and willing to preserve everything that can rightfully be saved forever. Therefore, as we have said, the most divine of visible things are unbreakable by their very nature.

<summary>Proclus explains how the Creator grants stability and immortality to the lower gods by linking them to eternal, intelligible principles. He distinguishes between permanent things created directly by the Creator and changeable things influenced by lesser causes.</summary>

<keywords>Proclus, Demiurge, Intelligible Triads, Eternity, Mundane Gods, Immortality, Divine Providence, Timaeus, Neoplatonism</keywords>

--- Page 349 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the Creator (the Demiurge) and how his divine will serves as the ultimate bond that maintains the stability and permanence of the universe.</meta>

<page-num>343</page-num>

<header>BOOK V.] THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO</header>

But they are also sustained by the creative <note>original: demiurgic</note> power which spreads through all things and connects them eternally. This power serves as the guardian and the divine law that holds everything together. However, a cause even greater and more fundamental than these is the creative will, which employs this power in its works. After all, what is superior to goodness? What bond is more perfect than the one that grants unity through its light <note>original: illumination</note>, connects an eternal essence, and serves as the bond and measure of all things? It is to this will that the Creator <note>original: Demiurgus</note> now attributes the cause of his unchanging power, saying, “*such being my will in its fabrication.*” He established his own will as a guard over his own works, as the force that gives unity, connection, and measure to the whole of existence.

However, the identity of the Creator and the "father" has been explained by us before, and we will briefly show it again here. There are four divine roles: the father alone; the maker alone; the father and maker; and the maker and father. 

1.  **The Father alone** is the ether (or the principle of "Bound"), which is the first proceeding from *the One*. 
2.  **The Father and Maker** is the divinity who exists according to the intelligible model <term>intelligible paradigm: The perfect, non-physical blueprint of the universe existing in the divine mind.</term> at the highest point of the intelligible order. Orpheus says the blessed Gods call him Phanes the First-born <note>original: Phanes Protogonus</note>. 
3.  **The Maker and Father** is Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus, used here in his role as the primary cosmic organizer.</note>, who is called the Creator by himself, but whom the Orphic writers would call the "father of works." 
4.  **The Maker alone** is the cause of the creation of individual parts <note>original: partible fabrication</note>, as the same writers would say. <note>This divinity is Vulcan.</note>

Therefore, all intelligible, intellectual, celestial <note>original: supermundane</note>, and worldly natures are subject to the **Father alone**. All intellectual, celestial, and worldly natures are subordinate to the **Father and Maker**. To the **Maker and Father**, who is an intellectual deity, the celestial and worldly natures are subservient. But to the **Maker alone**, only the worldly natures are in subjection. We learn all these details from the accounts of Orpheus; for according to the specific character of each of these four, there is a corresponding group of Gods. 

But what are the works of the Creator and father? Is it not evident that they include all physical bodies, the structure of living beings, and the entire count of participating souls? All these things are unbreakable through the will of the father. It is his will that grants them the power of unchanging permanence, and he connects and guards them with a superior excellence. However, the intellects that descend from above into souls cannot be called the "works" of the father. They did not have a beginning <note>original: generation</note>, but were revealed in a way that was never "born" <note>original: unbegotten</note>; they were shaped within and did not come out from the inner sanctuaries <note>original: adyta</note>. For there are no blueprints <note>original: paradigms</note> for the highest intellect, only for the intermediate and lowest levels of reality. For the soul is the first of the "images," but the whole entities—such as entire species of animals, animated beings, and those that participate in intellect—are lower.

<summary>This page explains that the universe is held together by the Creator's will and classifies four types of divine roles (Father, Maker, and their combinations) within the Orphic and Platonic hierarchy. It distinguishes between eternal intellects and the "works" of the Creator, such as souls and physical bodies.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the physical world is modeled after divine patterns and explores the nature of the "bond" that holds the universe together, specifically addressing why divine creations are considered both dissoluble and indissoluble.</meta>

<page-num>341</page-num>

<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.</header>

Creatures that are generated derive their existence from the intelligible models <term>intelligible paradigms: The eternal, non-physical blueprints for everything in the physical world.</term>, which are all contained within the "Living Being Itself" <note>original: animal itself; referring to the Platonic *Autozoon*, the divine template of all life</note>.

<margin>41 B</margin>
> "Everything, therefore, that is bound together can be dissolved; but to want to dissolve what is beautifully harmonized and well-composed is the mark of an evil nature."

It is necessary to consider how the terms "dissoluble" and "indissoluble" are applied to the Gods, and to link specific ways of dissolving things to their corresponding types of bonds. For not everything is bound in the same way, nor is something that is bound in one way dissolved in another. 

Rather, anything that is bound in a certain respect also has its dissolution according to that same mode. That which is bound in every respect is likewise dissolved in every respect. That which is bound by itself is also dissolved by itself. But that which is bound by something other than itself depends on that external force for its dissolution. Likewise, that which is bound within time is also dissolved according to time. But that which is granted an eternal bond must also be said to be perpetually dissolved. 

In short, the potential for dissolution is linked to every bond. A bond is not a simple union without variety, because the *One* <note>The absolute, simple source of all existence in Neoplatonism</note> does not require a bond. Nor is a bond a mere heap of many different things that no longer keep their unique characteristics. Such a thing would be "confusion"—a result where things are blended into a single corrupted mass rather than being truly bound. 

It is necessary for things that are bound to maintain their own identity; they are not truly "bound" if they are destroyed or corrupted in the process. Therefore, a bond only truly exists when there are many distinct parts that are preserved, yet held together by a single power that connects and collects them, whether that power is physical or non-physical. If this is the case, things that are bound are united through the bond but remain distinct because each preserves its own proper nature.

Everywhere, therefore, as we have said, a bond always has a corresponding dissolution connected with it. However, bonds and their dissolutions differ: they may exist in a specific way or simply; they may come from within the thing itself or from something else; and they may happen within time or exist perpetually. These are the ways they differ. 

We should not be surprised, then, if the same thing is both "dissoluble" and "indissoluble"—being indissoluble in one sense and dissoluble in another. The works of the Father <note>The Creator or Demiurge</note>, if they are indeed indissoluble, are so because they will not be dissolved by the passage of time. Yet they are "dissoluble" in the sense that they are composed of simpler elements that could be separated, according to the specific powers of the one who binds them. For just as that which is self-existing <note>original: self-subsistent</note> is said...

<summary>Proclus explains the paradox of divine bonds, arguing that while all joined things are theoretically dissoluble, the universe is indissoluble in time because it is held together by the perfect will of the Creator.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the "indissoluble" bond, specifically looking at how Proclus (commenting on Plato's Timaeus) distinguishes between things that are eternal and things that can be broken down or dissolved.</meta>

<page-num>345</page-num>

<header>BOOK 5] THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO.</header>

...to be so in two ways: first, as providing everything from itself alone; and second, as existing from itself while also coming from another source which is its cause. In the same way, the "indissoluble" exists both "from another" <note>original: *par’ heterou*; this phrase was missing in the Greek manuscript used for the original translation</note> and from itself, just as that which is moved exists in two ways and in a similar manner.

However, two modes of dissolution are opposed to these two modes of being indissoluble. Specifically, that which can be dissolved by another and by itself is the opposite of that which is indissoluble by another and by itself. The former is dissoluble in itself because it consists of separate parts. But because it has the causes of its existence in something else prior to itself, it becomes dissoluble by this cause and in this way alone. 

Again, that which is "simply dissoluble" in two ways—containing the cause of its dissolution within itself while also receiving it from another—is opposed to that which is "simply indissoluble" in two ways, from itself and from another. 

Therefore, there are four categories in total:
1. That which is **simply indissoluble** from another and from itself.
2. That which is **indissoluble in a certain way** in two respects.
3. That which is **dissoluble in a certain way** in two respects.
4. That which is **simply dissoluble** from itself and from another <note>original: *kai lyton haplos par’ heautou kai par’ heteron*; this phrase was omitted in the original Greek source.</note>.

Of these four, the first category belongs to **intelligibles** <term>intelligibles: eternal, non-physical realities or divine forms that can only be understood by the mind</term>. These are indissoluble because they are entirely simple, involving no composition that could be broken apart. 

The fourth category belongs to **mortal natures**. These are dissoluble from themselves and from others because they consist of many different parts and are put together by their causes in such a way that they will eventually be dissolved.

The middle categories apply to the **mundane Gods** <term>mundane Gods: the celestial bodies and deities that inhabit and govern the physical universe</term>, for the second and third modes coincide in them. In one sense, because they are the works of the Father <note>the Demiurge or Creator</note>, they are indissoluble; they are preserved by their own nature and through his will. Yet, in another sense, they are "dissoluble" because they were bound together by him, and he holds the primary power over the simple elements from which they are composed. Everything that is bound can be dissolved, and this applies even to the works of the Father.

Physical bodies are joined through **analogy** <note>In the *Timaeus*, Plato argues that the elements of the universe are held together by mathematical proportions</note>, for this is the most beautiful bond for them. Living beings, however, are held together with "animated bonds," as we have noted before. Finally, souls that contain a divisible nature are bound by "means" (specifically, by geometric, arithmetic, and harmonic ratios). Plato calls these ratios, and all the productive principles that make up the soul, "bonds." Only things that are "impartible" <term>impartible: simple and indivisible; having no parts</term> have no need for bonds; but those things that are bound...

<meta>This page continues the logical breakdown of the four categories of "dissolubility" and "indissolubility." Proclus is now applying these categories specifically to the "mundane gods"—the divine celestial bodies that make up the physical universe—to determine if they are eternal by nature or only by the will of their Creator.</meta>

<page-num>346</page-num>

<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK 5]</header>

...consist of things that exist independently; these are not separated according to time, but according to the causal understanding of simple natures within the Creator <term>Demiurgus: The "craftsman" or creator of the physical universe in Platonic philosophy.</term>. In this way, the capacity for the worldly gods to be dissolved exists as if coming from another source, or rather, as existing within another. Therefore, they are dissoluble in a certain sense, but they are by no means simply or absolutely dissoluble. 

For if they were dissoluble by their own nature, but held together only by the will of the Father <note>original: "the father," referring to the Demiurge</note>—as Severus, Atticus, and Plutarch are accustomed to say, and against whom many arguments are presented by many authors <note>original: *apo pollon* (from many)</note>—if this were the case, where would they derive this inherent capacity for being dissolved? If dissolution is natural to them, who gave them this natural power? It could not be anyone other than the Creator. However, if he is the provider of their nature, then he is also the cause of their dissolution. But if being dissoluble is contrary to their nature <note>original: "preternatural"</note>, then the opposite—being indissoluble—must be natural to them. 

And if being indissoluble is natural to them, they will possess this quality from within themselves; their very existence will be defined by it. In the same way, self-motion is natural to the soul, and lightness <note>original: "levity"</note> is natural to fire; these qualities exist essentially in those things. Thus, the worldly gods possess this indissolubility from themselves. When I say "from themselves," I mean they possess it from their own composition, which is their essential nature; I do not mean they exist without a prior cause. 

It is ridiculous, therefore, to say that while they are naturally dissoluble, they are only kept from dissolving through the will of the Father. These men assert this because they wish to preserve the axiom that "everything created must eventually decay <note>original: "corruption"</note>." They also argue that the world was created in time, so that Timaeus does not appear to contradict Socrates, whom he had heard the day before admitting that whatever is uncreated <note>original: *agenneton* (unbegotten)</note> is indestructible <note>original: "incorruptible"</note>. 

Hence, if the category of the worldly gods is of itself indissoluble, it is also of itself uncreated, and not only so through the will of the Father. For unless we admit this, how can we agree with Plato, who describes a twofold indissolubility: one according to nature, and another according to the Creator's will? If we deny this, must we not also speak disrespectfully of the Creator himself? For if he wishes to make his creations indissoluble but does not have the power to do so, we would be separating his will from his power. This would be absurd, as even virtuous men do not suffer from such a gap between intent and ability. But if he is both willing and able to make these things indissoluble, then because he is able, he *will* make them indissoluble by their very nature. For each of them was created indissoluble, but was...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's argument regarding the nature of the mundane gods. He explains that while they are composed of parts and therefore theoretically "dissoluble" (able to be broken apart), they remain "indissoluble" (eternal) through the power and will of the Creator.</meta>

<page-num>347</page-num>

<header>BOOK 5] THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO</header>

They were not created to be dissoluble and then later made indissoluble. Rather, the works of the Father <note>The "Father" refers to the Demiurge, the creator-god in Plato’s philosophy.</note> are indissoluble through the power which he possesses. They are likewise indissoluble due to the <term>demiurgic will</term> <note>The "crafting" or creative intent of the creator.</note>, since they are of a composite nature and are held in an indissoluble state by a divine bond. 

However, there is also a certain sense in which they are dissoluble, insofar as they consist of simple components, the definitive causes of which the Father contains within himself. Therefore, they are both indissoluble and dissoluble at the same time. They are not, however, as perfectly indissoluble as the <term>intelligible</term> <note>The realm of pure, abstract Ideas or Forms, which are non-physical and unchanging.</note>; for that realm is indissoluble because it transcends simplicity itself. These mundane gods, by contrast, are at once indissoluble and dissoluble because they are made of simple elements and yet are perpetually bound together. 

While all things that are bound are technically capable of being dissolved, those things that are perpetual—possessing beauty from the intelligible realm, divine union, and <term>demiurgic harmony</term> throughout all time—are effectively indissoluble. Only mortal natures are purely dissoluble, because they are connected to the deformity and unsuitability of matter. The former (the divine) are beautifully harmonized through the union placed in them by their cause of harmony. This is not the case for mortal things, however, because of the multitude of causes which no longer instill a similar union in them.¹ Their union is scattered through the sheer variety of elements mixed into their composition; as a result, they are quite properly assigned a relaxed² harmony.

Therefore, everything that is bound is technically dissoluble. But one kind of thing is both dissoluble and indissoluble in this way, while another is only dissoluble—just as the intelligible is indissoluble alone. Why, then, is that which is primarily bound both dissoluble and indissoluble at the same time? It is because it is beautifully harmonized and *well* composed. From being *well composed*, it achieves union, since *goodness* acts as a unifying force. From the intelligible realm, it achieves the *beautiful*, for beauty is derived from that source. And from the fabricating power of the creator, it achieves *harmony*, for the creator is the cause of the Muses <note>In this context, the Muses represent the source of mathematical and musical order in the cosmos.</note> and the source of the harmonic arrangement of the world. 

Thus, we again find the three causes: the final cause through the *good*, the <term>paradigmatic</term> <note>The "model" or "blueprint" cause upon which the world is based.</note> cause through the *beautiful*, and the demiurgic cause through the *harmonized*.³ It is necessary that a composition of this kind—harmonized by a single creative power, filled with divine beauty, and obtaining a <term>boniform</term> <note>Having the form or nature of "The Good."</note> union—should be indissoluble. For the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The Creator/Craftsman.</note> says that to dissolve such a work is characteristic of an evil nature.

³ After <note>original: "την παραδειγματικην" (the paradigmatic)</note>, it is necessary to supply the words <note>original: "δια του καλως, την δημιουργικην" (through the "well-composed," the demiurgic)</note>, which are missing in the original.

<summary>Proclus explains that the divine parts of the cosmos are both dissoluble (because they have parts) and indissoluble (because the Creator's will and beauty bind them). He distinguishes these from mortal things, which lack this divine harmony, and from the purely "intelligible" realm, which is simple and eternal.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the *Timaeus*, specifically focusing on the paradox of how the mundane gods and the universe can be both "dissoluble" (capable of being taken apart) and "indissoluble" (eternal/indestructible).</meta>

<page-num>348</page-num>

<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK 5] THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO</header>

Moreover, prior to this, Plato had said that the universe is indestructible <note>original: "indissoluble"</note> except by the one who bound it together. However, if it is entirely impossible for the universe to be destroyed by anyone else, and only the Father <note>The "Father" refers to the Demiurge, the creator-god in Platonic philosophy.</note> is able to dissolve it—and it is impossible for him to actually do this, for destruction is the hallmark of an evil nature—then it is impossible for the universe to be dissolved. 

For either <note>original: ειτε (eite)</note> he must dissolve it, or someone else must. But if some other person or force could do it, who would be able to offer violence to the Demiurge? It is impossible for a dissolution to be carried out except by the one who bound it. Yet if he himself were to dissolve it, how could he—being good—destroy that which is beautifully harmonized and well constructed? To subvert such things is to produce evil, just as subverting evil is the work of a benevolent nature. 

Hence, there is an equal necessity: either the Demiurge must be wicked (if it is even permitted to speak this way), or this world must be indestructible. [Essentially, both of these are considered equally impossible]. This is the logical necessity that Plato assigns to the immortality <note>original: "incorruptibility"</note> of the universe. 

Furthermore, Plato clearly shows that he grants an indestructible nature to the composition of the <term>mundane gods</term> <note>Gods that exist within and govern the physical world, such as the stars and planets.</note> when he orders them to bind mortal creatures, but not with those indestructible bonds with which they themselves are connected. For if the bonds that hold these gods together are indestructible, then the gods themselves must be essentially indestructible. 

Here, however, he says that they are not indestructible "in every respect." It is evident from both these assertions that they are <insert>and they themselves are</insert> <note>The Greek phrase "kai autoi" was omitted in the original transcription.</note> indestructible and yet, at the same time, dissoluble. They are not indestructible "in every respect" because of the specific way they are bound. 

But if these things are true, it is absolutely necessary that their "dissolution" be very different from what we call "corruption" <note>In ancient philosophy, "corruption" refers to the natural decay and death of physical things.</note>. For anything that is capable of being broken down in the same way as a perishable thing—because it is not indestructible—is so far from being "not indestructible in every respect" that it is actually "destructible in every respect." Therefore, it is not proper to say that the mundane gods are naturally perishable and only remain immortal through the will of the Father; rather, we should say that they are <note>original: αυτων φυσιν (auton physin), correcting the original's "his own nature" to "their own nature".</note> immortal in their very nature.

> “Therefore, since you are created <note>original: "generated"</note>, you are not immortal, nor are you indestructible in every respect; yet you shall never be dissolved, nor become subject to the fatality of death; for you have been granted my will, which is a much...

<summary>Proclus argues that the universe and the mundane gods are fundamentally indestructible because their creator, the Demiurge, is good and would never destroy a perfect, harmonized work. He explains that while they are technically "composite" and thus theoretically dissoluble, their divine nature and the creator's will ensure they are eternal.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*, specifically examining the speech of the Demiurge to the lesser gods. It addresses the philosophical problem of how created beings (the gods of the stars and planets) can be both "dissoluble" by nature but "indissoluble" by the will of the Creator.</meta>

<page-num>349</page-num>

<header>BOOK V.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

> "...a greater and more excellent bond than the vital connections <note>original: "connectives"</note> with which you were bound at the beginning of your creation <note>original: "generation"</note>."

Since all the gods of the physical world <note>original: "mundane Gods"</note> to whom these words are addressed consist of divine souls and the living beings <note>original: "animals"</note> linked to them—or, in other words, since they are souls shared with bodies <note>original: "participated souls"</note>—and since the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The "Divine Craftsman" who created the universe in Plato's philosophy.</note> calls them both indestructible <note>original: "indissoluble"</note> and yet capable of being dissolved, it is because their indestructibility is not of the purely spiritual <note>original: "intelligible"</note> kind, and their capability for being dissolved does not lead to death <note>original: "mortal"</note>. Rather, the former exists through a composition <note>original: "composition" (Greek: *synthesin*)</note>¹ from simple natures, for which the <term>Demiurge</term> understands the separate causes; and the latter exists through the unchangeable connection of the bond which the Father places within them. 

This being the case, he now wishes to gather into one viewpoint and one truth all that he had said separately about them. For at one and the same time, he takes away from them the status of being immortal and indestructible, and then grants these qualities back to them by removing their opposites. For "middle" entities <note>original: "media"</note> are assigned this kind of nature: they do not possess the full nature of either extreme, but appear to contain both. It is just as if someone should call the soul both indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> and at the same time divisible <note>original: "partible"</note>, as it consists of both; and yet it is neither truly indivisible nor divisible, as it is something different from those two extremes. 

Observe how such a "middle" state may be seen in the gods of the world. That which supplies itself with immortality is called primarily and principally immortal; for in the same way, "being" in its primary sense is that which exists from itself, "intellect" is that which is an intellect from itself, and "the one" is that which is one from itself. Everywhere, whatever primarily possesses a quality has it from itself; for if it did not have it from itself but from another, that other thing would be the primary source—whether it be intellect, life, "the one," or something else. Either this source would be primary, or if nothing is primary, the search for a source would go on forever <note>original: "the ascent will be to infinity"</note>. 

Thus, that which is truly immortal is immortal from itself and gives immortality to itself. But that which is neither vital in its entirety, nor self-existing <note>original: "self-subsistent"</note>, nor possesses immortality from itself, is not primarily immortal. Just as "secondary being" is not true being, so that which is secondarily immortal is not truly immortal; yet it is not mortal either. To be mortal would be a complete failure or departure from the immortal² <note>original: "the immortal" (Greek: *athanatou*)</note>, possessing neither an inherent life nor infinite power. For these three states exist in a successive order: that which possesses infinite life from itself; that which receives infinite life from another; and that which neither from itself nor another...

² For *of death* <note>original: του θανατου (tou thanatou)</note> here, it is obviously necessary to read *of the immortal* <note>original: του αθανατου (tou athanatou)</note>.

He distinguishes between primary immortality (self-derived) and the secondary immortality granted to created celestial beings.</summary>

Proclus is explaining how these beings occupy a middle ground between the purely eternal, simple spirits and the temporary, mortal creatures of the physical world.</meta>

...exhibits the infinity of life. The first level is truly immortal; the second is not purely immortal; the third is mortal; and the middle level is suited to the gods of the physical world <note>original: "mundane Gods"</note>. For they do not possess immortality from their own essence—since they derive it from that which is truly and primarily immortal, and since physical bodies are suspended from them—nor do they have a finite life. Instead, they are filled by the eternal Gods and, in turn, produce mortal natures. For the second stage of creation <note>original: "fabrication"</note> is connected with the first, proceeds from it, is governed by it, and directs the production of mortal categories <note>original: "genera"</note> back toward it.

Again, regarding that which is indestructible <note>original: "indissoluble"</note>, that which is principally and primarily so is simple and free from all composition <note>meaning it is not made of separate parts that could be pulled apart</note>. For where there is no composition, what possibility can there be of breaking apart <note>original: "dissolution"</note>? But that which is secondarily indestructible is that which is held together by a bond; this is simultaneously capable of being dissolved because it proceeds from divided causes. It is not simply "dissoluble" in a general sense, but only by the power of its cause <note>meaning only the Creator who bound it together has the power to unbind it</note>. For that which is bound before all time is bound only according to its cause; and that which is bound only by a cause can only be dissolved by that same cause. For everything is suited to be dissolved only by that which bound it, and in the same manner in which it was bound. The third level, following that which is properly indestructible, is that which was indestructible for a certain time; the first is properly indestructible because of its simplicity, the second is so in a subordinate way despite being a composition, and the third—falling short of both—is by its own nature capable of being dissolved.

Therefore, the gods of the physical world are not entirely indestructible, for that quality belongs only to the most simple natures. Nor are they dissolvable by time, for their composition proceeds from the union created by the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The divine craftsman or creator of the material world in Platonic philosophy.</note>. Just as in the first cause, union precedes things of a simple nature, in the same way here, a bond precedes dissolution; for a bond is more excellent and is the likeness of a more divine power. This is seen in souls, for there were "bonds" and "means" <note>original: "media"</note> within them, as was previously observed in the generation of the soul. It is also seen in bodies, for mathematical proportion <note>original: "analogy"</note> acts as a bond. It is likewise seen in living beings; for by being bound with "animated bonds," they became living beings. Hence, while perfect immortality and indestructibility do not entirely belong to the gods of the physical world, they do belong to them in a certain way. Because these qualities are not present in them in every respect—nor in the same way they exist in the purely spiritual realms <note>original: "intelligibles"</note>—absolute immortality must be distinguished from them. For in the *Symposium* <note>original: "Banquet"</note> as well, Plato does not think it right to call Love <note>Eros</note> immortal, yet he does not call him mortal either; instead, he asserts Love to be something between both of these. For there is a vast range between the mortal and the immortal, and they are joined together by many middle stages. It appears likewise, with respect to the...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the speech of the Demiurge in Plato’s *Timaeus*. The discussion focuses on categorizing different types of "immortality"—ranging from the absolute eternity of the divine to the cyclical or "essential" life of human souls—and identifying the specific beings (gods, spirits, or souls) that correspond to each level.</meta>

<page-num>351</page-num>

<header>BOOK 5.] PLATO'S TIMÆUS.</header>

...immortal, meaning that one type of immortality is common to all beings that differ from a mortal nature,¹ and which consists in not being deprived of the life it possesses. According to this sense of the word, Plato says that the Demiurge <note>The "craftsman" or creator of the material universe.</note> is the cause of immortal natures, but the lesser gods <note>original: "junior Gods"</note> are the cause of those that are mortal. 

However, another kind of immortality is specific to purely intellectual beings <note>original: "intelligibles"</note>, as they are eternal by their very nature. Another kind belongs to the gods of the physical world <note>original: "mundane Gods"</note>; this is an immortality that is perpetually rising into existence, and which finds its stability in a state of "always coming into being." 

Therefore, it may be said that the "immortal" and "mortal" are opposites with nothing in between if we use the general definition of immortality. However, they are not opposites without a middle ground if we consider that which is primarily immortal—that is, that which *is always immortal*. For the middle point between the strictly immortal and the mortal is that which *is always becoming immortal*. 

That which is properly immortal possesses the entirety of its life in eternity. However, that which has its life unfolded through the whole of time, and does not² always possess one and the same indivisible life, possesses an immortality that stretches along with the flow of generation, but is not immortal according to the unchanging stability of true Being. 

Furthermore, the middle ground between the immortality of the gods of the physical world and that of individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls is that which has a life always rising into existence, and which ascends and descends in its intellectual activity. This nature is closer to mortal beings; it leaves behind a more excellent form of thought to move into a lower one, but then returns to its original condition without forgetfulness <note>original: "oblivion"</note>. This is the specific characteristic of the gods of the physical world; but the latter is characteristic of spirits <note>original: "dæmons," referring here to mediating spirits, not evil entities</note> who attend these gods. 

But if a nature descends and becomes filled with forgetfulness, becoming very much like mortals and entirely losing the "true life" it once held—retaining only its "essential life"—such immortality belongs to individual souls. Therefore, the Demiurge in his speech calls the immortality in these souls "homonymous" <note>Sharing the same name but having a different definition</note> to that of the truly immortal beings. If, however, there is any nature after these which casts aside even its essential life, that nature alone³ is mortal. 

Thus, the primarily immortal and the mortal are the two extremes. The immortality of the gods of the physical world and that of individual souls are the levels just below those extremes. And the immortality which is truly the middle point between these is that of spirits. Therefore, spirits are in reality entirely of a middle nature. This concludes the discussion concerning the overall intent of these words.

<summary>Proclus defines a hierarchy of immortality, distinguishing between the eternal life of pure intellects, the "continual becoming" of celestial gods and spirits, and the "essential life" of individual souls which are prone to forgetfulness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the *Timaeus*, specifically focusing on the Demiurge's speech to the "mundane gods" (the gods of the physical universe). The discussion explores how these gods are "generated" (created) yet remains immortal through the divine will and the "bond" of goodness.</meta>

<page-num>352</page-num>

<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.</header>

Let us now, if you are willing, briefly return to the details. I have often shown how the process of being "generated" <note>original: "generation"</note> applies to the gods of the physical world <note>original: "mundane Gods"</note>. I have observed that it shows they are composed of parts, that their life is linked with time, and that they proceed from another cause. This life extends throughout the whole of time, but *is not always* eternal <note>Meaning it has a beginning in the divine order, even if it lasts forever within time.</note>. But the words, “*You are not immortal, nor are you indestructible,*” show that they were created to be immortal and indestructible. For *to be* each of these essentially belongs only to eternal beings; but *to be made* into each of them applies to created natures whose life spans the entirety of time. 

And the phrase *not to be entirely immortal, nor entirely indestructible*, reveals to us many types of immortality. Shortly after this, Plato calls divine souls immortal, but refers to individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls as immortal "by name only" <note>original: "homonymously"</note>. However, the words, “*You shall never be dissolved, nor become subject to the fate of death,*” take away from these gods all mortal-formed nature and any life that is constantly shifting or changeable. For mortality is a portion of life that is currently mixed with non-existence. 

Furthermore, “*the fate of death*” secretly reveals to us many different kinds of death. For the death belonging to those called spirits <note>original: "dæmons"</note> according to their habits is of one kind; that of individual souls is of another kind; that of animals, another; and that of living bodies is different from all of these. 
1. The first of these is like casting off a garment; 
2. The second is accompanied by a sympathy toward mortal nature, being the soul's "fall" into it; 
3. The third is the separation of the body and soul from each other; 
4. And the fourth is the loss of the life that exists within the physical body. 

But the gods of the physical world and the essential spirits who attend them are perfectly free from these. Even the first kind of death does not apply to them, as the divine Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) known for his work on the hierarchy of spiritual beings.</note> also asserts, who maintains that the true race of spirits is unchanging. 

Why, then, is there a bond for these beings?¹ Is it not because goodness—which defines the will of the Demiurge <note>The creator-craftsman of the universe.</note>—unites and measures all things, and leads them into a single harmony? It seems that it is especially according to this goodness that the gods of the physical world are perfectly produced. For it is a "bond of bonds," being superior² to the things that are bound together. The word *allotted* shows the distribution of beneficial providence by the many gods, coming from the one Demiurge. For being divided according to the assignments of Justice, they distribute the single and total providence of the Father, and the one...

² For the phrase "beyond the mind" <note>original: "υπερ τον νουν"</note> here, it appears to me to be necessary to read "superior" <note>original: "υπερτερον"</note>.

...the bond that comes from the creator-unit <term>original: demiurgic monad; the singular source of the creative power</term>. The celestial gods, and indeed all the gods of the physical world, are neither entirely indestructible nor entirely destructible; they are simply both. It is concluded, however, that they are neither immortal nor indestructible simply by the fact that they were created. For this is shown by the words, “*because you were created.*” <note>original: "generated"</note> For everything created has a renewed immortality and a bond given to it by something other than itself, because it is not able to sustain or give life to itself. But again, it is concluded that they are neither destructible nor mortal because of the bonds they essentially share, which they receive from the creator’s will. The latter is shown through their unity, while the former is shown through their plurality; for the Father's unity is a bond of bonds, and is the singular source <note>original: "monad"</note> for the unity of the participating gods.

->“Learn now, therefore, what I say to you,¹ indicating my desire.”<-

The first address to the gods of the physical world deified the listeners; for it proved all of them to be gods, inhabiting the bodies they guide. For these very bodies are also gods, being the physical images <note>original: "statues"</note> of the gods; since Plato likewise calls the earth the first and most ancient of the gods within the heavens. But these deified bodies participate in the gods truly so-called, from whom they are suspended and who exist prior to creation. For these bodies, as he says, have a beginning in creation. 

But the second address to these gods gave them an eternal power through their participation in an unbreakable connection. And the current words fill them with divine and creative conceptions, descending from above from the "Living Creature-in-itself" <note>original: "intelligible animal"; the divine blueprint or paradigm of the universe</note>. For being instructed in the fabrication of living things—insofar as it is a form of learning <note>original: "mathesis"</note>—is suited to the soul. These words fill the multitude of gods with the creative intelligence of all the forms contained in the divine blueprint of the "Living Creature." 

Through the word *now*, eternity is in a sense indicated; through the word *what*, that which is united and coiled together; through *I say*, that which proceeds into a multitude and is spread among the many gods; and through *indication*, a fullness derived from hidden and invisible causes is signified. For we only "indicate" things that are invisible to the crowd. But through all these words together, it is evident that the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> positions himself similarly to the divine Mind, and fills the number of physical gods with intellectual concepts. Furthermore, these words turn this multitude toward the...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the speech of the Demiurge (the divine Craftsman) in Plato's Timaeus. It explores the relationship between the primary Creator and the "junior" or physical gods who are tasked with creating mortal life.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.

This single creative intellect <term>original: demiurgic intelligence; the mind of the divine Craftsman</term>, before turning its providential care toward lesser beings, illuminates the world with pure, unmixed, and stable thought <term>original: intellection</term>. Just as the Creator <term>original: Demiurgus</term> acts by thinking, and brings things into being from an internal power that moves outward, he also wants the gods of the physical world <term>original: mundane Gods</term> to first learn and understand their father’s will, and then afterwards to imitate his power.

> “Three types <term>original: genera</term> of mortal creatures still need to be produced. Without the creation of these, the universe will be imperfect, for it will not contain every kind of animal. But it must contain them all to be truly complete. Yet, if these creatures were created by me and received life directly from me, they would be equal to the Gods.”

The most universal, primary, and divine of Ideas do not only bring eternal physical beings into existence from a separate, higher level, but they also produce all mortal beings from a single, unified cause. For example, the Idea of "winged beings" in the divine mind is the model <term>original: paradigm</term> for all birds and flying creatures; the Idea of "aquatic beings" is the model for all sea life; and the Idea of "land beings" <term>original: pedestrial</term> is the model for all land animals. 

As these higher forms <term>original: intelligibles</term> descend into the realm of thought, they divide the unified Ideas into many specific causes and reveal the distinct principles of many different forms. In the highest realm of thought, there isn't just one cause for all air-breathing animals, because there isn't a separate thought <term>original: intellection</term> for the eternal versions of those animals. Nor is there just one cause for sea or land animals. Instead, the power of "difference" in the intellectual realm divides the whole into parts and breaks down singular principles <term>original: monads</term> into numbers. 

Therefore, the causes for divine animals—which the Creator uses to establish the ranks of Gods and spirits <term>original: dæmons</term> that oversee birth—exist within him separately from the causes for mortal beings. It is for these mortal beings that he calls upon the "younger gods" to create. The Creator exists before the creative energy of these younger gods; he creates simply by saying that a thing should be made. *For the words of the Father are creative thoughts, and his thoughts are acts of creation.* However, the immediate act of creating is suited to the assembly of physical gods. Here, you see how the order of productive and creative causes is revealed. For the choir of physical gods produces mortal animals, but they do so in connection with movement and change <note>original: "mutation"</note>. And the Creator...

***

<note>¹ Instead of "with consultation" <note>original: μετα βουλῆς</note>, I read it as "with change" <note>original: μεταβολης</note>. In the *Timaeus*, the physical gods are never shown consulting or debating about how to build things. Consultation is not suited to a divine nature because it suggests they are seeking an answer they do not already have <note>original: "implies imperfection"</note>.</note>

<summary>Proclus explains that while the primary Creator (Demiurge) holds the perfect "Ideas" of all creatures, he leaves the creation of mortal animals to the "junior gods" so that these mortals do not become equal to the gods themselves. This distinction preserves the hierarchy of the universe while ensuring it contains every possible type of life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of how different levels of divinity—the Creator (Demiurge) and the primary "Living Being" (the Paradigm)—produce different types of existence, moving from the eternal and silent realm of thought down to the fragmented and changing realm of mortal life.</meta>

He also produces them simply by speaking, namely, through intellectual thought <term>original: intellection</term>. For he speaks indeed through intellectual perception, in a way that is unchanging and intellectual. The Living Being itself <term>original: Animal itself; the Platonic Form of the Living Being</term> also produces them, for it contains the primary cause of all winged, aquatic, and land animals. But it produces them in silence through its very essence and in a purely intelligible way. For the creative <term>original: demiurgic</term> speech receives the fatherly silence, just as the intellectual production receives the intelligible cause; the generation that exists through active energy <term>original: energizing</term> receives the divine care that comes from pure existence. Motion also receives the creative words, but the orderly arrangement <term>original: distribution</term> that is mixed with a physical <term>original: sensible</term> nature receives the intellectual energy. For the physical creations that exist at the furthest edge of things require a producing cause of this kind.

*Everything, therefore, which is subject to change, which changes in quality, and which is created and perishable, is generated from a cause that is unchanging in its essence but moves in its active energy. For the motion which is separated from essence in that higher realm produces here an essence that is constantly in motion.* 

Because that which creates does so both according to its essence and its energy—which are woven together—the change of essence in this world derives its progression from that higher source. Mortal natures, therefore, require causes that can move, and those that are very changeable require many such causes. It is impossible for these causes to remain "only-begotten" <term>original: unique and unproduced</term>; if they did, mortal types <term>original: genera</term> would not have a way to exist.

It is necessary, however, for mortal nature to exist. First, this ensures that everything capable of being created has a place in existence—both eternal beings and those that eventually cease to exist. Beyond these lies only that which does not exist in any respect. Second, this is necessary so that divine natures and beings are not the very last things in the chain of existence; for the power that produces something is more excellent and divine than the thing it creates. Third, it is necessary so that the world may be perfect, containing everything whose cause is held within the Living Being itself. For the "winged" nature that exists there is the cause of all winged creatures here; the aquatic is the cause of all sea life; and the terrestrial is the cause of all land creatures, whether they are divine or mortal. 

For this reason, Orpheus says that the life-giving cause <note>original: Proserpine; referring to the goddess Persephone</note> of fragmented <term>original: partible; referring to souls divided into bodies</term> natures was a nymph while she remained in the higher realms, weaving the order of the heavens. In that state, she was pure and undefiled, connected with Jupiter <note>original: Jupiter; the Roman name for the Greek god Zeus</note> and living in her proper way. But when she left her proper home, she left her weaving unfinished and was carried away <term>original: ravished; referring to the abduction of Persephone by Hades</term>. Having been carried away, she was married, and being married, she gave birth so that she might give life to things that have a temporary life <term>original: adventitious life; life that is added to a body from the outside</term>. The unfinished state of her weaving...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the *Timaeus*, specifically addressing the transition from the creation of eternal, divine beings by the primary Creator (the Demiurge) to the creation of mortal life by the secondary ("junior") gods.</meta>

<page-num>356</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.</header>

The mention of "webs" <note>original: "webs' indicates I think..." Proclus is referring to the Orphic myth where Proserpine weaves the fabric of the universe.</note> indicates, I believe, that the universe would be imperfect or unfinished if it only contained eternal <term>original: perpetual</term> animals. Hence Plato says that the one Creator <term>original: Demiurgus</term> calls on the many secondary creators <term>original: Demiurgi; the "junior gods" such as the stars and planets</term> to "weave together" mortal and immortal natures. This reminds us that adding mortal species <term>original: genera</term> is the final perfection of the universe's "weaving" life. It also prompts us to remember the divine Orphic myth and provides us with the underlying causes of the "unfinished webs" of Proserpine.

The divine number of beings, therefore, has its own proper boundary and end, and it is perfect. However, it is also necessary for mortal nature to exist and to have its own appropriate limits. This happens in three ways: in the air, in the water, and on the earth. It is impossible for mortality to exist in the heavens, because the summit and the highest species of every order is pure and eternal, since it is made to resemble the cause that came before it. Just as the highest of the "intellectual" beings <term>original: intellectuals; those that think</term> is "intelligible" <term>original: intelligible; that which is thought of</term>, and the highest of the angels is a God, so also the highest of the things we can perceive <term>original: sensibles</term> is eternal and divine. 

In the process of creation <term>original: generation</term>, however, the mortal nature is joined with the divine. For this reason, Plato calls the mortal species "the remainder" <note>original: "the remainder"; the leftovers after the primary creation is finished</note>, as if they were the scraps or residue left over from the divine craftsmanship—the dregs produced by the Gods themselves. But how can these be called "not yet generated"? Is it because they haven't been created yet at that point in the narrative? Because there is an order in the things that complete the universe, and the Creator has clearly made those that are secondary in order differ from those that come before them, he says the former are "not yet generated" while the latter already exist. 

Perhaps, in another sense, they may be said to be "not generated" because they are produced by the single creative source <term>original: demiurgic monad</term> through an unchanging and eternal power. Yet they are mortal because they are produced by the "junior Gods" <term>the celestial deities tasked with forming bodies</term>. These mortal beings still participate in a certain kind of eternity; they are indestructible in their form or species, even though they are individually perishable. In these beings, the "form" <term>the blueprint of the species</term> is distinct from the individual. The whole form is not contained within the individual as it is in the divine, eternal animals, because mortal beings are unable to receive the full extent of their eternal models <term>original: paradigms</term>. Therefore, the permanence of mortal natures comes from the primary creation, which keeps the species one and unchanging across many individuals. However, the changeability caused by the fragmented motion of the secondary causes alters the nature of the things produced. It is necessary, nonetheless, for mortal nature to exist so that the world may be perfect—not in a fragmented way, due to its intellectual cause, but so that it may be fully impressed with every variety of life.

forms. For those things which the single cause of all winged creatures <note>original: "natures"</note> includes, the sensible world receives in parts; and the single unit <note>original: "monad"</note> that exists there generates the plurality <note>original: "number"</note> that is here. But if these things are admitted, the <term>Demiurgus</term> <note>The Creator or "Craftsman" of the universe in Platonic philosophy.</note> (perceiving each mortal nature intellectually, insofar as each is eternal <note>original: "unbegotten"</note> because he contains the cause of mortality in an eternal manner) possesses not only the four primary Forms [contained in the "Animal Itself"], but also their subdivisions into the eternal causes of both immortal and mortal beings. The <term>Intelligible animal</term> <note>The abstract, perfect Form of "Living Being" in the realm of Ideas.</note>, therefore, is one thing, and the <term>intellectual animal</term> within the <term>Demiurgus</term> is another; the latter employs more specific <note>original: "partial"</note> animals, which are more numerous but possess less power than the <term>intelligible animal</term>.

Since, however, there are many perfections of the world—for it is perfect as a "whole of wholes," it is perfect by receiving the flow of time, and it is perfect by containing all living beings—<term>Plato</term> indicates the form of this perfection by adding, "*that it may be sufficiently perfect.*" For the world will thus be all-perfect by containing all animals within itself, embracing all intelligible and intellectual powers, and receiving the distributed images of the unified primary models <note>original: "paradigms"</note>. One might ask: if it is necessary for the world to contain all animals, including mortal ones, to match its perfect model, why does the <term>Demiurgus</term> himself not create them? <term>Plato</term> immediately provides the reason for this by adding, "*but if these were to receive life through me, they would become equal to the Gods.*" By these words, he directly confirms what was observed earlier: that everything produced by an unchanging <note>original: "immoveable"</note> cause is eternal and unchangeable. However, a thing produced by an unchanging cause through a "moving" cause (acting as a medium) is partly eternal and partly subject to change. It receives unity, existence, and Form from the unchanging cause, but it receives individuality and the process of "becoming" from the moving cause. Through this process, it is preserved according to its general Form but perishes as an individual. 

Since, therefore, one might say that the <term>Demiurgus</term> himself creates rational souls (which makes them equal to the Gods), why does <term>Plato</term> shortly after call these souls "homonymous" <note>sharing the same name but having a different nature</note> to divine souls regarding their immortality? It must be said that the word *isazoito* <note>original: ισάζοιτο; meaning "equalized" or "made similar to the equal"</note> is added with great caution. The <term>Demiurgus</term> does not say that they will be *entirely* equal to the Gods, but that they will be *similar* to them. For that which is "equalized" transitions into a likeness of the equal. Indeed, the "Equal" is a symbol of the gods of this world <note>original: "mundane Gods"</note>, as we may learn from the <term>Parmenides</term> <note>One of Plato’s most complex dialogues, dealing with the nature of "the One" and "the Many."</note>. To this we may add that the rational form of life, when it is purified and becomes perfect, is divine; so that some people do not hesitate to call it divine.

<summary>Proclus explains that while the Demiurge contains the eternal blueprints for all life, he delegates the creation of mortal beings to secondary causes so they remain mortal; otherwise, anything created directly by him would be an eternal god.</summary>

it is a God, through a divine nature being exerted within it, according to which it is also joined with the truly existing Gods. And thus much concerning this particular point.

It is likewise accurately said, "**through me**." For the mortal kinds <note>original: "genera"</note> are generated by the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The "Craftsman" or Creator of the universe in Platonic thought.</note>, but eternal natures are generated **through him**. For he possesses, according to one united cause, both the **by which** and the **through which**. As a father, he produces all things **by himself**; but as the Demiurge, he produces eternal natures **through himself**. Mortal natures are generated by him in a divided manner, but **through the junior Gods** <note>These are the secondary, celestial deities to whom the Demiurge delegates the creation of mortal bodies.</note>. This secondary creation <note>original: "junior fabrication"</note> must not be despised, however, because it stands in the relation of "through which" to the supermundane <note>beyond the physical world</note> cause. For more proximate causes always hold the rank of "through which" in reference to higher productions. For **nature is the instrument <note>original: "organ"</note> of the secondary creation, and of nature again, the instrument is internal <note>original: "innate"</note> heat**. 

Hence, those Platonists—such as the great Theodorus—who assign to the First Cause of all things the terms "**from which**" and "**to which**"; but to Intellect, the terms "**on account of which**" and "**with relation to which**"; and to Soul, the terms "**by which**" and "**according to which**," introduce a certain division of names that is not without merit <note>original: "inelegant"</note>, but they wander from the decision of Plato. For Plato assigns both the "**by which**" and "**through which**" to the demiurgic Intellect, and it is not at all necessary to divide these names according to the divine orders; except that "**on account of which**" denotes the final cause, while "**with relation to which**" denotes the paradigmatic <note>the ideal model or "Form"</note> cause. 

Nothing, however, hinders us from observing all of these in the Demiurge: as a God, he is the "**on account of which**" (for goodness is the end and goal of all things); but as an intellectual being, he is the "**through which**." For he produces through intellectual activity; his knowledge is not merely a precursor, but contributes through itself to the creation, acting beforehand according to intellect. Moreover, the words **participating in life** are very divinely added. For what if the elements as a whole had been generated by the Demiurge—namely fire, air, earth, and water—but were at the same time without life? Would they in that case have been equalized to the Gods, in the same way that we call the earth a God, and fire a God? By no means. For it is the soul which primarily deifies entire bodies, as it is said in the *Laws* <note>Plato's last and longest dialogue.</note>. But if they were generated through him and participate in life through him, they will have life and soul. For life <note>original: "βιος" (bios)</note> resides in souls. And if they also possess life in conjunction with their wholeness, they will be equalized to the Gods. For when he first gave a soul to the world, he then first celebrated it as a blessed God, because the soul possesses a deifying power in relation to everything corporeal and is essentially divine.
