“...that the universe may be truly all-encompassing, turn yourselves <note>original: "convert yourselves"</note> according to nature to the creation <note>original: "fabrication"</note> of animals, imitating the power which I employed in your own creation.”

A twofold purpose of creation is delivered here: one is providential, while the other is "assimilative" (intended to make the copy like the model). The first is more immediate, but the second is more universal. To create for the sake of giving existence to mortal natures indicates providence and the perfection¹ of power. This is because any overflowing abundance of power naturally produces other things subordinate to itself. 

However, to create for the sake of completing the universe indicates an energy based on an "assimilative" power—doing so so that this universe may be rendered similar to the **All-Perfect Living Being** <note>original: "all-perfect animal"; referring to the *Autozöon*, the divine intellectual model containing the forms of all living things</note>, by being adorned with all the various ranks of divine and mortal animals. If all things were immortal, the most divine² of sensible natures (those perceived by the senses) would be unproductive <note>original: "unprolific"</note>. Furthermore, if the universe were not filled with all forms of life, it would not be perfect, nor sufficiently similar to the All-Perfect Living Being. 

To ensure that neither of these defects occurred, the first **Demiurge** <note>The supreme Creator</note> stirs the "secondary creation" <note>original: "second fabrication"</note> from his own exalted vantage point above. He also pours life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note> and creative <note>original: "demiurgic"</note> power onto the gods of this world <note>original: "mundane Gods"</note>. Through this power, they generate secondary essences from themselves, fill them with life, and give them their distinct species. The unique quality of a life-giving deity is to grant life, while the quality of a creative deity is to produce form. The expression "turn yourselves," therefore, is a call to action; it is similar to the mandate given by Jupiter to the gods in Homer’s *Iliad*:

->Haste, to the Greek and Trojan hosts descend.³<-

Just as that command calls the gods to the "war of generation" (the world of change and becoming), so this command in Plato stirs them to the creation of mortals, which they accomplish through motion. This is achieved by all the gods within the world, but especially by the "governors of the world" (the planets). It is they who are "turned" or "converted," and most eminently by the sovereign **Sun**. For the Demiurge gave the Sun dominion over the whole, created him as a guardian, and ordered him, as **Orpheus** says:

->To rule over all.<-

The words "according to nature" also limit their creative work according to measure and goodness. Furthermore, these words place all physical production under their control as an instrument for their energies. Therefore, they move and govern that which is subservient to their will. Thirdly, these words define their existence as "media" (intermediaries); for it is the role of the middle to create the extremes.

according to nature. For things that have a temporary existence are dependent on those that are perpetual in time; and these perpetual things are, in turn, dependent on eternal entities. Primary natures generate intermediate ones, and intermediate natures produce those beings that are last in the series of all things. The word “*yourselves*,” which implies active crafting <note>original: "manual operation"</note>, rouses the divine lives themselves to the work of creation <note>original: "fabrication"</note>. 

Nor should we wonder how creative <note>original: "demiurgic"</note> power is granted to divine souls, since this is a characteristic of the superessential <note>Existing beyond the level of "being" or "essence"; a term for the highest gods in Neoplatonism</note> Gods. For just as Orpheus places a divine mind <note>original: "intellectual essence"</note> in Jupiter to make him a creator, Plato similarly shows that by receiving words from the Father <note>The Demiurge</note>, universal souls <note>original: "souls which rank as wholes"</note> are rendered divine and creative. 

We must not doubt why some worldly beings <gloss>1</gloss> are immortal while others are mortal, even though all are created according to divine models <note>original: "intelligible causes"</note>. This is because some proceed from one cause, and others from a different, more immediate cause. It is necessary to look at these immediate causes, and not just at the perfect archetypes <note>original: "paradigms"</note>. Furthermore, we should not search for "Ideas" of specific individuals like Socrates or Plato. The Demiurge divides mortal animals according to their types <note>original: "genera"</note> and focuses on universal divine thoughts <note>original: "total intellections"</note>; through these, he encompasses everything of a specific, individual nature. 

Just as the Demiurge creates material things using immaterial power, and creates the changing world using unchanging power, he also produces mortal natures in an immortal way <gloss>2</gloss>. He creates these indeed, but he does so through the agency of the junior Gods; prior to their physical making, he created them through divine thought <note>original: "intellection"</note> alone. We must also recognize that mortal natures exist in a divine way, not just a mortal one. The things the Demiurge now describes in his speech are the underlying realities <note>original: "hypostases"</note> of the junior or worldly Gods, which the heavens receive first, and according to which the Gods craft the mortal species. The primary units <note>original: "monads"</note> of every mortal life-form descend into the heavens from the divine forms. From these divine units, the entire multitude of material animals is generated. If we adopt these views, we will agree with Plato and remain true to the nature of things.

> “*Imitating the power which I employed in your creation <note>original: "generation"</note>,*” 

we must understand that the highest goal of this secondary creation is to imitate the one supreme, transcendent act of crafting and to return to its likeness. For it is necessary that self-moving <gloss>3</gloss> things should follow immovable natures, and that highly changeable things should follow those that are always in motion. There must be a perpetual series of secondary beings made in the likeness of those that—

He also makes this clear by adding, "*which I employed in your generation.*" For the father is the cause of this in conjunction with power, just as a human father, in conjunction with the female, is the cause of the propagation of the human species. He attributes this to the junior gods and shows them to be the lords of all mortal nature. He also received everything visible that was moving in a disorderly manner—which existed prior to him from another cause—and brought it into order from disorder. Thus, he delivers the final stages of the production of the universe to other powers, namely to the junior gods. Consequently, by both receiving and delivering, he acts as a mediator between the "Intelligible God"—who exists according to the *Animal-Itself* <note>original: "animal itself"; the Platonic Form or "Paradigm" of all living things</note>—and the many secondary creators <note>original: "Demiurgi"</note>.

For he produced the first of the immortals as well as those beings that share the name of the immortals. If he had committed the generation of the latter to the junior gods, he might appear to be the immediate cause of the celestial beings alone—producing sublunary <note>original: "sublunary"; referring to the earthly realm below the moon</note> natures from these, and souls from all of these combined. However, he has managed, through the production of the extremes, to show that the generation of all immortal natures, whatever they may be, comes from the one Demiurge. He shows this later when he says that the Demiurge is the father of immortals, but that he assigned the generation of mortals to other gods. This concludes the general meaning of these words.

From these points, however, we are compelled to speak freely against those Platonists who claim that our soul is of equal dignity with the gods and has the same essence as divine souls. We also speak against those who say that the soul becomes the *intellect itself*, the *intelligible itself*, and the *one itself*—leaving every soul-like quality behind and being established in total union. Plato is very far from asserting such a thing, since he calls the human soul "immortal" only in name <note>original: "homonymously immortal"</note> compared to divine souls. According to him, the soul does not possess this status from its own generation but is assigned this order by the Demiurge. It is *called* divine, but it is not *simply* divine. For "divine" pertains to undefiled souls that are always intellectual <note>original: "intellective"</note>; and "immortal" pertains to those souls that are established far away from mortal natures. 

But a soul that falls into the realm of generation—which has an essence of this kind and is capable of being mingled with mortal natures—is neither simply divine nor simply immortal. Again, you see different levels and a specific order of things. Some beings are primarily immortal; others are immortal in a secondary way; others share the name of immortality; and others are mortal. The nature of beings extends as far as these; and beyond these lies that which does not exist in any respect whatsoever. It must not be said, therefore, that our soul is simply divine, nor that it is simply immortal, even though it is frequently demonstrated to be immortal. <meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, specifically discussing the nature and origin of the human soul. It explains why the soul is considered immortal yet also connected to the mortal realm, and how it is produced through a hierarchy of causes—from the Demiurge down to the World Soul.</meta>

# [BOOK 5] PLATO'S TIMAEUS 363

[sub]sistence <note>original: "sistence"; part of the word "subsistence," meaning a distinct state of existence or reality</note>, yet exists genuinely, but it has that which is mingled with the mortal nature; because of this, some who have focused on this mixture have mistakenly believed that the soul is mortal. Moreover, we must not admit that the soul is the same as the Forms <note>original: "forms"; the perfect, abstract archetypes in Plato's philosophy</note> that are separate from matter, nor that it is the same as irrational life. 

For as Plato says here, the soul is granted a ruling nature by the Father <note>The Demiurge, or creator of the universe</note> who generated it. Hence, it is natural for the soul to have authority over irrational life. It likewise follows Justice and the Gods, as it is turned toward them, filled by them, and serves them. Every such form of life, specifically the rational soul, derives its existence from the "one fabrication" <note>The singular act of creation by the Demiurge</note>. For it is necessary that it should be produced by intellect—and specifically by a "total" or universal intellect. 

Consider these three categories of causes:
1. That which is of the same rank as the effect, but is universal.
2. That which is of a higher rank than the effect, but is partial.
3. That which is of a higher rank and is also universal.

There is no ambiguity regarding a fourth type—that which is partial and of the same rank—acting as a creator; it cannot be a primary cause because it does not <note>original: "το γαρ" (for); the translator notes it should be "ου γαρ" (for not)</note> differ enough from the thing it generates. This is because the effect is partial, and this cause would be of the same rank. 

It is impossible for a nature arranged in a higher rank, but which is only partial, to have the same authority over the generation of things as "wholes" (universal entities). It is absolutely necessary that what is truly a cause should be more powerful than its effect. Furthermore, that which is universal but of the same rank does not have the true power of generating, because it belongs to the same series as the thing generated. 

Therefore, the only "most principal" cause is that which is a "whole" or universal entity in a higher rank. This is because it surpasses its offspring in both rank and scope. The Demiurge, therefore, produces and crafts other things in conjunction with this universal cause. 

On this account, the individual soul proceeds through three stages:
1. Primarily from the Demiurge.
2. Secondarily from the universal soul of the universe.
3. Immediately from a "partial intellect." 

By a "partial intellect," I mean an intellect that holds the same place in the order of intelligible things that an individual soul holds in the series of souls. This intellect makes the soul an individual, but the universal soul makes it rational. The Demiurge makes it both. Therefore, he is the primary cause. This is why we say here that the Demiurge presides over the generation of the soul. 

In the *Philebus* <note>One of Plato's later dialogues concerning pleasure and the good life</note>, Plato gives the individual soul an essence derived from the universal soul. For just as the fire within us comes from the cosmic fire, and the earth, water, and air within us come from the universal elements, he says that the individual soul is generated from the Soul of the Universe. This concludes our discussion on this particular point.

Plato also quite properly aligns Justice with the worldly gods.

<summary>Proclus explains that the individual rational soul is created through a hierarchy: the Demiurge provides its essential nature, the World Soul makes it rational, and a "partial intellect" makes it an individual entity.</summary>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK 5]

### THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO. 364

For Justice is, as Orpheus says, the companion of Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus, the king of the gods</note>; since, according to him,

->Laborious Justice <note>original: "Laborious Justice"; often translated from the Greek *Dike* as "exacting" or "avenging" justice</note> follows Jove.——<-

And the Athenian guest <note>The main speaker in Plato's *Laws*</note> also asserts that Justice always follows Jupiter. But Justice is co-established with the mundane <note>original: "mundane"; gods belonging to the physical world/cosmos</note> Gods and governs the universe according to what is deserved, in conjunction with them. For from the center of the solar sphere, Justice entirely extends its providential inspection and disseminates the distribution of good.

What, however, are we to understand by the *semination* <note>original: "semination"; from the Latin *seminatio*, meaning a sowing or scattering like seeds</note>? Is it that which many of the Platonists speak of so much—the distribution of souls among the stars? For Plato says that the Demiurge <note>The Divine Craftsman or Creator of the universe</note> disseminated some of them into the earth, others into the sun, and others into the moon. We admit that there is a two-fold semination: one regarding the Gods, and the other regarding generation <note>The realm of physical birth and change</note>, which is described in the *Politicus* <note>Plato's dialogue *The Statesman*</note>. Now, however, Plato refers the cause of the essence of souls to the Demiurge. For it is necessary that they should first be generated, and then afterwards that different souls should be distributed among different leaders. 

It is better, therefore, according to the decision of our preceptor <note>Likely Syrianus, Proclus's teacher</note>, to understand this "semination" as generation, since it pertains to a father to disseminate and to generate "reasons" <note>original: "reasons"; translated from the Greek *logoi*, meaning productive principles or formative powers</note>. For the soul is a "reason of reasons" and proceeds from the Father who is the Demiurge of wholes. This, indeed, is the first semination. The second is that which involves the junior Gods <note>The secondary deities who create the mortal parts of the soul and body</note>. And the third is about the realms of generation. Of the first, divine souls participate; of the second, dæmons <note>original: "dæmons"; intermediary spirits between gods and men, not to be confused with modern "demons"</note> participate, for their orders are distributed around the Gods. But the third alone pertains to those souls that are distributed within the realm of generation. 

Very properly, the Demiurge says that he will deliver the *beginning*, or that he will *begin* the production of the rational soul, because other causes also generate it in conjunction with the Demiurge—I mean, for instance, such causes as the vivific <note>original: "vivific"; life-giving powers, often associated with the goddess Rhea or Hecate in Neoplatonism</note>. He likewise very properly says this because he generates the vehicle <note>original: "vehicle"; the *augoeides ochema* or "luminous body" that carries the rational soul</note> of the soul and all the life contained in it, which the junior Gods weave together with the mortal form of life. Hence, it appears to me that the "immortal" is assumed in both the rational soul and its vehicle—this being a common trait, rather than just the "rational" trait—and that this is indicated by the words, "*and so far as among these, it is fit there should be that which is homonymous <note>original: "homonymous"; having the same name but a different definition</note> to the immortals*," meaning it proceeds from the one fabrication. For every vehicle, together with its appropriate life and the rational soul from which it is suspended, is essentially perpetual. Both, therefore, are generated by the Demiurge, accord-

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the Demiurge (the Divine Craftsman) creates the soul and its "vehicle" according to the patterns of the stars, and how he delegates the creation of the mortal aspects of life to the junior gods.</meta>

<page-num>365</page-num>
<header>BOOK 5] TIMAEUS OF PLATO.</header>

According to a likeness of the stars, the Demiurge <note>The Divine Craftsman or Creator of the universe</note> produces both the souls and the vehicles <note>The "spiritual" or "astral" body that serves as a carrier for the soul</note> in which they reside. He sows the soul, acting as the "father of reasons" <note>The source of the rational principles that define a soul</note>; but in producing the vehicle, he provides the *beginning*. For this is now the beginning of the life formed in a mortal shape.

> “It is your <note>The original Greek text erroneously used *hemeis* (we) instead of *hymeis* (your)</note> business to accomplish the rest, and to weave together the immortal <note>The original Greek text erroneously used *thanate* (mortal) instead of *athanate* (immortal)</note> and mortal nature.”

The interpreters of Plato have unfolded the meaning of this immortal nature and this mortal nature. Some, leaving only the rational soul immortal, believe that all irrational life and the pneumatic <term>Pneumatic: Derived from *pneuma*, meaning "breath" or "spirit"; here it refers to a subtle, air-like body that clothes the soul.</term> vehicle of the soul are destroyed. They argue that these only exist because of the soul's tendency toward physical birth. These thinkers preserve only the intellect as immortal, as it is the only part that remains, is likened to the Gods, and does not suffer decay. This is the explanation of the more ancient interpreters, such as Atticus and Albinus <note>Platonist philosophers from the 2nd century AD</note> and those like them, who follow Plato’s words and explain why he destroys the irrational part, which they call the "mortal nature."

But others, more moderate and mild than these—such as Porphyry <note>A significant Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note> and his followers—refuse to admit this "corruption" <note>meaning destruction or decay</note> that supposedly dissipates the vehicle and the irrational soul. Instead, they say that these parts are renovated and dissolved <note>original: "analysed"</note> in a certain way back into the celestial spheres from which their composition was originally drawn. They add that these are mixtures derived from the celestial spheres and collected by the soul as she descends; thus, they exist and yet do not exist, for they have no individual identity, nor does their specific character remain. The authors of these claims appear to follow the *Chaldean Oracles* <note>A collection of mystical poems from the 2nd century AD, highly regarded by Neoplatonists</note>, which, in speaking of the soul's descent, say that it collects a portion of ether, of the sun, the moon, and things contained in the air as it travels downward. However, one must argue against these views using Plato’s own words, in which he clearly does not destroy the whole of the irrational nature.

And finally, in the third place, there are others who remove all destruction from the irrational nature. They do not simply give it a reality <term>Hypostasis: A term in Greek philosophy referring to the underlying reality or "substance" of a thing.</term> derived from divine bodies—lest, being generated from moving causes, it should be naturally changeable—but rather from the Gods themselves who govern the world and produce all things eternally.

Such, then, are the many opinions on this subject. There is, however, an explanation that immediately preserves the mortal nature and accords with the truth...

...with the nature of things themselves and all the Platonic doctrines <note>original: "dogmas"</note>. For it is clear that Plato believes the irrational life is preserved after the material body decays. He shows this by describing the soul being punished in Hades <note>The realm of the dead or the afterlife in Greek mythology</note> through anger and desire; yet the soul would not require any punishment if it were completely liberated from all passion. For the soul, existing as pure reason before it entered a body, chose its lives based on its previous dispositions: some chose tyrannical lives through greed <note>original: "voracity"</note>, while others chose the lives of sophists or popular figures through a desire for glory. These experiences happen to the soul during its first descent from the heavens and also to the soul that has been recently perfected.

Furthermore, it is evident that he considers the vehicle of the soul to be perpetual, as he represents souls using these vehicles in Hades. As Socrates says in the *Phaedo*, they cross the river [Acheron] by ascending into their vehicles. Now, he also establishes that the Demiurge <note>The Divine Craftsman or Creator</note> generates this vehicle. It is the Demiurge who causes the soul to ascend into its vehicle, modeled after the likeness of divine souls. For how could a soul belong to the world <note>original: "mundane"</note> without having a vehicle within the universe? Everything that belongs to this world has a specific place and order within it and contributes to the completion of a part of it. 

Consider this: would an individual <note>original: "partial"</note> soul be in a better state before or after a vehicle is attached to it? If it were better without one, it would be more divine than the "total" souls <note>The greater souls that animate the cosmos or the stars</note> to which the Demiurge gave vehicles. But if it were in a worse state without one, why would the Demiurge cause it to ascend into a vehicle immediately after it was created? Eternal things do not begin in an unnatural state, but in their natural condition of being. Therefore, it is evident that these ideas are consistent with Plato's opinion.

However, since he clearly calls the part woven together by the mundane gods "mortal," is the theory proposed by some scholars true? They say the life within the vehicle is woven by the junior gods <note>The subordinate deities who assist the Demiurge</note>. They suggest he calls it "mortal" because it takes a physical form and is involved with mortal nature. They argue that in another place, he calls that which is woven by the junior gods "immortal" so that we might understand the "mortal nature" mentioned here in that specific light. 

But how does this fit with his general rule that the Demiurge is the cause of immortal natures, while the creation of mortals is committed to the junior gods? Thus, after the initial act of creation <note>original: "fabrication"</note>, the junior gods are the sole creators of mortal natures. Or is the theory correct that the vehicle and the irrational soul both remain and are dissolved by being analyzed <note>Broken back down into their component elements</note> into the celestial spheres from which they were derived? If so, they would be "mortal" and yet "not mortal" at the same time. This idea, however, is inherently absurd. When a union is dissolved, how can we say that the same thing still remains? For the irrational soul is not a mere heap <note>original: "coacervation"</note> of animal parts, but a single life with many forms. In addition to these things, it must...

be admitted that at one time something is taken away from, and at another, something is added to the celestial bodies—an idea that is entirely foreign to their nature. Is the irrational soul, therefore, subject to decay <term>corruptible</term>, and should we admit that this life is scattered and lost <note>original: "dissipated"</note> along with the body? But if this were the case, how could there be punishments? How would there be purifications? How would there be the choosing <note>original: "elections"</note> of lives—some based on imagination <note>original: "phantasy"</note>, others on anger, and others on desire? And how would there be the entering into <term>ingressions</term> <note>The text suggests correcting the Greek from "euseis" to "eisdyseis," meaning the soul's entry or sinking into a body</note> the bodies of irrational animals? For contact with what is analogous is through analogy <note>The text suggests correcting the Greek from "pos di alogias gar" to "di analogias gar," meaning "through analogy"</note>, just as contact with the intellect is through the intellect.

Would it not, therefore, be better to say with our teacher that the spirit (the "pneumatic" or airy part of the soul) contains the highest points of the irrational life? These exist forever, along with the soul's "vehicle," having been produced by the Demiurge <note>The Divine Creator or Craftsman in Platonic philosophy</note>. These elements, when expanded and divided into parts, create the mortal life "woven" by the lesser <term>junior</term> gods. This life is mortal because the soul must eventually set aside this divided state; once it has been purified, it is restored to its original state of happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note>. 

However, this pneumatic life lasts longer than the life of the physical body. This is why the soul possesses this kind of life when it is in Hades <note>The realm of the afterlife</note> choosing its next existence. Because of its leaning or inclination toward the physical body, it receives this mortal life from the lesser gods. If we admit this, then the Demiurge creates the summit of the irrational life, but does not create the specific mortal life itself. In creating spirits <term>daemons</term> <note>In this context, these are intermediate spiritual beings, not necessarily evil</note>, he clearly also creates the irrational life within them, but not the specific kind of life that the lesser gods weave into us. 

This latter kind of life is only suited for souls that descend into the cycle of birth and death <term>generation</term>. The gods of this world <term>mundane</term>, possessing intellectual souls, illuminate their own vehicles with lives shaped by reason. But daemons, who are specifically defined by reason, use irrational powers over which they have control. Our souls likewise have an irrational life within their vehicle; however, our souls go beyond daemons in this: they receive an *additional* irrational life, which is a departure from the life in the spirit and is woven by the lesser gods. 

Therefore, everything the soul possesses that is immortal comes from its imitation of the universal "wholes." But any addition belongs to a second, mortal-shaped life. If, then, there is one unaffected <term>impassive</term> life in the ethereal vehicle, it will produce one sensitive <term>passive</term> sense in the airy <term>pneumatic</term> vehicle. This, in turn, will produce many sensitive senses in the shell-like <term>testaceous</term> <note>referring to the hard, outer physical body</note> body. In the same way, the power of desire <term>orectic power</term> in the ethereal vehicle will produce many powers of desire in the spirit <note>original: "pneuma"</note>—

It is likewise necessary to understand that he gives existence to the irrational soul prior to this outward body. But if the latter is the case, this soul may very properly be called mortal; and we shall no longer be able to maintain what is said of it elsewhere—namely, the choosing of lives and the punishments in the underworld <note>original: Hades</note>, in which the irrational nature is entirely involved. And if we say that this soul is in the [ethereal] vehicle, it will necessarily be immortal, and the claim that makes it immortal will prevail; it would then no longer be true that the one Demiurge <note>The supreme Creator</note> is the cause of immortals while the many junior <term>lesser</term> gods are the causes of mortal natures. ### THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO.

—weaving together the mortal with the immortal nature. And he states this generally, and not for all animals; because Plato, further on, calls plants "animals" also, and shows that it is necessary to name them as such. Through the immortal soul, therefore, the junior Gods <note>The secondary deities or celestial powers created by the Demiurge to fashion the mortal world.</note> produce animals—specifically those that not only possess the lowest form of life, the *desire-driven* <term>epithymetic</term> <note>original: "epithymetic"; referring to the appetitive part of the soul concerned with basic desires and survival.</note>, and are for this reason called "animals," but also every mortal animal. 

If, however, the Demiurge <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the Great Architect or Creator of the universe in Platonic thought.</note> calls on the junior Gods not only to fashion man by interweaving the mortal with the immortal nature, but also other animals, they evidently fashion all other animals as well. Hence, Timaeus very properly, towards the end of this dialogue, represents other animals as being generated through the transformation of the human soul into them. This occurs in accordance with the command of the Demiurge, while the junior Gods alone produce plants without the assistance of this rational soul. For in plants, there is no rational soul. 

Because this soul is the principle of motion, it is necessary that it should be the principle of the first motion in animals. But the first motion for these is "motion according to place" (local motion), as Aristotle also has shown. So every animal that moves from place to place has a self-moving soul present within it. On this account, a plant rooted in the earth does not have this soul. Thus, the junior Gods very properly generate and develop other animals (except plants) by weaving the mortal with the immortal nature. 

But they provide other animals with nourishment by arranging the growth of plants, through which humans and other animals are fed. For nothing prevents certain animals from being nourished by the same things that feed humans, as well as by other things to which their nature is related, just as the nature of the animals we eat is related to us. Through this careful workmanship, therefore, the junior Gods complete the production started by the one Demiurge. For he imparts only the beginning [or the highest point], but they develop and, through the process of generation, constitute the whole animal. 

Indeed, through this workmanship they imitate the power of the Demiurge, but through the act of generation, they imitate the paternal <note>original: "paternal"; the author notes a correction here from "spiritual" (pneumatic) to "paternal" (patric), signifying the fatherly role of creation.</note> power. Through their workmanship, they also produce the mortal parts of rational animals; but through generation, they produce irrational animals, insofar as they lack reason. For they constitute the entirety of such animals. But if they receive the immortal nature which the Demiurge produces, and which he orders them to weave with the mortal nature to fashion animals, it is evident that—according to the will of the Demiurge—every soul has an immortal life prior to its mortal life. The junior Gods develop the latter, but the one Demiurge creates the former. And if, indeed, the Demiurge constituted both irrational and rational...

souls, nothing would hinder that which is immortal in them from being irrational. *But since, in this case, he alone generates rational souls—to whom he also speaks, instilling in them the laws of Fate—it is evident that every animal which is properly an animal (by possessing the power of local motion) necessarily has a rational and immortal soul.* Therefore, when Plato speaks of the soul entering into irrational bodies, he does not agree with those who say these are human souls acting according to a human’s irrational nature; rather, he means they are truly the souls of irrational animals. This is evident not only through these arguments but also from what he says regarding other animals during the creation of mortal beings: that the creation of all of them is achieved through the human soul. By transferring <note>original: "μεγιστας" (megistas - greatest); the text suggests reading "μεθιστας" (methistas - transferring or changing).</note> this soul into different animals, he shapes the forms of their bodies according to the soul's transition and its chosen way of life, through which it develops an inclination <term>habitude</term> toward these animals. The Father [the Demiurge], therefore, orders the junior gods to build and generate all animals by weaving together the mortal nature with the immortal nature. And we have shown that the immortal nature is twofold (consisting of the soul and its vehicle <note>The "astral body" or ethereal carriage of the soul in Neoplatonic philosophy.</note>), and in a similar way, the mortal nature is twofold, with each mortal part corresponding to its immortal counterpart.

Next, the gift of nourishment is what brings mortals to completion. For this reason, the junior gods produced all plants for the sake of more honorable beings. The Demiurge <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine craftsman or creator of the material world.</note>, therefore, is very far from approving of the eating of animals, since after the generation of all animals, he commands the junior gods to produce plants as food for them. The creative work of these gods also ends beautifully in regeneration, according to the will of the Father. For to receive back again things which have decayed is nothing other than a renewal of creation—a turning of corruption back into generation. Because of this, nothing ever vanishes into total non-existence; the gods who preside over creation link the cycles of birth and death with their own eternal cycles. They make creation continuous with decay, giving form to the non-being of the latter and circularly leading "lack" <term>privation</term> back into a physical **form** <note>original: "morphe"; the Greek word for shape or visible form.</note>. The Demiurge, therefore, gave the junior gods the task of creating mortal beings and the cause of regeneration from the very beginning. Similarly, he placed the creation of all worldly natures into the single source <term>monad</term> of the junior gods—that is, in Bacchus—whom Orpheus also calls the "Juvenile God." You see, therefore, how the Demiurge imparts to them unifying and deifying powers by calling them "gods of gods"; connecting and stabilizing powers through the balance of the temporary and the eternal; powers of knowledge through instruction; and powers of completion through...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Proclus' analysis of Plato's Timaeus. It focuses on how the Demiurge (the primary Creator) delegates the creation of mortal life to secondary gods, who utilize various divine powers to maintain the cycle of birth and decay.</meta>

<page-num>371</page-num>
<header>BOOK 5.] THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO.</header>

...giving perfection to the world by adding mortal beings; creative <note>original: "demiurgic"</note> powers through their craftsmanship; and moving and matching powers by imitating the Father. We can also say he gave them Vulcanian <note>relating to Vulcan (Hephaestus), the god of fire and craftsmanship, representing natural energy.</note> powers through their natural actions; Minerval <note>relating to Minerva (Athena), goddess of wisdom and weaving.</note> powers through the command to weave the mortal and immortal natures together; Cerealian and Coric <note>relating to Ceres (Demeter) and Core (Persephone), goddesses of agriculture, growth, and the underworld.</note> powers through the command to give birth and nourish; Titanic <note>relating to the Titans, who in Neoplatonism represent the division of unity into many perishable parts.</note> powers by ordering them to produce mortal and temporary things; and Dionysian <note>relating to Dionysus, representing the return of the many back into one through regeneration.</note> powers through regeneration. 

For they receive back the things they create when those things decay <note>original: "corrupted"</note>, returning them to the universal wholes from which they came, and distributing each part to its proper source. From these sources, they take other parts again and combine them to create new things. All the elements are at their disposal to create mortal animals, and they constantly and without ceasing complete the cycle of birth and decay. Thus, they reclaim what they gave to created beings when those beings die, returning to the universal whole that which they originally took. This process continues in an infinite cycle of change, driven by the unchanging <note>original: "immobility [i. e. immutability]"</note> nature of the gods who create mortal beings.

> "**These things the Father spoke to those whom he assigned the task of creating mortal beings.**"

Plato divides the entire creation <note>original: "fabrication"</note> of things into two categories: the generation of divine beings and the generation of mortal beings. He further divides the creation of divine beings into the creation of the entire world (before its individual parts) and the creation of the great, everlasting parts within it. These are then divided into heavenly and earthly <note>original: "sublunary"</note> beings. 

Regarding mortal beings, he divides their creation into the production of their divine, immortal parts and the shaping <note>original: "plastic"</note> of their mortal parts. This shaping is further divided into the creation of souls and bodies. Finally, the creation of bodies is divided into the creation of the whole organism and its specific parts, such as the head, the heart, and the liver. 

The Demiurge <term>Demiurge: From the Greek 'demiurgos,' meaning craftsman; the primary creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy.</term> of the whole universe handles all the primary creation himself. However, for the secondary creation, he produces the immortal part but assigns the remaining tasks to the many "junior" creators <note>original: "Demiurgi"</note>. Since these junior gods are the shapers of mortal animals and are always full of life themselves, they provide their own caring energy to the mortal parts of creation as much as those parts can receive it, filling them with the life of the physical world <term>genesiurgic: relating to the production of the physical world or the process of birth and generation.</term> and material creation. For every—

<summary>Proclus explains how the Demiurge delegates the creation of mortal life to secondary gods, who use various divine attributes to manage the endless cycle of birth, decay, and regeneration. He outlines Plato's hierarchy of creation, from the universal whole down to the individual organs of mortal bodies.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the speech of the Demiurge (the Creator) in Plato’s Timaeus. <page-num>372</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK 5.</header>

...where the lowest things are created by those that rank as intermediaries <note>original: "media"</note>. These intermediaries between the first immortals and mortal beings are those that are always filled with a life that is constantly renewed. Therefore, the beings that are immortal by their own nature resemble fountains of water. Those that are filled by these fountains can be compared to perpetually flowing rivers, and those that sometimes lose their life <note>original Greek: "τα δε απολειποντα" (those failing); Proclus notes it should be read as "ποτε δε απολειποντα" (those failing at some time)</note> are like rivers that stop flowing. But everywhere, that which is more full desires to fill others and is eager to create. For this reason, it is necessary that intermediaries should pass on existence to the lowest things, and those that are always filled with life should pass it on to those that are only able to live for a time. This concludes the discussion on the relationship between these different orders of existence.

The words "*He spoke these things*" carry a remarkable meaning. In the first place, they indicate perfection and that which is defined by its proper limits. Since we cannot grasp the unified <note>original: "unical"</note> perfection, eternal activity, and infinite power of divine beings in a single word, we understand them in parts using terms related to time. We use the past tense to signify perfection, but the present tense to signify that which never fails. Therefore, the word *spoke* is a symbol of the perfection of the Creator’s <note>original: "demiurgic"</note> thoughts <note>original: "intellections"</note>. For just as those thoughts are all-perfect, so too are the Creator’s words—which are the expressions of those thoughts—that reach out to the many gods. 

In the same way, in the *Chaldean Oracles* <note>A collection of mystical poems from the 2nd century AD, highly regarded by Neoplatonists.</note>, the activities of the gods and of the Father himself are revealed through the word *spoke*, as when they say: "The intellect of the eternal Father, governing all things by intellect, *spoke* and said, 'into three.'" <note>This likely refers to the Chaldean triad of Father, Power, and Intellect.</note> To "speak" in this context is not an activity of mere existence or life, but of pure thought. This is the first thing these words indicate. 

Furthermore, the word *spoke* shows that *words* are suited to souls, for speaking is an activity familiar and closely related to them. This is because the verb *to speak* <note>original Greek: "to eipein"</note> is derived from the noun *word* <note>original Greek: "to epos"</note>. Reason <note>original Greek: "logos"</note> or speech belongs to souls and their order, as Plato observed earlier when he mentioned reason acting upon both the intellectual and the sensory world, and when he equated "intellectual perception" with "speaking." 

Again, adding the words *these things* unites the many individual thoughts around the single intelligence of the Creator and gathers the various powers of speech into the single source <note>original: "monad"</note> of the Father's thought. We must also understand that regarding divine speeches in Plato, all of them are either addressed to souls or exist for the sake of souls. For example, the speech of the Muses and the speech of the prophet in the *Republic* are addressed to souls. Likewise, the speech in the *Symposium* <note>original: "Banquet"</note> by Aristophanes—

<header>BOOK V.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

...and also the discussions delivered in the *Statesman* <note>original: "Politicus"</note> are focused on souls. The former concerns souls that are about to descend into the physical world, while the latter concerns those already involved in the world of change and "generation" <note>the realm of birth, death, and physical existence</note>. The reason for this, as we have said, is because speech is a quality that especially belongs to souls.

<margin>41 D</margin>
> "And once more, into the same mixing bowl <note>original: "Crater"</note> in which he had previously blended the soul of the universe, he poured the remains of the same ingredients, mixing them together."

These words show that for the divine mind of the Creator, "thinking" and "making" are the same thing. Among the Gods, there is no difference between perceiving something intellectually and producing it. No external movement is necessary for them to generate things; they create everything simply through their very being and existence. This is shown by the fact that as soon as the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> finishes speaking, he immediately turns to the mixing bowl and the blending of the various kinds <note>original: "genera"</note> of being. 

There is no gap between his words and his actions. If we perceive the work as separate from the words, it is only because of our own human weakness <note>original: "imbecility"</note>; we are unable to grasp in a single moment both the father’s transcendent intelligence and his creative act that produces individual souls. Any person who is not completely blind can see from these words that the category of individual souls proceeds according to its own order and differs entirely from divine souls, since they are created separately and at a different time. 

This distinction does not just come from the limitations of our language; it matches the actual nature of things. In reality, if you consider "participated time" <note>time as experienced by created beings</note>, the time experienced by total, divine souls is not the same as that of individual souls. They do not share the same way of thinking <note>original: "intellection"</note> or the same form of motion. Furthermore, Plato shows that individual souls come from the same father, but not in exactly the same way. The word *again* indicates that their progression follows a more limited power of the Creator. In one sense, this process is the same as what came before, yet in another, it is different. Because the word *again* does not refer to a sequence in time—since it is not right to think of eternal beings as acting step-by-step in time—it instead shows a different level of creation. Thus, in a certain respect, they have the same father, and yet not the same.

Furthermore, individual souls come from the same mixing bowl <note>original: "Crater"</note> as the total (universal) souls, but they are created with a certain "diminution" <note>a reduction in purity or power</note>. While divine souls remain and proceed within the mixing bowl, [these partial souls...]

² Instead of "order" <note>original Greek: "ταξιν"</note> here, it is necessary to read "mixture" <note>original Greek: "μιξιν"</note>.

### PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.

and do not depart from there. But our souls are entirely separated from it, and their separation is obvious. To this, we may also add that the kinds <note>original: "genera"</note> are both the same and different. For all souls come from the middle kinds, but some come from the first of these, and others from the remains and the last part of the mixture from which the souls before them were made. 

Again, the method of creation is at once the same and not the same: for in individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls, difference is more abundant than sameness. This is why, when speaking of these souls, there is a more frequent mention of "mixture." We must not, therefore, accept the opinion of those more recent interpreters who try to show that our soul is of equal dignity, or of the same essence—or whatever phrase they wish to use—with a divine soul. This is despite the fact that Plato asserts that individual souls are lacking in a second and third degree, separates them from the Mixing Bowl <note>original: "Crater"</note>, and has them produced by the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> according to a "secondary" intelligence (which is the same as saying a more partial intelligence). 

For he who says these things introduces essential differences between souls, and not differences based on their activities <note>original: "energies"</note> alone, as the divine Plotinus shows. For let it be admitted that some souls look toward total intellects, while others look to partial ones; that some employ pure intellectual perceptions <note>original: "intellections"</note>, while others sometimes abandon real beings; that some always create and adorn the whole of things, while others only sometimes travel in the company of the Gods; that some always move and govern Fate, while others sometimes fall under the power of Fate and fatal laws; that some are leaders to the intelligible realm, while others are sometimes assigned the order of followers; that some are purely divine, while others are at different times transferred to a different rank—either demoniacal <note>referring to "daemons," intermediary spirits between gods and humans</note>, heroic, or human; that some use horses which are all good and made of good things, while others use horses mixed from good and evil <note>This refers to the chariot allegory in Plato's *Phaedrus*</note>; that some have only that life which they received from the one primary creation, while others also have a mortal form woven by the lesser <note>original: "junior"</note> Gods; and that some act according to all their powers, while others live different lives at different times. 

Even if we accept these as the differences between souls, an essential change and a division by the Creator precede all of them. Through these, souls are separated by time, by cause, by their progression, by their way of existing <note>original: "mode of subsistence"</note>, and by the lowering of their kinds. Since they differ by all these details, how is it possible that they should be of the same essence? For,

[BOOK V.] THE *TIMAEUS* OF PLATO.

the rest, namely: the rational principles, the form of life, intelligence, and time. For these exist divinely in divine souls, but in a human manner within our own. This should suffice as an argument against those who imagine that our soul shares the same essence as the soul of the universe and other divine souls. Such people claim we are all things without any specific relationship <note>original: "habitude"; from the Greek *schesis*, meaning a relative condition or disposition</note>—meaning we are the planets, the fixed stars, and everything else in the same way the stars themselves are. This is an idea that Theodorus of Asine <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Iamblichus</note> also suggests somewhere. Such grandiose language on this subject is very far removed from the actual theory of Plato.

With respect to the **Mixing Bowl** <note>original: "Crater"; the vessel in which the Creator mixes the ingredients of the soul in Plato’s *Timaeus*</note>, however, let us see what it is, what rank it holds in relation to the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note>, and what effects it causes in souls. There is much discussion concerning this, and it deserves the most thorough consideration. The aforementioned Theodorus claims there is a twofold Mixing Bowl and asserts that the "mixture" itself is one of these. According to him, the second Mixing Bowl is the mixture; but the other Mixing Bowl consists of the portions of that mixture—namely, the soul of the universe, the souls of the celestial Gods, and our souls. He calls the soul itself the first Mixing Bowl, as it is the universal soul; but he labels the Bowl and the mixture together as the second Mixing Bowl. 

However, Plato speaks of only *one* Mixing Bowl, and in it he mingles all souls—some primarily and others secondarily—but he makes no mention at all of a second Bowl or a mixture within it. Indeed, if there were a second Mixing Bowl, what need would there be for the first one in the creation of our souls? I am surprised, therefore, that the most hardworking Atticus <note>A 2nd-century Platonic philosopher</note> should say he found a twofold Mixing Bowl in the *Timaeus*, since he usually follows Plato's words very strictly. Nevertheless, when interpreting the *Phaedrus*, he does mention a twofold Mixing Bowl. 

But according to the divine Iamblichus, the Mixing Bowl is the single life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note> cause that encompasses the whole of life and gathers it together. It sustains itself through certain creative principles <note>original: "demiurgic reasons"</note> that pervade all life and all levels of the soul <note>original: "psychical orders"</note>. It assigns to each soul in its proper rank the appropriate measures of connection; it grants the first measures to some from the beginning through the first mixture, and secondary measures to those that have been mingled again. For the rank they hold in relation to each other is the same as the progression they are assigned from the Mixing Bowl, receiving from it the boundaries of their lives. These, then, are the doctrines we have received from these men.

Our teacher <note>likely referring to Syrianus, Proclus' mentor</note>, however—viewing true reality from a high vantage point, as if from a watch-tower, and following the accounts of the theologians—places a productive power within the Father and Creator of the whole universe himself. According to this power, and by imitating the intelligible God, the Creator possesses both a maternal and paternal cause in relation to the gods of this world <note>original: "mundane Gods"</note>, being himself the source of essence, of life, and of form.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Mixing Bowl" (Crater) from Plato's Timaeus, exploring its role as the source of the soul's life and its relationship to the Creator (Demiurgus).</meta>

PROCLUS ON THE *TIMAEUS* [BOOK V.]

However, since it is necessary <note>The Greek text here requires the word *dei*, meaning "it is necessary."</note> for there to be a definite and distinct cause for the life of the soul—one that works together with the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> to build the entire world and generate the whole essence of the soul—this cause, he says, is conveyed to us through the Mixing Bowl <note>original: "Crater"</note>. He adds that theologians, speaking in mystery about their doctrines, have devised marriages and offspring for the Gods. Through these stories, they obscurely signal the natural connection of offspring among the Gods. Plato, however, used myths to introduce mixtures and blends; he used the "genera of being" <note>The basic categories of reality: Being, Sameness, and Difference</note> instead of seeds, and "mixture" instead of marriage. For while souls are produced by the Creator according to the "being" (essence) within them, they are produced from the Mixing Bowl according to the "life" within them. This Bowl is the life-giving cause of essential life. Since souls are "lives" to a greater degree than they are "beings," and are allied to the life-giving order of the universe, the mixture begins with the Creator but is brought to perfection in the Mixing Bowl. For this Bowl contains within itself all the types of souls and generates them in conjunction with the Creator. There are, therefore, four parts to this process: the one who mixes (the Father/Creator), the Mixing Bowl (the generative cause that defines the form of souls), the ingredients being mixed (the "genera of being"), and the resulting mixture itself. The first holds the rank of father; the second is the generative power that defines the form of souls; the third comes from both but more so from the father; and the fourth is given form by the generative cause so as to become a single thing through the Mixing Bowl.

But if it is necessary to explain the ideas of our teacher <note>Likely referring to the Neoplatonist Syrianus, Proclus’s mentor</note> on this subject, we must observe that just as the life-giving goddess <note>original: "vivific deity," referring to Rhea</note> contains within herself all the fountains of life—those that generate souls and the rank of spirits <note>original: "dæmoniacal"</note>, those that bring forth the angelic series, and those that produce nature in the lowest realm of things—so too does a specific life-giving goddess <note>original: "vivific deity," referring here to Juno or Hera</note> proceed from her. This goddess is the fountain for the entire development and generation of souls. Working alongside the Creator, she produces the whole order of souls—every soul both above the world and within it—and she reaches into all things and gives life to the entire world. Orpheus praises this life-giving goddess as being equal to the Creator; by connecting and joining her with him, Orpheus makes her the one mother of all the things for which Jupiter <note>Zeus</note> is the father. But Plato calls her the Mixing Bowl, as she is the fountain of the life of the soul. For this Mixing Bowl receives the creative energy of the "father of souls," and through this, the form of the soul receives its unique identity. This is why this form is called a "mixture." Jupiter indeed contains within himself a "royal soul," as Socrates says in the *Philebus* <note>A Platonic dialogue concerning the nature of pleasure and the good</note>, but he also contains this fountain <note>Hera</note> who works with him in the production of the order of the soul.

# BOOK V. THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO

The non-Greek sages <note>original: "Barbarians"; here referring to the Chaldean oracles and their practitioners.</note> call this life-giving cause the "source-soul" <note>original: "fontal soul"</note>. It is revealed alongside source-virtue <note>This refers to Vesta/Hestia.</note> from the inner depths of the great life-giving Goddess <note>Rhea</note>, who contains the fountains of all life—the divine, the angelic, the demonic, and the soul-based <note>original: "psychical"</note>. The Greek theologian <note>Referring to Orpheus</note> names this life-giving cause Juno <note>Hera</note>. She appears alongside Vesta from the mighty Rhea, who holds all life-giving powers within herself and eventually brings forth Nature itself. However, he connects Juno with the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> as a mother with a father. He depicts her as the source of all "Titanic division"—the process by which souls are divided into individual portions and separated. Plato, however, focuses on the Mixing Bowl <note>original: "Crater"</note>, the mixture, and the portions themselves, because the Bowl is the cause of that division. Therefore, Plato does not describe the division until he has sown the various types <note>original: "genera"</note> into the Mixing Bowl.

In short, based on these observations, we say it is clear that the Mixing Bowl is distinct from the Creator. In every case, the one who mixes, the bowl itself, and the ingredients being mixed are distinct from one another. It is also clear that the Mixing Bowl is different from the Creator because it is "soul-generating" <note>original: "psychogonic"</note>. This Bowl is not used in the production of pure Intellect or the construction of physical bodies; it is only used to give existence to souls. This is because a "mixture" is suited to souls, as they possess a middle nature <note>Souls exist between the eternal world of forms and the temporary world of matter.</note>. 

If the Mixing Bowl is soul-generating, it is undoubtedly the specific <note>original: *idios*</note> cause of souls. If it is on the same level <note>original: "co-ordinate"</note> as the Creator—so that it does not lack anything that comes after it, nor does it have anything more universal than itself—then it must be the cause of all the same things the Creator causes. If the Creator is an intellectual God and the best of causes, then the Mixing Bowl must also be intellectual. If the Creator is a "source-head" <note>original: "fontal"</note>, then the Bowl is also a source-head. And is it even necessary to mention that the non-Greek sages also call the specific causes <note>original: *aitias*</note> of individual souls "source-bowls"? 

Therefore, this Mixing Bowl is a source-bowl, since it is the cause of souls specifically as souls, rather than the cause of all life in general (for it is not the cause of purely intellectual or purely physical life). Elsewhere, Plato calls the soul itself the "fountain of wisdom" <note>original: "prudence"</note>, and in the *Phaedrus*, he calls it the "fountain and principle of motion." Therefore, according to Plato, we should definitely call the first soul a "source" and the Mixing Bowl a "source," provided there is a Mixing Bowl established alongside the Creator of the universe; since other "Bowls" are also described by Orpheus—

² For the Greek word meaning "particular" (*idion*) here, it is necessary to read "specifically" (*idios*).
³ The word "causes" (*aitias*) is omitted here in the original Greek.

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V. OF THE TIMAEUS]

...and Plato. For Plato, in the *Philebus*, mentions two Mixing Bowls <note>original: "Craters"; the Mixing Bowl is a symbolic vessel where the ingredients of the soul are blended.</note>: one belonging to **Vulcan**, and the other to **Dionysus** <note>original: "Dionysiacal"</note>. And **Orpheus** certainly knew of the Mixing Bowl of Bacchus <note>Another name for Dionysus.</note>, but he also establishes many others around the solar table. Regarding **Homer**, does he not represent **Hebe** as pouring out wine, and **Vulcan** drinking from a bowl and distributing nectar to all the Gods? These matters, however, require a much more extensive discussion. But what has been said will be sufficient for our present purpose, since in another work, we shall investigate a more complete development of each particular detail, if it pleases the Gods.

Someone, however, may doubt why Plato, when generating the soul of the universe, makes no mention of the Mixing Bowl, but only of the "mixture and commixture"; yet, in the generation of individual souls <note>original: "partial souls"; these are souls like those of humans or animals, rather than the single soul that animates the entire cosmos.</note>, he mentions it and reminds us of the mixture used for the soul of the universe? 

In answer to this, it must be said first that divine souls, in their progression, remain within the Mixing Bowl and do not depart from their fountain. Individual souls, however, are separated from it and frequently proceed out of it by leaning toward physical birth <note>original: "verging to generation"</note>. In the case of the universal soul, because it is so powerfully united with its source, Plato does not separate the Mixing Bowl from the mixture itself. Hence, some people mistakenly believe that the soul of the universe is the "first soul," and others call it **Juno** <note>Hera</note>, because they are unable to distinguish it from its own source. But in the case of these individual souls—since they are separated from the Mixing Bowl—Plato distinguishes the cause (the Mixing Bowl) from the things that come after it. 

Secondly, it must be said that the entire order of the soul is constituted by both the "Mingler" <note>The Creator or Demiurgus.</note> and the Mixing Bowl. But since one part of this order remains stable while the other proceeds outward—and one part rejoices in union while the other prefers division—the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> is responsible for the former to a greater degree than the Mixing Bowl is. The latter part (individual souls), being more material, is more closely allied to the productive <note>original: "prolific"</note> cause—that is, the Mixing Bowl. For this reason, in the case of the universal soul, everything is attributed to the Creator; but in the generation of individual souls, the Mixing Bowl is specifically mentioned. 

The myths of the Greeks also assert similar things. For they say that **Juno** is the cause of "insanity" <note>In a Neoplatonic sense, this refers to the soul's "frenzy" or movement into the material world.</note>, but **Jupiter** <note>Zeus</note> is the cause of temperance; and that Juno is the cause of the labors involved in physical birth, while Jupiter is the cause of rising above it. For Juno excites all things to progress, multiplies them, and causes them to be fruitful through her light. And that is enough to answer that doubt.

But I think it is right that the divine **Iamblichus** should look to these words of Plato and understand from them that Plato is constituting the soul of the world—and not the "super-celestial" soul—from the mixture of the middle types <note>original: "middle genera"</note>. For how, since his design was to build the universe, could he appropriately mention the soul that exists beyond the world? Especially since when he mentions Time (which is assigned a rank beyond the physical world), he organizes it together with the universe at the same time? For he says that...

# BOOK V. THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO

Time was created together with the heavens. And so much for this warning. But whether Plato knew, or did not know, that there are super-mundane <note>original: "supermundane"; refers to souls that exist beyond or above the physical universe.</note> souls is a matter to be investigated. It is a worthy inquiry, since he nowhere clearly states that there is a soul of this kind. To those who do not admit that there are super-mundane souls, it must be said that it is necessary for such souls to exist. These souls would be imparticipable <note>original: "im-participle"; in Neoplatonism, this describes a primary principle that acts on lower things without being "divided" or fully immersed in them.</note>, yet they understand things "transitively" <note>meaning they process thoughts in a sequence rather than all at once like a pure intellect.</note>; in this way, they differ from pure intellect. They also intellectually perceive more than one thing at a time, and in this, they transcend mundane <note>original: "mundane"; souls belonging to the physical world (the cosmos).</note> souls. For the progression of consciousness does not jump all at once from understanding everything simultaneously to the intellectual perception of only one thing at a time. Instead, it moves through the perception of more than one thing, yet not all things at once. It follows, therefore, that those who—for these reasons—admit that there are souls prior to the world should show how these souls are intermediaries <note>original: "media"</note> between the indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> and divisible essence. If they are divisible, what does this divisibility consist of? And if they are distributed into parts and fashioned similarly to cosmic souls, by what mechanism are they "prior" to them, since they would not differ at all in their fundamental reality <note>original: "hypostasis"</note>?

If it is also necessary that I should pay some attention to my own oracle <note>Proclus likely refers to the *Chaldean Oracles*, a text he considered divinely inspired.</note>, I would say that each of these super-mundane souls possesses an intellectual nature, which it receives from the indivisible reality above it. For that super-mundane intellect is the primary thing that can be participated in. Each soul also has a divisible nature—not in a simple sense, but insofar as the multitude of worldly natures is suspended from them <note>Lower levels of reality were thought to "hang" or depend upon higher ones.</note>. Hence, they are more indivisible than divisible, just as, on the contrary, the lowest souls are more divisible than indivisible, because divisibility—and not indivisibility—is the defining characteristic of their essence.

Therefore, each of these characteristics belongs to the souls that exist between the super-mundane and the lowest souls. Indivisibility is peculiar to them because a specific intellect is established above each of them; and divisibility is also present because a specific body is suspended from each. And as there are so many differences in the range <note>original: "latitude"</note> of souls, these differences cause the soul either not¹ always to remain on high, or to remain and be super-mundane, or to remain and be cosmic. 

By conceiving of the soul which ranks as a middle-ground between these to be this kind of thing, we will not wonder if souls were created equal in their division <note>original: "section"</note>, yet some of them have their boundaries limited to surfaces <note>original: "superficies"</note>, while others extend as far as solids. This extension makes the latter cosmic and causes them to enter into bodies, while it preserves the former prior to the world and without any contact with a body. Perhaps, too, some of them proceed only as far as linear boundaries, while others reach as far as surfaces. Hence, some of them are solely super-mundane, while others are intermediaries...

¹ The word "Or" is omitted here in the original.

He explains that these souls differ in their "latitude" or range, with some remaining above the world and others descending into it.</summary>

# PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS [BOOK V.]

...between super-mundane <note>original: "supermundane"; refers to souls that exist above or beyond the physical universe.</note> and mundane <note>original: "mundane"; refers to souls belonging to the physical world.</note> souls, just as surfaces <note>original: "superficies"</note> are intermediaries <note>original: "media"</note> between linear boundaries and solid bodies.

Moreover, it is not at all surprising that the harmony of these higher souls should be different from the three types of musical modulations found in physical things. For it is not necessary that there should be only three harmonies; rather, it is only this number of them that can be perceived in sounds that the human senses can measure. It is not impossible, however, for there to be certain harmonies more excellent than these, since these three types are not identified by logic alone, but through experience and sensory perception. We may also admit that these harmonies exist in super-mundane souls by inserting two intermediaries as far as the linear boundaries, and as far as the surfaces, in the first double <note>original: "duple"; the ratio 2:1.</note> and triple <note>ratio 3:1</note> intervals alone, or in the intervals that follow, and by producing two circles in these. *Here* <note>meaning in the physical world.</note> likewise, the internal circles are cut only in half, because there are two intervals; but *there* <note>in the super-mundane realm.</note>, they are cut into three parts. For there are that many intervals among the five boundaries. Hence *here*, one and three are generated, but *there* one and five, just as Plato, in describing mundane souls, makes one and seven. Therefore, in all things, it is possible for super-mundane souls to differ from mundane souls, both according to the intermediary and the number of circles. 

The ratios described by Plato also have a common quality that extends to every kind of soul essence. They elevate us from the soul-generation <note>original: "psychogony"</note> which proceeds into solid numbers <note>representing 3D reality</note>, to that which is simpler and proceeds only as far as surfaces <note>2D</note>, and from there to that which proceeds only as far as lines <note>1D</note>. They also produce three types of soul-generation which correspond with the three types of souls. For the progression from an essence that is perfectly indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> into one that is distributed according to all numbers does not happen without an intermediary; here also, as in all other things, the progression happens through middle stages. 

If this is the case, it is not at all wonderful that partial souls <note>individual souls, such as those of humans</note>—in which the divisible nature exists directly, but the indivisible nature exists only through other intermediaries that are elevated above them toward pure intellects—should cause the divisions to become more numerous within the divisible nature, more so than with the indivisible nature. I mean, for instance, that the 9:8 ratios <note>original: "sesquioctaves"</note> should be divided with the apotomes <note>original: "apotomæ"; a musical interval in the Pythagorean tuning system.</note> and the limmas <note>original: "leimmas"; the "remainder" interval in Pythagorean tuning.</note>, and that this same diatonic scale <note>original: "diatonic genus"</note> should be in them, with two intervals that define the Fourth <note>original: "diatessaron"</note> and the Fifth <note>original: "diapente"</note>, the same ratios being preserved in the extremes. So, in these souls also, the soul-generating ratios take place, but with a more abundant difference. For among the middle types, when "Essence" predominates, it creates a divine soul; when "Sameness" predominates, it creates a daemonic <note>original: "dæmoniacal"; referring to *daemons*, spirits that act as intermediaries between gods and mortals.</note> soul; and when "Difference" predominates, it creates a partial soul. Because these qualities predominate in different ways, many divine, many daemonic, and many partial souls are formed. Plato also indicates this when he says that the Demiurge <note>the Divine Craftsman or Creator.</note>, taking the second and third gradations of the mixture, gave...

<summary>Proclus explains the geometric and harmonic differences between divine, daemonic, and individual souls, arguing that soul-generation follows mathematical ratios that become more complex as they descend toward the physical world.</summary>
