<meta>This page continues Proclus’s detailed analysis of the nature of the soul. He provides a formal definition of the soul as a bridge between the eternal realm and the physical world of change, and defends the existence of individual souls for celestial bodies and lesser gods.</meta>

# BOOK V.] TIMAEUS OF PLATO.

Giving existence <note>original: "subsistence"</note> to individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls. For by assuming that these souls contain something similar to the universal soul, we will be able to determine their differences in relation to all the intermediate and primary souls. We can also provide the following common definition for all of them:

The soul is a fundamental substance <note>original: "essence"</note> which acts as a bridge between truly-existing reality <note>original: "essence"</note> and the world of physical change <term>original: "generation"; the realm of birth, death, and becoming.</term>. It is composed of the intermediate categories, divided according to essential numbers, and bound together by all the mathematical ratios <note>original: "middles"</note>. It is harmonized according to musical scales <note>original: "diatonically harmonized"</note>, living both a single and a dual life, and possesses the capacity for knowledge <note>original: "gnostic"</note> in both a single and dual manner. 

By adding specific characteristics to this definition, we can identify the specific qualities <note>original: "proper numbers"</note> of divine, dæmoniacal <note>original: "dæmoniacal"; here referring to "daimons," spirits intermediate between gods and humans, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense.</note>, or individual souls based on the fundamental nature <term>original: "hypostasis"</term> of each. 

Furthermore, we will be far from saying that the soul is the **actualization** <note>original: "entelecheia"; Aristotle’s term for the "perfection" or "actualization" of a body’s potential.</note> of the body, or of a physical organ that has the potential for life. This Aristotelian definition fails on two counts: it defines the soul only by its relationship to something else (the body) without saying what the soul is in itself, and it does not cover every kind of soul. For divine souls are not the souls of organic, physical bodies. This definition also fails to avoid circular reasoning. For that which "has the potential for life" already implies it has a soul in potentiality. All these problems are avoided by the definition we provided above. Our definition is a true definition because it captures what is common to all types of souls, explains its nature as an intermediate substance, and does not use the thing being defined as part of the definition itself. We have spoken at length on this to fully express the "birth-pains" <note>original: "parturitions"; a Platonic metaphor for the labor of bringing forth intellectual ideas.</note> of our own soul, even though Plato might not be speaking specifically about the soul that exists beyond the physical world <note>original: "super-mundane soul"</note> here.

But if someone should wonder why Plato does not mention other types of souls—the divine and the dæmoniacal—the answer is that Plato assumes the same basic mixture for these as well. Although dæmoniacal souls differ from divine souls, he views the entire "pure" category of souls as one group when compared to the souls involved in physical creation <term>original: "genesiurgic"</term>. At the same time, by mentioning the souls at the extreme ends of the spectrum and stating that they originate from the **Mixing Bowl** <note>original: "Crater"; the symbolic vessel in the *Timaeus* where the Demiurge mixes the ingredients of the soul.</note>, he shows that the form of all intermediate souls comes from there as well. 

By "extremes," I mean the Soul of the Universe and individual human souls. That Plato assigns specific souls to the stars and to the gods who dwell below the moon <note>original: "sublunary Gods"</note> is clear from what he says in the *Laws*. There, he states that we do not see the soul itself, but only the body it inhabits, and he asks how the soul moves that body. It is also clear from what he previously said in this dialogue, where he calls the stars "divine animals." If they are animals, where does their divine nature and their specific motion come from? If someone were to argue that a divine animal does not differ in its individual life from the lowliest animals on earth, it would mean it only receives its "actualization" <note>original: "entelecheia"</note> from the universe as a whole. Should we not, then, grant individual souls to those gods below the moon, who are the offspring of...

<summary>Proclus provides a formal Platonic definition of the soul as a bridge between the eternal and physical worlds, rejecting Aristotle's definition of the soul as the body's actualization. He argues that all divine and intermediate beings, like stars and sublunary gods, possess their own distinct souls derived from the same divine source.</summary>

# BOOK V.] COMMENTARY ON THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO.

What then shall we say of Heaven and Earth, and of Ocean and Tethys? In this case, how will they still be considered Gods? They must either be more excellent than souls, or they must possess souls. If they are cosmic <note>original: "mundane"</note> Gods, then divine souls must be dependent on them. The same reasoning applies to spirits <term>original: "dæmons"; in Neoplatonism, these are intermediary beings between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense.</term>. 

If, however, as we have said, Plato does not mention these here, it is not surprising. The way these beings exist <note>original: "mode of subsistence"</note> is not the same as that of individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls. For all divine souls, it is common to be unchanging, stable, and firmly rooted in the intellectual realm <note>original: "intelligibles"</note>. However, the tendency toward the physical world of change <note>original: "realms of generation"</note>, the "audacity," and the "loss of wings" <note>A reference to the *Phaedrus*, where Plato describes the soul losing its metaphorical wings and falling into a body.</note> begin with the individual souls that are now being produced.

We should also ask: how do divine, spirit-like <note>original: "dæmoniacal"</note>, and individual souls differ from the cosmic soul according to the soul-generating <note>original: "psychogonic"</note> diagram? For it is impossible for secondary souls <note>original: "secondary souls"; The original Greek footnote notes a grammatical correction: instead of *tais deuterais* (to the secondary ones), it should read *tas deuteras* (the secondary ones).</note> to consist of exactly the same things as those that came before them. In response to this, we must say that the same mathematical ratios exist in all of them. Plato mentions that these same ratios exist in individual souls: for instance, the 9:8, 4:3, and 3:2 ratios <term>original: "sesquioctaves, sesquitertian, and sesquialter ratios"; these are the fundamental musical intervals—the whole tone, the perfect fourth, and the perfect fifth—used to construct the harmony of the soul.</term> 

However, the specific numbers or boundaries <note>original: "terms"</note> which contain these ratios are different. In the soul-generating diagram of the cosmic soul, the boundaries used are primary ratios. Therefore, nothing prevents there being double ratios in divine souls, or an increase in these ratios in the souls of spirits in another manner. This is because the further existence progresses, the more variety and quantity <note>original: "multitude"</note> increases.

There must, therefore, be a difference either in the specific numbers used or in the ratios themselves. But a difference in ratios is impossible, because as we have already noted, Plato mentions these same ratios existing in individual souls. Hence, we must assume the difference lies in the specific numbers. Just as individual souls differ from higher souls in their numbers, they also differ in how certain ratios are divided. Thus, the ratios are common to all, but the specific numbers are different. 

Being unified and exempt from being split into parts will be a common trait of all spirit-level <note>original: "dæmoniacal"</note> souls. However, the increase in the number of ratios in individual souls causes them to be more divisible than spirits, and leads them to descend into the body instead of remaining in the higher realms. Such are the conclusions of my investigation <note>original: "oracle"</note> into these details.

What, however, is the meaning of the words, “*mingling he tempered*”? Shall we say that in those levels of life, unity is arranged in a way that is more ancient and venerable than division? And how could we not assert this? For "mixture" occurs in things that are divided, and separation follows afterward.

<summary>Proclus argues that while all souls share the same harmonic ratios, individual souls are distinguished by having a greater number of mathematical "terms," making them more divisible and prone to descending into the material world. He concludes that for higher beings, unity and "mixture" take precedence over the division into parts.</summary>

to mixture." <gloss>¹</gloss> In the case of individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls, on the contrary, Plato gives priority <note>original: "precedaneous order"</note> to the act of mingling. For he says, "*mingling them, he poured them out*"; he says this because in these souls, division is more prevalent. And Socrates says in the *Phaedrus* that the horses and charioteers <note>In Plato's allegory of the soul in the "Phaedrus," the charioteer represents reason, while the two horses represent the spirited and appetitive aspects of the soul.</note> of other souls are mixed. Likewise, the expression *he poured out* signifies a downward progression and a limitless <note>original: "indefinite"</note> <gloss>²</gloss> outpouring. 

But if you understand the term *pouring out* as if it referred to liquid substances, you might see that this also applies to the soul. This is because moisture is a symbol of life. Therefore, both Plato and the Gods before him <note>This likely refers to the "Chaldean Oracles," a text Proclus and other Neoplatonists considered divine revelation.</note> call the soul a "drop" of total animation <note>original: "vivification"</note> at one time, and a "fountain" at another. 

Furthermore, in the phrase "*the remainder of the former things*," we must assume that "the former" refers to the intermediate classes <note>original: "middle genera"</note> of beings. Plato cannot be referring to the original *mixture* used for the world-soul, because that entire mixture was used up in the creation, division into parts, and harmonization of the soul of the universe, as he states there. 

Among these intermediate classes, however, it is clear that some natures are supreme and intellectual, others are middle-ranking, and others are last. Analogy shows that some are primary, some are in the middle, and others exist at the very end. Since the extremes between which these middle elements exist are different, it follows that the middle elements must also differ proportionally. This is why we previously noted that the indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> part in each soul is one thing, and the part that is divisible throughout bodies is another—just as different bodies are attached to different souls. 

Therefore, because the extremes are different, the intermediate beings will necessarily be different as well. Using the elements that rank as the highest, the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> constructs divine souls; using the middle elements, he constructs spirit-like <note>original: "dæmoniacal"</note> souls; and using those that rank last, he constructs individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls. 

These last ones are now called "*the remainder of the former*" because in a certain respect they are similar to the others, but they are subordinate to them. A "remainder" is entirely similar to the whole of which it is a part, yet it is inferior to that which is more perfect and has priority. Therefore, we should accept both the views of those who say these individual souls are the remains of the intermediate classes, and the views of the divine Iamblichus. Iamblichus grants a superior excellence <note>original: "exempt transcendency"</note> to the classes that complete the divine souls, while also maintaining the similarities and variety of all the intermediate classes.

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.]

"**no longer pure and incorruptible in the same way, or to the same degree, but belonged to the second and third ranks.**"

Through these words, <term>Timaeus</term> <note>The speaker in Plato’s dialogue who describes the creation of the universe.</note> indicates the similarity of individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls to those that are universal <note>original: "total"</note>, as well as their lower status and different levels of development. He does not only describe their differences and their connection based on the primary and secondary <term>demiurgic energy</term> <note>The creative power of the Demiurge, the divine craftsman of the world.</note>. Nor does he only distinguish them by their union with or separation from the <term>Crater of life</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, the "Crater" (mixing bowl) is where the Demiurge mixes the ingredients of souls.</note>, or by the presence or lack of certain essential qualities. Instead, he also explains it through the method of their mixture, which is both similar and yet not the same. 

For neither the blending of the essential qualities nor the purity of the element of "Difference" is identical. In individual souls, "Difference" <note>In the "Timaeus," souls are made of "Sameness," "Difference," and "Essence." Individual souls have more "Difference," making them more prone to change.</note> is more prominent. This is why in these souls, "one of the horses is good, but the other is bad"; they consist of opposites—as stated in the <term>Phaedrus</term> <note>Plato’s dialogue where he uses the allegory of a charioteer (reason) and two horses (spirit and appetite) to describe the soul.</note>—because the principle of diversity prevails. 

Therefore, he shows that in a certain way they are the same, yet they also possess the unique traits of their specific composition. The total mixtures are no longer pure and incorruptible in the same way or to the same degree; they belong to the second and third ranks because they involve a loss of status and a specific hierarchical ordering. 

What, then, are the natures he calls "pure and incorruptible"? He does not mean they are simply incapable of being affected by outside forces <note>original: "impassive"</note>. It would be a small thing if divine souls differed from individual souls only in that one regard. This state of being affected by emotions and the physical world <note>original: "passivity"</note> is the very last thing to occur. It happens only after the soul flees from true reality, after its downward urge and inclination, and after the shedding <note>original: "defluxion"</note> of its wings, as <term>Socrates</term> says in the *Phaedrus*. 

It is better, therefore, to say that "pure and incorruptible" signifies the unchanging, the unbending, the inflexible, and the complete and undefiled form of essence. This essence is never turned toward lower <note>original: "secondary"</note> things, never undergoes change, never suffers a loss of life, is established far from all mortality, and is exempt from the laws of <term>Fate</term>. These qualities are common to every type of soul that always stays above <term>generation</term> <note>The physical realm of birth, death, and change.</note>. 

The opposites of these qualities belong to souls that are capable of descending into the world of physical birth, of changing their life from <term>intellection</term> <note>Pure intellectual contemplation.</note> to physical action, of becoming subject to the rule of Fate at certain times, and of being mixed with mortal affairs. Therefore, the "immovable" quality is not present in these souls in the same way, since they sometimes enter the world of change. Even when that quality is present, it is not there in the same manner. For a soul that is always engaged in intellectual thought is more excellent than one that sometimes leaves its proper intellectual activity.

Since, however, there is also an arrangement or order within these souls, and some

Some of them are undefiled, being familiar with the realm of physical change <note>original: "generation"; the world of birth, death, and material existence</note> and departing <note>The original text suggests a correction from *uphistamenai* (subsisting) to *aphistamenai* (departing).</note> from their own divine order for only a short time. Others, however, are entangled in all sorts of "flowers" <note>Metaphorically, the varied distractions or attachments of the material world.</note> and wander for very extended periods. Plato also indicates the difference between these by saying, "*that they were of the second and third order.*" For souls that descend and are defiled by vice are far removed from those that always remain on high and are without sin. 

The intermediaries between these are those souls that indeed descend, yet are not defiled by vice. The opposite—to be defiled by vice and yet remain on high—is not possible. For evil does not exist among the gods, but only in the mortal realm and in material things. 

Again, from what has been said, it appears that the first class <note>original: "genus"</note> of souls is divine. Everywhere that which is capable of receiving the divine has a ruling and leading order—in essences, in intellects, in souls, and in bodies. 

The second class of souls is that which is always connected to the gods; through this class, the souls which sometimes depart may be called back to the gods. 

The third class is that which indeed descends into the physical world, but descends with purity. It exchanges a more divine life for a lower one, but remains free from vice and passions. <note>This is the "heroic" class of souls. They descend into mortality partly for the benevolent purpose of leading the fourth class back to the spiritual world, and partly to satisfy the law of Fate, which requires them to descend at set times.</note> This class exists in continuity with the souls that always remain on high and are always undefiled. 

The fourth and last class is that which wanders extensively, descending as far as <term>Tartarus</term> <note>In Greek mythology and Platonic thought, a deep abyss used as a dungeon of torment or a place for the purification of souls.</note> before being raised up again from there. It develops all kinds of different lives, adopts various behaviors, and experiences different passions at different times. It assumes various forms of animals—the <term>daemonic</term> <note>original: "dæmoniacal"; referring to intermediate spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense.</note>, the human, and the irrational. Yet, at the same time, it is governed by Justice. It returns from earth to heaven and is led in a circle from matter back to intellect, according to the orderly cycles of the universe. 

Therefore, the words, "*no longer pure and incorruptible in the same way, or to the same degree,*" signify that individual souls are incorruptible in one respect—namely, in their essential nature alone. However, in another respect, they are not incorruptible; that is, in their activities <note>original: "energies"</note>, they are filled with all sorts of fated outcomes and are carried along <note>The original text suggests a correction from *emphairomenas* to *empheromenas* (carried along).</note> with flowing and mortal beings. They do not possess these activities always in the same manner or with undefiled purity. Instead, they experience them sometimes to a greater and sometimes to a lesser degree, as there is a vast inequality in souls.

<summary>Proclus describes a four-tier hierarchy of souls, ranging from divine souls that never sin to "wandering" souls that descend into physical forms and Tartarus to undergo purification and eventual return.</summary>

...in relation to their habit of descending to mortal nature, through which they are deprived of purity and the incorruptibility of life.

> “But having established the universe, he divided souls equal in number to the stars, and distributed each one to each star.”

Every order of souls depends on these two sources: the creative <note>original: "demiurgic"; relating to the Demiurge or divine craftsman</note> and the life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note>. The first, middle, and final parts of this hierarchy proceed from these sources and are defined by these gods. However, since within this hierarchy some souls are universal <note>original: "total"</note> while others are individual <note>original: "partial"</note>, and some do not leave their original principles while others proceed as far as descending into matter, and some act as leaders while others act as followers, the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> placed the former over the latter. He made the individual souls subject to the universal ones, distributed the multitude of souls according to their kinds <note>original: "genera"</note> under their presiding gods, and organized different souls into groups <note>original: "herds"</note> under the government of various leaders. 

And now, having established the divine souls, he makes the individual souls their attendants. Shortly after, when he brings them forth, he also arranges their "vehicles" <note>original: "vehicle"; in Neoplatonism, this refers to the "astral body" or a subtle, celestial carrier that allows the soul to interact with the physical world</note> under the divine celestial movements, aligning parts with their wholes. For just as one soul relates to another, so one vehicle relates to another, and both sets relate to each other according to a geometric arrangement. 

But more on this later. For now, before he has even made them part of the physical world <note>original: "mundane"</note>, he distributes them among the starry gods. The word *stars* here refers to the souls of the celestial bodies. Therefore, he divides the multitude of souls so they are equal in number to the divine souls and distributes each into its own star once he has, as Plato says, "established the universe." 

Plato, however, does not say that he made a single mixture as he did for the Soul of the World—where he made it one from three components: Being <note>original: "essence"</note>, Sameness <note>original: "same"</note>, and Difference <note>original: "different"</note>—and then divided souls from this by taking parts away <note>original: "ablation"</note>. He does not immediately jump from the mixture to distributing these souls among the divine souls while skipping over the division into numbers, harmonic ratios, and the teaching about the soul's vehicle. Instead, he includes all these things at once—the mixture, the division into parts, and the taking of a shape—in the phrase "having established the universe." From this process, all individual souls were distributed and organized. 

Thus, he formed the multitude of all these souls. The birth of each soul can be called a "formation" <note>original: "constitution"</note>, just as he claimed for the Soul of the World, because it is completed from many components. For he said then: “*Since the entire formation of the soul was carried out in accordance with the intention of its composing craftsman <note>original: "artificer"</note>.*” Therefore, having formed the entire multitude of souls, he divided—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how individual (partial) souls are distributed among the stars by the Creator (the Demiurge), exploring the meaning of "equal in number" and the hierarchy of beings surrounding each celestial god.</meta>

<page-num>387</page-num>
<header>BOOK V.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

...them equal in number to the stars, separating the former from each other, according to the peculiarities of the latter.

Will you therefore say that he distributed them equal in number, so that one individual soul <note>original: "partial soul"</note> is arranged under one of the stars, and that there are exactly as many souls as there are starry Gods? This might seem to be the case when he adds that each soul was distributed to each star. But how can we call this a Platonic teaching <note>original: "dogma"</note>, since Plato says shortly afterward that the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> scattered some souls into the earth, others into the sun, and others into the moon? These words suggest that he places a large number of souls in each star. 

Perhaps we should say that "equal in number" should not be looked at as a simple 1-to-1 count <note>original: "monadically"</note>, but according to a ratio or analogy? In mathematics, a group of ten (a decad) is analogous to a single unit (a monad); thirty is analogous to three (a triad); fifty is analogous to five (a pentad). In short, all numbers after ten are analogous to those within the first ten, and the second set is "equal in number" to the first in terms of their structure. This does not mean that five is equal in quantity to fifty, or three to thirty; rather, they are equal only by analogy. Just as the number three exists among single units, thirty exists among tens. 

Perhaps, then, "equal in number" should be understood this way regarding individual souls. Since each divine soul contains a certain appropriate number—which it holds beforehand and as a unified whole—this number, when expanded, defines the total number of individual souls arranged under it. The souls that are primarily attached to it are fewer in number but greater in power; those that are secondarily attached to it have less power but are greater in number. Each, however, develops in a way that is analogous to the leading soul. In the same way, the number four among tens, hundreds, and thousands is analogous to the very first "four." These points may be offered as an answer to this inquiry.

It may also be added that the "form" and character of the follower souls come from their leading Gods. This form is a number that defines the specific quality of their lives. As many leaders as there are, there are just as many forms of life following them—such as Saturnian, Jovian <note>relating to Jupiter</note>, Solar, or Lunar, and so on for the other Gods. This form, originating from on high, spreads all the way down to the last attendants and makes all of them similar to their leading God. 

For around every God, there are many smaller Gods; there are angelic orders that reveal divine light; there are spirits <note>original: "dæmons"; in Neoplatonism, these are intermediary beings between gods and humans, not necessarily evil</note> who travel with, guard, or attend the God; and there is the noble and magnificent army of heroes. These heroes suppress the disorder arising from matter, connect the divine carriers <note>original: "vehicles"; the subtle, celestial bodies of the gods</note>, and purify the individual carriers that revolve around them, making the lower ones like the higher. Finally, around every God, there is a choir of pure souls, shining with holiness, and a multitude of other...

...souls, sometimes raising the head of the charioteer to the intelligible realm <note>original: "the intelligible"; in Neoplatonism, this refers to the realm of pure forms and intellect beyond the physical world</note>, and at other times aligning themselves with the worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note> powers of the Gods. Among these souls, some are distributed¹ across one power of their leading God, while others are assigned to another. For this reason, among solar souls (those following the Sun), some depend on the healing <note>original: "Pæonian," referring to Apollo/the Sun as the healer</note> power, others on the prophetic, others on the creative <note>original: "demiurgic"</note>, and others on the God’s power to elevate. In other Gods as well, the souls that follow the same divinity do not all have the same rank. Instead, some are distributed² across different powers of that God, and others participate more closely or more distantly in that same power. However, all of them share equally³ in the general form of their God. For within the Gods themselves, unity comes before many-ness, and a single identity comes before the differences found in their separate powers. Therefore, through these points, it is clear how souls are "equal in number" to the stars.

However, it is necessary to mention the view of Acyllus⁴ on this subject. He suggests that individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls are equal in number to the souls of the stars not by being divided among them, but because they were created in a similar way. This means they consist of the same quantity of numbers that each starry soul consists of. This thinker interprets the "equality in number" of individual to universal souls as meaning that each individual soul is divided into the same number of parts as the starry soul it is arranged under and distributed by the Father <note>The "Father" refers to the Demiurge or Creator of the universe</note>. Consequently, the individual soul is similar to the universal soul. Thus, not every soul possesses a vast variety of different numbers; some have fewer and others have more, though the ratios in all of them remain the same. Plato does not define the specific numbers, but rather the ratios of the parts. We have already noted that nothing prevents individual souls from differing from those that come before them in the total quantity of their terms, and we have demonstrated how that difference works. So much for this particular point.

Now, the first distribution of individual souls among divine souls happens before they even enter the physical world <note>original: "become mundane"</note>. Because of both a heavenly <note>original: "supermundane"</note> and a worldly arrangement, parts are woven together with wholes. Thus, if in the temples found here on earth, there is a certain ritual "throning"⁵ <note>original: "establishment"</note> of those that—

When we are initiated into these mysteries, it provides us with an image of how the Creator <note>original: "demiurgic"</note> arranges individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls alongside universal <note>original: "total"</note> souls, and how they are distributed among their leaders. For divine souls themselves are distributed according to the powers of the universal soul of the universe. They proceed according to the many forms of power contained within it and are established there; some are placed in the orbit of the *Same* <note>In Platonic philosophy, the "Same" refers to the outermost, uniform rotation of the heavens</note> within this soul, while others are placed in the cycles of the orbit of the *Different* <note>The "Different" refers to the inner, varying orbits of the planets</note>. 

Furthermore, individual souls are arranged around these divine souls, distributing their own universal powers. They are raised up together with these divine souls to the intellectual realm <note>original: "the intelligible"</note>, filled by them with unchanging intelligence, and organized according to the numbers of their specific leaders. Therefore, just as these worldly divine souls ascend through the twelve Gods¹ to the realm beyond the heavens, individual souls also ascend to it through the divine souls. For they are united to them according to an arrangement that exists beyond the physical world, which Timaeus calls *distribution*. This process is carried out according to the divine law that sits beside Jupiter <note>the Roman name for Zeus, the king of the gods</note>, as described in Plato's *Gorgias*, and together with him, it organizes the more universal and more individual orders in the world. Hence, there is a single likeness shared by all individual souls and a distribution based on the kingdoms of the Gods. The Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> is the cause of both. These matters also pertain to souls in a manner that transcends the physical world. Thus, the differences between souls do not arise from temporary states or conditions, as some claim, but from their very essence. Their arrangement with different leaders and their distribution is essential to what they are. For whatever they possess from the one act of creation <note>original: "fabrication"</note>, they possess as part of their core nature.

Since individual souls are said to be distributed among the stars, it is evident that they hold the fourth rank below the soul of the universe. For with this universal soul, the souls of the celestial spheres and the souls of the sublunary <note>the region below the moon, typically the Earthly realm</note> spheres—which contain all the elements—exist. Beneath these are the stars and those more specific types of Gods² that are contained within the whole systems of all the previously mentioned orbits. And finally, beneath these are the individual souls. 

Hence, the soul of the universe is the only truly *universal* soul. The souls that are assigned to govern the celestial orbits are *universal-individual* <note>meaning they are broad in scope but specific to a sphere</note>. Those contained within these orbits are, conversely, *individual-universal*. And in the last place, individual souls have an *individual existence* alone. Plato, therefore, calls all the divine souls that are contained within their greater wholes—

For all of them possess definite, star-like vehicles; even Socrates compares individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls descending into physical birth <note>original: "leaping into generation"</note> to the stars, according to their vehicles. It would be illogical if individual souls were only distributed among what are properly called the stars, while the other Gods were not leaders of the groups of souls that exist in each element corresponding to them—namely, the aerial, aquatic, and terrestrial Gods, of whom he says that they become visible whenever they choose.¹ But as we have said, he gives them a common name from things obvious to everyone, because he does not neglect to observe that which is perceived by the senses <note>original: "sensible"</note>.²

<margin>41 E</margin>
> "And causing them to ascend as into a vehicle, he pointed out to them the nature of the universe,"

Therefore, those who say—such as the great Theodorus—that the "vehicle of the soul" is the "nature of the universe," speak in a way that does not match the facts or the words of Plato. For the nature of the universe is not the vehicle of an individual soul; it is enough for such a soul to govern its own individual nature correctly. Nor can we reconcile the phrase *he pointed out* with what follows in that interpretation. Furthermore, those who look not to the following phrase, but to the preceding one, and say that the "vehicle" signifies a literal star, do not speak in accordance with the nature of the thing. For where is the vehicle of an individual soul, which descends into physical birth, ever said to be an actual star? Even if you were speaking of a physical star, a star always remains in the high heavens. 

It seems that both of these thinkers were persuaded to adopt these opinions because the Creator did not first create the vehicle and then later cause the soul to ascend into it. However, they should have seen that because the vehicle is formed at the same time as the soul, it would be redundant to describe the Creator making the body first. To this, we may add what has been shown before: that the Creator produced bodies in conjunction with souls. Therefore, if it is necessary to follow both the reality of the matter and the doctrine of Plato, it must be said that the "nature" which is pointed out by the Creator is one thing; the star under which the soul is arranged is another (and this is incorporeal); and this vehicle which serves the souls is yet another. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul’s relationship with its "vehicle" (an ethereal or astral body) and how the Creator (Demiurge) organizes souls within the cosmic order, citing the authority of Iamblichus and the Chaldean Oracles.</meta>

It is also necessary to say that souls, by ascending into their vehicles, became citizens of the universe. They entered into and were arranged in relation to the whole world, and these souls were distributed along with the stars. They surveyed Nature and the entire worldly order, being themselves positioned above the nature of the world while still receiving their own specific worldly assignment. 

For in the first place, they were created; afterwards, they were distributed among the divine administrations; and finally, in the third place, they ascended into vehicles, surveyed Nature, and listened to the laws of Fate. From all of this, it is easy to perceive that, according to Plato, souls are superior to Fate according to their highest level of life. For that which the Father of all things gave to them is according to nature. Hence, as the *Chaldean Oracle* says: "By understanding the works of the Father, they fly from the shameless <note>original: *anaides*</note> wing of Fate. But they rest in God, drawing upon vigorous torches descending from the Father; and from these, the descending soul gathers heavenly <note>original: empyrean</note> fruits—the flower that nourishes the soul."

What, therefore, is the "vehicle" of the soul, and how does the Creator <note>original: Demiurgus</note> cause souls to ascend into it? It is necessary to understand that the great Iamblichus and his followers are accustomed to say that the composition of these soul-vehicles is generated from the entire ether, which possesses a life-giving <note>original: prolific</note> power. Divine bodies are neither diminished by this process, nor do they create these vehicles by simply piling matter together <note>original: co-acervation</note>. Instead, they proceed according to divine lives, giving form <note>original: *morphē*</note> to individual spirit-like <note>original: partial pneumatic</note> substances. 

However, it is necessary to understand something even more true: that the development of these vehicles proceeds from the works of the Creator. For the maker of every physical existence <note>original: hypostasis</note> constitutes these vehicles—the same maker who also prepares the seats for the Gods in the world <note>original: referring to Vulcan or Hephaestus, the divine blacksmith</note>. He receives souls that are sent from the realm of pure thought <note>original: the intelligible</note> into the world and gives different abodes to different souls. The Creator of the universe likewise constitutes them, and he is the first of all to do so. Hence, he now causes them to ascend into vehicles, clearly producing the vehicle himself. For this vehicle was not fashioned in what was previously described, but the Creator himself, having constituted it along with the "wholes" <note>the major components of the universe</note>, causes souls to ascend into it and imparts to them the principle of their own organs. For he is the Creator of all living beings and of the fullness <note>original: plenitudes</note> of the universe. Therefore, he not only produces souls, but he produces them together with their appropriate vehicles. On a survey of Plato's conception, we shall find that it is truly admirable and secret <note>original: arcane</note>, since he does not represent the Creator as fashioning these vehicles from the larger "wholes" that already existed, nor does he—

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.

...the vehicles of the planets and the **fixed** stars <note>original: *aplanon*</note>; but he says that the Demiurge <note>The "Demiurge" is the divine Craftsman or Creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy.</note> produced these, with the younger Gods contributing parts and causing the bodies to come together from these elements. This, therefore, is a clear argument that each of these vehicles is, *in a certain sense, self-constituted*, and not created by cutting away parts of other things; otherwise, it would be necessary for them to eventually be returned to the source from which they were taken. For everything that exists by being cut off from other things must necessarily be entirely restored to the whole, since the cutting away causes a reduction in the original whole. It is necessary for each of the great "wholes" of the universe to always remain complete; for this reason, every soul-vehicle of this kind is eternal, and the same vehicle is always joined to the same soul. For each is naturally designed to exist in this way, just as it was first created by the Demiurge.

How could we still consider the soul to be "mundane" <note>original: *mundane*—meaning belonging to the world or universe.</note> if we were to destroy its vehicle? And how could a soul be called mundane if nothing of it remained within the universe? For if <term>partial souls</term> <note>Individual human souls, as opposed to the "soul of the world" or the souls of gods.</note> were superior to a life lived in union with these vehicles, they would be even greater than the divine souls themselves. And if they were inferior to such a life, why would the Demiurge place them into these vehicles immediately upon their creation, as is described here? Likewise, how do souls use vehicles both in the afterlife <note>original: *Hades*</note> and in the heavens if these bodies are not permanently attached to them? It is clear that they do use them, based on what Socrates says in the *Phaedo* and the *Phaedrus*. In the first, he says that *souls entering into vehicles travel to <term>Acheron</term>* <note>A river in the underworld.</note>; and in the second, he says that *while the vehicles of the Gods are easily controlled and move in balance, the vehicles of other souls following the Gods move with difficulty and hardly [attain the vision of the place above the heavens]*.

This can also be proven through other arguments; we have clearly stated these points before, and they are now brought back to our memory.

From this, we can also see the difference between partial souls and divine souls. In divine souls, the Demiurge placed the bodies *within* the souls, so that the souls surround them on all sides. These divine souls do not turn their attention toward the physical things they rule, but instead use a single, unchanging <term>intellection</term> <note>original: *intellection*—the act of pure, divine thought or understanding.</note>. But in the case of individual souls, he causes the souls to enter into vehicles because they are prone to being frequently overcome by physical bodies and focusing their attention on the material world they govern <note>original: *dioikoumena*</note> when they become parts of the universe. In this way, their vehicles are subject to the laws of Fate and no longer live purely under the divine light of Providence. And so much for the vehicle of the soul.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "vehicle" of the soul—a subtle, celestial body—and explains how human souls relate to the higher "Intellect" and intermediate spirits known as daemons.</meta>

<page-num>393</page-num>

It is worth revisiting and carefully considering what has been frequently said: since the whole of our soul is a middle ground between an indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> essence and that essence which is divided among bodies, we clearly receive this latter, divisible essence from its vehicle. For a vehicle that is born with the soul <note>original: "connascent"</note> is attached to it, possessing its own appropriate form of life, just like the vehicles of divine and daemonic <note>original: "dæmoniacal"—referring to "daemons," which in Greek philosophy were intermediate spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> souls. This life is the "partial essence" for which the soul already holds the blueprint <note>original: "paradigm"</note>. Therefore, "opinion" is established in the soul as the model for sensory perception, while the power of deliberate choice serves as the model for the appetite <note>original: "orexis"</note> in its specific vehicle. It is through this appetite that the soul is moved from place to place and driven to perform various actions. These are the most immediate "partial" natures within the soul. Above these lies the soul's inner differentiation—the various divisions of its essence—which allow it to be distributed into parts while still possessing an indivisible core and remaining a whole. 

Since we are making these claims about how the soul is divided, we should ask: what is the indivisible essence that exists *above* our soul? This is a relevant question because every soul higher than ours has an Intellect <note>original: *νουν* (nous)—the highest form of reason or divine mind.</note> existing prior to it. However, individual <term>partial souls</term> <note>Individual human souls, as opposed to universal or divine souls.</note> do not each have a unique, essential Intellect directly above them. If they did, they would always remain in the higher realms like the superior souls do, because the Intellect would keep the soul anchored in the intelligible world by constantly sharing its light with it. We have discussed this more than once already, but we will now explain more clearly what we believe to be the truth and what the divine has revealed to our own intellect. 

Thus, we have often spoken about the nature of the "indivisible" within each individual soul—a truly difficult <note>original: "dubious"</note> subject—by directing our minds toward the divine. For the idea that every single soul has its own individual Intellect is simply not acceptable. Might we not say, then, that each of these partial souls is essentially attached to a specific daemon, and every daemon has its own daemonic Intellect above it? An individual soul, therefore, shares the same Intellect as the daemon to which it is attached; that Intellect serves as the indivisible essence preceding the soul. Consequently, the daemonic soul is the primary participant in this Intellect, while the individual souls beneath it participate only secondarily—which is precisely what makes them "partial" or limited. Each soul has its own unique, divisible nature, but it shares its indivisible nature with the daemons above it, for whom that indivisibility is a natural trait. This explains why daemons stay in the higher realms, while individual souls sometimes descend, scattering their essence among physical bodies because they are more suited to them. For if the "element of difference" <note>In Platonic thought, "Difference" is one of the five Great Kinds of being; here, it refers to the quality that allows for multiplicity, change, and the descent into the physical world.</note> is excessive in individual souls, it makes them unable to always...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how individual souls relate to the higher Intellect and the hierarchy of spirits (daemons), exploring the soul's position between the indivisible realm of pure thought and the divisible realm of the physical body.</meta>

<page-num>394</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.</header>

Because these souls act according to all their powers, it necessarily follows that they must be more familiar with the life that is divided among bodies and more remote from an indivisible essence. In this way, they preserve a proportional relationship between the two extremes. Similarly, the most divine souls, by being like the divine Intellect, are more exempt from fragmented natures and more closely united to the indivisible essences above them, from which they are naturally suspended <note>original Greek: *exērtēsthai*. The author notes it is necessary to read this as *exērēsthai*, meaning "set apart" or "exempt."</note>; they also establish an intellectual order within souls. It also appears that the intellect of each daemon <note>original: "dæmon"—in Greek philosophy, these are intermediate spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note>, being a single whole, is the intellect of the specific daemon that directly shares in it. However, it also contains the total number of souls underneath it and their intellectual models <note>original: "paradigms"—divine blueprints or patterns.</note>. <note>The original text notes that instead of "of it" (Greek: *autou*), we should read "of them" (Greek: *autōn*).</note> Therefore, each individual soul will have its own specific model—contained within this Intellect as an indivisible essence—and not simply the whole Intellect in the same way as the daemon who is the essential leader of these souls. 

We say, therefore, that the indivisible part of each individual soul above it can be more accurately defined as its "form." This form is contained within the single Intellect assigned to rule the daemonic hierarchy under which each individual soul is organized. Thus, both claims are true: that the Intellect of each soul alone is established among the eternal natures in the higher realms, and that each soul is a middle ground between the indivisible essence above it and the divisible nature that follows it. So much for these details.

But in what way does the Demiurge <note>The divine "Craftsman" or creator of the material world in Plato's philosophy.</note> point out the nature of the universe to these souls? Is it by turning them toward the world and preparing them to observe the rational principles <note>original: "reasons"—the *logoi* or organizing principles of the cosmos.</note> contained in nature? Doing this, however, would make the souls less excellent; it would turn them away from independent rational principles toward those that cannot be separated from physical, sensible things. On the contrary, the Demiurge raises souls toward the intelligible realm, turns them toward himself, separates them from matter, and fills them with divine powers and his own creative thoughts. Might we say, then, that because he holds the cause of nature within himself, he turns the souls toward himself? For anyone who points something out looks entirely at what he is indicating. But the Demiurge looks only at what is above him and at himself. Therefore, he sees the nature that he points out to the souls within himself. For he contains the unified principles of all things and has established within himself the powers capable of producing both nature and all other things. Just as he contains the blueprints for physical bodies in a non-physical way, he also understands nature in a way that transcends nature. These points are correctly stated. However, it is necessary to speak further...

In another way, he does not only place the Form <note>original: "idea"—referring to the Platonic Ideas or divine blueprints</note> within the Demiurge <note>The divine craftsman or creator of the material world in Plato's philosophy</note> in a philosophical sense, but also, as theologians teach, he views Nature primarily as it pre-exists intellectually within the life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note> deity. Being dependent upon that deity, Nature governs this visible world, makes material things similar to immaterial principles <note>original: "reasons"—from the Greek *logoi*, meaning the formative, rational patterns of reality</note>, and relates physical movements back to their original, primordial motions. 

However, it is also necessary to view Nature in a secondary way, according to the worldly <note>original: "mundane"—meaning belonging to the physical cosmos</note> order of the life-giving Goddess <note>In this Neoplatonic context, this likely refers to Rhea or Hecate, who was seen as the source of the world's soul and life</note>, consistent with what the Oracles <note>The Chaldean Oracles, a sacred text for later Platonists</note> say: *that immense Nature is suspended from the back of the Goddess.* From its primary existence in the life-giving deity, Nature proceeds into the demiurgic intellect. It is also necessary for souls to study the fountains and roots of Nature so they may recognize their own dignity and the entire chain from which they are suspended; by holding onto this, they may contemplate the universe. For by focusing their sight on Nature itself, they align themselves with Fate. 

Just as the Demiurge himself governs the universe by first understanding the model <note>original: "paradigm"</note> of Nature, he also desires that souls—by looking to the first intellectual cause of Nature—should rise to the heights and guide the whole world. This is the highest destiny <note>original: "allotment"</note> of souls. The Demiurge, therefore, points out to souls that source-like <note>original: "fontal"</note> Nature which pre-exists in the entire life-giving Goddess, according to that very oracle of the Gods delivered to their true initiates <note>original: "mystics"</note>. But since souls have second and third lives <note>Referring to the cycles of reincarnation or descent into lower states of being</note>, the Demiurge also gives them the principles or productive foundations for these.

<insert>41 E</insert>

->“He also announced to them the Laws of Fate.”<-

It is clear that this is the second speech of the Demiurge, reaching out once more to souls through words suited to their nature. The Demiurge's first speech was addressed directly to the lesser <note>original: "junior"—the gods created by the Demiurge to assist in the creation of mortal life</note> Gods, as "Gods of Gods." But this second speech shows that the Demiurge also fills these souls with divine principles <note>original: "words or reasons"</note>, though not as directly as he does the lesser Gods. 

The purpose of the first speech was to reveal the principles of providence, while the second reveals the laws of Fate. Having established this, we say—turning now to the subject at hand—that Fate must not be described merely as a limited <note>original: "partial"</note> nature, as some of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle</note> claim...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of Fate, distinguishing it from physical Nature and pure Intellect by critiquing earlier philosophical definitions from the Peripatetics and others.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.

...Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note>, such as Alexander [of Aphrodisias] assert it to be. For this [kind of] nature is weak <note>original: "imbecile"—meaning lacking inherent power or stability</note> and not eternal. But we assume beforehand, based on common understanding, that the power and dominion of Fate are immense and stable. Nor is Fate simply the order of the world's cycles <note>original: "mundane periods"</note>, as Aristotle claims, who calls any growth that deviates from order "beyond fate" <note>original: "preter-fatal"</note>, as if this order were established by Fate. In reality, the cause of order is one thing, but the order itself is another. 

Nor should we say that Fate is the soul in a state of disposition <note>original: "soul in habitude"—referring to the soul's relationship or orientation toward the material world</note>, as Theodorus asserts. For such a form of life is not a primary principle in the whole of reality <note>original: "wholes"</note>. Nor is it simply Nature, as Porphyry says. For many things that are supernatural and outside the domain of Nature are produced by Fate—such as nobility, fame, and wealth. For how could purely physical movements be the cause of these things? 

Nor is it the intellect of the universe, as Aristotle says again in a certain work (if the treatise *On the Universe* <note>original: "concerning the World"—referring to the *De Mundo*, a text then attributed to Aristotle</note> was actually written by him). For the intellect produces everything it creates all at once; it does not require a governing process that operates through time, cycles, or a continuous, well-ordered series. This, however, is the specific characteristic of Fate: a series of many causes, an organized order, and production through cycles <note>original: "periodical production"</note>. 

But if we must concisely define its entire nature, we should say that Fate is "Nature" in terms of its substance, but it is a Nature that has been deified and filled with divine, intellectual, and spiritual <note>original: "psychical"—relating to the Soul</note> illuminations. For the order of the Gods known as the *Moiregetae* <note>original: *tōn moirēgetōn kaloumenōn*—meaning "the ones called Leaders of the Fates"</note> and the higher classes of beings <note>original: "more excellent genera"—referring to angels, daemons, and heroes in the Neoplatonic hierarchy</note> culminate in Fate. For these beings impart powers from themselves into the single life of Fate; and the Demiurge <note>The divine craftsman or creator</note> of the universe <note>original: "wholes"</note> collects and unites all these gifts and all these divine fullnesses <note>original: "plenitudes"</note>, showing them to be a single power. For if visible physical bodies are filled with divine $^1$ powers, then Nature is deified with even greater priority. And if the entire visible world is a unity, then the whole essence of Fate is even more so a unity, with its structure fully composed of many different causes. 

Because Fate is suspended from the providence of the Gods and the goodness of the Demiurge, it is made into a unity and governed with righteousness by them. It is a rational principle <note>original: "reason"—meaning a formative, blueprint-like power (*logos*)</note> consisting of many rational principles, a single multiform power, a divine life, and the order of things that are arranged before it. $^2$ 

Thus, the ancients, observing this variety and the multifaceted nature of Fate, were led to different opinions about it. Some called it a God because it participates in divinity; others called it a spirit <note>original: "dæmon"—in the Greek sense of a mediating power, not an evil entity</note> because of its effective and multifaceted way of producing results; others called it Intellect because a certain share of intellect flows into it; and others called it "Order" because everything that is arranged is invisibly contained within it. But Plato alone [truly]...

# BOOK V.] THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

...surveyed the essence of it; for he indeed calls it Nature, but considers it dependent upon the Demiurgus <note>The "Demiurgus" is the divine Craftsman or Creator who fashions the universe in Plato's philosophy.</note>. For how else could the Demiurgus point out Nature unless he contained the principle of it within himself? Similarly, how could he announce the laws of Fate—after pointing out the nature of the universe—unless he established Nature as the single, connected container for these laws? 

In the *Statesman* <note>original: "Politicus"</note>, Plato explains even more clearly that the secondary life of the universe depends on Fate. This occurs after the one guiding spirit <note>original: "dæmon"</note> that governs the universe, and the many spirits attending him, separate themselves from it. Consequently, he removes their providential care from the world and leaves it only under the government of Fate. Although the world always possesses both providence and Fate, the philosophical myth separates them for the sake of explanation. For he says that Fate and innate <note>original: "connascent"—meaning born together with or inherent</note> desire revolve the world; just as the Chaldean Oracles say: 

> "Nature rules over the worlds and their works, and draws them downward, so that heaven may run an eternal course; and so that the other cycles of the sun, the moon, the seasons, night, and day may be completed." 

Thus, Plato also says that the second cycle of the world is revolved by Fate, but not the first, intellectual cycle. He almost explicitly asserts that he conceives this Fate—which immediately moves the perceptible <note>original: "sensible"—meaning that which can be perceived by the senses</note> world—to be dependent on the invisible providence of the Gods. Indeed, establishing that "Necessity" is the mother of the Fates, he has the world revolve on her knees, as he describes in the tenth book of the *Republic*. <note>The original text used a Greek word meaning "nourishes" (trephei), but Proclus clarifies it should be "revolves" (strephei).</note>

If it is necessary to state my opinion, Plato places these three causes of order in succession: **Adrastia**, **Necessity**, and **Fate**. The first is intellectual, the second is beyond the physical world <note>original: "supermundane"</note>, and the third belongs to the physical world <note>original: "mundane"</note>. *For the Demiurgus, as Orpheus says, was indeed nurtured by Adrastia, but he associates with Necessity and produces Fate.* 

Just as Adrastia encompasses the divine institutions <note>original: "thesmōn" (θεσμῶν). The source text mistakenly used "desmōn" (chains/bonds), but Proclus notes it should be "thesmōn" (divine laws).</note> and gathers together all kinds of laws, Fate also encompasses all the physical laws of the world. The Demiurgus now writes these laws into souls so that he may guide them along with the cosmic wholes <note>The "wholes" refer to the universal structures and celestial bodies of the cosmos.</note>, and may definitely assign to them what is appropriate according to the different lives they choose. *Because of this, a mistaken choice leads the soul to a dark and godless life, but a pious choice conducts it to heaven under the guidance of the cosmic wholes. This is because every choice is filled with the laws of Fate, and souls—as Plotinus says—betake themselves to the place assigned to them by the law they carry within themselves.* This is the unique quality of the Gods' providence: to guide the subjects of their care from within. And why should this be surprising, since Nature, by inserting material and...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how Fate and Providence govern souls. ## BOOK V. PROCLUS ON THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO

If physical powers in material objects move them—earth through gravity and fire through lightness <note>original: "levity"</note>—how much more do the Gods move souls through the powers they have sown within them? Therefore, if they lead souls according to the laws of Fate, these laws reside within the souls themselves. These laws pre-exist intellectually in the Demiurge <note>The divine Craftsman or Creator in Plato's philosophy.</note>, for with him the divine law is established. However, they also exist in divine souls, because according to these laws, they are the leaders of the universe. Finally, they are shared by individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls; for through these laws, as souls move themselves, they lead themselves to an appropriate place. 

Through their own deliberate choice, souls may fail or act rightly; but through law, they assign to themselves an order suited to their past conduct. When, therefore, souls become mundane <note>Belonging to the physical, worldly realm.</note>, they observe the power and rule of Fate hanging from above, originating in providence, and they receive the laws of Destiny. For the Demiurge pointed out Nature to them as something different from themselves, but he announced the laws of Fate to them as if writing them into their very essence. For the Demiurge’s creative words <note>original: "logoi"</note> proceed through the essence itself of souls. Just as he placed his words into the younger gods <note>The secondary deities who assist in the creation of the mortal world.</note> prior to this, he now places these laws in individual souls.

<margin>41E</margin>
> “And he showed them that the first birth <note>original: "generation"</note>, arranged in an orderly manner for all of them, would be one and the same, so that no particular soul would be assigned a smaller share of life than another.”

Souls are essentially supernatural, beyond the world, and beyond Fate, because their primary existence is separate from this world. However, regarding their vehicles <note>The subtle or astral bodies that carry the soul into the physical world.</note> and the assigned domains they were destined to govern, they were created as worldly beings by the Demiurge and received this order. 

Hence, after assigning their vehicles to them, the Demiurge announces the laws of Fate, by which they are assigned the government of bodies. It is as if someone—desiring <note>The original Greek text uses *apheimenos* (neglectful), but it should likely be *ephiemenos* (desiring).</note> political activity and high office—should distribute his wealth appropriately, though not yet perfectly <note>The original Greek here is *oud' outōs eisin hai psychai hypo tēn heimarmenēn*, but the phrase is obscure and appears to have missing or erroneous words in the source manuscript.</note>. Such is the condition of souls under Fate. For not only the vehicles of these individual souls, but even those of the Gods themselves, are led by Fate. In order, therefore, that these souls and their vehicles may be placed under the rule of Fate, it is necessary that they should descend and join with the realm of "generation" <note>The world of birth, death, and constant change.</note>, which is the second...

### BOOK V. THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO

...events after their planting <note>original: "semination"</note>. For that planting is the primary cause; but this is a secondary distribution of the vehicles <note>In Platonic philosophy, the "vehicle" is a subtle, spiritual body that carries the soul as it descends from the divine realm into the physical world.</note> under the divine circulation <note>original Greek: περιφοράς (periphoras); the text corrects an error in the original manuscript which used "differences" (διαφοράς) instead of "circulations."</note>.¹ This is similar to the distribution of the souls themselves into the souls of the stars,² which was brought about by the single demiurgic <note>The "Demiurge" is the divine Craftsman or Creator who shapes the material world.</note> cause. 

Therefore, this distribution is eternal, and it is impossible for such leaders to change. It is also brought about by Fate. For Fate has dominion over cycles <note>original: "periods"</note>; it connects both universal and individual cycles, and it brings together similar qualities in both divine and individual souls. Through the union of these souls with one another, their vehicles are also born together <note>original: "connascent"</note>. Thus, when an individual soul aligns itself with a universal soul, its vehicle also follows the vehicle of that divine soul. Just as the individual soul imitates the thinking of the divine soul, its body also mirrors <note>original: "adumbrates"</note> the motion of the divine soul.

The first planting, therefore, is that of the vehicles. This not only clearly shows that the soul belongs to the world <note>original: "mundane"</note>, but also organizes its entire composition under its proper leader. For it is one thing to belong generally to the world, and another to be specifically "lunar" or "mercurial" <note>Influenced by the Moon or the planet Mercury</note>, since the latter is a more specific <note>original: "partial"</note> form of life. Just as the soul becomes a citizen of the universe after ascending into its vehicle, so too when it is planted alongside its vehicle, it becomes a citizen of a specific lunar, solar, or other celestial orbit. 

The attachment of the soul's vehicle to the universe causes it to be more complex <note>original: "multitudinous"</note> than the life lived above the physical world; as some say, it is almost split in two. As this planting continues, the soul gains a more specific dominion. After this planting, however, every soul has one definite birth <note>original: "generation"</note>; but souls make second and third descents into the world according to their own choices. There is, therefore, one birth common to all of them. It is necessary for every individual soul to descend into physical birth. Because individual souls cannot remain in the higher realms forever, they occasionally fall under the rule <note>original: "sceptres"</note> of Necessity. 

These souls also receive a mortal form of life from the universe, along with this outward body and a physical disposition <note>original: "habitude"</note>. However, by leading a good life, they are able even while on earth to be purified from the conditions imposed by Fate, as long as they avoid connecting with the body more than absolute necessity requires. For what effect can the works of Fate have on the "Coryphæan philosopher" <note>The "leading" or ideal philosopher described by Plato.</note> mentioned in the *Theaetetus*, who studies the stars above the heavens and does not even know where on earth he lives? But when souls turn toward the body, they must necessarily interact with the gifts of Fate. And when they are—

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.

...vanquished by the mortal form of life, they become the slaves of Fate. *For the universe uses them as irrational animals.* And this again happens to them because of their own nature. For their choice was made in this way, and having chosen, they lead a life consistent with their choice. It also happens to them because of the "wholes" <note>The "wholes" refer to the universal structures and the World-Soul that govern the cosmos as a whole.</note>. For everything is guided according to its natural fitness; every form of life is of some use to the universe; and nothing is left disorderly or undefined within the universal systems. Instead, all things are led toward a harmony of life. Thus, souls proceed step-by-step from a life that is always well-ordered and primary, down to the final life ruled by fate, passing through intermediate states of being. From an order that exists above Fate, they are distributed under the laws of Fate and travel through various destinies under the throne of Necessity.

What, however, should we say the "first generation" <note>In Plato's *Timaeus*, the "first generation" refers to the initial state or birth of souls as decreed by the Creator.</note> is, which the philosopher Plato now describes, and which the Demiurge <note>The divine Craftsman or Creator of the material world.</note> announces to souls while proclaiming the laws of Fate? There is more than one opinion on this matter. The divine Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who emphasized theurgy and the soul's descent.</note> calls the planting <note>original: "semination"</note> of the vehicles <note>The "vehicle" (*ochema*) is a subtle, ethereal body that carries the soul during its descent from the divine realm into the physical world.</note> the "first generation," and what follows in the text supports his claim. For Plato adds, as a continuation of this: “*But it was necessary that having disseminated them, etc.*” Another person, however, interprets the first generation of souls to be their single descent into the world. For it is necessary that each of these souls should be entirely familiar with the realm of "generation" <note>The physical world of change and rebirth.</note>, since this is their specific characteristic. He therefore simply decides that there is one specific descent for each soul.

But the solution provided by our teacher <note>Proclus is likely referring to his mentor, Syrianus.</note> is more accurate. For he says that for every individual <note>original: "partial"</note> soul, one descent is defined—not simply once in all time, but once according to each cycle <note>original: "period"</note> *of the divinely generated nature*. For it is not likely that any individual soul—whether of those called "undefiled" <note>Souls that remain pure and close to the divine.</note> or those capable of being stained by vice and wandering—should remain in the high heavens for every cosmic cycle. For if a soul is able to stay on high for one whole cycle, staying constant and without leaning toward the physical world, it could not descend into the world in another cycle. This is because it has kept itself free from fault during the entire movement of all the patterns of the universe. *And these cosmic patterns always repeat again and again.* Furthermore, the life of an individual soul is shorter than the great cycle of the universe. Therefore, if it is capable of remaining <note>1</note> on high through the whole of this cycle, it has been granted an unchanging intellectual power. This is because it will live with the same unchanging nature through all of time. So, if the passage of all time creates nothing new in this soul, it is one of those beings that always stays in a state according to its nature. Consequently, it is necessary that every individual soul should make one descent in each cosmic cycle...

...cycle; but some souls undergo a greater number of descents than others because they exercise an abundant freedom of will. Plato, however, calls this descent the "first generation" <note>original: "generation"; here meaning the soul's first birth or entry into the world of change.</note>. This is evident from his later remark when speaking of the destinies assigned after the first birth: “*that the corrupt soul should, in the second birth, be transformed into the nature of a woman.*” Consequently, he refers to the "first generation" as the descent from the intelligible <note>The "intelligible" realm refers to the world of pure, divine ideas that exist beyond physical perception.</note> realm. But since this first descent occurs after the sowing <note>original: "semination"</note> of the "vehicles" <note>The "vehicle" (*ochema*) is the subtle, ethereal body that carries the soul during its descent.</note>—at which point souls first become subject to Fate—he adds:

<margin>41E</margin>
> “But it was necessary—having sown them respectively into the instruments of time <note>The "instruments of time" are the planets and stars that govern the cycles of the physical world.</note> suited to each—that the most god-fearing of living beings should be born.”

For this was necessary after the sowing into the appropriate stars; and this is the first law of Fate: that every individual <note>original: "partial"</note> soul in each cosmic cycle <note>original: "mundane period"</note> should be joined with birth. It is necessary that the cycle of such a soul be shorter than the cycle of the universe, and this condition is common to all individual souls. 

However, these souls differ from each other according to the divine authority <note>original: "empire of the Gods"</note> they follow, for different groups of souls are organized under the dominion of different Gods. They also differ according to the rational principles <note>original: "reasons"</note> they exercise. For among the souls governed by the same divinity, some choose a life suited to that God, while others do not. Some participate in the same divinity through a different power, and others according to a different rank. For example, what if some of the souls who are attached to the prophetic power of the Sun should lead a medical or <term>initiatory</term>¹ life, while others lead a Mercurial life, and still others a Lunar life? The way these lives vary is not always the same. 

Furthermore, souls also differ according to their deliberate choices. For even if two souls should choose an <term>initiatory</term>² life, it is possible for one to practice it with integrity, but the other in a distorted manner. Every life has the potential to be lived well or poorly. To speak summarily, souls either: (1) are under the authority of the same power, choose the same life, and live in the same manner; (2) are under the same power, but do not choose the same life, yet live similarly; or (3) are neither under the same power, nor choose the same life, nor live in the same manner. This last category represents the ultimate difference between them. These, then, are the various ways in which souls differ. Since there are three factors involved, we must either deny all of them, affirm all of them, or deny two but affirm one, or—
