# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK 5]

...democracy from an aristocracy; but Plato describes a gradually subsiding change <note>original: "mutation"</note> of political concerns, and in accordance with this, he leads souls descending from the intelligible world <note>The realm of pure thought and divine forms, above the physical world.</note> into men. For he creates from them a living being <note>original: "animal"</note> which would afterwards be called *man* <note>original: "ανηρ" (aner), specifically meaning a male or a man of vigor</note>, receiving its name from the grandeur and vigor of its nature; according to which it is also better adapted to souls that are currently descending. This should be sufficient as an answer to the previously mentioned doubt concerning the first descent of souls.

From these points, therefore, we may gather as a logical conclusion <note>original: "corollary"</note> that the creation <note>original: "fabrication"</note> of this universe did not have a beginning in time. For if the universe was generated from a specific beginning, it is also necessary that the descent of souls must have taken place from a specific beginning, and that there must have been a first soul that descended. 

But the Demiurge <note>The "Divine Craftsman" or creator god in Platonic philosophy.</note> leads the first descent of each soul into the birth of a man. Therefore, it is necessary that the descent which makes a man should not have been carried out through a woman, nor proceed into physical birth through a woman, as the female would not yet exist. Similarly, the descent which makes a man does not provide a birth for a woman, since in this case it would be possible for the female to be generated not from both the male and female, but from a specific male alone. 

If, therefore, these things are impossible, it is impossible that the male and the female [should have had a beginning in time].¹ Souls always descend into the male gender before the female, the former not² being generated from the latter. And the speech of the Demiurge is addressed to beings which are always generated in the universe, and not to those that once received a beginning in time. 

What then, it may be asked, shall we say of the male and the female? Are they not also present in souls themselves, so that some are of a masculine and others of a feminine nature? And how can it be said that this is not necessary? For if these qualities exist in the Gods primarily, and in physical things <note>original: "sensibles"</note> ultimately, it is also necessary that they should exist in the middle levels. For from where else is their progression down to a physical nature derived, except through the middle nature <note>original: "essence"</note>? 

Furthermore, if the Demiurge, by connecting each soul with a vehicle <note>The "astral vehicle" or "spirit-body" that carries the soul into the physical realm.</note>, produces a certain living being <note>original: "τι ζωον" (ti zoon)</note>,³ it is entirely necessary that the difference between male and female in the soul should be apparent at the same time. For this is how living beings are divided. Must we not, therefore, admit that these qualities are in souls? And how is it possible we should not, since they are made to resemble their leading Gods? For as they derive every other form from them, so they also receive from them the unique characteristic of the—

# BOOK 5: THE TIMÆUS OF PLATO

Male and female souls are divided according to the types of animals found here in the physical world. However, as souls change their form <gloss>original: "ηθη" (customs), but corrected to "ειδη" (forms/species)1</gloss> of life, they also change these powers. Some souls are rendered more feminine, while others descend into a more robust and vigorous form of life. 

In this physical <note>original: "sensible"</note> region, that which has the quality of a "limit" <note>In Platonic thought, "Limit" (bound) represents order and form, while the "Infinite" represents chaos or potential.</note> is more vast than the infinite that exists in the higher realm—the state souls occupy before their descent. Consequently, any fall or lapse will be entirely into a state that is less excellent. This descent to a less excellent state sometimes leads to something near the higher excellence, and at other times to something more remote from it, yet it always corresponds to the arrangement found in the divine realm. 

For instance, it is said that a "Lunar" soul <note>A soul particularly influenced by the sphere of the Moon.</note> descended into human nature to become the soul of Musæus <note>A legendary Greek philosopher, poet, and polymath.</note>, and that an "Apollonian" soul became the soul of the Sibyl <note>An ancient prophetess who spoke the oracles of the god Apollo.</note>. The myth told by Aristophanes in the *Banquet* <note>Plato’s dialogue, the *Symposium*, where Aristophanes describes original humans as being split into two halves.</note> also shows that souls are divided into male, female, and a common gender <note>Androgynous.</note>. It is also evident that masculine souls do not exclusively enter into the birth of men, nor do feminine souls only enter into the birth of women. This is shown by Timaeus saying that every soul makes its first descent into a male body; this is natural because the female nature contains within it the cause of the male in animals, as we have observed before.

<margin>424</margin>

> “And as souls are by necessity implanted in bodies, and as one thing joins but another leaves these bodies.”

While souls remain on high with the Father <note>The Demiurge or Creator.</note> and are filled with intelligence from divine natures, they have no need for a mortal-shaped life. Instead, they use immaterial, pure, and "starry-form" organs <note>The *augoides* or "astral body," a luminous vehicle for the soul.</note>, revolving together with the Gods and governing the entire world alongside them. 

But when they descend into the world of generation <note>The physical world of birth, death, and constant change.</note>, become connected with a material body, and are assigned a nature that is constantly flowing in and out <note>A reference to the metabolic processes of eating and excreting, or the flux of matter.</note>, the binding of the mortal life—which draws its existence from the souls themselves—becomes necessary. This is because souls already contain the highest points of *this* <gloss>2</gloss> life within their spirit. This principle of sensory perception derives its existence both from the souls themselves <gloss>3</gloss> and from the junior Gods <note>The lesser deities created by the Demiurge to fashion the mortal parts of the soul and body.</note>. It comes from the souls because they have dominion over the entire irrational life, which they also organize; but they would neither govern nor...

# BOOK V: PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS

The junior gods <note>In Platonic philosophy, these are the celestial deities created by the Demiurge to oversee the physical world.</note> would not adorn the soul unless they were the primary causes of its essential nature. The soul also derives its existence from these Gods because its individual parts work together with the whole of the universe, and the ability to produce life is present in individual souls through their alignment with the whole. 

Therefore, if the junior Gods produced mortal life and created another mortal animal when souls were implanted in bodies, it follows that the animation of the material body is one thing—whether it exists in simple garments or in those that are composite and shell-like <term>original: "testaceous"; referring to the hard, oyster-like shell of the physical body</term> <note>The text suggests a correction here: instead of "starry" <note>original: *astrinous*</note>, it is necessary to read "shell-like" <note>original: *ostreinos*</note>.</note>—and the animation within the soul's "vehicle" <note>The "vehicle" (okhema) is an ethereal or subtle body that carries the soul through the heavens.</note> is another. The Demiurge <note>The supreme Creator-God.</note> establishes the latter vehicle, which is immortal. However, the former mortal life, which is mortal from the very beginning, originates from the junior Gods because it cannot be separated from material bodies. 

The specific life of the soul’s vehicle also differs from other types of life, just as an immortal life differs from a mortal-formed one. Furthermore, the life that exists in "simple garments" differs from the life in a composite body because the latter follows the physical temperament of the body, while the former can be disciplined and is able to master those physical temperaments. 

The vehicles of the soul are therefore three-fold <note>The text suggests a correction here: for "third" <note>original: *trita*</note>, read "triple" or "three-fold" <note>original: *tripla*</note>.</note>:
1.  Simple <note>The text suggests a correction here: instead of the masculine "simple" <note>original: *aplos*</note>, it is necessary to read the neuter form "simple" <note>original: *aploun*</note>.</note> and immaterial.
2.  Simple and material.
3.  Composite and material. 

Consequently, there are three types of lives corresponding to these: the first is immortal; the second lasts longer than the physical body; and the third perishes along with the body. This concludes this particular point. 

The word *implanted* refers to the seed-sowing of generation <note>original: "genesiurgic semination"; the process of planting the soul into the world of physical birth.</note>, while simultaneously signifying that this form of life is self-perfecting, just as a plant is grafted into another part of nature. Additionally, the phrase *from necessity* indicates that this "sowing" of the soul is material in nature, rather than divine and celestial.

> "He declared to them that, in the first place, one innate <term>original: "connascent"; meaning born at the same time or naturally united</term> sense, produced by violent passions, was necessary to all; in the second place, love mingled with pleasure and pain; and in addition to this, fear and anger, and all other such things that either follow these or are naturally out of harmony <note>original: "discordant"</note> because they are of a contrary nature."

The Demiurge encompassed all material and mortal-formed life within three boundaries and placed the causes of these within souls so that they might rule over and subdue them. For true dominion can only come from a state of inherent priority <note>original: "essential precedency"</note>. Therefore, the irrational life exists intellectually within the Demiurge, but rationally within souls. This is not surprising at all, since the body exists...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of sensation and the different levels of the soul's life, distinguishing between the cognitive powers of the immortal soul and the passive sensations of the mortal body.</meta>

# BOOK V: THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO

...exists <note>The text begins mid-word: [con]sists.</note> incorporeally within the intelligible causes of all things. However, what else can we call each of these powers but a material <note>original Greek: *enylo*, corrected from the OCR's *enydro* (watery)</note> life that takes a physical form? This life gains knowledge from things that affect it from the outside and produces this knowledge through sensory organs. It does not depend on itself, but on the objects it perceives. It is mixed with material matter, and the knowledge it gains is always accompanied by "passion" <note>In Platonic philosophy, "passion" (pathos) refers to the state of being acted upon by an external force, including physical sensations and emotions.</note>.

As Socrates says in the *Philebus*, not every feeling produced in a living being gives us a sensation; only those that cause significant agitation do so. It is necessary for a certain agitation to be produced in the sensory organs <note>original: sensoria</note>. Not all motions of the soul are felt by the body; some, such as intellectual motions, belong to the soul itself <note>original Greek: *autês*, corrected from the OCR's *autois*</note>. Likewise, not all motions of the body reach the soul; some are too faint or obscure to move it.

Sensation, therefore, is not produced by every feeling, but only from those that are violent and cause great agitation. This "mortal-formed" sense is divisible <term>original: partible; meaning it is split among different organs like eyes and ears</term>, is material, and is influenced by passions when it makes judgments. However, there is another type of sense that exists prior to this one, located in the "vehicle" <note>The *okhema*, or subtle body, which acts as an intermediate carrier for the soul between the spiritual and physical realms.</note> of the soul. Compared to the physical sense, this one is immaterial and pure. It is a form of "impassive" knowledge—meaning it is not altered by what it perceives—and exists on its own. Yet, it is not entirely free from form <note>original: *morphē*</note> because it still has a physical-like nature, as its fundamental reality <term>original: hypostasis</term> is assigned to a body.

This sense has the same nature as the imagination <note>original: phantasy</note>. They share a single essence. When it looks outward, it is called "sensation"; but when it remains within and observes forms <note>original: *morphai*</note> and figures in the spirit, it is called "imagination." Furthermore, when it is divided among the spirit, it is sensation. 

Additionally, "opinion" <note>The rational processing of sensory information.</note> is the foundation of the rational life, while the imagination is the peak of the second (irrational) life. Opinion and imagination are linked to each other, and the irrational life is filled with powers from the more excellent, higher life. The middle part of the irrational life cannot receive higher forms but can only receive things situated on the outside. At the same time, it is "common" (shared) and perceives sensible things through being acted upon. 

In contrast, the material sense only perceives things that strike it from the outside and move it. It cannot hold onto these sights because it is divisible and not a single unit; it is spread across the various sensory organs. 

Thus, there are three types of sense:
1. The impassive and common sense (belonging to the soul's first, highest vehicle).
2. The common but passive sense (belonging to the irrational life).
3. The distributed and passive sense (belonging to the animation of the physical body).

<meta>This page continues the analysis of the mortal parts of the soul as discussed in Plato's Timaeus, moving from the faculty of sensation to the lower faculties of desire and anger.</meta>

# BOOK V: PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS

Following sensation, however, Plato places ***desire***. <note>original: *epithymia*. Desire is well-defined by the followers of Pythagoras as a specific tendency or impulse of the soul to be filled with something, to enjoy something present, or to experience a sensory activity. It can also stem from the absence or lack of perception of certain things. See my translation of Iamblichus' *Life of Pythagoras*, p. 146.</note> This is a type of life that takes a physical form; it is constantly rebuilding the body and relieving its needs. It is also the realm where pleasure and pain are found. While these passions are present in other parts of the soul—for you can find pleasure and pain within both reason and anger—physical pleasure and pain are specifically generated through desire.

For the body, the path toward what is contrary to nature <note>original: preternatural</note> and the loss of life produce pain; however, the return to a state that conforms to nature and the restoration of life produce pleasure. The part of the soul that is either calmed or stimulated <note>original Greek: *diakechymenon*, corrected from the OCR's *diadechomenon*</note> by these passions is the <term>epithymetic</term> (desiring) part. Since these two passions—pleasure and pain—are the primary sources and the "fountains" of all other passions (as Plato says in the *Philebus* and the *Laws*), he explains the birth of other passions through the mixture of these two. 

For instance, he describes **love** as a mixture of pleasure and pain. Love relates to all things. As long as the object of love is in sight, love is accompanied by pleasure; but as long as that object is not yet fully possessed or present, love is mingled with pain. Plato characterizes the entire life of desire through love because this passion is the most intense expression of it.

In the third place, he lists **anger**. Anger is a faculty of life aimed at removing anything that causes pain or disturbs the body. For this reason, the fear that the body might be destroyed also agitates it. We can see both excess and deficiency in this faculty, such as audacity and cowardice, and their related traits: ambition, competitiveness, and all such effects produced by a state of agitation <note>original Greek: *ptoian*, corrected from the OCR's "astonishment"</note> regarding mortal concerns. The higher soul employs this faculty to move the body.

These three <term>genesiurgic</term> (life-generating) powers follow a specific order. As soon as a body is born, according to the progression of life, it participates in sensation. It would not be a living animal, nor would it possess an appetite, unless it were first made capable of sensing. While appetites are always accompanied by sensation, sensation <note>The words "but senses" were missing in the original text but are necessary for the logic of the sentence.</note> is not always accompanied by appetite. Therefore, an animal is defined more by its <term>sensitive</term> faculty than by its <term>orectic</term> (appetitive) faculty. After the body begins to participate in sensation, it appears to...

# BOOK V: PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS

The soul is affected by pleasure and pain. It is contracted by external cold, but it is comforted by swaddling bands and guided toward a condition that conforms to nature. As a child grows older, the soul begins to manifest the passion of anger. Anger is a power belonging to a more robust and vigorous nature. For this reason, among irrational animals, those that are more "material" (driven by physical needs) live according to desire alone and experience only pleasure and pain. However, animals that are more "perfect" or complex are granted a more spirited <note>original: irascible</note> life. 

Before these appetites develop, however, there is a certain "summit" or highest point of these faculties within the <term>pneuma</term> <note>The *pneuma*, or "spirit-vehicle," was considered by Neoplatonists to be a subtle, quasi-physical body that carries the soul into the material world.</note> of the soul. This summit is a specific impulsive power that moves the spirit, but it also guards and holds the spirit's essence together. At times, this power is extended and divided into parts; at other times, it is led toward boundaries and order, regulated by reason.

> "And that those souls who subdue these passions would live justly, but those who are conquered by them would live unjustly."

How, then, can souls subdue these physical lives unless they possess the underlying causes <note>original: "reasons" or "productive principles" (logoi)</note> of those lives? Through these principles, they make the passions more harmonious with reason. Everything that naturally has authority over the passions contains within itself the "reason" or rational principle of those passions; by looking to this principle, the soul can define the proper limits of their movement. 

For example, Ulysses suppressed the anger in his breast <note>A reference to Homer’s *Odyssey*, where Odysseus (Ulysses) famously strikes his chest and tells his heart to endure, restraining his impulse for immediate revenge.</note> because he had already disciplined it. The soul also brings order to external anger so that its expression may be just. If Ulysses’s internal anger had given itself over to raw passion and physical impulse, it would have entirely corrupted the other well-ordered parts of his soul. Therefore, when souls subdue material passions and bring beauty to their inner lives, they live justly. But when they are conquered by these passions, they imperceptibly fall into injustice. By following the immoderate appetites of the body, their powers become disordered and unrefined, and they become more focused on the world of physical change <term>generation</term> <note>original: generation; in this context, it refers to the realm of birth, death, and material flux.</note> than is proper. 

But how do souls follow justice at one time and not at another? It was previously said of them: "Of those that are always willing to follow justice and you."* Can it be said that they are always indeed willing to follow justice and the Gods, but that they do not always actually follow them? This relates to the arguments in Plato's *Gorgias*, which distinguish a person’s true "will" (which always seeks the good) from "opinion," which is governed by how things appear. Or may it not be said that souls follow justice and—

# BOOK V: PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS

...the Gods, because of a divine nature presiding within them? For he who desires what is good also desires to follow justice. This is what was meant in the previously cited passage: "*that a divine nature has dominion over those who are always willing to follow justice and the Gods.*" Our divine part naturally follows justice, while the irrational forms of life follow the divine nature that resides within us.

> "He who lived well during his appointed time [on the earth] shall return again to the habitation of his kindred star, and there enjoy a happy life."

Again, these outcomes are brought about by the souls themselves. Because they are self-moving, they arrange themselves in an appropriate place. But they are also influenced by Fate. This power defines the appropriate assignments of each soul and adapts them to their proper forms of life. Thirdly, these things are carried out by the Gods, who organize the parts of the universe in an orderly manner. They distribute to all things what is deserved; for this reason, it is said that Justice—proceeding into the universe from the middle sphere of the Sun—governs all things according to rectitude. Just as in the universal systems <note>original: "wholes"</note>, Justice follows Jupiter <note>original: Zeus</note> and is the avenger of those who abandon divine law, so too does the energy of Justice act upon individual souls. It brings order to those who forget the laws of Fate and trade a more excellent life for an inferior one. So much for these general points.

But what is the *proper time*, what is the *kindred star*, and what is the *happy life*? The *proper time* is that which Plato defines in the *Phaedrus* for the souls that are led in a cycle from this world after their first generation—namely, a period of a thousand years, or some other similar duration. Just as this time pertains to those who choose a life of philosophy, other periods, either more or less extended, are adapted to those who make a different choice. This time does not exist in a single, uniform way <note>original: monadically</note>, but is defined according to the specific form of life. 

The <term>kindred star</term> <note>In Platonic thought, every soul is "assigned" to a star that matches its character and divine origin.</note> is the place where the distribution of souls and their vehicles is made. So, if there are some souls which, from the start, have their assignment on the earth, these souls—after their first life, and provided they follow Justice and the Gods—will return to the <term>ethereal vehicle</term> <note>The subtle, celestial body that the soul inhabits before descending into a physical, "terrestrial" body.</note> of the whole earth, leaving behind the physical body. Establishing themselves in this state, along with the organ inherently connected <note>original: connascent</note> to them (that is, their ethereal vehicle), they will be filled with intellectual life. They will also fill their vehicles with divine light and creative <note>original: demiurgic</note> power. Furthermore, if there are certain souls that proceed from the Sun, these will return to their universal source <note>original: "wholeness"</note>. Together with the Sun, they will organize the universal systems in an orderly manner, being assigned through a coordinated system...

# BOOK V: PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS

...with it, a power of such a kind as not to depart from the intellectual understanding of themselves while they pay providential attention to the universe. And the *happy life* is that life defined according to the specific character of the leading powers. For these powers are in the order of spirits <note>original: dæmons; in Greek philosophy, these are intermediate beings between gods and humans that act as guardians or guides, not evil entities.</note>, having individual <note>original: partial</note> souls in their possession and raising them to the intelligible realm <note>the realm of pure thought and reality above the physical world</note>, in the same manner as the leaders of the liberated Gods. Hence also, Plato elsewhere calls these souls happy, as being suspended from these leaders who are happy <note>original: εὐδαιμονῶν ὄντων (eudaimonōn ontōn), meaning "being happy" or "possessing a good spirit"</note>—that is, who are beneficent spirits. For everywhere, that which is established directly above a nature that is considered deserving of its providential care has the rank of a beneficent spirit with respect to it.

It is necessary also to examine the uninterrupted connection of these philosophical principles. For Plato established souls from the creator <note>original: demiurgic</note> and life-giving <note>original: vivific</note> cause; and after their creation, he arranged different individual souls under different divine souls, making their progression and distribution occur in the realm beyond the world <note>original: supermundane</note>. After these divine souls, he also introduces individual souls into the universe, gives them vehicles <note>the "astral body" or subtle carrier of the soul</note>, and distributes them among the stars. In the next place, he leads them into the realm of birth <note>original: generation</note> and imparts to them the mortal form of life; and after these things, he divides their lives and distributes assignments <note>original: allotments</note> adapted to their lives. For their progression is from natures beyond the world into the world; but their descent from the universal <note>original: total</note> life is into the realm of birth. 

Now, therefore, since he speaks of souls that are restored to their kindred star after their first lifetime, and says that by leaving the body they obtain a happy life, how can we show that these things agree with what is asserted in the *Phaedrus*? For in that dialogue, he who chooses a philosophical life is restored to his original perfection through three lifetimes. Or may we not say that the assignment which is delivered here is not a return to the place from which each soul originally came (for that is achieved through three periods, each of which consists of a thousand years), but is a return to the star under which it was essentially organized, and in conjunction with which it possesses a common life? 

For it is possible for souls that have not led a philosophical life to be raised by Justice to a certain place in the heavens, and there to receive the reward of the life which they passed in the human form. For this is asserted in the *Phaedrus* regarding the souls of those who are not philosophers. For the restoration <note>original: *apocatastasis*; the return of a soul or the cosmos to its original state</note> into the same situation again is one thing, but the ascent to the kindred star is another. For the former requires three periods, but the latter may be achieved through one period. And the former raises the soul to the intelligible realm from which it descended, but the latter leads it to a secondary form of life. For there are different <note>original: διαφορά (diaphora); this word is omitted here in the original Greek text.</note> measures of happiness, and the return is twofold: one of ascending souls, but the other, of...

# BOOK V: PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS

...those that have ascended. Its return, however, to the intelligible realm <note>the realm of pure, non-physical reality and truth</note> itself requires a period of three thousand years. For through this process, the soul regains its highest "winged" state <note>A reference to Plato's *Phaedrus*, where the soul is described as having wings that grow when it contemplates truth and wither when it falls into the physical world.</note>.

<margin>42 B</margin>
> "But he whose conduct was depraved should, in the second generation, be changed into the nature of a woman."

We have previously observed that Plato does not call the planting <note>original: semination</note> of souls the "first generation," but rather the first descent from the intelligible realm, which is common to all individual <note>original: partial</note> souls. He therefore calls the second descent the "second generation" and establishes that this second descent is into the nature of a woman—just as the third descent is into the nature of an animal <note>original: brutal nature</note>. This indicates a systematic lessening of the soul's quality of life. Thus, in the *Phaedrus*, he also names all subsequent lives after the first generation according to these "second lives."

<margin>42 C</margin>
> "That both of these, at the expiration of a thousand years, should return to the allotment and choice <note>The original Greek text here was corrected from *aithin* to *hairesin*, meaning "choice."</note> of a second life, with each soul receiving a life suited to its choice. And that in this selection, the human soul could pass into the life of an animal <note>original: brute</note>."

Plato here displays another order of life, leading the soul from a more powerful to a weaker nature, and from an intellectual life to one deprived of intellect. Why is it necessary that the soul should not descend directly from the first generation into the nature of a woman? If the female gender existed only as a deviation from the male, it would be necessary for souls that were recently perfected to begin only from that which follows nature (the male); this is because anything "unnatural" <note>original: preternatural</note> is always secondary and accidental. However, since the female nature also exists among the Gods, what should prevent souls—which in this respect are imitating their proper divine leaders—from not only choosing lives adapted to themselves <note>The text was corrected here from "herself" to "them."</note> but also the nature of animals allied to them? It is not, however, surprising that these alternations should take place, as we observed before. For the male and the female exist not only in mortal beings but also in the...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the second descent of the soul, specifically addressing the transition into a female nature and the logical implications for the eternity of the soul and the universe.</meta>

# BOOK V: TIMAEUS OF PLATO

The indivisible <note>original: impartible; the translator notes that the Greek text should be read as "ameristais" (indivisible) rather than "meristais" (divided)</note> lives of souls can be inferred by recalling what was previously stated: that these sexual differences exist both in natures that come before and those that come after individual <note>original: partial</note> souls. However, we should not be skeptical if the "vehicles" <note>The subtle, ethereal bodies or "chariots" that carry the soul</note> are naturally born and permanently joined to universal souls, while in individual souls, they are only sometimes joined and sometimes not. For in universal souls, this connection is essential, but in individual souls, it is the result of deliberate choice. Therefore, in universal souls, the division of these vehicles is tied to the soul's very essence, but in individual souls, it is tied to the differences in their choices.

This can also be inferred from what is said in the *Symposium* <note>original: Banquet</note>, specifically in the myth told by Aristophanes. As we noted before, that text clearly describes the division of souls according to these vehicles and how choices regarding mortal life alternate. If you understand these words to directly imply the nature of women, then I would interpret the passage in this way. However, if "woman" is instead a symbol for every form of life that is weak, effeminate, and focused on physical reproduction <note>original: generation</note>—as some distinguished thinkers before us have believed—then the words would not require the explanation I just gave. You may choose either of these explanations, though it should be noted that Plato often deliberately hides deeper meanings behind symbols. Whichever solution you choose, it is clear that the soul is not placed in a female body during its first descent into the physical world.

From this, I also conclude that according to the character Timaeus, the soul, humanity, and indeed the entire universe are "unbegotten" <note>eternal and having no beginning in time</note>. For if the soul were created at a specific time and descended for the first time into physical existence <note>original: first generation</note>, it would provide life to a man. But if this man were entirely a created being, he would have to be born from a woman. This woman would then need a soul. That soul would either be one descending for the first time—in which case Timaeus’s claim that the soul's first descent is into a male is false—or it would not be the first soul, meaning a male soul must have existed before her to produce the soul within her.

But then, that male must have been born from a female; if not, his existence would have to be the result of mere chance. However, if that were the case, his existence would be pointless, as there would be no female through whom the male could reproduce. This female, like the male, would either have to exist by chance—with a soul that descended for the first time and was created with her—or she would have to be produced by the male. But both of these are impossible. Therefore, neither the male nor the female was ever "created" at a single point in time. Neither the soul, nor certainly the universe, belongs to the category of things that have a beginning in time.

# PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS: BOOK V

> “And if vice does not cease in these individuals even then, but continues according to a likeness of the way they were born <note>original: "similitude of the mode of generation"</note>, then the soul shall always be changed into a brutal nature <note>The nature of a "brute," or an animal lacking human reason</note> corresponding to its disposition.”

It is common to investigate what is meant by the descent of souls into irrational animals. Some thinkers believe that what are called "brutal lives" are simply instances of humans acting like animals. They argue it is impossible for a rational essence <note>The core, thinking part of a human soul</note> to actually become the soul of a creature without reason. 

Others, however, admit that a soul may be directly introduced into irrational animals. They claim that all souls are of a similar form, meaning they believe a human soul could literally become a wolf, a leopard, or even one of the sea creatures called *pneumones* <note>original: marine fishes called "pneumones," likely referring to jellyfish or lung-fish</note>. 

The true answer to this inquiry, however, is this: the human soul may enter into animals, but it does so while retaining its own proper life. The soul that is inserted "rides" upon the animal nature, so to speak, and is bound to it by sympathy. We have demonstrated this through many arguments in our *Commentaries on the Phaedrus*, where we have also shown that this is the only way such an insertion occurs. 

If it is necessary to remind the reader that this is a Platonic doctrine, we can look at the *Republic*, where the soul of Thersites <note>A soldier in the Trojan War known for being vulgar and rebellious</note> is said to have been clothed with the *nature* of an ape, rather than its *body*. Similarly, in the *Phaedrus*, the soul is said to descend into a *brutal life*, not a brutal body; for the "life" is what functions alongside the soul itself. Here, Timaeus says the soul is changed into a brutal *nature*. A "brutal nature" is not the physical body of the animal, but the animal's way of living. As we mentioned, this can be understood more fully from our *Commentaries on the Phaedrus*. 

Furthermore, we can recall that it is impossible for a recently perfected soul to immediately become the soul of an animal. As Aristotle says, "brutality" is something that exists beyond the scope of human vice. Therefore, it is necessary to first descend into human vice, and only afterward into the vice suited to animals. It is not possible to jump from the highest forms of life directly to their complete opposites. This is why Timaeus says, “*And if vice does not cease in these individuals even then*,” with "then" referring to the soul's descent into a female form. If they continue to be depraved in that state, they are then changed into an animal nature of this kind. 

Through a process of decline, irrational forms of life are produced from the primary and more intellectual <note>original: "νοερωτέρων" (noerōterōn). The translator notes the original Greek text mistakenly used "νεωτέρων" (neōterōn), which means "newer" or "younger."</note> forms. Forms that exist in a state of earthly attachment <note>original: "habitude"</note> come from those that are remote from such attachments, and the weak come from the robust. However, since vice takes many forms, the animal nature may be seen...

<summary>Proclus explains the Neoplatonic view of reincarnation, arguing that human souls do not literally become animals but "ride" upon an animal nature as a result of persistent vice and spiritual decline.</summary>

### PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS [BOOK V]

...universal, when she lives in conjunction with her middle vehicle <note>The "middle vehicle" refers to the ethereal or astral body that Neo-Platonists believed acted as an intermediate between the pure soul and the physical body</note>, as a citizen of the realm of generation <note>The world of physical birth, change, and decay</note>. Dismissing, therefore, her first state <note>original: "habit"</note> which exists according to an alliance to the whole of the material world, and laying aside the irrational nature which connects her with physical birth, while also governing her irrational part by reason and elevating opinion to intellect, she will be led back in a circle to a happy life, away from wandering through the regions of the senses. This is the life which those initiated by Orpheus into the mysteries of Dionysus <note>original: "Bacchus"</note> and Persephone <note>original: "Proserpine"</note> pray to obtain, along with the assigned portions of the celestial sphere and a rest <note>original: *anapausai*; the footnote indicates the Greek text should be corrected from *apapeusai* to *anapausai*, meaning "to rest" or "to cease"</note> from evil. 

But if our soul necessarily lives well when living according to the "circle of sameness" <note>A Platonic term for the intellectual, unchanging, and divine motion of the soul</note>, this must be even more true for divine souls. It is possible, however, for our soul to live according to the circle of sameness when it is purified, as Plato says. Therefore, purifying <note>original: "Cathartic"</note> virtue alone must be called the salvation of souls; for it cuts away and powerfully erases material natures and the passions that cling to us from physical birth. It separates the soul and leads it back to the intellect, causing it to leave behind on earth the vehicles with which it is clothed. For as souls descend, they receive different vehicles from the elements—airy, watery, and earthy—and finally enter into this dense physical bulk. For how could they proceed from immaterial spirits into this body without an intermediate step? Therefore, before they enter this body, they possess an irrational life and its vehicle, which is prepared from the simple elements. From these, they become clothed in "tumult" [or the world-generating <note>original: "genesiurgic"</note> body], which is named so because it is foreign to the soul's natural vehicle, composed of all sorts of garments that make the soul heavy.

The word *clinging* <note>original: "adhering"</note> also shows that this type of vehicle is placed around the soul externally, and points to the binding <note>original: "colligation"</note> to the single nature contained within it. After this, the final physical body—made of dissimilar and varied parts—is hung from the soul. For how is it possible for the descent to happen [immediately] from a life that governs the entire world to the most specific and limited form of life? This particular and indivisible "outward man" cannot be directly connected to the universe; instead, a prior descent into a middle state between the two is absolutely necessary. This middle state is not a specific animal, but the source of many lives. For the descent does not directly produce the life of a specific man, but—prior to this and before the birth of an individual—it produces the life of the universal <note>original: *katholikou*; the translator notes this word is likely missing in the Greek text here</note> man. <meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the soul's descent, specifically detailing the different "vehicles" or layers of embodiment—celestial, generative, and physical—that the soul assumes as it moves from the divine realm into the material world.</meta>

# BOOK V.] TIMAEUS OF PLATO.

[The soul descends from the] celestial vehicle; so from this, the descent is into a generative body <term>genesiurgic</term> <note>original: "genesiurgic"; pertaining to the realm of "generation" or physical birth and change</note>, according to which the soul exists in the realm of generation. From this, it descends into a terrestrial body, according to which it lives within the shell-like <term>testaceous</term> <note>original: "testaceous"; literally "shell-like," referring to the hard, physical body that encases the soul like a shell</note> body. Hence, before it is surrounded with this last body, it is invested with a body which connects it with all generation. For this reason, it only leaves this [middle] body when it leaves the realm of generation entirely. But if this is the case, it must have received that body when it first came into generation. It came into generation, however, prior to its lapse into this last physical body. Therefore, prior to this last body, it received that vehicle, and it retains it after the dissolution of the physical one. It lives, therefore, in this vehicle through the whole of its period in the realm of generation.

On this account, Plato calls "the adhering tumult" the irrational <note>original: *alogon*. The translator notes the original Greek text likely had a typo, reading "rational" (*logon*) when it should have been "irrational" (*alogon*)</note> form of life in this vehicle; he does not mean that which adheres to the soul in each of its specific incarnations, but that which has circularly invested it from the first. The innate <term>connascent</term> <note>original: "connascent"</note> vehicle, therefore, makes the soul a part of the universe <term>mundane</term>; the second vehicle causes it to be a citizen of generation; and the shell-like vehicle makes it a terrestrial being. And as the life of souls is to the whole of generation <note>The original Greek text here was corrupt; the translator has reconstructed the meaning to show the proportional relationship between the soul's life, the realm of change, and the universe</note>, and the whole of generation is to the world, so are these vehicles to each other. 

With respect to the arrangement of the vehicles: one is perpetual and always part of the universe; another exists prior to this outward body and remains after it (for it both precedes and follows it within the realm of generation); and a third exists only when the soul lives a certain partial life on the earth. Plato, therefore—by using the term *adhering* and by making the irrational nature depend on the soul throughout all its lives—distinguishes this irrational nature from this outward body and its specific life. But by adding the words *externally* and *afterwards*, he distinguishes it from the innate vehicle in which the Creator <term>Demiurgus</term> <note>The divine craftsman or architect of the universe in Platonic thought</note> caused it to descend. Hence, this vehicle which causes the soul to be a citizen of generation is a middle ground between both.

Timaeus, therefore, knew the vehicle of the irrational life which adheres to us prior to this outward body. For it is evident that this irrational and tumultuous crowd of passions, which adheres to us from fire, earth, air, and water, does not belong to the first [celestial] vehicle. This must be emphasized again, because some interpreters have not fathomed the depth of Plato’s theory concerning the soul’s vehicles <term>psychical vehicles</term>. Consequently, some of them—by rejecting the [first] vehicle—are compelled to make the soul exist sometimes without any body at all. But others, while preserving it, are forced to make the vehicle of the irrational life immortal; neither of them separating...

<summary>Proclus explains the Neoplatonic doctrine of the soul's three vehicles: the eternal celestial vehicle, the intermediate generative vehicle, and the temporary physical body. He argues that the irrational part of the soul belongs to the intermediate vehicle, which exists before and after any single physical life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s analysis of the soul's different "vehicles" or envelopes. It distinguishes between the soul's original, innate vehicle and the secondary, irrational layers it acquires as it descends toward physical incarnation.</meta>

# BOOK V.] PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO.

[It is necessary to distinguish] the innate vehicle from the *adherent vehicle* <note>original: "adherent vehicle"; a secondary, temporary body or energy field the soul acquires during its descent</note>, and the prior from the posterior. We must also distinguish that which was fashioned by the one Demiurgus <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the supreme Creator or "Craftsman" of the universe</note> from that which was woven into the soul by the many "junior" creators, even though Plato clearly distinguishes these. 

It is evident, therefore, that this "irrational crowd" <note>the collection of irrational impulses and lower soul-faculties</note> is not located in the innate vehicle of the soul—the vehicle in which the Demiurgus originally placed the soul. Plato clearly states that this irrational nature "adhered to the soul afterwards." It is also manifest that this is not the life within the shell-like <term>testaceous</term> <note>original: "testaceous"; referring to the hard, physical body</note> body. If it were, why would Plato say that the soul, in its cycle of changing bodies, will not be freed from its labor until it subdues the tumultuous and irrational crowd that later adhered to it? 

He says, therefore, that the soul exchanges one life for another, and that the irrational crowd adhered to it but is not innate to it. To claim otherwise would mean the soul is changing its own essential and allied nature. Consequently, in each of the soul's lives, there is no change to the irrational life in the same way there is a change of physical bodies. 

This irrational life is different from the <term>entelecheia</term> <note>original: "entelecheia"; the "actualization" or the animating principle that gives a specific physical body its life and form</note>, which is unique to each body and inseparable from it. For the one is inherent, descending with us into the realms of physical birth <note>original: "generation"</note>; but the other is changed along with the bodies from which it cannot be separated. 

Thus, Timaeus knew that the irrational life is different from the life of the primary vehicle and from the life of the final physical body. It differs from the former because he calls it *posterior* (coming after), and from the latter because it does not change along with the outward body. Indeed, the soul must subdue this irrational nature while it is present. The soul is eventually separated from the *entelecheia* of the body; then, as it changes bodies between the life of the ethereal vehicle and the life of the physical body, it completes its <term>genesiurgic period</term> <note>original: "genesiurgic period"; the cycle of birth and reincarnation</note>. 

During this time, however, the soul is disturbed by the irrational life. To cast off such vehicles as these—where Plato specifically names each of the elements involved—the philosophic life certainly contributes. But in my opinion, the <term>telestic art</term> <note>original: "telestic art"; theurgy or the high art of sacred rituals and initiations</note> is the most effective for this purpose. As the Oracles <note>referring to the *Chaldean Oracles*</note> teach us, this art uses divine fire to wipe away all the stains caused by physical birth, as well as everything foreign that the spirit and the irrational nature of the soul have attracted to themselves.

In these words, Plato completes the doctrine regarding the first stage of creation <note>original: "fabrication"</note> and establishes the beginning of the second stage. He preserves...

He argues that while philosophy helps, sacred ritual (the telestic art) is the most effective way to purify the soul from these material stains.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the *Timaeus*, specifically discussing how the Demiurge establishes the laws of the universe and the role of the "decad" (the number ten) in the administration of Fate.</meta>

# BOOK V.] THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO.

The first [divine law] is free, singular <note>original: "monadic"</note>, transcendent <note>original: "exempt"</note>, pure, and unmixed with lower natures. It hangs the secondary laws from itself, delivering all the measures, the arrangement, and the boundaries of creation <note>original: "production"</note> as a consequence. These secondary laws are perfected and governed by the first, receiving all their power from it. This is the goal of the words we are considering. 

Directing our attention, however, to the sacred law of the Demiurge <note>The "Divine Craftsman" or creator of the physical world</note>, we must not say that it resembles the law of a city established by a human legislator, which only acts upon things that already exist. For the will of the Demiurge comes before the action that establishes things in existence; in short, it is not right to think of human concerns and divine concerns as the same. For human laws, though they are sometimes made to resemble a divine nature, are only partially similar—imitating the stability in one respect, the effectiveness in another, and the perfecting power of divine natures in another. 

Nor should we admit that a sacred law of this kind is ambiguous. For example, we should not think that "if someone does *these* things, *those* will follow, but if not, the opposite results will occur," based on a varying way of thinking <note>The original Greek text here should be read as "dissimilar" (anomoion) rather than "him" (auton)</note>. For the Father of all things contains the causes of all effects within himself. He does not understand them through vague ideas, but through stable and uniform categories. He perceives created things in an uncreated way, things that are uncertain as being necessary, and divisible things in an indivisible way. 

Time and place were created together with the universe. Therefore, the Demiurge of the universe established the principles of all things within himself, without time and without space. Thus, it is necessary to admit that the divine decree <note>original: *thesmos*</note> of the Demiurge is the intellectual order contained in the divine law that spreads through all things, is present with all things without hindrance, and guards all things with purity. I believe that a "divine decree" <note>original: *thesmos*</note> possesses something more than a standard "law," just as a deity is more excellent than the human intellect. We say that "law" is the distribution of the intellect, but a "divine decree" <note>original: *thesmos*</note> is a divine order and a unified boundary. This is enough regarding these details.

Proceeding to the words of the text, we shall first demonstrate that Plato understands all the laws of Fate through the number ten <note>original: "the decad"</note>, because the number ten is born together with the cause of the Demiurge. For the blessings that the Demiurge gives to the world end in this number—all of them being ten. For the number ten belongs to the world, as the Pythagorean hymn says; it calls the number ten the "receiver of all things, ancient and venerable," which places a boundary around all things, and is named the "unchanging and tireless number ten." All the laws of Fate mentioned above regarding souls are ten in number. For it is necessary that souls...

<keywords>Proclus, Timaeus, Demiurge, thesmos, Fate, the decad, Pythagoreanism, divine law, intellect</keywords>

--- Page 426 ---
<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the *Timaeus*, focusing on the ten laws established by the Demiurge (the Divine Craftsman) to govern the descent, moral conduct, and eventual salvation of souls within the realm of Fate.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.

The laws established that souls should be spread abroad; that there should be one common descent for all of them in each time period; that the soul descending in the first generation should enter a righteous <note>original: "pious"</note> creature; that the soul descending into human nature should first pass into the seed of man; that the soul within a body should produce divided <note>original: "partible," meaning fragmented or localized</note> and material lives; that the soul which masters its material life should be considered just, but the soul mastered by it, unjust; that the just soul should return to its kindred star; that the failing soul should descend again in the second generation into the nature of a woman; that the soul in the second generation should, in its third descent, pass into the nature of a brute animal; and finally, the tenth law is the law of the Demiurge <note>The "Divine Craftsman" or creator of the physical world</note>, which is the sole savior of the soul, being the life that raises it back to the cycle of the "same and the similar," and causes the wandering circle of rebirth <note>original: "generation"</note> to cease. 

All the laws mentioned above are contained within the number ten <note>original: "decad"</note>, because the Pythagoreans consider the number ten to be suited to both the Demiurge and to Fate. These laws are planted within souls so that they may guide themselves, since the Gods wish to rule over self-moving beings as self-moving beings. Likewise, this ensures that the souls themselves are the causes of any evils that may later befall them, rather than the Demiurge. For if they did not already understand the laws of Fate—even if they were once superior to Fate—they would not descend into the world of change. But if they are eventually to be under Fate's power, how could they be blamed for doing wrong if they had not previously learned the punishment ordained for such mistakes? Therefore, so that the Demiurge might not be blamed for the guilt of souls, he established the laws of Fate within their very essences.

Consequently, the nature of evil must not be blamed on divinity; for it is stated here that the maker of the entire world is not the cause of it. This is not only asserted here regarding the Demiurge, but also in the *Republic*, where the prophet proclaiming the decree of Lachesis <note>One of the three Fates in Greek mythology, who measures the thread of life</note> says: "*the one who chooses is responsible, but God is blameless.*" <note>original: "the electing soul is the cause... but God is blameless"</note> Thus, divinity is neither the prior cause nor the cause of evil at all, but is without fault. As was said before, divinity willed that wickedness should, as much as possible, have no existence. 

Therefore, evil must not be attributed to a divine nature, nor should it be said to be without a beginning or root <note>original: "principle"</note>. For if it had no root, it would be disorganized and limitless, and would harm the entire structure of creation. For what could bring order to it if it has no place among existing things? Yet, a root must not be given to it as a "whole" or "total" reality. Nothing that exists as a complete "whole" is capable of receiving evil. Instead, all wholes perpetually preserve the same pure nature, free from evil. Thus, it is clear that evil arises from a partial or individual source <note>original: "partial principle"</note>.

<summary>Proclus explains the ten laws of the Demiurge that govern the soul's journey through various lives and asserts that the soul, being self-moving, is responsible for its own moral failures, exonerating the Divine from the existence of evil.</summary>
<keywords>Proclus, Timaeus, Demiurge, Fate, Decad, Soul's Descent, Justice, Rebirth, Lachesis, Origin of Evil</keywords>

--- Page 427 ---
<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the *Timaeus*, specifically examining why the Demiurge (the Divine Craftsman) is not responsible for evil and how souls are distributed throughout the cosmos.</meta>

[BOOK V.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 421

In what way does evil exist because of this? Shall we say it exists as a primary substance <note>original: "precedaneous hypostasis," meaning something that exists by design from the beginning</note>? By no means. For things that exist in that way are limited, have a clear purpose, and are naturally aligned with their creator. Evil, therefore, is implanted in souls as a byproduct <note>original: "parypostasis," a Neoplatonic term for evil as a "deviation from existence" or a side-effect rather than a primary creation</note>, or a deviation from true existence, occurring either through a lack of harmony <note>original: "symmetry"</note>, through a mixing of different natures, or in some other way. Plato, knowing this, says, "*in order that the Demiurge might not be the cause of the future wickedness of each.*" For the word *future* shows that the existence of wickedness is something added later, foreign to the soul’s nature, and implanted from the outside. 

But what is this "legislative announcement"? For evils have already been discussed before this point. May we not say that it signifies the single understanding within the Demiurge of all the laws of Fate? For the *divine ordinance* <note>original: "thesmos"</note> encompasses all laws. The *ordinance* in Adrastia <note>a goddess representing inescapable destiny</note> includes the laws of Saturn and Jupiter, and also the laws of Fate; but the *ordinance* in the Demiurge both encompasses and gives existence to all worldly natures. This announcement, however, with the addition¹ [of the words, "*all these things to souls*,”] signifies that the authority of this *ordinance* extends to all things, and that its protective oversight reaches even to the very last of things.

<margin>42 D</margin>
> “He scattered some of them into the earth, others into the moon, and others into the other instruments of time <note>the planets and stars</note>.”

It must not be supposed that this sowing <note>original: "semination"</note> of souls was done by chance. For how could the indefinite or random intervene in things that exist eternally with unchanging consistency? Nor should it be thought of as a mere distribution by the creator. For the souls being sown are neither moved only by external forces, nor do they act without deliberate choice. Instead, this sowing is accomplished from above, in harmony with the divine intellect of the Demiurge, and with the full agreement of the souls’ own wills. For each soul both knows and chooses its proper place, and establishes its "vehicle" <note>the subtle body or light-shell that carries the soul</note> in appropriate parts of the universe. Each soul is not the same as the Gods around whom it is sown—as some people claim—for that would make a part the same as the whole. If that were true, the arrangement of leaders and followers would be confused, and the order of pure <note>original: "undefiled"</note> souls and those that are not pure would be destroyed. Nor does each of these souls connect itself with random parts of the universe. Rather, an essential similarity exists before this kind of sowing occurs. For what else could someone point to as the cause of this division? Is it that individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls should exist without being coordinated with universal <note>original: "total"</note> souls?

¹ Instead of "preface" <note>original: "προθεσεως" (protheseos)</note> here, it is necessary to read "addition" <note>original: "προσθεσεως" (prosthetheos)</note>.

<summary>Proclus explains that evil is a "byproduct" rather than a primary creation of the Demiurge and describes the "sowing" of souls into the planets and Earth as a deliberate process involving both divine intellect and the soul's own choice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, focusing on how souls are distributed ("sown") throughout the universe and the relationship between individual souls and the "younger Gods" who oversee the material world.</meta>

### PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V. TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 422]

And should we say that their vehicles <note>original: "ochema," the subtle or "astral" body that carries the soul</note> ought to be separated from the universal circulations? This, however, is impossible, for parts everywhere follow the whole. Is it, therefore, because souls differ from each other? And how, in short, do they differ from each other, since they exist in immaterial forms? Shall we say then, that they differ from each other, but were not distinguished according to the primary measures of divine souls? And how, in this case, is ascent and perfection imparted <note>The translator corrects the Greek *apheken* (sent away) to *epheken* (imparted or sent into).</note> to them through divine souls? We must say, therefore, that this sowing <note>original: "semination," the process of distributing souls into the cosmos</note> is entirely <note>The Greek *panta* (all things) is corrected to *pante* (entirely/wholly).</note> defined according to a divine and perfect intellect. And that is enough regarding this particular point.

But let us, in the next place, connect this with a survey of the specific words used. *The sowing of souls, therefore, along with their vehicles among the younger Gods <note>the celestial deities or planetary powers created by the Demiurge</note>, precedes every other creation performed by these Gods.* For it is necessary that souls should have leaders not only as souls, but as worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note> natures; and that, being granted the government of living beings, they should be arranged under some of the divine orbits. 

The term "sowing," however, reveals through its very name the divided distribution of the vehicles. It shows the power that invisibly contains all individual souls within the universal souls, and the productive energy of divine bodies, by which they fill these individual vehicles with their own life and unique character. For everything that is sown receives something from the earth in which it is planted. 

Hence, from all that has been said, this is first of all evident: there is no "sowing" regarding the soul of the universe. For it is not proper to contrast the sowing of this universal soul with the sowing of other souls, nor to contrast the whole world with its parts. For if it were possible <note>The original Greek *adunaton* (impossible) is corrected to *dunaton* (possible).</note> for an individual soul to remain on high during the whole period of the universe, it would be possible for a sowing of souls to take place even around the soul of the universe. *But this universal soul is arranged in the world as a monad <note>a singular, unified principle</note>. For it is the primary unity of the worldly souls that distribute <note>The Greek is corrected from the singular *kataneimamenes* to the plural *kataneimamenon* to match the plural "souls."</note> its powers.* 

Indeed, a power of the soul of the universe is present with each of the divine bodies. Around this number, however, the classes of beings that are superior to us, as well as individual souls, are divided—these having the rank of attendants. Secondly, there is a sowing of souls in each of the elements below the moon <note>original: "sublunary elements"—earth, water, air, and fire</note>, in the celestial spheres, and in the stars. We have already shown the types of natures around which the distribution of souls takes place, so that the sowing is also centered around these.

<summary>Proclus explains the "semination" or sowing of individual souls into the cosmos, arguing that they are distributed among the "younger Gods" and celestial spheres while remaining connected to the universal Soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, specifically discussing how the individual vehicles of souls are distributed throughout the celestial spheres and their relationship to the measurement of time.</meta>

### BOOK V. TIMÆUS OF PLATO [423]

...vehicles of them. For all of them contribute to the creation of time—some by themselves, and others together with whole systems, in the same manner as the stars. All of them are the instruments of time. For all the fixed stars, and every cosmic God, being moved in a circle, have entire periods of time by which the whole duration of the cosmic life is measured. They also have "restorations" <note>original: "apocatastases," the return of celestial bodies to the same relative positions</note> in common with this life and with each other. 

However, Plato only mentions those instruments of time whose cyclic periods <note>original: "apocatastatic periods"</note> can be perceived through the senses. Dividing the whole world into the heavens and the realm of generation <note>the material world of change and growth</note>, he treats the moon and the earth as the two extremes of these based on their position. He is satisfied with these two because he is discussing the division of the "lowest" souls and the sowing <note>original: "semination"</note> of the most individual vehicles. These vehicles are naturally suited to change and are designed to approach and enter into the densest physical bodies.

After these details, it is also worthwhile to understand, thirdly, that vehicles are likewise distributed among the fixed stars. For every part of the world is full of individual souls who are placed under their savior Gods and follow the daimons <note>original: "dæmons," intermediate spirits that act as guides or attendants to the Gods</note> that depend on them. 

One might ask whether any of these individual bodies are raised above the sphere of Saturn <note>original: *sphairan* (sphere); the translator notes that this word was missing in the original Greek text and should be inserted</note>, or whether all of them are arranged in the planetary spheres according to an alliance with the fixed stars. This deserves consideration. Regarding the planets themselves, those skilled in these matters say that different planets are allied to different signs of the zodiac. It is not at all surprising, then, if the vehicles of souls exist in the planetary spheres while different vehicles revolve in conjunction with different fixed stars. 

One might find this more rational than placing them above the sphere of Saturn, since the planetary sphere is better suited to a variety of life, a tendency toward physical birth, and a nature composed of bodies that have both circular and straight-line motion. However, it is better to say that there is a sowing of souls among the fixed stars, and that those vehicles which are purified, star-like, and unencumbered—having a simple life and a motion centered on intellect and wisdom, following the cycle of the "Same" <note>The "Circle of the Same" refers to the rotation of the fixed stars/celestial equator in Plato's cosmology</note>—ascend as far as the "inerratic" sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, so called because they do not "wander" like planets</note>. It would be ridiculous for souls to be distributed among the fixed stars while their vehicles were sown somewhere else. For just as one soul relates to another soul, so a vehicle relates to its kindred <note>The translator replaces the original *symmiges* (mixed) with *syngenei* (kindred/related)</note> vehicle. It is better, therefore, to admit this.

<summary>Proclus explains that all celestial bodies act as instruments of time and argues that the subtle vehicles of souls are distributed among both the planets and the fixed stars according to their purity.</summary>
<keywords>Proclus, Timaeus, Plato, apocatastasis, vehicles of the soul, fixed stars, planetary spheres, Saturn, semination, cosmology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, specifically discussing the distinction between the "distribution" of souls to the stars and their "semination" (sowing) into the material world via their immortal vehicles.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.
[424]

It is better to claim that souls are scattered there, but that their vehicles <term>The "vehicle" (ochema) is the soul’s immortal, subtle body that allows it to interact with the material world.</term> do not rise as high as the vehicles of the fixed stars. In nature, parts everywhere naturally move toward the wholes to which they belong, unless they are broken apart by forces foreign to their nature. These soul-vehicles, however, are indestructible and immortal because they were created by the one Demiurge <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine craftsman or creator of the universe</note>. These claims are more acceptable than the previous ones regarding the sowing <note>original: "semination"</note> and distribution of souls and their vehicles, both of which are carried out by the Demiurge.

Since this sowing involves souls along with their vehicles—and not just souls alone, as was the case with the earlier distribution—Plato correctly says that the Demiurge sowed some of them into the earth and others into the moon. This indicates *that each of these souls is now a human being, and specifically the first man.* The definition here also applies: a human is a soul using a body, and the immortal human uses an immortal body. It is also necessary to distinguish this immortal body from every mortal body, so that a human can become what they were before falling into the cycle of birth <note>original: "lapse into generation"</note>. For the sowing now concerns human beings, rather than just souls. It is very fitting, then, to say that some were sowed into the earth and others into the moon.

These points must be considered along with what was said before. Additionally, we should note that souls will never be located outside the physical universe <note>original: "supermundane situation"</note>, even according to those who believe there are other spheres beyond the fixed stars. However, the highest and simplest of the vehicles do share in the heavenly light <note>original: "ethereal splendor"</note>. But the *distribution* is different from the *semination*. The former refers to souls alone, while the latter refers to souls joined with their vehicles. This is why, when speaking of the former, Plato says the Demiurge *distributed* each soul to its own star; but here, he says he *disseminated* (sowed) them—some into the earth and others into the moon—because they are now expressing human characteristics. In the stars, a human is a soul using an immortal body, and that human is eternal. 

The *distribution* is therefore different from the *semination*; the former is said to be into the stars, but the latter is into the "instruments of time" <note>the planets and celestial bodies that measure time</note>. Consequently, it might seem that each of these processes leads to a different place. The earth is not a star, so there will not be a *distribution* of souls to it; similarly, the fixed stars are not called instruments of time, so there will not be a *semination* among them. But the planets alone are both stars and instruments of time; so, regarding the planets, there will be both a distribution and a semination. It would be clearly absurd, however, if both of these did not take place regarding the earth and the—

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s discussion of the Demiurge’s role in placing souls throughout the cosmos. It specifically addresses how souls are both "distributed" to the stars and "sown" into planetary bodies like the Earth and Moon, and how these processes relate to the soul's eventual restoration (apocatastasis).</meta>

# BOOK V.] TIMAEUS OF PLATO.
[425]

fixed stars. For if the Demiurge <note>original: "Demiurgus"; the divine craftsman</note> is the one who both distributes and sows the souls, both these actions are essentially inherent in the nature of souls. If this is the case, it is necessary that both actions should concern the same goal, so that the restoration <term>original: "apocatastasis"; the return of a soul to its original, perfected state</term> of every soul may be into one single thing. Otherwise, through the "distribution," a soul might return to its kindred star, but be forced through "sowing" to return to something else entirely. For whatever is sown is naturally allied and adapted to the place in which it is essentially scattered. 

Therefore, if these things are true, the Earth itself must be called a "star"—not because of its visible physical mass, but because of its ethereal and star-like vehicle <term>The "vehicle" (ochema) is the soul’s immortal, subtle body that allows it to interact with the material world.</term>, since our own soul-vehicle is also a thing of this kind. It must also be admitted that the fixed stars cooperate in the creation of time. Consequently, insofar as they have cycles—even if those cycles are unknown to us—they measure the whole of time, each in its own different way. For not every fixed star has the same period of restoration <note>original: "apocatastasis"</note>, yet we have no certain sensory evidence of their movement as we do for the revolutions of the planets.

Therefore, all parts of the world receive scattered individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls, and every worldly God is the overseer of the individual Gods and souls¹ distributed and sown around him, in accordance with the divine intellect of the Demiurge. But Plato says that the "distribution" primarily concerns the stars, while the "sowing" concerns the lowest of the universal wholes—the moon and the earth. By this, he indicates the proper status of each: the former is more divine because it is incorporeal <note>not composed of matter</note>, while the latter is subordinate because the sowing involves physical bodies. 

This distinction is evident because he mentions the preceding causes of the distribution and the sowing separately at different times, even though both involve the same things; in this way, he shows how they differ from each other. Therefore, while there is a "distribution" of the soul regarding the earth, this only applies insofar as the earth possesses something star-like and incorporeal. Conversely, while there is a "sowing" of the soul regarding a star, this only applies insofar as the star has something allied to the earth, which is its physical body. 

The Earth and the Moon were likewise included in the sowing because of their similarity to each other, as both produce shadows. What the Earth is among the universal wholes, the Moon is among the heavenly bodies. Consequently, there will be a restoration <note>original: "apocatastasis"</note> to the Earth for those souls that were originally sown into it, and they will receive their assigned places there. It is not surprising that Plato says in the *Phaedrus* that the better assignments are heavenly, while the lowest are underground. In that dialogue, his only intention was to speak of the two extremes, without mentioning the fortunate assignments in the air or on the earth. Hence,
