<meta>This page continues Proclus’s analysis of the Demiurge’s "sowing" (semination) of souls. Proclus argues that the Earth and Moon are destinations for souls that will eventually inhabit human bodies, and he explores the various "types" of humanity described across Plato's dialogues.</meta>

# BOOK V.] PROCLUS ON THE [426]

When he <note>Plato</note> mentions those souls that are the last, he does not simply say that they are terrestrial <note>of the earth</note>. Instead, he reveals what they are through the tribunals <note>judgment seats</note> under the earth. The divine allotments within the earth—insofar as the earth itself is a divinity—are different from those allotments characterized by punishment. As we have already said, however, "distribution" must be distinguished from "semination" <note>original: "semination"; the scattering of souls like seeds</note>. For semination pertains especially to certain physical natures. But distribution—which is a separation according to form, and not like semination, the placing <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original footnote: For "theois" (gods) here, it is necessary to read "thesin" (placing/positioning).</note> of some things in others—transcendently belongs to incorporeal <note>spiritual or non-physical</note> natures. 

But since the assertion that the Demiurge <note>the divine craftsman of the universe</note> disseminated some souls into the earth and others into the moon refers to human beings, as we have said, it may be assumed from the *Politicus* <note>Plato’s dialogue *The Statesman*</note> that Plato knew of a "man" who is an immortal soul using an immortal vehicle <term>In Neoplatonism, the "vehicle" (ochema) is a subtle body that carries the soul through the heavens.</term>. For he says there that souls were "men" in the Saturnian period <note>the Golden Age of Cronus</note>, during which only the immortal part of us lived. That he also knew of another "man"—namely, the soul which uses the "middle" vehicle—is evident from the *Phaedo*. There, he says that men dwell on the summit of the earth and live for a much longer time than the men here below. Moreover, he also knew the "last man," who lives in conjunction with this outward physical body. In every case, according to Plato, "man" is a soul using a body; it is either an immortal body, the second <note>middle</note> body, or the composite <note>physical</note> body. Hence, by adding the difference of the body and of the soul that uses it, we shall be able to define what a "man" is.

<margin>42 d</margin>
-> “But then after this semination, he delivered to the junior Gods.” <-

What this "semination" is, where it comes from for the souls, how it differs from "distribution," and how it is the specific characteristic of the creation of individual parts has been frequently mentioned by us in what was said before. But we must now show who the "junior Gods" are. It is evident that the worldly <note>mundane</note> Gods are called "junior Gods." They appear, however, to be named this by Plato for a few reasons. Either it is by comparing them with the ancient and venerable nature of the invisible creation, and the transcendence of power and perfection of intellect contained within it (for that which is more intellectual in the Gods is more ancient: 
> "But Zeus <note>original: "Jove"</note> was born the first, and more he knows," 
says Homer <note>original: Iliad 13.355</note>). 

Or, they are named this because they always make the process of generation <note>the physical world of birth and decay</note> new. When it becomes old and weak through its material nature, they recall it to a state of existence according to nature through their motions. They do this by sending into it flows of all-various productive principles and powers, and thus they render it perpetually new. Or, they are called this because, while having intellectual essences...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, specifically discussing the nature of the "junior gods"—the celestial deities to whom the primary Demiurge delegates the creation of mortal life. Proclus explains why these eternal beings are described using terms of youth and "becoming."</meta>

# BOOK V.] PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO [427]

<warning>A vertical section on the right side of the first paragraph (lines 10-12) is affected by a printing error or paper crease, causing a gap and partial illegibility in the text.</warning>

Depending on them <note>the higher divine causes</note>, they eternally act with the highest degree of intellectual vigor. For, as the poets say, Hebe <note>the goddess of youth</note> pours out their wine, and they drink nectar and survey the entire sensible world. Therefore, employing unchanging and unswerving intellect, they fill all things with their demiurgic providence <note>the care and craft of a divine creator</note>. They are given this title because a Curetic deity <term>Curetic deity: Referring to the Curetes, a class of guardian gods in Greek theology who represent intellectual purity and stable, protective power.</term> is present with them—or a deity belonging to the order of the Curetes—illuminating their intellectual thoughts with purity and their motion with stability. This provides them with a firm power through which they govern all things without losing the essential characteristics of their nature. 

Or, and this is the truest reason of all, they are named this because their unified source <note>original: "monad"</note> is called a <unclear>recent God</unclear>. For theologians give this title to Bacchus <note>Dionysus</note>, who is the <unclear>monarch of all the second</unclear> fabrication <note>the "second fabrication" refers to the creation of the visible, material world as opposed to the eternal, ideal world</note>. For Jupiter <note>Zeus/the Demiurge</note> established him as the king of all <unclear>mundane Gods, and</unclear> distributed the first honors to him:

-> Though the God is young, he is an infant guest.<sup>1</sup> <-

For this reason, theologians are also accustomed to calling the sun a *recent God*, and Heraclitus says that the sun is a *daily youth*, as it participates in Dionysian power. 

Or, for a reason most appropriate to Platonic principles, they are named "junior" because the bodies that are generated are dependent upon them. The essence of these bodies is not granted an existence in eternity, but rather within the whole of time. They are "junior," therefore, not because they once began to exist, but because they are always being generated. As we have observed before, they exist in a state of "becoming" or are perpetually rising into existence. For anything that is "generated" <note>produced in the physical world</note> does not possess everything it has all at once in a single moment of infinity; rather, it has an infinity that is perpetually being supplied. Thus, they are called junior because their existence is stretched out alongside time, always advancing into existence and possessing a renovated immortality <note>an immortality maintained by constant renewal</note>.

<margin>42 d-e</margin>
> "The duty of fashioning mortal bodies, and besides this, to rule over whatever else remained necessary to the human soul, and over everything resulting from their creations."

The delivery of this first fabrication is a communication and generation of demiurgic powers. These powers are distinct from everything produced directly by the "second fabrication." It is a progression of production from the invisible into the visible, and a division of unified power into the many-sided government of the world. But the—

# BOOK V.] PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO [428]

<margin>Handwritten "428" in the left margin.</margin>

The formation of bodies makes the junior gods similar to the hidden <note>original: "unapparent"</note> process of creation. For that primary creation was the cause of universal bodies <note>bodies that exist as whole systems, like the elements or the heavens</note>, just as these gods are the causes of partial bodies <note>individual physical forms</note>, though they show a decrease in power. The Demiurge <term>Demiurge: The primary architect or "craftsman" of the universe in Platonic philosophy.</term> is the ultimate cause of the body that they make and shape; but they specifically form the partial bodies—those endowed with specific qualities. Therefore, "body" in a general sense is not "born" in time and cannot be destroyed, a view also held by Aristotle. For, says he, an empty space <note>original: "vacuum"</note> would exist if a body could be created outside <note>original: εξω σωματος (exō sōmatos)</note>¹ the body of the entire universe. 

However, this *particular* body is subject to decay because it is limited in nature; for the *wholes* of the elements <note>the total mass of fire, air, water, and earth</note> brought their existence from the primary creation of the whole. The addition of the human soul, which was the final part <note>original: λοιπης (loipēs)</note>² to be created, makes the mundane <note>original: mundane; gods belonging to the physical world or cosmos</note> gods similar to the fatherly power of the Demiurge. For it is the duty of a father to generate life. Every father is a cause of life: the intelligible father produces intelligible life, the intellectual father produces intellectual life, and the supermundane <note>original: supermundane; existing above the physical world</note> father produces supermundane life. 

Thus, the mundane gods who create physical life are also fathers. The creative work assigned to these gods produces the nature of individual animals. For this individual animal, which is connected to the immortal soul, consists of both soul and body. The creation of all other things follows this rule: parts are created for the sake of the whole. But the authority which the Demiurge gave the junior gods activates their divine care <note>original: "providential inspection"</note>, their power to hold things together, and their protective oversight. Without these, the bodies they shape and the mortal forms of life would quickly vanish into nothingness. Therefore, before these were created, the Demiurge established their ruling gods to be their guardians and saviors. Thus, the junior gods possess creative powers <note>original: "demiurgic"</note> to give form to things; life-giving powers <note>original: "vivific"</note> to provide secondary life; and perfecting powers <note>original: "perfective"</note> to complete what is lacking in the process of birth. They also possess many other powers beyond these, which are impossible for us to grasp with our human understanding.

<margin>428</margin>

> “He likewise commanded them to govern the mortal animal in the best and most beautiful manner possible, so that it might not become the cause of evil to itself.”

Of everything the one Demiurge delivers to the junior gods, we must recognize three most beautiful boundaries: the good-shaped <note>original: "boniform"; having the form of the Good</note> will of him who...

Regarding the demiurgic <term>demiurgic: relating to the "Demiurge," the divine craftsman who shapes the physical world.</term> production of the junior gods <term>junior gods: lower-ranking deities who carry out the specific, material creation tasks assigned by the primary Creator.</term> themselves, we must again examine three major elements: a turning toward the Good, a shift toward intellectual beauty, and a free power sufficient to rule over everything they govern. 

For just as Phanes <note>original: Phanes. This refers to Jupiter, who Proclus identifies here with Phanes or the "First-born" (Protogonus), who serves as the model (paradigm) of the universe.</note>¹ himself—the Creator of entire systems—made the whole world as beautiful and good as possible, he also willed that the secondary creators should govern mortal animals in the most beautiful and best way. He poured beauty upon them from the intellectual realms, while filling them with that "good-forming" <note>original: "boniform"</note> power and will that he himself possessed when he created the whole world. In this way, the process of birth and change <note>original: "generation"</note> will also share in beauty and goodness, as far as its nature allows, provided the gods who connect and sustain it adorn it themselves, since they are transcendently decorated with beauty and good.

If, however, the secondary creators have such a nature, then nothing evil or unnatural is generated by the celestial gods. It is not proper to divide the gods in the heavens into "beneficent" and "malignant" groups, as many people do; for because they are gods, this is impossible. Instead, the mortal creature is the cause of evil to itself. For neither disease, nor poverty <note>original: πονηρια (ponēria/wickedness). The translator notes it is necessary to read this as κακια (kakia/vice).</note>², nor anything else of this kind is truly evil; the only true evils are the corruption of the soul, lack of self-control, cowardice, and every vice. 

We ourselves are the causes of these things. Even if we are pushed by others toward these vices and are negatively affected, it is still through our own agency, since we have the power to associate with the good and separate ourselves from the bad. According to Plato, therefore, we must not think that some gods are malicious and others kind. We must admit that all of them are the sources of all the good that mortals are able to receive. Things that are truly evil are not produced by the gods, but are only *signified* by them, as we have observed before. They present frightening appearances and signs to those who are able to see and read the "letters" in the universe—signs which the creators of mortal natures write through the patterns <note>original: configurations</note> of their orbital revolutions. 

And even if someone should derive a certain evil from the motions of the celestial gods—becoming cowardly or undisciplined—the gods act in one way, while their influences are received by souls in another. For the "overflow" <note>original: efflux</note> of intellect, says Plotinus <note>Plotinus: A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD).</note>, becomes "cunning" in someone who receives that influence poorly; the gift of a refined life becomes "excess" <note>original: "intemperance"</note> through a similar cause. In short, while...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the role of the Demiurge (the divine Creator) and the junior gods. It follows a discussion on why the gods are not the authors of evil, even though they oversee a world where evil exists.</meta>

# BOOK V.] PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS [430]

The gods produce everything with benevolence, but their gifts are received by earthly beings in a contrary or distorted way. Therefore, the givers who bestow these gifts with kindness are not to be accused as the authors of evil. Instead, the blame lies with the recipients, who ruin these gifts because of their own unfitness. 

Similarly, in Homer’s writings, Jupiter <note>original: "Jupiter in Homer." This refers to Zeus in the opening of the *Odyssey*, where he complains that mortals blame the gods for suffering that they actually bring upon themselves through their own folly.</note> blames souls for vainly accusing the Gods, while they themselves are the true causes of their own misfortunes. For the Gods are the sources of good and the providers of intellect and life; they are not the causes of any evil. Even a "partial nature" <term>partial nature: an individual nature, such as a human parent, as opposed to the universal nature of the cosmos.</term> is not the cause of evil to its own offspring. What, then, should we think concerning the Gods themselves? Is it not clear that they are even more the causes of good to their creations? Within them, there is power, a self-perfect nature, and universal goodness—all of which are the opposite of evil. Evil, by its own nature, is powerless, imperfect, and lacks any true measure.

<margin>432</margin>

->“At the same time, he who had orderly arranged all these details remained in his own accustomed manner.”<-

Plato, throughout his work, often summarizes a long explanation with a single concluding thought. He knew that in the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: the "Craftsman" or divine Creator who shapes the material universe according to an eternal, intellectual model.</term>, a single intellectual perception contains a multitude of ideas, a single power connects many powers, and a uniform cause unites many divided causes. 

Therefore, the previous words, "*Having therefore instructed souls in all these particulars*," and the words currently before us, "*He who orderly disposed all these particulars*," trace the distinct actions of the Demiurge back to a single, unified cause. Furthermore, the word "*all*" shows that the creation is fully realized within its proper boundaries. The phrase "*orderly disposed*" indicates the order pervading all beings which the Demiurge introduced to the "mundane gods" <term>mundane gods: the gods who govern the physical world, such as the stars and planets.</term> and to individual souls. This demonstrated that the mundane gods are themselves secondary creators (Demiurgi), while it inscribed the laws of Fate <note>original: "laws of Fate." In Neoplatonism, Fate governs the physical and temporal consequences of a soul's choices.</note> within individual souls. 

Moreover, the word "*remained*" does not simply indicate standing still or a fixed way of thinking, but rather an "establishment"¹ <note>original: εδραν (edran, meaning a seat or bench). Proclus suggests reading this instead as ιδρυσιν (idrusin), meaning a foundation or stable establishment.</note> in the One. In this state, the Demiurge is separate from the "wholes" (the entire created system) and is distinct from the beings who perceive him through their intellect. This establishment is eternal and always remains the same. These concepts are also indicated by the words "*accustomed*" and "*manner*." One shows that this permanence is always the same, while the other shows the unique way the Demiurge remains stable. For "manner" indicates a specific quality; the way something is held together is different from the way it remains unchanging, and both of these differ from the specific stability of the Creator.

---

<note>¹ For "seat" (edran), it is necessary to read "establishment" or "founding" (idrusin).</note>

He also analyzes Plato's description of the Demiurge's "remaining" in his own manner, explaining it as a state of divine stability and transcendence from the created world.</summary>

# BOOK V.] PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS [431]

<margin>42 e</margin>
> "But because he remained in his own nature, as soon as his children understood their father’s order, they became obedient to it."

When the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: the "Craftsman" or primary Creator in Platonic philosophy.</term> speaks, the junior gods take the role of listeners. When he perceives through intellect, they learn; for learning is dianoetic <term>dianoetic: relating to discursive thought or reasoning, as opposed to direct intellectual intuition.</term>. When he remains in his state of absolute unity, his children perceive intellectually. They always occupy an order inferior to his. Being filled by him, they maintain the role of listeners in relation to him; but as they unfold his singular power, they are like learners. For a student is one who unfolds the intellect of their teacher. 

However, because they are deified by him, they also act as those who perceive through pure intellect. For the intellect becomes divine through its contact <note>original: "aphē" (αφή). The text notes that "saphē" was a printing error for "aphē."</note> with *the One*. Therefore, while the father remains in his own state, his children rightly perceive him intellectually. They are intellects participating in divine souls that inhabit vehicles of pure, undefiled bodies. They intellectually perceive the father’s order, which existed within him even before the effects of that order were arranged—the plan by which he became the source of all things. This is consistent with what Orpheus says regarding the single source <note>original: "monad"</note> of the junior gods:

->Though all things by the father Jove were formed,<-
->Yet their completion they to Bacchus owe;<-
<note>original: Jove and Bacchus. In Neo-Platonic interpretation, Jove (Zeus) is the Demiurge who creates the universe's essence, while Bacchus (Dionysus) represents the distribution of that life into individual, multiple forms.</note>

The same must be said of the junior gods: they provide the finishing touches to the creation <note>original: "fabrication"</note> which the father established through his own intellectual activity. As the Chaldæan Oracle also says, "The father understood these things, and the mortal nature became animated for him." Mortal natures were thus fashioned and given life by the Demiurge's thought alone. However, the junior gods reveal and expand his total production through their own visible craftsmanship, being filled by the power of the Demiurge.

> "And receiving the immortal principle of the mortal animal, in imitation of their craftsman, they borrowed from the world the parts of fire and earth, water and air, as things which they should eventually restore; and they joined the received parts together, though not with the same unbreakable bonds that held their own bodies together."

Plato indicates to us here the distinction between the primary creation and the secondary creation...

<meta>This page continues the comparison between the primary Demiurge (the Great Architect) and the "junior gods" (lesser divine beings) who execute his creative plan. Proclus explains how the two levels of divinity work together to bridge the gap between eternal spiritual truths and the changing physical world.</meta>

<page-num>432</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.</header>

...through many words and stages <note>original: "bathmōn" (βαθμῶν). The text notes that "batheōn" (depths) was a printing error for "bathmōn" (steps or stages).</note>. For if the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: from the Greek *demiourgos*, meaning "craftsman." In Platonic thought, this is the divine mind that shapes the universe according to eternal patterns.</term> sets things in order, but the junior gods obey his commands, then the former is the cause of all created things simply by commanding them. The latter, being stirred into action by the Demiurge, receive the defined limits of their entire creative work from him. And if he remains centered in himself while they move around him, it is clear that he is the eternal cause of things that exist within time. They, being filled by him, act throughout the whole span of time. Furthermore, if he is perfectly established in his own usual way, but they emerge from him to reveal his unified and indescribable nature, then they derive the specific measurements of their creative work from him.

Moreover, he is said to have the dignity of a father, while they are called his children, expressing his creative power and his singular goodness. He is celebrated for delivering the principles of creation from his exalted home, while they are celebrated for receiving the immortal principle that helps organize the mortal realm. He is the fountain of life for eternal beings, but they are the cause of existence for animals with mortal forms. He extends himself as a model <term>paradigm: an eternal blueprint or model after which the physical world is patterned.</term> for the many gods, while they are said to imitate this creative intellect. He is said to produce the entire world and everything that fills it; they, however, are said to borrow parts from their father's creations in order to complete their own specific works. He employs entirely spiritual <term>incorporeal: having no physical body or substance.</term> powers, while they also use physical ones. He gives existence to unbreakable bonds, but they create bonds that can be dissolved. He is said to instill a unity that is older than the things it unites, while they introduce a secondary unity—one that comes after the creation—to beings made of many conflicting parts. Finally, he is said to produce all things as a whole, without division; they produce things with division, minutely distributing the existence of mortal natures into "small and invisible nails" <note>This is a reference to the *Timaeus* 43a, where Plato describes the junior gods pinning the soul into the body using tiny, invisible bolts or nails.</note>. 

From these points, we can understand the distinction between the two levels of creation. However, the union and connection between them can be seen in the words before us. Here, a connection is made between the second and the first creation—between the visible and the invisible, and between divided and unified production.

Therefore, it is necessary that the lowest part of the first, invisible creation should merge with the highest point of the second. In this same way, the heavens are joined with the "sublunary region" <term>sublunary region: the area "below the moon," referring to the Earth and its atmosphere, where things are subject to change and decay.</term>. The lowest of the celestial bodies shows the first principle of change, while the highest essence of...

<summary>Proclus contrasts the primary Demiurge, who acts eternally and through unity, with the junior gods, who act in time and through division to create mortal beings. He explains that these two levels of creation are joined together like a chain, linking the eternal spiritual realm to the physical world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "junior gods" and their role in the creation of the physical world. It explores how these lesser divine beings bridge the gap between the eternal Father (the Demiurge) and the mortal realm by crafting bodies from the four elements.</meta>

<page-num>433</page-num>
<header>BOOK 5.] TIMAEUS OF PLATO.</header>

Earthly natures <term>sublunary: literally "under the moon," referring to the physical world of change and decay below the celestial spheres.</term> move in connection with the heavens. For this reason, the rational soul is joined here with the mortal form of life—that is, the most humble and specific part of the Father’s creations is joined with the highest of the natures produced by the junior gods. As "fathers," these junior gods produce life; but as "craftsmen," they produce bodies. They imitate Hephaestus <note>original: "Vulcan"</note> by crafting bodies, and Hera <note>original: "Juno"</note> by bringing them to life. Through both of these actions, they imitate the Great Architect <term>Demiurge: from the Greek *demiourgos*, the divine "craftsman" who shapes the universe.</term>. For he is both maker and father, but the junior gods fashion bodies by borrowing parts from the cosmic "wholes" <note>The "wholes" refer to the total masses of the four elements: fire, earth, air, and water.</note>. 

Everywhere, parts are composed from their respective wholes. When these wholes are non-physical (incorporeal), they are not reduced when parts arise from them. But when the wholes are physical bodies, the parts created from them take away from the whole. Therefore, if there were a constant taking away <note>original: "ablation"</note> and the parts stayed separate, the wholes would eventually be destroyed. This would mean that the process of birth and creation <term>generation: the process of coming into being or creation.</term> would stop, and the works of the primary creation would be erased by the secondary creation—an outcome that is impossible to accept. 

To prevent this from happening in the universe, composite parts are eventually broken down again to replenish the wholes. Thus, the creation of one thing is the decay of another, and the decay of one thing is the creation of another, ensuring that the cycle of birth and death <note>original: "generation and corruption"</note> continues forever. If creation only happened for a limited time, it would eventually stop because it uses finite materials that would run out. If those were used up, decay would also stop because everything would be gone. Therefore, if one of these must exist, the other must exist as well. Everything produced by this secondary creation is a temporary composite that can be broken down; since it is made within time, it will also be dissolved by time. 

The junior gods, therefore, are correctly described as "borrowing" parts that must eventually be returned to the whole. They borrow these from the entire universe <margin>The text notes that the Greek word should be *pantos* (the universe) rather than *patros* (father).</margin>. What they borrow are the four elements—fire, earth, water, and air—and they return them to the universe <margin>The text notes that the Greek word should be *panti* (to the universe) rather than *patri* (to the father).</margin>. The Father intends for the cosmic "wholes" he created to remain intact. This concludes the discussion on the work of the junior gods.

Now, let us focus on the specific words used by Timaeus. The word *receiving* shows how the junior gods receive the immortal soul as it descends in its first "vehicle" <note>In Platonic thought, the "vehicle" is a subtle, celestial body that carries the soul into the physical world.</note>. He refers to this entire process as "the immortal principle." It also shows that the gods provide for us everywhere through divine providence: the Father cares for us from above, while his children (the junior gods) care for us below, if it <meta>be</meta>

² Here also, for "father," it is necessary to read "the universe" <note>original: "panti" (παντί)</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the human soul interacts with different levels of divine influence. <header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.</header>

It is necessary to speak about this in a divided way. For our soul lives at one time according to the characteristics of *Jupiter* <note>original: "Jupiter" refers to Zeus as the stabilizing, governing intellect.</note>, and at another according to those of *Bacchus* <note>original: "Bacchus" refers to Dionysus as the source of divided, individual life.</note>; but in its earthly arrangement, it lives in a Titanic manner<sup>1</sup> <note>original: "Titannically." This refers to the soul being fragmented or focused on the material world, like the Titans of myth.</note>. The

---

<sup>1</sup> This is excellently explained by *Olympiodorus* <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher known for his commentaries on Plato.</note>, in his manuscript commentary on that part of the *Phaedo* where *Plato* speaks of the prohibition of suicide in the secret doctrines <note>original Greek: απορρητα (aporrheta), meaning "unspoken" or "arcane" teachings.</note>: "The argument," he says, "which *Plato* uses here against suicide is derived from *Orphic* mythology, which celebrates four kingdoms. The first is the kingdom of *Heaven* <note>Uranus</note>, whom *Saturn* <note>Cronus</note> attacked, cutting off his father’s genitals. After *Saturn*, *Jupiter* <note>Zeus</note> succeeded to the government of the world, having hurled his father into *Tartarus* <note>The deep abyss used as a dungeon of torment.</note>. After *Jupiter*, *Bacchus* <note>Dionysus</note> rose to power. According to the story, through the schemes of *Juno* <note>Hera</note>, Bacchus was torn to pieces by the *Titans* who surrounded him, and who then tasted his flesh. But *Jupiter*, enraged by the deed, struck the offenders with his thunderbolts and consumed them to ashes. From the vapor of the smoke ascending from their burning bodies, a certain matter was formed, and from this, mankind was produced.

"Therefore, it is unlawful to destroy ourselves—not for the reason *Plato's* words seem to imply (that we are in the body as if in a prison secured by a guard, for this is obvious and *Plato* would not have called such a plain statement 'secret'), but because our body is *Dionysiacal* <note>Of or belonging to Dionysus/Bacchus.</note>, or the property of *Bacchus*. We are a part of this God, since we are composed of the vapors of the *Titans* who tasted his flesh. *Socrates*, therefore, being careful not to disclose the secret part of this story, adds nothing more to the fable except that we are placed in a kind of prison secured by a guard; but the interpreters explain the fable openly."

And the mythical argument is as follows: In the Orphic tradition, four kingdoms are handed down. The first is that of Heaven, which Saturn succeeded after cutting off the genitals of his father. After Saturn, Jupiter reigned after hurling his father into Tartarus. Then Dionysus succeeded Jupiter, whom they say, by the plot of Hera, the Titans around him tore to pieces and tasted his flesh. And Jupiter, being angry at this, struck them with lightning, and from the soot of the vapors rising from them, matter being formed, humans were created. We must not, therefore, commit suicide—not because (as the phrasing seems to suggest) we are in a certain bond in the body; for this is clear, and he would not have called this a secret. Rather, we must not kill ourselves because our body is Dionysiacal; for we are a part of him, since we are composed from the soot of the Titans who tasted his flesh. Socrates, therefore, showing the secret by his actions, adds nothing more of the myth than that we are in a certain "guard-house." But the interpreters add the myth from the outside. <note>original Greek: Και εστι το μυθικον επιχειρημα τοιουτον. Παρα τω Ορφει τεσσαρες βασιλειαι παραδιδονται... Οι δε εξηγηται τον μυθον προστιθεασιν εξωθεν.</note>

After this, he beautifully observes, "That these four governments obscurely signify the different levels of virtues, through which our soul contains the symbols of all the virtues—theoretical, purifying, political, and ethical. For the soul either acts according to the theoretical virtues, the model for which is the government of *heaven* (to begin from the highest); and for this reason, heaven is named for 'beholding the things above' <note>original Greek: παρα του τα ανω οραν (para tou ta ano oran).</note>. Or it lives a purifying <term>cathartic: from the Greek *katharsis*, meaning a cleansing or purification of the soul.</term> life, the model of which is the *Saturnian* kingdom; for this reason, *Saturn* is so named because he is a pure intellect who surveys himself; hence he is said to 'devour his own offspring,' signifying how he turns back into himself. Or the soul acts according to the political virtues, symbolized by the government of *Jupiter*; hence *Jupiter* is the *Demiurge* <term>Demiurge: the divine "craftsman" or "architect" of the physical universe.</term>, so called because he operates upon lower natures. Or finally, the soul acts according to both ethical and physical virtues, symbolized by the kingdom of *Bacchus*; for this reason, he is fabled to be torn in pieces by the *Titans*, because these lower virtues do not follow one another but are separated from each other."

They hint <gloss>read: they hint</gloss> at the different levels of the virtues, according to which our soul, possessing symbols of all the virtues—theoretical, purifying, political, and ethical. For it either acts according to the theoretical virtues as a model of the kingdom of heaven, so that we may begin from above; for this reason, heaven is named from "beholding the things above." <note>original Greek: Αινιττονται [lege αινιττονται] δε τους διαφορους βαθμους των αρετων καθ’ ας η ημετερα ψυχη συμβολα εχουσα πασων των αρετων... διο και ουρανος ειρηται παρα του τα ανω οραν.</note>

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*, specifically focusing on the division of labor between the supreme Creator (the Demiurgus) and the lesser "junior gods." It explores the origins of the human soul and body and references the Neoplatonist Olympiodorus to explain different states of the soul's existence through the lens of Greek mythology.</meta>

<page-num>435</page-num>
<header>BOOK V.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

The word *principle*, however, does not simply reveal what comes first in the composition of a human being. Instead, it signifies that which is the leader and ruler of secondary natures. This is how it exists according to nature, and it was produced by the Gods for this very purpose. Just as the <term>Demiurgus</term> <note>The supreme "Craftsman" or Creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy.</note> established the soul of the universe to rule over its body, so too did the various <term>Demiurgi</term> <note>The plural form, referring here to the "junior gods" or lesser celestial powers.</note> establish our soul as the ruling principle in the mortal animal. If we fail to rule over our mortal nature, the fault lies not with the power that arranged our soul, but with the laziness of the soul being governed. 

The word *immortal* encompasses every nature that the Demiurgus created. This includes both the soul's "vehicle" <note>An ethereal body that carries the soul between incarnations.</note> and the rational soul itself. The rational soul was perfectly produced by the Father, who scattered its essence throughout the world and from whom it originated. Again, <term>Timæus</term> <note>The main speaker in Plato's dialogue of the same name.</note> shows that the junior Gods are the life-giving causes and creators of the mortal animal. They perform each of these roles in conjunction with motion, so that their creations might be mortal.

Furthermore, the words "*in imitation of their artificer*" are appropriate. The junior Gods create bodies by imitating the creative characteristics of the Father. Just as he built the entire universe from the "wholes" of the elements <note>The pure, universal forms of fire, air, water, and earth.</note>, they fashion individual bodies from individual parts. They do this so that while they imitate him, a sense of "diminution" or smaller scale is preserved. Thus, they remain Creators, but they are creators of partial, individual things. 

The expression *they borrowed* reveals that the parts making up our bodies belong more to the universal "wholes" and to higher realms than they belong to us. If this is the case, why should people grieve when they die? And why is death — the dissolution of these parts — considered *dreadful*? How can it be anything but good if the universe receives back what is its own? It is easy to see that the parts of our bodies belong more to the universe than to ourselves, for their natural places are within the universal wholes, not within us. The phrase "*the gluing together of the received parts*" demonstrates that the union found in mortal natures is of a later origin and added after the fact. In the universe, the whole comes before the parts, and "the one" comes before the multitude. But in us, many separate things are brought together.

-> Either the soul lives a purificatory life, modeled after the kingdom of Saturn <note>original: η καθαρτικως ζη, ης παραδειγμα η κρονεια βασιλεια (hē kathartikōs zē, hēs paradeigma hē kroneia basileia)</note>, which is why Saturn is called "Pure-Mind" <note>original: κορο-νους (koro-nous), a philosophical pun on the name Cronus/Saturn</note> because he sees himself. This is also why he is said to swallow his own offspring, as he returns back into himself. Or it lives according to political virtues, symbolized by the kingdom of Jupiter <note>Zeus</note>; therefore Jupiter is the Creator <note>Demiurgus</note> because he acts upon secondary things. Or it lives according to ethical and physical virtues, symbolized by the kingdom of Dionysus; this is why he is torn to pieces, because these lower virtues do not always follow one another. <-

And thus far speaks Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>. In these passages, it is necessary to observe that since the Titans are the final craftsmen of things and are closest to what they create, humans are said to be composed from their fragments. This is because the human soul has a "partial" life, capable of descending into the most extreme divisions of matter while still being united with its own nature. While the soul is a slave to the body, she lives confined, as if in chains, under the dominion of this "Titanic" life.

...separated from each other, are glued together <note>original: "conglutinated"</note>, receiving a violent and renewed union. <margin>Plato, Timaeus 43a</margin>
> "But they gave them a strong connection using many small nails, invisible because of their smallness; crafting the body of each person from a mixture of all [the elements]; and binding the cycles of the immortal soul within a body that is constantly flowing in and out <note>original: "influxive and effluxive"</note>."

Because of what is said here, just as before, Plato establishes that the first "vehicle" of the soul that qualifies as a body is made from the elements. It is evident that this body is not indivisible, as it is generated from elements that must eventually be returned to the universe. It is also clear that just as that vehicle is a single unit, this shell-like body <note>The physical, material body; see "testaceous" below.</note> is likewise generated as a single unit. The former vehicle, however, has a simpler union of simple layers; but the physical body has a more varied union, as it is more complex in its nature.

Therefore, in that higher state, the combination of fire, water, air, and earth—which we said was like a "crowd"—represented the second vehicle and the life contained within it. But in the current passage, the <term>testaceous body</term> <note>original: "ostreodes," meaning shell-like. Neoplatonists compared the physical body to a shell that encases the soul like an oyster.</note> is what is meant. When Plato speaks of it, he is not satisfied with simple things; he adds qualities suited to an organic body. For it is not possible that an organic body should consist only of simple elements.

Beginning, therefore, from things that are more imperfect and material, and producing things made of "similar parts," and from these the organic body, he allows the body to participate in the soul. For the junior Gods, borrowing parts from the universal "wholes," took simple parts and made the vehicles for the irrational souls. He previously called these vehicles a "tumultuous and irrational crowd" composed of fire, earth, air, and water. By gluing these together, they generated things with similar parts made from the four elements. By causing these generated things to stick together through "many small nails," they completed the organic body. For it is this body, as he says, which requires *all those small and invisible nails*.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s analysis of Plato’s *Timaeus*, specifically the section where the "junior gods" (lesser divine beings) construct the human body and the soul enters this physical form. Proclus explains the mechanism of how the material elements are held together and the distinction between the mortal and immortal souls.</meta>

<page-num>437</page-num>
<header>BOOK V.] PLATO'S TIMAEUS.</header>

The body is created through a composition of different natures and held together by "thick-set nails," allowing the composition to eventually be dissolved.

We say, therefore, that these "thick-set and invisible nails" are the insertions of tiny, invisible elements into the solid parts <note>original: "τοις μελεσι στερεοις" (tois melesi stereois)</note> of the body. The <term>colliquefaction</term> <note>A melting together or blending of substances; original Greek: "συντηξιν" (suntexin).</note> is suited to "Vulcanian works" <note>Metaphorical reference to Vulcan/Hephaestus, the god of the forge; meaning the work of crafting with fire.</note>. Fire, through <term>rarefaction</term> <note>The process of becoming less dense; original: "αραιωσεως" (araioseos).</note> during this melting process, allows all things to flow through each other. Just as in things that are melted together, the smaller parts enter into the larger parts during the melting, and thus the mixture is completed.

It follows, then, that by gluing <note>original: "conglutinating"</note> the elements they have received, the junior gods produce a body. This body does not consist of unbreakable bonds, but of parts that stick together firmly through these thick-set, small, and invisible nails. Both melting <note>original: "τηξεως" (texeos)</note> and gluing <note>original: "κολλησεως" (kolleseos)</note> are necessary to create things made of similar parts; moisture provides the gluing <note>original: "παρεχεται" (parechetai)</note>, and heat provides the melting. For everything is liquefied by fire, but bound together by water. 

The soul joins <note>original: "accedes"</note> the body after many different natures have been united. First, the soul which is entirely mortal arrives. It is through this mortal soul that the "effluxive" body exists—that is, the body that is constantly losing and gaining matter. This is sustained through the physical, sensitive, and <term>orective</term> <note>Related to desire, appetite, or the drive toward an object.</note> life. 

Secondly, the immortal soul arrives. This soul does not simply enter a "body," but enters a body that is in a constant state of influx and efflux <note>The continuous process of matter flowing into the body (through nourishment) and out of the body (through decay/waste).</note>. The mortal soul is generated along with the body, but the immortal soul enters the body from the outside. 

This is the order of divine crafting <note>original: "fabrication"</note>, and it follows a logic that is consistent with the truth. All creation begins with what is imperfect and moves steadily toward what is perfect. In the universe as a whole, this crafting proceeds from intellect and soul down to bodies; this happens outside of time. [But in mortal natures, the crafting happens in conjunction with the body,] <note>The translator notes this phrase was missing in the original Greek and added it for clarity.</note> for it is <term>temporal</term> <note>Existing within or governed by time.</note>. 

Anything created in time begins its existence as something imperfect. Therefore, if there is anything that does not begin as imperfect, that thing was not created in time <note>original: "ου κατα χρονον" (ou kata chronon)</note>. Consequently, the universe itself was not created in time. For the <term>Demiurgus</term> <note>The divine craftsman or creator of the world in Platonic philosophy.</note> did not first create the body and then the soul, as we have observed before. This shows that what is called "generation" is when...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*. It focuses on the timing and mechanism of how the immortal soul is joined to the physical body, which has been constructed by the "junior gods" using "thick-set nails" and "colliquefaction."</meta>

<page-num>438</page-num>

applied to the universe, an unbegotten and simultaneous composition. In the universe, the whole exists prior to the parts, and the "one" exists before the "multitude"; but in mortal natures, the many parts are generated before the one whole. These parts, being liquefied through closely packed <note>original: "thick set"</note> nails, give completion to a single thing. For simple bodies are liquefied, these liquefied bodies are nailed together, the nailed bodies are given life <note>original: "vivified"</note>, and these living bodies are then adapted to fit the immortal soul.

From these things, it is also evident that we must say the insertion of the soul, according to Plato, takes place at the moment the infant comes out of the womb; for only then is the fetus complete, and not before. Nature would not uselessly detain it in the womb if it were already complete. Therefore, when the fetus becomes a single, whole entity, the immortal soul enters deeply into it. The fetus becomes a "one" when it is complete, and it is complete when it has come into the light of day. For while it remains inside, $^1$ it is merely a part of another thing <note>Meaning it is part of the mother's body rather than an independent individual.</note>. The soul, therefore, is not bound to the seed by the Gods, nor is it—as some think—released along with the seed. Instead, only when the body is fully generated are the cycles <note>original: "periods"</note> of the soul connected with it. $^2$ For where in the seed is there a body generated from many closely packed nails? Hence, when the instrument <note>The body, viewed as a tool for the soul to use.</note> is rendered complete, the Gods then bind to it the soul that is intended to use it. And that is enough regarding this particular point.

*But Plato calls the cycles of the soul its "energies," which proceed into the animal, as well as the twofold powers of the "Same" and the "Different."* <note>Platonic terms for the fundamental components of the soul's structure in the *Timaeus*.</note> According to Plato, the entire soul descends. Because he alone gives the soul two circles and two cycles and leads both of them downward, the claim made by Plotinus <note>A later Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD).</note>—who argues that the whole soul does not descend—is a more modern <note>original: "novel"</note> assertion. Regarding the "closely packed nails," some suppose them to signify the joining of the triangular elements. However, according to Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD).</note>, they indicate the sharing of physical productive powers, just as the "melting together" <note>original: "colliquefaction"</note> $^3$ signifies the craftsman-like <note>original: "demiurgic"</note> connection and union of them. But we have already shown what the nails, the glues, and the meltings are, and what theory best fits the nature of all these.

<page-num>439</page-num>
<header>BOOK V.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.</header>

...relating to the descent of the soul: the prophet, the assigned lots, the choices of life, the guardian spirit <term>daimon</term>, the pitching of tents in the plain of Lethe <note>Lethe is the "Plain of Forgetfulness" in the underworld where souls drink water to forget their previous existence.</note>, the thunder and lightning, and all such details discussed in the fable in the tenth book of the *Republic*. Nor does he describe here what happens after the soul leaves this life—namely the terrors, the rivers, Tartarus, those savage and fiery spirits <term>daemons</term>, the thorns, the bellowing mouth, the triple path, and the judges—all of which we are taught by the myths in the *Republic*, the *Gorgias*, and the *Phaedo*. 

Why, then, someone might ask, is this omitted? I reply that it is because Plato maintains a focus appropriate to the specific goal of this dialogue. Here, he only adopts as much of the theory of the soul as is physical, describing the soul's association with the body. Aristotle also followed Plato’s example in his treatise *On the Soul*; because he was discussing it from a physical perspective, he mentions neither the descent of the soul nor its assigned lots. However, in his *Dialogues*, Aristotle speaks of these separately and makes them his primary subject of consideration. This is enough regarding those details.

We must, however, investigate this from the beginning: why does the soul descend into bodies? <note>See my translation of Plotinus, *On the Descent of the Soul*.</note> The answer is that it wishes to imitate the providential energy of the Gods. For this reason, it sets aside pure contemplation and descends into the realm of generation <note>The world of birth, change, and physical matter.</note>. Since divine perfection is twofold—one being intellectual and the other "providential" (caring for the universe), with one existing in stillness and the other in motion—the soul reflects these two states. It mirrors the stable <note>original: *monimon*; the text previously used *gonimon* (productive), but *monimon* (stable/permanent) is the correct reading here.</note>, intellectual, and unchangeable energy of the Gods through contemplation, but it mirrors their providential and active energy through a life of worldly creation <term>genesiurgic life</term>. 

Just as the soul’s intelligence is partial (limited) compared to the Gods, so too is its providential energy. Because it is limited, it is concerned with a limited, individual body. Furthermore, its descent contributes to the perfection of the universe. It is necessary that there should not only be immortal and intellectual beings (like the Gods) or only mortal and irrational animals (the lowest part of creation), but also those that exist between these two: beings that are not immortal themselves <note>The original reads "not at all immortal," but the grammar suggests a correction is needed to clarify they are intermediate beings.</note> but are able to participate in reason and intellect. There are many such beings in various parts of the world. Man is not the only rational mortal being; there are many other such types <term>genera</term>, some of which are more spirit-like <term>daemoniacal</term> in nature, while others are closer to our own essence. The descent of an individual <note>original: "partial"</note> soul also contributes to the makeup of all living beings that are mortal and...

<summary>Proclus explains that the Timaeus focuses on the physical union of soul and body rather than the soul's journey in the afterlife. He argues the soul descends into matter to imitate the "providential" or caring nature of the Gods, ensuring the universe is populated with rational, intermediate beings.</summary>

<page-num>440</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.</header>

...and rational. Why, therefore, are individual <term>partial</term> souls filled with such great material disturbance and so many evils when they descend into the realm of birth and change <term>generation</term>? 

It happens through the inclination arising from their free will; through their intense attachment to the body; through their sympathy with the soul's reflection, which is called animation; and through their total shift from the world of pure thought <term>intelligible world</term> to the world of the senses <term>sensible world</term>, moving from a state of still energy to one entirely occupied with motion. It also results from a disordered state of being naturally produced by the combination of opposite natures: the immortal and the mortal, the intellectual and that which lacks intellect, the indivisible <term>impartible</term> and that which possesses physical dimensions <term>endued with interval</term>. 

All of these factors cause the soul great turmoil and labor within the realms of physical birth. We are disturbed by the many changes and connections that occur within an essence that is in constant motion. In this state, we pursue a mockery that is forever fleeing from us. By leaning <insert>toward a material life,</insert> the soul kindles a light in the body but finds herself placed in darkness. By giving life to the body, she destroys both herself and her own intellect <insert>as much as these things are capable of being destroyed</insert>. 

Thus, the mortal nature participates in intellect, but the intellectual part participates in death. As Plato observes in the *Laws*, the whole being becomes a marvel—a "prodigy" composed of the mortal and the immortal, of the intellectual and that which lacks intellect. This natural law <insert>which binds the soul to the body</insert> is the death of the immortal life, even as it gives life to the mortal body. 

In the *Phaedrus*, Plato describes the causes of this descent coming from the soul itself: namely, forgetfulness <term>oblivion</term>, the loss of its "wings," and the consequences that follow. But here, he describes the causes derived from the Gods, for it is the Gods who join the soul to the body. However, he does not add at this point the specific way <note>The original Greek text uses *houtos* ("thus"), but it should be read as *hopos* ("how" or "in what manner").</note> in which the soul turns away <insert>from the sphere of light</insert>, nor through what forms of life she proceeds <insert>into the realms of generation</insert>. In the *Republic*, he provides the causes arising from both the soul herself and the Gods. There, the prophet and the Fates, the guardian spirit <term>daemon</term> and the lots, and the models and choices of lives are all included. These details, therefore, must be explored in those specific dialogues.

We must, however, consider what is stated here: specifically, what is meant by *the river, the binding, and the vast*, for this "river" is described as vast. We must also consider what it means for souls neither to conquer nor be conquered. 

The "river" signifies more than just the human body; it represents the entire world of change and physical birth <term>generation</term> that surrounds us externally with its rapid, violent, and unstable flow. Similarly, in the *Republic*, Plato calls the entire world of creation the *river of Lethe* (Forgetfulness). In this river, as Empedocles says, are contained *Oblivion* and the *meadow of Ate* <note>original: "Ate." In Greek mythology, Ate refers to delusion, infatuation, or ruin.</note>...

<page-num>441</page-num>
<header>BOOK 5] PLATO'S TIMAEUS</header>

...the hunger of matter and the dark world <note>original: "light-hating world," likely referring to the material realm or Hades</note>, as the Gods say; and the twisting currents <note>original: "winding streams"</note> which pull many people down, as the *Chaldean Oracles* claim. This *binding* represents a life that is restricted and has reached its lowest point. Once bound, the soul is stopped from moving forward; no longer able to advance, it remains at the very end of its journey. 

However, by sharing its powers with the body, the soul reaches the final stage of its descent. The word *vast* indicates the complex and constantly changing flow of physical existence <term>generation</term>, which can be broken down in every way. The phrase *neither conquering nor being conquered* means that each substance <term>essence</term> keeps its own nature when they come together. The union of the soul and body is not like a chemical reaction where both parts are destroyed <note>original: "mutual corruption"</note> to create something new. The body does not transform into the soul, and the soul does not take on the specific physical qualities of the body; if that happened, neither would be able to make the other like itself. 

Therefore, the soul is not defeated by the body, as it does not lose its life <term>become inanimate</term>. Nor does the soul defeat the body, because it does not turn the body into something spirit-like <term>incorporeal</term>. In another sense, however, the soul masters the body by holding it together, while it is mastered by the body whenever the body gets in the way of the soul's higher thought <term>intellection</term>. Plato denies both possibilities so that we might understand the unique nature of each part within their union—how they are joined together while remaining distinct.

It has become clear from what we have discussed that the <term>genesiurgic</term> <note>The "genesiurgic" river refers to the constant flow of physical matter and birth that surrounds the soul.</note> river disturbs the soul entirely. This disruption is especially strong in youth because the flow of matter into and out of the body is so heavy. Since the body is heavy, earth-bound, and prone to decay <term>cadent</term>, it must be directed by the soul. Meanwhile, the soul—which is intellectual by nature—is stripped of its intellect through its connection with the body. 

For this reason, Plato says that souls *carry and are carried with violence*. The word *violence* points to the unnatural and forced way that a mortal animal is given life <term>vivification</term> <note>original Greek: "For *to thneton* [the mortal] here, it is necessary to read *tou thnetou* [of the mortal]."</note>. <header>PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.]</header>

...of motion; instead, it is carried by that motion through sympathy toward a nature concerned with physical birth <term>genesiurgic</term>. Therefore, Plato rightly says that the entire living being <note>original: "animal"; here meaning the composite of soul and body</note> is moved. This is because the body is moved by the soul, and the soul—setting aside its own higher existence—lives the life of the combined body and soul. The whole living being, therefore, is moved.

In another sense, you could also say that Plato emphasizes that the *whole* moves in order to distinguish the individual living being from the universe. The universe, as we noted before, does not move as a single whole from place to place, but only its parts move within it. However, because the stars move with a forward motion <note>original: *in antecedentia*</note>, each moves as a complete unit rather than just in its parts. Yet they move in an orderly way, unlike us, because they follow the rhythm of the universe. 

But Plato adds the word *disorderly* to show that this motion is material and completely inconsistent. It begins from a lower nature, which turns the natural order upside down. In divine beings, however, motion must always begin from the superior or more excellent part of their nature. Similarly, the word *casually* refers to the impulsive and unstable nature of this movement. The word *proceeds* indicates how souls depart from their own true nature. All of these conditions are secondary to those of divine beings, where the intellect is the cause <note>original: *aitios*</note> of all activity, and every being goes forth while simultaneously remaining rooted in its source. The word *irrationally* follows quite appropriately. For wherever order is lost, irrationality creeps in. Reason <note>original: *logos*</note> is the source of order, measure, and the ability to share in what is good.

Furthermore, the many different types of motion become clear here, along with the total number of motions possible for a mortal being. Since bodies have three dimensions and are composed of opposites—and because "opposition" is a pair <note>original: *duas*</note>—combining this pair with the triad of dimensions produces this specific number of motions. There must be exactly three intervals or dimensions. This is because an interval is a "reasoning principle" <note>original: *logos*</note> that proceeds from the indivisible world into matter, giving it shape <term>morphe</term>. 

The indivisible source is "monadic" (a unity); the process of moving forward is "dyadic" (a pair); and the final shape is "triadic" (a three-part whole). For when something that has moved outward returns or turns back toward its source, it gains a boundary and a definite form <term>morphe</term>. It is also necessary for there to be opposition in these motions based on their position. For the two ends of any straight line are opposite to one another. Therefore, within the three dimensions, the opposites at each end are: up and down, right and left, and forward and backward. Thus, the combination of these opposites with the three dimensions produces the six motions, a number that is perfectly suited to a living body. According to the Pythagoreans, the monad (the One)...

<page-num>443</page-num>
### BOOK 5: THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO

The monad <term>the number one</term> is analogous to a point; the duad <term>the number two</term> to a line; the triad <term>the number three</term> to a surface <note>original: "superficies"</note>; the tetrad <term>the number four</term> to a solid body; the pentad <term>the number five</term> to a body endowed with a specific quality¹; and the hexad <term>the number six</term> to a living body <note>original: "animated body"</note>. This number of motions, therefore, is appropriately attributed to mortal animals, whose birth <note>original: "generation"</note> proceeds from the even² number and a formless nature. 

One should not wonder, however, that animals have so many different types of motion while inanimate objects have only one. For example, a clod of earth only moves downward, while flame has the opposite motion (upward). Through careful observation, we find that the extremes are often simpler than the middle points, while the middle is more complex than the extremes.³ 

For instance, we see that nature and matter are simpler than the physical body, just as the irrational life and the pure intellect are simpler than the rational soul. The intellect is "simple" because it is more excellent; irrationality is "simple" because it is less excellent. The irrational lives without deliberate choice and acts according to its basic nature. 

If, therefore, we see that divine animals and inanimate bodies have a simpler motion, while the middle beings wander and are carried along in many forms, what reason is there to wonder? The simplicity of divine motion is superior to the variety found in mortal natures; however, the simplicity of inanimate beings is inferior. It is just as divine bodies are essentially simple because they are better than composite natures, whereas the inanimate parts of the elements are simpler than physical masses because they are less excellent⁴—they lack the specific life that belongs to living beings.

<margin>43c</margin>
> "For though the flooding and draining waves <note>original: "inundating and effluxive waves"</note> which provide nutrition to the animal pour along with a powerful abundance, an even greater chaos and disturbance is produced by the sensations arising from external impacts. This happens when the body is disturbed by the sudden attack of external fire, or by a solid mass of earth, or is shaken by the swirling blasts of the air. From all of these, through the medium of the body, various motions are hurried along and strike the soul with distress <note>original: "molestation"</note>."

² For "wild" <note>original Greek: ἀγρίου (agriou)</note> here, it is necessary to read "even" <note>original Greek: ἀρτίου (artiou)</note>.

<page-num>444</page-num>
### PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK 5]

In these remarks, the philosopher <note>Plato</note> attributes all this chaos <note>original: "tumult"</note> to **two causes**: the life of nutrition and the life of sensation. These causes represent the desiring <term>orectic</term> and the knowing <term>gnostic</term> parts of our entire irrational nature. We usually divide all the powers of the soul into these categories, asserting that some are "vital" <note>governing life functions</note> while others are "knowing."

The life of nutrition, as it turns toward physical bodies, creates a constant flow within them. Because of the moisture in bodies, it releases a great deal of physical matter <note>original: "material efflux"</note>, but through its life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note> heat, it draws in other substances. Meanwhile, the life of sensation is affected by the physical elements of fire, earth, air, and water as they encounter it. Because this level of life is so unrefined <note>original: "vile"</note>, it perceives all these sensations as overwhelming, which causes agitation and disturbance in the soul.

For those who have reached adulthood, these sensations have become a habit. However, for the newborn, even the smallest things cause astonishment because they are so unusual. What a massive fire is to an adult, the flickering flame <note>original: "snuff"</note> of a candle is to an infant. What a towering mountain is to an adult, the smallest pebble is to a baby. This small stone is enough to cause them pain, and by blocking their movements, it brings them to tears. What stormy winds and heavy rain are to adults, a slight breeze or a slip on a little moisture is to infants. Because the senses are shaken by the impact of all these things, the soul of the newborn is astonished, leading it into difficulty and chaos. These, in short, are the causes of the soul’s disturbance: the movement of the nutritive power and the impact of the senses.

We must not, however, imagine that the soul itself actually suffers from these things. Imagine someone standing on the bank of a river, looking at their own image and form reflected in the flowing water. The person's actual face remains unchanged, but because the stream is constantly moving, the reflection changes. At different times, the image appears different—sometimes slanted, sometimes upright, sometimes broken apart, and sometimes continuous. 

Let us also suppose that this person, being unused to such a sight, should think that they themselves were undergoing this distortion <note>original: "τον πασχοντα διαστροφην ταυτην"</note> simply because they are looking at their shadow in the water. Thinking this, they would be distressed, disturbed, astonished, and hindered. In the same way, the soul—beholding the reflection of herself in the body, which is carried along in the "river of generation" <term>the cycle of physical birth and change</term>—perceives herself through internal passions and external impacts. The soul itself is actually unaffected <term>impassive</term>, but she *thinks* she is suffering. Because she is ignorant of her true nature and mistakes the reflection for herself, she becomes disturbed, astonished, and perplexed. This state of passion particularly exists...

# BOOK V.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO. 445

This is evident in newborn children, but it also shows itself in the dreams of adults. For instance, when someone—because their nature is exhausted from the digestion <note>original: "concoction"</note> of food—imagines in a dream that they are tired, or that they are traveling along a difficult road, or that they are carrying heavy burdens, or suffering some other similar hardship, then this physical experience <note>original: "passion," meaning a state of being acted upon by external forces</note> becomes apparent. It is possible from these examples to examine the nature of the physical experiences of children. <note>The original Greek text here should read *paidōn* ("children") instead of *pedōn* ("plains" or "fetters").</note> And this should be enough to say about these details for now.

It is necessary, however, to proceed to the words of Plato and to say that the *waves* do not represent the wind blowing from the outside, as some claim, but rather the accumulated lack of reason <note>original: *aphrosynēn*, "folly" or "unreason"</note> existing in youth, and the constant flow of matter in and out of the body. The *inundation* <note>or "flood"</note> signifies, first, that the spiritual vehicle <term>pneumatic vehicle</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, the "pneumatic vehicle" is a subtle, airy body that acts as an intermediary between the immaterial soul and the physical corpse.</note> is agitated and made heavier; for it is this vehicle that shows within itself stains and vapours. Secondly, it signifies the soul itself, for the soul is disturbed by these gathered impulses.

<margin>43 C</margin>
> "And on this account all these were then, and are still now denominated senses."

According to Plato, the senses receive their name <note>original: "appellation"</note> from physical experience <note>original: "passion," from the Greek *pathos*</note>. If we were to say that the senses are merely motions placed deep inside us, that claim would face much criticism from a grammatical perspective. But if we say that the senses are a mixture of internal motions and physical experience, perhaps ancient usage would support that claim. For the word "sensation" (*aisthesis*), when spoken with four syllables, is a certain *a-is-the-sis*.
-> "And he groaned, breathing out his life," <note>original Greek: *O d' ebrachen thymon aisthō (lege aisthōn)*</note> <-
says Homer. The word *aisthesis* (sensation) is derived from *aiein* <note>original: "to hear, blow away, or understand"</note> and *thesis* <note>meaning "position"</note>. In this view, sensible objects move externally, but those motions travel through the body to the soul and produce—as Plato says—sensations. Therefore, those who first recognized the nature of this physical experience, and those today who do not entirely understand it, were very correct to name the senses this way. And those who still use this name for the senses do so because there is a similar process occurring.

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.

a complication in them of physical experience <note>original: "passion," meaning the state of being acted upon by external forces</note> and judgment, or of motion and position. For the motion of the soul alone is unaffected by outside forces; but that which travels from the body to the soul is accompanied by physical experience.

<margin>432 (cont.)</margin>
> "And these [senses] indeed, both then and now, receiving the most abundant and greatest movement, and being moved along with that incessantly flowing stream, and violently shaking the orbits of the soul, they entirely bind the circulation of *the same*, which flows in the opposite direction, and they hinder its activities as it rules and moves forward; but they agitate the circulation of *the different*."

Sense is concerned with the present, just as memory is with the past and hope is with the future. Therefore, both then and now, sensation moves the soul in connection with the nutritive power. Through the intake of food, this power provides a remedy for the body's natural waste <note>original: "effluxions"</note>, and it recombines what had been broken down, just like the unweaving and reweaving of the web of Penelope <note>A reference to Homer's *Odyssey*, where Penelope unwove her work every night to delay her suitors, symbolizing a constant cycle of construction and deconstruction</note>. For this is "the incessantly flowing stream," which is very appropriately called a stream because it is a part of the vast river of generation <note>The cycle of birth and material existence</note>, which, as was observed before, is abundant.

In company with this stream, therefore, sense disturbs and causes an uproar in the cycles or orbits of the immortal soul. It binds the cycle of the circle of *the same*, but agitates the cycle of the circle of *the different*. Since there are two types of circles within the soul—imitating the souls of the gods—the circle that contemplates intellectual truths (the rational or dianoetic <term>dianoetic</term> circle) is only hindered in its activity but does not actually suffer distortion. However, the circle of opinion <term>doxastic circle</term> is distorted, and this follows quite logically. For it is possible to hold a wrong opinion, but it is not possible to have "false" scientific knowledge. 

If, however, someone should say that the rational part of the soul may be ignorant in two ways, and that the thing which suffers this will be distorted, let them learn from us that twofold ignorance <note>original: "twofold ignorance is, when a man is not only ignorant, but is ignorant that he is ignorant. And this is the disease of the multitude."</note> does not simply belong to the reasoning power <note>original: *dianoia*</note>. Rather, it begins there and takes root in the part of the soul that forms opinions. For twofold ignorance—insofar as it is ignorance and a lack of science—originates from the reasoning power because it is a failure of the power of knowledge to move. After all, ignorance exists regarding the same things that knowledge exists. But insofar as this ignorance also adds the false suspicion that one actually possesses knowledge, it exists in the part of the soul that forms opinions.

### BOOK V.] THE TIMAEUS OF PLATO.

...in the <term>doxastic</term> <note>The part of the soul responsible for forming opinions (doxa), as opposed to certain knowledge.</note> part. For that which is nothing more than a false suspicion of knowledge is this. And ignorance, indeed, is only the loss of intellect in the <term>dianoia</term> <note>The faculty of discursive reason or "thinking through" a problem.</note> when it is bound <note>The original notes specify that the Greek word should be read as "fettered" (pepedemenēs) rather than "educated" (pepaideumenēs).</note> and concealing its productive powers; but <term>deception</term> <note>original: "ἀπάτη" (apatē)</note>, or a false suspicion of knowledge, is the loss of intellect in the faculty of opinion, being a certain distortion of it. For being false, it injures its possessor. *For what evil is in action, the false is in knowledge.*

The period of the Circle of the *Same*, therefore, is alone bound, and resembles those who are in captivity and, for this reason, are prevented from acting <note>original: "energizing"</note>. This circulation, however, remains in the souls that are bound without being distorted. But the period of the Circle of the *Different* is agitated, being filled with false beliefs <note>original: "dogmas"</note>. For the proximity of this circle to the irrational part of the soul causes it to be affected by external things. 

From these points, however, we are impelled to speak freely in opposition to Plotinus and the great Theodorus, who maintain that there remains in us something unaffected <note>original: "impassive"</note> which always perceives intellectually. For Plato assumes only two circles in the essence of the soul, one of which—according to him—is bound, while the other is agitated; and it is not possible for either that which is bound or that which is agitated to act intellectually. Therefore, the divine Iamblichus rightly argues against those who adopt this opinion. For what is it that is faulty in us when we fall back into an unrestrained imagination through the stimulation of our irrational nature? Is it not our own deliberate choice? And how could it be otherwise, since it is by this choice that we differ from those who imagine things impulsively? 

But if our deliberate choice is faulty, how can the soul be guiltless? Also, what is it that makes our whole life happy? Is it not because reason possesses its proper virtue? We say entirely so. But if we are *wholly* happy when the most excellent part of us is perfect, what prevents us all from being happy right now, if the summit of our nature always perceives intellectually and is always with the Gods? For if this summit is purely intellect, it has nothing to do with the soul; but if it is a part of the soul, then the rest of the soul would also be happy.
