### PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS [BOOK V.

Because the soul sublimely reaches toward the place beyond the heavens, yet at other times enters into the heavens, and at still other times becomes "lame" and suffers a loss <note>original: "defluxion"</note> of its wings, it clearly follows that the highest part of our nature exists in different states at different times. This subject, therefore, the reader will find discussed more extensively elsewhere.

If, however, these things are true, it is very appropriate to say that the rotation of the *Circle of the Same* <note>In Platonic philosophy, this represents the rational, unchanging part of the soul.</note>, as it governs and moves forward, is "fettered." For having a twofold perfection—the practical <note>original: "practic"</note> and the contemplative <note>original: "theoretic"</note>—it is deprived of both. It is neither able to rule over the lower natures subject to its command (because of their unstable motion), nor to move forward—that is, to perceive intellectually. For "to proceed" is the activity of a rotation, and to proceed through reasoning <note>original: "dianoetically"</note> is the activity of the reasoning faculties. The senses, therefore, collide with this internal rotation; flowing inward from external objects in the opposite direction, they block intellectual activity <note>original: "energy"</note>. Hence, the period of the *Circle of the Same* is deprived of both action and contemplation. 

What then, someone might ask, is the soul motionless? And how can the soul be motionless? We might answer that it is indeed moved by itself, but not with a physical motion (for it is incorporeal), nor with a motion based on images <note>original: "phantastic motion," referring to the faculty of phantasia or imagination</note> (for it has no physical form), nor with a motion of conscious knowledge (for it is ignorant of itself); instead, it moves with an essentially vital motion. Just as perceiving intellectually is the activity of the intellect, and existing is the activity of "Being," so too living is the activity of life. The soul does not possess a life-force added from the outside <note>original: "adventitious"</note>, but derives it from itself. It is life generating and producing itself. Since all life is motion, it follows that everything which lives is moved; therefore, that which lives by its own power <note>original: "εαυτῃ" (eautē). The original text notes a correction from "εαυτο" (eauto).</note> will be moved, and that which always lives will always be moved—vitally, though not necessarily intellectually. 

Hence, the soul is always moved, and yet not always. *For it is intellect in potential <note>original: "capacity"</note>, but life in actuality <note>original: "energy"</note>.* And there is a third thing—matter—which exists only in potential, but never in actuality. Since there is a triple order within us—according to essence, according to power, and according to activity—our essence remains entirely the same, as something that exists, lives, and is intellectual. Being the primary image of the Divine Intellect, the soul is intellectual, just as the first image of the soul is "animated" (endowed with life). 

However, the powers of the <term>dianoia</term> <note>The faculty of discursive reason or "thinking through" a problem.</note> are fettered, and the powers of opinion are shaken. Since these powers correspond to different levels of life, the power of one life (the intellectual) is restrained, while another is agitated. The essential life is always in motion. Regarding our activities, however, those of the reasoning mind are stripped away, while those of opinion are distorted. As these are analogous to the intellectual realm, it is evident that the soul is prevented from perceiving intellectually. The essence of the soul, therefore, is per—

<summary>Proclus explains how the soul's rational "Circle of the Same" is hindered by sensory input and material life, arguing that while the soul's essence remains constant and "vitally" active, its intellectual functions can be temporarily disabled or "fettered."</summary>

# BOOK 5] PLATO'S TIMAEUS.

It is perpetually vital and perpetually moved; but the powers and activities <note>original: "energies"</note> pertaining to its life and intellect are naturally prone <note>original: "adapted"</note> to err.

> “So that they turn with every kind of revolution, each of the three intervals of the double and triple, together with the means <note>original: "media"</note> and conjoining bonds of the four-to-three <note>original: "sesquitertian"</note>, three-to-two <note>original: "sesquialter"</note>, and nine-to-eight <note>original: "sesquioctave"</note> ratios which cannot be dissolved by any one, except by him by whom they were bound. And besides this, they introduce all the fractures and diversities of circles which it is possible to effect.”

All things are in all souls, but in a way appropriate to each: in some divinely, in others dæmonically <note>In Platonic philosophy, "dæmonic" refers to a level of being between gods and humans, not "demonic" in the modern sense.</note>, and in others partially. For the means, the three-to-two, the four-to-three, and the nine-to-eight ratios, together with the remainder <note>original: "leimma," a term for a Pythagorean semitone</note>, are in all souls. For how else could the soul know universal <note>original: "total"</note> harmony and produce <note>original: "procreate"</note> such beautiful ratios, unless she contained the causes of them within herself? She is, according to her own rank <note>original: "order"</note>, a certain harmony of harmonies. This is not a harmony consisting of things harmonized from the outside (since that kind of harmony exists in something else, is moved by another <note>original: "alter-motive"</note>, and depends upon another moving cause), but rather a harmony that organizes itself and is organized by the whole of reality <note>original: "wholes"</note>. 

Therefore, the soul possesses all harmonized ratios and, in addition to these, the sevenfold divisions of the *Circle of the Different* <note>In the *Timaeus*, the soul is divided into circles representing the motions of the planets.</note>. For the creator's division <note>original: "demiurgic section"; a footnote in the original text suggests reading the Greek word *tome* (section) instead of *to men* (the indeed).</note> begins from above with divine souls and proceeds down to the most partial <note>individual or human</note> souls; it includes all those other things we have examined regarding the Soul of the Universe. The method of interpretation is also the same, except that we must add the specific character of each soul, attaching the divine quality to some, the dæmonic to others, and the partial quality to others. 

We have, however, previously observed that although all ratios—the divine, dæmonic, and partial—exist in all souls after the World Soul <note>original: "mundane soul"</note>, it is not at all surprising that the boundary terms should differ. This is because they become more numerous <note>original: "multiplied"</note> in the lower souls than in the souls that precede them. For while the ratios of the Soul of the Universe were primary or radical terms <note>original: "pythmenes," or *πυθμενες*, referring to the base numbers of a ratio</note>, nothing prevents them from later becoming double, triple, or, in short, multiples of these. Through a process of decrease <note>original: "diminution"</note>, they are multiplied in orderly ratios all the way down to individual souls. And in some of these souls, they are more multiplied than in others. For divine souls are not all equal in rank <note>original: "dignity"</note>, nor are the dæmonic souls that follow them, nor the individual souls. Thus, they have some things in common, but differ in other ways according to their essence.

Socrates, therefore, in the *Phaedrus*, compares the powers of the soul to a charioteer and horses, and asserts that one of the horses is better than the other. At still other times, they are turned in every direction because the better part is subjected to the worse.

But when the soul wavers, there is first a hostile struggle within her regarding what is the same as a certain thing and what is different from it. Next, the worse means is victorious by leaning toward total divisibility <note>original: "all-various partibility"</note> instead of observing itself. Third, there is a total weakening of the better means because the soul hands over supreme power and ruling authority to the less excellent means.

The means pertaining to sameness leads the soul to a divine nature, while the one pertaining to difference leads it to a mortal nature. Hence, the soul becomes irrational in this way: the means in the circle of difference are broken and turned, and prior to this, they disagree with each other; this turning completely drags this circle down toward the passions. <meta>This page continues the discussion of how the soul's internal harmony is disrupted when it descends into a physical body, focusing on the concepts of "fracture," "turning," and "discord" within the soul's proportions.</meta>

# BOOK 5] PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS.

The soul of the universe is perfectly free from any tendency toward the physical things it governs. However, in an individual soul, this tendency is reversed; it is completely inclined toward matter, falling into a body and entering deeply into it. This "fracture" forces the soul into a motion <note>original: "lation"</note> toward multiplicity and variety, creating a distribution into different parts because of the soul's weakness and lack of power. For things that are fractured lose their strength and become "many" instead of remaining "one." 

This discord <note>original: "dissention"</note> produces nothing but opposition and hostility. The "turning" completely ruins the soul's uprightness; the "fracture" causes the one to become many; and the discord alone introduces conflict. 

To visualize this:
*   The effect produced by **discord** resembles a person who is running but cannot stand firmly.
*   The **fracture** resembles someone who has fallen and broken their limbs, leaving them in a slanted <note>original: "oblique"</note> position.
*   The **turning** is like someone lying on their back <note>original: "supine"</note> who fixes their head in the dirt but raises their feet as high as possible. 

A slanted position is a middle ground between standing upright and being completely upside down, because in that situation, the head is downward but the feet are upward. 

The part of the soul responsible for opinion <note>original: "doxastic part"</note> becomes distorted through the senses; it forms false opinions and is disorderly <note>The original Greek text uses "πολυμελες" (having many parts), but it is necessary to read "πλημμελες" (discordant or erroneous).</note> and mistaken. This occurs in the "circle of the *different*," as we observed before, which is the realm where opinions and beliefs are formed in the universal soul. Consequently, this part of the soul becomes filled with false beliefs, as it is split apart by the senses and is in conflict with itself. 

All these "passions" (or sufferings) affect the powers and activities of the soul, but the essence of the soul itself cannot be destroyed <note>original: "indissoluble"</note>, except—as Timaeus says—by the one who binds it together. For the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> holds within himself the definite causes of the soul’s mathematical ratios and its circular motions. That which can only be dissolved by the same cause that perpetually connects it is, for all intents and purposes, indestructible. Just as something produced by "the Good" alone is without evil, something produced by evil alone is corrupt <note>original: "depraved"</note>, and something produced by cold alone lacks heat. It is not the nature of cold to provide heat, nor of the Good to cause harm <note>original: "vitiate"</note>, nor of that which connects things to pull them apart. Therefore, the statement that only the Creator can dissolve the soul is a hidden way of affirming the soul's immortality.

<meta>This page continues the analysis of the soul's motions—contrary, oblique, and supine—and how these geometric metaphors describe the internal conflict or harmony between the rational and irrational parts of the soul.</meta>

# BOOK 5] PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS.

These motions move in opposite directions; however, the "fractures" cause them to move at an angle <note>original: "obliquely"</note>, and the "turnings" cause them to move face-up <note>original: "supinely"</note>. These three states <note>original: "passions"</note> are examined within the rational soul, but they are also seen consistently within the irrational part. When the rational soul is in harmony with itself—and even when it is in discord—it opposes the irrational soul even more fiercely. For the virtues follow one another: the intellectual <term>dianoetical</term> virtues follow the moral <term>ethical</term> ones, and the moral follow the intellectual. 

How, then, are these three states to be identified in the rational part? We may say that "opposition" <note>original: "contrariety"</note> is observed when one opinion fiercely opposes another, and yet the better opinion is not defeated by the worse one. Even in those who believe false things, there is always a certain true principle <note>original: "dogma"</note> from which the person holding the false opinion may be proven wrong. After all, how could Socrates have proven Thrasymachus, Callicles, and others who were similarly and shamelessly bold to be wrong, unless they also held certain true principles? By starting from a truth they both acknowledged, Socrates could deduce the logical conclusions that followed. 

For example, when a person says that the Divine is good, but then says that God does not provide for all things, these principles <note>The original text uses "δειγματα" (deigmata/examples), but it should be read as "δογματα" (dogmata/principles).</note> contradict each other. The person simply does not see that the opposite of their second claim follows logically from the first position—that God is good. 

The "oblique" or slanted position occurs when two principles are distorted and cannot maintain a logical connection; they are then said to be inconsistent <note>The original text uses "ακολουθα" (akoloutha/consequent), but it should be read as "ανακολουθα" (anakoloutha/inconsistent).</note>. In this state, the entire opinion collapses and becomes obvious to the senses. In such cases, it is not that one part is true and the other false, but that the whole idea is false. Such are the claims that "justice is folly" and "injustice is wisdom." 

If someone imagines that justice is folly, but simultaneously says that injustice is depravity <note>original: "badness"</note>, he contradicts himself; by calling injustice "bad," he is also admitting that justice is not "folly." However, the person who says that justice is folly and injustice is wisdom is consistent with himself, but he asserts both ideas in a distorted way. Therefore, he is much harder to argue with and more "incurable" than the first person. 

Finally, the "supine" (face-up) position occurs when the worse opinions completely defeat the better ones, and the information gathered from the senses subdues the wisdom drawn from within. In a state like this, excellent things are enslaved and become subject to lower things.

Again, regarding the irrational part of the soul, "opposition" can be observed in those who possess self-control <note>original: "continent"</note>. In these individuals, the better part fights with the worse—the mental image of beauty struggles against the appetite for what is ugly. On the other hand, "obliquity" (distortion) is seen...

# BOOK 5] PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS.

...in the harmonious agreement of judgment with appetite, when both move in the same way and are affected similarly. A state of being face-up <note>original: "supineness"</note> occurs in lives lacking self-control, in which the rational part is entirely dominated by the irrational part. Here, you can see how the slanted <note>original: "oblique"</note> disposition develops in a systematic way from its opposite. 

When, after a great struggle, the rational part yields to the irrational part, it then moves in a slanted direction, and from this, it ends up face-up. Because the worse part continually defeats the better part, there is eventually no need for a struggle; the better part is enslaved and led wherever the worse part pleases. This is the lowest form of life, just as the most perfect life is the one that is in harmony with itself, without slanting, and in accordance with nature—where the more excellent part maintains its own order without hostile opposition. 

Likewise, harmony is produced from temperance, the lack of slanting comes from courage <note>original: "fortitude"</note>, and the arrangement according to nature comes from justice. Their opposites are produced as follows: 
- Conflict produces opposition.
- Fracture produces a slant <note>original: "obliquity"</note>, for things that are fractured become slanted.
- Turning produces the face-up <note>original: "supine"</note> position. 

This turning entirely flips the order of leaders and followers. The opposition appears to tear apart the unified life of the soul and makes the rational life disagree with itself. The slanting produces irrationality itself, for this state tends entirely toward the body and toward matter. And the face-up position¹ causes the rational life to be ranked with plants; for in plants, the "head" (the root) is buried in the earth. 

Since this is how the soul's powers are divided and affected, Plato very properly says *that they are hardly² connected with each other.* For it is the existence of their essential nature—which is indestructible unlike mortal things—that holds them together. Thus, conflict, fracture, and turning are produced when matter defeats form; matter is like the feet, while form is like the head.

> "It is as if someone in a face-up position were to press their head against the earth and raise their feet high in the air. In such a situation, both the inverted person and the observers would mistakenly imagine that the parts on the right are on the left, and the parts on the left are on the right. The very same disturbances, and others of a similar kind, occur with great force regarding the cycles <note>original: "circulations"</note> of the soul. Therefore, when anything external occurs that is characterized by the nature of 'the same' or 'the different,' they name things..."

# BOOK 5] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

"...the same with, or different from others, in a manner contrary to the truth, and become false, and destitute of intelligence."

In what is here said, Plato uses dramatic language <note>original: "tragically describes"</note> to describe the final suffering of the soul, in which the better part is deceived and enslaved, while the worse part rules—a lowly rule over the heavenly <note>original: "Olympian," referring to the divine or highest part of the soul</note> part, and a material rule over divine natures. He also compares the head to our divine part, and our inferior part to the feet. For the former governs, but the latter has the rank of the governed. As he says further on, the slavery of that which is divine and ruling within us is similar to fixing the head in the earth, while the tyranny of the irrational part is like raising the feet high. What occurs from a posture of this kind is similar to what takes place within the soul. In the body, it happens that the right- and left-hand parts are seen in reversed positions. Consequently, it happens in the soul that things that are "the same" and things that are "different" are swapped from the perspective of observers. For *the same* is similar to the right hand, but *the different* is similar to the left, according to Pythagorean tradition. This is the general meaning of the text.

But let us direct our attention to the specifics. In the first place, we must examine the order: how Plato describes the body moving from a standing position to a slanted <note>original: "oblique"</note> position, then from a slant to lying face-up <note>original: "supine"</note>, and finally to having the feet raised on high. Fixing the head in the earth creates a figure of this kind. In the soul, there is first a departure from good; secondly, a slanted or crooked way of life; thirdly, an extension toward matter¹ <note>original: "materiality"</note>, a movement toward the physical world <note>original: "generation"</note>, and a joining of the divine with that which is without God; and in the last place, the unbearable tyranny of foolish natures. 

Likewise, among political systems <note>original: "polities"</note>, the one that loves conflict is formed according to this kind of opposition; the one that loves riches exists according to a slant; the one that loves pleasure exists unlawfully according to a face-up <note>original: "supineness"</note> life; and the tyrannical system exists according to the elevation of the feet. This is the figure described in what Plato now says.

In the second place, it is necessary to examine how a posture of this kind displays the right-hand parts on the left and the left on the right, both to the person in this position and to the spectators. Imagine one person looking to the north and another to the south. The first person will have their right hand toward the east and their left hand toward the west. But the other person will have these the other way around <note>original: "vice versa"</note>. However, let the person who looks to the north be lying face-up—not as Timaeus [might seem to] say, having his head fixed in the earth, but his feet...

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK 5] TIMAEUS OF PLATO.

...elevated, as we are accustomed to say of someone who lies in a prone position [but with his face upward]. And again, he will have the east to his right hand, but the west to his left. In order, however, that he may be supine <note>lying on the back, face upward</note> in the way mentioned by Timaeus, let his feet be raised, but his head be fixed on the ground, so that his face may be turned away from the north. Looking, therefore, toward the south, he will similarly have the right-hand parts to the east and the left-hand parts to the west. 

However, the opposite should occur for those who stand and look toward the south. Consequently, since he looks south, he will imagine that things located to the east are on the left hand, and those located to the west are on the right hand. Spectators will also imagine this to be the case. He will therefore imagine things on the left to be on the right, and things on the right to be on the left; this is the result of his supine position. It is also clear that he will perceive things related to an upright spectator to exist in reverse <note>original: "vice versa"</note>, although the right and left parts will refer to the same objects for both. For each person looking south will imagine that the east is to the left and the west is to the right, and will say that if one exists this way, the rest must also exist the same way. This, however, will not be true for someone lying face down, even if he looks south. It is well said, therefore, that each will imagine things pertaining to both—and not just to one of them—will have a reversed position.

Thirdly, it is necessary to show how these things may be analogously observed in the soul. For when the soul buries her reason but stimulates the imagination <note>original: "phantasy," the faculty of the soul that deals with sensory images</note> and the irrational powers, she becomes more like a plant [than a rational nature] and imitates the life of plants. For in plants, the head (the root) is buried downward, while everything else grows upward, overcoming the better part. Because of this, the soul judges things contrary to the truth. This affects not only the soul in this condition but also the soul that does not yet suffer this but looks toward her. 

It is evident, therefore, that he who fixes his head downward resembles those who are perfectly distorted. However, he who stands in a natural position but is affected by looking at the former resembles those who are distorted by others, just as the former is similar to those who are distorted by themselves. Thus, the soul, by imitating a merely physical life, thinks different things are the same and, again, that the same things are different. For she thinks that pleasure is the same as the Good, though it is different; but she separates the divine from the Good, and virtue from the Beautiful, even though they are the same. As a consequence of this way of thinking, the soul possesses the lowest form of life, departs from herself, and follows this life. Hence, her opinions are false, and are thus affected not only regarding the "Same" and the "Different," but also regarding motion and permanence. For...

They believe that the nature which is constantly in motion has stood still—as the common people <note>that is, the Christians of that time</note> believe regarding the sun—and also that what is permanent is moved, as some believe regarding the earth. And in many other details, they perceive things in a way that is changed from what they actually are. These disturbances <note>original: "passions"</note>, however, occur regarding the activities of the circles in the cycle <note>original: "period"</note> of the *different*. Because of this, Plato says that the seven rotations in the circle of the *different* suffer these and other similar conditions. For one of the circles—namely, the circle of the *same*—is bound <note>original: "fettered"</note>, as was observed before. Therefore, he alone is gifted with intellect who uses the circle of the *different* correctly but frees the circle of the *same*; and he will be entirely whole <note>original: "one"</note> who liberates his own inner Prometheus, who was bound by Epimetheus. For through this¹ <note>that is, through possessing the lowest form of life</note>, the soul becomes bound to the irrational order, which Epimetheus himself is said to organize <note>original: "adorn"</note>.²

<margin>74 A</margin>
> “And in this situation, there is not any one of the rotations <note>original: "circulations"</note> which possesses a ruling and leading authority.”

For since there are many cycles <note>original: "periods"</note> in the circle of the *different*, in imitation of the Soul of the Universe, they are all damaged, distorted, and weakened <note>original: "imbecile"</note>, and they exist in slavish subjection to irrational movements. It is not appropriate to call these movements *cycles*, because they rush in a *straight line* <note>original: "right line"</note> toward physical birth <note>original: "generation"</note>. For a *cycle is a movement from the same point back to the same point*. But every irrational form of knowledge and desire rushes from one thing to a different thing, extending toward that which is outside of itself. For both the object of desire and the object of knowledge are external—the former to irrational desire, and the latter to irrational knowledge. Therefore, neither does the cycle of the *same*³ govern, for it is bound and resembles a king in chains because he is in the power of his enemies; nor does the cycle of the *different* govern, for it is distorted and resembles a general who supports the interests of his enemies. > "But when certain senses, carried in from the outside, strike the soul and pull the whole vessel of it along with them, then the rotations that are ruled appear to be the ones ruling."

It has already been stated that none of the soul’s internal cycles <note>original: "periods"</note> acts as a ruler or leader; instead, our "head" is buried in matter while our "feet" are lifted high. Through these words, it is added that mortal natures rule over immortal ones. The senses are "carried in from the outside" because they report on external things; they "strike the soul" because their reports are accompanied by emotion <note>original: "passion"</note>. 

Therefore, if they pull the "cavity" of the soul—meaning its entire essence—along with them, they become the leaders of the soul's entire life. (The word *kutos* <note>original: κυτος</note>, meaning "vessel" or "cavity," refers to things that are folded together). They cause the soul to speak and think only what the senses report. This leads a person to imagine that whatever they can touch, eat, or drink is the only "true existence," while believing that the *intelligible* <term>the realm of pure thought and eternal forms</term> and the things chosen by philosophy are non-existent. 

When these senses lead, the appetites take control, and the "multitude" <note>referring to the many irrational parts of the soul</note> holds supreme power. Rational choice and reason, reduced to a subservient role, eventually end up serving the passions. But does sense-perception actually lead and govern in reality? How could it, since it is mortal and material? It only *appears* to govern reason, while in truth, it is rightfully governed by other forces. Sense is characterized by "Difference" <note>referring to the "Circle of the Different" in the soul, which deals with changing, physical things</note>; because of this, it depends on external things, is overcome by them, and is changed constantly. The irrational life creates its own slavery. Thus, it does not truly govern, as it lacks a ruling power that cannot be defeated. Instead, while being a slave to external things, it rules over natures better than itself (like reason) because those higher natures have been deceived.

# BOOK 5] PLATO'S TIMAEUS. 459

This is the conclusion of all that has been said concerning the incarnation of souls. From this, Plato reveals the causes of the soul's disturbance and upheaval resulting from its birth into the physical world <note>original: "generation"</note>, and finally, the confusion <note>original: "insanity"</note> seen in those who are recently born. Because of this, it is evident that he believed the rational soul exists even in children, but that it is bound and inactive <note>original: "sluggish"; the text notes a correction from "ruling" (archein) to "inactive" (argein)</note>, being overcome by other forces. It does not arrive at a later time, as some people imagine it does. He explains the reasons why reason is present but not effectively active. Concluding his list of these reasons, he says that because of them, the soul was originally made senseless <note>original: "stupid"</note> when it was first tied to a mortal body, and it remains so at present. For what difference is there between being young in years and being young in the way one lives? Therefore, just as reason stays quiet in adults who lack wisdom <note>original: "stupid"</note>, in the same way, in newborns <note>original: "those just born"; the text notes a correction from "young" (neais) to "newborns" (neagnesis)</note>, reason is indeed present but is made sluggish by being overcome by senselessness.

<margin>Stephanus 44B</margin>
> “However, when the flood of growth and nourishment slows down, the soul's rotations are restored to peace and follow their proper path. In the course of time, they become more stable and steady, taking on a form suited to their nature. Consequently, when the revolutions of each circle move correctly—properly identifying both 'the same' and 'the different'—they make the person who possesses them wise and prudent.”

In the *Phaedrus*, Plato teaches us about the blissful life of the soul, where it rotates alongside the gods, returns to the realm above the heavens <note>original: "supercelestial place"</note>, and contemplates Justice herself, Temperance herself, and every divine virtue. He shows how the soul moves from supreme happiness: sometimes raising its "charioteer's head" above the heavens and other times descending within them. Eventually, through a decline, it no longer sees these holy sights but follows along out of habit. For the soul's fall from a full vision of the *intelligible* <term>the realm of pure thought and eternal forms</term> into physical birth <note>original: "generation"</note> is not sudden, but happens through many intermediate stages. In this passage, however, he uses dramatic language <note>original: "tragically"</note> to describe the soul's suffering as it falls into physical birth—detailing its diversions, breaks, and turbulent flows—and he intends to...

<summary>Proclus explains that the rational soul is present even in infants but is temporarily overwhelmed by the physical processes of growth and nutrition. As the body matures and these physical "floods" subside, the soul's internal cycles stabilize, allowing for the return of reason and wisdom.</summary>

# PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS [BOOK 5] 460

[These revolutions] lead the soul gradually back to an intellectual life, and to a life that conforms to its true nature. In the higher realms, when the influence of more excellent things—and the benefits granted by the Intellect and the Gods—comes to an end, worse things follow. These include "lameness," a shedding <note>original: "defluxion"</note> of the soul's wings, forgetfulness, encounters with evil spirits <note>original: "dæmons"</note>, and a heavy downward pull. 

Here in the physical world, however, as these worse things cease and the obstacles created by matter are removed, the soul's internal circulations immediately begin to proceed according to nature. More excellent qualities then present themselves, namely: order, reason, and a prudent, wise state of being. As we reach maturity, we become more prudent and considerate, and we enter the progression <gloss>There is a gap in the original text here; the translator suggests the word "progression" (original Greek: τὴν πρόοδον) is missing.</gloss> of a stable and orderly life, with nature acting as our leader. 

Why, then, should Galen <note>A famous Greek physician and philosopher (c. 129–216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> argue that the powers of the soul simply follow the physical temperaments of the body? He claims that when the body is moist, unstable, and in a constant state of flux, the soul is stupid and unstable; but when the parts of the body are properly balanced so that the whole is in symmetry, the soul acts correctly and becomes prudent and wise. How can we possibly accept this? Since the immortal soul exists before the body, it is not right to claim it becomes "intellectual" because of the body. Rather, we should say that at one time the body acts as an obstacle to the soul in its pursuit of a well-ordered life, and at another time, it simply disturbs the soul less. 

Consider this analogy: if we lived near a trivial and talkative neighbor, we would not become more childish because of him. However, he might hinder us more or less from enjoying a quiet life. In the same way, the soul's connection to the body disturbs it at one time and eases the disturbance <note>original: "remits the tumult"</note> at another. The soul, however, does not truly become tranquil until education <note>original: "erudition"</note> arrives. Therefore, the body is an obstacle to achieving a prudent life, but it is by no means the cause of it. So much for these details.

Regarding the specific words of the text, it should be noted that the phrase "**the stream of growth and nutrition**" refers to the "physical river" <note>A Platonic metaphor for the constant flux of matter and sensory input that floods the soul at birth.</note>. It is necessary that as greater growth occurs, there must be a greater amount of nourishment. This growth is greater because "nature"—the force that provides growth—is more powerful at that time. In the young, nature flourishes and is very robust; but in those of advanced age, where the soul is more thoughtful, nature is weak <note>original: "imbecile"</note>. You can see that the soul is affected differently not only by age, but also by different times. *For the soul, in those who are awake, is...*

# BOOK V.] TIMEUS OF PLATO.

[The soul] is more vigorous [when awake], but during sleep it is indeed sluggish; yet it is then that nature especially operates and performs its proper work. Therefore, it follows quite reasonably that when the physical stream <note>Referring to the "stream" of nutrition and growth that floods the soul at birth.</note> diminishes, tranquility and order take hold of the soul. We must say, then, that "the path of the circulations" is a progression into wisdom, balance, and order. For those who are advanced in years are generally more prudent, more balanced, and more steady than those who are young. 

The various circles—into which the periods of the "circle of difference" <note>In Plato’s cosmology, the Soul is composed of the circle of the "Same" (fixed stars/intellect) and the "Different" (planets/opinion).</note> are divided—must be seen as a renovation from breakage and a perfect restoration to a circular form when they revolve correctly. An unbroken line serves as a middle ground between a broken straight line and a circumference, imitating the simplicity, balance, and likeness of a perfect circle. 

Furthermore, the circulations themselves, along with "sameness" and "difference," are referred to by their proper names in both intellectual <note>original: "dianoetic"</note> and perceptible <note>original: "sensible"</note> essences. For things are no longer moved in a childish <note>original: "puerile"</note> way; instead, there is an effort to connect and divide each thing appropriately. We should also note that knowledge <note>original: "science"</note> and ignorance are always defined by how we handle "sameness" and "difference," whether following a straight line or by alternation. For example, we affirm some things that we ought to deny, which is to treat something "different" as if it were the "same." Conversely, we deny things we should affirm because we are ignorant of the thing we are denying. 

Therefore, when the power of knowing <note>original: "gnostic power"</note> is properly developed, we name all things according to their nature, asserting that some things are the same as each other, while others are different. In this way, as our internal circulations proceed according to nature, they make the person who possesses them prudent and wise. Plato also very appropriately uses the word <term>becoming</term> <note>original Greek: γιγνομενον (gignomenon)</note> here, because anyone who becomes prudent through these circulations is undergoing a physical process of change. It also sometimes happens, in addition to these things, that there is a right education, about which he says the following:

<margin>44C</margin>
> "He, therefore, who receives education <note>original: "erudition"</note>, in conjunction with proper nourishment <note>original: "nutriment"</note>, will be perfectly whole and consistent <note>original: "same"</note>, and will avoid the greatest disease."

The soul's natural path toward wisdom is described through these words. However, Plato connects this with political education, which perfects one's natural aptitude. Through proper nourishment, this education gives the irrational part of our nature the habit of good conduct and a life that aligns with correct opinion.

<summary>Proclus explains how the soul's rational "circulations" recover their circular, orderly motion as a person matures and the physical body's growth slows. He emphasizes that true wisdom comes from correctly identifying what is "the same" and what is "different," aided by both natural development and a proper education.</summary>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.

...through education <note>original: "erudition"</note> [the soul] nourishes its rational essence by means of various studies and dialectic <note>The philosophical method of investigating truth through logical discussion.</note>. It is necessary that the irrational part of the soul be instructed by morality, while reason is instructed by the sciences, so that the former becomes obedient to a rational life and the latter, returning to the intellect, can observe the nature of all things. When these things happen, the soul is rendered **entire** and **the same**. It is **entire** because all its powers are unencumbered, and the "circle of the same" <note>In Plato’s cosmology, the "Circle of the Same" represents the soul's intellectual, unchanging movement, while the "Circle of the Different" represents its involvement with changing, physical things.</note> is freed from its chains. It is **the same** because it has applied a remedy to the distorted cycle of the "circle of the different," restoring it to an unbroken and straight condition.

Or it may be said that the soul is **entire** as it pursues whole truths instead of mere parts, raising itself from the confusion produced by things in the physical world. It rouses itself toward the intellect, surveying existence from on high and shaking off the salty waters of the "sea of generation" <note>A Neoplatonic metaphor for the material world of birth, change, and death.</note>. It is **the same** because it is returning to its own natural order and running back toward true knowledge. For ignorance is the soul's greatest disease, burying and blinding its intellectual eye.

<margin>44C</margin>
> “But whoever neglects this will proceed through the path of life in a lame condition and will pass into Hades <note>The underworld or the state of the soul after death.</note> once again imperfect and lacking intelligence.”

The philosopher [Plato] shows through these words that something is achieved by both natural growth and social education. He calls someone "imperfect" if they do not receive the right nourishment and education. Like a person whose feet are injured, such a person walks, but not well; they are not entirely deprived of the ability to move, but they cannot use their limbs in a way that is complete and perfect. In the same way, whoever neglects themselves—that is, whoever looks only downward and ignores self-knowledge—will proceed through life in a "lame" condition, having only progressed as far as nature alone could move them. 

Hence, Plato says that such a person will **again** pass into Hades imperfect and lacking intelligence, being unable to bring their intellect to perfection, because "the living come from the dead" <note>Referring to the Platonic cycle of reincarnation.</note>. Passing into Hades signifies moving into a state that is dark and without light. For this journey is not guided by the good and wise god Pluto <note>In Greek mythology, the god of the underworld; Neoplatonists often interpreted Pluto as a purifying force for the soul.</note> through the passage leading down into the subterranean place. For someone who has not purified themselves cannot know that which is wholly pure and incorruptible. <note>1</note> Hence, he is sent to—

# BOOK V.] PLATO’S TIMAEUS

...that place where he will be purified. He who has lived in accordance with Fate alone will be directed onto the right path by Fate through orderly cycles of time <note>original: "orderly periods of time"</note>.

<margin>44C</margin>
> "These details, however, occur later; but it is necessary to discuss more accurately the matters that are currently proposed for our consideration."

The discussion of the body's composition—both as a whole and in its parts—along with the irrational life <note>The part of the soul concerned with emotions and physical desires, rather than reason.</note>, follows the consideration of the soul's incarnation. A precise discussion of the soul's "allotments" <note>The specific destinies or roles assigned to souls after death.</note> is found in the investigations within *The Republic*, which aims to lead souls toward a prudent and wise life. However, it is the role of the natural philosopher <term>physiologist</term> <note>In this context, someone who studies the nature of physical things (*physis*).</note> to complete the discussion concerning the living being. 

Therefore, the philosopher correctly sets aside ethical speculations for now and moves on to physical doctrine. For this reason, he says that these details—specifically the destinies of souls—happen after the things that are now proposed for more accurate discussion. Although the sentence seems somewhat difficult, he is saying that everything just asserted will happen in the future. It is now necessary to speak about those matters we have proposed to discuss: those pertaining to the life of the body. Others, however, rearrange the words for the sake of clarity <note>original: "perspicuity"</note>, writing: *It is necessary to discuss more accurately the things now proposed to be considered.* Yet, the text that follows contradicts this rearrangement.

<margin>44C-D</margin>
> "Before these things, therefore, it is necessary to speak about bodies according to the generation of their parts,¹ and about the soul. We must show, by sticking closely to probable reasoning, through what causes and through what providence of the Gods they were created. For in this way, and for those who proceed in accordance with these matters, it is necessary to discuss the remaining details."

In these lines, Plato defines the scope of what he is about to present.

***

¹ That is, to speak of how the various parts of bodies are created <note>original: "generation of the parts of bodies"</note>.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, transitioning from the purification of the soul to the specific creation of the human body and the mortal soul by the "junior Gods."</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE [BOOK V.

...namely, that it concerns the creation <note>original: "generation"</note> of bodies and the soul. For it was clearly stated that his intention was to speak about both, and to show the specific elements from which the secondary Demiurges <term>Demiurges</term> <note>Divine craftsmen or creators in Platonic philosophy; the primary Demiurge creates the universe, while the "junior" or secondary ones create mortal life.</note> formed the soul and the body. In line with this, he had previously asserted that in forming the soul and body, it was necessary to introduce the Gods and to carry out the subsequent steps: the divisions of the soul and a more detailed discussion of the parts of the body. In this way, after a general discussion of the whole universe, he spoke about the parts it contains.

He also follows a defining principle of Platonic philosophy: to trace all creation back to the Gods. He does this now by placing the primary causes of mortal bodies and the inseparable forms of life within the Gods. This does not mean that the Gods contain specific blueprints <note>original: "definite reasons [or productive powers]"</note> for individual beings or for things that decay. A divine nature is very far removed from crafting individual, finite things. Instead, they preside over created things in an uncreated manner, and over material things in an immaterial way. They gather from many individual and immediate causes that which is individual in its effects through eternal motions and through well-arranged, multifaceted causes. 

Just as the first Demiurge <note>The primary Creator of the universe.</note> hands over the production of mortal beings to the junior Gods, so too does their providence proceed through spirits <note>original: "dæmons"</note> down to material and individual principles. In this process, they use specific natural forces as helpers <note>original: "adjutors"</note>, along with the various unique movements of these forces which differ in their powers. They also employ all the immediate causes of created beings. From these, a created being reaches its completion. It is crafted as a specific individual nature instead of a whole, and it receives an existence <note>original: "hypostasis"</note> defined by different circumstances and unique characteristics. 

Therefore, it is necessary here to speak about the body according to its parts—for instance, the head, the chest <note>original: "thorax"</note>, and the legs—and about the organs contained within each of these. It is also necessary to speak about the mortal soul, which together with the body makes up the mortal animal; this is the work of the junior Gods. We must also discuss its parts, both the cognitive <note>original: "gnostic"</note> and the appetitive <note>original: "orectic"; relating to desire or appetite.</note>. If we properly understand these through logic, we will have thoroughly discussed what it means to be human.

However, it is necessary that a human being should be considered as a complete whole, just like the entire world, because man is a small universe <term>microcosm</term>. For he has intellect and reason, and a divine and a mortal body, in the same way the universe does. He is divided in a way that corresponds to the universe. For this reason, some are accustomed to say that his intellectual part is arranged similarly to the sphere of the fixed stars, but his faculty of reason—specifically the part that contemplates—is similar to Saturn, and

# BOOK V.] TIMÆUS OF PLATO.

The political aspect of the soul is analogous to Jupiter. Of the irrational part as well, the spirited nature <note>original: "irascible nature"; referring to the part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and vigor</note> is analogous to Mars; the part endowed with the faculty of speech is analogous to Mercury; the <term>epithymetic</term> <note>The desiring or appetitive part of the soul, concerned with physical needs and pleasures.</note> part is analogous to Venus; the sensory part is analogous to the Sun; and the vegetative part <note>The part responsible for growth and nutrition.</note> is analogous to the Moon. The <term>luciform vehicle</term> <note>The "astral body" or "star-like" vehicle; in Neoplatonism, this is a subtle, immortal body that carries the soul between incarnations.</note> is likewise analogous to the heavens; but this mortal body is analogous to the sublunary region <note>The realm of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) located below the moon, characterized by change and decay.</note>. Therefore, so that you may understand the universe in its specific parts, the discourse about humanity is organized alongside the study of all nature <note>original: "physiology"</note>. And that is enough on this particular point.

But how are the *causes and protective care <note>original: "providential energies"</note> of the Gods to be divided?* Is it not that the former are essential foundations <note>original: "hypostatic"</note>, or the sources of existence, while the latter are protective in nature? The former provide essence, while the latter provide goodness. The former are the creators of mortal beings, while the latter are the saviors of immortal souls. For the Gods look after these souls with care, receive them when they descend into the realms of physical birth, and again, when the souls are willing to ascend, the Gods extend their hands and share the compassion that resides with them. 

However, both the cause and the providence of the "junior Gods" <note>The celestial deities who, in Plato’s Timaeus, craft the mortal parts of humans.</note> are both many and yet united. For how could union be passed from them to created beings, unless the Gods who produce them were themselves united to each other by a much higher priority? For this reason, Plato calls their <term>demiurgic</term> <note>Creative or craftsmanship-related; from the "Demiurge" or divine creator.</note> powers both their providence and their causes. For there are many <term>Demiurgi</term> <note>Divine creators or craftsmen.</note>, and the production of each is multifaceted. And yet, he unites this multitude of Gods. For union and a consistent power are granted to all beings—and by a much greater priority to the Gods themselves—from their divine uniqueness. This is just as intelligence is present in whole systems, and in a much greater degree within the intellectual orders themselves, stemming from the primary Intellect. 

When, in short, he refers the cause of created beings to the providence of the Gods, he grants them a primary transition into existence that is beyond words and superior to ordinary knowledge. Hence, Iamblichus <note>A highly influential Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) whom Proclus frequently cites.</note> rightly says that it is not possible to prove through logic <note>original: "collect syllogistically"</note> how the Gods produce the body and the life within it, or how they connect the two. For these things are unknown to us. Indeed, we firmly assert that all things are created by the Gods because we look toward their goodness; however, we are not able to know exactly how they proceed from that source. The reason for this is that to act with providence and to create are the prerogatives of a divine <term>hyparxis</term> <note>The essential existence or "the summit of being" of a god.</note> and possess a transcendence beyond our understanding. 

It has been shown, therefore, what the subject of this discussion is. But he reminds us again of the nature of this inquiry: that it is mixed with probability. For insofar as it is connected with nature and the creation of mortal beings, it is accompanied by probability <note>Plato famously described his account of the physical world as a "likely story" (eikos mythos) because the physical world is constantly changing and cannot be known with the absolute certainty of mathematics or metaphysics.</note>; but insofar as it returns to a divine intellect—

### ADDITIONAL NOTES.

**Vol. I. p. 1. *On this account we have prefixed the treatise of Timaeus to these Commentaries.***
This treatise by Timaeus <note>referring to Timaeus of Locri, to whom the authorship of a work on the world-soul was attributed</note>, which has been passed down to us through Proclus, is not, however, placed at the beginning of the printed edition of these Commentaries. But the reader may find it in Thomas Gale's *Small Works on Mythology* <note>original: "Opuscula Mythologica"</note>.

**P. 4. *The two co-ordinations of things.***
These two sets of opposites <note>original: "co-ordinations"</note> are as follows: limit and the unlimited <note>original: "bound the infinite"</note>; the odd and the even; the one and the many <note>original: "multitude"</note>; the right hand and the left hand; the masculine and the feminine; the stationary <note>original: "quiescent"</note> and that which is in motion; the straight and the curved; light and darkness; good and evil; the square and the oblong.

**P. 14. *Who celebrate number, &c. and the tetractys.***
For an explanation of the way in which the Pythagoreans philosophized about number, and also concerning the <term>tetractys</term> <note>The tetractys is a triangular figure of ten points arranged in four rows, which the Pythagoreans considered a sacred symbol of the organization of the universe.</note>, see my *Theoretic Arithmetic*.

**P. 17. *Our preceptor Syrianus.***
This very extraordinary man was the first who thoroughly understood and explained the hidden doctrines of the philosophers and theologians of the highest antiquity. He did not write much himself, but entrusted the public spreading of his teachings <note>original: "dogmas"</note> to Proclus.

**P. 35. *Sirens.*** The following beautiful account of the Sirens is given by Proclus in his manuscript notes <note>original: "MS. Scholia"</note> on Plato's *Cratylus*: "The divine Plato knew that there are three kinds of Sirens: the celestial, who are under the government of Jupiter; the <term>genesiurgic</term> <note>concerned with the process of physical birth and generation</note>, who are under the government of Neptune; and the <term>cathartic</term> <note>concerned with purification</note>, who are under the government of Pluto. It is common to all these to draw all things through a harmonious motion toward their ruling Gods. Hence, when the soul is in the heavens, they desire to unite it to the divine life which flourishes there. But it is proper that souls living in the world of generation should sail past them, like Ulysses in Homer’s poems, so that they may not be lured by physical existence <note>original: "generation"</note>, of which the sea is a symbol. And when souls are in the underworld <note>original: "Hades"</note>, the Sirens desire to unite them through intellectual understanding to Pluto. So, Plato knew that in the kingdom of the underworld, there are Gods, spirits <note>original: "daemons"</note>, and souls, who dance as it were around Pluto, lured by the Sirens who dwell there."

**P. 35. *Dialectic.*** The dialectic of Plato, to which Proclus refers here, is not the same as the dialectic that deals with opinion and is accurately investigated in the *Topics* of Aristotle. For the former is beyond reproach and most efficient; since it is 

<column-break/>

innate <note>original: "connate"</note> with things themselves and employs a variety of powers in order to attain the truth. It likewise imitates the intellect, from which it receives its principles, and rises through well-ordered stages to being itself. It also ends the soul's wandering among things perceived by the senses <note>original: "sensibles"</note> and explores everything by methods which cannot be disproven, until it arrives at the unspeakable <note>original: "ineffable"</note> first principle of things. The business of this supreme science is also to employ definitions, divisions, analysis, and proofs as primary tools in the investigation of causes. In doing so, it imitates the way beings proceed from the first principle of things and their continual return <note>original: "conversion"</note> to it as the ultimate object of desire. For a full account of this master science, see the notes to my translation of the *Parmenides* of Plato, and also my translation of *Select Works of Plotinus*.

**P. 43. *Physical virtues.*** The physical virtues are those common to both humans and animals, being mixed with our physical constitutions <note>original: "temperaments"</note>, and for the most part, they are often in conflict with one another; or rather, they belong to the animal nature. Or it may be said that they are flashes of light from reason when it is not blocked by a certain bad physical constitution, or that they are the result of actions in a previous life. Plato speaks of these in the *Statesman* <note>original: "Politicus"</note> and the *Laws*. For an account of the other virtues—namely, the ethical, the political, the purifying <note>original: "cathartic"</note>, the contemplative <note>original: "theoretic"</note>, and the exemplary <note>original: "paradigmatic"</note>—see the notes to my translation of the *Phaedo* of Plato, and also the additional notes included in my translation of *Select Works of Plotinus*.

**P. 58. *Sceptre of twenty-four measures.***
The sceptre of Jupiter, as we are informed by Proclus in his notes on the *Cratylus*, was—according to Orpheus—twenty-four measures in length. By this, says Proclus, the theologian signifies Jupiter's establishment of those two divine orders, the celestial and the super-celestial, and his reign over two series of Gods, each of which is characterized by the number twelve.

**P. 91. *For the relation subsisting among you, that Phaeton, the offspring of the Sun, &c.***
The following explanation of the myth <note>original: "fable"</note> of Phaeton is given by Olympiodorus in his notes <note>original: "Scholia"</note> on the *Meteorology* <note>original: "Meteors"</note> of Aristotle. "Phaeton signifies a comet, by which large parts of the earth are destroyed from time to time. But he is said to have been the child of the Sun because a comet is a <term>sublunary</term> <note>located in the atmosphere beneath the moon</note> body, consisting of a collection of dry vapors raised and set on fire by the Sun. He is also said to have desired the government—"

...management of the chariot of the Sun, because a comet desires to imitate the circular motion of the Sun. He did not keep to the track observed by his parent because a comet does not move in a direction parallel to that of the Sun. He was struck by lightning <note>original: "blasted by thunder"</note> through the anger of Jupiter because this comet was extinguished by damp vapors. For this reason, he is said to have fallen into the river Eridanus because the comet was extinguished through moisture. He was mourned by the Heliades because the vapor resulting from the dissolution of the comet flowed downward; being watery in nature, it corresponded to tears. The myth, therefore, obscurely signifies that the sap of the poplar tree is produced from moisture similar to that which was produced by the dissolution of the comet.

<margin>Page 44.</margin> *The horses, therefore, and charioteers of the Gods, are all of them good, etc.*

These are beautifully explained by Hermeas in his scholarly notes <note>original: "Scholia"</note> on the *Phaedrus*, as follows:

What are we to understand by the charioteer and the two horses? In the first place, we must consider whether it is necessary to classify <note>original footnote 1: "Instead of <term>to do</term> (πραττειν) here, it is obviously necessary to read <term>to arrange</term> (ταττειν)."</note> them according to essences, according to powers, or according to activities <note>original: "energies"</note>. For there are different opinions on this subject. I say, then, that they must be classified according to powers. Their arrangement cannot be according to activities, since the horses are represented as acting, but there are no "activities of activities"; and because the activities of the soul change over time, but the horses are always the same. For the soul does not receive different horses at different times but always has the same ones. Nor can the arrangement be according to essences, since even in our souls, the essences remain unstained by vice. For the essence of the soul is never corrupted; if it were, it would perish. But its powers can become depraved, and this is even more true of its activities. Plato himself likewise says, "*that the horses and charioteers of the Gods are all of them good, and consist of such things as are good;*" but of ours he says, "*that they become depraved, and suffer a shedding of the wings <note>original: "defluxion"</note>.*" Therefore, if the essence of our soul remains unstained by vice, but its powers become distorted, the horses and charioteers may be very properly classified according to powers. Plato himself clearly proclaims this when he says, "*Let it be similar to the innate <note>original: "connascent"</note> power of a winged chariot and charioteer.*" If, however, someone should say that the words "*all of them are good and consist of things good*" are spoken to signify that these horses and charioteers are derived from benevolent causes, the words that follow will testify against this interpretation. For our horses and charioteers are also from things that are good, as from causes; so by that logic, all of them would be good. Plato, however, says that ours are stained with vice. But Plato is not the first who assumes a charioteer and horses: for before him, they were used by the divinely inspired poets Homer, Orpheus, and Parmenides. 

<column-break/>

By them, however, as being inspired, they are mentioned without an explained cause, for they spoke with divine enthusiasm. But since Plato introduces nothing into his philosophy that he cannot derive from a cause, let us show why—though he speaks with greater dignity about these particulars—he omits to mention their causes. In the meantime, we should observe that the theologians before him appear to have assumed the charioteer and horses as pertaining to powers. For Jupiter in Homer <note>Iliad, book 8, verse 440.</note> uses horses, which Neptune is said to unharness <note>original: "unbrace"</note>, and he does not always use them but is sometimes represented sitting on a throne. But if the essence of Jupiter consisted in riding in a chariot, and Jupiter was the same as the charioteer, he would always drive a chariot. Now, however, he is represented as doing other things. Therefore, the different powers of Jupiter are honored through the horses and charioteer. In the meantime, it must be observed that the assertions respecting a divine and human soul ought to be common to both.

Plato, therefore, in the *Timaeus*, says that the Demiurge <note>The divine craftsman or creator of the material world in Platonic philosophy.</note>, in constituting the essence of the soul, took a middle essence from the "genera of being"—namely, from [the three categories] essence, sameness, and difference. And this middle nature which he assumed is a medium between an indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> essence and the essence which is divided among bodies. But the irrational life, nature, and the ways the soul participates in the body constitute the essence which is divided among bodies. And again, the Demiurge assumed a middle "sameness," which is a medium between indivisible sameness and the sameness which is divided among bodies. The same also takes place with respect to the middle "difference." The Demiurge likewise, says Plato, mixing these three, formed the essence of the soul. These "middles," however, in divine souls consist of pure and incorruptible categories, but this is not the case in our souls. As Plato says, "the Demiurge poured and mixed the remainder of the former mixture; in a certain respect, indeed, after the same manner, yet not similarly incorruptible, but inferior to the first, falling to a second and third degree." *The horses, therefore, and the charioteer, are the powers of these three; and the one power of the soul, which produces these three powers, is the Form <note>original: "idea"</note> of the soul.* The power of being (that is, of essence), which is one of the categories, is the charioteer; the power of sameness is the better of the two horses; and the power of difference is the inferior horse. Hence, if we conceive of two horses and a charioteer that are made to unite, then the one power which generates and produces the charioteer and the horses is the Form of the soul. *Power*, however, must here be understood in the way geometers use the term, as when they say that a straight line is "potentially" <note>original: "in power"</note> a square. In what was said before, Plato discussed the essence of the soul; but here, he speaks about its powers; and in what follows, about its activities. These being three—namely, essence, self-motion, and immortality—three powers are assumed here analogous to them: the Form of the soul, the horses, and the more specific lives of the horses. For the Form of the soul is assumed as analogous to the...

<meta>This page continues a detailed Neoplatonic explanation of the soul’s nature, using the allegory of the chariot and horses from Plato’s *Phaedrus*. It interprets the "horses" and "charioteer" as symbolic of the soul's different powers and its relationship to both the divine and the physical worlds.</meta>

<page-num>469</page-num>
<header>ADDITIONAL NOTES.</header>

...one essence of the soul, which uniquely possesses both self-motion and immortality. However, the horses and their self-moving nature are considered analogous to the soul's self-motion. The more specific aspects of the soul’s life—namely its ascents and descents, the shedding <note>original: "defluxion"</note> of its wings, and their regrowing <note>original: "germination"</note>—are analogous to its immortality.

But why does Plato call the power of the *Same* and the power of the *Different* the "horses," while calling the power of "Essence" (one of the primary categories <note>original: "genera"</note> of being) the "charioteer"? It is evident that all these categories participate in one another, but each is named according to whichever quality is most dominant. Essence, which is here used to describe the composition of the soul, is the highest point and is most perfect; because of this, it has dominion over the rest. For this reason, the soul is not forced to move according to its fundamental nature <note>original: "essence"</note>.¹ However, the remaining two powers—the *Same* and the *Different*—are likened to horses because they are seen in motion and in regular, repeating cycles <note>original: "periodic progressions"</note>. These powers are also the circles or wheels of the *Same* and the *Different*. When they are viewed as moving toward the realm of pure thought <note>original: "intelligible"</note>, they are seen as horses; but when they return to their original state, they are seen as circles or wheels.

The superior wheel—the circle of the *Same*—is the one that revolves around divine realities and has the power to lift the soul upward; for this reason, it is called "agile" or "nimble." But the less excellent wheel—the circle of the *Different"—is generative <note>original: "genesiurgic," meaning involved in the creation of physical life</note>; it revolves around the physical world <note>original: "sensible"</note> and the realm of opinion <note>original: "doxastic"</note>. This wheel is called "upright" when it possesses its proper virtue (indicating a correct orientation) and "oblique" when it reports physical sensations without distortion. 

For example, if the faculty of opinion wishes to perceive something in the physical world, "deliberate choice" <note>original: "pre-election"</note> is sufficient to excite and direct the spirit. If necessary, it even sends out rays through the eyes. These rays dart out toward the physical object, and the sense of sight—reflecting back through the eyes—reports what it sees to the spirit, then to the faculty of opinion. Thus, this "reflection" is not perfectly circular, but by running in a straight line from the goal to the starting line and back again, it imitates a circle. This entire process represents an "upright" circle. But when it reports things in a distorted way, it is said to suffer from various "fractures." In individual <note>original: "partial"</note> souls, this circle has a downward-pulling, generative power. In divine souls, however, it provides providential care for lower forms of life.

We may also make the following division: the "Intellect" of the soul is the charioteer; the "Circle of the Same" (the better horse) is the soul’s reasoning faculty <note>original: "dianetic part"</note>; and the "Circle of the Different" (the inferior horse) is the faculty of opinion <note>original: "doxastic part"</note>. However, it must be noted that reasoning participates in "difference," and opinion participates in "sameness." Every part of the soul you might identify participates in both. If we examine the horses and charioteer according to the highest part of the soul—its supreme union with divine thoughts and the Gods—then that union itself is the charioteer. But the better horse

<column-break/>

will be that power of the soul which always aspires toward divine realities <note>original: "intelligibles"</note>. The inferior horse will be that power which comes into contact with thoughts that involve division and transition. 

These definitions apply if you look at the charioteer and horses within the reasoning <note>original: "dianoetic"</note> soul alone. But if you look at them within the soul of opinion, then the reasoning faculty must be seen as the charioteer; the power of opinion that always desires to align with reason is the better horse; and the power that yearns for physical creation <note>original: "generation"</note> and the governance of lower things is the inferior horse. It is also possible to view the charioteer as the combination of both reason and opinion, with the better horse representing reason alone and the inferior horse representing opinion. It should be observed that when the soul devotes itself to more excellent realities, opinion yields itself entirely to reason and wishes to belong to it alone—though when it grows weary, it wishes to act on its own. These things—the horses and the charioteer—can be observed within the rational soul alone.

However, since the soul descends so that an "irrational nature" is woven into it, and since each horse resists being connected to this irrational form, we must consider them in this condition as well. The soul possessed its original form through its eternal progression from the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> alone. But the qualities I am about to describe are received by the soul from the "Junior Gods" <note>the subordinate deities who build the mortal body</note> and from its connection with the mortal form of life. 

In this state, the charioteer resides in the faculty of opinion. The better horse is "anger" <note>original: "anger," likely referring to the spirited part or *thymos*</note>, and the inferior horse is "desire." Thus, when opinion is upright, it produces a balanced, right-thinking man and a balanced charioteer. But when opinion is distorted, it produces a distorted man, resembling a charioteer dragged along by the will of the horses. When these "horses of opinion" and their charioteer are properly disciplined, they produce the highest type of citizen <note>original: "political man"</note>; but the "reasoning horses" and charioteer produce the philosopher <note>original: "contemplative or theoretic man"</note>. 

These horses and their charioteer change according to the planetary spheres and the elements, and according to every form of life. In the sphere of the Sun, they are "Solar"; in the sphere of Jupiter, they are "Jovian"; in the sphere of Mars, they are "Martial." In short, they are always established according to the specific character of the God they are following. If they are established according to a divine form, they are divine; if according to an angelic form, they are angelic; if according to a daemoniacal form, they are daemoniacal; if according to a heroic form, they are heroic; and so on through all other forms of life.

But what are we to understand by the word *hypopteron* <note>original: ὑπόπτερον</note>?³ First, let us see what a "wing" signifies. The wing of the soul is its "upward-leading" <note>original: "anagogic"</note> power, which is most clearly seen in the better of—

² That is, a man belonging to a middle class of excellence.
³ This word means literally "having wings" or "under-winged."
