**The two horses.** We therefore call this horse a wheel—or rather the circle of the *Same*—because it is a lover of beauty, aspires toward the realm of pure thought <note>original: "intelligibles"</note>, and never resists the charioteer. Instead, it acts rightly and even errs in harmony with the charioteer. But the other horse, which represents the origin-generating <term>original: "genesiurgic"</term> power of the soul that pulls it downward, gravitates toward the earth and resists the charioteer. 

All souls, therefore, have wings, for all of them possess all these powers; this is also true of the charioteer and the horses. However, in divine souls, the wings are always unencumbered. Because of this, they are said to be "winged" <note>original: πτερωτοι (pterotoi)</note> rather than "partially winged" <note>original: υποπτεροι (hypopteroi)</note>. On the contrary, in our human souls, the wings are not always expanded but are sometimes closed and sluggish. We possess the power of these wings (since we never lose our inherent powers), but we do not always have the active energy to use them. Therefore, the term "partially winged" is more appropriate for us, as we possess the potential power but not the complete active energy of wings. 

To the gods, however, the term "winged" is suited, as they possess both the power and the energy in full effect. This is why Plato later says of our soul that *formerly it was winged*. By choosing a word that applies to both divine souls and our own, he uses "partially winged." All souls have an upward-leading <term>original: "anagogic"</term> power, though some have it constantly, while others have it only occasionally in active expression. Alternatively, it could be said that the term "partially winged" is accurately applied to both divine souls and ours: for divine souls, it means their wings are focused on their lowest powers nearest to the earth, while their main energies remain fixed on pure thought. For our souls, "partially winged" is used because "fully winged" is only true for us at certain times.

->P. 54. *Plato divides poetry into the divinely inspired and the technical <note>original: "artificial"</note>.*<-

Since Proclus uses "divinely inspired poetry" to mean what Plato in the *Phaedrus* calls the "offspring of poetic madness" <note>original: "mania"</note>, and since the energy of divine inspiration <note>original: "enthusiasm"</note> is frequently mentioned in these commentaries, the following account is added. This explanation of divine inspiration and the different kinds of madness mentioned by Plato is taken from the writings <note>original: "Scholia"</note> of Hermeas on that dialogue for the benefit of the English reader interested in Plato.

> "Since Plato here describes four kinds of madness <note>original: "mania"</note>—by which I mean divine inspiration <note>original: "enthusiasm"</note> and possession by the gods—namely the musical, the initiatory <term>original: "telestic"</term>, the prophetic, and the amatory, we must first discuss divine inspiration itself. We must show which part of the soul this inspired energy belongs to; whether every part of the soul possesses it; if all inspiration comes from the gods; and in which part of the soul it is produced, or if it exists in something even more excellent than the soul. 
> 
> Where then does that which is properly and primarily called divine inspiration exist, and what is it? The rational soul has two parts: one is discursive reason <term>original: "dianoia"</term>, and the other is opinion. Of discursive reason, one part is the lowest (which is properly called reason), but another part is the highest, which is 

<column-break/>

> the intellect of the soul. It is through this part that the soul becomes truly intellectual, and some call it the 'potential intellect.' There is also something even above this, which is the very summit of the whole soul and most closely allied to 'the One.' This part wishes well to all things, always gives itself up to the gods, and is ready to do whatever they please. This is called the 'one' of the soul; it bears the image of the divine 'One' that exists beyond all being and unites the entire soul. 
> 
> We can learn that things exist this way as follows: the rational soul derives its existence from all causes prior to itself—that is, from the divine Intellect and the gods. But it also exists from itself, for it perfects itself. Therefore, as far as it comes from the gods, it possesses 'the one,' which unites all its powers and its internal variety, joining them to 'the One itself.' This part is the first to receive the gifts granted by the gods. It also makes the entire essence of the soul 'good-formed' <term>original: "boniform"</term>, through which it is connected and united to the gods. 
> 
> However, as far as the soul comes from the Intellect, it possesses an intellectual nature. Through this, it understands forms by direct insight or intuition rather than through step-by-step reasoning, and it is joined to the Intellect above it. And as far as the soul creates itself, it possesses the power of discursive reason <term>original: "dianoetic power"</term>. Through this, it creates sciences and principles, works through logical steps, and draws conclusions from propositions. It is evident that the soul gives existence to itself because it brings itself to perfection; since that which leads itself to perfection and gives itself well-being will certainly give itself existence, for well-being is a greater thing than mere being. If the soul gives the greater thing to itself, it will certainly give the lesser. 
> 
> Therefore, true divine inspiration from the gods is achieved according to this 'one' of the soul, which is above reason and above the soul’s intellect. This 'one' is at other times in a relaxed and dormant state. When this 'one' is illuminated by the gods, the entire life of the soul is illuminated—including the intellect, the reason, and even the irrational part—and a shadow of this divine inspiration is transmitted even to the body itself.
> 
> "Other types of inspiration are produced in other parts of the soul,¹ as certain spirits <term>original: "dæmons"</term> excite them,² or even the gods themselves, though usually through the intervention of spirits. For example, the reason is said to work with divine inspiration when it discovers sciences and principles in a very short time and to a greater degree than other men. Likewise, opinion and imagination <note>original: "phantasy"</note> are said to be inspired when they discover arts and accomplish wonderful works. Examples include the statues made by Phidias, or as Homer says³ of the man who made the belt of Hercules: 'that he neither did, nor would technically produce such another.' Even anger is said to be inspired when, in battle, it acts with supernatural power:
> 
> > 'Like Mars, when brandishing his spear, he raged.'⁴

² Because of this same mistake, the Greek word for "it" <note>original: αυτο</note> must be read as "them" <note>original: αυτα</note> in this context.

<columns>

But if someone, giving in to desire, should eat something that reason forbids, and through this unexpectedly becomes well, you might say that desire also in this instance acted "enthusiastically"—though in an obscure way. In this sense, enthusiasm is also produced in the other parts of the soul. However, enthusiasm properly so called occurs when the **"one"** of the soul—that part which is above the intellect—is stirred by the Gods and receives inspiration from them. 

At different times, the soul is possessed according to its own readiness by different Gods. It is more or less possessed when the intellect or <term>original: "dianoia"</term> <note>Dianoia refers to the soul's ability to reason through logic and steps, rather than direct intellectual intuition.</note> is what is being moved. Just as when we ask what philosophy is, we do not always define it accurately but frequently—through an improper use of the word—call mathematics or physics "philosophy" and "science," we do the same with respect to enthusiasm. For even if it is the imagination <note>original: "phantasy"</note> that is excited, we are accustomed to calling that excitation enthusiasm. 

Furthermore, those who attribute enthusiasm to the "temperatures" <note>This refers to the balance of humors or physical states within the body.</note> of bodies, the excellent quality of the air, the influence of vapors, the suitability of times and places, or the movement of the planets, are speaking of the cooperating and material causes of the phenomenon rather than its true causes. You have, therefore, the Gods as the producing cause of enthusiasm; the material cause is the soul itself (which acts enthusiastically) or external symbols; the formal cause is the inspiration of the Gods upon the **"one"** of the soul; and the final cause is "the Good."

"If, however, the Gods always wish for what is good for the soul, why does the soul not always act enthusiastically? We might say that while the Gods always wish for the soul's good, they also wish for the order of the universe to prevail. Because of many different causes, the soul is not always adapted to enthusiasm, which is why it does not always act in that state. Some say that the <term>original: "telestic art"</term> <note>The "telestic art" refers to theurgy or the practice of sacred rites and mysteries used to purify the soul and invoke the divine.</note> extends only as far as the sublunary region <note>The realm "below the moon," which in ancient cosmology was the world of change and decay (the Earth).</note>. If they mean that no celestial or higher being acts upon the sublunary region, they are clearly asserting something absurd. 

But if they mean that the <term>original: "telestæ"</term>—those who perform these mystic rites—are not able to act above the lunar sphere, we say that if all soul-assignments were sublunary, their assertion would be true. However, there are also assignments for souls above the moon (for some are attendants of the Sun, others of the Moon, and others of Saturn, since the <term>original: "Demiurgus"</term> <note>The Divine Craftsman or Creator of the physical universe.</note> distributed some into the Earth, others into the Moon, and others elsewhere). Since this is the case, it is possible for the soul to act above the moon. For what the whole order of things gives to the soul over a very long period, the soul is also able to give to itself for a short time when assisted by the Gods through the telestic art. A soul can never act beyond its own assigned level, but it can act to the full extent of it. For instance, if a soul was assigned to the level of philosophy, even if it chose a different life, it could still act somewhat philosophically. There are also said to be certain "supermundane" <note>Existing beyond the physical world.</note> souls. And thus we have shown how the soul acts with divine enthusiasm.

"But how are statues said to have an enthusiastic 

<column-break/>

energy? We might say that a statue, being inanimate, does not itself act toward divinity. Instead, the telestic art purifies the matter of which the statue consists. By placing certain characters and symbols around it, the art first makes the statue "animated"—causing it to receive a certain life from the world-soul. Next, it prepares the statue to be illuminated by a divine nature, through which it always delivers oracles as long as it remains properly adapted. 

For the statue, once perfected by the telestic art, remains endowed with a prophetic power until it becomes entirely unsuited to divine illumination. However, a human who receives the inspiring influence of the Gods receives it only at certain times, not always. The cause of this is that the soul, when filled with deity, acts through that power. Because it is acting above its own natural strength, it becomes weary. It would be a God, similar to the souls of the stars, if it did not become weary. But the statue, according to its participation, remains illuminated. Therefore, the statue's loss of power only happens when it is no longer fit to receive it, unless it is perfected and animated *anew* <note>original: "de novo"</note> by the mystic operator. We have shown, then, that enthusiasm properly so called is achieved in the **"one"** of the soul and is an illumination from divinity.

"Next, let us discuss the order and use of the four <term>original: "manias"</term> <note>In this context, "mania" does not mean insanity, but "divine madness" or inspired states described by Plato in the *Phaedrus*.</note>, and show why the philosopher mentions only these. Is it because there are no others, or because these were sufficient for his purpose? Plato himself indicates as he proceeds that there are many other divine inspirations and 'madnesses,' mentioning earlier the inspiration from the Nymphs. There are also inspirations from Pan, the Mother of the Gods, and the Corybantes. Here, however, he only presents these four manias. He does so, first, because these alone are sufficient for the soul to achieve its proper <term>original: "apocatastasis"</term> <note>The restoration of the soul to its original, divine state.</note>, and second, because he is presenting the most direct steps for the soul's ascent. 

The gifts of the Gods to all beings are many and beyond comprehension, but here he presents the energies of the Gods that extend to souls. He presents these four manias not as if one—especially the "amatory" <note>Inspired love of beauty.</note>—was not enough to lead the soul back to its original happiness, but to show the series, regular gradation, and orderly perfection of the soul. 

Just as a tyrannical life can be suddenly changed into an aristocratic one through intense effort and divine help—though the gradual ascent is from tyrannical to democratic, then oligarchic, then timocratic, and finally aristocratic—the same is true here. As the soul is about to ascend and be restored to its former happiness, it is first possessed by the **musical mania**, then the **telestic** <note>mystic/ritual</note>, then the **prophetic** <note>original: "μουσικην" (musical), but corrected by the author to "μαντικην" (prophetic)</note>, and finally the **amatory mania** <note>original: "μαντικην" (prophetic), but corrected by the author to "ερωτικην" (amatory)</note>. These inspirations work together and need one another, so great is their connection. For the telestic requires the prophetic mania..."

It also details how "telestic art" (theurgy) can animate statues to deliver oracles and outlines the four types of divine madness—musical, telestic, prophetic, and amatory—that lead the soul back to its divine origin.</summary>

interprets many things pertaining to the former. And again, the prophetic requires the telestic mania <note>original: "telestic mania"; this refers to initiatory or ritual inspiration used in religious mysteries</note>. For the telestic mania perfects and establishes oracular predictions. Furthermore, the prophetic uses the poetic and musical mania. For prophets, so to speak, always speak in verse. And again, the musical uses the prophetic mania spontaneously, as Plato says.

But what need is there to speak about the amatory and musical manias? For nearly the same persons exercise both of these—as, for instance, Sappho, Anacreon, and the like—because these cannot exist without each other. But it is very evident that the amatory mania contributes to all of these, since it is subservient to enthusiasm of every kind: for no enthusiasm can be achieved without amatory inspiration. And you may see how Orpheus appears to have applied himself to all of these, as they are necessary to and dependent upon each other. For we learn that he was most telestic and most prophetic, and was excited by Apollo; and besides this, he was most poetic, which is why he is said to have been the son of Calliope <note>The Muse of epic poetry</note>. He was likewise most amatory, as he himself acknowledges to Musaeus, extending divine gifts to him and rendering him perfect. Hence he appears to have been possessed by all the manias, and this by a necessary consequence. For there is an abundant union, cooperation, and alliance among the Gods who preside over these manias: namely, the Muses, Bacchus, Apollo, and Love.

"It remains, therefore, that we should explain the nature of each of the manias. We should first observe that those which are internal—originating from the soul itself and giving perfection to it—are of one kind; but their external energies, which preserve the outward man and our physical nature, are of another. The four external forms, however, are analogous to the four internal manias. 

Let us consider, first, the internal ones, which alone originate from the soul itself, and let us see what they effect in the soul. In order that this and their arrangement may become manifest, let us survey from on high the descent (as Plato says) and the "shedding of the wings" of the soul. From the beginning, the soul was united to the Gods, and its own unity was joined to their "One." But afterwards, the soul, departing from this divine union, descended into the intellect. It no longer possessed real beings in a united and singular way, but understood and surveyed them by simple mental focus and, as it were, intellectual contact. 

Next, departing from the intellect and descending into reasoning and <term>dianoia</term> <note>original: "dianoia"; the soul's ability to reason through logic and steps</note>, it no longer understood real beings by simple intuition, but through logic and transition, proceeding from one thing to another, from premises to conclusions. Afterwards, abandoning true reasoning and its analytical character, it descended into the world of "generation" <note>The physical world of birth and decay</note> and became filled with much irrationality and confusion. It is necessary, therefore, that it should return to its proper principles and go back to the place from which it came. 

To this ascent and <term>apocatastasis</term> <note>original: "apocatastasis"; the restoration of the soul to its original divine state</note>, these four manias contribute. The musical mania leads the agitated and disturbed parts of the soul—which were swept away into chaos and unfitness and filled with great tumult—back to symphony and harmony. But the telestic mania causes the soul to be perfect and entire, and

<column-break/>

prepares it to act intellectually. For while the musical mania alone harmonizes and calms the parts of the soul, the telestic mania causes the whole of it to act, preparing it to become a complete whole so that its intellectual part may function. For the soul, by descending into the realms of generation, resembles something broken and weakened. The "circle of the same" (the intellectual part) is fettered, and the "circle of the different" (the part concerned with opinion) suffers many fractures and distortions. Hence, the soul acts only partially, and not according to its whole self. 

The Dionysian inspiration <note>Relating to Bacchus/Dionysus</note>, therefore, once the parts of the soul are harmonized, renders the soul perfect; it causes it to act according to its whole self and to live intellectually. But the Apollonian mania converts and excites all the multiplied powers and the whole of the soul toward its "One." Hence Apollo is so named because he elevates the soul from multitude to unity. And the remaining mania, the amatory, receiving the soul now united, joins this "One" of the soul to the Gods and to intelligible beauty. 

Just as the givers of these inspirations are transcendently united and exist within each other, the gifts also participate in and communicate with each other; thus, the recipient soul possesses an adaptation to all these gifts. This, therefore, is the order, and these are the internal energies and powers of these four manias within the soul itself.

"But let us also consider their external effects on man. The musical mania causes us to speak in verse, to act and move rhythmically, and to sing in meter the splendid deeds of divine men, their virtues, and their pursuits. Through these, we discipline our lives, just as the inward manias harmonize our souls. 

The telestic mania, by expelling everything foreign, contaminating, and harmful, keeps our life perfect and blameless. By banishing insane and diabolical illusions <note>original: "phantasy"</note>, it causes us to be sane, whole, and perfect, just as the internal telestic mania makes the soul perfect and entire. 

Again, the prophetic mania contracts the extension and infinity of time into one; it sees all things—the past, the future, and the present—as one single "now." Because it sees the future as present to itself, it predicts what will be. It thus allows us to pass through life in a blameless manner, just as the internal prophetic mania contracts and elevates all the many powers and lives of the soul to the "One," so that it may be better preserved and connected. 

Finally, the amatory mania draws young people to us and makes them our friends. It is instructive to youth, leading them from physical beauty to the beauty of the soul, and from there toward intelligible beauty—just as the internal amatory mania joins the "One" of the soul to the Gods.

"All the manias mentioned above are superior to the soul's ordinary energies of prudence and temperance. Nevertheless, there is a mania that is equal to temperance, and which we say has, in a certain respect, a prerogative above it. For certain inspirations are produced according to the middle and opinion-based levels of the soul. According to these, artists achieve certain things and discover theories beyond expectation, as Asclepius did, for¹"

instance, in medicine, and Hercules in the practical life."¹

Afterwards, in commenting on what Plato says of the divine madness <note>original: "mania"</note> from the Muses—namely, "that it adorns the countless deeds of the ancients"—Hermeas observes: "The inward energy in the soul of the poetic madness, by applying itself to superior and intelligible natures, imparts harmony and order to lower natures. However, external divinely inspired poetry celebrates the deeds of the ancients and instructs both its contemporaries and posterity, extending its energies everywhere." But Plato says, "He who, without the divinely inspired madness of the Muses, expects to become a divine poet, will, by merely imagining it, become imperfect himself; and his poetry will be surpassed and hidden by the poetry which is the offspring of divine madness." Hermeas adds, "For what similarity is there between the poetry of Choerilus and Callimachus, and that of Homer and Pindar? For the divinely inspired poets, being filled by the Muses, always invoke them and direct everything they say toward them." For a fuller and most admirable account of poetic madness, and of the different species of poetry according to Proclus, see the notes on the 10th book of the *Republic* in my translation of Plato, and also the Introduction to my translation of the *Rhetoric, Poetics,* and *Nicomachean Ethics* of Aristotle.

From what is said here by Hermeas about enthusiasm, the intelligent reader will easily see that none of the Roman poets whose works have been preserved for us possessed that which is primarily, properly, and truly "enthusiasm." They lacked that highest species of it, in which the "one" of the soul <note>The "one" of the soul refers to the highest, most unified part of the human spirit that is capable of direct union with the Divine</note> is illuminated by a divine nature and is united to it through transcendent similarity. As for Virgil, indeed the leader of these poets, although he invokes the Muse at the beginning of the *Aeneid*, his invocation of her is only a partial and secondary thing. For he only calls on her to explain to him the causes that involved a man of such remarkable piety as Aeneas in so many misfortunes:
> Muse, remind me of the causes, etc. <note>original Latin: "Musa, mihi causas memora, &c."</note>
And, trusting in his own genius, he begins his poem without asking for heavenly inspiration:
> I sing of arms and the man, etc. <note>original Latin: "Arma, virumque cano, &c."</note>
To this may be added that placing himself before the Muse resembles the "I and my king" <note>original Latin: "ego et meus rex"</note> of Cardinal Wolsey. On the contrary, divinely inspired poets, as Hermeas well observes, knock, as it were, at the gates of the Muses, and being filled from that source, they exclaim:
-> Tell me now, O Muses— <-
<note>original Greek: "Εσπετε νυν μοι Μουσαι"—Iliad 2.484</note>
And,
-> Sing, O Goddess, of the wrath— <-
<note>original Greek: "Μηνιν αειδε θεα"—Iliad 1.1</note>
And,
-> Tell me, O Muse, of the man— <-
<note>original Greek: "Ανδρα μοι εννεπε Μουσα"—Odyssey 1.1</note>
For being always directed toward them, they arrange the

<column-break/>

whole of what they afterwards say as something derived from the Muses' inspiring influence. With an arrogance, too, peculiar to the Romans, who, as a certain Greek poet says,² were a people
-> "Beyond measure proud," <-
Virgil associates himself in his 4th *Eclogue* with the Muses as their equal:
-> Sicilian Muses, let us sing of slightly greater things: <-
<note>original Latin: "Sicilides Musæ, paulo majora canamus:"</note>
This reminds me of what Suetonius relates of Caligula: that he would place himself between the statues of Castor and Pollux and confer privately with Jupiter Capitolinus, imagining that he was intimate with and equal in dignity to these divinities. And as for the poets who have lived since the fall of the Roman Empire, it would be ridiculous to suppose that they possessed this highest enthusiasm, as they did not believe in the existence of the sources from which it is alone genuinely derived.

### P. 61. *As therefore, Jupiter in Homer sends the Gods, who preside over the mundane contrariety, to the Grecian war.*—

The following beautiful explanation of the hidden meaning of the Trojan War in Homer is given by Hermeas in his *Scholia* on the *Phaedrus* of Plato:

"By Ilium <note>Troy</note> we must understand the realm of generation and matter, which is named from 'mud' and 'matter' <note>original Greek: <term>παρα την ιλυν και την υλην</term>, "para ten ilun kai ten ulen," a wordplay on the Greek words for mud and matter</note>, and in which there are war and rebellion. But the Trojans represent material forms and all the lives that exist around bodies. Hence, the Trojans are also called *genuine* or *native-born* (<term>ithageneis</term>). For all the lives that exist around bodies and irrational³ souls are favorable and attentive to their own matter. On the contrary, the Greeks are rational souls, coming from Greece—that is, from the intelligible realm into matter. Hence, the Greeks are called *foreigners* (<term>epelydes</term>) and defeat the Trojans, as they belong to a superior order. But they fight with each other over the phantom of Helen, as the poet says (about the image of Aeneas):
> Around the phantom, Greeks and Trojans fight.⁴
Helen signifies intelligible beauty, being a certain 'vessel' (<term>elenon tis ousa</term>) that attracts intellect to itself. An outflow <note>original: "efflux"</note> of this intelligible beauty is granted to matter through Venus; and over this outflow of beauty, the Greeks fight with the Trojans (that is, rational lives fight with irrational ones). And those who oppose and defeat matter return to the intelligible realm, which is their true country; but those who do not, as is the case with the masses, are bound to matter. Therefore, just as the prophet in the 10th book of the *Republic*, before the descent of souls, announces to them how they may return to their original happiness after periods of ten thousand years; so also Calchas predicts to the Greeks their return in ten years—the number ten being a symbol of a perfect period. And as in the lives of souls, some are raised up through philosophy, others through the art of love,⁵"

See my translation of the *Dissertation of Maximus Tyrius, On the Practical and Theoretical Life*.
² See Olympiodorus in *Aristotle's Meteorology*.
³ For "analogous souls" here, it is necessary to read "irrational souls" (<term>alogoi psuchai</term>).

For the beauty in the realms of generation is an outflow of intelligible beauty.

**P. 292.** *The essence which is without shape, etc., and the plain of truth.*
Proclus alludes here to the following passage in Plato’s *Phaedrus*: "The region above the heavens <note>original: "supercelestial place"</note> has not yet been celebrated by any of our poets, nor will it ever be praised according to its true dignity and worth. It exists, however, in the following manner (for we should dare to speak the truth, especially when speaking about the truth): without color, without shape, and without physical contact, existing as true essence, it is perceived only by the contemplative intellect, the governor of the soul; around this essence, the category of true science resides." On these words, Hermeas comments as follows:
> "Why does Plato say that no poet before him, or any who might follow him, will celebrate the region above the heavens according to its dignity and worth? He was not so arrogant as to think that he alone had deservedly praised it. Rather, his assertion means this: if we understand 'poets' to be those who are 'three steps removed from the truth' <note>Plato argues in Book 10 of the *Republic* that art is an imitation of an imitation, making poets 'third from the truth.'</note>—that is, the multitude of merely human poets who are not divinely inspired—then the truth of his statement is evident. This excludes Homer and Orpheus, as well as Hesiod and Musaeus, who have spoken about this place. No one among the common crowd of such poets and artists has celebrated this place as it deserves; this has been accomplished only by divinely inspired poets like Homer and Orpheus. But if we understand 'all poets' to include Homer and Orpheus, then Plato must also include himself, as he is also unable to speak of this place in a manner suited to its dignity. It is <unclear>just</unclear> as if he had said: 'No human poet has deservedly praised the region above the heavens; this has only been achieved by Apollo and the choir of the Muses.'"

But having said that no one has celebrated the region above the heavens according to its merit, why does he now say, "We should dare to affirm the truth"? Is it because the truth must be asserted as it exists in human understanding? For it is possible to speak the truth, yet

<column-break/>

not speak it adequately. For example, he who says that Socrates was not a bad or impious man says what is true, yet he does not say what Socrates deserves; that is done by the person who asserts that he was a good man, that he possessed scientific knowledge, was wise in divine matters, and was dear to the gods. He who says these things praises Socrates in a way that matches his merit. Plato, therefore, says something similar regarding the region above the heavens. 

The words, "Especially when speaking concerning the truth," are stated very mysteriously and theologically. By "Truth" here, he signifies the entire order of the "Nights" <note>In Orphic theology, "Night" refers to a high-ranking divine principle or goddess.</note>; and the *Plain of Truth*, which he mentions later, obscurely points to these. Theologians likewise specifically establish Truth in that place. For Orpheus, speaking about Night, says, "that she possesses the truth <gloss>¹</gloss> of the Gods," and:
> To her, prediction wholly true was given.

She is also said to prophesy to the Gods. Homer, too, points toward this Goddess. For speaking about Jupiter <note>original: "Zeus"</note>, Sleep says: <gloss>²</gloss>
> Night, the great tamer of both Gods and men,
> To whom I fled, preserved me from his wrath;
> For he was fearful of offending swift <gloss>³</gloss> Night.

Plato says he shall "dare to speak" concerning it because he is going to make an affirmative statement about it. The *dread*, however, is that we might be led toward something inappropriate or trivial in such high teachings. His words about the region above the heavens also agree with what he asserts in the first part of the *Parmenides* concerning the first principle of all things. There, he describes this principle through negations—except that he absolutely denies all things of the first principle, whereas of the region above the heavens, he denies some things and affirms others. For the Goddess Night is superior to certain divine orders but inferior to others; and just as the first principle of things is beyond being <note>original: "super-essential"</note>, so Night is above the heavens <note>meaning she is above the intellectual order called "Heaven."</note>. 

Why, however, are souls not said to "see" Heaven, but rather to be "situated in" and "joined with" it, while they are not joined with the natures above Heaven, but only perceive them? In answer to this, it <gloss>⁴</gloss> may be said that it is necessary for physical contact to exist only up to a certain point. Why only to that point? Because not even the Gods under Jupiter are said to be united to Phanes <note>Phanes is the primary creator deity in Orphic myth.</note>; this is only asserted of Jupiter, and he is said to be united through Night as a mediator.

But why does Plato say that the region above the heavens is *without color*? Is it in the same way we say that nature and the soul have no color? What would be so remarkable about asserting that? And if we admit this, what <gloss>⁴</gloss> would be superior about the region above the heavens, since nature and the soul possess that same quality? We might say that Plato follows the aforementioned theologians very closely here and arranges his words to match theirs. For after the order of the "Nights," there are three orders of Gods: Heaven, the Cyclopes, and the Centimani <note>the "Hundred-Handed" giants/gods</note>, the proper—

---

¹ In the original text here, a word <unclear>...</unclear> is omitted.
² *Iliad*, book 14, verse 259, etc.
³ The Chaldean Oracles call the intelligible Gods *swift*, and Night exists at the highest point of the order of Gods which is both intelligible and intellectual; she is therefore absorbed in the intelligible. Hence, Homer divinely calls Night "swift."
⁴ For the Greek word **το** (the), here, it is necessary to read **τι** (something), and to treat the sentence as a question.

# ADDITIONAL NOTES.

...names of those whom Plato excludes from the region above the heavens <note>original: "supercelestial place"</note>. For among the Gods who dwell within Phanes <note>The first-born deity in Orphic cosmogony</note>, Heaven is the first to become visible through him. Both Heaven and Earth first emerged from Phanes, and Heaven is first illuminated by the divine light of Phanes, since Orpheus says that Night is united to him:
> No eye but that of sacred Night alone,
> Beheld the First-born <note>original: "Protogonus"</note>: for all the rest
> Were lost in wonder at the unexpected light,
> Which glittered from immortal Phanes' skin.

But whatever is visible and illuminated has color, since colors are specific types of illumination. Therefore, Night and the entire region above the heavens—being above the visible Heaven—are very properly described as being "without color." Night is also the opposite of day because the latter is illuminated and colored. By describing it as lacking color, Plato shows that the realm of Night is above the kingdom of Heaven. Furthermore, by describing it as "without shape" <note>original: "privation of figure"</note>, he shows that it is above the order of the Cyclops. For theology says that shape is first revealed in the Cyclops, and that these divinities are the primary principles and causes of the shapes that exist everywhere. Thus, theology calls them "manual craftsmen" <note>original: "artificers"</note>, for this group of three <note>original: "triad"</note> <note>1</note> brings shapes to perfection.

> And in their forehead, one round eye was fixed. <note>2</note>

Similarly, in the *Parmenides*, when Plato speaks of the straight, the circular, and that which is a mixture <note>3</note> of both, he obscurely points to this divine order. These Cyclops, as the first causes of shapes, taught Minerva <note>Athena</note> and Vulcan <note>Hephaestus</note> the various types of shapes.

> These were the first manual artists, who taught 
> Pallas <note>Minerva</note> and Vulcan all things. [says Orpheus]. 

We should not be surprised to hear that Vulcan and Minerva are the causes of shapes. Vulcan is the cause of physical shapes and every shape in the material world; Minerva is the cause of the shapes of the soul and the intellect; and the Cyclops are the cause of divine shapes and shapes that exist everywhere. Therefore, it is clear that the region above the heavens is above the order of the Cyclops.

By the "absence of physical contact," Plato shows that this place is above the Hundred-handed ones <note>original: "Centimani"</note>. These deities are the first to come into "contact," as it were, with the entire creation of things. Theology calls them "hundred-handed" because we use our hands to touch, make, and distinguish all things. Furthermore, the sense of touch spreads through the entire body. Theology, therefore, symbolically calls these "hundred-handed" because they touch and cause the entire creation of things. This group of three <note>4</note>, however, is protective <note>original: "of a guardian nature"</note> in nature. Plato uses negative terms to describe what the theologian Orpheus celebrated with positive terms. What Orpheus calls "Night," Plato calls "without color." And what Orpheus describes as "without falsehood," Plato celebrates

<column-break/>

as *having within it the category of true science, and as being truly existing essence*.
> Prediction without falsehood was given
> To Night above all things. [says Orpheus.]

Plato, having celebrated the region above the heavens with three negative descriptions, then adds three positive affirmations derived from "Being." Since this order is a grouping of three, Plato properly maintains that structure in both his negative and positive conclusions. Or, it could be said that since this realm is both "the One" and "Being," and is a group of three in both respects, he uses negative conclusions to describe the "One" (which is beyond essence) and positive affirmations to describe "Being." Here, also, the first concept of Number is revealed.

According to Hermeas, the "governor of the soul" signifies the "One of the soul" <note>The highest, most unified part of the human spirit</note>, which he tells us was also the opinion of Iamblichus. However, I prefer the explanation given by Proclus in these commentaries: that it is a specific intellect belonging to the series of Minerva.

Next, Hermeas lists the different kinds of truth as follows: "Superior natures illuminate subordinate ones with the light of truth. We must, therefore, look toward these four: first, the One, which is the first principle of all things; second, Phanes, who is the boundary of the Intelligible realm but the independent principle of the Intellectual Gods (for the 'Nights' are principles that rank alongside him); third, Jupiter <note>Zeus</note>, who is the king of the realm above the world but the boundary of those properly called the Intellectual Gods; and fourth, the Sun, who is the king of the physical <note>original: "sensible"</note> world. Each of these illuminates the beings below it <note>5</note> with the truth it holds from an order higher than the one it illuminates. Thus, the Sun gives light from above the world to physical things; hence its essence is said to come from natures above the world. Again, Jupiter illuminates essences above the physical world with intellectual light; Phanes illuminates the Intellectual Gods with intelligible light; and the Principle of all things fills the Intelligible Gods and all creation with the divine light proceeding from himself." <note>6</note>
Vol. 2. p. 116.

->*Socrates says in the Phaedrus that souls*<-
->*are carried round in a circle.*<-

This is well explained by Hermeas in his *Scholia on the Phaedrus* as follows:
"Heaven [meaning the middle of that order of Gods called 'Intelligible and Intellectual'] and the celestial intelligence revolve all these souls, who are at rest within their own proper activities. It also causes them to apply themselves to the intelligible realities above Heaven, and to act intellectually according to celestial intelligence. But the natures beyond Heaven are the 'Nights,' which Plato calls the 'region above the heavens' <note>original: "supercelestial place"</note>."
Vol. 2. p. 197. *Time, therefore, is a certain proceeding intellect, etc.*
For much more additional and important information concerning Time, see the Notes at the end of my translation of Aristotle's *Physics*.

# ADDITIONAL NOTES.

...and is the offspring of Melissus and Amalthea. Melissus, therefore, is to be understood as a power providentially attending to secondary natures; but Amalthea must be considered according to that which is steadfast <note>original: "uninclining"</note> and pure <note>original: "uneffeminate"</note>. Hence, Adrastea was generated from steadfast Providence, and she is the sister of Ida.

->The beautiful Ida and Adrastea sprung<-
->From the same father.<-

This Goddess, therefore, as a single unity <note>original: "unically"</note> comprehends and contains in herself at once the centers of all laws: namely, the mundane <note>pertaining to the physical world</note> and the supermundane <note>above the physical world</note>, the laws of Fate, and those of Jupiter; for there are Jovian and Saturnian, divine, supermundane, and mundane laws. On this account, she is called Adrastea, because her legislative decrees are inevitable <note>The name Adrastea is Greek for "the inescapable one"</note>. Hence, she is said to be seated with bronze drumsticks in her hands before the cave of Night, and through the sound produced by her cymbals, she renders all things obedient to her laws. For Phanes <note>the first-born deity</note> is indeed seated within the cave, in the inner sanctuary <note>original: "adytum"</note> of Night; but Night sits in the middle of the cave, prophesying to the Gods; and Adrastea sits in the entrance halls, legislatively proclaiming the divine laws. 

She differs, however, from the "Justice" who resides there in the same way that the legislative characteristic differs from the judicial. And the Justice which is there is said to be the daughter of the Law and Piety which are there. But Adrastea herself, who is the offspring of Melissus and Amalthea, is likewise inclusive of Law. These goddesses are said to have nurtured Jupiter in the cavern of Night; the theologian <note>Likely referring to Orpheus</note> directly asserting that which Plato says about Jupiter. For Plato represents him as fabricating and proclaiming laws. But divine law is imparted by Adrastea to the Gods as well: for the order within them is derived from this Goddess. It is, however, likewise imparted to the attendants of the Gods, both to everyone in common and specifically to each individual.

P. 410. *The thousand years, which Plato defines in the Phaedrus.*

For the sake of more fully understanding what Proclus refers to in this place, and also for the benefit of the Platonic reader, the following translation of an extract from the *Scholia* <note>Commentaries</note> of Hermeas on the *Phaedrus* is given. The text of Plato, regarding the first descent of the soul from the intellectual world <note>original: "intelligible world"</note> into the realms of physical birth <note>original: "generation"</note>, on which the extract is a comment, is as follows:

> "This is the law of Adrastea: that whatever soul, attending on a divinity, has beheld something of reality, shall be free from damage until another period takes place; and if she is always able to accomplish this, she shall be perpetually free from the attacks of evil. But when, through an inability to accomplish this, she has not perceived reality, and from some chance occurrence—being filled with forgetfulness and depravity—she becomes heavy and sluggish, breaks her wings, and falls again to the earth, then this law prevents her, in her first rebirth, from being implanted in some animal <note>original: "brutal"</note> nature. Instead, it commands the soul which has seen the most to inhabit the body of a philosopher, or of one who desires beauty; of a musician, or of one devoted to love. 
> 
> But it orders the soul whose perceptions rank in the second class to descend into a legitimate king, or a man studious of empire and war. But it distributes a soul of the

<column-break/>

> third order into a certain political character, or the ruler of a family, or the master of a trade. And again, it distributes a soul of the fourth rank into one engaged in gymnastic exercise, or in procuring remedies and taking care of the body. But souls of the fifth order it distributes into a prophetic life, or a certain life of religious initiation <term>telestic</term>. In the sixth, it makes a distribution into a poetic or imitative life. In the seventh, into a farmer <note>original: "husbandman"</note> or a craftsman. In the eighth, into a sophist or a popular demagogue. And in the ninth, into the life of a tyrant. 
> 
> But in all these, he who passes his life justly will afterwards obtain a better condition of being; but he who acts unjustly will pass into a worse state of existence. For no soul will return to its original condition until the expiration of ten thousand years, since it will not recover the use of its wings before this period—except for the soul of one who has practiced philosophy sincerely, or who has been a lover of youth alongside philosophy. These indeed, in the third period of a thousand years, if they have thrice chosen this mode of life in succession and have thus restored their wings to their natural vigor, shall in the three thousandth year return to their original home."

The *Scholia* of Hermeas on this passage are as follows:

> "Whatever soul," says Plato, "following its proper God, is able to perceive something of the realm of pure thought <term>intelligibles</term>, will remain without injury during the whole of that period—that is, it will not fall into the cycle of birth <note>original: "generation"</note>. For to fall into the cycle of birth is to be injured. And you may see how accurately here, in the same manner as before, he exhibits to us the difference between divine and human souls. For he does not merely say, *if it has seen* reality, but, *if it has seen something* of reality; that is, if it has seen what is partially and individually real. 
> 
> If, therefore, in the beginning of the period, it has seen something of real being, it will remain uninjured until another period. For the sacred law of Adrastea beforehand encompasses the progressions of all the Gods and of all souls, and imparts that which is adapted to each. Hence, as the reward for having seen something of reality at the beginning of the period, it will, during the whole of that period, remain on high and revolve in conjunction with the Gods. For its adaptation to the period will sustain it; just as here, some things live for one solar period, others for two, and others only for a day, by being adapted to a certain position of the stars. 
> 
> Certain guiding spirits <note>original: "dæmons"</note> also, by their sustaining aid, keep souls from falling into the cycle of birth, just as we see here that bodies of good constitution, though they should be poorly nourished, yet at the same time remain healthy through their natural condition from the beginning; and though they try to perform certain defiled actions, they are prevented by certain good spirits from accomplishing them. In the same manner, therefore, the soul that has once beheld something of the realm of thought is assisted and supported by good spirits and heroes, so as not to fall into birth in that period. But when the soul, being unable to follow the Gods, no longer perceives something of reality, Plato enumerates many causes for its lapse into birth. The first cause, therefore, which he assigns for this is its inability to follow the [perpetual] attendants of the Gods. The second is its being unable to perceive something of the realm of pure thought. The third is a chance occurrence; and this is probably

---

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul's journey and the cosmic laws governing its descent into the physical world, specifically examining the causes of the soul's "fall" and the classification of human lives as described in Platonic philosophy.</meta>

# ADDITIONAL NOTES.

...the occurrence of certain harmful demons <note>original: "malefic dæmons"</note>. When the soul departs from the Gods, it encounters evil demons who ignite its desire to associate with the world of physical birth <note>original: "generation"</note>. A similar thing happens when someone follows a teacher—Socrates, for instance, or another worthy instructor. In that case, the student becomes modest and worthy, sharing in a certain goodness. But if he abandons his teacher, he meets intemperate and impudent men who incite desires in him that are contrary to modesty and worth. 

The fourth cause for the soul's fall is a total forgetfulness of the "intelligibles" <note>the realm of pure, divine truths or spiritual realities</note>. It also involves the soul's power to create distinctions and its tendency toward a life preoccupied with physical birth. Because of these causes, the soul becomes "heavy." It is filled with the "potion of oblivion" <note>referring to the mythical River Lethe, which causes souls to forget their divine origin</note> and is fettered by the bonds of physical birth. It departs from and becomes entirely forgetful of the higher spiritual realms. This is the depravity of the soul, which causes its "wings" to fall away and leads to its descent to earth.

When Plato says, "the soul falls again on the earth," he may mean "earth" to represent the entire realm of physical existence <note>original: "all generation"</note>. He may also mean this specific planet, or he may mean the human body itself, which the soul enters because the body is so heavily composed of the element of earth. The law of Adrastea <note>the goddess of inescapable destiny</note> grants this to the soul during its first fall from the spiritual realm into the physical: that it shall not enter the body of a beast, but only that of a human. Plato defines this "first generation" as the soul's initial descent into the physical realms to give life to a human frame after it has glimpsed the divine truths.

Next, we must observe that the nine types of lives described here differ from those mentioned in the tenth book of Plato's *Republic*. The lives listed here are nine in number, while those in the *Republic* are infinite. The lives in the *Republic* are assigned based on the soul's own choices; however, the lives here are distributed according to the reward and honor earned by the soul's vision of divine truths. In the *Republic*, a soul may transition from a human to a beast or vice versa. In this text, the transition is only into a human, and specifically into a male rather than a female. Most importantly, in this context, the soul is proceeding for the first time from the spiritual realm into physical birth, whereas in the *Republic*, it is moving from one physical life to another. In short, a careful survey reveals many differences between these two sets of lives. Furthermore, we must note that the specific *categories* <note>original: "species or forms"</note> of lives are listed here, rather than their specific fortunes or external circumstances—such as a specific military or royal career, or a life defined by specific weapons or a particular type of luck.

It remains to be investigated whether the entire range of human existence is divided into these nine lives, or if there is another division that would result in ten or more lives. It is possible to divide the same subject into more or fewer parts depending on one's perspective. For example, in the *Philebus*, the division is into three; in the *Republic*, it is five. We must demonstrate, however, that the entire span of human life can be categorized into these nine. These four aspects of a human must be considered: **reason, anger, desire,** and **nature.** When the soul descends into physical birth, it lives according to **reason** alone,

<column-break/>

yielding nothing to the passions and suffering nothing from them. In this case, the soul produces the first life: the **philosophic** life. Alternatively, the soul may live according to anger while reason still maintains control; this produces the second life: the **royal and military** life. Or, it lives according to desire while reason still holds power, creating the third life: the **political** life, which also includes the acquisition of wealth. This life is focused on procuring necessary food for the individual and the city. Again, the soul may be preoccupied with "nature" <note>the physical body and its functions</note> while reason still presides; this produces the fourth life: the **gymnastic and medicinal** life. This life is directed toward the body, providing care and remedies for it. 

Since we have reached the end of the progression of lives focused on nature, the fifth life remains: the **telestic** <note>related to religious rites and initiations</note> life. This life does not possess a unique power of its own, for it is directed toward the Gods and provides assistance to the lives that came before it. Plato refers here to the prophetic and ritualistic life, not the "enthusiastic" <note>divinely inspired or possessed</note> one. The enthusiastic life is considered philosophic and scientific in the extreme, being entirely inspired by divinity. Instead, he refers here to the "artificial" and medicinal religious life which offers aid to humanity through sacrifices and prayers. These five lives are conducted according to "right reason" and resemble the activities of the Gods. Just as each God remains in their source, goes forth, and returns to their beginning, the soul here either remains in reason (the philosopher), goes forth into nature (the next three lives), or returns to the Gods (the fifth life).

The remaining four lives are imitative—they are "images" of the previous five. Two of them (the sixth and seventh) truly imitate the earlier lives, one through words and the other through actions. The other two imitate them poorly or "dissimilarly." The sixth and seventh lives differ because the sixth imitates the philosopher or king through words to discipline men (the poet or artist), while the seventh imitates through deeds (the craftsman or artificer <note>original: "artificer"</note>). In the category of "poetic," we should include every imitative character, including painters; as Plato says in the *Republic*, these are "three steps removed from the truth." For the "demiurgic" <note>creative/craftsman</note> character, we include those who bring something from non-existence into being, such as the carpenter, potter, or shoemaker. This also includes the farmer, insofar as he attends to nature so that her growth is healthy and excellent. 

The *sophistical* and *popular* characters differ in that the *sophist* is a teacher of laws and virtue, while the *popular* character practices rhetoric among the common people. We should not view these "sophistical" and "tyrannical" lives as inherently corrupt here, but rather as those who use these powers for a good purpose—the former through persuasion <note>original: "deception"</note> and the latter through authority <note>original: "force"</note>. As Plato implies, it is possible to use these powers for either good or ill. This concludes the discussion of the nine lives.

# ADDITIONAL NOTES.

<margin>* The fundamental categories <note>original: "genera"</note> of being are: essence, permanency, motion, sameness, and difference.</margin>

It now remains for us to gather, through human scientific reasoning, the nature of the "intelligibles" <note>the realm of pure, spiritual forms or divine truths</note>. By contemplating these, the soul descends into its first, second, and subsequent lives. The soul that has surveyed the beautiful, the wise, and the good—since these begin from first principles and extend to the very last of things—descends into the "first life." 

Because of this, it is reasonable to suppose that a soul which has surveyed wisdom itself will choose the philosophic life. However, a soul that has surveyed beauty itself will choose a life devoted to elegance; Plato divides this into the musical and the amatory <note>romantic or love-focused</note> life. By receiving beauty through either the eyes or the ears, we obtain a reminiscence of that higher, intelligible beauty. Ultimately, the path back to all these lives leads toward the "Good." 

Again, the soul that has surveyed the fundamental categories <note>original: "genera"</note> of being will choose the "second life." A king establishes all things and is therefore analogous to *permanency*. From this stability, he is named a king <note>original: "βασιλεὺς" (basileus)</note>, a title derived from "foundation" and "stability," as he gives firmness to all things <note>original: "παρα την βασιν, και το εδραιον, και το βεβηκεναι απ' αυτου τα πραγματα"</note>. He also moves or excites all things by arranging and adorning everything, making him analogous to *motion*. He is the cause of friendship and union for all through common laws, which is the work of *sameness*. Furthermore, he divides every thing and represses whatever is hostile and injurious, which is the work of *difference*. He rules over all things, and for this reason, he is called warlike and a prince. Yet, as the cause of everything [in the city] *existing*, he may be said to exist in a way analogous to *essence*, because he leads each thing from non-being into existence.

Again, when the soul has surveyed the categories of being more partially rather than as a whole—or has primarily surveyed justice itself—she produces the "third life." Those who enter the third life are concerned with justice to a greater degree. The soul that has surveyed health itself and the body itself produces the "fourth life." The soul that has beheld the "elevating Gods" produces the prophetic or initiatory <note>original: "telestic"</note> life. The remaining four lives, however, involve souls that have surveyed "similitude" <note>likeness</note> and "dissimilitude" <note>unlikeness</note> itself; the first two surveyed similitude more closely, and the last two surveyed dissimilitude.

Plato, having spoken about these lives and how they are distributed to souls descending into the physical world <note>original: "generation"</note> from the spiritual realm, briefly discusses what remains: the conduct of the soul during its fallen condition. This is consistent with what is said in the *Republic*: that a soul that has passed through this life in a just and holy manner shall obtain an excellent condition of being, but the soul that has acted unjustly will face a worse one. 

Having led the soul into the realms of physical birth, he again elevates it to the spiritual realm. He says that every soul, such as the souls of the common multitude, is restored to the spiritual realm over ten thousand years; however, the soul of a philosopher is restored in three thousand years. Since he mentions periods of ten thousand years <note>original: "myriad"</note>, three thousand years, and one thousand years for the progression from one birth to the next, let us first explain the mathematical meaning of these statements and then investigate what he intends to signal by them.

<column-break/>

<margin>† Pindar, Olympian Ode ii. v. 123, etc.</margin>

In the *Republic*, Plato defines the measure of a human life as one hundred years. This number is the square of ten, which contains within itself all forms of numbers. If you multiply one hundred by ten, you produce the cube: one thousand. Because this number is terrestrial and adapted to the earth, Plato attributes it to the physical world. He says that the progression of the soul "under the earth"—that is, its journey from birth to birth—consists of a thousand years. This is so that the punishment for its offenses or the reward for its good deeds may take place in a "tenfold degree" <note>100 years of life x 10 = 1,000 years</note>. 

Furthermore, we must assume that a soul about to be restored to its original happiness must have chosen a philosophic life. Imagine a soul that has lived through the nine types of lives; it still requires one final restorative <note>original: "apocatastatic"</note> life. Thus, we have ten lives in total. Since each life’s progression under the earth consists of a thousand years, ten times one thousand produces a "myriad" <note>10,000</note> of years. 

Because it is necessary for a soul returning to its original happiness to have "philosophized thrice," as Plato says, this results in three thousand years. Perhaps Plato also took this from history. For instance, Hermes Trismegistus received the title "Thrice-Greatest" because he had lived as a philosopher on earth three times, and on the third time, he truly "knew himself." As the poet Pindar says:

> But those who, strong in true virtue, 
> Can endure the third purification; 
> And keep their minds from deceitful wrongs, 
> and stay pure from the contagion of guilt; 
> They travel through the starry paths of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> 
> To the blissful tower of Saturn.

Such is the mathematical meaning of the words. In short, the numbers three and ten multiply the journey of a thousand years under the earth—the progression from birth to birth—to create the cycles of three thousand and ten thousand years.

What, then, does Plato obscurely signify through these numbers? It must be said that three thousand and ten thousand are symbols of perfection. Plato does not literally mean the mathematical counts. If that were the case, every soul would be restored in ten thousand years, and eventually, this physical world would be left entirely empty of souls. But this is impossible, as is evident from the story of Aridæus in the tenth book of the *Republic*. Aridæus remained under the earth for many thousands of years and was still unable to ascend, even while other souls were leaving. 

Therefore, Plato does not intend to signify a literal count of years, but rather measures of spiritual perfection and the different grades of souls (first, middle, and last). Some souls achieve their restoration <note>original: "apocatastasis"</note> quickly, while others move more slowly; some require only a little purification, while others need a great deal. Three is a "perfect number," containing a beginning, middle, and end. Ten is also a perfect number, representing a different form that encompasses all numbers within itself. Three is analogous to three thousand, and ten to ten thousand: each acts as a "monad" <note>a primary unit</note> that represents a complete cycle. For all these reasons, Plato uses these numbers to show that those who philosophize perfectly complete their restoration to the...

# ADDITIONAL NOTES.

...intelligible in a shorter time, as requiring little or no purification; but the souls of the common people achieve their restoration <note>original: "apocatastasis," the return of the soul to its original divine state</note> over a longer period, as they are in need of much punishment and cleansing. The number one thousand also represents a specific measure of the perfection of a soul that is purified beneath the earth. Having obtained this perfection, the soul enters the cycle of birth again; after living well or poorly on earth, it again seeks its required perfection in the afterlife. Therefore, these periods do not literally mean such a vast number of years that souls only achieve restoration after such a long time. Instead, they symbolically represent a specific measure of perfection. Through this process, the soul receives what it is suited for, achieves its perfection, and is restored to its original happiness.

### P. 411. *The happy life, etc.*

The supreme happiness of the soul in another life consists in the vision of "intelligibles" <note>pure, divine truths or forms</note> in a far more perfect way than can be achieved in this life. In the *Phaedrus*, Plato calls this vision the "initiation into the most blessed of mysteries." His beautiful words are translated as follows: 

"At that time, we were permitted to see splendid beauty when, along with that happy choir, we attained that blessed spectacle and vision. We followed in the company of Jupiter <note>the Roman name for Zeus</note>, while others followed other gods, seeing and being initiated into those mysteries which may truly be called most blessed. These divine rites <note>original: "orgies," referring to sacred religious ceremonies</note> were performed by us while we were still whole and free from the evils that awaited us in later times. With our internal eyes <note>original: "closed eyes," meaning looking inward rather than through physical senses</note>, we were spectators of the highest mysteries <note>original: "epoptic spectators"</note> in a pure light, seeing simple, stable, and happy luminous appearances. We were pure ourselves and free from the weight of what now surrounds us, which we call the 'body,' and to which we are bound like an oyster to its shell."

All of this is admirably explained by Hermeas <note>a 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note>: "Plato everywhere says that the sovereign Sun is analogous to the first principle of all things. For just as the sun is the ruler of the entire physical world, the first principle <note>the Good or the One</note> rules the intelligible world. And as light descends from the sun to join the power of sight with the objects we see, so the light proceeding from the first God—which Plato calls 'truth'—joins the intellect with the intelligible truths. You see, therefore, that beauty imitates this light. It is, as it were, a light emitted from the fountain of the divine world to this visible world, alluring and calling all things upward to itself and uniting the lover with the object of love. Thus, spiritual elevation is achieved through beauty. Plato summarily says that these 'intelligibles' are the objects to which Love elevates us. The beauty we find here is obscure and perceived only by the senses (just as the light here is mixed with air), and it leads us to remember Beauty itself.

"But when he says, 'We were then permitted to see splendid beauty,' he means Beauty itself shining brightly, without any mixture of its opposite. The 'happy choir' we moved with consists of divine souls, called a 'choir' because of their united existence. He now calls this a choir, though he previously called it the 'army of gods and spirits' <note>original: "dæmons"</note>. He rightly calls it 'happy,' for truly, anyone who surveys those divine forms is happy and blessed.

"Again, when he says, 'We indeed following with

<column-break/>

Jupiter,' it must be observed that in the *Timaeus*, Plato represents the Creator <note>original: "Demiurgus"</note> as disseminating souls equal in number to the stars—that is, equal according to their forms. Making some souls solar, others lunar, and others Jovian <note>related to Jupiter/Zeus</note>, he distributed them into the Earth and other 'instruments of time' <note>the planets</note>. Plato now says, 'We followed with Jupiter,' as one who knows his own specific God <note>the deity to whose spiritual lineage the soul belongs</note>. For the happiness of the human soul is to move in conjunction with its appropriate Gods, since it is impossible to go beyond the Gods.

"When he says 'Being initiated,' he derives the word for initiation (*telete*) from the soul being made *perfect* by it <note>original: $\tau\epsilon\lambda\epsilon\tau\eta$ (telete) from $\pi\alpha\rho\alpha\ \tau\omicron\ \tau\epsilon\lambda\epsilon\alpha\nu\ \tau\eta\nu\ \psi\upsilon\chi\eta\nu\ \alpha\pi\omicron\tau\epsilon\lambda\epsilon\iota\nu$, 'because it makes the soul perfect'</note>. You see, therefore, that the soul was once perfect. When it is on earth, it becomes divided, and the whole of it cannot act by itself. He also says, 'Which may be lawfully called,' because the vision of them is not simply the highest blessing; the observer still sees them as something different from themselves. It is necessary for a union to take place. Therefore, being established within these objects of vision is the highest blessing. 

"It is necessary to know that *telete* <note>initiation</note> is one thing, *muesis* <note>secret instruction</note> another, and *epopteia* <note>direct vision</note> another. *Telete* is like the preparation and purification. *Muesis*, named from 'closing the eyes,' is more divine; to close the eyes is to no longer receive divine mysteries through the senses, but to behold them with the soul itself. And *epopteia* is to be established in them and become a direct spectator of them. He says 'These divine rites were performed by us' because to perform these mysteries is called *orgiazein* <note>original: $\omicron\rho\gamma\iota\alpha\zeta\epsilon\iota\nu$, to celebrate sacred rites</note>.

"Again, when Plato says, 'Being ourselves then entire,' he speaks as a spectator of those divine mysteries, using the word 'entire' to mean 'perfect.' When he mentions 'the evils which awaited us in a posterior time,' he means that joining with a physical body causes the soul's fall. By the word 'stable,' he indicates the firm and constant nature of divine truths. The expressions 'closed eyes' and 'epoptic spectators' are taken from the Eleusinian mysteries <note>the most famous secret religious rites of ancient Greece</note>. He also says we were spectators 'in a pure light, being ourselves pure,' because light in the world below the moon is not pure, being mixed with air. But we were pure then, because it is not permitted for what is impure to join with what is pure. And finally, just as oysters are bound to their shells, so are we bound to the body."

### P. 451. *Socrates in the Phaedrus says that the horses of the soul sometimes fight with each other, etc.*

For the benefit of the reader of Plato, I will provide the entire passage from the *Phaedrus* that Proclus refers to here, along with Hermeas' commentary on it. The passage is as follows:

> "As for other souls, those that follow divinity most closely and become similar to its nature, they raise the head of the charioteer <note>the intellect</note> into the place above the heavens. There, the charioteer is carried along with the celestial rotation, but is disturbed by the struggle of the horses and only barely catches a vision of perfect realities. Other souls, however, sometimes raise and sometimes lower the head of the charioteer; because of the violence of the horses, they see some things but are deprived of others. And again,

<meta>catchword: Again,</meta>

<summary>This page explains the Neoplatonic interpretation of the soul's journey, detailing how the soul undergoes purification cycles and eventually achieves a state of "perfection" through various stages of divine initiation as described in Plato's Phaedrus.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Phaedrus, Hermeas, soul's restoration, apocatastasis, initiation, telete, muesis, epopteia, Eleusinian mysteries, intelligible beauty, Jupiter/Zeus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Additional Notes" on Plato's Phaedrus, specifically Hermias's commentary on the different types of souls and their ability to perceive divine truth.</meta>

# ADDITIONAL NOTES.

...other souls follow, all of them desiring the vision of this superior place. But because they are unable to accomplish this goal, they are carried around in a submerged condition, trampling on and attacking each other in a struggle for priority in their path. Because of this, the chaos, conflict, and exertion are extreme. Indeed, many become "lame" through the fault of their charioteers, and many break their wings. All of them, involved in great labor, depart without achieving a perception of reality. After their departure, they consume a *nutriment of opinion* <note>original: "doxastic nutriment," referring to knowledge based on belief rather than direct truth</note>; because of this, they strive greatly to see where the *plain of Truth* is located. From a meadow of this kind, the highest part of the soul receives the proper nourishment; from this, the nature of the wing is fed, which enables the soul to ascend."

The following are the explanations of Hermias on this passage: "Plato, having spoken concerning divine souls and those that always remain invariably the same, now turns to our individual and human souls, which are sometimes able to follow divinity and sometimes abandon their divine nature. Therefore, he describes them using the indefinite word *others*, as they possess much depravity and wandering. He also divides these into three categories: first, middle, and last. He had likewise given a three-fold <note>original: "triadic"</note> division to the beings of a superior order. Regarding the visions, he says that some are within the Heaven, others are in the sub-celestial arch, and others are beyond the Heaven. 

Again, regarding the visions beyond the Heaven, he says that the truly-existing reality in the super-celestial place is without color, without shape, and cannot be touched. Before this, he also made a division into Jupiter and Vesta, and the ten leaders; and again into Jupiter, Gods, and demons; or again, into Jupiter and those who always follow him when they are willing and able.¹ Generally, everything that has once proceeded from the first principle ought to be three-fold. For being perfect, it will have a beginning, middle, and end, matching what the [Chaldean] Oracle says: 'The triad measuring all things.' 

Thus, regarding our souls, he says that some of them raise the head of the charioteer—that is, the summit of our intellect—to the super-celestial place. Others sometimes raise the head and sometimes do not; and others are unable to raise it at all but are carried downward into the cycle of birth <note>original: "generation"</note>. We must also accurately observe how he indicates the difference between our souls and those that are divine. In speaking of our highest happiness, and assuming the soul that is most perfectly made like divinity, he says it is barely able (because of being disturbed by the "horses" of desire) to raise the head of the charioteer to the place beyond the Heaven to perceive something of real beings. It then stands on the rim of the Heaven, as if in a watch-tower,² surveying different objects at different times. Divine souls indeed are said to be carried around by the rotation of the Heaven; but our souls are carried around in conjunction <note>original Greek: *symperiagesthai*, to be carried round together</note> with those that are divine.

By the 'head of the charioteer,' we must understand the highest and most intellectual part of the soul, which alone possesses all its intellectual power. Since the soul has many powers <note>original: "multipotent"</note> and its other powers also wish to act, souls of the first rank are very properly said to be disturbed by the horses. But souls of the middle rank, which have not perfectly disciplined their other powers, are not merely said to be disturbed, but to be *forced* by the horses. Therefore, at one time they act according to their highest part, and at another time according to their lower parts. Souls of the third rank are entirely defeated by the horses; for this reason, being unable to raise the head of the charioteer, they remain in a submerged condition. 

Consider examples of these from characters on the earth. Let an example of a soul of the first rank be a philosopher who is at peace³ with himself and dedicated to contemplation, but who provides only good to his other faculties and to everything around him. Let the statesman <note>original: "political character"</note> be the image of souls of the middle rank; at one time stretching toward contemplation, and at another time turning back to organize things of a lower nature. And let souls of the third rank be like the common and emotion-driven <note>original: "impassioned"</note> man. 

Furthermore, there is a great variety in souls of the middle rank because they perceive some things but not others. Some have seen many things but missed a few; others, vice versa, have seen a few but missed many; and others have seen and missed things in equal measure. This must be noted, for it helps us understand the types of lives that follow. Therefore, the souls that are the last of those following the Gods, as they naturally aspire to the super-celestial place, revolve together with the Gods; but because they lack the power to see it, they sink downward. At last, will and desire leave them, for will begins first and ends last. Just as the common, emotion-driven man on earth naturally desires what is good but is unable to identify or discover true reality, souls in that state are affected in the same way.

You may also use other examples of the three orders of souls. Of the first order, the temperate man; of the second, the self-controlled <note>original: "continent"</note> man, where—though there is a conflict between the lower and higher parts of the soul—reason still tries to maintain its authority. Of the last order, you may use the self-indulgent or intemperate man as an example. And again, you may take as an example of the first order the worthy man, who neither accuses himself nor another.

***

¹ And these, as they are sometimes willing and able to follow Jupiter, and sometimes not, make a three-fold division along with Jupiter.
² For "at leisure" (*epi scholes*) in this place, I read "from a watch-tower" (*epi skopes*).
³ Matching what Plato says elsewhere: that the genuine philosopher is nourished in truth and leisure. But at present, as true philosophy is not studied and there are consequently no genuine philosophers, every man is busily employed with external concerns. No one is at leisure for reflections of the highest importance. "I am too busy; I have not a moment to spare for such things," is the common language of the high and the low, the rich and the poor.
