<meta>This page continues the "Additional Notes" on Plato's Phaedrus, specifically Hermias's commentary on the different types of souls and their struggle to perceive divine truth.</meta>

# ADDITIONAL NOTES.

Regarding the first rank of souls, they are not disturbed because of their own corruption, but because of the nature of the material world, which is inherently designed to cause disturbance. From this, we can also resolve the question of how it is said *that the soul, when perfect and winged, revolves on high and governs the whole world.* For as long as the soul follows the Gods and devotes itself to them, it is happy. However, souls of the middle rank must be categorized as those making progress, who blame only themselves for their failings.

Again, when Plato adds that souls of the third rank are carried around in a submerged state, he does not mean they "fall" in the traditional sense. Instead, he means they are submerged because they are overpowered by the violence and conflict of other forces. At the same time, they are revolved along with the attendants of the Gods because they still long for the super-celestial realm <note>original: "supercelestial place," the realm beyond the physical heavens where true reality exists</note>. It is said of divine souls that the rotation of the Heavens carries them along because they are naturally suited for it and give themselves over to that motion. But regarding souls of the third rank, it is said they are revolved "together with" the rest because they are pulled along by force. They naturally tend toward a straight-line descent into physical birth <note>original: "generation"</note>, yet at the same time, they are pulled in a circle because they are still carried by the movement of the Heavens and the divine attendants—much like how flammable matter at the very top of the atmosphere is said to be carried around in a circle by the heavens. These souls, therefore, enter a submerged state because their life-generating <term>genesiurgic</term> power pulls them down and seeks to be active; it is to this power that the lower, irrational form of life is connected. When it is said that they trample on each other, we should not imagine they use physical feet in that realm; rather, it means one soul is trying to get ahead of another. Thus, the superior soul may be said to "trample" the lower one, and the lower one to "attack" the superior. Souls of this kind do not reach the intellectual realm <note>original: "intelligible"</note> but instead look toward each other, competing and striving to surpass one another.

Consequently, a disturbance is produced in their rational mind <term>dianoetic part</term>, and a conflict arises in their spirited part <note>original: "anger"</note>; for it is the spirited part of the soul that craves honor and status. There is also an extreme exertion of the desiring and life-generating parts <term>epithymetic and genesiurgic</term>, which later leads to physical birth. This exertion is called "extreme" to distinguish it from the "divine exertion" of souls that are ascending, which Plato mentions later. Here, however, Plato blames the "charioteer" <note>In Plato's allegory, the charioteer represents Reason guiding the soul</note> for souls of the third rank, because the charioteer is the cause of this confusion. This is similar to his statement in the *Republic* that it is impossible for the stable order of a city to be destroyed without the corruption of its leaders. You may also conclude from this that, according to Plato, the *entire* soul descends if the charioteer (the highest part of the soul) becomes corrupted. This contradicts 

<column-break/>

Plotinus, who says that one part of the soul descends while another part remains in the high, divine realm.

Furthermore, regarding the "lameness" of these souls, this is understood by observing how lame people walk. They move slowly and clumsily and are always at risk of falling. In the same way, these souls are slower and less refined in their intellectual thoughts and are always in danger of being pulled down into physical life. Therefore, Plato compares their thinking to the walking of the lame, since walking is a fitting metaphor for their shifting, step-by-step intelligence.<sup>1</sup> He also beautifully notes that many of these souls *break their wings*. He does not say they "destroy" them, because the soul never truly loses its power to ascend <term>anagogic power</term>; rather, its activities become sluggish. In this sense, the wings are said to perish, even though the power itself remains, albeit broken. We can understand this better by looking at winged animals: if a bird breaks its wing, it might be lifted up for a moment by its winged nature, but it is quickly pulled back down. These souls depart, he says, *destitute of the perception of reality*—that is, they fly toward that which is without God and dark.

> Heavens' exiles straying from the orb of light,

<note>original: A quote from the philosopher Empedocles</note>. But they depart *destitute, imperfect, or uninitiated*. For the vision of the intellectual realm is the only true spiritual initiation. They also consume *nutriment of opinion* <note>original: "dorastic [doxastic] nutriment"</note>; that is, they rely on the logic and forms of physical things and live according to them, no longer seeing the true intellectual realities, but only physical objects.

Furthermore, in the phrase *through which there is a great endeavor*, etc., he describes what is common to all three ranks of souls: those that achieve the vision of true reality and those that do not. So, to those who ask why all souls work so hard and weary themselves to gain this vision, the answer is that all of them naturally desire to perceive true beings. By the "nourishment suited to the best part of the soul," he means that which is suited to the intellect; for the intellect is nourished only by true reality <note>original: "the intelligible"</note>. The "wing" of the soul—its upward-reaching power—is also nourished by nothing else but this reality. The *meadow* represents the fertile power of forms. This meadow may also be called "Night," for that is where the sources of life are held. However, there is a different meadow mentioned in the 10th Book of the *Republic*, where souls dwell for a time before being born into the world. That meadow is a luminous appearance <term>phasma</term> located beneath the moon. Nevertheless, the meadow in the *Republic* is analogous to the one mentioned here, as it contains the principles of nature and of life in the physical world.”

---

<sup>1</sup> For the word "sensation" <term>aisthesei</term> used here, it is clearly necessary to read "intellection" <term>noesei</term>.
